A relay publishes the outbox to an SNS topic, which fans out to three SQS queues, each with a dead-letter queue.

One more queue appears only in the choreographed saga (11.03): the ledger publishes its own events, such as LedgerReserved, on its SNS topic ledger-events, and Payouts reads them from the SQS queue payouts-ledger-events.

The names in the diagram are used everywhere in Part IV: PayoutSaga, OutboxRelay, payout-events, ledger-confirm. When an entry says "the ledger", it means the ledger service the saga reserves money in.

The code is for reading

The listings in Part IV are short, at most 15 lines. They show the part that matters and leave out the rest, such as imports, unless the imports are the point. They are not run against the companion project. Every version, limit and default they rely on is recorded in research/claims.md, with the page it came from and the date it was checked. Java syntax itself lives in the handbook, Java for C# Developers, which each entry points to by chapter title.

Finding your way

  • By mistake. Each part ends with a review checklist: what you might see in a pull request, why it hurts, and the entry that fixes it. All the checklists are collected in the first index.
  • By import. Found com.netflix.hystrix or org.springframework.cloud.sleuth in old code? The second index lists the imports that date a codebase, with the entry that shows the modern way.
  • By old way. The third index lists every older way, with its era and its replacement.
  • By number. The fourth index lists every entry.

Part IV · The how-to1. Build and project#

Every Payouts change goes through Maven, Java's standard build tool, before it reaches a pod. Maven reads each project's POM (Project Object Model), a pom.xml file, much as dotnet build reads a .csproj. This part covers the build as a developer meets it: starting a service, deciding where a version is set, finding where a jar came from, building one module, keeping builds identical everywhere, and making the build refuse what it should refuse. It also shows the Ant files, archetypes and hand-copied jars you will find in older services, and what replaced them.

★What a veteran knows
  • The pom.xml you read is not the build Maven runs, because it inherits from a parent. Run ./mvnw help:effective-pom (through the Maven wrapper, 1.05) before you argue about where a version or a setting comes from.
  • A version written in a module's POM is a decision taken without the parent. If it has to exist, it needs a comment saying why, and when it can go.
  • Nearest wins, Maven's rule that the version declared closest to your project beats any other, is the rule, not a bug to work around. Manage versions in one place, and distance stops mattering.
  • A green build that prints warnings is a build that will break later. Make each rule fail the build, or delete it.
  • When the build is slow, time it before you blame Maven. In most services the minutes are in the tests, not the compiler.
  • The jar you ship, the zip of compiled classes and libraries, is the truth. jar tf, which lists the files inside it, settles more arguments than reading POMs.
◷How we got hereIn 1999 Sun gave the code of Tomcat, its Java web server, to the Apache Software Foundation.

In 1999 Sun gave the code of Tomcat, its Java web server, to the Apache Software Foundation. James Duncan Davidson, who had written Tomcat, had also written a small tool to build it. The Apache Ant FAQ is plain about its ambition: "Ant was there to build Tomcat, nothing else." In January 2000 Ant became a project of its own, and Ant 1.1 shipped on 19 July 2000. Davidson had chosen XML for its build files because it was the easiest way to describe a tree without writing his own parser. In 2004 he looked back. He had seen build files "hundreds, and even thousands, of lines long", and he had built "70-80% of a scripting environment" without recognising it. Maven took the other road. A Maven project declares what it is, and plugins decide how to build it. The build.xml you find in an old service is a script, and every service that has one builds in its own way.

1.01 Start a new service from the parent POM, not a generator's defaults

Then.

  • Spring era: A Maven archetype, a project template, run with mvn archetype:generate. The maven-archetype-quickstart template produced an App.java, an AppTest.java and a dependency on JUnit 3.
  • Boot era: Copy an existing service and delete what you do not need. The company's rules came across, along with everything else the old service had collected.
<dependency>
  <groupId>junit</groupId>
  <artifactId>junit</artifactId>
  <version>3.8.1</version>
  <scope>test</scope>
</dependency>

Archetypes were right when every project was laid out by hand, and a company archetype was the only way to stamp out the same skeleton. Copying a service was right when the parent POM was thin and the real rules lived in each service. A generator for the code and a parent POM for the rules replaced both.

Recognise it by. App.java, and AppTest extends TestCase in src/test/java. Also junit:junit at 3.8.1, a <name> that still says the old service's name, and <repositories> blocks copied from somewhere else.

The rookie version. Generate the project on start.spring.io and commit it as it comes:

<parent>
  <groupId>org.springframework.boot</groupId>
  <artifactId>spring-boot-starter-parent</artifactId>
  <version>4.1.2</version>
</parent>
<artifactId>payouts-reports</artifactId>
<properties>
  <java.version>17</java.version>
</properties>

What goes wrong. The new payouts-reports service builds and runs. It has none of Sorrel's rules. It compiles for Java 17, the generator's default, while payouts-api and payouts-domain compile for 25. It is on Boot 4.1 while they are on 3.5, because start.spring.io no longer offers 3.5. Maven does all its work through plugins, such as the compiler, and these plugin versions are whatever Boot chose, not the ones the platform team approved. The parent's enforcer rules, the checks that stop a bad build (1.09), never run, so a SNAPSHOT dependency can reach the main branch. (A SNAPSHOT is an unreleased build of a library that can change under the same version number.) Six months later the security scan shows payouts-reports as the one service on a different toolchain. Nobody decided that. It was the generator's default.

Do this now.

  1. Use Spring Initializr, at start.spring.io or through IntelliJ's new-project wizard, to generate the code. Choose the package com.sorrel.payouts.reports and the starters you need. A starter is a Boot dependency that brings the libraries for one job, such as the web starter for an HTTP API.
  2. Replace the <parent> block with Sorrel's parent POM. A parent POM is a POM that other projects inherit from. It carries properties, agreed library versions and plugin settings.
  3. Rename the starters to their Boot 3.5 names. The generator wrote Boot 4 names, such as spring-boot-starter-webmvc and spring-boot-starter-webmvc-test. Boot 3.5 has no such artifacts, so the build stops with a missing version. They become spring-boot-starter-web and spring-boot-starter-test.
  4. Delete every <version> on a dependency the parent manages. Delete <java.version> too. The parent sets both.
  5. Replace the generated Maven wrapper files with the company's, so every service runs the same Maven (1.05).
  6. Run ./mvnw help:effective-pom. It prints the full POM Maven will use after inheritance. Check that the Java release, the Boot version and the enforcer rules are the parent's.
<parent>
  <groupId>com.sorrel</groupId>
  <artifactId>sorrel-parent</artifactId>
  <version>14</version>
  <relativePath/>
</parent>
<artifactId>payouts-reports</artifactId>
<dependencies>
  <dependency>
    <groupId>org.springframework.boot</groupId>
    <artifactId>spring-boot-starter-web</artifactId>
  </dependency>
</dependencies>

Maven names every library by groupId, artifactId and version, as NuGet names a package by ID and version. The empty <relativePath/> tells Maven to fetch the parent from the repository instead of looking in the folder above. The dependency has no version, because the parent's imported Boot list supplies it. When the service moves to Boot 4, rename the starter back to spring-boot-starter-webmvc. The old name still works there, but it is deprecated.

Also seen. A company archetype that stamps out the whole skeleton, parent included. It saves the edits, and it goes stale unless someone owns it. A template repository on the Git server does the same job at the same cost.

When to break it. A throwaway spike that will never be deployed can keep the generator's parent. Delete the spike when it ends, or it will quietly become a service.

.NET anchor. dotnet new webapi is the generator, and Directory.Build.props carries the company's settings. The difference is how they connect. A .NET project picks up Directory.Build.props from the folders above it without being asked. A Maven project inherits only from the parent it names.

See also. 1.07, 1.08, 1.12, The Yard, chapter 1, Maven vs csproj, Spring Boot orientation

1.02 Pin a transitive dependency version in the right place

Then.

  • Spring era: Exclude the unwanted version from every dependency that brought it, then declare the wanted version directly. It worked before teams had a shared parent to manage versions in, and each exclusion was repeated in every service.
  • Boot era: Override a version property, such as <jackson-bom.version>, under spring-boot-starter-parent. That still works with the starter parent. It does nothing when Boot's list is imported instead, as Sorrel's parent does (1.07).
<dependency>
  <groupId>com.sorrel</groupId><artifactId>policy-client</artifactId>
  <exclusions>
    <exclusion>
      <groupId>org.apache.commons</groupId><artifactId>commons-compress</artifactId>
    </exclusion>
  </exclusions>
</dependency>

Recognise it by. The same <exclusions> block repeated across services for one artifact. Also a direct dependency with a comment such as "forces version", and properties named after Boot's managed libraries, such as <snakeyaml.version>.

The rookie version. Add the library to the module that needed the fix, with a version:

<!-- payouts-api/pom.xml -->
<dependency>
  <groupId>org.apache.commons</groupId>
  <artifactId>commons-compress</artifactId>
  <version>1.27.1</version>
</dependency>

What goes wrong. A transitive dependency is a library you did not name, brought in because a library you did name needs it. Maven chooses its version by nearest wins: the declaration closest to your project in the dependency tree beats any declaration further down. The rookie pin works in payouts-api, because a direct declaration is as near as it gets. Two weeks later payouts-domain gets the old commons-compress 1.21 through a different library. Nobody fixes it there, because the finding only named payouts-api. Then policy-client moves to a newer commons-compress, and the pin in payouts-api now holds it back. The pin has no comment, so nobody knows it can go.

Do this now.

  1. Find the path with dependency:tree (1.03), so you know which library brings the version.
  2. Put the version in the <dependencyManagement> of the POM every affected module inherits from. For one service that is its root POM. For all services it is sorrel-parent. dependencyManagement lists versions without adding any library. If any module, or any library deep in its tree, uses that artifact, it gets this version, however far down it sits.
  3. Write the reason beside it, with the condition for removing it.
  4. Remove any <version> for that artifact from the modules.
  5. Run dependency:tree again and check that every module shows the pinned version.
<dependencyManagement>
  <dependencies>
    <!-- policy-client 3.2 brings 1.21, flagged by the scanner on 2026-10-12.
         Remove when policy-client 3.4 is the oldest version in use. -->
    <dependency>
      <groupId>org.apache.commons</groupId>
      <artifactId>commons-compress</artifactId>
      <version>1.27.1</version>
    </dependency>
  </dependencies>
</dependencyManagement>

An entry written directly in <dependencyManagement> beats one that arrives through an imported list such as Boot's. So the same block can override a version Boot manages. Do that for a security fix, not for taste, because Boot tested its versions together. For a family of libraries that publishes its own list, such as Jackson, import that list above Boot's import. When two imported lists disagree, the first one declared wins.

Also seen. An <exclusion> when you want the library gone, not changed. A property override when the service inherits spring-boot-starter-parent.

When to break it. A module that genuinely needs a different version from its siblings, such as a migration tool that reads an old file format. Pin it in that module, with a comment. The cost is that two versions now ship from one repository, and every scan shows both.

.NET anchor. Central package management in Directory.Packages.props, with transitive pinning on, is the closest match. When two packages ask for different versions, NuGet takes the higher of the minimums. NuGet also lets a direct reference win, as Maven does, but it reports a resulting downgrade as NU1605 (1.09). Maven takes the nearer, even when it is older, and says nothing. That is why a Maven version can go backwards when you add an unrelated library.

See also. 1.03, 1.09, 19.06, The Yard, chapter 9, The Yard, chapter 10, Maven vs csproj

1.03 Find out which dependency pulled in a jar

Then.

  • J2EE era: Jars copied into a lib/ folder and committed, with an Ant build.xml that put the folder on the classpath, the list of jars and folders the JVM loads classes from. The only record of why a jar was there was the commit that added it.
  • Spring era: Apache Ivy, which added dependency resolution to Ant through an ivy.xml file next to build.xml.
<path id="compile.classpath">
  <fileset dir="lib" includes="*.jar"/>
</path>
<javac srcdir="src" destdir="build/classes" classpathref="compile.classpath"/>

A lib/ folder was right when there was no shared repository of libraries to resolve from. The jar was the dependency. Maven Central replaced it. Each library published there names what it needs, so a tool can tell you why every jar is present.

Recognise it by. build.xml or ivy.xml, a committed lib/ or WEB-INF/lib folder of jars with version numbers in their names, and <fileset dir="lib">.

The rookie version. Search the POMs, find nothing, close the finding:

# security says commons-compress 1.21 ships in payouts-api
grep -r "commons-compress" --include=pom.xml .
# no output, so the finding is marked "not ours"

What goes wrong. The search finds nothing because nobody declared the library. It arrived transitively, two levels down, through a library the team did choose. The jar is still inside payouts-api.jar, and so it runs in both pods. Closing the finding as "not ours" leaves it there until the next audit, which now has a closed ticket saying it was looked at.

Do this now.

  1. Ask Maven for the path. dependency:tree prints every library and what brought it, and -Dincludes narrows it to one artifact. Run it from the root, so payouts-domain's tree comes from its current source, not from an old copy (1.04). It prints one tree per module:
./mvnw dependency:tree \
  -Dincludes=org.apache.commons:commons-compress
  1. Read the answer for payouts-api from the top down. Each indent is one step further from your project:
[INFO] com.sorrel:payouts-api:jar:1.0.0
[INFO] \- com.sorrel:policy-client:jar:3.2.0:compile
[INFO]    \- com.sorrel:sorrel-commons:jar:2.1.0:compile
[INFO]       \- org.apache.commons:commons-compress:jar:1.21:compile
  1. The last field is the scope. A compile or runtime dependency ships in the jar, and a test dependency does not. The version shown is the one Maven chose, not every version that was asked for.
  2. When a dependency has no version anywhere you can see, find where it was decided. ./mvnw help:effective-pom -Dverbose prints the POM Maven actually uses, with a comment on each line naming the file it came from. The answer is nearly always the parent or an imported list such as Boot's.
  3. For the whole list rather than one path, run ./mvnw dependency:list. Then check the artifact itself, the jar the build produced, with jar tf (1.11).

Also seen. IntelliJ's Maven tool window shows the same tree, and its dependency analyser highlights conflicts. It reads the same model, and it is quicker to browse. A CycloneDX software bill of materials, generated in CI by cyclonedx-maven-plugin, is the record a security team should read instead of guessing.

When to break it. Do not trust the tree alone when a library is shaded. A shaded jar has copied another library's classes inside itself, often under a renamed package. The tree does not show them, and jar tf on the shaded jar does. When the tree and the artifact disagree, believe the artifact.

.NET anchor. dotnet list package --include-transitive lists the packages, and dotnet nuget why in recent SDKs shows the path to one of them. Maven's tree adds the scope, which decides whether the library ships at all.

See also. 1.02, 1.09, 1.11, 15.12, The Yard, chapter 9, Maven vs csproj

1.04 Build and test one module without building everything

Then.

  • Spring era: cd into each module and build it alone, after running mvn install on the modules it needs. That was right when each module had its own version and its own release. A module was meant to build against the last released version of its sibling.
cd payouts-domain && mvn install
cd ../payouts-api && mvn test

Recognise it by. A README that says "install payouts-domain first", scripts that cd into each module in turn, and modules with their own version numbers instead of ${project.version}.

The rookie version.

# from the root, build only the module I changed
./mvnw -pl payouts-api test

What goes wrong. -pl (project list) builds only the named module. Its dependency, payouts-domain, then comes from the local repository: the cache at ~/.m2/repository where Maven keeps every jar it has downloaded or installed. That copy is whatever you last installed, perhaps last Tuesday. This morning you changed Money in payouts-domain. payouts-api compiles against last Tuesday's Money, and its 214 tests pass. A colleague with a newer copy runs the same command and gets 3 failures. CI, which builds every module from source, fails too. "Passes here, fails there" is the sign.

Do this now.

  1. Run from the root and add -am (also make). Maven then builds payouts-domain from source, then payouts-api, in one reactor: Maven's name for the set of modules in a single build, ordered so each comes after what it depends on.
  2. To run one test class, add -Dtest=PayoutServiceTest. The other modules in the reactor have no such class, so also add -Dsurefire.failIfNoSpecifiedTests=false. Surefire is the plugin that runs unit tests.
  3. To see what your change breaks downstream, use -amd (also make dependents). ./mvnw -pl payouts-domain -amd verify builds payouts-domain and every module that depends on it.
  4. After a failure late in a long build, -rf :payouts-api (resume from) restarts the reactor at that module.
  5. Prefer verify to install. A Maven build runs in phases, in a fixed order, and naming one runs every phase before it: compile, test, package (make the jar), verify (run the checks), install (copy the jar into the local repository). verify runs every test and check, and it does not write your half-finished work into the local repository.
# one module and one test class, against the current source of what it needs
./mvnw -pl payouts-api -am verify \
  -Dtest=PayoutServiceTest \
  -Dsurefire.failIfNoSpecifiedTests=false

Also seen. Running the test from IntelliJ. It compiles the modules it needs from source, so it avoids the stale copy. It is not the build CI runs, though, so a plugin or enforcer failure only shows up later. Gradle's :payouts-api:test builds project dependencies from source without being asked.

When to break it. When payouts-domain has its own release cycle and you want to test against its published version. Then building alone is the point. The version in the POM should be a release, not a SNAPSHOT, so the copy you build against is the copy everyone gets.

.NET anchor. dotnet test Payouts.Api.Tests builds every project reference from source, every time. Maven's -pl without -am has no .NET equivalent. It behaves as if a project reference had quietly become a package reference to an old local package.

See also. 1.12, 1.14, 16.01, The Yard, chapter 1, The Yard, chapter 4, Maven vs csproj, Gradle and multi-module builds

1.05 Keep the build reproducible on every laptop and in CI

Then.

  • Spring era: Maven installed by hand on each laptop and on the build server, with the version written on a wiki page. It was right when tools were installed by hand and builds ran in one place.
  • Boot era: The Takari Maven wrapper, a separate project that gave Maven its mvnw script before Apache Maven took the wrapper in. The idea was right, and it moved upstream.
# .mvn/wrapper/maven-wrapper.properties, Takari era
distributionUrl=https://repo.maven.apache.org/maven2/org/apache/maven/apache-maven/3.6.3/apache-maven-3.6.3-bin.zip
wrapperUrl=https://repo.maven.apache.org/maven2/io/takari/maven-wrapper/0.5.6/maven-wrapper-0.5.6.jar

Recognise it by. A README that says "install Maven 3.6", a bare mvn in the CI script, and io/takari/maven-wrapper in the wrapperUrl of maven-wrapper.properties. A wrapperUrl or a .mvn/wrapper/MavenWrapperDownloader.java on its own does not date it, because Apache's own wrapper writes them too unless it runs in its default script-only mode.

The rookie version.

# ci/build.sh
mvn clean install

What goes wrong. The laptop has Maven 3.9 from a package manager, and the CI image has Maven 3.10. Maven 3.10 fails the build on a dependency declared twice in one POM, and 3.9 does not. The pull request is green on the laptop and red in CI. A plugin with no version in the POM gets whichever version that Maven release defaults to, so two machines can run different Surefire versions on the same commit. On 3.9, without a fixed timestamp, two builds of one commit give jars with different checksums. When an incident needs "is this the binary we tested?", nobody can say yes.

Do this now.

  1. Commit the Maven wrapper: mvnw, mvnw.cmd and .mvn/wrapper/maven-wrapper.properties. The wrapper is a script that downloads the exact Maven version named in that file and runs it. Add it with mvn wrapper:wrapper -Dmaven=3.10.0, and update it later with ./mvnw wrapper:wrapper -Dmaven=<version>.
  2. Run ./mvnw everywhere, CI included, and never a mvn from the machine.
  3. Pin every plugin version in the parent's <pluginManagement>, the section that sets a plugin's version and settings for every module that uses it (1.07). The enforcer rule requirePluginVersions fails a build that leaves one out.
  4. Pin the JDK. requireJavaVersion in the enforcer stops a build on the wrong major version. The CI image and the README name the same JDK.
  5. Set project.build.outputTimestamp in the parent. It fixes the timestamps written into the jar, so one commit gives the same bytes on any machine. Maven 3.10 turns this mode on by default, and the property pins the value. On 3.9, the property is what turns it on.
  6. In CI, run ./mvnw -B -ntp verify. -B is batch mode, and -ntp drops the download progress lines from the log.
  7. Now and then, prove it on a released version: ./mvnw clean verify artifact:compare rebuilds it and compares the result with the copy already published to the repository.
# .mvn/wrapper/maven-wrapper.properties
distributionUrl=https://nexus.sorrel.example/repository/maven-public/org/apache/maven/apache-maven/3.10.0/apache-maven-3.10.0-bin.zip

<!-- sorrel-parent -->
<properties>
  <project.build.outputTimestamp>2026-10-01T00:00:00Z</project.build.outputTimestamp>
</properties>

The wrapper downloads Maven through the company mirror (1.06), so a build on a locked-down CI runner still works.

Also seen. Gradle's gradlew does the same job for Gradle. A dev container, or the CI image run locally, pins the JDK and Maven together. SDKMAN's .sdkmanrc pins the JDK per project for those who use SDKMAN.

When to break it. A team that builds inside one pinned container image everywhere, laptops included, can drop the wrapper, because the image already pins Maven. The cost is that every developer builds inside Docker, and IntelliJ's own Maven runs outside it.

.NET anchor. global.json pins the SDK version for a repository. The wrapper goes further: it downloads the pinned Maven itself, so a laptop needs only a JDK. The C# compiler's <Deterministic> setting does the job of outputTimestamp, and SDK-style projects have it on already.

See also. 1.06, 1.08, 1.09, The Yard, chapter 2, Maven vs csproj

1.06 Run the build through the company mirror

What goes wrong. A mirror is a repository server that stands in for Maven Central and keeps a copy of every jar it serves. Sorrel's is Nexus. One developer's settings.xml has no mirror, so their builds fetch from Maven Central directly. CI passes the mirror, and laptops mostly do not. The platform team can count only what passes through Nexus, so when security asks which builds used a library, half of Payouts has no answer. When Nexus is down for 20 minutes, builds needing a new jar fail, and builds with a full local cache pass. That hides the outage from whoever is not affected.

Do this now.

  1. In ~/.m2/settings.xml, send every repository through the mirror with <mirrorOf>*</mirrorOf>. The settings file belongs to the user or the machine, not the project.
  2. Put credentials in a <server> whose <id> matches the mirror's. In CI, read them from environment variables and pass the file with -s.
  3. Remove <repositories> blocks from POMs. The mirror decides where jars come from.
<settings>
  <mirrors><mirror>
    <id>sorrel-nexus</id>
    <mirrorOf>*</mirrorOf>
    <url>https://nexus.sorrel.example/repository/maven-public/</url>
  </mirror></mirrors>
  <servers><server>
    <id>sorrel-nexus</id>
    <username>${env.NEXUS_USER}</username>
    <password>${env.NEXUS_PASSWORD}</password>
  </server></servers>
</settings>

.NET anchor. A nuget.config with <clear/> and one company feed.

See also. 1.05, 15.12, The Yard, chapter 2, Maven vs csproj

1.07 Choose between starter-parent and importing the Boot BOM

Then.

  • Boot era: Spring IO Platform, a curated list of versions for Spring and many other libraries, imported as io.spring.platform:platform-bom. It was right when Boot's own list was smaller. Boot's spring-boot-dependencies grew to cover the same ground, and the platform project was wound down.
<dependency>
  <groupId>io.spring.platform</groupId>
  <artifactId>platform-bom</artifactId>
  <version>${platform-bom.version}</version>
  <type>pom</type>
  <scope>import</scope>
</dependency>

Recognise it by. io.spring.platform, platform-bom, and release versions named after cities, such as Brussels and Cairo.

The rookie version. Switch a module to Spring's parent, to "use Boot properly":

<!-- payouts-api/pom.xml: sorrel-parent used to be here -->
<parent>
  <groupId>org.springframework.boot</groupId>
  <artifactId>spring-boot-starter-parent</artifactId>
  <version>3.5.16</version>
</parent>

What goes wrong. A POM can have only one parent. Switching payouts-api to the starter parent drops sorrel-parent for that module. Gone with it are the Java release, the enforcer rules, the pinned plugin versions and the fixed timestamp. Nothing fails. The difference surfaces weeks later, when payouts-api passes a build that payouts-domain would fail, and nobody can work out why the two modules behave differently.

Do this now. A BOM, a bill of materials, is a POM whose only content is a list of library versions known to work together. Boot publishes one as spring-boot-dependencies. There are two ways to use it, and one question decides: does the company already have a parent POM?

  1. No company parent, as for a standalone tool: inherit spring-boot-starter-parent. It gives you Boot's BOM and plugin settings. It declares the repackage step that makes a runnable jar (1.11). It sets the compiler's -parameters flag and UTF-8 encoding. It filters resource files with @...@ placeholders, so they do not clash with Spring's ${...}. You can change a managed version with a property such as <jackson-bom.version>.
  2. A company parent exists, as at Sorrel: the parent imports the BOM. An import scope in <dependencyManagement> copies the BOM's version list into yours, and nothing else.
  3. With an import, add back what the starter parent gave you: the plugin settings below, and project.build.sourceEncoding set to UTF-8 in the parent's properties. The -parameters flag matters most. Spring reads method parameter names, such as id in @PathVariable Long id, from the data that flag writes. Without it, a mapping with no explicit name fails at runtime.
  4. Version properties do nothing with an import. To change one managed version, declare it in <dependencyManagement>, or import that library's own BOM above Boot's (1.02).
<properties><spring-boot.version>3.5.16</spring-boot.version></properties>
<dependencyManagement>
  <dependencies>
    <dependency>
      <groupId>org.springframework.boot</groupId>
      <artifactId>spring-boot-dependencies</artifactId>
      <version>${spring-boot.version}</version>
      <type>pom</type>
      <scope>import</scope>
    </dependency>
  </dependencies>
</dependencyManagement>

<pluginManagement><plugins>
  <plugin>
    <artifactId>maven-compiler-plugin</artifactId>
    <version>3.16.0</version>
    <configuration><parameters>true</parameters></configuration>
  </plugin>
  <plugin>
    <groupId>org.springframework.boot</groupId>
    <artifactId>spring-boot-maven-plugin</artifactId>
    <version>${spring-boot.version}</version>
    <executions>
      <execution><goals><goal>repackage</goal></goals></execution>
    </executions>
  </plugin>
</plugins></pluginManagement>

Both plugins carry a version, because the import brings no plugin versions and requirePluginVersions (1.05) refuses a plugin without one. Settings in <pluginManagement> apply only to a module that uses the plugin. The compiler runs in every jar module, so parameters reaches them all. The Boot plugin runs only where a module declares it, so the application module declares spring-boot-maven-plugin with no version, and the library modules do not declare it (1.12).

Also seen. A company parent that itself inherits from spring-boot-starter-parent. That gives one chain and all of Boot's plugin settings. It also ties the company's release cycle to Boot's: every Boot patch is a new company parent.

When to break it. A service outside the company's build, such as a demo for a supplier, can use the starter parent. It then follows none of Sorrel's rules, and its README should say so.

.NET anchor. The starter parent is like an SDK such as Microsoft.NET.Sdk.Web: it sets build behaviour as well as versions. The BOM import is like including someone else's Directory.Packages.props into your own. A .NET project can combine an SDK with several props files. A Maven project gets one parent, and as many imported BOMs as it likes.

See also. 1.01, 1.02, 1.11, 19.02, The Yard, chapter 1, The Yard, chapter 3, Maven vs csproj, Spring Boot orientation

1.08 Set the Java version once, with maven.compiler.release

Then.

  • Spring era: <source>1.8</source> and <target>1.8</target> in the compiler plugin, often with animal-sniffer-maven-plugin to catch calls to newer APIs. That pairing was right before the compiler could check APIs itself. Its release option replaced both.

What goes wrong. A Payouts batch job that still runs on a Java 21 base image sets source and target to 21, and compiles on JDK 25. It calls Stream.gather, which became final in Java 24. It compiles, because source and target only control the language level and the class file format. In the pod it fails with NoSuchMethodError at the first payout that reaches that line.

Do this now. Set release to the Java version of the image the code runs on. release makes the compiler produce classes for that version and reject any API newer than it, so with 21 the Stream.gather call fails on the laptop instead. For Payouts, set <maven.compiler.release>25</maven.compiler.release> once, in the parent's properties. Delete source, target and java.version from the modules. Add <requireJavaVersion><version>25</version></requireJavaVersion> to the enforcer's rules (1.09), so the build refuses an older JDK.

.NET anchor. <TargetFramework>net9.0</TargetFramework>, set once in Directory.Build.props.

See also. 1.05, 19.05, The Yard, chapter 1, Getting a JDK, and the release train

1.09 Fail the build on conflicting or banned dependencies

Then.

  • Spring era: A reviewer who read every POM change against a list of banned libraries on a wiki page. It worked for a few services and a team that did not change.
  • Spring era: Excluding commons-logging from every Spring dependency and adding jcl-over-slf4j. Spring once logged through Commons Logging, and this routed its logs to SLF4J. Spring's own spring-jcl module made the exclusion unnecessary, and the enforcer's ban list replaced the habit of repeating it. In Boot 4, Spring depends on Apache Commons Logging 1.3 again, which does the same routing, so a commons-logging jar in the tree is expected.
<dependency>
  <groupId>org.springframework</groupId><artifactId>spring-context</artifactId>
  <exclusions><exclusion>
    <groupId>commons-logging</groupId><artifactId>commons-logging</artifactId>
  </exclusion></exclusions>
</dependency>
<dependency><groupId>org.slf4j</groupId><artifactId>jcl-over-slf4j</artifactId></dependency>

Recognise it by. jcl-over-slf4j, commons-logging exclusions repeated on each Spring dependency, and <fail>false</fail> in the enforcer's configuration.

The rookie version. Use a class because it compiles:

// payouts-api: compiles, because policy-client happens to bring commons-lang3
import org.apache.commons.lang3.StringUtils;

String reference = StringUtils.leftPad(payout.id(), 12, '0');

What goes wrong. payouts-api never declared commons-lang3. It arrived through policy-client. Six months later policy-client 3.4 drops it, and the upgrade pull request fails to compile in a class nobody touched. Meanwhile a new client library brought an older commons-compress nearer the top of the tree. Nearest wins took the older version, and the build said nothing. The payouts-api image went from 1.27.1 back to 1.21 in a change about something else.

Do this now. Make the build refuse three things, with rules that fail. The enforcer is a plugin that checks rules about the build and stops it when one is broken.

  1. Downgrades. requireUpperBoundDeps fails when the version Maven chose is lower than a version some library in the tree asked for. That is nearest wins going backwards. dependencyConvergence is stricter: every path must ask for the same version. It suits a small library. On a service it fails often, and each failure needs a managed version to settle it.
  2. Banned libraries. bannedDependencies lists artifacts that must never appear, at any depth. Log4j 1.x reached end of life on 5 August 2015, so log4j:log4j belongs there. So does JUnit 4's junit:junit, once the team has moved to JUnit 5 and nothing else needs it. Check the tree first: Testcontainers 1.x still brings it, so a service on Testcontainers 1.x cannot ban it yet. The listing leaves it out for that reason.
  3. Undeclared use. The dependency plugin's analyze-only goal, with failOnWarning, fails a module that uses classes from a jar it does not declare. Bind it to the verify phase in an <execution>. It suits payouts-domain, which declares everything it uses. In a Boot module every Spring class arrives through a starter, so the goal flags Spring's own jars as undeclared, and each starter as unused, because a starter has no classes. Ignore those with ignoredUsedUndeclaredDependencies set to org.springframework* and ignoredUnusedDeclaredDependencies set to org.springframework.boot:spring-boot-starter*. What is left is short: libraries such as Jackson that you use on purpose, which you then declare, and jars you lean on by accident, such as commons-lang3.
<plugin> <!-- version from the parent's pluginManagement (1.05) -->
  <artifactId>maven-enforcer-plugin</artifactId>
  <executions><execution>
    <id>enforce-dependencies</id>
    <goals><goal>enforce</goal></goals>
    <configuration><rules>
      <requireUpperBoundDeps/>
      <bannedDependencies><excludes>
        <exclude>log4j:log4j</exclude>
      </excludes></bannedDependencies>
    </rules></configuration>
  </execution></executions>
</plugin>

Leave the enforcer's fail setting at its default, true. A rule that only warns is read as often as a changelog. Maven 3.10 also fails a POM that declares the same dependency twice. On 3.9, banDuplicatePomDependencyVersions gives the same check.

Also seen. Gradle's failOnVersionConflict() in a resolution strategy. A vulnerability scanner in CI (15.12) catches known-bad versions, but not a quiet downgrade to a version nobody has reported yet.

When to break it. requireUpperBoundDeps sometimes flags a library that asks for a newer version it does not need. Exclude that one artifact from the rule, with a comment and a review date. The cost is one hole that someone has to remember to close.

.NET anchor. NuGet reports a detected package downgrade as NU1605, and the SDK treats it as an error. Maven has no such default. The enforcer is how you get one.

See also. 1.02, 1.03, 1.10, 15.12, The Yard, chapter 10, Maven vs csproj

1.10 Keep SNAPSHOT dependencies off the main branch

What goes wrong. payouts-api depends on sorrel-commons 1.4-SNAPSHOT. A SNAPSHOT version can be republished under the same number, and Maven fetches the newest one. On Thursday the commons team publishes a snapshot that renames a method. No commit on the Payouts main branch changed, and the 14:00 build fails. A build that passes is worse. Rebuild the same commit tomorrow and it may contain different classes.

Do this now.

  • Depend on released versions on the main and release branches. Use a SNAPSHOT only on a feature branch, while two teams change things together.
  • Add the enforcer's requireReleaseDeps rule to the main-branch build. The rule also checks each module's parent. If the service's own modules carry a SNAPSHOT version between releases, as many do, exclude them and the root POM with the rule's excludes, such as com.sorrel:payouts-*.
  • Pass -U to force a check for newer snapshots, and only on the branch that uses one.
  • Treat a version range such as [1.2,2.0) the same way. It resolves to the highest version in the range, which changes when a new one is published. Write one version.

See also. 1.09, 19.06, 20.14, The Yard, chapter 10, Maven vs csproj

1.11 Package a runnable jar and know what is inside it

Then.

  • Spring era: A WAR file, copied to a Tomcat server that another team ran.
  • Spring era: A fat jar built by maven-shade-plugin or maven-assembly-plugin, which unpacked every library into one jar. Files with the same name from two libraries overwrote each other.

What goes wrong. mockito-core is declared in payouts-api without <scope>test</scope>. It ships in the jar, in both pods, and the scanner reports its findings against production.

Do this now.

  • The repackage goal of spring-boot-maven-plugin turns the plain jar into a runnable one, and keeps the plain one with .original on the end.
  • Maven names the jar payouts-api-1.0.0.jar by default. Payouts sets <finalName>payouts-api</finalName> in the module's <build>, so it is target/payouts-api.jar in every version, the name the Dockerfile in 17.01 copies.
  • Your classes sit under BOOT-INF/classes, and each library stays a separate jar under BOOT-INF/lib. The manifest, META-INF/MANIFEST.MF, names the class java -jar starts. Its Main-Class is Boot's org.springframework.boot.loader.launch.JarLauncher, and Start-Class is your application class. An older Boot jar names org.springframework.boot.loader.JarLauncher.
  • Look before you ship: jar tf target/payouts-api.jar | grep BOOT-INF/lib.

See also. 1.03, 1.12, 17.01, 17.11, Packaging and native images

1.12 Lay out a multi-module service

Then.

  • J2EE era: Modules by deployment format: payouts-ejb, payouts-web and payouts-ear, assembled by maven-ear-plugin into one archive for an application server. It was right when the server ran several components and the packaging had to mirror them.
  • Spring era: Modules by technical layer: payouts-dao, payouts-service, payouts-web and payouts-common. It was right when each layer had its own Spring XML context. Splitting by what changes together replaced it, because a layer split makes every feature touch every module.
<modules>
  <module>payouts-common</module>
  <module>payouts-dao</module>
  <module>payouts-service</module>
  <module>payouts-web</module>
  <module>payouts-ear</module>
</modules>

Recognise it by. <packaging>ear</packaging> or <packaging>ejb</packaging>, maven-ear-plugin, application.xml, and module names that are layer names, such as -dao, -service and -common.

The rookie version. Put the Boot plugin in the root POM, so every module gets it:

<!-- payouts/pom.xml, the root -->
<build><plugins>
  <plugin>
    <groupId>org.springframework.boot</groupId>
    <artifactId>spring-boot-maven-plugin</artifactId>
  </plugin>
</plugins></build>

What goes wrong. Every module now runs repackage, payouts-domain included. payouts-domain has no main method, so ./mvnw verify stops there with Unable to find main class, while ./mvnw test passes, because it never reaches the package phase. Give the module a main class to quiet that, and it is repackaged. A repackaged jar keeps its classes under BOOT-INF/classes, where another module's compiler cannot see them. payouts-api then fails with cannot find symbol: class Money, on some builds and not others. It compiles when the build stops before package and Maven hands it the sibling's compiled classes, and fails when Maven hands it the jar. A team that also split by layer pays twice: adding one field to Payout touches all 4 modules, common, dao, service and web.

Do this now.

  1. Give the service a root POM with <packaging>pom</packaging>. It does two jobs. It is the aggregator: it lists the <modules>, so one command builds them all. It is also the parent each module names in <parent>. It inherits from sorrel-parent in turn.
  2. payouts-domain is plain Java: Claim, Payout, Money, PayoutStatus and the rules. It has no web framework and no database driver. It changes when the business changes.
  3. payouts-api is the Boot application: PayoutController, PayoutService, PayoutRepository, the clients and the configuration. It depends on payouts-domain, and it alone declares spring-boot-maven-plugin.
  4. Manage the sibling's version in the root's <dependencyManagement> as ${project.version}, so modules declare it with no version.
  5. Add a module only when something is built or released separately, such as a payouts-client library other teams consume. Two modules is a good number for one service.

Also seen. One module for the whole service, which is the right start for a small one. A split by ports and adapters, such as -domain, -application and -adapters, which enforces the dependency direction at the cost of more POMs and a longer build.

When to break it. A service with a small domain can stay as one module until a second deployable or a client library appears. The cost is that nothing stops domain code importing the database driver's classes. Review has to catch it instead of the compiler.

.NET anchor. A solution with a Payouts.Domain class library and a Payouts.Api web project, joined by a project reference. The root POM is the .sln and Directory.Build.props in one file. A .sln only lists projects. The root POM also sets what they inherit.

See also. 1.04, 1.07, 1.11, 21.01, 21.07, The Yard, chapter 4, Gradle and multi-module builds, Maven vs csproj

1.13 Use Maven profiles without making two builds

Then.

  • Spring era: One profile per environment, dev, test and prod, each filtering its own database URL into the property files at build time. It was right for a WAR configured inside the archive. Configuration read at runtime replaced it.

What goes wrong. A Maven profile is a named block of POM settings, switched on with -P or by a condition. It acts at build time, unlike a Spring profile, which chooses configuration when the application starts (4.03). A prod profile in payouts-api swaps in a different logback.xml. CI builds with -Pprod, and laptops build without it, so the jar that ships is not the jar anyone tested. A second trap: a profile marked activeByDefault is switched off as soon as any other profile is named with -P.

Do this now.

  • Build one artifact for every environment. Environment differences belong in Spring configuration at runtime (4.03, 4.15).
  • Use profiles for optional work on the same artifact, such as an owasp profile that adds the vulnerability scan (15.12), run with -Powasp.
  • Run ./mvnw help:active-profiles to see which profiles are on.

See also. 1.05, 4.03, 4.15, Maven vs csproj

1.14 Speed up a slow build before changing tools

What goes wrong. The payouts-api CI build takes 8 minutes, and someone proposes moving to Gradle. 6 of the 8 minutes are tests, running one class at a time in one JVM. The tests would be as slow in Gradle.

Do this now.

  1. Measure. Maven's reactor summary prints the time per module. Time compilation and tests separately.
  2. Run tests in parallel. Surefire's default is one JVM per module, running classes one after another. Set forkCount to 1C, one JVM per CPU core, with reuseForks true. JUnit 5 can also run tests in parallel inside one JVM: set junit.jupiter.execution.parallel.enabled=true and junit.jupiter.execution.parallel.mode.default=concurrent in src/test/resources/junit-platform.properties. The first alone runs nothing in parallel.
  3. Build independent modules in parallel with -T 1C. A chain of modules that each depend on the last stays a chain.
  4. Cache ~/.m2/repository in CI, keyed on a hash of the POM files, not on the branch name.
  5. Run verify, not clean install, unless you need either.
  6. Only then compare tools, one change at a time.

Also seen. The Maven Daemon, mvnd, keeps a warm JVM between builds on a laptop.

See also. 1.04, 16.07, 16.08, 18.01, The Yard, chapter 4, Gradle and multi-module builds

⚠Review checklist
  • If you see spring-boot-starter-parent as the parent of a new Sorrel service: it has dropped the company parent and every rule in it. See 1.01.
  • If you see a <version> on a dependency in a module POM, with no comment: it silently overrides the parent, and nobody will know when it can go. See 1.02.
  • If you see a security finding closed because no POM names the jar: transitive jars ship too. See 1.03.
  • If you see -pl without -am in a script or README: the module builds against a stale copy in the local repository. See 1.04.
  • If you see mvn instead of ./mvnw in CI, or a plugin with no version: two machines build the same commit differently. See 1.05.
  • If you see <repositories> in a POM, or a CI job with no settings file: builds bypass the mirror, and nobody can count what they used. See 1.06.
  • If you see a module switching its parent to spring-boot-starter-parent: a POM has one parent, so the company's is lost. See 1.07.
  • If you see <source> and <target> in the compiler plugin: calls to newer APIs compile, then fail at runtime on the older Java. See 1.08.
  • If you see an import from a jar the module does not declare, or <fail>false</fail> on the enforcer: an upgrade elsewhere will break it, and the warning will not be read. See 1.09.
  • If you see -SNAPSHOT or a version range in a dependency on the main branch: the build can change with no commit. See 1.10.
  • If you see a test library without <scope>test</scope>: it ships to production. See 1.11.
  • If you see spring-boot-maven-plugin under <plugins> in the root POM: every module is repackaged, the domain module included. See 1.12.
  • If you see a Maven profile named after an environment: the jar you tested is not the jar you ship. See 1.13.
  • If you see a build-tool migration justified by test time: the tests will be as slow in the new tool. See 1.14.

Part IV · The how-to2. Core Java#

This part covers the language and the standard library underneath every Payouts service: money, time, values, equality, null, collections, streams, exceptions and resources. Each entry shows what a developer who has written Java for many years reaches for today, the mistake a newcomer from C# makes by analogy, and the older code you will find in services written before records and java.time. Syntax lives in the handbook. These entries are about the choices.

★What a veteran knows
  • Money is a BigDecimal plus a Currency, with the scale fixed once. Every rounding is a business decision with a named RoundingMode.
  • Store an Instant for anything that happened. A LocalDateTime in a stored document is a bug waiting for the clocks to change.
  • A type that overrides equals overrides hashCode too, and neither looks at anything that can change.
  • Decide about null at the edges of the service. Inside the domain, a null is a bug, not a value.
  • A record is only as immutable as its components. Copy every collection it receives.
  • Let the compiler review for you: sealed types switched over with no default (2.12), and packages marked @NullMarked (2.06).
  • Inherited code tells you its age. Modernise it in its own pull request, never inside a fix.
◷How we got hereStephen Colebourne started Joda-Time in 2002 because the date classes that shipped with Java were, in the…

Stephen Colebourne started Joda-Time in 2002 because the date classes that shipped with Java were, in the words of its own site, poor. java.util.Date and java.util.Calendar were both mutable, so any method that received a date could change it under the caller. Both counted months from zero, so 2 meant March. In January 2007 Colebourne and Michael Nascimento Santos took a replacement to the Java Community Process as JSR 310, a Java Specification Request, the process's name for a proposed standard API. The rationale listed the zero-indexed months and the mutability as causes of many bugs. Roger Riggs of Oracle joined the work later. On 4 March 2014 Riggs told the mailing list that JSR 310 was approved and complete, and JDK 8 shipped java.time on 18 March 2014. It had taken twelve years to get from library to platform. Joda-Time's own site now asks Java 8 users to migrate to java.time. Every Date you meet in a Sorrel service is code that was written before that migration reached it.

2.01 Represent money without losing pennies

Then.

  • J2EE era: amounts as a long count of pence, in fields called amountPence or amountMinor. This was right for a single-currency system and is still defensible in a hot path. It made every boundary convert, and a pounds value sometimes slipped into a pence field.
  • Boot era: a money library, Joda-Money or Moneta, the reference implementation of JSR 354. Both are sound. JSR 354 never became part of the JDK, so most teams now own a small Money type instead of a dependency.
Money fee = Money.of(CurrencyUnit.GBP, new BigDecimal("18.60"));    // Joda-Money
Money total = payout.getAmount().plus(fee);

MonetaryAmount amount = org.javamoney.moneta.Money.of(1240.50, "GBP");  // JSR 354

Recognise it by. org.joda.money.Money, CurrencyUnit.GBP, javax.money.MonetaryAmount, org.javamoney.moneta, and long fields named ...Pence or ...Minor.

The rookie version.

BigDecimal amount = new BigDecimal(1240.10);            // built from a double
BigDecimal fee = amount.multiply(new BigDecimal("0.015"));
BigDecimal net = amount.subtract(fee);
if (net.equals(new BigDecimal("1221.50"))) { ... }      // equals compares scale too

What goes wrong. The newcomer knows not to use double, so they reach for BigDecimal, the JDK's arbitrary-precision decimal type. Then they build it from a double literal. A double cannot hold 1240.10 exactly, and new BigDecimal(double) faithfully copies the error, with a long tail of digits. The fee then carries more decimal places than any currency has. Nobody rounds it, so the ledger receives a reservation for an amount with 44 decimal places and rejects it. The equals check fails even when the value is right, because BigDecimal.equals treats 1221.5 and 1221.50 as different. In the nightly reconciliation of 20,000 payouts, a total built this way disagreed with the ledger by 3p, and the batch was held for a day.

Do this now. Give money a type, and make that type refuse bad values.

  1. Write one Money record, a BigDecimal amount and a java.util.Currency.
  2. Build BigDecimal from a String, or from a whole number of pence with BigDecimal.valueOf(124050, 2). Never from a double.
  3. Fix the scale in the constructor, to the currency's own number of decimal places. RoundingMode.UNNECESSARY makes setScale throw an ArithmeticException if the value would need rounding, so £1,240.505 is rejected at the door.
  4. Round only where the business rounds, with a named mode. Fees and interest are where it happens. Whether that is HALF_EVEN or HALF_UP is a question for finance, not for the developer.
  5. Compare amounts with compareTo or signum. With the scale fixed in the constructor, the record's equals is also safe.
  6. Give the type a named zero, such as ZERO_GBP, for sums that start from nothing (2.08).
public record Money(BigDecimal amount, Currency currency) {
    public static final Money ZERO_GBP = gbp("0.00");
    public Money {
        amount = amount.setScale(currency.getDefaultFractionDigits(), RoundingMode.UNNECESSARY);
    }
    public static Money gbp(String a) { return new Money(new BigDecimal(a), Currency.getInstance("GBP")); }
    public Money plus(Money other) {
        if (!currency.equals(other.currency)) throw new IllegalArgumentException("currency mismatch");
        return new Money(amount.add(other.amount), currency);
    }
    public Money minus(Money other) { return plus(new Money(other.amount.negate(), other.currency)); }
    public Money applyRate(BigDecimal rate, RoundingMode mode) {
        return new Money(amount.multiply(rate).setScale(currency.getDefaultFractionDigits(), mode), currency);
    }
}

Also seen. A long of minor units, when one currency is certain and arithmetic speed matters. Moneta, when the service converts between currencies and wants exchange-rate providers. Joda-Money, in code that already uses it.

When to break it. A counter that sums millions of amounts per second can use long pence internally. The cost is a conversion at every boundary and a unit in every variable name, so a pounds value cannot hide in a pence field.

.NET anchor. C#'s decimal is a 128-bit value type with operators, so a + b and a == b work. Java's BigDecimal is an immutable object with methods and no operators. In .NET 2.0m == 2.00m is true. In Java new BigDecimal("2.0").equals(new BigDecimal("2.00")) is false.

See also. 2.04, 2.18, 5.13, 8.10, Numbers, money and time

2.02 Store and compare points in time

Then.

  • J2EE era: java.util.Date, java.util.Calendar and java.sql.Timestamp. A Date is a moment on the timeline despite its name, but it prints itself in the server's zone and it is mutable. These were the only types the platform had.
  • Spring era: Joda-Time's DateTime, LocalDate and DateTimeZone. It was the right answer from 2002 until JDK 8, and java.time was designed by the same author.
Calendar cal = Calendar.getInstance();
cal.set(2016, 2, 31);                 // 31 March: months count from 0
Date due = cal.getTime();
payout.setDueDate(due);               // the caller can still change it

DateTime paidAt = new DateTime(DateTimeZone.UTC);   // Joda-Time

Recognise it by. java.util.Date, java.util.Calendar, java.sql.Timestamp, org.joda.time.DateTime, @Temporal(TemporalType.TIMESTAMP), and getTime() used to get milliseconds.

The rookie version.

public record Payout(String id, Money amount, LocalDateTime paidAt) {}

var payout = new Payout(id, amount, LocalDateTime.now());

What goes wrong. LocalDateTime is a date and a time of day with no zone or offset. It looks like a timestamp and is not one. LocalDateTime.now() reads the wall clock in whatever zone the JVM runs in. Payouts runs as 2 pods, and one of them was built from a base image that set TZ=Europe/London. During British Summer Time the two pods stored times an hour apart for the same moment. The London pod's times were an hour ahead, so its payouts from the last hour before the 17:00 cut-off looked as if they came after it. The bank file missed 212 of them, and they went out a day late. On the last Sunday of October, 01:30 happens twice in London, and a LocalDateTime cannot say which one it meant.

Do this now. Choose the type by what the value means.

  1. A moment that happened, such as paid, requested or received, is an Instant. It is a point on the UTC timeline with no zone attached.
  2. A calendar date with no time, such as a claim's date of loss or a policy's start date, is a LocalDate.
  3. Convert to a zone only to show a value to a person or to apply a calendar rule. Use atZone(ZoneId.of("Europe/London")).
  4. Use OffsetDateTime at a boundary where the offset is part of the data, such as a timestamp the bank sends back.
  5. Compare with isBefore, isAfter and Duration.between, not with compareTo on strings or millisecond arithmetic.
  6. If the store keeps less precision than Instant does, truncate before you store, so a value read back equals the value written. DocumentDB stores dates to the millisecond (8.10).

The clock here is an injected java.time.Clock, so tests can fix the time (2.16).

static final ZoneId LONDON = ZoneId.of("Europe/London");

Instant paidAt = Instant.now(clock).truncatedTo(ChronoUnit.MILLIS);
LocalDate bankDay = paidAt.atZone(LONDON).toLocalDate();
ZonedDateTime cutoff = bankDay.atTime(17, 0).atZone(LONDON);
boolean late = paidAt.isAfter(cutoff.toInstant());
Duration waited = Duration.between(payout.requestedAt(), paidAt);

Also seen. ZonedDateTime, for a value that must keep its region, such as a schedule in London time. OffsetDateTime, in JSON and JDBC code where the offset travels with the value.

When to break it. A future local appointment, such as "pay at 09:00 London time on 1 April", is a LocalDateTime plus a ZoneId, stored as two fields. Zone rules can change before the date arrives, and an Instant computed today would then be wrong. The cost is two fields and a conversion at the moment of use.

.NET anchor. Instant is closest to a UTC DateTimeOffset, and LocalDate to DateOnly. LocalDateTime is DateTime with DateTimeKind.Unspecified, with the same traps. If you have used NodaTime, it began as a port of Joda-Time, and the names Instant and LocalDate mean the same things.

See also. 2.15, 2.16, 5.13, 8.10, Numbers, money and time

2.03 Model a value with a record

Then.

  • Spring era: a JavaBean, a class with private fields, a no-argument constructor, getters, setters, and equals, hashCode and toString generated by the IDE. Frameworks needed the setters to fill objects in.
  • Boot era: generated value classes, from Lombok's @Value, Google's AutoValue or the Immutables library. They removed the boilerplate before the language could. Records replaced them because the compiler now does the same job with no annotation processor, a compiler plug-in that generates code from annotations.
@Value                                 // Lombok: final fields, getters, equals
public class Money {
    BigDecimal amount;
    Currency currency;
}

@AutoValue abstract class ClaimId { abstract String value(); }

Recognise it by. lombok.Value, lombok.Data, com.google.auto.value.AutoValue, org.immutables.value.Value, and accessors named getAmount() rather than amount().

The rookie version.

public record ClaimId(String value) {}
public record PayoutBatch(String id, List<Payout> payouts) {}

var list = new ArrayList<Payout>();
var batch = new PayoutBatch("b-17", list);
list.add(extraPayout);                 // the "immutable" batch just changed

What goes wrong. A record is a class whose fields are fixed at construction, with accessors, equals, hashCode and toString generated from its components. The newcomer takes "fields are final" to mean "the value cannot change". It means the reference cannot change. The list behind it still can. In Payouts a batch of 12 payouts was signed and handed to the relay, then a second caller added a 13th to the same list. The ledger received 13 and the audit log recorded 12. The batch's hashCode had also changed, so a HashSet of sent batches no longer found it. Separately, new ClaimId("") compiled and ran, and an empty claim id reached the policy system before anything rejected it.

Do this now.

  1. Write one record per value: ClaimId, Money, PayoutBatch. A wrapper such as ClaimId needs a converter to be stored as a plain string (8.18).
  2. Validate in the compact constructor, the constructor with no parameter list that runs before the fields are assigned. Throw IllegalArgumentException for bad input.
  3. Copy every collection with List.copyOf, Set.copyOf or Map.copyOf. The copy is unmodifiable and rejects null elements.
  4. Add behaviour as methods. Compute derived values in methods rather than storing them as extra components.
  5. Put parsing in a static factory, such as ClaimId.parse(String), so the constructor stays the one place that validates.
  6. In Java 25, a constructor may run statements before it calls this(...) (JEP 513, flexible constructor bodies). An extra record constructor can now check its input before it delegates.
public record PayoutBatch(String id, List<Payout> payouts) {
    public PayoutBatch {
        if (id == null || id.isBlank()) throw new IllegalArgumentException("batch id is blank");
        payouts = List.copyOf(payouts);
    }
    public Money total() {
        return payouts.stream().map(Payout::amount).reduce(Money.ZERO_GBP, Money::plus);
    }
}

Also seen. A final class with private fields, when the representation must stay hidden. A record exposes every component through an accessor. Lombok, in services that predate the decision to drop it.

When to break it. A type with an identity that moves through states, such as a payout, is an entity, not a value. In a service that uses JPA, the Java standard for mapping objects to SQL tables, an entity must be a class, because JPA needs a no-argument constructor and non-final fields. Spring Data MongoDB maps records directly, so Payouts keeps Payout a record whose changes return new copies (8.01). The cost of a class is writing equals and hashCode by hand (2.04). The cost of a record entity is that its equals compares every component, as 2.04 explains.

.NET anchor. C# record and record struct are the nearest thing. Java records are always final and cannot extend another class. Java has no with expression, so you write a withStatus method yourself. The accessor is amount(), a method, not a property.

See also. 2.04, 2.07, 5.03, 8.01, 8.18, The Yard, chapter 5, Records

2.04 Make equals and hashCode agree

Then.

  • Spring era: hand-written methods with Apache Commons Lang's EqualsBuilder and HashCodeBuilder, or Guava's Objects.equal and Objects.hashCode. They were tidier than the IDE's 31 * result output, and they were correct.
  • Boot era: Lombok's @EqualsAndHashCode, usually through @Data, which included every field, mutable ones too.
@Override public boolean equals(Object o) {
    if (!(o instanceof Payout)) return false;
    Payout other = (Payout) o;
    return new EqualsBuilder().append(id, other.id).isEquals();
}
@Override public int hashCode() {
    return new HashCodeBuilder(17, 37).append(id).toHashCode();
}

Recognise it by. org.apache.commons.lang3.builder.EqualsBuilder, HashCodeBuilder, com.google.common.base.Objects, lombok.EqualsAndHashCode, lombok.Data, and result = 31 * result + ....

The rookie version.

public class Payout {
    private final String id;
    private PayoutStatus status;

    public boolean equals(Payout other) {      // an overload, not an override
        return id.equals(other.id);
    }
}

What goes wrong. HashSet, HashMap and List.contains call equals(Object). The method above takes a Payout, so it is a new overload and the collections never call it. They fall back to identity, where two objects are equal only if they are the same object. The nightly retry job loaded the same failed payout twice, from two queries, and its de-duplicating Set kept both. A payout of £1,240.50 went to the bank twice. The second common form overrides equals correctly and forgets hashCode. Then two equal payouts land in different hash buckets, and the set still holds both.

Do this now.

  1. Decide what "the same" means. A value, such as Money, is equal when every component is equal. An entity, such as a payout, is the same payout when its identifier is equal.
  2. For values, use a record. It generates both methods from all components.
  3. For an entity written as a class, as in JPA services and older Sorrel code, override equals(Object) with @Override, so the compiler catches an overload. Use the instanceof pattern: o instanceof Payout other tests the type and, if it matches, gives you o already cast as other. Compare the id, and build hashCode from the same fields.
  4. For an entity written as a record, as Payout is in Payouts (8.01), the generated equals compares every component, version and status included. Two loads of the same payout at different versions are not equal. De-duplicate by id instead, with a Set of ids or Collectors.toMap(Payout::id, p -> p, (first, second) -> first).
  5. Never base either method on a field that can change while the object sits in a HashSet or is a HashMap key. A changed hash strands the object in the wrong bucket.
  6. Watch the components. BigDecimal.equals compares scale (2.01). Arrays compare by identity, so a record with an array component is never equal to a copy. Use a List.
  7. Keep compareTo consistent with equals. A TreeSet uses compareTo and a HashSet uses equals, and BigDecimal gives different answers in the two.
public final class Payout {                 // the class form, in older services
    private final String id;
    private PayoutStatus status;
    // constructor and behaviour elided

    @Override
    public boolean equals(Object o) {
        return o instanceof Payout other && id.equals(other.id);
    }

    @Override
    public int hashCode() {
        return id.hashCode();
    }
}

Also seen. Objects.hash(id, currency) for several fields. It allocates an array per call, which matters only in a hot loop. EqualsVerifier, a test library, checks the whole contract in one line. By default it fails if equals ignores a field, or if a null field makes equals throw, so an entity says which fields count and that they are never null: EqualsVerifier.forClass(Payout.class).withOnlyTheseFields("id").withNonnullFields("id").verify().

When to break it. Objects with no natural identity, such as services, listeners and builders, keep the identity equals they inherit from Object. An entity with no id until it is saved has no stable equality. Keep it out of hash collections until it has one.

.NET anchor. The contract is the same as Equals and GetHashCode. In C#, writing Equals(Payout other) is the right pattern, because IEquatable<T> makes collections call it. Java has no such interface, and the collections ignore an overload. In Java == on objects always compares references, and there is no operator overloading to change that.

See also. 2.03, 2.07, 2.11, Equality, hashing and comparison

2.05 Return "maybe nothing" without returning null

Then.

  • J2EE era: return null and say so in the Javadoc. It was the only option, and it relied on every caller reading the comment.
  • Boot era: Guava's com.google.common.base.Optional, with absent(), fromNullable() and or(). Guava had it years before the JDK did, and java.util.Optional copied the idea.
/** @return the payout, or null if there is none */
public Payout findByClaim(String claimId) { ... }

Optional<Payout> p = Optional.fromNullable(found);     // Guava
Payout payout = p.or(Payout.NONE);

Recognise it by. com.google.common.base.Optional, Optional.absent(), fromNullable, @CheckForNull, and Javadoc that says "or null".

The rookie version.

Optional<Payout> payout = repository.findById(id);
if (payout.isPresent()) {
    return payout.get().status();
}
return null;

private Optional<String> bankReference;     // a field, and sometimes null itself

What goes wrong. Optional<T> is a box that holds one value or none. The code above uses the box and then returns null anyway, so the caller is back where it started. The status endpoint returned "status": null for an unknown payout instead of a 404. The claims portal read that as "not started" and resubmitted the claim. Only the idempotency key stopped a second payout. The Optional field is worse. It can hold a value, hold nothing, or be null, so bankReference.isPresent() threw a NullPointerException on payouts loaded from older documents. A bare get() on an empty box throws NoSuchElementException with no useful message.

Do this now.

  1. Return Optional<T> from a method where "nothing" is a normal answer, such as a lookup by id. A Spring Data repository is an interface whose implementation Spring Data writes for you at start-up. MongoRepository<Payout, String> names the document type and the type of its id. Its findById already returns Optional. So does a derived query, a method such as findByIdempotencyKey whose query Spring Data works out from its name (8.03), if you declare it that way. Use Optional only where at most one document can match. A claim can have several payouts, so a lookup by claim returns a List.
  2. Consume it in one expression. map transforms the value if there is one. orElseThrow turns absence into an exception you choose.
  3. Use orElseGet for a default that is expensive to build. orElse evaluates its argument even when the value is present.
  4. Use ifPresentOrElse when both branches have side effects.
  5. Do not use Optional for fields, parameters or collections. A field is non-null or marked nullable (2.06). A collection is empty, never absent.
public interface PayoutRepository extends MongoRepository<Payout, String> {
    Optional<Payout> findByIdempotencyKey(String idempotencyKey);   // unique (8.16)
    List<Payout> findByClaimId(String claimId);                     // empty, never absent
}

public PayoutStatus statusOf(String payoutId) {
    return repository.findById(payoutId)
            .map(Payout::status)
            .orElseThrow(() -> new PayoutNotFound(payoutId));       // a 404 (6.14)
}

Also seen. A nullable return marked with JSpecify's @Nullable (2.06), in internal code where allocation matters. A sealed result type (2.12), when "nothing" has several reasons the caller must tell apart.

When to break it. A tight loop that looks up millions of values can return a nullable reference to avoid allocating a box per call. The cost is that the compiler no longer reminds the caller to handle absence, unless a null checker runs in the build.

.NET anchor. C# nullable reference types (Payout?) give the same signal through the compiler, with flow analysis and warnings. Java has no nullability in the language, so Optional is a library type and the compiler treats it like any other object. Nullable<T> is not the analogue, because it is for value types only.

See also. 2.06, 2.12, 6.14, 8.03, 8.16, Nullability: Optional and JSpecify

2.06 Handle null at the boundaries

Then.

  • Spring era: the JSR 305 annotations, javax.annotation.Nullable and @Nonnull, from the FindBugs jar, with @ParametersAreNonnullByDefault on a package. JSR 305 was never finished, and different tools read the annotations differently.
  • Boot era: Spring's own org.springframework.lang.Nullable and @NonNullApi. Spring Framework 7, which Boot 4 uses, deprecates them in favour of JSpecify.
// package-info.java
@NonNullApi
package com.sorrel.payouts.domain;

import org.springframework.lang.NonNullApi;

Recognise it by. javax.annotation.Nullable, javax.annotation.Nonnull, com.google.code.findbugs:jsr305, org.springframework.lang.Nullable, @NonNullApi, org.jetbrains.annotations.NotNull.

The rookie version.

public Money net(PayoutTerms terms) {
    if (terms == null) return null;
    if (terms.gross() == null) return null;
    if (terms.fee() == null) return terms.gross();
    return terms.gross().minus(terms.fee());
}

What goes wrong. Every method guards against null, so no method knows whether null is allowed. The checks pass null along until something far away throws, or, worse, until a guard makes a silent decision. Here a missing fee means the claimant is paid the gross amount. PayoutTerms is what Payouts maps the policy system's answer into. The policy system started omitting the fee field on one product after a change on its side. Over a weekend 37 payouts went out without their fee deducted, £18.60 each on a typical payout of £1,240.50. No exception was thrown, so nobody was paged.

Do this now. Check null where data enters the service, and nowhere else.

  1. List the boundaries: HTTP request bodies, SQS messages, documents read from DocumentDB, and responses from LedgerClient, PolicyClient and BankGatewayClient.
  2. At the HTTP boundary, use @NotNull from Bean Validation, the Jakarta standard for constraints written as annotations, on the request record (6.01). For messages and client responses, such as the policy system's terms, validate when you map them to domain types.
  3. In domain records, call Objects.requireNonNull in the compact constructor (2.03). The object cannot exist with a missing field.
  4. Mark each package @NullMarked, from JSpecify (org.jspecify:jspecify). Every type in it is then non-null unless it says @Nullable. A package annotation lives in a file named package-info.java in that package. It does not cover subpackages, so each package needs its own.
  5. Annotations do nothing at run time. Add a build-time checker so a possible null becomes a compile error. NullAway is one: a check that runs inside Error Prone, Google's plug-in that adds checks to the Java compiler. Both are configured in the maven-compiler-plugin section of the POM, as NullAway's README shows.
// src/main/java/com/sorrel/payouts/domain/package-info.java
@NullMarked
package com.sorrel.payouts.domain;

import org.jspecify.annotations.NullMarked;

public record PayoutTerms(String claimId, Money gross, Money fee, @Nullable String waiverReason) {
    public PayoutTerms {
        Objects.requireNonNull(claimId, "claimId");
        Objects.requireNonNull(gross, "gross");
        Objects.requireNonNull(fee, "fee");          // no fee is Money.ZERO_GBP, said explicitly
    }
}

Also seen. Optional for return values (2.05). The null object pattern, a real object that does nothing, such as a NoFee policy. IntelliJ's own inspections, which read JSpecify annotations, as a first step before a build checker.

When to break it. A library you call may return null by design. Wrap the call at your boundary and convert the null to Optional or an exception there. Inside a tight loop, a local null is fine if it never leaves the method.

.NET anchor. @NullMarked with a checker is the Java version of <Nullable>enable</Nullable> in a .csproj. The difference is that C#'s compiler does the checking itself, and Java's needs a plugin. Objects.requireNonNull is ArgumentNullException.ThrowIfNull.

See also. 2.05, 6.01, 6.12, 7.10, Nullability: Optional and JSpecify

2.07 Choose the right collection and make it unmodifiable

Then.

  • J2EE era: Vector, Hashtable, Stack and Enumeration, often as raw types with no generics. Every method was synchronised, which was a reasonable default before the newer collections existed.
  • Spring era: Collections.unmodifiableList to protect a field, and Guava's ImmutableList and ImmutableMap when a real copy was wanted. Guava filled a gap that List.of and List.copyOf later closed.
Vector payouts = new Vector();                    // raw and synchronised
Hashtable byClaim = new Hashtable();

List<Payout> view = Collections.unmodifiableList(list);    // a view, not a copy
ImmutableList<Payout> copy = ImmutableList.copyOf(list);   // Guava

Recognise it by. java.util.Vector, java.util.Hashtable, java.util.Stack, java.util.Enumeration, com.google.common.collect.ImmutableList, Collections.unmodifiableList, Arrays.asList.

The rookie version.

public class PayoutBatch {
    private final List<Payout> payouts = new ArrayList<>();
    public List<Payout> getPayouts() { return payouts; }
}

List<String> currencies = Arrays.asList("GBP", "EUR");
currencies.add("USD");                     // UnsupportedOperationException

What goes wrong. The getter hands out the batch's own list. A caller removed failed payouts from it with removeIf while the outbox relay was iterating the same list, and the relay failed at 02:14 with a ConcurrentModificationException. The batch of 64 payouts was half published. Arrays.asList looks like a list and is a fixed-size view of an array. add throws at run time. Java's List interface has add on every list, including the ones that refuse it, so the compiler cannot warn you.

Do this now.

  1. Pick by how the collection is used. ArrayList is the default list. ArrayDeque is the queue and the stack, in place of Stack and LinkedList. HashMap is the default map, LinkedHashMap keeps insertion order, and TreeMap keeps keys sorted. EnumMap and EnumSet are the fastest choice when the keys are an enum.
  2. Make literals with List.of, Set.of and Map.of. Make copies with List.copyOf. Stream.toList() also returns an unmodifiable list.
  3. Know their rules. They reject null elements and null keys. Set.of and Map.of reject duplicates when they are created. The iteration order of Set.of and Map.of is unspecified, so never depend on it.
  4. Remember that Collections.unmodifiableList is a view. Changes to the list underneath still show through it.
  5. Use the sequenced-collection methods from Java 21: getFirst(), getLast() and reversed().
public record PayoutBatch(String id, List<Payout> payouts) {
    public PayoutBatch { payouts = List.copyOf(payouts); }
}

Map<PayoutStatus, Long> counts = new EnumMap<>(PayoutStatus.class);
Deque<SagaStep> done = new ArrayDeque<>();      // push on success, pop to compensate
Set<String> currencies = Set.of("GBP", "EUR");
Payout latest = batch.payouts().getLast();

Also seen. Guava's immutable collections, in code that already depends on Guava. ConcurrentHashMap for maps shared between threads (3.07). Eclipse Collections, for large collections of primitives.

When to break it. A method that builds an ArrayList locally and returns it can skip the copy, because nobody else holds a reference. Copying 100,000 elements on every call has a real cost. The cost of skipping it is a list the caller can change, so say so in the method name or the Javadoc.

.NET anchor. Java's ArrayList is List<T>, not .NET's old untyped ArrayList. HashMap is Dictionary<TKey,TValue>, and List.copyOf is close to ToImmutableList().
