The difference is that .NET has IReadOnlyList<T>, an interface without Add. Java has no read-only collection interface, so an unmodifiable list fails at run time, not at compile time.

See also. 2.03, 2.08, 3.07, Collections

2.08 Transform collections with streams and keep them readable

Then.

  • Spring era: for loops with an explicit Iterator, and Guava's FluentIterable, Iterables.transform and Collections2.filter with anonymous classes. Before lambdas, that was the only way to pass behaviour, and Guava made it bearable.
List<Money> paid = new ArrayList<>();
for (Iterator<Payout> it = payouts.iterator(); it.hasNext(); ) {
    Payout p = it.next();
    if (p.getStatus() == PayoutStatus.PAID) paid.add(p.getAmount());
}
Iterable<String> ids = Iterables.transform(payouts, new Function<Payout, String>() {
    public String apply(Payout p) { return p.getId(); } });

Recognise it by. com.google.common.collect.FluentIterable, Iterables.transform, com.google.common.base.Function, org.apache.commons.collections.CollectionUtils, and new Function<...>() { inline.

The rookie version.

List<String> failed = new ArrayList<>();
BigDecimal[] total = {BigDecimal.ZERO};
payouts.parallelStream()
       .filter(p -> p.status() == PayoutStatus.FAILED)
       .forEach(p -> {
           failed.add(p.id());                          // not thread-safe
           total[0] = total[0].add(p.amount().amount());
       });

What goes wrong. A stream is a pipeline over a source: a chain of steps such as filter and map, ended by one terminal step that produces a result. The code above uses the stream as a loop and collects its results by side effect. With parallelStream the work runs on several threads at once, and ArrayList and the array slot are not safe to share. Additions are lost without an error. The nightly report showed 41 failed payouts out of 44, with the total £3,712.20 short. parallelStream also runs on the common pool, one ForkJoinPool of threads that the whole JVM shares, so a big report slows every other user of that pool.

Do this now.

  1. Produce the result from the pipeline. Use toList(), Collectors.groupingBy, Collectors.toMap or reduce, never forEach adding to an outside list.
  2. Keep each step short. A lambda longer than a line becomes a named method, used as a method reference such as Payout::isFailed.
  3. Stay sequential. Use parallelStream only for large, CPU-bound work you have measured (18.01).
  4. Know the collectors. Stream.toList() is unmodifiable. Collectors.toList() makes no promise about mutability. Collectors.toMap throws on a duplicate key unless you pass a merge function.
  5. Streams do not accept lambdas that throw checked exceptions. Translate the exception in a helper method (2.09), or use a loop.
  6. Use a gatherer (Stream.gather, final in Java 24) for steps the built-in operations lack, such as fixed-size batches.
List<String> failedIds = payouts.stream()
        .filter(Payout::isFailed)
        .map(Payout::id)
        .toList();

Map<PayoutStatus, Long> byStatus = payouts.stream()
        .collect(Collectors.groupingBy(Payout::status, Collectors.counting()));

Money total = payouts.stream()
        .map(Payout::amount)
        .reduce(Money.ZERO_GBP, Money::plus);

List<List<Payout>> batches = payouts.stream().gather(Gatherers.windowFixed(25)).toList();

Also seen. A plain for loop. It is the right tool for early exit, index arithmetic, checked exceptions, or logic that reads as steps. Experienced Java developers use both, and neither is a sign of age.

When to break it. A CPU-heavy calculation over a very large in-memory list may justify parallelStream. The cost is contention for the common pool, which the rest of the JVM also uses, and code that must be free of shared state.

.NET anchor. Streams are LINQ to Objects with different names: Where is filter, Select is map, Aggregate is reduce, GroupBy is the groupingBy collector. A stream can be consumed once. Enumerating it twice throws, where a LINQ query would run again. parallelStream is AsParallel. No stream translates into a database query the way IQueryable does.

See also. 2.07, 2.09, 18.01, Streams vs LINQ

2.09 Throw, wrap and translate exceptions

Then.

  • J2EE era: checked exceptions, the kind the compiler forces every caller to catch or declare, carried all the way up: throws RemoteException, SQLException, NamingException. The designers wanted failures handled close to where they happened. In practice they were declared and passed on.
  • Spring era: Spring's DataAccessException, an unchecked hierarchy that translated SQLException into meanings such as DuplicateKeyException. Most Java code since has followed it, and the hierarchy is still current.
public void pay(String claimId) throws RemoteException, SQLException, NamingException {
    try {
        ledger.reserve(claimId);
    } catch (SQLException e) {
        e.printStackTrace();
        throw new EJBException(e);
    }
}

Recognise it by. throws Exception on interfaces, javax.ejb.EJBException, e.printStackTrace(), org.springframework.dao.DataAccessException, org.springframework.core.NestedRuntimeException.

The rookie version.

try {
    ledgerClient.reserve(payout);
} catch (Exception e) {
    log.error("Ledger reserve failed: " + e.getMessage());
    throw new PayoutException("Ledger reserve failed: " + e.getMessage());
}

What goes wrong. The new exception keeps the message and drops the original, its type and its stack trace. catch (Exception e) also catches the service's own bugs. One night the logs filled with 3,000 lines of Ledger reserve failed: null. The ledger was healthy. The real exception was a NullPointerException from an Objects.requireNonNull call with no message, in Payouts' own request mapping, and the code had thrown away the stack trace that pointed at it. The same failure was also logged twice, once here and once by the handler above (12.05).

Do this now.

  1. Define a few unchecked exceptions that say what happened. Keep business refusals, such as PayoutRejected, apart from technical failures, such as LedgerUnavailable (6.04).
  2. Translate at the boundary. LedgerClient turns the HTTP client's failures into its own type. Where there is an original exception, it passes it on as the cause, the constructor argument super(message, cause) receives. The stack trace then shows both.
  3. Catch the narrowest type you can do something about. Let everything else reach one handler (6.03).
  4. Log or rethrow, not both.
  5. If you catch InterruptedException, restore the flag with Thread.currentThread().interrupt() before you throw.
  6. Wrap an IOException you cannot handle in UncheckedIOException, keeping the cause.
public final class LedgerUnavailable extends RuntimeException {
    public LedgerUnavailable(int status) { super("ledger answered " + status); }
    public LedgerUnavailable(Throwable cause) { super("ledger unreachable", cause); }
}
public Reservation reserve(ReserveRequest request) {
    try {
        return restClient.post().uri("/reservations").body(request).retrieve()
                .onStatus(HttpStatusCode::is5xxServerError, (req, res) -> {
                    throw new LedgerUnavailable(res.getStatusCode().value());
                })
                .body(Reservation.class);
    } catch (ResourceAccessException e) {          // timeout or refused connection
        throw new LedgerUnavailable(e);
    }
}

restClient is Spring's RestClient, built once in the client's constructor from the builder Boot provides (7.01). onStatus turns a 5xx answer into LedgerUnavailable. ResourceAccessException is what RestClient throws when no answer came at all. The full status mapping, 409 refusals included, is in 6.09.

Also seen. A sealed result type (2.12) for expected outcomes, such as a bank rejection, so the caller must handle each one. Vavr's Try, in code that adopted functional style.

When to break it. The top of an SQS listener may catch Exception, because a message must be acknowledged, retried or dead-lettered whatever went wrong (6.11). Do that in exactly one place. A checked exception is still right in a library API whose callers must decide what to do, such as a parser. The cost is noise at every call site.

.NET anchor. .NET has only unchecked exceptions, so Java's checked ones are the new idea. The cause is .NET's InnerException. Java records the stack trace when the exception is created, so throw e; keeps the original trace. There is no equivalent of C#'s throw ex; mistake.

See also. 2.10, 2.12, 6.03, 6.04, 6.09, 7.01, 12.05, Exceptions and resources

2.10 Close resources reliably

Then.

  • J2EE era: try and finally, with a null check and a second try inside the finally, because close() can throw too. It was correct, and nobody wrote it the same way twice.
  • Spring era: Commons IO's IOUtils.closeQuietly, deprecated for several releases because it hid failures, then restored, and Spring's templates, such as JdbcTemplate, which open and close for you. The templates are still current.
InputStream in = null;
try {
    in = new FileInputStream(file);
    return parse(in);
} finally {
    if (in != null) try { in.close(); } catch (IOException ignored) { }
}

Recognise it by. finally { if (x != null) x.close(); }, org.apache.commons.io.IOUtils.closeQuietly, catch (IOException ignored).

The rookie version.

long failed = Files.lines(Path.of("/data/payouts-2026-10-23.csv"))
        .filter(line -> line.contains(",FAILED,"))
        .count();

What goes wrong. Files.lines returns a stream backed by an open file. The stream is not closed when it finishes, and the garbage collector does not close it at any predictable time. The reconciliation job read 300 bank files a night in one pod. It ran for weeks without trouble, then failed with "Too many open files" on the first night the bank sent more files than usual. The same shape leaks with Files.list, Files.walk, S3 object streams and database cursors. A cursor left open also holds resources on the database server.

Do this now.

  1. If you opened something that implements AutoCloseable, close it with try-with-resources: declare it in the parentheses after try, and Java closes it when the block exits, normally or by exception.
  2. Declare several resources in one header. They close in reverse order.
  3. If the block throws and close() throws too, the block's exception propagates and the close failure is attached to it. getSuppressed() returns it, so neither is lost.
  4. Know who owns what. A bean is an object that Spring creates, hands to the classes that need it, and closes at shutdown (4.01). Beans such as MongoClient belong to Spring. Never close an injected bean. A stream over an in-memory collection needs no closing. A stream from Files does.
try (Stream<String> lines = Files.lines(report)) {
    return lines.filter(line -> line.contains(",FAILED,")).count();
}

try (var in = s3.getObject(request);
     var reader = new BufferedReader(new InputStreamReader(in, StandardCharsets.UTF_8))) {
    return reader.lines().map(BankFileLine::parse).toList();
}

Here s3 is the AWS SDK v2 S3Client, injected as a bean. Its getObject returns an open stream over the object's bytes, which you must close.

Also seen. MongoTemplate and JdbcTemplate callbacks, which manage the cursor or connection for you. java.lang.ref.Cleaner, for native resources in library code. Application code rarely needs it.

When to break it. A resource meant to live as long as the application, such as a client or a connection pool, should not sit in a try block. Make it a bean, and Spring closes it at shutdown. The cost of forgetting to make it a bean is a leak on every restart of the context, which tests notice first.

.NET anchor. Try-with-resources is the using statement, and AutoCloseable is IDisposable. Java has no using var declaration that lasts to the end of the scope, so there is always a block. When both the body and Dispose throw in C#, the body's exception is lost. Java keeps it and attaches the other as suppressed.

See also. 2.09, 4.01, 18.06, Exceptions and resources, Files and I/O

2.11 Compare strings and boxed numbers correctly

What goes wrong. if (currency == "GBP") passed every unit test and failed on a currency parsed from JSON. Long ids compared with == worked for the test data, ids 1 to 50, and failed for production ids. Both are one rule: == on objects compares references, and the tests happened to share objects. The week-one gotchas shows why literals and small boxed values are shared, and why unboxing a null throws.

Do this now. Compare objects with equals. Put the constant first, as in "GBP".equals(code), or use Objects.equals(a, b) when either side may be null. Use equalsIgnoreCase for case-insensitive checks, never toUpperCase and ==. Use primitive long and int for values that are always present, and compare those with ==. Use Long.compare in comparators.

.NET anchor. C# overloads == for string, so it compares values. Java has no operator overloading, and == on any object compares references.

See also. 2.04, The week-one gotchas, Equality, hashing and comparison

2.12 Model a closed set of outcomes with sealed types and pattern matching

Then.

  • Spring era: a result class with boolean flags and fields that are set only in some cases, or an exception for every outcome that is not success. Closed hierarchies used the visitor pattern, which was the only way to make the compiler check every case.
  • Boot era: instanceof chains with a cast on the next line, and switch over an enum with a default that throws.
public class BankResult {
    private boolean success;
    private String reference;        // set when success
    private String errorCode;        // set when not
    private boolean pending;         // added later, checked by some callers
}
if (result instanceof Accepted) { Accepted a = (Accepted) result; ... }

Recognise it by. boolean flags beside nullable fields, accept(Visitor v) methods, instanceof X followed by (X), and default: throw new IllegalStateException().

The rookie version.

String describe(BankOutcome outcome) {
    return switch (outcome) {
        case Accepted a -> "paid " + a.bankReference();
        case Rejected r -> "rejected " + r.code();
        default -> "unknown";                 // hides the next new case
    };
}

What goes wrong. A sealed interface lists every type allowed to implement it, so the compiler knows the full set. A switch over it with no default must handle every type, or it does not compile. The default above throws that check away. When the bank added a fourth outcome, Returned, for money sent back after 3 days, the compiler said nothing. Returned payouts were reported as "unknown". Over a month, 14 of them never reached the claimant notification queue, and claimants waited for money that had come back.

Do this now.

  1. Declare the outcomes as a sealed interface with one record per case. Records nested inside the interface are permitted without a permits clause.
  2. Switch over it with a pattern for each case and no default. Adding a case then breaks every switch that must decide what to do with it, which is what you want.
  3. Deconstruct records in the pattern, as in case Accepted(var ref), and add a condition with when.
  4. Use an enum instead when the cases carry no data (2.13).
  5. Keep exceptions for the unexpected (2.09). Use a sealed result for outcomes the caller is expected to handle.

Sealed types arrived in Java 17, and pattern matching for switch and record patterns in Java 21.

public sealed interface BankOutcome {
    record Accepted(String bankReference) implements BankOutcome {}
    record Rejected(String code, boolean retryable) implements BankOutcome {}
    record Pending(Instant checkAgainAt) implements BankOutcome {}
}

SagaStep next(BankOutcome outcome) {
    return switch (outcome) {
        case Accepted(var ref) -> SagaStep.recordInstruction(ref);
        case Rejected r when r.retryable() -> SagaStep.retryLater(r.code());
        case Rejected r -> SagaStep.compensate(r.code());
        case Pending(var at) -> SagaStep.waitUntil(at);
    };
}

Also seen. The visitor pattern, in older code that wanted the same guarantee. An enum with behaviour (2.13), when the cases carry no data.

When to break it. An open set, such as a plug-in point other teams extend from their own code, cannot be sealed. A sealed type also needs care at the edge of the service. Jackson, the JSON library Spring Boot uses, deserialises a hierarchy only with type information, such as @JsonTypeInfo and @JsonSubTypes, and the JSON then carries a type field that is part of your contract.

.NET anchor. C# switch expressions with type patterns read almost the same. Up to C# 14, the compiler cannot know every subtype of an ordinary class hierarchy, so you end with a _ arm. C# 15, which ships with .NET 11, adds closed classes, the nearest match to a sealed interface, and union types, and both let the compiler check a switch without one. Java has had the check since Java 21. F#'s discriminated unions are the older match.

See also. 2.09, 2.13, 6.04, 11.02, Sealed types and pattern matching, Switch expressions and statements

2.13 Give an enum behaviour

What goes wrong. Status rules end up as if chains spread across PayoutService, the saga and a listener. One chain allowed FAILED to move to PAID on a late retry, and a payout of £1,240.50 was paid after it had been compensated. A second trap is storing ordinal(), the constant's position. Inserting a new status in the middle renumbers every stored document. Inherited JPA code does this by default: JPA stores an enum by ordinal unless the field says @Enumerated(EnumType.STRING).

Do this now. A Java enum is a class with a fixed set of instances, so it can carry fields and methods. Put the rule on the enum, in one switch the compiler checks for completeness. Use EnumSet and EnumMap for sets and maps of statuses. Store the name, never the ordinal.

public enum PayoutStatus {
    PENDING, RESERVED, INSTRUCTED, PAID, FAILED, CANCELLED;

    public boolean canMoveTo(PayoutStatus next) {
        return switch (this) {
            case PENDING -> next == RESERVED || next == FAILED || next == CANCELLED;
            case RESERVED -> next == INSTRUCTED || next == FAILED || next == CANCELLED;
            case INSTRUCTED -> next == PAID || next == FAILED;     // past the pivot: no cancel
            case PAID, FAILED, CANCELLED -> false;
        };
    }
}

.NET anchor. A C# enum is a named integer and cannot have methods, only extension methods. A Java enum is a full class. EF Core stores an enum as its integer by default, which is safe in C# because you can pin each number. A Java ordinal is only a position, and nothing pins it.

See also. 2.12, 11.02, Enums

2.14 Build strings and use text blocks

What goes wrong. Building the 4,000-line bank file with += in a loop copies the whole string on every pass, so the time grows with the square of the length. A second trap is locale. String.format("%,.2f", amount) uses the JVM's default locale, and a pod with a different default wrote 1.240,50 into a file the bank parsed as English. Java has no string interpolation, and string templates were withdrawn after two previews.

Do this now. Use StringBuilder in loops, and Collectors.joining or String.join for lists. Use "...".formatted(...) for templates. It always uses the default locale, so format numbers for a machine with String.format(Locale.ROOT, ...). Write multi-line text, such as test JSON, as a text block: three quotes, a line break, the text. Java removes the indentation common to every line, counting the closing quotes when they sit on a line of their own, so their position sets the margin. Use BigDecimal.toPlainString(), which never switches to scientific notation.

String body = """
        {
          "claimId": "%s",
          "amount": { "value": "%s", "currency": "GBP" }
        }
        """.formatted(claimId, amount.toPlainString());
String file = lines.stream().map(BankLine::render).collect(Collectors.joining("\n"));

.NET anchor. There is no $"...". Text blocks resemble C# 11 raw string literals, but a text block still reads escapes such as \n, so a backslash in a regex must be doubled.

See also. 2.10, 5.13, 16.17, var, strings and text blocks

2.15 Format and parse dates without SimpleDateFormat

Then.

  • J2EE era: SimpleDateFormat, often in a static final field so it was built once. Before java.time it was the only formatter in the JDK.
private static final SimpleDateFormat FMT = new SimpleDateFormat("dd/MM/yyyy");

Recognise it by. java.text.SimpleDateFormat, java.text.DateFormat, and ThreadLocal<SimpleDateFormat>, the old workaround.

What goes wrong. SimpleDateFormat keeps state while it works, so a shared one is not thread-safe. Under load, two request threads interleave and parse each other's digits. Payouts saw due dates moved by months and an occasional NumberFormatException. A second trap survives into java.time: the pattern YYYY means the week-based year, so in the last days of December it prints next year's number.

Do this now. Use DateTimeFormatter. It is immutable and safe to share as a constant. Use the ISO forms, Instant.parse and LocalDate.parse, for anything a machine reads. Give a formatter for people an explicit Locale and zone. Use uuuu or yyyy for the year. A bad input throws DateTimeParseException.

private static final DateTimeFormatter STATEMENT = DateTimeFormatter
        .ofPattern("d MMM uuuu, HH:mm", Locale.UK).withZone(ZoneId.of("Europe/London"));

String shown = STATEMENT.format(payout.paidAt());        // 24 Oct 2026, 14:05
Instant parsed = Instant.parse("2026-10-24T13:05:00Z");

See also. 2.02, 5.13, Numbers, money and time

2.16 Inject a Clock so time can be tested

Then.

  • Spring era: new Date() and System.currentTimeMillis() wherever the code needed the time. Tests that used Joda-Time froze it with DateTimeUtils.setCurrentMillisFixed, a global switch that had to be undone after every test.
  • Boot era: PowerMock, which rewrote classes so a test could replace static methods such as LocalDate.now(). It worked, and it was slow and fragile. Teams that disliked both wrote their own TimeProvider interface, which was the right idea.
@Before
public void freezeTime() {
    DateTimeUtils.setCurrentMillisFixed(1477958400000L);    // 1 November 2016
}
@After
public void unfreeze() { DateTimeUtils.setCurrentMillisSystem(); }

Recognise it by. org.joda.time.DateTimeUtils, setCurrentMillisFixed, org.powermock, @PrepareForTest, a home-grown TimeProvider or SystemClock interface, and Thread.sleep inside tests.

The rookie version.

public boolean isOverdue(Payout payout) {
    return Instant.now().isAfter(payout.requestedAt().plus(Duration.ofHours(48)));
}

@Test
void overdueAfterTwoDays() {
    var payout = payoutRequestedAt(Instant.now().minus(Duration.ofHours(48)).minusSeconds(1));
    assertTrue(service.isOverdue(payout));
}

What goes wrong. The method reads the real clock, so the test must be built around the real clock. It cannot test the boundary exactly, because time moves between the two calls. It cannot test a clock change, a month end or a leap day at all. Payouts' overdue alert counted working days with LocalDate.now(), which reads the pod's zone, UTC. All summer, between midnight and 01:00 London time, it still thought it was the day before, so payouts requested in that hour were given an extra day. Nobody could write a test that showed it, and 23 overdue payouts went unflagged until the claimants phoned.

Do this now.

  1. java.time.Clock is an abstract class that supplies the current instant and a zone. Every now() method in java.time has an overload that takes one: Instant.now(clock), LocalDate.now(clock).
  2. Declare one Clock bean, Clock.systemUTC(), from a @Bean method in a @Configuration class. Spring registers what the method returns as a bean (4.05).
  3. Inject it through the constructor into each class that asks the time (4.01). @Service marks a class that Spring finds and creates as a bean. For a calendar rule, convert to London first, as in Instant.now(clock).atZone(LONDON).toLocalDate() (2.02), because this clock's zone is UTC.
  4. In a unit test, pass Clock.fixed(instant, ZoneOffset.UTC). For time that moves, build a new clock with Clock.offset(base, duration), or write a small mutable test clock that extends Clock.
  5. In a Spring test, supply a fixed clock from a @TestConfiguration, a configuration class that only tests load. Mark it @Primary, which tells Spring to inject it wherever both clocks qualify (4.06).
  6. If a class needs only instants and no zone, depend on java.time.InstantSource, which Clock implements.
@Configuration
class TimeConfig {
    @Bean Clock clock() { return Clock.systemUTC(); }
}

@Service
class PayoutDeadlines {
    private final Clock clock;
    PayoutDeadlines(Clock clock) { this.clock = clock; }

    boolean isOverdue(Payout p) {
        return Instant.now(clock).isAfter(p.requestedAt().plus(Duration.ofHours(48)));
    }
}

var requested = Instant.parse("2026-10-24T09:00:00Z");
var clock = Clock.fixed(requested.plus(Duration.ofHours(48)).plusSeconds(1), ZoneOffset.UTC);
assertTrue(new PayoutDeadlines(clock).isOverdue(payoutRequestedAt(requested)));

Also seen. Mockito's mockStatic(Instant.class). It works inside a try-with-resources block and is fragile, because it relies on which static method the code happens to call. A TimeProvider interface in older services. It does the same job as Clock, so leave it until the code is touched for another reason.

When to break it. Logging and metrics take their own timestamps, and threading a Clock into them adds nothing. A one-off script can call Instant.now(). The cost appears only when someone later wants to test it.

.NET anchor. Clock is .NET 8's TimeProvider, and Clock.fixed plays the part of FakeTimeProvider. ISystemClock was the older .NET pattern. Java's Clock has no timers, so a scheduled task still needs its own seam.

See also. 2.02, 4.01, 4.05, 4.06, 16.13, Numbers, money and time

2.17 Generate identifiers

What goes wrong. A System.currentTimeMillis() id works on one laptop. Payouts runs as 2 pods, and two requests in the same millisecond on different pods got the same id. The second document overwrote the first, and one claimant's payout disappeared until the ledger reconciliation found it. A counter kept in one database document makes every insert wait on it.

Do this now. Let the database assign a document's id where it can: Payout's String id is filled with an ObjectId on insert (8.01). For ids the service creates, such as the saga's idempotency keys (11.02), use UUID.randomUUID(), which gives a random version 4 UUID. Store it in one form everywhere. Wrap an id in a record, such as ClaimId (8.18), so a claim id cannot be passed where a payout id is expected. If index locality matters, use time-ordered version 7 UUIDs, from Java UUID Generator's Generators.timeBasedEpochGenerator() on Java 25 or from UUID.ofEpochMillis once the service runs on JDK 26 or later. Never use the client's Idempotency-Key as the payout's id (9.10). Use SecureRandom for anything a caller must not guess.

.NET anchor. UUID.randomUUID() is Guid.NewGuid(). Recent .NET has Guid.CreateVersion7().

See also. 2.03, 8.01, 8.16, 8.18, 9.10, 11.02

2.18 Avoid integer overflow in counters and amounts

What goes wrong. An int holds values up to about 2.1 billion, and Java arithmetic wraps silently when it passes that. Payouts' annual report summed amounts in pence into an int. The year's total was £25 million, which is 2,500,000,000 pence. The sum wrapped to −1,794,967,296 pence, and the report showed −£17,949,672.96. Nothing threw. The same happens to an int of milliseconds after about 24 days.

Do this now. Use long for counts, pence and durations in milliseconds, and BigDecimal for money (2.01). Where overflow would be a bug, use Math.addExact, Math.multiplyExact and Math.toIntExact, which throw ArithmeticException instead of wrapping. Use Duration rather than raw numbers for time. For counters shared between threads, use AtomicLong or LongAdder (3.07).

.NET anchor. C# has checked blocks that throw OverflowException. Java has no such keyword, only the Math.*Exact methods.

See also. 2.01, 3.07, Numbers, money and time

2.19 Read code written for older Java versions

Then.

  • J2EE era: raw collections such as List with no type parameter, Vector, Hashtable, StringBuffer and Enumeration. Generics did not exist yet, and synchronised classes were the safe default.
  • Spring era: anonymous inner classes for every callback, Date and Calendar, explicit Iterator loops, and Guava for what the JDK lacked, such as Optional, Function and Preconditions.
  • Boot era: lambdas and streams, but JavaBeans with getters and setters, Lombok, javax.* imports and instanceof followed by a cast.
Collections.sort(payouts, new Comparator<Payout>() {
    @Override
    public int compare(Payout a, Payout b) {
        return a.getRequestedAt().compareTo(b.getRequestedAt());
    }
});
StringBuffer line = new StringBuffer();
Preconditions.checkNotNull(claimId, "claimId");

Recognise it by. new Comparator<...>() {, StringBuffer, java.util.Vector, com.google.common.base.Preconditions, @SuppressWarnings("unchecked"), <maven.compiler.source>1.8</maven.compiler.source>.

The rookie version.

PR #412  Fix rounding in fee calculation
  47 files changed, 1,903 insertions(+), 2,118 deletions(-)
  - Converted beans to records
  - Replaced anonymous classes with lambdas
  - Replaced Date with Instant
  - Fixed fee rounding (FeeCalculator.java, line 88)

What goes wrong. The fix is one line, and it is buried in 47 files of modernisation. The reviewer cannot read 4,021 changed lines, so they skim and approve. Replacing Date with Instant changed how paidAt was written to JSON. The notification service could not parse the new format, and 2,300 PayoutCompleted events went to its dead-letter queue over a weekend. When the bug was found, the fee fix could not be reverted without reverting everything else.

Do this now.

  1. Find the language level. Read maven.compiler.release or maven.compiler.source in the POM, Maven's pom.xml build file (1.08), and check which JDK the image runs. Code compiled for Java 8 often runs on 25 unchanged.
  2. Read the file by era, with the table below. Old idioms are not bugs, and most can stay.
  3. Modernise in a separate pull request, with no behaviour change, and tests green before and after. Use OpenRewrite, a tool that applies scripted refactorings called recipes, or IntelliJ's inspections for the mechanical part (19.03).
  4. Change a public contract last, and on purpose: JSON shapes, stored documents, event payloads.
  5. Know which rewrites are not neutral. In an anonymous class this is the anonymous object, and in a lambda it is the enclosing one. Vector to ArrayList drops synchronisation. Date to Instant changes serialisation.
You see Today
new Comparator<Payout>() { ... } Comparator.comparing(Payout::requestedAt)
StringBuffer StringBuilder, unless threads share it
Vector, Hashtable ArrayList, HashMap, or ConcurrentHashMap if shared
Date, Calendar, Joda-Time Instant, LocalDate (JDK 8, 2014)
Guava Optional, Function java.util.Optional, java.util.function
JavaBean or Lombok @Value a record (Java 16)
visitor, instanceof and cast sealed types (17), pattern switch (21)
list.get(list.size() - 1) list.getLast() (21)

Also seen. Leaving untouched code untouched. A file that works and nobody changes earns nothing from modernising. Tidying only the method you are already changing is a reasonable middle way.

When to break it. Sometimes the old idiom is the bug. A shared SimpleDateFormat (2.15) is fixed by replacing it, so the replacement belongs in the fix. Keep that change as small as the bug, and say so in the description.

.NET anchor. This is reading C# 2 code: ArrayList, anonymous delegate methods, no LINQ and no var. OpenRewrite plays the part of Roslyn code fixes and dotnet format. Java removes old APIs more rarely than .NET does, so Vector still compiles.

See also. 1.08, 19.03, 19.05, The Yard, chapter 1, Appendix C: The Java you'll inherit, Appendix A: Java 9 to 25

2.20 Use var without hiding meaning

What goes wrong. var declares a local variable whose type the compiler infers from the right-hand side. In a pull request on the web, there is no IDE to show that type. var result = ledgerClient.reserve(payout); hides whether result is a reservation, an Optional or a status code. var amount = 1240.50; is a double. var ids = new ArrayList<>(); is an ArrayList<Object>, because the empty diamond has nothing to infer from.

Do this now. Use var when the type is visible on the same line, as in var payout = new Payout(...) or var clock = Clock.fixed(...). It also suits loop variables and try-with-resources headers. Write the type when the right-hand side is a method call whose return type matters to the reader. var works only for local variables and lambda parameters, so fields, method parameters and return types always say their type. Agree the rule once as a team, and let review enforce it.

.NET anchor. It is C#'s var, with the same trade-off. Java has no target-typed new().

See also. 2.19, var, strings and text blocks

⚠Review checklist
  • If you see double amounts, or new BigDecimal(someDouble): pennies are lost or invented in arithmetic. See 2.01.
  • If you see equals between two BigDecimal amounts: 1240.5 and 1240.50 are not equal. See 2.01.
  • If you see LocalDateTime.now() or a LocalDateTime field for something that happened: the value depends on the pod's zone. See 2.02.
  • If you see a record with a List or Map component and no copyOf in its constructor: the value can change under its owner. See 2.03.
  • If you see equals(Payout other) without @Override, or equals without hashCode: hash collections keep duplicates. See 2.04.
  • If you see Optional.get(), an Optional field, or a method returning Optional that also returns null: absence is unhandled again. See 2.05.
  • If you see null checks that return null deep in the domain: a missing value turns into a silent decision. See 2.06.
  • If you see a getter returning an internal ArrayList, or Arrays.asList followed by add: shared mutation or a run-time exception. See 2.07.
  • If you see forEach adding to an outside collection, or parallelStream with shared state: results are lost without an error. See 2.08.
  • If you see catch (Exception e) that rethrows with e.getMessage() only: the cause and its stack trace are gone. See 2.09.
  • If you see Files.lines, Files.list or an S3 stream outside try-with-resources: file handles leak until the pod fails. See 2.10.
  • If you see == between strings or boxed numbers: it passes tests and fails on real data. See 2.11.
  • If you see default in a switch over a sealed type: the compiler can no longer flag a new case. See 2.12.
  • If you see status transitions in if chains, or an enum stored by ordinal(): rules drift and stored data renumbers. See 2.13.
  • If you see += on a string in a loop, or String.format without a locale for machine output: slow builds and unparseable files. See 2.14.
  • If you see SimpleDateFormat in a field, or YYYY in a pattern: garbled dates under load and wrong years in December. See 2.15.
  • If you see Instant.now() or LocalDate.now() without a clock in a service: the rule cannot be tested. See 2.16.
  • If you see a timestamp or a random int used as an id: two pods produce the same id. See 2.17.
  • If you see an int summing pence or milliseconds: it wraps silently to a negative number. See 2.18.
  • If you see a fix and a modernisation in the same pull request: the fix cannot be reviewed or reverted alone. See 2.19.
  • If you see var with an empty diamond, or on a method call whose type matters: the reader cannot tell what the variable is. See 2.20.

Part IV · The how-to3. Concurrency#

Payouts serves many requests at once, and each one waits on the ledger, the bank gateway and DocumentDB. This part shows how to do that waiting cheaply on virtual threads, how to make calls in parallel, and how to keep context, shared state and limits correct when work crosses threads. It also shows the thread pools, futures and locks you will find in older code, and what replaced them.

★What a veteran knows
  • A Spring bean, an object Spring creates once and injects wherever it is needed, is shared by every request at once, so a mutable field in a @Service is shared state whether anyone meant it or not.
  • Every concurrency limit in a service is per pod: 20 permits on 2 pods is 40 calls at the ledger.
  • Work handed to another thread leaves its logging context, its security identity and its transaction behind, unless something carries them across.
  • A queue of tasks in memory dies with the pod, so anything that must happen goes into DocumentDB or SQS first.
  • A thread pool was often the only limit a service had, and removing it for virtual threads removes the limit too.
  • Never hold a lock while you wait for the network.
◷How we got hereIn July 1998 Doug Lea, a computer scientist at SUNY Oswego, released a library called util.concurrent.

In July 1998 Doug Lea, a computer scientist at SUNY Oswego, released a library called util.concurrent. Java's own tools for threads were then synchronized, wait and notify, and every team wrote its own pool and its own queues. Lea's overview called his code "implementations of ideas that have been around for ages", "merely intended to save you the trouble of coding them". Teams used it outside the JDK for more than three years. In January 2002 a Java Specification Request, JSR 166, went to ballot with Lea as its lead, citing "Doug Lea's package" and the usage experience it had built up. The final release came on 30 September 2004, the day J2SE 5.0 shipped with java.util.concurrent inside it. Lea then told the users of his own package to "plan to convert your applications". The executors, atomics, locks and concurrent maps in this part are his work, standardised. When you meet EDU.oswego.cs.dl.util.concurrent in a very old codebase, that is where it came from.

3.01 Run blocking work on virtual threads

Then.

  • Spring era: a fixed pool of platform threads, sized by hand. A platform thread is a Java thread backed by one operating-system thread, with its own fixed-size stack. The pool size was the number of tasks that could wait at once.
ExecutorService pool = Executors.newFixedThreadPool(50);
Future<LedgerEntry> f = pool.submit(() -> ledgerClient.reserve(payout));
LedgerEntry entry = f.get(5, TimeUnit.SECONDS);
  • Boot era: server.tomcat.max-threads=200 in application.properties, later renamed server.tomcat.threads.max. The number was chosen when every waiting request held a whole operating-system thread.
  • Boot era: a move to WebFlux, Spring's reactive web stack, and Reactor, the library behind its Mono and Flux types, so that a few threads never block. It was the right answer when threads were expensive and every library in the path could be reactive.

Recognise it by. Executors.newFixedThreadPool, ThreadPoolTaskExecutor beans with a hand-picked maxPoolSize, server.tomcat.max-threads or server.tomcat.threads.max, and Mono or Flux return types on code that calls a blocking client.

The rookie version.

@Bean
ExecutorService ledgerExecutor() {
    // "virtual threads are cheap, so pool 200 of them"
    return Executors.newFixedThreadPool(200, Thread.ofVirtual().factory());
}

What goes wrong. A virtual thread is cheap to create and meant to be thrown away after one task. Pooling them brings back the ceiling the pool was meant to remove. When the ledger stalls for 2 seconds, the 200 threads fill, and task 201 waits in the pool's queue. A fixed pool's queue has no bound, so it grows for as long as the ledger is slow. The service has the old ceiling of 200 threads with a modern name on it. If the 200 was meant as a limit on ledger calls, it is the wrong tool. It limits threads, not calls, and it hides the limit inside an executor nobody reads.

Do this now.

  1. Set spring.threads.virtual.enabled=true in application.properties. It defaults to false. With it on, the web server runs each request on a new virtual thread: a thread the JVM schedules itself, which hands back its underlying carrier thread while it waits. Boot's own task executor switches to virtual threads too.
  2. Keep the code blocking. The MongoDB driver, RestClient and the AWS SDK's synchronous clients all block, and blocking is what virtual threads are for.
  3. For work the service starts itself, create one virtual thread per task and let it end. Catch each task's failure inside the task, because nobody reads the Future that submit returns.
  4. Put the limit where it belongs, on the call to the downstream service (3.09).
  5. Check it once, in a test or a log line, with Thread.currentThread().isVirtual().
ThreadFactory named = Thread.ofVirtual().name("reconcile-", 0).factory();
Semaphore inFlight = new Semaphore(10);               // at most 10 at the ledger

try (ExecutorService exec = Executors.newThreadPerTaskExecutor(named)) {
    for (Payout p : batch) {
        exec.submit(() -> {
            inFlight.acquireUninterruptibly();
            try { payoutService.reconcile(p); }
            catch (RuntimeException e) { log.error("reconcile failed: {}", p.id(), e); }
            finally { inFlight.release(); }
        });
    }
}   // close() waits for every task to finish

The name prefix makes a thread dump readable. Executors.newVirtualThreadPerTaskExecutor() does the same without names. Without the catch, one payout that throws is lost silently, and the rest of the batch carries on as if nothing happened. Without the semaphore, a batch of 5,000 payouts starts 5,000 ledger calls at once. In a batch, waiting for a permit is what you want, so acquire has no timeout here. A request should not wait like that (3.09).

Two habits change. Stop caching expensive objects in a ThreadLocal, a variable that holds one value per thread. There is now one thread per task, so the cache is never reused. And keep CPU-heavy work off virtual threads. A virtual thread that never waits never hands its carrier back.

Also seen. WebFlux, for a service that streams to many open connections and needs back-pressure. Thread.startVirtualThread(runnable) for a single task that needs no executor.

When to break it. A batch job that only calculates, such as hashing 40,000 bank statements, belongs on a fixed pool sized to the pod's CPUs. Virtual threads give it nothing, and the bounded pool stops it starving the request threads.

.NET anchor. The nearest thing is async and await over the .NET thread pool, where the thread is released while I/O waits. The difference is that Java needs no async keyword and no Task return type. The blocking code stays as it is, and the JVM does the releasing.

See also. 3.02, 3.09, 13.07, 18.05, The Yard, chapter 12, Threads are cheap now

3.02 Avoid pinning virtual threads

Then.

  • Modern: on Java 21 to 23, teams replaced synchronized with ReentrantLock around blocking calls. A virtual thread that waited inside synchronized was pinned: it could not hand back its carrier thread. The advice was right then. Java 24 removed nearly all of that pinning, so on Java 25 the rewrite buys nothing.
private final ReentrantLock lock = new ReentrantLock();   // was: synchronized

public Token token() {
    lock.lock();
    try { return refreshIfExpired(); } finally { lock.unlock(); }
}
  • Modern: the system property -Djdk.tracePinnedThreads=full in start-up scripts, which printed a stack trace when a virtual thread blocked while pinned on those versions. Java 24 removed the property, and setting it now does nothing.

Recognise it by. ReentrantLock fields with a comment about virtual threads or Loom, -Djdk.tracePinnedThreads in a Dockerfile or in JAVA_TOOL_OPTIONS, and upgrade notes that say "virtual-thread friendly".

The rookie version.

@Component
class BankTokenCache {
    private Token token;
    synchronized Token get() {
        if (token == null || token.expired()) {
            token = bankGatewayClient.fetchToken();   // 800 ms network call
        }
        return token;
    }
}

What goes wrong. Holding a lock while waiting on the network is wrong in any era. Every payout that needs a token queues behind the one that is fetching it. When the token endpoint takes 800 ms, every request on the pod waits up to 800 ms in a line. On Java 21 to 23 it was worse. Each queued virtual thread was pinned to a carrier, and the JVM keeps only a small, fixed set of carriers. A 2-core pod could stop answering anything, including its readiness probe. On Java 25 the pinning is gone, but the queue is not.

Do this now.

  1. Keep waits outside locks. Lock only to read or swap a value in memory, and make the network call with no lock held.
  2. Accept that two threads may occasionally fetch at the same moment. For a token, that is cheaper than a queue.
  3. Know the causes of pinning that remain on Java 25. The main one is a virtual thread waiting inside native code, reached through JNI, the Java Native Interface, or the foreign function API. Some compression, cryptography and driver libraries do that. The other is blocking while a class is being loaded or initialised, as in a static initialiser that makes a network call.
  4. Find pinning with Java Flight Recorder (JFR), the JDK's built-in recorder. Its jdk.VirtualThreadPinned event records the stack of a thread that blocked while pinned.
  5. When a library pins, move just that call to a small platform-thread executor, so it holds a platform thread instead of a carrier.
private final AtomicReference<Token> token = new AtomicReference<>();

Token get() {
    Token current = token.get();
    if (current != null && !current.expired()) return current;
    Token fresh = bankGatewayClient.fetchToken();   // no lock held
    token.set(fresh);
    return fresh;
}

# record 60 seconds under load, then print the pinned events
jcmd <pid> JFR.start duration=60s filename=/tmp/pin.jfr
jfr print --events jdk.VirtualThreadPinned /tmp/pin.jfr

Also seen. A ReentrantLock with tryLock and a timeout, when a lock around the wait cannot be avoided and callers should give up rather than queue (3.08). A cache with refresh ahead of expiry, for tokens and slow lookups (7.13).

When to break it. A lock around a short update in memory is cheap and correct, so keep synchronized there. A lock around a wait is acceptable when two fetches at once would do harm, such as a token endpoint that revokes the old token on every fetch. Then use tryLock with a timeout, and accept that callers queue for that one call.

.NET anchor. C# refuses to compile an await inside a lock block, which steers you away from this mistake. Java allows a blocking call inside synchronized, so the rule has to be a habit. Native pinning resembles a P/Invoke call that blocks a thread-pool thread.

See also. 3.01, 3.08, 18.07, The Yard, chapter 12, Threads are cheap now, Locks, atomics and the memory model

3.03 Make several calls in parallel and wait for all of them

Then.

  • Spring era: a Future, the result of a task on an ExecutorService, collected with a blocking get and a timeout on each one.
Future<Policy> policy = pool.submit(() -> policyClient.find(claim.policyId()));
Future<Balance> balance = pool.submit(() -> ledgerClient.balance(claim.claimantId()));
return decide(policy.get(2, SECONDS), balance.get(2, SECONDS));
  • Boot era: @Async methods returning Spring's ListenableFuture, and AsyncRestTemplate for HTTP. CompletableFuture and WebClient replaced them, and ListenableFuture is gone in Boot 4.
  • Boot era: Mono.zip over two WebClient calls in a reactive service, or Observable.zip with RxJava.

Recognise it by. java.util.concurrent.Future, ListenableFuture, AsyncRestTemplate, AsyncResult, Mono.zip, and io.reactivex imports.

The rookie version.

List<Decision> decisions = claims.parallelStream()
        .map(c -> decide(policyClient.find(c.policyId()),
                         ledgerClient.balance(c.claimantId())))
        .toList();

What goes wrong. parallelStream() runs on the common pool, one ForkJoinPool shared by the whole JVM and sized for calculation, not for waiting. So does CompletableFuture.supplyAsync when no executor is passed, on a pod with more than 2 CPUs. On a 2-core pod the common pool has 1 thread, and supplyAsync starts a new platform thread for every task instead. Twelve claims, each waiting 700 ms on two services, go through a few at a time. Every other user of the common pool in the JVM waits behind them. The calls inside each claim still run one after the other. And if one claim's call fails, the stream throws, but the calls already running for other claims carry on.

Do this now.

  1. Start each call as its own task on an executor you own. A virtual-thread executor makes the waiting free.
  2. Wait for the group with CompletableFuture.allOf. It completes when every call has finished, and fails if any of them failed.
  3. Put one deadline on the group with orTimeout, so a slow call cannot hold the request past its budget.
  4. Read each result with join, and unwrap the CompletionException it throws to reach the real cause (3.06).
  5. Give every client its own timeout as well (7.03). Cancelling a CompletableFuture does not stop the call that is running inside it.
// callExecutor: a SimpleAsyncTaskExecutor bean on virtual threads (see below)
var policy = CompletableFuture.supplyAsync(
        () -> policyClient.find(claim.policyId()), callExecutor);
var balance = CompletableFuture.supplyAsync(
        () -> ledgerClient.balance(claim.claimantId()), callExecutor);

CompletableFuture.allOf(policy, balance)
        .orTimeout(2, TimeUnit.SECONDS)
        .join();             // throws CompletionException on failure or timeout

return decide(policy.join(), balance.join());

With the policy call at 300 ms and the balance at 400 ms, the request now spends about 400 ms waiting instead of 700 ms. Make the executor a Spring bean rather than a try-with-resources block in the method. Closing an executor waits for its tasks, so a timed-out call would hold the request anyway. Build it as new SimpleAsyncTaskExecutor("call-") with setVirtualThreads(true) and setTaskDecorator(...), so the MDC and the trace travel with each call (3.04, 13.07). A bare Executors.newVirtualThreadPerTaskExecutor() carries neither.

Also seen. StructuredTaskScope, from structured concurrency, which keeps the calls inside one block and cancels the others when one fails. It is a preview API in Java 25 and needs --enable-preview, so keep it out of production code until it is final. ExecutorService.invokeAll with a timeout, for a list of tasks of one type. Mono.zip in a service that is already reactive.

When to break it. Two calls of 20 ms each are not worth the thread hop, the extra error handling and the harder stack trace. Parallelise when the saving is measured and real. Calls that need each other's results stay in sequence.

.NET anchor. This is Task.WhenAll followed by WaitAsync(timeout). The difference is cancellation. .NET passes a CancellationToken into each call. Java's CompletableFuture.cancel does not stop the running call, so the client's own timeout does that job.

See also. 3.01, 3.06, 7.03, 7.15, CompletableFuture and Task, Structured concurrency and cancellation

3.04 Pass request context across threads

Then.

  • Spring era: InheritableThreadLocal, or Spring Security's inheritable mode. A new thread copied its parent's values when it was created. That worked for a thread per task. With pools it gave wrong answers, because pool threads are created once and then reused by other requests.
SecurityContextHolder.setStrategyName(
        SecurityContextHolder.MODE_INHERITABLETHREADLOCAL);
  • Boot era: Spring Cloud Sleuth wrapped executors so that trace IDs crossed threads, with classes such as LazyTraceExecutor. Sleuth does not work with Boot 3, and its core moved to Micrometer Tracing.
  • Boot era: MDC copied by hand at each submit, with MDC.getCopyOfContextMap() before and MDC.setContextMap inside the task.

Recognise it by. InheritableThreadLocal, MODE_INHERITABLETHREADLOCAL, org.springframework.cloud.sleuth.instrument.async, DelegatingSecurityContextRunnable, and MDC.getCopyOfContextMap scattered through service code.

The rookie version.

public void approve(Payout payout) {
    payoutRepository.save(payout.approved());
    CompletableFuture.runAsync(() -> {
        String who = SecurityContextHolder.getContext()
                .getAuthentication().getName();     // runs on another thread
        auditLog.record(payout.id(), "APPROVED", who);
        log.info("audit written");                  // no payoutId in the MDC
    }, auditExecutor);
}

What goes wrong. Much of a request's context lives in ThreadLocals: the security context, the MDC (the Mapped Diagnostic Context, a map of values that the logger adds to every line written through SLF4J, the logging API most Java code calls), the trace and the transaction. The task above runs on a thread from auditExecutor, which has none of them. getAuthentication() returns null, and the task dies with a NullPointerException. The approval of a payout of £1,240.50 is saved with no audit record. The log line has no payoutId and no trace ID, so nobody can connect it to the request. On a reused pool thread it can be worse than empty. If an earlier task set the MDC and never cleared it, this line carries another payout's ID.

Do this now.

  1. Capture what the task needs as plain values on the request thread, and pass them in. A String approvedBy parameter cannot go missing. This is the first choice.
  2. For context that every task needs, such as the MDC, decorate the executor once. A TaskDecorator is a Spring interface that wraps each Runnable at the moment it is submitted. It runs on the submitting thread, so it can capture there and restore on the worker.
  3. Restore inside a try, and in finally put back whatever the thread held before. A reused pool thread is left empty, and a request thread that runs the task itself (as CallerRunsPolicy does in 3.05) keeps its own values.
  4. For the trace, Spring's ContextPropagatingTaskDecorator uses the Micrometer context-propagation library to carry every registered ThreadLocal (13.07).
  5. Boot applies a TaskDecorator bean to the executor it configures. On Boot 3.5 it does so only when there is exactly one such bean, so declaring the MDC decorator and a ContextPropagatingTaskDecorator side by side silently applies neither. Declare one bean that combines them, new CompositeTaskDecorator(List.of(mdc, tracing)) from org.springframework.core.task.support, and keep the parts as plain objects rather than beans. In Boot 4 several beans are combined for you. An executor you build yourself needs setTaskDecorator.
@Bean
TaskDecorator mdcDecorator() {
    return task -> {
        Map<String, String> mdc = MDC.getCopyOfContextMap();   // on the caller
        return () -> {
            Map<String, String> before = MDC.getCopyOfContextMap();   // on the worker
            if (mdc != null) MDC.setContextMap(mdc); else MDC.clear();
            try { task.run(); }
            finally {
                if (before != null) MDC.setContextMap(before); else MDC.clear();
            }
        };
    };
}

Your own request values, such as the idempotency key, can use a scoped value. ScopedValue is final in Java 25. It is bound for the length of one call and cannot leak into the next task. It flows into structured-concurrency subtasks only, so for executors you still pass values or decorate.

Do not try to carry a transaction across. A @Transactional transaction belongs to one thread, and work on another thread runs outside it (9.01).

Also seen. Spring Security's DelegatingSecurityContextExecutor, which wraps an executor so the caller's identity travels with each task. Choose it when the task really must act as the caller.

When to break it. A metric flush or a cache warm-up needs no context. An executor that only runs such work can skip the decorator. Name it plainly, so nobody adds request work to it later.

.NET anchor. .NET flows ExecutionContext across await and Task.Run without being asked, so AsyncLocal<T> values follow the work. Java's ThreadLocal does not flow at all. The nearest .NET habit is passing values explicitly instead of reading HttpContext from a background task.

See also. 3.05, 9.01, 12.04, 13.07, Structured concurrency and cancellation, Actuator and observability

3.05 Make @Async actually asynchronous, on a bounded executor

Then.

  • Spring era: the executor and the annotation switched on in XML.
<task:annotation-driven executor="mailExecutor"/>
<task:executor id="mailExecutor" pool-size="5-10" queue-capacity="100"/>
  • Spring era: @Async methods returning new AsyncResult<>(value), a Future wrapper of Spring's own. Today the method returns CompletableFuture.completedFuture(value).
  • Boot era: a class implementing AsyncConfigurer, or extending the older AsyncConfigurerSupport, to supply the executor and the handler for uncaught exceptions.

Recognise it by. <task:annotation-driven>, AsyncResult, AsyncConfigurerSupport, ListenableFuture return types, and @EnableAsync on a class far from the code that uses @Async.

The rookie version.

@Service
class PayoutService {
    public Payout complete(Payout p) {
        Payout done = payoutRepository.save(p.completed());
        sendReceipt(done);                 // a call on "this", not on the proxy
        return done;
    }
    @Async
    public void sendReceipt(Payout p) { notifier.email(p); }   // 3 s SMTP call
}

What goes wrong. @Async asks Spring to run a method on an executor. It works through a proxy, a wrapper object Spring places in front of the bean, and only calls that arrive through the proxy are intercepted. The call to sendReceipt goes from the object to itself. Nothing intercepts it, and it runs on the request thread. Every completed payout takes 3 seconds longer, and nothing in the code says why. When the method moves to another bean, a second problem appears. The executor keeps its pending receipts in a queue in memory. A deploy stops a pod with 400 receipts queued, and those claimants never hear. A failure in a void method has no caller to tell, so it reaches a handler that only logs it.

Do this now.

  1. Put @EnableAsync on one configuration class.
  2. Put the @Async method on a different bean from its caller, so the call crosses the proxy.
  3. Name the executor, as in @Async("receiptExecutor"). One executor per kind of work stops slow receipts from delaying other background work.
  4. Bound it, with a core size, a maximum, a queue capacity and a rejection policy. Overload then shows up as a decision, not a growing heap.
  5. Know how the pool grows. A ThreadPoolTaskExecutor adds threads beyond the core size only when its queue is full. With a large queue, the maximum is never reached.
  6. Return CompletableFuture<T> when the caller needs the result or the failure. For void methods, register an AsyncUncaughtExceptionHandler that counts failures in a metric.
  7. Anything that must happen even if the pod dies goes into the outbox and SQS, not into an executor's queue (9.07). Even the executor below drains only what its 20 seconds allow: 8 threads at 3 seconds a receipt finish about 50, so a full queue of 100 is not cleared.
@Bean(name = "receiptExecutor")
ThreadPoolTaskExecutor receiptExecutor(TaskDecorator taskDecorator) {  // MDC and trace (13.07)
    var exec = new ThreadPoolTaskExecutor();
    exec.setCorePoolSize(4);
    exec.setMaxPoolSize(8);
    exec.setQueueCapacity(100);
    exec.setThreadNamePrefix("receipt-");
    exec.setRejectedExecutionHandler(new ThreadPoolExecutor.CallerRunsPolicy());
    exec.setTaskDecorator(taskDecorator);
    exec.setWaitForTasksToCompleteOnShutdown(true);
    exec.setAwaitTerminationSeconds(20);
    return exec;
}

CallerRunsPolicy runs a rejected task on the caller's thread. That slows the caller down, which is a crude but honest form of back-pressure. With spring.threads.virtual.enabled on, Boot's own executor becomes a SimpleAsyncTaskExecutor on virtual threads, which starts a new thread for every task. Give it a limit with spring.task.execution.simple.concurrency-limit, or use named executors like the one above. Declaring any Executor bean of your own, as here, makes Boot skip its own executor unless spring.task.execution.mode is force. An unnamed @Async may then fall back to a SimpleAsyncTaskExecutor with no limit at all.

Also seen. @Async on an @EventListener, for side effects that should not slow the publisher (4.13). An SQS queue, when the work must survive a restart or belongs to another service (10.04).

When to break it. An unbounded executor is acceptable for work that is tiny, rare and harmless to lose, such as warming a cache at start-up. Name it even then, so it shows up in a thread dump.

.NET anchor. The nearest is a BackgroundService reading a bounded Channel<T>. A bounded channel with BoundedChannelFullMode.Wait plays the part of the queue capacity and rejection policy here. .NET has no proxy in the way, so it has no self-invocation trap.

See also. 3.04, 3.11, 4.08, 9.02, 9.07, How Spring actually works, Caching, scheduling and events

3.06 Use CompletableFuture without losing exceptions

What goes wrong. A compensating step calls CompletableFuture.runAsync(() -> ledgerClient.release(reservationId, key)) and never looks at the future again. The release fails with a 503. The exception is stored inside the future, nobody reads it, and nothing is logged. The ledger keeps £1,240.50 reserved for a payout that has already failed.

Do this now.

  • Keep the future, and end every chain in something that sees the failure: join, whenComplete, handle or exceptionally.
  • Know the wrappers. join throws CompletionException and get throws ExecutionException. The real exception is getCause().
  • A stage such as thenApply is skipped when an earlier stage failed, and the failure passes on to the end of the chain.
  • Always pass an executor (3.03).
  • Logging the failure is the minimum. Work that must happen belongs in the saga, which retries it (11.05).
CompletableFuture.runAsync(() -> ledgerClient.release(reservationId, key), callExecutor)
        .whenComplete((ok, ex) -> {
            if (ex != null) log.error("release failed for {}", payout.id(), ex);
        });

.NET anchor. An unobserved Task exception is lost in .NET too, apart from TaskScheduler.UnobservedTaskException. Java has no global hook for futures.

See also. 3.03, 11.05, CompletableFuture and Task

3.07 Share state between threads safely

Then.

  • J2EE era: Hashtable, Vector and Collections.synchronizedMap, where every method takes one lock on the whole collection. Each single call was safe. A check followed by a put was still a race.
private final Map<String, Integer> counts =
        Collections.synchronizedMap(new HashMap<>());
  • Spring era: a ThreadLocal<SimpleDateFormat>, because SimpleDateFormat is not safe to share and was costly to create. java.time's DateTimeFormatter is immutable and replaced it (2.15).
  • Spring era: synchronized on whole service methods, which made a bean safe by letting one request in at a time.

Recognise it by. java.util.Hashtable, Vector, Collections.synchronizedMap, ThreadLocal<SimpleDateFormat>, and synchronized on the public methods of a @Service.

The rookie version.

@Service
class PayoutLimits {
    private final Map<String, Money> paidToday = new HashMap<>();
    boolean allow(String claimantId, Money amount) {
        Money soFar = paidToday.getOrDefault(claimantId, Money.ZERO_GBP);
        if (soFar.plus(amount).amount().compareTo(DAILY_CAP.amount()) > 0) return false;
        paidToday.put(claimantId, soFar.plus(amount));
        return true;
    }
}

What goes wrong. A Spring bean is a singleton by default: one instance, shared by every request thread. Two requests for the same claimant arrive together. Each reads £0 paid, each adds £1,240.50, and each passes the £2,000 daily cap. The claimant receives £2,481.00. A HashMap written by two threads at once can also lose entries or corrupt itself while it resizes. And the map is per pod, so with 2 pods a claimant can reach the cap on each.

Do this now.

  1. Prefer no shared mutable state. Make values records (2.03) and pass them along.
  2. When state must be shared inside one JVM, use the java.util.concurrent types, and make each update one atomic call: - ConcurrentHashMap.compute or merge for a read-modify-write on one key. - AtomicLong or AtomicReference for a single value. - LongAdder for a counter that many threads increment and few read.
  3. Keep the function you pass to compute short. It runs while the map holds that key's lock, so it must not call another service.
  4. Mark a field volatile when one thread writes a flag and others only read it. It guarantees they see the new value, and nothing more.
  5. When the state must be right across pods, it does not belong in memory. Use one atomic update in DocumentDB (8.04) or a unique index (8.16).
private final ConcurrentHashMap<String, Money> paidToday = new ConcurrentHashMap<>();

boolean allow(String claimantId, Money amount) {
    var allowed = new AtomicBoolean(false);
    paidToday.compute(claimantId, (id, soFar) -> {
        Money next = soFar == null ? amount : soFar.plus(amount);
        if (next.amount().compareTo(DAILY_CAP.amount()) > 0) return soFar;
        allowed.set(true);
        return next;
    });
    return allowed.get();
}

This removes the race inside one pod, and nothing more. A daily cap on money must hold across both pods, survive a restart and start again each day, which this map does not. So in Payouts the cap belongs in one conditional update in DocumentDB, the pattern in 8.04. The map pattern fits figures that are honestly per pod, such as a local counter or a cache.

Also seen. A ReentrantReadWriteLock, for data read constantly and written rarely. An immutable snapshot swapped through an AtomicReference is usually simpler. Caffeine, for a bounded cache shared between threads (18.08).

When to break it. A plain HashMap is safe to share when it is filled in a constructor, never changed again and held in a final field. Wrap it with Map.copyOf so nobody changes it later by accident.

.NET anchor. ConcurrentHashMap is ConcurrentDictionary, and compute is close to AddOrUpdate, with one difference that bites. AddOrUpdate may run your function more than once and does not lock, so a side effect inside it, like allowed.set(true) here, is unsafe in .NET. Java's compute runs the function once, under the key's lock. AtomicLong does what Interlocked does. A @Service field is like a field on a service registered with AddSingleton: every request shares it.

See also. 2.03, 2.07, 3.08, 8.04, 8.16, Locks, atomics and the memory model, Legacy concurrency you will still meet

3.08 Choose between synchronized and ReentrantLock

What goes wrong. Advice copied from a Java 21 migration guide replaces every synchronized block in payouts-domain with a ReentrantLock. The diff touches 31 files and adds a finally to each, and one of them misses its unlock. The first exception on that path leaves the lock held, and every later caller waits for ever.

Do this now.

  • Use synchronized for short critical sections. On Java 25 it no longer pins virtual threads in nearly all cases, and it always releases the lock when an exception escapes.
  • Use ReentrantLock for what synchronized cannot do: tryLock with a timeout, lockInterruptibly, a fair ordering of waiters, or several Conditions on one lock.
  • Pair every lock() with unlock() in finally.
if (!lock.tryLock(500, TimeUnit.MILLISECONDS)) throw new LedgerBusyException();
try { reserveLocally(payout); } finally { lock.unlock(); }

.NET anchor. synchronized is C#'s lock. ReentrantLock with tryLock is closer to Monitor.TryEnter with a timeout.

See also. 3.02, 3.12, Locks, atomics and the memory model

3.09 Limit concurrency to protect a downstream service

Then.

  • Boot era: the thread pool as the limit. A Tomcat pool of 200 meant no more than 200 ledger calls in flight per pod, whether anyone intended it or not.
  • Boot era: Hystrix thread-pool isolation, which ran each dependency's calls on its own small pool. Hystrix has been in maintenance mode since 2018, after 1.5.18, and Resilience4j, Java's nearest thing to Polly, replaced it.
@HystrixCommand(threadPoolKey = "ledger",
        threadPoolProperties = @HystrixProperty(name = "coreSize", value = "20"))
public LedgerEntry reserve(Payout p) {
    return ledgerClient.reserve(p);
}
  • Spring era: a hand-written java.util.concurrent.Semaphore field around the call.

Recognise it by. com.netflix.hystrix, @HystrixCommand, threadPoolKey, hystrix.threadpool.* keys, a bare Semaphore field in a client class, and a server.tomcat.threads.max with no comment.

The rookie version.

private final Semaphore permits = new Semaphore(20);

public LedgerEntry reserve(Payout p) throws InterruptedException {
    permits.acquire();
    LedgerEntry entry = ledgerClient.reserve(p);
    permits.release();
    return entry;
}

What goes wrong. A semaphore holds a fixed number of permits: a caller takes one before the call and gives it back after. Here release is not in a finally, so every call that throws keeps its permit. After 20 ledger timeouts the semaphore is empty, and it stays empty. acquire has no timeout, so every later payout waits in it for ever. The pod looks alive and pays nothing until someone restarts it. The developer also chose 20 without knowing that payouts-api runs 2 pods, so the ledger sees up to 40.

Do this now.

  1. Agree the number with the team that owns the downstream service, as total calls in flight, and divide it by the most replicas you ever run at once. The ledger team allows 40. Payouts runs 2 pods, but 3 during a rolling deploy (17.06), so each pod gets 13. Revisit it whenever the replica count changes.
  2. Use a bulkhead: a named limit on concurrent calls to one dependency, with a short wait for a free slot and a clear failure when there is none. On Boot 3.5 this is Resilience4j's @Bulkhead, which by default is a semaphore bulkhead. It needs the same starter and AOP setup as the circuit breaker in 7.05, and it works only on calls from another bean, through the proxy (3.05).
  3. Keep the wait for a slot short. A caller that cannot get in should fail fast with a 503 that says to retry, not queue.
  4. Map BulkheadFullException to that 503 in one place (6.03).
  5. Order the bulkhead with the retry and the circuit breaker on purpose (7.06), and graph its metrics so the moment it fills is visible.
@Bulkhead(name = "ledger")
public LedgerEntry reserve(Payout p) {
    return ledgerClient.reserve(p);
}

resilience4j:
  bulkhead:
    instances:
      ledger:
        max-concurrent-calls: 13    # 40 agreed with the ledger team, over 3 pods
        max-wait-duration: 100ms

In Boot 4, Spring Framework 7 adds @ConcurrencyLimit in org.springframework.resilience.annotation, switched on with @EnableResilientMethods. It limits concurrent calls to a method without a library. Spring describes it as working like a pool that blocks when full, so callers over the limit wait for a slot rather than fail. That is the queueing step 3 warns against. Core Spring has no circuit breaker, bulkhead or timeout, so a service that already uses Resilience4j for its breaker keeps the bulkhead there too.

Also seen. A thread-pool bulkhead, type = Bulkhead.Type.THREADPOOL, which also runs the calls on their own threads. With virtual threads that isolation buys little. A plain Semaphore with tryAcquire and a timeout, and release in finally, in a library with no Spring.

When to break it. A managed AWS service such as SQS needs no bulkhead to protect it. You may still want one to protect yourself, if a stall there could tie up every request on the pod.

.NET anchor. A SemaphoreSlim with WaitAsync(timeout), or Polly's concurrency limiter. Both are limits per process, exactly like this one, so the same division by replicas applies.

See also. 3.01, 7.05, 7.06, 10.16, The Yard, chapter 11, HTTP clients and resilience

3.10 Run @Scheduled work once across several pods

Then.

  • Spring era: Quartz with a clustered JDBC job store, org.quartz.jobStore.isClustered=true, where the nodes agreed through row locks in a shared database.

What goes wrong. @Scheduled(cron = "0 0 2 * * *") starts the nightly repair of stuck payouts. payouts-api runs 2 pods, and each pod runs the job at 02:00. Both find the same 14 stuck payouts, and both send them to the bank gateway again.

Do this now.

  • Make the job idempotent first (9.09). A lock makes duplicates rare, not impossible.
  • Take a lock in DocumentDB before the job runs. ShedLock does this. Add net.javacrumbs.shedlock:shedlock-spring and shedlock-provider-mongo, put @EnableSchedulerLock(defaultLockAtMostFor = "PT10M") beside @EnableScheduling, and declare the lock store.
  • Set lockAtMostFor longer than the job ever takes. Set lockAtLeastFor too, or a 2-second job releases the lock and a pod whose clock runs behind starts it again.
@Bean
LockProvider lockProvider(MongoTemplate mongoTemplate) {
    return new MongoLockProvider(mongoTemplate.getDb());   // a shedLock collection
}

@Scheduled(cron = "0 0 2 * * *")
@SchedulerLock(name = "repairStuck", lockAtMostFor = "PT10M", lockAtLeastFor = "PT1M")
public void repairStuck() { ... }
  • Or move the job out of the service into a Kubernetes CronJob with concurrencyPolicy: Forbid, so runs never overlap.

.NET anchor. Hangfire or Quartz.NET with a shared store solves the same problem. A BackgroundService with a PeriodicTimer has the same per-pod trap as @Scheduled.

See also. 9.09, 11.09, 17.08, Caching, scheduling and events

3.11 Shut executors down cleanly

What goes wrong. OutboxRelay creates Executors.newFixedThreadPool(4) in its constructor, so Spring does not manage it and never shuts it down. A deploy stops the pod, and the JVM exits in the middle of a batch. The relay has published 6 events to SNS and not yet marked them sent, so the next pod publishes them again.

Do this now.

  • Make executors Spring beans, so Spring closes them. A ThreadPoolTaskExecutor with setWaitForTasksToCompleteOnShutdown(true) and setAwaitTerminationSeconds finishes running and queued tasks for that long.
  • Boot's own executor takes spring.task.execution.shutdown.await-termination and spring.task.execution.shutdown.await-termination-period.
  • Outside Spring, call shutdown(), then awaitTermination, then shutdownNow() for whatever is left. Try-with-resources does the waiting part, since close() waits.
  • Fit the waits inside the grace period. A ThreadPoolTaskExecutor waits when its bean is destroyed, after the web drain, so its wait adds to the sum in 17.05: a 5-second sleep before SIGTERM, 20 for listeners, 20 for the drain, 5 spare, 50 in all. The receipt executor's 20 (3.05) makes it 70.
  • A killed pod still republishes, so consumers of payout-events must tolerate duplicates (10.07).

.NET anchor. IHostApplicationLifetime.ApplicationStopping and HostOptions.ShutdownTimeout play the same part.

See also. 3.05, 17.05, The Yard, chapter 14, Threads are cheap now

3.12 Recognise a deadlock and get out of it

What goes wrong. One thread locks payout A and then wants the claimant's ledger account. Another locks the account and then wants payout A. Each waits for the other for ever. A quieter version needs no locks. Four tasks on a pool of 4 threads each submit a second task to the same pool and wait for it. No thread is left to run them. The pool stops, and the CPU sits near zero.

Do this now.

  • Take a thread dump with jcmd <pid> Thread.print. The JVM finds lock cycles and prints "Found one Java-level deadlock" with both stacks.
  • For virtual threads, use jcmd <pid> Thread.dump_to_file -format=json /tmp/threads.json.
  • Restart the pod to get out. Then fix the cause:
  • take locks in one fixed order, for example by payout ID
  • use tryLock with a timeout, so a cycle becomes an error instead of a hang (3.08)
  • never wait on a task submitted to the pool you are running on.

.NET anchor. The classic .NET deadlock is .Result blocking a SynchronizationContext. Java has none, so its deadlocks are lock cycles and starved pools.

See also. 3.08, 17.10, 18.05, Locks, atomics and the memory model

⚠Review checklist
  • If you see Executors.newFixedThreadPool(n, Thread.ofVirtual().factory()): pooling virtual threads brings back the ceiling and hides a limit inside an executor. See 3.01.
  • If you see a network call inside synchronized, or between lock() and unlock(): every caller queues behind the slowest call. See 3.02.
  • If you see parallelStream(), or supplyAsync with no executor, around an HTTP or database call: the waiting happens on the JVM's shared common pool. See 3.03.
  • If you see SecurityContextHolder or MDC read inside runAsync, submit or an @Async method: the context is empty, or belongs to another request. See 3.04.
  • If you see an @Async method called from its own class: it runs on the caller's thread. See 3.05.
  • If you see @Async with no named executor, or an executor with no queue capacity: overload grows the heap and a deploy loses the queue. See 3.05.
  • If you see a runAsync or supplyAsync whose future is never joined or handled: its exception disappears. See 3.06.
  • If you see a mutable HashMap, counter or non-final field in a @Service: every request thread shares it. See 3.07.
  • If you see lock() without unlock() in finally: the first exception leaves the lock held. See 3.08.
  • If you see Semaphore.acquire() with no timeout on a request path, or release() outside finally: permits leak until the pod pays nothing. See 3.09.
  • If you see a new @Scheduled method with no lock and no idempotency: it runs once per pod. See 3.10.
  • If you see an ExecutorService created in a constructor or a field, not as a bean: it is never shut down. See 3.11.

Part IV · The how-to4. Spring configuration and dependency injection#

How a Spring Boot service gets its objects and its settings. Spring's container is the part of Spring that creates your objects, called beans, and hands each one the others it needs. This part covers wiring beans together, binding settings to typed records, keeping environments and secrets apart, and what Spring's wrappers do to your classes. It ends with writing auto-configuration, the setup Boot applies by itself when a library is on the classpath, for a shared library, and with finding out why a bean exists.

★What a veteran knows
  • A constructor with eight parameters is not a reason to switch to field injection. It is a class doing too much, and the constructor is the only place that says so.
  • Every @Value("${...}"), an annotation that reads one setting into one field, is a setting nobody can list. One record per prefix makes the record the list.
  • A profile is a named switch that turns on extra settings and beans (4.03). It should name a capability, such as fakeledger, not a place. Environments differ by values, and values come from the environment.
  • A proxy is the wrapper Spring puts around a bean to apply annotations such as @Transactional (4.08). An annotation that works through a proxy works only on a public, non-final method, called from another bean. Test what it does, never that it is there.
  • Bad configuration should stop one pod at startup, not fail the first payout at 02:14.
