  • Read the conditions report, Boot's list of what it switched on and why (4.12), before you exclude anything. Write the reason beside the exclusion, because nobody will remember it.
◷How we got hereIn January 2004 Martin Fowler published an article on his website, "Inversion of Control Containers and the…

In January 2004 Martin Fowler published an article on his website, "Inversion of Control Containers and the Dependency Injection pattern". A rush of lightweight containers had appeared to assemble components from different projects into one application. They all described themselves by the same phrase, and Fowler objected to it. Inversion of control, he wrote, is a common characteristic of frameworks. Calling these containers special for it "is like saying my car is special because it has wheels." What they inverted was narrower: how a component looks up the implementation it needs. "Inversion of Control is too generic a term, and thus people find it confusing," he wrote. After "a lot of discussion with various IoC advocates" they settled on Dependency Injection. The community had numbered its styles type 1, type 2 and type 3. Fowler gave them the names still used: interface, setter and constructor injection. The first entry below is still choosing between the last two.

4.01 Inject dependencies through the constructor

Then.

  • Spring era: XML bean definitions wired through setters. Spring called a no-argument constructor, then one setter per dependency. This was right when wiring was meant to change without a recompile.
<bean id="payoutService" class="com.sorrel.payouts.PayoutService">
    <property name="repository" ref="payoutRepository"/>
    <property name="ledgerClient" ref="ledgerClient"/>
</bean>
  • Spring era: @Autowired on private fields. It was short, and it moved the wiring next to the class. Most code written in the 2010s looks like this.
  • Boot era: @Autowired on a constructor. Spring once needed the annotation to choose a constructor. Current Spring uses a class's only constructor without it.

Recognise it by. @Autowired on fields, import org.springframework.beans.factory.annotation.Autowired in every class, javax.inject.Inject, <property name="..." ref="..."/> in applicationContext.xml, and setters nobody else calls.

The rookie version.

@Service
public class PayoutService {
    @Autowired private PayoutRepository repository;
    @Autowired private LedgerClient ledgerClient;
    @Autowired private BankGatewayClient bankGatewayClient;

    public Payout pay(Claim claim) { ... }
}

It reads like a C# property with an attribute, and it compiles.

What goes wrong. A unit test writes new PayoutService() and gets an object with three null fields. Nothing fails until pay runs and throws NullPointerException from inside. The test author then reaches for @SpringBootTest, which starts the whole application inside the test, to get the fields filled, and a 40 ms test becomes a 9-second one. Field injection also hides growth. Adding a dependency is one line, so PayoutService reached 11 of them before anyone noticed. The fields cannot be final either, so nothing stops later code from replacing ledgerClient.

Do this now. Make the constructor the only way in.

  1. Declare each dependency as a private final field.
  2. Write one constructor that takes them all. With exactly one constructor, Spring uses it, and @Autowired is noise.
  3. Mark the class @Service or @Component so that Spring finds it (4.05).
@Service
public class PayoutService {
    private final PayoutRepository repository;
    private final LedgerClient ledgerClient;
    private final Clock clock;

    public PayoutService(PayoutRepository repository, LedgerClient ledgerClient, Clock clock) {
        this.repository = repository;
        this.ledgerClient = ledgerClient;
        this.clock = clock;
    }
}

A unit test is now plain Java: new PayoutService(fakeRepository, fakeLedger, Clock.fixed(...)). A missing dependency is a compile error, not a null at runtime. If two beans need each other, startup fails at once instead of working by accident (4.07). Spring creates one instance of each bean and shares it, so the class must hold no per-request state in its fields. When the parameter list passes five or six, split the class rather than hide the list.

Also seen. Setter injection, for an optional dependency with a sensible default. ObjectProvider<T> as a constructor parameter, when the dependency may be absent or must be looked up at call time (4.06).

When to break it. Test classes. @Autowired fields in a @SpringBootTest class are normal, because nobody constructs a test class by hand. The cost is small: the test reads a little less plainly.

.NET anchor. This is ASP.NET Core's default. IServiceCollection fills constructor parameters and has no field or property injection at all. The difference is registration. Spring finds the class by scanning, where .NET needs AddScoped<PayoutService>() in Program.cs. Spring's shared instance is like AddSingleton, not AddScoped.

See also. 4.05, 4.07, 2.16, 16.01, The Yard, chapter 15, Dependency injection and configuration

4.02 Bind configuration to a typed record with @ConfigurationProperties

Then.

  • Spring era: @Value on fields, reading a .properties file loaded by <context:property-placeholder/> or @PropertySource. In ${ledger.timeout:5000}, the text after the colon is the default used when the key is missing. It was right for a handful of values in a service with one file.
@Value("${ledger.url}")
private String ledgerUrl;

@Value("${ledger.timeout:5000}")
private int ledgerTimeoutMs;
  • Boot era: @ConfigurationProperties on a mutable class with getters and setters. It was typed, but any bean could call setReadTimeout. @ConstructorBinding arrived for immutable classes. Current Boot binds through a single constructor without it, so on a record it is noise.

Recognise it by. @Value("${, PropertyPlaceholderConfigurer, <context:property-placeholder location="..."/>, @PropertySource("classpath:..."), @ConstructorBinding, and *Properties classes full of setters.

The rookie version.

public LedgerClient(RestClient.Builder builder,
        @Value("${payouts.ledger.base-url}") String baseUrl,
        @Value("${payouts.ledger.timeout:5000}") int timeout) { ... }

public LedgerHealthCheck(
        @Value("${payouts.ledger.timeout:5}") int timeout) { ... }

RestClient.Builder is the builder Boot provides for its HTTP client (7.01).

What goes wrong. Two classes read the same key with different defaults and different units. The ConfigMap sets payouts.ledger.timeout: 2000. LedgerClient reads that as 2,000 ms. LedgerHealthCheck reads it as seconds, so it waits up to 33 minutes. In uat the key was spelt payouts.ledger.time-out, and neither class noticed, because a default hides a missing key. Nobody can list the service's settings without searching the code for ${.

Do this now. One record per prefix, bound once, injected where it is needed.

  1. Write a record whose components are the settings, with real types.
@ConfigurationProperties(prefix = "payouts.ledger")
public record LedgerProperties(
        URI baseUrl,
        @DefaultValue("1s") Duration connectTimeout,
        @DefaultValue("5s") Duration readTimeout,
        @DefaultValue("3") int maxRetries) {
}
  1. Register it. Put @ConfigurationPropertiesScan on the application class, the one marked @SpringBootApplication that holds main, or @EnableConfigurationProperties(LedgerProperties.class) on a configuration class.
  2. Inject LedgerProperties through the constructor of LedgerClient and anything else that needs it.
  3. Write the values with their units.
payouts:
  ledger:
    base-url: http://ledger.ledger.svc.cluster.local
    connect-timeout: 1s
    read-timeout: 5s

This base value of 5 seconds is overridden to 2 seconds in production by an environment variable (4.15).

Boot uses relaxed binding: read-timeout, readTimeout and the environment variable PAYOUTS_LEDGER_READTIMEOUT all reach the readTimeout component. A Duration accepts 500ms, 5s or 2m, so the unit lives in the type and names like timeoutMs disappear. Always write the unit. @DurationUnit decides what a bare number means, and a reader should not have to look it up.

  1. Add spring-boot-configuration-processor as an annotation processor: list it under annotationProcessorPaths in the maven-compiler-plugin section of pom.xml, Maven's build file. The processor writes metadata, so the IDE completes payouts.ledger.* keys and flags unknown ones.

The record is immutable, so no bean can change a timeout while the service runs. Validation of the values is 4.10. In Boot 4, mark an optional component with JSpecify's @Nullable, which replaces Spring's own.

Also seen. @Value for one value used in one place, such as ${spring.application.name}. Environment.getProperty(...) in framework code that does not know its keys until runtime.

When to break it. A small library that must read one key without owning a prefix may use @Value. The cost is that the key is missing from the metadata and from any list of settings.

.NET anchor. This is the options pattern: services.Configure<LedgerOptions>(config.GetSection("Payouts:Ledger")) and an injected IOptions<LedgerOptions>. The record behaves like IOptions<T>, bound once at startup. There is no built-in IOptionsMonitor<T> equivalent that changes underneath you.

See also. 4.10, 4.15, 7.03, 16.18, Dependency injection and configuration

4.03 Use profiles for environments without forking the configuration

Then.

  • Boot era: A profile is a named switch, such as uat, that turns on extra configuration and beans when it is active. Old code put one application.yml with several documents separated by ---, each guarded by a spring.profiles key. Boot replaced that key with spring.config.activate.on-profile, which says plainly that the document applies when a profile is active.
spring:
  profiles: prod
payouts:
  ledger:
    base-url: http://ledger.prod.internal
---
spring:
  profiles: uat
  • Spring era: Before profiles, a Maven profile, a named block of build settings in pom.xml, filtered ${...} placeholders into the properties file at build time. Each environment got its own WAR, the archive deployed to Tomcat, built from the same source. Spring then added <beans profile="uat"> blocks to XML, and -Dspring.profiles.active on the Tomcat command line chose one.

Recognise it by. spring.profiles: as a key inside a YAML document, <beans profile="...">, <filtering>true</filtering> on resources in the POM, and application-dev.yml, application-uat.yml and application-prod.yml side by side.

The rookie version.

src/main/resources/
  application.yml         340 lines
  application-dev.yml     330 lines, copied from application.yml
  application-uat.yml     335 lines, copied from application-dev.yml
  application-prod.yml    338 lines, copied from application-uat.yml

The same developer writes if (environment.acceptsProfiles(Profiles.of("prod"))) around the call to the real bank.

What goes wrong. Each profile file here has become a fork. After six months the four files differ in 41 places, and 6 of those differences are deliberate. A fix that raised max-retries in uat never reached prod. The prod check in code is worse: the path that pays the bank is the one path no test runs, because the tests run with no profile.

Do this now. One base file, values from the environment, profiles for capabilities.

  1. Keep one application.yml with what every environment shares and safe defaults.
  2. Take the values that differ by environment, such as URLs and pool sizes, from environment variables or a ConfigMap (4.15). The same jar then runs in dev, uat and prod.
  3. Name profiles after what they switch on. In Payouts, fakeledger replaces the real ledger with a stand-in and local points at a Mongo container. Each profile file holds only what it changes.
# application-local.yml
spring:
  data:
    mongodb:
      uri: mongodb://localhost:27017/payouts   # Boot 4: spring.mongodb.uri
payouts:
  ledger:
    base-url: http://localhost:8089
  1. Activate with SPRING_PROFILES_ACTIVE=local. Group profiles that always go together with spring.profiles.group.local=fakeledger in the base application.yml. Boot refuses a group defined inside a profile's own file.
  2. Put @Profile("fakeledger") on the configuration class that declares the stand-in bean, and @Profile("!fakeledger") on the real one, so that exactly one LedgerClient bean exists. Never use an if in business code.

Values arrive in layers, and a later layer wins:

When several profiles are active, the last one listed wins where they disagree.

Also seen. spring.config.activate.on-profile inside a multi-document application.yml, when the overrides are few and you want them in one file.

When to break it. Environments sometimes differ in structure, not only in values. Uat may talk to the bank's sandbox, which needs a different client. A profile is right there, named for what it does: sandbox-bank. The cost is one more combination to start and test.

.NET anchor. ASPNETCORE_ENVIRONMENT with appsettings.Production.json layered over appsettings.json is the same layering. Spring differs in two ways. Several profiles can be active at once, and a profile can switch beans on and off, where .NET code usually calls IWebHostEnvironment.IsProduction().

See also. 4.14, 4.15, 4.16, 17.07, Dependency injection and configuration

4.04 Keep secrets out of application.yml

Then.

  • J2EE era: The application server held the credentials. JNDI is the server's directory of named resources. A JNDI data source in Tomcat's context.xml carried the database password, and the application looked it up by name. That was right: the server team owned the secret, and the code never saw it.
  • Boot era: Encrypted values committed to the YAML, decrypted at startup with one key. jasypt-spring-boot used ENC(...). Spring Cloud Config used {cipher}... and a bootstrap.yml that pointed at a config server. It kept everything in git, but every environment needed the one key.
payouts:
  bank:
    api-key: ENC(G6N718UuyPE5bHyWKyuLQSm02auQPUtm)
jasypt:
  encryptor:
    password: ${JASYPT_PASSWORD}

A starter is a dependency that brings a library together with the setup that switches it on, such as jasypt-spring-boot-starter. Modern Spring Cloud reads bootstrap.yml only with spring-cloud-starter-bootstrap on the classpath. spring.config.import replaced it.

Recognise it by. ENC(, jasypt.encryptor.password, com.github.ulisesbocchio:jasypt-spring-boot-starter, {cipher}, bootstrap.yml, spring.cloud.config.uri, and <Resource name="jdbc/..."> in context.xml.

The rookie version.

# application-prod.yml, committed
payouts:
  bank:
    api-key: sk_live_4f9a1c7e2b
spring:
  data:
    mongodb:
      uri: mongodb://payouts:Winter2025@payouts-db:27017/payouts

What goes wrong. The repository is readable by about 200 developers at Sorrel, and by every CI job. Deleting the line later does not help, because git keeps history. Rotating the bank key now needs a commit, a build and a release, which took 2 days the one time it was urgent. A copy of the repository on a lost laptop is a copy of the bank key.

Do this now. The file names the setting. The platform supplies the value.

  1. Leave secret values out of every file in the repository. The record that binds them can still have the component, such as apiKey in BankProperties.
  2. On Kubernetes, mount the Secret as files and import the directory as a config tree, where each file name is a property name and its content is the value.
spring:
  config:
    import: "optional:configtree:/etc/payouts/secrets/"

Put this in application.yml. Mount the Secret at that path with a volumes entry and a volumeMounts entry in the pod spec (17.07). A file /etc/payouts/secrets/payouts.bank.api-key then binds to payouts.bank.api-key. The optional: prefix lets the service start on a laptop, where the directory does not exist. A missing key still stops startup once the record is validated (4.10). Rotating the key means updating the Secret and restarting the pods, with no build.

  1. To read from AWS Secrets Manager instead, add Spring Cloud AWS's io.awspring.cloud:spring-cloud-aws-starter-secrets-manager and write spring.config.import=aws-secretsmanager:payouts/bank. Each key in the secret's JSON becomes a property, so the secret holds {"payouts.bank.api-key": "..."}. Use its 3.4.x line on Boot 3.5 and 4.x on Boot 4. Entry 15.06 covers it, including the pod's AWS permissions.
  2. Override toString() on any record that holds a secret. A record's generated toString() prints every component, so one log.info("config {}", props) prints the key.

Also seen. Environment variables filled from a Secret with envFrom. It is simpler, but every child process inherits them, and any tool that dumps the environment prints them. Spring Cloud Vault, with spring.config.import=vault://, where Vault is the company's store.

When to break it. Local development against a fake bank may use a dummy key in application-local.yml, if it is obviously fake and the real gateway rejects it. The cost is that someone copies it into a real profile one day, so make startup refuse that key outside local.

.NET anchor. dotnet user-secrets locally and the Azure Key Vault configuration provider in production. spring.config.import is how Spring adds a configuration provider. A config tree is the same idea as AddKeyPerFile. C# records have the same toString() trap: their generated ToString() prints every property too.

See also. 15.06, 17.07, 12.06, 4.15, Security

4.05 Choose between component scanning and @Bean methods

What goes wrong. Clock is a JDK class, so nobody can put @Component on it. A developer calls Clock.systemUTC() inline in 6 classes, and no test can fix the time (2.16). Elsewhere, a @Component in com.sorrel.shared is never found, because the application class lives in com.sorrel.payouts. Startup fails with NoSuchBeanDefinitionException.

Do this now. Component scanning means Spring searches the package of the @SpringBootApplication class, and every package below it, for classes marked @Component, @Service, @Repository, @Controller or @Configuration. Use it for your own classes. Use a @Bean method for objects you do not own, or that need construction logic:

@Configuration(proxyBeanMethods = false)
class TimeConfig {
    @Bean
    Clock clock() {
        return Clock.systemUTC();
    }
}

proxyBeanMethods = false stops Spring wrapping the class (4.08). Ask for other beans as method parameters rather than calling other @Bean methods. Keep the application class at the root of com.sorrel.payouts, so the scan covers the whole service and nothing else. A class in a shared library reaches services through auto-configuration instead (4.11).

.NET anchor. Microsoft's container has no scanning. Scrutor adds it. A @Bean method is a factory registration: services.AddSingleton(_ => TimeProvider.System).

See also. 4.01, 4.11, 2.16, Dependency injection and configuration

4.06 Pick one of several beans of the same type

Then.

  • Spring era: Matching by name. XML wired ref="ledgerRestTemplate" by bean id, and @Resource(name = "...") from javax.annotation did the same in code. @Autowired with @Qualifier on a field came next. The qualifier is still current. The field is not (4.01).
@Resource(name = "ledgerRestTemplate")
private RestTemplate ledgerTemplate;

@Autowired
@Qualifier("bankRestTemplate")
private RestTemplate bankTemplate;

Recognise it by. javax.annotation.Resource, javax.inject.Named, @Qualifier on fields, and several RestTemplate beans named after the services they call.

The rookie version.

@Bean @Primary
RestClient ledgerRestClient(RestClient.Builder builder, LedgerProperties props) {
    return builder.baseUrl(props.baseUrl().toString()).build();
}

@Bean
RestClient bankRestClient(RestClient.Builder builder, BankProperties props) {
    return builder.baseUrl(props.baseUrl().toString()).build();
}

Startup had failed with "required a single bean, but 2 were found". @Primary made it start.

What goes wrong. @Primary marks one bean as the default whenever a type has several candidates. BankGatewayClient asks for a RestClient without saying which, and gets the ledger's. Every bank instruction goes to the ledger's URL and fails with 404. The tests fake both clients, so they pass. In production the instructions for 37 payouts, the first for £1,240.50, fail for 50 minutes until the rollback. @Primary did not answer "which one?". It stopped Spring asking.

Do this now. Avoid the choice first, then make it visible where it remains.

  1. Prefer not to have two beans of a general type. Build each RestClient inside the client class that owns it, from the injected RestClient.Builder (7.01). Each injection point gets its own builder, so a base URL set for the ledger does not leak into the bank client. Then LedgerClient and BankGatewayClient are distinct types, and there is nothing to choose.
  2. When two beans of one type must exist, name the choice at the injection point with @Qualifier.
@Bean
@Qualifier("bank")
RestClient bankRestClient(RestClient.Builder builder, BankProperties props) { ... }

public BankGatewayClient(@Qualifier("bank") RestClient restClient) { ... }
  1. For a family of implementations, inject them all. A List<PayoutRule> parameter receives every PayoutRule bean, sorted by @Order. A Map<String, PayoutRule> receives them keyed by bean name.
  2. Use ObjectProvider<T> when the bean may be missing or there may be several. It offers getIfAvailable(), getIfUnique() and orderedStream().
  3. Keep @Primary for a genuine default that other code, such as an auto-configuration, should pick up without asking.

Spring can also match a parameter name to a bean name, when the code is compiled with -parameters. The Boot parent POM, the pom.xml your build inherits its settings from, sets that flag. Do not rely on it, because renaming a parameter then changes the wiring.

Also seen. A custom qualifier annotation, such as @BankClient, itself annotated with @Qualifier. It is worth it when the same string would repeat in many places. Current Spring also has @Fallback, which marks a bean as the one to use only when no other candidate exists.

When to break it. @Primary on a bean in a test configuration that replaces a production one is fine. So is @Primary on a library bean that services are expected to override. The cost is that the injection point no longer shows which bean arrives.

.NET anchor. Keyed services in .NET 8: AddKeyedSingleton and [FromKeyedServices("bank")] do what @Qualifier does. Typed clients, AddHttpClient<BankGatewayClient>(), are step 1. The defaults differ. Microsoft's container lets the last registration win silently, while Spring refuses to guess and fails at startup.

See also. 7.01, 7.02, 4.01, 4.11, Dependency injection and configuration

4.07 Break a circular dependency properly

Then.

  • Spring era: With field or setter injection, Spring resolved most cycles quietly. It created PayoutService, handed a half-built reference to PayoutSaga, then finished PayoutService. Code from that era often has cycles nobody knows about. Spring Boot now refuses them at startup unless told otherwise, so upgrades of such code fail with a cycle report. Many teams added the escape hatch and moved on.
# added during the Boot upgrade, never removed
spring.main.allow-circular-references=true

Recognise it by. spring.main.allow-circular-references=true, @Lazy on a constructor parameter, setters that exist only to break a cycle, and ApplicationContextAware used to fetch a bean by hand.

The rookie version.

@Service
public class PayoutService {
    public PayoutService(PayoutRepository repository, @Lazy PayoutSaga saga) { ... }
}

@Service
public class PayoutSaga {
    public PayoutSaga(LedgerClient ledger, PayoutService payoutService) { ... }
}

The service started the saga, the saga called back into the service, and @Lazy made the startup error go away.

What goes wrong. Startup had failed with a clear message:

The dependencies of some of the beans in the application context form a cycle:

┌─────┐
|  payoutService defined in file [.../PayoutService.class]
↑     ↓
|  payoutSaga defined in file [.../PayoutSaga.class]
└─────┘

@Lazy injects a stand-in that finds the real bean on its first call, so the startup check passes and any wiring failure moves to the first call. The design stays tangled. The saga retries a step by calling payoutService.pay, which starts a second saga for the same payout. One claim gets 2 sagas and 2 ledger reservations of £1,240.50. Neither class can be unit-tested without the other.

Do this now. Read the cycle as a design review that Spring did for you. Fix it in one of three ways, in this order.

  1. Extract what both need. Usually the saga does not need all of PayoutService, only a way to update a payout's status. Give the saga PayoutRepository directly, or a small PayoutStatusUpdater that both depend on.
  2. Invert one direction with an in-process event (4.13). The saga publishes an event, and the service listens. The dependency then points one way. Such events live only in memory and are lost on a crash, so use this only for work that may be lost, such as a metric. A status change takes option 1.
  3. Merge the two classes, if they are one responsibility that was split only for size.

Let dependencies run one way: from the coordinator to the parts.

@Service
public class PayoutSaga {
    private final LedgerClient ledger;
    private final PayoutRepository payouts;

    public PayoutSaga(LedgerClient ledger, PayoutRepository payouts) {
        this.ledger = ledger;
        this.payouts = payouts;
    }
}
// PayoutService depends on PayoutSaga. PayoutSaga no longer depends on PayoutService.

Also seen. @Lazy on one constructor parameter, or an ObjectProvider<PayoutService> resolved at call time. Both are acceptable as a bridge during a refactor, with a ticket to remove them.

When to break it. A cycle between two library beans you do not own may need @Lazy until the library is fixed. The cost is that a wiring failure now appears on the first call, not at startup.

.NET anchor. Microsoft's container throws InvalidOperationException with "A circular dependency was detected" when it resolves the service. The fix is the same. The Spring-only twist is the old quiet resolution through fields, which .NET never had, and which you will find in inherited code.

See also. 4.01, 4.13, 11.02, 21.01, How Spring actually works

4.08 Know what a Spring proxy does to your bean

Then.

  • Spring era: Proxies declared by hand. TransactionProxyFactoryBean in XML wrapped a target bean, and later <aop:config> and <tx:annotation-driven/> did it by rule. The XML had one virtue: you could see that payoutService was a wrapper around payoutServiceTarget.
<bean id="payoutService"
      class="org.springframework.transaction.interceptor.TransactionProxyFactoryBean">
    <property name="target" ref="payoutServiceTarget"/>
    <property name="transactionAttributes">
        <props><prop key="pay*">PROPAGATION_REQUIRED</prop></props>
    </property>
</bean>
  • Spring era: An interface for every service, PayoutService beside PayoutServiceImpl. Spring proxied through interfaces by default, so a class needed one to be wrapped. Class-based proxies, now the default in Boot, removed that need. The *Impl pairs in old code are often that, not design.

Recognise it by. TransactionProxyFactoryBean, ProxyFactoryBean, <aop:config>, <tx:annotation-driven proxy-target-class="true"/>, @EnableAspectJAutoProxy(proxyTargetClass = true), one-interface-one-*Impl pairs, and $$EnhancerBySpringCGLIB$$ in old stack traces.

The rookie version.

@Component
public class LedgerClient {
    private final RestClient client;   // set in the constructor, omitted

    @CircuitBreaker(name = "ledger")
    public final LedgerReservation reserve(Payout payout) {
        return client.post().uri("/reservations").body(payout)
                .retrieve().body(LedgerReservation.class);
    }
}

A C# habit: seal what you do not mean to be overridden.

What goes wrong. A proxy is a wrapper object Spring puts in front of your bean. Other beans receive the proxy, and it applies annotations such as @CircuitBreaker, @Transactional, @Cacheable and @Async around each call. @CircuitBreaker comes from Resilience4j, Java's counterpart to a Polly circuit breaker (7.05). The code that runs around the call, such as the breaker's logic, is called an aspect, and the technique is AOP, aspect-oriented programming. Spring's usual proxy is a generated subclass of your class, created without running your constructor. A subclass cannot override a final method. So the call runs reserve on the proxy object itself, where client was never set. The first payout after the deploy throws NullPointerException. If the method had touched no fields, it would be worse. It would work, and the breaker would never count a failure. In a ledger outage like the one in The Yard, chapter 11, the breaker would stay closed.

The same silent bypass happens to private and static methods, to calls on this (9.02), and to calls made from a constructor or @PostConstruct. A final class cannot be subclassed at all, and every record is final. Startup then fails with an error that names the class.

Do this now. Respect the subclass, and prove the effect.

  1. Put proxied annotations only on public, non-final methods of a non-final class.
  2. Call them from another bean (9.02).
  3. Do not compare classes. On a proxied bean, getClass() returns a name such as LedgerClient$$SpringCGLIB$$0. Use AopUtils.getTargetClass(bean) and AopUtils.isAopProxy(bean) from org.springframework.aop.support.
  4. Test what the annotation does, not that it is present. The ledger breaker in 7.05 decides nothing before 10 calls, so make a fake ledger fail 10 times, then assert that the breaker is open and that the next call fails without reaching the fake.
  5. Read the stack trace when in doubt. Frames such as CglibAopProxy$DynamicAdvisedInterceptor and the aspect's own frames sit between the caller and your method when the proxy did its work.
  6. A @Configuration class is proxied too, so that one @Bean method calling another returns the shared bean. proxyBeanMethods = false drops that wrapper. Then ask for other beans as parameters instead of calling their methods.

Also seen. AspectJ weaving, at compile time or load time, rewrites the bytecode itself. Final methods and calls on this then work. @EnableTransactionManagement(mode = AdviceMode.ASPECTJ) turns it on for transactions. Choose it only when proxies cannot do the job, because it needs a build plugin or a -javaagent.

When to break it. Making a class final on purpose is legitimate for a pure-logic bean that carries no proxied annotations. The cost arrives the day someone adds @Cacheable: startup fails. That is the right failure, and it is loud.

.NET anchor. Castle DynamicProxy, which Autofac's interceptors use, can intercept only virtual members. Java methods are virtual unless marked final, so the rule flips. In C# you opt in with virtual. In Java you opt out with final, often without knowing you have.

See also. 9.01, 9.02, 7.05, 3.05, The Yard, chapter 15, How Spring actually works

4.09 Run code at startup safely

What goes wrong. PolicyClient warms a cache of 12,000 policies in a @PostConstruct method, which Spring calls once the bean is built. That runs on the bare object before Spring's proxies are ready, so its retry and breaker do not apply. One morning the policy system is down. The call throws, the context fails, and both pods restart in a loop until it returns.

Do this now. Put startup work in an ApplicationRunner bean and call other beans through their proxies.

@Component
class PolicyCacheWarmer implements ApplicationRunner {
    private final PolicyClient policies;

    PolicyCacheWarmer(PolicyClient policies) { this.policies = policies; }

    @Override
    public void run(ApplicationArguments args) {
        policies.warmCache();   // through the proxy: retry and breaker apply
    }
}

Runners run after the context has started and before Boot reports the application ready for traffic. So a runner keeps the pod out of the Service until it finishes, which is right for a warm-up. Work that must not delay traffic belongs in an @EventListener(ApplicationReadyEvent.class) method that hands off to an executor. Keep the warm-up to what the first requests need, inside the startup probe's budget (17.04), because a slow start slows every rollout (18.09). Decide what a failure means. An exception from a runner stops startup, as before. If the cache is optional, catch the exception and log it.

.NET anchor. IHostedService.StartAsync, or a callback on IHostApplicationLifetime.ApplicationStarted.

See also. 4.08, 14.04, 17.04, 18.09

4.10 Fail fast on bad configuration

What goes wrong. The uat ConfigMap is missing payouts.ledger.base-url. The service starts, and readiness is green. The first payout at 09:02 throws deep inside LedgerClient, and 14 payouts fail before anyone looks at the logs.

Do this now. Validate the record when it is bound. Add spring-boot-starter-validation, then annotate the record with @Validated and its components with Bean Validation constraints, the Jakarta annotations such as @NotNull that play the part of .NET's data annotations:

@Validated
@ConfigurationProperties(prefix = "payouts.ledger")
public record LedgerProperties(
        @NotNull URI baseUrl,
        @DefaultValue("1s") Duration connectTimeout,
        @DefaultValue("5s") Duration readTimeout,
        @DefaultValue("3") @Min(0) @Max(5) int maxRetries) {
}

A missing URL or a max-retries of 9 now stops startup with "APPLICATION FAILED TO START". The report names the property, the value and the rule it broke. The new pod never becomes ready, so the rollout stalls while the old pods keep serving (17.06). For a rule that spans two values, such as a connect timeout shorter than the read timeout, throw IllegalArgumentException from the record's compact constructor, the constructor body a record may declare without repeating its parameter list. Binding fails the same way.

.NET anchor. ValidateDataAnnotations() with ValidateOnStart() on the options builder.

See also. 4.02, 6.12, 16.18, 17.06

4.11 Write an auto-configuration for a shared library

Then.

  • Spring era: A shared @Configuration class that each service brought in with @Import(AuditConfig.class), or a shared XML file pulled in with <import resource="classpath:audit-context.xml"/>. It was explicit, and right when each service chose what to switch on.
  • Boot era: Auto-configuration registered in META-INF/spring.factories, under one long key. Current Boot no longer reads auto-configurations from that file.
# META-INF/spring.factories
org.springframework.boot.autoconfigure.EnableAutoConfiguration=\
  com.sorrel.audit.AuditAutoConfiguration

Recognise it by. spring.factories with an EnableAutoConfiguration= key, plain @Configuration classes inside a library, @Import of another team's configuration, and scanBasePackages or @ComponentScan("com.sorrel") that reach into libraries.

The rookie version.

package com.sorrel.audit;

@Component
public class AuditRecorder {
    public AuditRecorder(MongoTemplate mongo) { ... }
}

// and in every service that uses the library:
@SpringBootApplication(scanBasePackages = {"com.sorrel.payouts", "com.sorrel.audit"})

What goes wrong. Every service must know the library's packages. A service that forgets the second package gets no recorder, and nothing says so. A service without MongoDB that adds the package fails to start. No service can supply its own AuditRecorder, because that makes two candidates (4.06). In Payouts the scan also found FakeAuditRecorder, a test helper marked @Primary that had been shipped in the main jar, so every service received it. For 3 weeks, audit records went nowhere.

Do this now. Auto-configuration is a configuration class that Boot applies by itself when its jar is on the classpath, guarded by conditions. A starter is a dependency that brings a library and its auto-configuration together.

  1. Write an @AutoConfiguration class in a package no application scans, with conditions.
@AutoConfiguration(after = MongoDataAutoConfiguration.class)
@ConditionalOnClass(MongoTemplate.class)
@ConditionalOnProperty(prefix = "sorrel.audit", name = "enabled",
        havingValue = "true", matchIfMissing = true)
@EnableConfigurationProperties(AuditProperties.class)
public class AuditAutoConfiguration {

    @Bean
    @ConditionalOnMissingBean
    @ConditionalOnBean(MongoTemplate.class)
    AuditRecorder auditRecorder(MongoTemplate mongo, AuditProperties props) {
        return new MongoAuditRecorder(mongo, props.collection());
    }
}

AuditProperties is a record bound to sorrel.audit.*, as in 4.02. AuditRecorder is now an interface, and MongoAuditRecorder implements it.

  1. List the class, one per line, in src/main/resources/META-INF/spring/org.springframework.boot.autoconfigure.AutoConfiguration.imports.
  2. Keep @ConditionalOnMissingBean on every bean. A service that declares its own AuditRecorder then wins, and the library steps aside.
  3. @ConditionalOnBean is reliable only when your class runs after the one that creates that bean. Name it with @AutoConfiguration(after = ...), as the listing does: in Boot 3.5, MongoDataAutoConfiguration from org.springframework.boot.autoconfigure.data.mongo. In Boot 4, Boot's own auto-configurations moved into per-technology spring-boot-<technology> modules, and that class became DataMongoAutoConfiguration in org.springframework.boot.data.mongodb.autoconfigure.
  4. Publish a sorrel-audit-spring-boot-starter. Names that begin with spring-boot belong to the Spring Boot project.
  5. Test the conditions without starting a service, using ApplicationContextRunner.
new ApplicationContextRunner()
        .withConfiguration(AutoConfigurations.of(AuditAutoConfiguration.class))
        .withPropertyValues("sorrel.audit.enabled=false")
        .run(context -> assertThat(context).doesNotHaveBean(AuditRecorder.class));

Every service's conditions report now lists AuditAutoConfiguration, with the reason it did or did not apply (4.12).

Also seen. An @EnableSorrelAudit annotation that imports the configuration. Choose it when switching the library on should be a visible decision in each service.

When to break it. A library used by one service needs no auto-configuration. A @Bean method in that service is plainer. Auto-configuration has a cost too: every consumer receives behaviour just by depending on a jar (21.07).

.NET anchor. A NuGet package with an AddSorrelAudit() extension method, using TryAddSingleton where Spring uses @ConditionalOnMissingBean. The difference is who calls it. In .NET, Program.cs calls AddSorrelAudit(). In Spring, the jar on the classpath is the call.

See also. 4.12, 1.12, 20.14, 21.07, The Yard, chapter 15, How Spring actually works

4.12 Find out why a bean was or was not created

What goes wrong. A cache experiment adds spring-boot-starter-data-redis. Boot creates a Redis connection factory, and /actuator/health reports DOWN on both pods. Actuator is Boot's set of operational endpoints under /actuator. A developer excludes the Redis auto-configuration to make it green. Two months later the real cache needs it, and nobody remembers why it is off.

Do this now. Ask Spring, then change the cause.

  1. Start with --debug: java -jar payouts-api.jar --debug. With the Maven plugin, run ./mvnw spring-boot:run -Dspring-boot.run.arguments=--debug, because -Ddebug never reaches the forked process. Search the conditions report, Boot's list of every auto-configuration with the condition that applied or skipped it.
  2. On a running pod, read /actuator/conditions and /actuator/beans. Only health is exposed by default, so add them to management.endpoints.web.exposure.include, on an internal port (14.09).
  3. A bean that exists because of a jar: ./mvnw dependency:tree finds who brought the jar in (1.03).
  4. To replace Boot's bean, declare your own. Exclude with spring.autoconfigure.exclude only after reading the condition, with a comment that says why.

See also. 4.11, 1.03, 14.09, The Yard, chapter 15, How Spring actually works

4.13 Use application events inside one service

Then.

  • Spring era: Events extended ApplicationEvent, and listeners implemented ApplicationListener<PayoutEvent>. Any object can be an event now, and any bean method can listen.

What goes wrong. PayoutService publishes an event after the bank accepts an instruction, and a listener updates a dashboard. The listener throws. Listeners run in the publisher's thread, so the exception reaches pay, and a payout the bank accepted is reported as failed. Moved to @Async, the listener loses the event when a pod restarts before handling it, because events live only in memory.

Do this now. Publish a record and listen with @EventListener:

public record PayoutMarkedPaid(String payoutId) {}

publisher.publishEvent(new PayoutMarkedPaid(payout.id()));   // ApplicationEventPublisher

@EventListener
void on(PayoutMarkedPaid event) { paidCounter.increment(); }

The publisher injects ApplicationEventPublisher through its constructor. A plain listener still runs in the publisher's thread, so catch and log inside any listener whose failure must not fail the caller.

Use events to decouple classes in one service (4.07), for work that may be lost. @TransactionalEventListener runs after commit, and only when a transaction is active. Otherwise the event is dropped silently, unless the listener sets fallbackExecution = true. Anything that must survive a crash or reach another service goes through the outbox (9.07).

.NET anchor. MediatR's INotification handlers: in-process and in-memory.

See also. 4.07, 9.07, 3.05, Caching, scheduling and events

4.14 Override configuration in tests

What goes wrong. Someone adds src/test/resources/application.yml. It has the same name as the main file, and test resources come first on the classpath, the list of folders and jars Java loads classes and files from, so it hides the main file completely. For 8 months the tests ran with a 30-second read timeout while production used 2 seconds.

Do this now. Layer test settings on top of the main file, never instead of it.

  • For one test class, use @SpringBootTest(properties = "...") or @TestPropertySource.
  • For values known only at runtime, such as a fake server's port, use @DynamicPropertySource. For Testcontainers, the library that starts Docker containers from a test, @ServiceConnection does this for you on the containers Boot supports.
  • For settings every test shares, use src/test/resources/application-test.yml with @ActiveProfiles("test").
@SpringBootTest(properties = "payouts.ledger.read-timeout=1s")
class LedgerTimeoutTest {
    @RegisterExtension   // a fake ledger on a free port (16.09)
    static WireMockExtension LEDGER = WireMockExtension.newInstance()
            .options(wireMockConfig().dynamicPort()).build();

    @DynamicPropertySource
    static void ledger(DynamicPropertyRegistry registry) {
        registry.add("payouts.ledger.base-url", LEDGER::baseUrl);
    }
}

Each distinct set of properties builds a new Spring context, so keep the sets few (16.07). Replacing beans uses @MockitoBean, because Boot 4 removed @MockBean (16.06).

.NET anchor. WebApplicationFactory<T>.WithWebHostBuilder, with UseSetting or an in-memory configuration source.

See also. 16.06, 16.07, 16.18, 4.03

4.15 Configure a service on Kubernetes through environment variables

What goes wrong. The Deployment sets PAYOUTS_LEDGER_READ_TIMEOUT=2s. Boot reads that as payouts.ledger.read.timeout, which nothing binds, so the 5 seconds from application.yml stays. Nothing warns.

Do this now. To turn a property into an environment variable, replace dots with underscores, remove dashes, and use upper case. payouts.ledger.read-timeout becomes PAYOUTS_LEDGER_READTIMEOUT.

These lines go under the container in the Deployment's pod spec:

env:
  - name: PAYOUTS_LEDGER_BASEURL
    value: "http://ledger.ledger.svc.cluster.local"
  - name: PAYOUTS_LEDGER_READTIMEOUT
    value: "2s"

Environment variables override application.yml, as the diagram in 4.03 shows. Check the result on a running pod through /actuator/configprops, which shows each bound record once it is exposed (4.12). Boot masks the values as ****** unless management.endpoint.configprops.show-values allows them. For a larger block, mount a ConfigMap as a file and point spring.config.additional-location at it.

Kubernetes also injects variables of its own. Each Service in the namespace adds <NAME>_SERVICE_HOST and <NAME>_PORT. A Service called payouts would set PAYOUTS_PORT=tcp://10.0.0.11:80, which Boot binds to payouts.port. Set enableServiceLinks: false in the pod spec if that could collide.

.NET anchor. .NET uses a double underscore, Payouts__Ledger__ReadTimeout, and keeps the rest of the name.

See also. 17.07, 4.02, 4.03, 4.04

4.16 Add a feature flag without a framework

What goes wrong. A flag for the bank's new API is read with @Value("${payouts.features.new-bank-api:false}") in 9 classes. Two of them spell it differently. The new API is fully live a year later, and the flag is still there, alongside 13 others nobody dares to remove.

Do this now. One record holds the flags, and one place branches on each.

@ConfigurationProperties(prefix = "payouts.features")
public record PayoutFeatures(boolean newBankApi) {}

Inject PayoutFeatures where the choice is made. To choose an implementation at startup instead, put @ConditionalOnProperty(name = "payouts.features.new-bank-api", havingValue = "true") on one of two beans of the same interface. Put havingValue = "false", matchIfMissing = true on the other, so that exactly one exists. Changing a flag means changing the ConfigMap and restarting the pods. During the restart both values run at once, so both paths must be safe together. Write the removal date beside the flag when you add it.

Also seen. Unleash, LaunchDarkly or OpenFeature, when a flag must change without a restart, per caller or by percentage.

.NET anchor. Microsoft.FeatureManagement and IFeatureManager.IsEnabledAsync.

See also. 20.05, 4.02, 4.10

⚠Review checklist
  • If you see @Autowired on a private field in production code: dependencies are hidden, the field cannot be final, and a unit test gets nulls. See 4.01.
  • If you see @Value("${...:default}") reading the same key in two classes: defaults and units drift apart, and a misspelt key is hidden by the default. See 4.02.
  • If you see a new application-<environment>.yml copied from application.yml: the files fork and drift. See 4.03.
  • If you see a profile check such as acceptsProfiles in business code: the production path is the one no test runs. See 4.03.
  • If you see a password, token or API key in any YAML or properties file: it stays in git history, and rotating it needs a release. See 4.04.
  • If you see a record holding a secret with no toString() override: one log line prints the secret. See 4.04.
  • If you see @Primary added in the same change as a second bean of that type: it hides which bean each client receives. See 4.06.
  • If you see @Lazy on a constructor parameter, or spring.main.allow-circular-references: a cycle has been papered over. See 4.07.
  • If you see final, private or static on a method that carries @Transactional, @Cacheable, @Async or @CircuitBreaker: the proxy cannot intercept it. See 4.08.
  • If you see a test that asserts an annotation is present: it proves nothing about what happens at runtime. See 4.08.
  • If you see a network call in a @PostConstruct method: it runs before proxies are ready and can stop every pod starting. See 4.09.
  • If you see a @ConfigurationProperties record without @Validated: bad values fail the first request instead of startup. See 4.10.
  • If you see @Component in a shared library, or scanBasePackages naming another team's package: consumers cannot override it or switch it off. See 4.11.
  • If you see spring.autoconfigure.exclude with no comment: nobody will know what it removed or why. See 4.12.
  • If you see an @EventListener doing work that must not be lost or must reach another service: in-memory events vanish on a restart. See 4.13.
  • If you see src/test/resources/application.yml: it hides the main configuration from every test. See 4.14.
  • If you see an environment variable such as PAYOUTS_LEDGER_READ_TIMEOUT, with an underscore where the property has a dash: it binds to nothing. See 4.15.

Part IV · The how-to5. REST API design#

This part is about the HTTP interface of payouts-api: the URLs, methods, status codes and JSON that other teams build against. It shows how Spring MVC routes a request to a controller, how to keep that controller thin, and how to make a POST that moves money safe to send twice. It covers long-running work, pagination, versioning and changes that do not break clients, and the limits every public endpoint needs. Along the way it shows the older styles you will meet: SOAP services, JAX-RS resources, Springfox, Joda-Time in JSON and hand-written DTO mappers.

★What a veteran knows
  • The URLs and the JSON are a contract with clients you cannot see. Whatever you publish will be depended on, including the mistakes.
  • Never return a storage document from a controller. The day you rename a field in the database, you break a client you have never met.
  • Every client retries, whether or not its authors meant it to. A POST that moves money needs an idempotency key from the first release.
  • Additive changes are free and everything else costs a version. Most "v2" APIs could have been one new optional field.
  • Decide the money and time formats on the first day: an amount as a string with a currency, a point in time as an ISO-8601 instant in UTC.
  • A limit you do not set is set for you, by the first client that sends 40 MB or 4,000 requests a minute.
◷How we got hereIn 2000 Roy Fielding finished his doctoral dissertation at UC Irvine.

In 2000 Roy Fielding finished his doctoral dissertation at UC Irvine. Its fifth chapter described an architectural style he called Representational State Transfer, or REST. He defined it by four interface constraints. The last was "hypermedia as the engine of application state": a client finds its next move in the links the server sends back. Within a few years "REST" had come to mean any HTTP interface that returned JSON. On 20 October 2008 Fielding lost patience on his blog. "I am getting frustrated by the number of people calling any HTTP-based interface a REST API," he wrote. Of that day's example he said, "That is RPC. It screams RPC." He asked API authors to follow the constraints "or choose some other buzzword for your API." The word stayed attached to resource URLs, methods and status codes. That everyday sense is the one this part uses, and hypermedia survives mostly in libraries such as Spring HATEOAS.

5.01 Design resource URLs and methods for payouts

Then.

  • J2EE era: SOAP services built with JAX-WS. One URL took every request as a POST, and the operation was named inside an XML envelope described by a WSDL file.
@WebService
public class PayoutWebService {
    @WebMethod
    public PayoutResult createPayout(PayoutRequest request) { ... }
}
  • Spring era: Spring MVC with page-style URLs, one per action, often ending in .do or .htm.
@RequestMapping(value = "/createPayout.do", method = RequestMethod.POST)
public @ResponseBody PayoutResult createPayout(@RequestBody PayoutForm form) { ... }
  • Boot era: JAX-RS resources on Jersey, with @Path and @GET. JAX-RS is the Java standard for REST endpoints, and Jersey is its best-known implementation. The URL design is often fine. Only the annotations differ from Spring MVC.

SOAP was right when enterprise tooling wanted a formal contract and generated clients. Resource URLs replaced it because any HTTP client, cache and proxy understands them without a toolkit.

Recognise it by. javax.jws.WebService and @WebMethod, a .wsdl file under src/main/resources, RequestMethod.POST with a verb in the path, javax.ws.rs.Path, and jersey-server or spring-boot-starter-jersey in the POM. The POM is pom.xml, the build file of Maven, Java's usual build tool, and plays the part of a .csproj. A starter is a Spring Boot dependency that brings in a library together with Boot's automatic setup for it, so one line in the POM is enough.

The rookie version.

@GetMapping("/payouts/{id}/cancel")
PayoutResponse cancel(@PathVariable String id) {
    return PayoutResponse.from(payoutService.cancel(id));
}

@PostMapping("/getPayouts")
List<PayoutResponse> list(@RequestBody PayoutFilter filter) { ... }

What goes wrong. GET is meant to be safe: it reads and changes nothing. Browsers, proxies and link checkers rely on that promise. A monitoring tool that crawls the claims back office follows every link it finds. In one afternoon it cancels 37 pending payouts by fetching their cancel URLs. The POST used for a read has the opposite cost. Nothing can cache it, and a client library will not retry it after a timeout, because a POST might not be safe to repeat.

Do this now. Spring MVC is Spring's web framework. It runs on the Servlet API, Java's standard interface between a web server such as Tomcat and application code, and Boot embeds the Tomcat server in the service. In Spring MVC a controller is a class annotated @RestController. Its methods carry mapping annotations such as @GetMapping and @PostMapping, and Spring routes each request to the method whose path and method match. Whatever the method returns is written as the response body.

  1. Name resources with plural nouns. The collection is /payouts. One member is /payouts/{payoutId}.
  2. Nest only for real ownership, and only one level: /claims/{claimId}/payouts lists one claim's payouts.
  3. Let the HTTP method carry the verb. GET reads. POST creates in a collection. PUT replaces a whole resource, PATCH changes part of it, and DELETE removes it.
  4. Model an action that is not create, read, update or delete as a noun you create. Cancelling a payout is POST /payouts/{id}/cancellation, which returns the cancellation with its own status.
  5. Use lower-case, hyphenated path segments and opaque IDs. Never put an internal key format in a URL you would struggle to change.
@RestController
@RequestMapping("/payouts")
class PayoutController {
    @GetMapping("/{payoutId}")
    PayoutResponse get(@PathVariable String payoutId) { ... }

    @PostMapping
    ResponseEntity<PayoutResponse> create(@RequestBody CreatePayoutRequest body) { ... }

    @PostMapping("/{payoutId}/cancellation")
    ResponseEntity<CancellationResponse> cancel(@PathVariable String payoutId) { ... }
}

@PathVariable binds a segment of the path to a parameter. ResponseEntity is a response with a status, headers and a body, used when the status is not always 200.

Also seen. RPC-style paths such as POST /payouts/{id}:cancel are a reasonable house style when the whole company uses them. gRPC suits internal calls between services with generated clients, at the price of browser and tooling support.

When to break it. A search whose filter is too large for a query string can be a POST to /payouts/searches. The cost is that the result cannot be cached, and the call reads like a write in logs and metrics.

.NET anchor. This is an ASP.NET Core controller with [Route("payouts")], [HttpGet("{id}")] and [HttpPost]. @RestController plays the part of [ApiController] on a ControllerBase, and @PathVariable is [FromRoute].

See also. 5.02, 5.04, 5.06, Controllers, routing and binding

5.02 Keep a controller thin

Then.

  • Spring era: controllers extended framework base classes such as SimpleFormController and returned a ModelAndView, because Spring MVC began as a framework for server-rendered pages.
public class PayoutFormController extends SimpleFormController {
    protected ModelAndView onSubmit(Object command) throws Exception {
        PayoutForm form = (PayoutForm) command;
        payoutDao.save(form.toPayout());
        return new ModelAndView("payoutSaved");
    }
}
  • Spring era: plain classes annotated @Controller, with @ResponseBody on every method, before @RestController combined the two.

The base classes went because annotations let any plain class be a controller, and a plain class is easier to test.

Recognise it by. org.springframework.web.servlet.mvc.SimpleFormController, ModelAndView, a *-servlet.xml file, @Controller with @ResponseBody on each method, and a DAO field in a controller. A DAO, a data access object, is the older name for a class that reads and writes one table or collection.

The rookie version.

@PostMapping("/payouts")
ResponseEntity<?> create(@RequestBody Map<String, Object> body) {
    try {
        var claim = policyClient.claim((String) body.get("claimId"));
        if (!claim.approved()) return ResponseEntity.badRequest().body("not approved");
        var payout = repository.save(Payout.from(body));
        ledgerClient.reserve(payout);
        return ResponseEntity.ok(payout);
    } catch (Exception e) { return ResponseEntity.status(500).body(e.getMessage()); }
}

What goes wrong. The rule "only approved claims are paid" now lives in an HTTP method. Later the team adds an SQS listener that requests payouts from claim events. The rule is not there, and the listener pays 4 unapproved claims, £3,180.00 in all, before anyone notices. Testing the rule needs the web layer and three mocks. The catch turns every failure into a 500 carrying the exception's message, which can include a database host name.

Do this now. A controller does four things, and only these:

  1. Bind the request: path variables, headers and a body record.
  2. Check the shape with Bean Validation, the standard annotations such as @NotBlank that Spring checks when a parameter is marked @Valid (6.01).
  3. Call one method on a service, passing domain types.
  4. Map the result to a response record and a status code.

A service here is an ordinary class annotated @Service, which makes it a bean: an object Spring creates once and injects wherever it is needed. PayoutService holds the rules and knows nothing about HTTP. Failures leave it as exceptions, and one @RestControllerAdvice class turns them into responses (6.03).

@PostMapping
ResponseEntity<PayoutResponse> create(@Valid @RequestBody CreatePayoutRequest body,
                                      @RequestHeader("Idempotency-Key") String key) {
    Payout payout = payoutService.accept(body.toCommand(), key);   // the rules live here
    return ResponseEntity
            .accepted()
            .location(URI.create("/payouts/" + payout.id()))
            .body(PayoutResponse.from(payout));
}

The answer is 202 Accepted, not 201, because the payment itself runs later (5.06). There is a simple test of thinness. Could an SQS listener call the same service method with no changes? If it could, the rule is in the right place.

Also seen. Functional endpoints, built from RouterFunction and HandlerFunction, route requests without annotations. They suit a team that wants routing as plain code. Most Spring MVC code you meet uses annotations.

When to break it. A read-only endpoint that returns one document and applies no rules can call the repository directly. A repository is the interface that Spring Data implements for you to read and save documents (8.01). The cost is small until the first rule arrives. Then someone has to remember to move it.

.NET anchor. It is the same advice as for an ASP.NET Core controller that delegates to an application service or a MediatR handler. @Valid @RequestBody is [FromBody] with model validation. The @RestControllerAdvice does the job of exception-handling middleware or an IExceptionHandler.

See also. 5.03, 6.01, 6.03, 16.04, Controllers, routing and binding

5.03 Map request and response bodies with records, not documents

Then.

  • Spring era: DTO classes with a no-argument constructor, getters and setters, because Jackson, the JSON library Spring uses (5.12), and JSP, Java's old server-rendered page templates, needed JavaBeans: classes of exactly that shape. Libraries such as Dozer copied fields between entity and DTO by reflection.
public class PayoutDto {
    private String claimId;
    private BigDecimal amount;
    public String getClaimId() { return claimId; }
    public void setClaimId(String claimId) { this.claimId = claimId; }
    // ... and the same for every other field
}
  • Boot era: @Data from Lombok, a compiler plug-in that writes getters, setters and constructors from annotations, on the DTO, and ModelMapper to copy fields. Both cut the typing. Both hide the mapping from the compiler, so a renamed field fails at runtime.

Records replaced them. A record is immutable, gets its constructor and accessors for free, and Jackson reads and writes it without setters.

Recognise it by. org.dozer or org.modelmapper.ModelMapper imports, lombok.Data on classes in a dto package, and @JsonIgnore scattered over a @Document class. @Document is the Spring Data MongoDB annotation that maps a class to a DocumentDB collection (8.01).

The rookie version.

@Document("payouts")
public class Payout {
    @Id String id; String claimId;
    BigDecimal amount;
    PayoutStatus status;
    @Version Long version;
    String bankReference;
}
@PostMapping("/payouts")
Payout create(@RequestBody Payout payout) { return repository.save(payout); }

What goes wrong. Three things. A client can send "status": "PAID" in the body, and the save stores it. This is mass assignment: the client sets fields it should never touch. The response also carries version, the optimistic-locking counter (8.05), and the bank's internal bankReference, so clients start to rely on them. And the API is now welded to storage. When the team renames amount to amountPence in DocumentDB, every client of payouts-api breaks on the same deploy.

Do this now. A record is a Java class declared by its components. The compiler writes the constructor, the accessors, equals, hashCode and toString.

  1. Write one record per direction. CreatePayoutRequest holds only what a client may send. PayoutResponse holds only what a client may see.
  2. Map by hand, in a small static method on the record. The compiler then checks every field.
  3. Keep the @Document class in the persistence package, and never let it reach a controller.
public record CreatePayoutRequest(
        @NotBlank String claimId,
        @NotNull @Valid MoneyJson amount) {   // payee left out here (6.01)

    PayoutCommand toCommand() { return new PayoutCommand(claimId, amount.toMoney()); }
}

public record PayoutResponse(String id, String claimId, MoneyJson amount,
                             PayoutStatus status, Instant requestedAt) {
    static PayoutResponse from(Payout p) {
        return new PayoutResponse(p.id(), p.claimId(), MoneyJson.of(p.amount()),
                p.status(), p.requestedAt());
    }
}

MoneyJson is the money record from 5.13. Three types for one payout look like duplication. They are three contracts that change for different reasons: the client's, the stored shape's and the domain's.

Also seen. MapStruct generates mapping code at compile time, so the compiler still checks it. It pays off with dozens of large types. @JsonView shows different fields of one class to different callers. It keeps one type, but every change to that type then risks every view.

When to break it. An internal endpoint that returns a read model built only for that endpoint can return it directly. That type is already a response record in all but name.

.NET anchor. It is the rule against returning an EF Core entity from a controller, and against binding a request to one. A Java record is close to a C# positional record. MapStruct is the compile-time cousin of AutoMapper, closer to Mapperly.

See also. 5.10, 5.13, 6.01, 8.01, Records, Controllers, routing and binding

5.04 Return the right status code

Then.

  • Spring era: the status set by hand on the servlet response, or fixed to an exception class with @ResponseStatus.
@ResponseStatus(HttpStatus.NOT_FOUND)
public class PayoutNotFound extends RuntimeException { }

public void cancel(String id, HttpServletResponse response) {
    response.setStatus(HttpServletResponse.SC_CONFLICT);
}
  • Boot era: client code that reads getStatusCode() on a ResponseEntity or a RestTemplate exception as the HttpStatus enum, or calls getRawStatusCode(). In Spring 6 getStatusCode() returns the HttpStatusCode interface, so a switch on the enum needs changing.

@ResponseStatus on an exception still works. It fell out of favour because it ties a domain exception to HTTP.

Recognise it by. HttpServletResponse.SC_* constants, @ResponseStatus on exception classes, and getRawStatusCode().

The rookie version.

@PostMapping("/payouts")
Map<String, Object> create(@RequestBody CreatePayoutRequest body) {
    try {
        return Map.of("success", true, "payout", payoutService.request(body.toCommand()));
    } catch (ClaimNotApproved e) {
        return Map.of("success", false, "error", "Claim not approved");
    }
}

What goes wrong. Every answer is 200 OK. The claims portal checks the status code, as HTTP clients do, and marks a refused payout as sent. A claimant is told that £1,240.50 is on its way. The dashboard shows a 0% error rate during an outage, because every error is a 200. Other teams' retry logic cannot tell a refused request from a server fault, so it retries neither or both.

Do this now. Payouts uses this table:

Situation Status
A read succeeded 200 OK
A resource was created, and is complete 201 Created, with Location (5.14)
Accepted, the work continues, as for POST /payouts 202 Accepted (5.06)
Succeeded, nothing to return 204 No Content
Malformed JSON or failed validation 400 Bad Request
No token, or an invalid one 401 Unauthorized
A valid token that may not do this 403 Forbidden
No such payout 404 Not Found
Clashes with the current state, such as cancelling a completed payout 409 Conflict
If-Match did not match 412 Precondition Failed (5.11)
Well-formed, but breaks a business rule 422
Too many requests 429, with Retry-After (5.21)
A bug in Payouts 500
A dependency failed or timed out 502, 503 or 504
  1. Return ResponseEntity when the status varies. Return a plain record when it is always 200.
  2. Throw domain exceptions from the service. Map them to statuses in one @RestControllerAdvice, with a ProblemDetail body, Spring's form of the standard JSON error body (6.02, 6.03).
  3. Keep 4xx for "the client must change something" and 5xx for "the client may try again later". Client retry policies depend on that line (7.04). Two 4xx answers are exceptions, and say so with a Retry-After header: 429, and the 409 that 5.05 returns while the first request with the same key is still running. Both mean "send the same request again, later".
  4. Write down whether a broken business rule is 400 or 422. Payouts uses 400 for shape and 422 for rules. Some teams use 400 for both. Either works if every endpoint agrees.

The static builders on ResponseEntity name the common cases: ok(), created(uri), accepted(), noContent(), notFound() and status(...).

Also seen. Some teams return 400 for every client error and let clients tell cases apart by the problem type. It is defensible, and it keeps the table short.

When to break it. A batch endpoint that handles 50 payouts in one call cannot describe 50 outcomes with one status. It returns 200 with a result per item, or 207 Multi-Status. The cost is that every client must read every item.

.NET anchor. These are Ok(), CreatedAtAction(), NotFound(), Conflict() and UnprocessableEntity() on ControllerBase, or TypedResults in minimal APIs. Spring's builders on ResponseEntity do the same job.

See also. 5.14, 6.02, 6.03, 6.14, 7.04, Validation and error responses

5.05 Make POST safe to retry with an Idempotency-Key

Then.

  • Boot era: deduplication on a business key. A unique index on claimId meant a second POST for the same claim failed. It was a good design while one claim had one payout. It broke when partial payouts arrived.
@Indexed(unique = true)
private String claimId;   // one payout per claim, by construction
  • J2EE era: the synchronizer token for HTML forms. The server put a one-time token in a hidden field, so a double-clicked submit button could not post twice. It was the same idea, for browsers only.

Recognise it by. @Indexed(unique = true) on a business field with a comment about duplicates, a hidden token field in old JSP forms, and a requestId field in a request body that nothing checks.

The rookie version.

@PostMapping("/payouts")
ResponseEntity<PayoutResponse> create(@Valid @RequestBody CreatePayoutRequest body) {
    Payout payout = payoutService.request(body.toCommand());   // a new payout every call
    return ResponseEntity.created(URI.create("/payouts/" + payout.id()))
            .body(PayoutResponse.from(payout));
}

What goes wrong. The claims portal posts a payout of £1,240.50. Payouts creates it and instructs the bank. The response is lost when the ingress times out at 30 seconds. The portal's HTTP client retries twice, as configured. The claimant receives £3,721.50, and neither service logged an error. The same happens with no timeout at all, when a pod is restarted between the bank call and the response.

Do this now. The client generates a key for each logical operation and sends it in an Idempotency-Key header. The header name comes from an IETF draft, and payment APIs have used it for years.

  1. Require the header on every POST that creates a payout or moves money. Reject a request without one with 400.
  2. Before doing any work, insert a record into idempotency_keys whose _id is the caller's identity and the key together, with a hash of the body. The _id index is always unique, so two parallel retries cannot both get through (8.16, 9.10).
  3. If the insert succeeds, do the work. Then store the response status and body against the key.
  4. If the key exists with the same body hash and a stored response, return that response again, unchanged.
  5. If it exists with a different body hash, return 422. The client reused a key for a different request.
  6. If it exists with no stored response yet, the first request is still running. Return 409 with Retry-After, and the client retries later.
  7. If the work throws, delete the record, so the client's retry can run. Otherwise every retry gets 409 until the key expires.
  8. Expire keys after a period agreed with clients, 24 hours in Payouts, with a TTL index, an index that deletes documents once they are old enough (8.17).
@PostMapping
ResponseEntity<PayoutResponse> create(@RequestHeader("Idempotency-Key") String key,
                                      @Valid @RequestBody CreatePayoutRequest body,
                                      @AuthenticationPrincipal Jwt caller) {
    return idempotencyKeys.execute(caller.getSubject(), key, body, () -> {
        Payout payout = payoutService.accept(body.toCommand(), key);   // unique on key (8.16)
        return ResponseEntity.accepted().location(URI.create("/payouts/" + payout.id()))
                .body(PayoutResponse.from(payout));
    });
}

@RequestHeader binds a header to a parameter. @AuthenticationPrincipal Jwt gives the validated token of the caller (15.01). idempotencyKeys is a bean of your own, injected through the controller's constructor, and 9.10 shows its execute method. The key also goes into the payout, whose unique index on it (8.16) stops a second payout if a retry ever runs the work twice. This entry is the HTTP contract. The store, its race conditions and what to save are in 9.10.

Also seen. A natural key in the body, such as a claim and instalment number, needs no new header when one exists. PUT /payouts/{clientChosenId} makes creation idempotent under HTTP's own rules, at the cost of trusting clients to generate good IDs.

When to break it. An endpoint whose only caller is an SQS listener that already deduplicates by message ID does not need a second key. The cost arrives with the next caller, which is unprotected.

.NET anchor. ASP.NET Core has no built-in idempotency support either. Teams write an action filter or middleware backed by a store with a unique constraint. The Java version has the same shape: a wrapper around the handler, or a servlet filter.

See also. 7.07, 8.16, 8.17, 9.09, 9.10, The Yard, chapter 11

5.06 Accept long-running work with 202 Accepted and a status resource

Then.

  • Spring era: the request held open for the whole job, with long timeouts set on every proxy in the path.
  • Spring era: Servlet 3 asynchronous requests through DeferredResult or Callable. They free the request thread while the work runs, but the client still waits on the connection. They remain useful for that narrower job.
@PostMapping("/payouts")
public DeferredResult<PayoutResult> create(@RequestBody PayoutForm form) {
    DeferredResult<PayoutResult> result = new DeferredResult<>(120_000L);
    bankGateway.instructAsync(form, result::setResult);
    return result;
}

Recognise it by. DeferredResult, Callable or WebAsyncTask return types on controller methods, spring.mvc.async.request-timeout, and client read timeouts measured in minutes.

The rookie version.

@PostMapping("/payouts")
PayoutResponse create(@Valid @RequestBody CreatePayoutRequest body) {
    Payout payout = payoutService.reserve(body.toCommand());
    BankResult bank = bankGatewayClient.instruct(payout);   // 5 to 40 seconds
    return PayoutResponse.from(payoutService.complete(payout, bank));
}

What goes wrong. The bank gateway answers in 5 to 40 seconds. The claims portal gives up at 30 seconds and shows an error, while the bank goes on to pay. On the busiest morning 1 call in 9 times out, and staff press "pay" again. Each waiting request also holds a thread on one of the 2 pods. During a deploy, a pod that stops mid-call leaves a payout whose outcome nobody recorded.

Do this now.

  1. Validate the request, then save the payout as PENDING and the first state of its saga, in one transaction (11.02).
  2. Return 202 Accepted, a Location header that points at /payouts/{id}, and a Retry-After header with the seconds to wait before asking again.
  3. Run the saga outside the request. A worker in each pod polls payout_sagas for due sagas, claims one, and runs its next step (11.02, 11.07). It moves the payout through RESERVED and INSTRUCTED to PAID or FAILED. Because the saga is a saved document, a pod that stops mid-step loses nothing: another worker picks it up.
  4. Serve GET /payouts/{id} at every stage with 200 and the current status. The resource exists from the first moment, so a client never sees 404 for a payout it was told about.
  5. Offer events for clients that do not want to poll. Payouts publishes PayoutCompleted and PayoutFailed to SNS (10.02).
@PostMapping
ResponseEntity<PayoutResponse> create(@Valid @RequestBody CreatePayoutRequest body,
                                      @RequestHeader("Idempotency-Key") String key) {
    Payout payout = payoutService.accept(body.toCommand(), key);   // saved as PENDING
    return ResponseEntity.accepted()
            .location(URI.create("/payouts/" + payout.id()))
            .header(HttpHeaders.RETRY_AFTER, "5")
            .body(PayoutResponse.from(payout));
}

The idempotency key still matters here (5.05). A lost 202 is retried like any other response. The listing leaves out 5.05's idempotencyKeys.execute wrapper for space. In Payouts this call runs inside it.

Also seen. A separate job resource, such as /payout-requests/{id}, that links to the payout when it is done. It suits work whose result is a different resource. Callbacks to a client's URL suit outside partners. Server-sent events suit a browser that watches one job.

When to break it. If the work finishes well inside a second, even at the slowest percentile you measure, return 201 with the finished resource. The cost of 202 is a polling client, and a status field that every client must handle.

.NET anchor. It is Accepted() or AcceptedAtAction() in ASP.NET Core, with a queue and a BackgroundService doing the work. Neither framework has a built-in job abstraction. In Payouts the saga document is the job.

See also. 5.05, 5.14, 9.13, 10.02, 11.02, 17.05

5.07 Paginate a large collection

Then.

  • Boot era: Spring Data's Pageable and Page<T>, bound from ?page=3&size=20 and returned straight from the controller. Spring Data is the library that writes repository implementations from interfaces. Offset pages are still fine for small collections. Returning Page itself as JSON is not, because its JSON shape is an internal detail. Recent Spring Data versions log a warning when it happens.
@GetMapping("/payouts")
public Page<Payout> list(Pageable pageable) {
    return repository.findAll(pageable);
}
  • Boot era: Spring HATEOAS's PagedResourcesAssembler, which wrapped a Page and added next and prev links.

Recognise it by. org.springframework.data.domain.Pageable as a controller parameter, Page<...> as a return type, JSON with content, pageable and totalElements, and a logged warning about serialising PageImpl.

The rookie version.

@GetMapping("/payouts")
List<PayoutResponse> list(@RequestParam PayoutStatus status) {
    return repository.findByStatus(status).stream()
            .map(PayoutResponse::from)
            .toList();
}

What goes wrong. In the first month ?status=PAID returns 900 payouts. A year later it returns 180,000. One call reads every match into the pod's heap, builds 180,000 records and serialises them. The pod has a 512 MiB memory limit, and Kubernetes kills it for going over, which it reports as OOMKilled (17.09). The client retries and takes out the second pod. Offset pages fail more slowly. Skipping reads and discards every earlier document (8.08). Inserts between two calls shift the pages, so a client sees one payout twice or misses another.

Do this now. Use keyset pagination, also called cursor pagination: each page starts after the last item of the one before.

  1. Sort on a unique, indexed key, here requestedAt and then _id, with an index on {status: 1, requestedAt: 1, _id: 1} (8.06). Because requestedAt alone can tie, "after" means a later requestedAt, or the same one with a later _id. 8.08 builds that filter.
  2. Accept a limit, with a default and a maximum that you enforce.
  3. Return the items and a next cursor. The cursor is an opaque string that encodes the last item's sort key, such as Base64 of a small JSON object. Opaque means clients pass it back and never build it.
  4. The next request sends ?cursor=..., and the query asks for items after that key, using the index.
  5. Leave out the total count. Counting 180,000 documents on every page is a second query nobody needs.
public record PayoutPage(List<PayoutResponse> items, String next) { }

@GetMapping
PayoutPage list(@RequestParam PayoutStatus status,
                @RequestParam(required = false) String cursor,
                @RequestParam(defaultValue = "50") @Min(1) @Max(100) int limit) {
    PageCursor after = PageCursor.decode(cursor);              // null on the first page
    List<Payout> found = payoutService.findAfter(status, after, limit + 1);
    boolean more = found.size() > limit;
    List<Payout> page = more ? found.subList(0, limit) : found;
    return new PayoutPage(page.stream().map(PayoutResponse::from).toList(),
            more ? PageCursor.of(page.getLast()).encode() : null);
}
