Asking for one more item than the limit tells you whether a next page exists, without a count. @Min(1) matters: with limit=0 and one match, the page is empty but more is true, so getLast() throws and the client gets a 500. Spring MVC checks these constraints on the parameters itself, with no @Validated on the class (6.05).

Also seen. Page with a total, for an admin screen with page numbers over a few thousand rows. Spring Data's Slice fetches one extra row like the listing above and skips the count. Spring Data's Window and ScrollPosition do keyset scrolling inside repository methods. A Link header with rel="next" carries the cursor in a header instead of the body.

When to break it. A collection that is small by nature, such as one claim's payouts, can be returned whole. Write the bound into the API documentation, and cap it in code anyway.

.NET anchor. It is the choice between Skip().Take() and keyset pagination in EF Core, with the same costs. Pageable resembles a paged-list helper bound from the query string.

See also. 5.08, 8.06, 8.08, 17.09, Document data: Amazon DocumentDB and the MongoDB API

5.08 Filter and sort through query parameters safely

What goes wrong. GET /payouts?sort=bankReference is passed straight to Spring Data's Sort.by(sort). A client can now sort 180,000 payouts on a field with no index, and 3 such calls a minute slow every other query on the collection. A filter that copies parameter names into a query lets clients filter on fields you never meant to expose, or slip in query operators such as $ne (15.08).

Do this now.

  1. Bind each filter as a typed @RequestParam: an enum for the status, an Instant for a date. Spring converts the value and answers 400 when it cannot.
  2. Model the sort as an enum of allowed orders, each backed by an index.
  3. Build the query in the repository from those types, never from raw strings.
enum PayoutSort { REQUESTED_AT_DESC, REQUESTED_AT_ASC, AMOUNT_DESC }

@GetMapping
PayoutPage list(
        @RequestParam(required = false) PayoutStatus status,
        @RequestParam(required = false)
        @DateTimeFormat(iso = DateTimeFormat.ISO.DATE_TIME) Instant from,
        @RequestParam(defaultValue = "REQUESTED_AT_DESC") PayoutSort sort,
        @RequestParam(required = false) String cursor) { ... }

See also. 5.07, 6.05, 8.06, 15.08

5.09 Version an API without breaking clients

Then.

  • Boot era: the version in a custom media type, selected with produces.
@GetMapping(value = "/payouts/{id}",
            produces = "application/vnd.sorrel.payout.v2+json")
public PayoutV2 getV2(@PathVariable String id) { ... }

It follows HTTP's design closely. It lost ground because browsers, curl users and gateways rarely set an Accept header, and caches need Vary: Accept to keep the versions apart.

  • Spring era: a whole copy of the application per version, payouts-v1.war and payouts-v2.war, deployed side by side on one application server.

Recognise it by. application/vnd. in a produces attribute, an X-API-Version header checked in a filter, and v1 and v2 packages holding near-identical controllers.

The rookie version.

// Before: public record PayoutResponse(String id, BigDecimal amount, ...)
public record PayoutResponse(String id, MoneyJson amount, PayoutStatus status) { }

What goes wrong. amount changes in place from a number to an object, {"value": "1240.50", "currency": "GBP"}. Payouts' own tests pass, because they were updated in the same pull request. The claims portal and the finance export both read amount as a number. Both break at 09:00 on deploy day, and the rollback takes 25 minutes. The opposite mistake is common too: a new version for every change. Two years later Payouts runs v1 to v6, and nobody knows who still calls v2.

Do this now.

  1. Avoid new versions. Most changes can be additive (5.10), and an additive change needs no version.
  2. When a change cannot be additive, add the new shape beside the old one in the same version. Add amountMoney next to amount, move clients across, then remove amount (20.01).
  3. Start a new major version only when the resource itself changes meaning. Payouts puts the major version in the path, as in /v2/payouts. It shows in every log line, routes easily at the ingress and is easy to try with curl. The first release had no version in its paths, so /payouts keeps working as v1, as the listing shows.
  4. Serve both versions from one service layer. The v1 controller maps the same domain object to the v1 response record.
  5. Count v1 calls per client (14.02). Agree a date, send Deprecation and Sunset headers, then remove v1 (20.06).
@RestController
@RequestMapping({"/payouts", "/v1/payouts"})   // the unversioned path stays v1
class PayoutControllerV1 {
    @GetMapping("/{id}")
    PayoutResponseV1 get(@PathVariable String id) {
        return PayoutResponseV1.from(payoutService.get(id));   // same service, old shape
    }
}

In Boot 4, Spring Framework 7 adds built-in API versioning. The mapping annotations gain a version attribute, such as @GetMapping(version = "2"). The ApiVersionConfigurer passed to WebMvcConfigurer.configureApiVersioning, or the spring.mvc.apiversion.use.* properties, says whether the version arrives in a path segment, a header, a query parameter or a media type parameter. On Boot 3.5 you write the version into the path yourself, as above.

Also seen. A version header such as API-Version: 2 keeps URLs clean, but the version is invisible in a browser and in most access logs. Media-type versioning works as in Then. Date-based versions pinned per client, as some large public APIs use, need a translation layer for every version.

When to break it. A breaking change with exactly one known client can be made in place, on a date agreed with that team. The cost is a coordinated deploy, and any client you did not know about breaks with no warning.

.NET anchor. It is Asp.Versioning.Mvc, formerly Microsoft.AspNetCore.Mvc.Versioning, with [ApiVersion("2.0")] and readers for the URL segment, a header or the media type. Framework 7's versioning offers the same choices.

See also. 5.10, 14.02, 16.16, 20.01, 20.06, Migrating Spring Boot 3 to 4

5.10 Make backward-compatible changes to JSON

Then.

  • Boot era: @JsonIgnoreProperties(ignoreUnknown = true) on every class a client read, because the client's mapper was set to fail on any field it did not know. Setting that once on the shared mapper (5.12) made the annotation unnecessary.
@JsonIgnoreProperties(ignoreUnknown = true)
public class LedgerEntryDto { ... }
  • Spring era: XML validated against an XSD, where a new element broke a strict validator. Teams added xs:any extension points to leave room for growth.

Recognise it by. @JsonIgnoreProperties(ignoreUnknown = true) on many classes, DeserializationFeature.FAIL_ON_UNKNOWN_PROPERTIES in a mapper setup, and xs:any in an .xsd file.

The rookie version.

public enum PayoutStatus { PENDING, RESERVED, INSTRUCTED, PAID, FAILED, CANCELLED }
// CANCELLED added on Tuesday. Consumers read status into their own copy of the enum.

public record PayoutResponse(String id, String claimantName, PayoutStatus status) { }
// claimantName was called payeeName until this release.

What goes wrong. Adding an enum value looks additive, and it is not. The notification service has its own copy of PayoutStatus. Its copy was written before CANCELLED existed, and the first cancelled payout makes its JSON reader throw. The message lands in notify-claimant-dlq, and 212 claimants get no letter. The rename is worse. Every client that reads payeeName now gets null and prints an empty name on the letter.

Do this now. These changes are safe for clients:

  • adding an optional field to a response
  • adding an optional field to a request, with a default when it is absent
  • adding a new endpoint, or a new optional query parameter

These break clients:

  • removing or renaming a field, or changing its type or format
  • making an optional request field required, or changing what a value means
  • adding an enum value, unless clients were told to expect new ones

Four habits make the safe list longer:

  1. Make every client a tolerant reader, one that ignores fields it does not know. Configure that once on the mapper (5.12), and test it (16.17).
  2. Treat enums in responses as open, and say so in the API documentation. In your own Java clients, map unknown values to a fallback with @JsonEnumDefaultValue. The annotation does nothing until the mapper has DeserializationFeature.READ_UNKNOWN_ENUM_VALUES_USING_DEFAULT_VALUE on, which on Boot 3.5 is spring.jackson.deserialization.read-unknown-enum-values-using-default-value: true.
  3. Rename by expanding, then contracting. Write both names for a while, accept both with @JsonAlias, and drop the old one when no client reads it (20.01).
  4. Run each consumer's contract test in your build (16.16). A breaking change then fails your build, not theirs.
// A consumer's copy, older than CANCELLED, with a fallback for values it has not seen
public enum PayoutStatus {
    PENDING, RESERVED, INSTRUCTED, PAID, FAILED,
    @JsonEnumDefaultValue UNKNOWN
}

// The provider, while a field is being renamed
public record CreatePayoutRequest(
        String claimId,
        @JsonAlias("payeeName") String claimantName,   // the old name is still accepted
        MoneyJson amount) { }

Also seen. A JSON Schema for each response, compared in CI against the last release. Avro or Protobuf with a schema registry for events, where tooling checks compatibility (20.02).

When to break it. Before the first client exists, change anything. After that, the only clean break is a new version (5.09).

.NET anchor. System.Text.Json ignores unknown properties unless told otherwise, and JsonStringEnumConverter throws on an enum name it does not know. That is the same trap as a closed Java enum. @JsonAlias has no direct System.Text.Json equivalent.

See also. 5.09, 5.12, 10.12, 16.16, 16.17, 20.01, 20.02

5.11 Handle concurrent edits over HTTP with ETag and If-Match

What goes wrong. Two back-office users open payout p-81 for £1,240.50. One corrects the sort code. A minute later the other corrects the amount to £1,204.50 from a stale copy and PUTs the whole payout. The sort-code fix is silently undone, and the bank rejects the payment two days later.

Do this now. The payout document already has an @Version number for optimistic locking (8.05). Expose it as an ETag, a response header that names one version of a resource, such as ETag: "7".

  1. Send the ETag on every GET and every write.
  2. Require If-Match: "7" on PUT and PATCH. Answer 428 Precondition Required when it is missing.
  3. Pass the expected version to the update. If the stored version has moved on, answer 412 Precondition Failed. The client re-reads and tries again.
@PutMapping("/{id}")
ResponseEntity<PayoutResponse> replace(@PathVariable String id,
        @RequestHeader(value = HttpHeaders.IF_MATCH, required = false) String ifMatch,
        @Valid @RequestBody UpdatePayoutRequest body) {
    if (ifMatch == null) return ResponseEntity.status(HttpStatus.PRECONDITION_REQUIRED).build();
    long expected = Long.parseLong(ifMatch.replace("\"", ""));
    Payout saved = payoutService.update(id, expected, body.toChange());   // 412 on mismatch
    return ResponseEntity.ok().eTag(String.valueOf(saved.version()))
            .body(PayoutResponse.from(saved));
}

A bare parseLong turns * or a weak W/"7" into a 500. Payouts puts the check and the parsing in one helper, IfMatch.version, which 5.17 reuses. Spring's older ShallowEtagHeaderFilter hashes a response body to save bandwidth on GET. It cannot protect a write.

See also. 5.17, 8.05, 9.11, The Yard, chapter 8

5.12 Configure Jackson once for the whole service

What goes wrong. A developer writes new ObjectMapper() in LedgerClient to parse one response. That mapper has none of the service's settings or modules. On Boot 3.5 it has no java.time support, so the first Instant throws. It may also fail on a field the ledger added last week. The client works in tests with old fixtures and fails in production.

Do this now. Jackson is the JSON library Spring MVC uses to read request bodies and write responses. Boot builds one ObjectMapper with its modules and your settings.

  1. Inject that ObjectMapper wherever you need one.
  2. Set service-wide choices under spring.jackson.* in application.yml.
  3. Put anything a property cannot express in one customizer bean: a @Bean method that returns a lambda, which Boot calls while it builds the mapper. On Boot 3.5 it is a Jackson2ObjectMapperBuilderCustomizer, such as builder -> builder.featuresToEnable(...). In Boot 4 it is a JsonMapperBuilderCustomizer, and Jackson 3's packages move from com.fasterxml.jackson to tools.jackson. Some keys move too: the date setting below becomes spring.jackson.datatype.datetime.write-dates-as-timestamps, and Jackson 3 already has it off.
# Boot 3.5 keys
spring:
  jackson:
    default-property-inclusion: non_null
    deserialization:
      fail-on-unknown-properties: false
    serialization:
      write-dates-as-timestamps: false

See also. 5.10, 5.13, 16.17, Migrating Spring Boot 3 to 4

5.13 Serialise money and dates in JSON

Then.

  • Spring era: java.util.Date written as milliseconds since 1970, or with a pattern on each field, and amounts held as double.
@JsonFormat(shape = JsonFormat.Shape.STRING, pattern = "dd/MM/yyyy HH:mm")
private Date requestedAt;
private double amount;
  • Boot era: Joda-Time's DateTime, written through the jackson-datatype-joda module. Joda-Time was the right answer before Java 8. Java 8 brought java.time, designed by Joda-Time's author, and Joda-Time's own site asks users to migrate.

Recognise it by. java.util.Date or org.joda.time.DateTime fields, jackson-datatype-joda in the POM, double or float amounts, and @JsonFormat(pattern = ...) with no time zone.

The rookie version.

public record PayoutResponse(String id, double amount, LocalDateTime requestedAt) { }
// {"id":"p-81","amount":1240.5,"requestedAt":"2026-03-29T01:30:00"}

What goes wrong. A double cannot hold most decimal fractions exactly. In Java, 0.1 + 0.2 is 0.30000000000000004. The finance export adds 10,000 payouts as doubles and is out by £0.03 against the ledger. JavaScript reads every JSON number as a double too, so even a correct BigDecimal on the server can lose digits in a browser. 1240.5 has also lost its trailing zero and says nothing about the currency. LocalDateTime has no time zone. Is 01:30 in GMT or in British Summer Time? On 29 March 2026 the clocks in London jumped from 01:00 to 02:00, so 01:30 London time never happened that day.

Do this now.

  1. Write an amount as a string, with an ISO 4217 currency code beside it: "amount": {"value": "1240.50", "currency": "GBP"}. A string passes through every JSON parser unchanged.
  2. In Java, hold the amount as a BigDecimal at the currency's scale, inside the Money value type (2.01). Map it to a JSON record at the edge.
  3. Write a point in time as an Instant, which Jackson writes in ISO-8601 in UTC, such as "2026-03-29T00:30:00Z". Keep a zone only where the business needs local time, in a separate ZoneId field.
  4. Write a date without a time, such as a claim's incident date, as a LocalDate: "2026-03-28".
  5. Tell Jackson to write dates as strings, not numbers, once for the service (5.12). On Jackson 2, java.time support comes from the jackson-datatype-jsr310 module, which Boot 3.5 registers for you.
public record MoneyJson(
        @NotNull @DecimalMin("0.01") @Digits(integer = 9, fraction = 2)
        @JsonFormat(shape = JsonFormat.Shape.STRING) BigDecimal value,
        @NotNull @Pattern(regexp = "[A-Z]{3}") String currency) {

    static MoneyJson of(Money m) {
        return new MoneyJson(m.amount(), m.currency().getCurrencyCode());
    }

    Money toMoney() { return new Money(value, Currency.getInstance(currency)); }
}

@JsonFormat(shape = STRING) makes Jackson write the BigDecimal as "1240.50". On the way in, Jackson reads either a string or a number into it, so clients that still send numbers keep working. Currency.getInstance throws IllegalArgumentException for a code that fits the pattern but does not exist, such as XYZ. Catch it in toMoney and throw a validation exception of your own, which the advice answers with 400 (6.03). Otherwise the catch-all answers 500.

Also seen. Integer minor units, such as "amountPence": 124050, as several payment providers use. It is exact and simple, but every client must know each currency's number of decimal places. Epoch seconds suit high-volume telemetry, where size matters more than reading the value by eye.

When to break it. An outside partner's API dictates its own format. Match it in the client for that partner only (7.01), and keep your own API in yours.

.NET anchor. C# decimal is the money type, and System.Text.Json writes it as a JSON number, so the browser-precision risk is the same. JsonNumberHandling.WriteAsString is the fix there. Instant is a DateTimeOffset in UTC. LocalDateTime is a DateTime with DateTimeKind.Unspecified, with the same ambiguity.

See also. 2.01, 2.02, 5.12, 8.10, Numbers, money and time

5.14 Return a Location header for a created resource

What goes wrong. POST /payouts returns 202 and a body, but no Location. The claims portal builds each payout's URL itself, from "/payouts/" + id. When Payouts moves to /v2/payouts, every link in the portal returns 404. Tools that follow Location after a create find nothing to follow.

Do this now. Send Location with the URL of the new resource on every 201 Created and every 202 Accepted. Build it from the current request, so path prefixes and versions stay right.

URI location = ServletUriComponentsBuilder.fromCurrentRequest()
        .path("/{id}")
        .buildAndExpand(payout.id())
        .toUri();
return ResponseEntity.created(location).body(PayoutResponse.from(payout));

For a 202, pass the same URI to ResponseEntity.accepted().location(location). The listings earlier in this part write URI.create("/payouts/" + id) to stay short. That hard-codes the prefix this entry warns about, so use the builder in real code.

Behind an ingress, an absolute URL uses the host and scheme the pod sees, unless Spring trusts the proxy's X-Forwarded-* headers. Boot turns that on for some platforms it detects. Set server.forward-headers-strategy to native or framework explicitly, so the behaviour does not depend on detection. A relative URI, which HTTP allows, avoids the question.

See also. 5.04, 5.06, 5.09

5.15 Document the API with OpenAPI

Then.

  • Boot era: Springfox, which generated Swagger 2 documents from Spring MVC controllers.
@Configuration @EnableSwagger2
public class SwaggerConfig {
    @Bean
    public Docket api() {
        return new Docket(DocumentationType.SWAGGER_2).select()
                .apis(RequestHandlerSelectors.basePackage("com.sorrel.payouts")).build();
    }
}
  • Boot era: Swagger 2 annotations such as @Api, @ApiOperation and @ApiModelProperty, from io.swagger.annotations.

Springfox was the usual way to get Swagger UI on a Spring service for years. Its releases stopped before the move to jakarta.* packages, so it does not run on Boot 3. springdoc-openapi replaced it, reading the same controllers and producing OpenAPI 3.

Recognise it by. io.springfox in the POM, @EnableSwagger2, a Docket bean, io.swagger.annotations.* imports, and a swagger.json that begins "swagger": "2.0".

The rookie version.

# docs/payouts-api.yaml, written by hand, last edited a year ago
paths:
  /payouts:
    post:
      requestBody:
        content:
          application/json:
            schema: { $ref: '#/components/schemas/Payout' }   # amount: number

What goes wrong. The file says amount is a number. The code has sent a money object since last spring. A new team generates a client from the file. It fails on the first response, and they lose two days finding out that the documentation is wrong, not their code. The opposite mistake also happens: a document generated from the @Document class (5.03), which publishes version and bankReference to every reader.

Do this now. OpenAPI is a standard JSON or YAML description of every path, parameter, body and response of an HTTP API. Swagger UI is a browsable page built from it.

  1. Add springdoc-openapi's Web MVC starter, org.springdoc:springdoc-openapi-starter-webmvc-ui. It reads your controllers and records and serves the document and Swagger UI.
  2. Describe what the code cannot say. @Operation gives an endpoint a summary. @ApiResponse lists each status it returns. @Schema adds descriptions and examples to record components. @Tag groups endpoints.
  3. Document the error body, the Idempotency-Key header and the security scheme. springdoc cannot infer them.
  4. Generate the document in the build and commit it. springdoc's Maven plugin, org.springdoc:springdoc-openapi-maven-plugin, does this: the Spring Boot Maven plugin's start goal runs the service during the build, and the plugin fetches the document from it and saves it as a file. A pull request then shows every contract change as a diff, and a reviewer can ask whether it is additive (5.10).
  5. Turn Swagger UI off in production with springdoc.swagger-ui.enabled=false, and the JSON document with springdoc.api-docs.enabled=false, or put both behind authentication.
@Operation(summary = "Request a payout for an approved claim")
@ApiResponse(responseCode = "202", description = "Accepted, poll the Location URL")
@ApiResponse(responseCode = "409", description = "Same Idempotency-Key, still running")
@ApiResponse(responseCode = "422", description = "Claim not approved, or key reused")
@PostMapping
ResponseEntity<PayoutResponse> create(
        @Parameter(required = true) @RequestHeader("Idempotency-Key") String key,
        @Valid @RequestBody CreatePayoutRequest body) { ... }

public record PayoutResponse(
        @Schema(example = "p-81") String id,
        @Schema(description = "Where the payout's saga has got to") PayoutStatus status) { }

Each springdoc line is built for one Boot generation. Check springdoc's compatibility notes before the Boot 4 upgrade, and move to the release line built for it.

Also seen. Contract-first, where the YAML is the source and code is generated from it (5.16). Spring REST Docs builds documentation from tests, so every documented example is a passing test.

When to break it. An endpoint with one internal caller, such as an admin action (5.22), can stay out of the published document with @Hidden. The cost is that the next person to need it must read the code.

.NET anchor. springdoc is Swashbuckle, or Microsoft.AspNetCore.OpenApi in recent .NET versions. @Operation and @ApiResponse do the work of [EndpointSummary] and [ProducesResponseType].

See also. 5.03, 5.10, 5.16, 16.16, Controllers, routing and binding

5.16 Choose contract-first or code-first

What goes wrong. Neither choice fails on its own. Mixing them does. Payouts starts code-first. Then another team hands over a YAML file "as the contract". Nobody owns it, the code drifts away from it, and within a month two descriptions of one API disagree.

Do this now. Pick one per API, and write it down.

  • Code-first: controllers and records are the source, and springdoc generates the document (5.15). Choose it when one team owns both the API and its main client.
  • Contract-first: the OpenAPI YAML is the source, reviewed before any code. openapi-generator-maven-plugin generates Java interfaces at build time, and the controller implements them. Choose it when several teams or an outside partner must agree the shape first.
<plugin>
  <groupId>org.openapitools</groupId>
  <artifactId>openapi-generator-maven-plugin</artifactId>
  <version>${openapi-generator.version}</version>
  <executions><execution><goals><goal>generate</goal></goals></execution></executions>
  <configuration>
    <inputSpec>${project.basedir}/api/payouts-api.yaml</inputSpec>
    <generatorName>spring</generatorName>
    <configOptions>
      <interfaceOnly>true</interfaceOnly>
      <useSpringBoot3>true</useSpringBoot3>
    </configOptions>
  </configuration>
</plugin>

The plugin goes inside <build><plugins> in the POM, and openapi-generator.version is a property you set in its <properties> block. useSpringBoot3 makes the generated code import jakarta.*, which Boot 3 needs. The generated code also needs the libraries it imports, such as org.openapitools:jackson-databind-nullable, as ordinary dependencies.

Either way, check the published document in CI against the last release, so a breaking change fails the build (16.16).

See also. 5.15, 16.16, 1.01

5.17 Support PATCH without wiping fields

What goes wrong. PATCH /payouts/p-81 arrives with {"sortCode": "40-11-62"} and is bound to a record. Every other component is null. The service copies every field across, and the payout loses its claimant name and reference. A record cannot tell "absent" from "sent as null".

Do this now. Use JSON Merge Patch: the body lists only the fields to change, and the content type is application/merge-patch+json.

  1. Bind the body as a Jackson JsonNode, a tree that records which fields were present.
  2. Allow a fixed set of fields, and reject any other with 400.
  3. Apply each present field through the service, then validate the result as a whole.
  4. Require If-Match (5.11).
static final Set<String> PATCHABLE = Set.of("sortCode", "reference");
@PatchMapping(path = "/{id}", consumes = "application/merge-patch+json")
ResponseEntity<PayoutResponse> patch(@PathVariable String id, @RequestBody JsonNode body,
        @RequestHeader(value = HttpHeaders.IF_MATCH, required = false) String ifMatch) {
    body.fieldNames().forEachRemaining(f -> { if (!PATCHABLE.contains(f)) throw new InvalidPatch(f); });
    var change = new PayoutChange(text(body, "sortCode"), text(body, "reference"));
    Payout saved = payoutService.patch(id, IfMatch.version(ifMatch), change);   // 428, 412 (5.11)
    return ResponseEntity.ok().eTag(String.valueOf(saved.version())).body(PayoutResponse.from(saved));
}
static Optional<String> text(JsonNode body, String field) {   // empty when absent
    JsonNode value = body.get(field);
    if (value == null) return Optional.empty();
    if (!value.isTextual()) throw new InvalidPatch(field);   // null or not a string: 400
    return Optional.of(value.asText());
}

The header is optional so that a missing one gets 5.11's 428, not Spring's 400. In merge patch a null value means "remove this field". Neither field may be removed, so the listing refuses it, rather than let asText() return the string "null". In Boot 4, Jackson 3 renames isTextual() and asText() to isString() and asString(), and keeps the old names as deprecated.

JSON Patch, a list of operations such as replace and remove, suits clients that edit arrays.

See also. 5.03, 5.11, 6.10

5.18 Compress and cache responses

What goes wrong. A developer adds Cache-Control: max-age=300 to GET /payouts/{id} to speed up the claims portal. For 5 minutes after a payout completes, the portal shows it as PENDING, and staff pay it again by hand. A shared proxy could also serve one claimant's payout to the next caller.

Do this now.

  1. Compress at the ingress where you can. Otherwise turn on Boot's compression with server.compression.enabled=true and list the types in server.compression.mime-types. Responses below server.compression.min-response-size are left alone.
  2. Mark personal and fast-changing data Cache-Control: no-store. Payouts are both. Spring Security adds headers that stop caching by default, but a Cache-Control your code sets replaces them, so do not set one on payouts.
  3. Cache only public, slow-changing data, such as the list of supported currencies. Send max-age and an ETag, so clients can revalidate with If-None-Match and get 304 Not Modified. Spring MVC sends the 304 itself when a GET's If-None-Match matches the ETag on the ResponseEntity you return.
return ResponseEntity.ok()
        .cacheControl(CacheControl.maxAge(Duration.ofHours(1)).cachePublic())
        .eTag(currencies.version())
        .body(currencies.all());

See also. 5.11, 7.13, 18.08

5.19 Upload and download files

Then.

  • Spring era: Apache Commons FileUpload through CommonsMultipartResolver. The servlet container's own multipart support replaced it.

What goes wrong. A claim-evidence endpoint reads each upload with file.getBytes(). Ten claimants upload 25 MB videos at once. That is 250 MB of byte arrays, and the copies the code makes on the way to S3 double it, on a pod with a 512 MiB limit. A download built as a byte[] does the same in reverse.

Do this now.

  1. Accept a MultipartFile with @RequestPart, and stream it with getInputStream() to its destination, usually S3.
  2. Cap sizes with spring.servlet.multipart.max-file-size and max-request-size (5.20).
  3. Check the type from the bytes, not the file name. Never use the client's file name as a path.
  4. Stream downloads as a Resource or StreamingResponseBody, with Content-Disposition: attachment.
  5. For large files, return an S3 pre-signed URL, and let the client talk to S3 directly. S3Presigner, from the AWS SDK for Java, signs a URL that lets whoever holds it upload or download one object for a limited time.
@GetMapping("/{id}/remittance")
ResponseEntity<StreamingResponseBody> remittance(@PathVariable String id) {
    return ResponseEntity.ok()
            .contentType(MediaType.APPLICATION_PDF)
            .header(HttpHeaders.CONTENT_DISPOSITION,
                    ContentDisposition.attachment().filename(id + ".pdf").build().toString())
            .body(out -> remittances.writePdf(id, out));
}

See also. 5.20, Files and I/O

5.20 Limit request size and time

What goes wrong. POST /payouts/batches accepts any body. A client bug sends a 40 MB JSON array. Jackson builds it all in memory, two such requests arrive together, and the pod is OOMKilled. With no time limits, a slow client that trickles bytes holds a request thread for minutes.

Do this now.

  1. Cap body size at the ingress first, such as with the NGINX ingress annotation nginx.ingress.kubernetes.io/proxy-body-size.
  2. Cap uploads in Boot with the multipart properties, and headers with server.max-http-request-header-size. Neither caps a JSON body. Failing the ingress, a servlet filter can refuse a large Content-Length with 413.
  3. Bound what Jackson accepts. Its StreamReadConstraints limit string length, number length and nesting depth. Set them on the shared mapper's factory, in the customizer from 5.12. Cap collection sizes in request records with @Size(max = 100). It runs after Jackson has read the body, so it saves no memory.
  4. Bound time where it is spent: the server's connection timeout, which limits the wait between bytes rather than the whole request, and a timeout on every outbound call (7.03) within the request's deadline (7.15). Spring MVC cannot stop a running handler after N seconds.
spring:
  servlet:
    multipart:
      max-file-size: 25MB
      max-request-size: 26MB
server:
  max-http-request-header-size: 16KB
  tomcat:
    connection-timeout: 5s

See also. 5.19, 7.03, 7.15, 17.03

5.21 Rate-limit a client

Then.

  • Boot era: RateLimiter from Guava, Google's general-purpose Java library, in front of a handler. It limits one JVM, and it makes callers wait instead of refusing them.
private final RateLimiter limiter = RateLimiter.create(20.0);   // permits a second

@PostMapping("/payouts")
public PayoutResult create(@RequestBody PayoutForm form) {
    limiter.acquire();                                           // blocks the thread
    return service.create(form);
}
  • Boot era: Netflix Zuul as the edge gateway, with a community rate-limit filter. Spring Cloud Gateway replaced Zuul in Spring Cloud.

Guava's limiter was right for smoothing calls out of one process. It went out of use for client limits once services ran as several pods behind a gateway.

Recognise it by. com.google.common.util.concurrent.RateLimiter, spring-cloud-starter-netflix-zuul in the POM, and @EnableZuulProxy.

The rookie version.

private final Map<String, AtomicInteger> counts = new ConcurrentHashMap<>();

@PostMapping("/payouts")
ResponseEntity<?> create(HttpServletRequest req, @RequestBody CreatePayoutRequest body) {
    int n = counts.computeIfAbsent(req.getRemoteAddr(), k -> new AtomicInteger()).incrementAndGet();
    if (n > 100) return ResponseEntity.status(500).body("slow down");
    ...
}
@Scheduled(fixedRate = 60_000) void reset() { counts.clear(); }

What goes wrong. There are four faults in nine lines. The count lives in one pod, so with 2 pods the limit is 200 a minute, and 300 while a rolling deploy runs a third. getRemoteAddr() returns the ingress's address, so every client shares one count. On a busy morning the claims portal and the finance export lock each other out. The fixed window lets a client send 100 requests at 10:00:59 and 100 more at 10:01:00. And a 500 tells the client the fault is Payouts', so a client that retries server errors (7.04) comes straight back, with no hint to wait.

Do this now.

  1. Decide what you are protecting. A limit per client stops one caller starving the others. A limit on the whole service protects its dependencies, and that is a concurrency limit, not a rate limit (3.09).
  2. Put the coarse limit at the edge. A gateway or the ingress refuses traffic before it reaches a pod. Spring Cloud Gateway has a RequestRateLimiter filter backed by Redis.
  3. Put a limit in the service only when it needs business identity, such as 20 payout requests a minute per calling client. Key it by the client ID in the validated token (15.01), never by IP address.
  4. Use a token bucket. Each client has a bucket of tokens that refills at a steady rate, and each request takes one. It allows short bursts and holds the average. Bucket4j is the usual Java library.
  5. Keep the buckets in a store that every pod shares, such as Redis, when the limit must hold across pods. A bucket per pod with the limit divided by the pod count is cheaper, and drifts whenever the pod count changes.
  6. Refuse with 429 Too Many Requests, a Retry-After header and a ProblemDetail body (6.02).
@Component
class ClientRateLimitFilter extends OncePerRequestFilter {
    private final ClientBuckets buckets;   // wraps Bucket4j and the shared store
    private final ProblemWriter problems;  // writes a ProblemDetail body (6.02)

    @Override
    protected void doFilterInternal(HttpServletRequest req, HttpServletResponse res,
                                    FilterChain chain) throws ServletException, IOException {
        Take take = buckets.tryTake(clientId(req));          // client ID from the JWT
        if (take.allowed()) { chain.doFilter(req, res); return; }
        res.setStatus(HttpStatus.TOO_MANY_REQUESTS.value());
        res.setHeader(HttpHeaders.RETRY_AFTER, String.valueOf(take.retryAfter().toSeconds() + 1));
        problems.write(res, "rate-limited");
    }
}

A OncePerRequestFilter is a servlet filter, the Java form of middleware, that Spring runs once per request. It must run after Spring Security's filters, so the token has been validated before clientId reads it from SecurityContextHolder. Boot registers a filter bean that has no @Order after Spring Security's chain, so this one is already in the right place. If you add it inside the chain instead, with http.addFilterAfter(...) in the SecurityFilterChain (15.05), do not also make it a @Component, or it runs twice.

Also seen. Resilience4j, the Java fault-tolerance library that plays the part of Polly, has a @RateLimiter that limits how often your code calls something else. It protects a dependency from you, not you from a client (7.06). A cloud API gateway with usage plans per API key suits a public API.

When to break it. Internal callers under the same team's control can go without a per-client limit and rely on the concurrency limit. The cost is that one runaway batch job can still fill every slot. Payouts limits internal callers too, since the finance export once sent 4,000 requests in a minute.

.NET anchor. ASP.NET Core's rate-limiting middleware, set up with AddRateLimiter and a partitioned token-bucket limiter, is the same idea in one process. Like a Bucket4j bucket held in memory, it counts per instance, and neither shares state across pods without a distributed store.

See also. 3.09, 6.02, 7.04, 7.06, 15.01, 15.05

5.22 Expose internal admin endpoints safely

Then.

  • Spring era: JMX beans marked @ManagedResource and @ManagedOperation, reached through JConsole, or over HTTP through Jolokia. JMX is the JVM's built-in management interface, and JConsole its desktop client.

What goes wrong. A developer adds POST /admin/payouts/{id}/retry to PayoutController to repair stuck sagas. It shares the public port and the public ingress. Any claims-portal token can call it, and it appears in the published OpenAPI document. One mistaken call re-instructs the bank for a payout that had already been paid.

Do this now.

  1. Put operational actions on Actuator, Spring Boot's built-in management endpoints. Serve them on a separate port with management.server.port, which the ingress does not route.
  2. Write the action as a custom endpoint, with @Endpoint and @WriteOperation. The listing below answers POST /actuator/sagas/{payoutId} on the management port, and @Selector binds the last path segment.
  3. Require an admin role in the SecurityFilterChain, the bean that holds Spring Security's rules, matching the path with EndpointRequest.to("sagas") (14.09, 15.05). Record every call (15.14).
  4. Expose only what you need. By default management.endpoints.web.exposure.include lists only health (14.09), so the new endpoint stays unreachable until you add it: health,prometheus,sagas.
@Component
@Endpoint(id = "sagas")
class SagaAdminEndpoint {
    @WriteOperation
    String retry(@Selector String payoutId) {
        return sagaRepair.retry(payoutId).name();   // audited inside the service
    }
}

See also. 11.09, 14.09, 15.05, 15.14, Actuator and observability

⚠Review checklist
  • If you see a @GetMapping that changes state, or a verb in a URL path: crawlers, proxies and retries repeat GETs freely. See 5.01.
  • If you see a repository, two downstream clients or a catch (Exception e) in a controller: the next entry point will skip the rules, and errors leak internals. See 5.02.
  • If you see a @Document class as a @RequestBody or a controller return type: clients can set any field, and storage changes break them. See 5.03.
  • If you see "success": false inside a 200 response: clients, dashboards and retry policies read failures as success. See 5.04.
  • If you see a POST that creates a payout without an Idempotency-Key: one client retry pays the claimant twice. See 5.05.
  • If you see a controller that waits for the bank gateway or another slow step: client timeouts cause duplicate requests, and waiting requests hold threads. See 5.06.
  • If you see a list endpoint with no limit, or offset paging on a growing collection: memory and latency grow with the data. See 5.07.
  • If you see a sort or filter parameter passed straight into a query: unindexed scans and operator injection. See 5.08.
  • If you see a response field renamed, retyped or removed in place: every client breaks on deploy day. See 5.09.
  • If you see a new enum value in a response, or a consumer with a closed enum: the first new value sends messages to a dead-letter queue. See 5.10.
  • If you see PUT or PATCH without If-Match on a resource people edit: the second writer silently undoes the first. See 5.11.
  • If you see new ObjectMapper() in application code: it ignores the service's JSON settings and modules. See 5.12.
  • If you see a double amount or a LocalDateTime in a JSON record: lost pennies and times that may not exist. See 5.13.
  • If you see a hand-written API YAML in a code-first service, or a schema built from a storage class: the documentation lies or leaks. See 5.15.
  • If you see a PATCH body bound to a record: absent fields become nulls and wipe stored data. See 5.17.
  • If you see file.getBytes() or a byte[] download: memory per request equals the file size. See 5.19.
  • If you see a rate limit held in a pod's memory or keyed by getRemoteAddr(): the limit multiplies with pods and lumps clients together. See 5.21.
  • If you see an /admin path in a public controller: public tokens reach operational actions. See 5.22.

Part IV · The how-to6. Validation and error handling#

Every request Payouts accepts is a claim on someone's money, and every error it returns is an instruction to a client. This part covers checking what comes in, at the edge and in the domain, and saying what went wrong in one standard shape. It shows how to keep business refusals apart from broken infrastructure, how to translate another service's errors into your own, and how to decide what to retry, what to fail and what to set aside.

★What a veteran knows
  • Apart from 408 and 429, a 4xx status is a promise that sending the same request again will fail again. Return one only when that is true, because clients and gateways decide whether to retry from the status alone.
  • The problem type is the contract and the detail is for people. A client that parses detail breaks the day someone fixes a typo.
  • Check shape at the edge, rules in the domain and facts in the database. A rule placed in the wrong layer is either skipped or checked against stale data.
  • Every exception should have one place that turns it into a response and one place that logs it. Two of either means two answers to the same question.
  • An error you forward unchanged from a downstream service is that service's API leaking into yours. Your callers start depending on a team they have never met.
  • A failed message has nobody waiting for the answer. Decide in advance what happens to it, or the queue decides for you after ten tries.
◷How we got hereOn 4 July 2012 Mark Nottingham, then at Rackspace, posted an Internet-Draft called "Indicating Details of…

On 4 July 2012 Mark Nottingham, then at Rackspace, posted an Internet-Draft called "Indicating Details of Problems to Machines in HTTP". Every API he looked at had invented its own error body, and every client had to learn each one. He proposed a single, extensible format instead. The draft carried a note to readers: "Using it before it becomes an RFC may subject you to ridicule; you have been warned." He also named the risk that it might couple clients to servers more tightly. His answer was that lots of people were doing this already. The draft became RFC 7807 in March 2016, written with Erik Wilde. Spring Framework 6.0 shipped support for it in November 2022. In July 2023 RFC 9457 replaced 7807, adding a registry of common problem types. The format had survived the ridicule.

6.01 Validate request bodies with Bean Validation

Then.

  • Spring era: a hand-written class implementing Spring's own Validator interface, attached to a controller in an @InitBinder method. The controller took a BindingResult and checked it by hand:
public void validate(Object target, Errors errors) {
    PayoutForm form = (PayoutForm) target;
    ValidationUtils.rejectIfEmptyOrWhitespace(errors, "claimId", "required");
    if (form.getAmount() == null || form.getAmount().signum() <= 0) {
        errors.rejectValue("amount", "positive");
    }
}
  • J2EE era: Struts 1 forms overrode ActionForm.validate(), or declared rules in a Commons Validator validation.xml.

This was right when there was no standard for declaring rules. Bean Validation replaced it with annotations that any framework can read, so the rule sits on the field it guards.

Recognise it by. implements org.springframework.validation.Validator, @InitBinder with binder.setValidator(...), if (result.hasErrors()), ValidationUtils.rejectIfEmpty, and javax.validation.constraints.* imports in code from before Boot 3.

The rookie version.

public record CreatePayoutRequest(
        @NotBlank String claimId,
        @NotNull MoneyJson amount,
        @NotNull Payee payee) {}

@PostMapping("/payouts")
ResponseEntity<PayoutResponse> create(@RequestBody CreatePayoutRequest request) {
    return ResponseEntity.status(201).body(payoutService.create(request));
}

What goes wrong. The annotations look like validation, so the review passes. Nothing reads them. Without @Valid on the parameter, Spring binds the JSON and calls the method. A request with an amount of "-1240.50" reaches PayoutService, and the ledger is asked to reserve minus £1,240.50. There is a second trap. A starter is a Boot dependency that brings in a library together with the configuration that switches it on. If the validation starter is missing from the POM, Maven's pom.xml build file, but another library has brought in the Jakarta Validation API, the annotations compile and there is nothing to run them. Even @Valid then does nothing, and the service starts without a warning.

Do this now. Bean Validation is the Jakarta EE standard for declaring rules as annotations on fields. Jakarta EE is the successor to Java EE, which is why the package moved from javax.validation to jakarta.validation. Hibernate Validator is the implementation Spring Boot uses. It needs no database, despite the name.

  1. Add the starter. The web starter does not bring it.
<dependency>
  <groupId>org.springframework.boot</groupId>
  <artifactId>spring-boot-starter-validation</artifactId>
</dependency>
  1. Put the rules on the request record, which is the boundary type. Keep them off the stored document.
public record CreatePayoutRequest(
        @NotBlank @Size(max = 20) String claimId,
        @NotNull @Valid MoneyJson amount,      // value and currency rules: 5.13
        @NotNull @Valid Payee payee) {}

@PostMapping("/payouts")
ResponseEntity<PayoutResponse> create(@Valid @RequestBody CreatePayoutRequest request) { ... }
  1. Mark nested records with @Valid, as on amount and payee. Without it the rules inside MoneyJson and Payee are skipped.
  2. A failure throws MethodArgumentNotValidException before your method runs. Spring answers 400. Entries 6.02 and 6.13 make that answer useful.
  3. Prove it with a @WebMvcTest, a test that starts only the web layer, which posts a negative amount and expects 400 (16.04).

Also seen. Checks in a record's compact constructor, a constructor body with no parameter list that runs before the fields are set, which throw IllegalArgumentException. Use them for invariants of a domain value such as Money, which must hold everywhere, not only over HTTP. Spring's Validator interface is still the right tool when a rule needs another bean, an object Spring creates and injects, such as a configured limit. Keep calls to other systems out of it (6.07).

When to break it. An internal endpoint that receives a message format you do not own may accept what it is sent and validate later, as in 6.12. The cost is that bad data travels further before anyone notices.

.NET anchor. DataAnnotations such as [Required] and [Range]. ASP.NET Core with [ApiController] validates automatically and returns 400. Spring validates only when the parameter says @Valid, which is why the rookie version compiles and runs. ASP.NET Core also walks into nested objects by itself. Spring does not, so a nested record without @Valid is never checked.

See also. 6.06, 6.07, 6.13, 16.04, Validation and error responses, Annotations and attributes

6.02 Return errors as ProblemDetail

Then.

  • Boot era: Boot's default error body from its /error controller, with timestamp, status, error, message and path. Most teams wrapped it in their own class:
public class ApiError {
    private String code;
    private String message;
    private List<String> details;
    // getters and setters
}
  • Boot era: Zalando's problem-spring-web library, which implemented RFC 7807 before Spring did, with Problem.builder() and ThrowableProblem.

Both were right at the time. The home-grown class gave clients a stable shape, and Zalando's library gave them a standard one. Spring now has the standard built in, so neither is needed in new code.

Recognise it by. org.zalando.problem.*, a class named ApiError, ErrorDto or ErrorResponse in your own package, a custom ErrorAttributes bean, and "application/problem+json" typed out as a string.

The rookie version.

@PostMapping("/payouts")
ResponseEntity<Map<String, Object>> create(@Valid @RequestBody CreatePayoutRequest request) {
    try {
        return ResponseEntity.ok(Map.of("ok", true, "payout", payoutService.create(request)));
    } catch (ClaimNotApproved e) {
        return ResponseEntity.ok(Map.of("ok", false, "error", e.getMessage()));
    }
}

What goes wrong. Every refusal is a 200. The claims portal's retry logic sees success and moves on. The dashboards count no errors. When claim CLM-204170 was refused 340 times in one afternoon, nothing alerted, because the metric for 4xx responses stayed at 0. Each controller also invents its own keys, so a client needs one parser per endpoint.

Do this now. ProblemDetail is Spring's class for the RFC 9457 format, a JSON body with five standard members: type, title, status, detail and instance. It is served as application/problem+json.

  1. Turn on Boot's support. It is off by default, on Boot 3.5 and Boot 4. With it on, Spring's own errors, such as a missing parameter or an unsupported media type, come back as ProblemDetail too.
spring:
  mvc:
    problemdetails:
      enabled: true
  1. Build your own problems with a stable type URI for each kind of error, and extra members for what the client needs.
ProblemDetail problem = ProblemDetail.forStatusAndDetail(
        HttpStatus.UNPROCESSABLE_ENTITY, "Claim CLM-204170 is not approved for payment.");
problem.setType(URI.create("https://errors.sorrel.example/payouts/claim-not-approved"));
problem.setTitle("Claim not approved");
problem.setProperty("claimId", "CLM-204170");

On Spring Framework 7, the version under Boot 4, the constant is HttpStatus.UNPROCESSABLE_CONTENT. UNPROCESSABLE_ENTITY still compiles there, but it is deprecated.

  1. Return it from one handler (6.03), or throw an exception that extends ErrorResponseException and carries it.
  2. Document each type in the OpenAPI description (5.15). Clients branch on type. They show title and detail to people.
{ "type": "https://errors.sorrel.example/payouts/claim-not-approved",
  "title": "Claim not approved", "status": 422,
  "detail": "Claim CLM-204170 is not approved for payment.",
  "instance": "/payouts", "claimId": "CLM-204170" }

Also seen. An organisation-wide error envelope that predates the RFC. Keep it if every client already parses it. ResponseStatusException, which produces a ProblemDetail with a status and a reason and suits a one-off error with no type of its own.

When to break it. When existing clients parse another error format, switching breaks them. Add the new format behind a new media type or version and retire the old one deliberately (20.01). The cost is two formats for a while.

.NET anchor. ASP.NET Core's ProblemDetails, ValidationProblemDetails and AddProblemDetails(). The shape is the same RFC. The difference is that ASP.NET Core with [ApiController] produces it for validation failures by default, and Boot needs the property.

See also. 6.03, 6.13, 5.04, 5.15, Validation and error responses

6.03 Handle exceptions in one place with @RestControllerAdvice

Then.

  • J2EE era: <error-page> elements in web.xml, mapping an exception class or status code to a JSP.
  • Spring era: a SimpleMappingExceptionResolver bean in XML, or @ExceptionHandler methods copied into every controller or inherited from a BaseController:
public abstract class BaseController {
    @ExceptionHandler(ClaimNotFoundException.class)
    @ResponseStatus(HttpStatus.NOT_FOUND)
    @ResponseBody
    public ApiError notFound(ClaimNotFoundException e) { return new ApiError("NOT_FOUND", e.getMessage()); }
}
  • Boot era: @ResponseStatus(HttpStatus.NOT_FOUND) on the exception class itself. It still works, but it cannot carry a body.

The base class was the natural way to share code before advice classes existed. It ties every controller to one hierarchy, and a controller that forgets to extend it gets no handling at all.

Recognise it by. extends BaseController, SimpleMappingExceptionResolver, <error-page>, @ControllerAdvice paired with @ResponseBody on each method, and @ResponseStatus on exception classes.

The rookie version.

@GetMapping("/payouts/{id}")
ResponseEntity<?> get(@PathVariable String id) {
    try {
        return ResponseEntity.ok(payoutService.find(id));
    } catch (Exception e) {
        log.error("Failed to get payout", e);
        return ResponseEntity.status(500).body(e.getMessage());
    }
}

What goes wrong. payouts-api had 9 controller methods, each with its own catch. A missing payout came back as 500, because the service threw PayoutNotFound and the catch did not distinguish it. A DocumentDB timeout returned the driver's message, host name included (6.08). Each failure was logged by the service, the controller and the client, so one bad request made 3 stack traces.

Do this now. An advice class is a Spring bean whose handler methods apply to every controller. @RestControllerAdvice is @ControllerAdvice with @ResponseBody added, so its return values are written as the response body.

  1. Write one advice class for the service. Extend ResponseEntityExceptionHandler, Spring's base class that already handles Spring MVC's own exceptions as ProblemDetail. Boot's own problem-details handler, switched on in 6.02, then steps aside, because yours does the same job.
  2. Add one @ExceptionHandler method per family of exceptions. Spring chooses the closest match by exception type, so specific handlers win over general ones.
  3. Return ProblemDetail from each one.
  4. Add a last handler for Exception. It logs once, with the stack trace, and returns a 500 with a fixed detail and no internals.
@RestControllerAdvice
class PayoutsExceptionHandler extends ResponseEntityExceptionHandler {
    private static final Logger log = LoggerFactory.getLogger(PayoutsExceptionHandler.class);
    @ExceptionHandler(PayoutRejected.class)
    ProblemDetail rejected(PayoutRejected e) {
        log.info("Payout refused: {}", e.getMessage());   // a refusal: no stack trace
        return e.toProblemDetail();                       // 409 or 422, see 6.04
    }
    @ExceptionHandler(Exception.class)
    ProblemDetail unexpected(Exception e) {
        log.error("Unhandled failure", e);
        return ProblemDetail.forStatusAndDetail(
                HttpStatus.INTERNAL_SERVER_ERROR, "The payout service failed. Quote the trace ID.");
    }
}

Controllers then contain no try blocks. They call the service and return the result. Add the trace ID to the 500's body as 13.10 shows, so the caller has an ID to quote. Each further family, such as LedgerUnavailable (6.09) or PayoutNotFound (6.14), gets its own handler here. Anything without one lands in the catch-all as a 500.

Exceptions thrown inside a servlet filter never reach the advice. A servlet is Java's standard unit of HTTP handling, and a filter is code that wraps it and runs before any controller. Spring Security's errors are an example. Handle those in the filter chain (15.05).

Also seen. Exceptions that extend ErrorResponseException carry their own status and ProblemDetail, and the base class from step 1 renders them with no handler method of your own. @ResponseStatus on an exception class suits a status with no body.

When to break it. A controller with a genuinely local concern, such as a file download that must answer with plain text, may keep a local @ExceptionHandler. Local handlers win over the advice. The cost is a second place to look. Limit an advice with basePackages when admin endpoints need a different shape.

.NET anchor. UseExceptionHandler middleware, IExceptionHandler and MVC exception filters. Spring's version dispatches on the exception type through annotations, rather than one handler that switches on the type itself. A servlet filter is the nearest thing to middleware, and here the two differ. UseExceptionHandler placed first catches what later middleware throws. The advice sits inside Spring MVC, so it never sees what a filter throws.

See also. 6.02, 6.04, 6.08, 5.02, 12.05, Validation and error responses, Exceptions and resources

6.04 Separate domain errors from technical failures

Then.

  • J2EE era: EJB split exceptions in two. Application exceptions, marked @ApplicationException or declared as checked, were business outcomes. System exceptions were failures and rolled the transaction back.
  • Spring era: checked business exceptions, declared on every method:
public Payout pay(String claimId) throws ClaimNotApprovedException, LimitExceededException {
    ...
}
public class ClaimNotApprovedException extends Exception { ... }

The checked exception was right in its day. The compiler forced every caller to handle the refusal. It fits badly with lambdas and streams, and Spring's @Transactional commits on a checked exception unless told otherwise. Modern code uses unchecked exceptions or result types.

Recognise it by. extends Exception on business errors, long throws clauses, javax.ejb.ApplicationException, and rollbackFor = Exception.class added to work around the commit.

The rookie version.

public class PayoutException extends RuntimeException {
    public PayoutException(String message, Throwable cause) { super(message, cause); }
}

// used for everything
throw new PayoutException("Claim not approved", null);
throw new PayoutException("Ledger call failed", timeout);

What goes wrong. One exception type cannot have two status codes. The team mapped PayoutException to 400. The claims portal treats 400 as final, so a ledger timeout that would have succeeded a minute later became a refused payout. Claimants rang the call centre about £1,240.50 that was never sent. The alert on 5xx responses stayed quiet, because the outage was reported as bad requests.

Do this now. A domain error is an expected outcome that the business has a rule for. A technical failure is something broken. They differ on every axis that matters:

Domain error Technical failure
Status 409 or 422 500, 502 or 503
Retry never with the same input perhaps, with backoff
Log INFO, no stack trace ERROR, once, with stack trace
Alert on a rising rate yes
  1. Model the domain errors as a sealed hierarchy, a class that lists the only subclasses allowed. The compiler then knows every case.
public sealed abstract class PayoutRejected extends RuntimeException
        permits ClaimNotApproved, PayoutLimitExceeded, DuplicatePayout, InsufficientReserve {
    protected PayoutRejected(String message) { super(message, null, false, false); }
    public abstract ProblemDetail toProblemDetail();
}
  1. Pass false, false to the superclass constructor. The first turns off suppressed exceptions, and the second skips the stack trace. A refusal does not need one, and filling it in costs time on every refused request. Each permitted subclass must itself be declared final, sealed or non-sealed, or the hierarchy does not compile.
  2. Keep technical failures as their own types, such as LedgerUnavailable, with the cause attached.
  3. Translate at the boundary. The advice in 6.03 maps each family to its status. Clients in 6.09 turn downstream failures into one or the other.

If toProblemDetail() puts Spring web types in the domain module, move the mapping into the advice and keep payouts-domain free of Spring imports.

Also seen. A sealed result type such as PayoutOutcome, with Paid and Rejected records, returned instead of thrown. It makes the refusal impossible to ignore (2.12). It suits code where refusal is common and callers must branch on it.

When to break it. A small internal tool with one caller can use one exception type. The cost appears the day a second caller needs to tell a refusal from an outage.

.NET anchor. The split between a domain exception and an HttpRequestException or TimeoutException, or a Result<T> type from a library such as FluentResults. C# has no checked exceptions, so the Spring-era throws clause has no .NET counterpart.

See also. 2.09, 2.12, 6.03, 6.09, 9.01, Exceptions and resources, Sealed types and pattern matching

6.05 Validate path and query parameters

Then.

  • Boot era: @Validated on the controller class, which wrapped it in a proxy, a generated object that intercepts each call before passing it on. A failure threw ConstraintViolationException, which became a 500 unless someone mapped it.

What goes wrong. GET /payouts?limit=100000 reads 100,000 documents from DocumentDB and serialises them all. A path ID of ../admin reaches the repository, and any downstream URL built from it, exactly as sent. Unchecked parameters are the cheapest way to make a service do expensive work.

Do this now. Put constraints directly on the parameters. Current Spring MVC applies them through its built-in method validation, with no @Validated needed.

@GetMapping("/payouts")
List<PayoutResponse> list(@RequestParam(defaultValue = "50") @Min(1) @Max(100) int limit,
                          @RequestParam(required = false) @ClaimId String claimId) { ... }

@GetMapping("/payouts/{id}")
PayoutResponse get(@PathVariable @Pattern(regexp = "p-\\d{1,12}") String id) { ... }

@ClaimId is the custom constraint from 6.06. A failure raises HandlerMethodValidationException, which the advice in 6.03 renders as 400. Use one mechanism. With a class-level @Validated as well, Spring leaves the work to the proxy, and you get ConstraintViolationException instead. The base class in 6.03 does not handle that one, so it reaches the catch-all as a 500.

See also. 6.01, 5.07, 5.08, Controllers, routing and binding

6.06 Write a custom constraint

What goes wrong. The same regular expression for a claim ID is pasted into 7 request records. Claims changes the format from CLM- plus 5 digits to 6 digits. Six records are updated, and one endpoint keeps refusing new claims with a 400.

Do this now. A constraint is an annotation plus a validator class that Bean Validation calls.

@Target({ FIELD, PARAMETER, RECORD_COMPONENT })
@Retention(RUNTIME)
@Constraint(validatedBy = ClaimIdValidator.class)
public @interface ClaimId {
    String message() default "must be a Sorrel claim ID, such as CLM-204170";
    Class<?>[] groups() default {};
    Class<? extends Payload>[] payload() default {};
}

class ClaimIdValidator implements ConstraintValidator<ClaimId, String> {
    private static final Pattern FORMAT = Pattern.compile("CLM-\\d{6}");

    @Override
    public boolean isValid(String value, ConstraintValidatorContext context) {
        return value == null || FORMAT.matcher(value).matches();
    }
}

Use it as @NotNull @ClaimId String claimId in every record and on every parameter that carries one, and the format lives in one class. The three attributes message, groups and payload are required by the specification. Return true for null and pair the annotation with @NotNull, so each annotation checks one thing. Keep validators free of I/O (6.07).

See also. 6.01, 6.07, Annotations and attributes

6.07 Validate rules that span fields and documents

Then.

  • Boot era: Hibernate Validator's @ScriptAssert, a class-level rule written as a script string:
@ScriptAssert(lang = "javascript",
        script = "_this.amount.compareTo(_this.approvedAmount) <= 0")
public class PayoutForm { ... }

It let a team express a cross-field rule without writing a validator class. The script is invisible to the compiler and to refactoring, and depends on a script engine being present at run time. A class-level constraint or a plain Java check replaced it.

Recognise it by. org.hibernate.validator.constraints.ScriptAssert, @AssertTrue on a method such as isDatesConsistent(), and validators that are Spring beans with repositories injected.

The rookie version.

class ApprovedClaimValidator implements ConstraintValidator<ApprovedClaim, String> {
    private final PolicyClient policyClient;

    ApprovedClaimValidator(PolicyClient policyClient) { this.policyClient = policyClient; }

    public boolean isValid(String claimId, ConstraintValidatorContext ctx) {
        return policyClient.claim(claimId).approved();      // an HTTP call
    }
}

What goes wrong. Every validation now calls the policy system, including in unit tests. When the policy system timed out, the exception escaped Bean Validation wrapped in a ValidationException. The team's advice mapped every ValidationException to 400, so clients were told a valid claim was invalid. The check is also stale by design. The claim was approved at validation time and withdrawn 200 milliseconds later, before PayoutService wrote the payout. The rule was checked in one place and acted on in another.

Do this now. Split rules by what they need.

  1. Shape, one field at a time: Bean Validation annotations (6.01).
  2. Consistency inside one request, such as "a payout to a third party needs a reason": a class-level constraint, or a check in the record's compact constructor. A class-level constraint is built as in 6.06, with TYPE in its @Target, and goes on the record itself, here as @ThirdPartyReason. @Valid runs it with the field rules, and it can point its error at the right field:
class ThirdPartyReasonValidator
        implements ConstraintValidator<ThirdPartyReason, CreatePayoutRequest> {
    public boolean isValid(CreatePayoutRequest r, ConstraintValidatorContext ctx) {
        if (r.payee().thirdParty() && (r.reason() == null || r.reason().isBlank())) {
            ctx.disableDefaultConstraintViolation();
            ctx.buildConstraintViolationWithTemplate("is required for a third-party payee")
               .addPropertyNode("reason").addConstraintViolation();
            return false;
        }
        return true;
    }
}
  1. State, such as "the claim is approved" or "the total paid stays within the approved amount": in PayoutService, against the data. Throw a domain error from 6.04, so the client gets a 422 with a type it can act on.
  2. Where the rule protects your own data against a race, make the write enforce it. A conditional update that only succeeds while the payout's status is still PENDING, or a unique index, closes the gap a read-then-write leaves open (8.04, 8.16). A fact another system owns, such as the claim's approval, cannot be locked from Payouts. Check it as late as you can, just before the step that acts on it, and accept the small gap that remains.

Also seen. @AssertTrue on a record method named like a getter, such as isThirdPartyReasonPresent(). It is quick, but the error lands on an invented property name that the client has never seen.

When to break it. A read-only lookup with no side effects may check a stored fact during validation if the result is only advisory. The cost is a dependency inside your validators that tests must now satisfy.

.NET anchor. IValidatableObject.Validate for cross-field rules, and FluentValidation's MustAsync for the rookie version's database call.

See also. 6.04, 6.06, 8.04, 8.16, 9.09, Validation and error responses

6.08 Never leak stack traces or internals in a response

Then.

  • Boot era: the Whitelabel error page, Boot's default HTML page for errors, and server.error.include-stacktrace=always set for local debugging and then shipped.

What goes wrong. A DocumentDB timeout reached a client as the driver's message, with the cluster's host name, port and replica set name. A bank gateway error echoed the full instruction, including the claimant's sort code and account number. Each is a gift to an attacker and, for the account number, a reportable data incident.

Do this now.

  1. Keep Boot's error properties closed in every environment. They govern Boot's fallback /error response, which still answers for errors the advice never sees, such as those from filters. never is already the default, so set them explicitly and refuse any profile that reopens them in review:
server:
  error:
    include-stacktrace: never
    include-message: never
    include-binding-errors: never
  1. Never copy e.getMessage() of a technical failure into detail. Write a fixed sentence.
  2. Return the trace ID instead, so support can find the full log line (13.10).
  3. Test it. Make the mocked service throw in a @WebMvcTest and assert that the body holds no class names.

See also. 6.03, 12.06, 13.10, 15.05, Validation and error responses

6.09 Map a downstream service's errors to your own

Then.

  • Spring era: a ResponseErrorHandler on RestTemplate, Spring's original synchronous HTTP client, often a subclass of DefaultResponseErrorHandler with hasError and handleError overridden.
  • Boot era: Feign, Netflix's declarative HTTP client, with an ErrorDecoder:
public class LedgerErrorDecoder implements ErrorDecoder {
    public Exception decode(String methodKey, Response response) {
        return response.status() == 409
                ? new LedgerRejectedException()
                : new LedgerUnavailable(response.status());
    }
}

Both were the right hook for their client. The Spring Framework 7 reference declares RestTemplate deprecated in favour of RestClient, which has the same idea built into its fluent API. The 7.0 code carries no @Deprecated annotation yet, so the compiler does not warn.

Recognise it by. implements ResponseErrorHandler, extends DefaultResponseErrorHandler, restTemplate.setErrorHandler(...), feign.codec.ErrorDecoder, and catch (HttpClientErrorException e) spread through service code.

The rookie version.

try {
    return ledgerClient.reserve(request);
} catch (HttpStatusCodeException e) {
    return ResponseEntity.status(e.getStatusCode())
            .body(e.getResponseBodyAsString());          // the ledger's body, as ours
}

What goes wrong. The ledger answered 404 because the cost-centre account was missing on its side. Payouts passed the 404 through on POST /payouts. The claims portal read it as "this endpoint does not exist" and raised a ticket against the wrong team. The ledger's body also named its internal account ACC-0093-RESERVE. When the ledger changed its error format in a release, the portal's error screen broke, though Payouts had not changed a line.

Do this now. Translate at the client, the one class that knows the ledger.

  1. Decide what each downstream outcome means for a payout. A 409 for insufficient reserve is a domain refusal. A 5xx or a timeout is a technical failure. A 400 means Payouts sent a bad request, which is a bug in Payouts.
  2. Map statuses with RestClient's onStatus, which runs before the body is read:
Reservation reserve(ReserveRequest request) {
    try {
        return restClient.post().uri("/reservations").body(request).retrieve()
                .onStatus(s -> s.value() == 409, (req, res) -> {
                    throw new InsufficientReserve(request.payoutId());
                })
                .onStatus(HttpStatusCode::is5xxServerError, (req, res) -> {
                    throw new LedgerUnavailable(res.getStatusCode().value());
                })
                .body(Reservation.class);
    } catch (ResourceAccessException e) {            // timeout or refused connection
        throw new LedgerUnavailable(e);
    }
}
  1. Unmapped 4xx statuses fall through to HttpClientErrorException. Let the catch-all in 6.03 turn them into a 500, because they are your bug.
  2. Log the downstream status and the downstream trace ID at the client. Return your own ProblemDetail, with your own type.
  3. Return 503 for LedgerUnavailable from its own handler in the advice, which logs it once at ERROR (12.05). To add a Retry-After header when you know when to try again, return a ResponseEntity with the header and the ProblemDetail as its body.
  4. Update the resilience configuration to match. The client now throws LedgerUnavailable for timeouts and 5xx, so a retry or circuit breaker that lists ResourceAccessException or HttpServerErrorException no longer matches anything (7.04, 7.10). InsufficientReserve belongs in the breaker's ignore list. A retried reservation is a POST, so it needs the idempotency key from 7.07.

Also seen. A declarative client from @HttpExchange (7.02), which accepts the same RestClient status handlers. Parsing the ledger's own ProblemDetail type instead of its status, when the ledger documents its types. That is more precise and couples you to its catalogue.

When to break it. A thin gateway whose whole job is to proxy one service may pass errors through. The cost is that its clients now depend on the service behind it.

.NET anchor. HttpClient with EnsureSuccessStatusCode and a DelegatingHandler, or Refit's ApiException. The pattern is the same: translate in the typed client, never in the controller.

See also. 6.04, 7.01, 7.02, 7.04, 7.07, 7.10, 12.05, The Yard, chapter 11, HTTP clients and resilience

6.10 Validate differently on create and update

What goes wrong. One PayoutRequest record served both POST and PUT. @NotNull on id broke creation, so it was removed. Updates then arrived with no ID, and Spring Data's save() treated each one as a new document. A correction to one payout became a second payout for the same claim.

Do this now. Prefer two records, CreatePayoutRequest and UpdatePayoutRequest. Each carries the rules for its own operation, and the OpenAPI description shows the difference. When the shared fields are many, use validation groups, marker interfaces that select which constraints run:

public interface OnCreate {}
public interface OnUpdate {}

public record PayoutRequest(
        @Null(groups = OnCreate.class) @NotNull(groups = OnUpdate.class) String id,
        @NotNull(groups = { OnCreate.class, OnUpdate.class }) BigDecimal amount) {}

@PostMapping("/payouts")
ResponseEntity<PayoutResponse> create(@Validated(OnCreate.class) @RequestBody PayoutRequest request) { ... }

@Validated is Spring's annotation that takes a group, where @Valid cannot. A constraint with no groups belongs to Default, which does not run when you name a group. That is the usual surprise.

See also. 6.01, 5.17, Validation and error responses

6.11 Decide what to retry, what to fail and what to dead-letter

Then.

  • Spring era: Spring Retry's @Retryable and RetryTemplate, from the separate spring-retry project. It was the standard for years. It is now archived, and Spring Framework 7 has @Retryable in core.
  • Boot era: JMS listeners with a broker redelivery policy, where every exception meant "try again" up to the broker's limit.

Recognise it by. org.springframework.retry.annotation.Retryable, @EnableRetry, RetryTemplate.builder(), @Recover methods, and broker settings named maximumRedeliveries.

The rookie version.

@SqsListener("ledger-confirm")
void onMessage(EventEnvelope<PayoutCompletedData> event) {
    try {
        payoutService.confirm(event);
    } catch (Exception e) {
        log.error("Confirm failed", e);                 // and the message is acknowledged
    }
}

What goes wrong. @SqsListener acknowledges a message when the method returns normally. Catching everything means every failure is acknowledged and deleted. During a 6-minute DocumentDB failover, 412 confirmations were logged and lost. The opposite rookie version, which throws everything, also hurts. A message with an unknown payout ID can never succeed, yet it is received 5 times, the maxReceiveCount set on ledger-confirm (10.08), before it reaches ledger-confirm-dlq.

Do this now. Classify each failure by one question: would the same input succeed later?

  1. Transient failures are worth retrying: timeouts, 503, 429, and optimistic-lock conflicts, where a save lost a race on a @Version field. Over HTTP, retry a few times in process with backoff (7.04). For a message, make one attempt and throw, so it is not acknowledged. SQS hides a received message for the visibility timeout, then delivers it again. That redelivery is the retry, so do not add in-process retries on top: 4 attempts inside each of 5 receives is 20 ledger calls (10.06).
  2. Permanent failures will never succeed: a body that fails validation, an unknown payout, a refusal. Over HTTP, return a 4xx at once. For a message, do not wait for maxReceiveCount. Send it to a parking queue, one of your own for messages set aside, with the reason, then return normally:
@SqsListener("ledger-confirm")
void onMessage(EventEnvelope<PayoutCompletedData> event) {
    try {
        payoutService.confirm(event);
    } catch (PayoutRejected | PayoutNotFound e) {
        sqsTemplate.send("ledger-confirm-parked", new Parked(event, e.getMessage()));
    }                                       // anything else propagates and is redelivered
}
  1. Set maxReceiveCount on the redrive policy, the queue setting that says after how many receives SQS moves a message to its dead-letter queue. Size it to cover the transient cases. ledger-confirm uses 5 receives 60 seconds apart, which gives a fault about 5 minutes to clear (10.06, 10.08). The 6-minute failover above outlasts that, so the confirmations that arrived early in it still reach ledger-confirm-dlq. They wait there, not lost, and are redriven once the database is back (10.09).
  2. Alarm on the depth of the dead-letter and parked queues. A message there is a decision a person must make (14.08).

Also seen. Throwing every failure and letting the redrive policy dead-letter the permanent ones. It is simpler and costs a few wasted receives per bad message. For the HTTP side on Boot 4, Spring Framework 7's own @Retryable, with includes naming the transient exception types.

When to break it. A FIFO queue keeps strict order within a message group, here the messages for one payout (10.10). When that order matters, parking a message and moving on breaks the order. AWS warns that a dead-letter queue breaks it too. Stop the group and page someone instead (10.10).

.NET anchor. Polly's HandleTransientHttpError for the HTTP side. For the message side, Azure Service Bus: an unacknowledged SQS message comes back like an abandoned peek-lock message, and maxReceiveCount plays the part of MaxDeliveryCount. The difference bites on permanent failures. Service Bus lets you dead-letter one message with a reason. SQS has no such call, which is why the listener sends it to a parking queue itself.

See also. 6.04, 7.04, 7.07, 10.06, 10.07, 10.08, 10.09, 10.10, 10.17, The Yard, chapter 11, Messaging and WebSockets

6.12 Validate configuration and messages, not only HTTP

What goes wrong. A typo set payouts.ledger.read-timeout to 0, which an HTTP client may read as "no timeout". The service started and ran, until the ledger slowed down. A PayoutRequested message published by another team without amount reached PayoutService and threw a NullPointerException on each of its receives.

Do this now. Bean Validation works on any object, not only request bodies.

@Validated
@ConfigurationProperties(prefix = "payouts.ledger")
public record LedgerProperties(
        @NotNull URI baseUrl,
        @DefaultValue("5s") @DurationMin(millis = 100) Duration readTimeout,
        @DefaultValue("3") @Min(0) @Max(5) int maxRetries) {
}

With the validation starter (6.01) present and the record registered with @ConfigurationPropertiesScan (4.02), Boot validates it at startup. It refuses to start if a rule fails, with the property name in the error (4.10). @DurationMin comes from Hibernate Validator. The default covers a missing key only, so a typed 0 is still refused. For messages, inject jakarta.validation.Validator into the listener and call validator.validate(event). A non-empty set of violations is a permanent failure, so park the message (6.11).
