See also. 4.02, 4.10, 6.11, 10.12, 10.17, Dependency injection and configuration

6.13 Return field errors a client can act on

What goes wrong. The claims portal received 400 with "Invalid request content." and nothing else. It could not tell the claimant which of 9 form fields was wrong, so it showed a generic message. Support took 31 calls in a week about the same missing sort code.

Do this now. Override the validation handler in the advice from 6.03 and add an errors member.

@Override
protected ResponseEntity<Object> handleMethodArgumentNotValid(MethodArgumentNotValidException ex,
        HttpHeaders headers, HttpStatusCode status, WebRequest request) {
    ProblemDetail problem = ProblemDetail.forStatusAndDetail(status, "The payout request has invalid fields.");
    problem.setType(URI.create("https://errors.sorrel.example/payouts/invalid-request"));
    problem.setProperty("errors", ex.getBindingResult().getFieldErrors().stream()
            .map(f -> Map.of("pointer", "#/" + f.getField().replace('.', '/'),
                             "code", f.getCode(), "message", f.getDefaultMessage()))
            .toList());
    return ResponseEntity.status(status).body(problem);
}

Give each error a JSON pointer to the field, a path into the body such as #/payee/sortCode, a stable code such as NotBlank, and a message. Never echo the rejected value, which may be an account number. Override handleHandlerMethodValidationException too, because constraints on parameters (6.05) arrive as HandlerMethodValidationException, not this one. Its errors come from getParameterValidationResults(), one result per parameter. Name the parameter there, because a query parameter has no place in the body to point at.

See also. 6.01, 6.02, 6.03, 12.06, Validation and error responses

6.14 Tell "not found" from "empty"

What goes wrong. GET /claims/CLM-204170/payouts returned 404 when the claim had no payouts yet. The portal showed "claim not found" to a claimant whose claim was being paid that day. Elsewhere, GET /payouts/p-12345 returned 200 with an empty body for a payout that did not exist.

Do this now. Decide per resource.

  • A single resource that does not exist is 404 with a ProblemDetail.
  • A collection that exists but has no members is 200 with []. It is never 404 or 204.
  • A collection under a parent that does not exist is 404, because the parent is missing.
@GetMapping("/payouts/{id}")
PayoutResponse get(@PathVariable String id) {
    return payoutRepository.findById(id).map(PayoutResponse::from)
            .orElseThrow(() -> new PayoutNotFound(id));
}

PayoutNotFound is not one of the refusals in 6.04, so give it its own handler in the advice from 6.03, returning a 404 ProblemDetail. Without one, the catch-all answers 500.

Repositories return Optional for one item and an empty list for many. Never return null for either (2.05).

See also. 2.05, 5.04, 6.03, Nullability: Optional and JSpecify

⚠Review checklist
  • If you see constraint annotations on a request record but no @Valid on the @RequestBody: nothing is checked, and bad input reaches the domain. See 6.01.
  • If you see a 200 response with an ok: false or success: false flag: clients, gateways and dashboards all count it as a success. See 6.02.
  • If you see try { ... } catch (Exception e) in a controller method: errors are handled nine different ways and logged more than once. See 6.03.
  • If you see one exception type thrown for both a business refusal and a timeout: it cannot have the right status for both. See 6.04.
  • If you see a @RequestParam page size or ID with no constraint: a client can make the service do unbounded work. See 6.05.
  • If you see a ConstraintValidator with a repository or client injected: validation now does I/O, fails as a 400, and checks stale data. See 6.07.
  • If you see e.getMessage() of a technical failure in a response, or include-stacktrace set to anything but never: internals leak to callers. See 6.08.
  • If you see a downstream status code or body passed through to your caller: your API now depends on someone else's. See 6.09.
  • If you see a listener that catches every exception and returns normally: every failure is acknowledged and the message is lost. See 6.11.
  • If you see a @ConfigurationProperties record without @Validated: a bad value starts the service and fails later, under load. See 6.12.
  • If you see 404 for an empty collection, or 200 with no body for a missing item: clients cannot tell absence from emptiness. See 6.14.

Part IV · The how-to7. Calling other services and resilience#

Payouts cannot pay a claim on its own. It reads the policy system, reserves money in the ledger and instructs the bank gateway, all over HTTP. This part is about those calls. It shows how to make them with RestClient and HTTP interfaces, how to bound them with timeouts, and how to retry, break and contain them without making things worse for the service at the other end. It also covers tokens, trace headers, testing against a fake server, and what to do when one call succeeds and the next one does not.

★What a veteran knows
  • Every outbound call has a timeout, and someone on the team can say why it is that number. A default you did not choose is a decision somebody else made for you.
  • A retry is load on another team. Before you add one, work out how many requests the other side receives in a bad minute.
  • A timeout on a write does not mean the write failed. It means you do not know, and the code needs a third outcome called "unknown".
  • Most resilience bugs are ordering bugs: a retry inside a breaker, a breaker that counts a 404, or a fallback that hides the failure the caller needed to see.
  • A circuit breaker nobody can see is worse than none. On Payouts the breaker's state is a graph on the team dashboard, next to the symptom alerts it explains.
  • The call that takes a service down is often not the business call. On Payouts it was the token request in front of it, which nobody had timed.
◷How we got hereIn March 2007 the Pragmatic Bookshelf published Michael T.

In March 2007 the Pragmatic Bookshelf published Michael T. Nygard's Release It! Design and Deploy Production-Ready Software. Its argument was that systems fail at the seams between them. "Integration points are the number-one killer of systems," he wrote. "Every socket, process, pipe, or remote procedure call can and will hang. Even database calls can hang." The circuit breaker was one of the book's stability patterns. In the second edition, in 2018, Nygard remembered a site with so many feeds that its manager tracked them in a database. "I was awakened every night at 3 a.m. for the latest crash or crisis," he wrote. "I'm sure that every single synchronous integration point caused at least one outage." In March 2014 Martin Fowler credited Nygard with having "popularized" the circuit breaker, to stop one unresponsive supplier causing "cascading failures across multiple systems". Hystrix in 2012, and the project that became resilience4j in 2015, turned those patterns into the Java libraries this part uses.

7.01 Call another service with RestClient

Then.

  • Spring era: RestTemplate, with one method per verb and response shape, and the URL as a string. It was Spring's HTTP client for well over a decade, and Spring Framework 7 deprecates it in favour of RestClient.
RestTemplate rest = new RestTemplate();
PolicySummary policy = rest.getForObject(
        "http://policy/policies/{id}", PolicySummary.class, claim.policyId());
  • Boot era: WebClient from Spring WebFlux, ending every call with .block(), in services that were not reactive at all. Before RestClient existed it was the only Spring client with a fluent API.

Recognise it by. org.springframework.web.client.RestTemplate, getForObject, postForEntity, exchange(..., new ParameterizedTypeReference<...>() {}), RestTemplateBuilder, and WebClient chains that end in .block().

The rookie version.

public PolicySummary find(String policyId) {
    RestClient client = RestClient.create();
    return client.get()
            .uri("http://policy-service:8080/policies/" + policyId)
            .retrieve()
            .body(PolicySummary.class);
}

What goes wrong. RestClient.create() builds a bare client that knows nothing about the service it runs in. It skips everything Boot attached to its builder: the service's Jackson settings, the tracing that adds a traceparent header, and any timeouts. Boot's documentation says it plainly: without the auto-configured builder, "automatic trace propagation won't work!" So when a payout of £1,240.50 fails, its trace stops at Payouts and the policy call is missing from it. The string concatenation is a second bug. A policy ID with a / or a space in it produces a different URL, because nothing encodes it. The host name is a third: it is written into the code, so the test environment calls the production name.

Do this now. RestClient is Spring's synchronous HTTP client, added in Framework 6.1. Use it like this:

  1. Inject the RestClient.Builder that Boot auto-configures. Each injection point gets its own copy, so what you add for the ledger does not leak into the policy client.
  2. Build the client once, in the constructor, and keep it in a field. A RestClient is safe to share between threads.
  3. Take the base URL from configuration, through a @ConfigurationProperties record bound to payouts.policy.* (4.02).
  4. Use URI templates: .uri("/policies/{id}", policyId). The template variables are encoded for you.
  5. Read the body with retrieve().body(PolicySummary.class). Use toEntity when you need status or headers, and toBodilessEntity when there is no body. For a generic type such as a list, pass a ParameterizedTypeReference.
  6. Map the response into a record that Payouts owns, in the client's package. Do not reuse the other team's classes (7.02).
@Component
public class PolicyClient {
    private final RestClient client;

    public PolicyClient(RestClient.Builder builder, PolicyClientProperties props) {
        this.client = builder.baseUrl(props.baseUrl()).build();
    }

    public PolicySummary find(String policyId) {
        return client.get()
                .uri("/policies/{id}", policyId)
                .retrieve()
                .body(PolicySummary.class);
    }
}

The client blocks its thread while it waits. That is fine. With spring.threads.virtual.enabled=true each request runs on a virtual thread, and a blocked virtual thread is cheap (3.01). This listing still has no timeout, and 7.03 adds one.

Also seen. WebClient when the service is reactive end to end, or when you need to stream a response. The JDK's own java.net.http.HttpClient in a library that must not depend on Spring. RestTemplate in code you are not otherwise changing: it still works on Boot 3.5, but it is deprecated from Framework 7, which Boot 4 uses.

When to break it. A throwaway script or a test may call RestClient.create(). The cost is that it gets none of the service's configuration, so never let one reach production code.

.NET anchor. The injected builder, built once, is close to a typed client registered with IHttpClientFactory: services.AddHttpClient<PolicyClient>(c => c.BaseAddress = ...). RestClient.create() per call is the Java cousin of new HttpClient() in a using block. The cost differs. In .NET it was socket exhaustion. Here it is mostly the configuration you silently lose.

See also. 7.02, 7.03, 7.09, 3.01, 4.02, The Yard, chapter 11, HTTP clients and resilience

7.02 Declare an HTTP client as an interface with @HttpExchange

Then.

  • Boot era: Spring Cloud OpenFeign. You wrote an interface with Spring MVC annotations, and Feign generated the client. It fitted the Netflix stack of its day, with load balancing and Hystrix built in.
// @EnableFeignClients on a @Configuration class
@FeignClient(name = "policy", url = "${payouts.policy.base-url}")
public interface PolicyFeignClient {
    @GetMapping("/policies/{id}")
    PolicySummary find(@PathVariable("id") String id);
}
  • Boot era: Retrofit, from Square, in teams that came from Android: @GET("policies/{id}") on an interface method returning Call<PolicySummary>.

Recognise it by. @FeignClient, @EnableFeignClients, org.springframework.cloud.openfeign, the spring-cloud-starter-openfeign artifactId, feign.client.config.* keys, and retrofit2 imports.

The rookie version.

import com.sorrel.ledger.api.LedgerApi;          // the ledger team's jar
import com.sorrel.ledger.api.LedgerEntryDocument; // their internal type

@Bean
LedgerApi ledgerApi(RestClient.Builder builder) {
    RestClient rest = builder.baseUrl("http://ledger").build();
    return HttpServiceProxyFactory.builderFor(RestClientAdapter.create(rest))
            .build().createClient(LedgerApi.class);
}

What goes wrong. The interface is fine. The dependency is the mistake. The ledger team's jar brings its own dependencies with it. When ledger-api 3.5.0 moved to a newer Jackson, Payouts' build resolved that Jackson too, by Maven's nearest-wins rule (1.02): when two libraries ask for different versions, the one declared closest to your project in the dependency tree wins. Then 2 serialisation tests failed in a release that changed nothing in Payouts. The interface also describes the ledger's whole API, 31 methods, of which Payouts calls 2. Every ledger release now forces a Payouts upgrade, and the two teams' deploys are tied together. LedgerEntryDocument is how the ledger stores an entry, not what it promises callers.

Do this now. An HTTP interface is a Java interface whose methods describe HTTP requests. Spring generates the implementation at startup and sends each call through a RestClient. This arrived in Framework 6.0, with RestClient support in 6.1, and needs no Spring Cloud.

  1. Write the interface in Payouts, with only the calls Payouts makes, and records Payouts owns.
  2. Put @HttpExchange on the type for the common path, and @GetExchange, @PostExchange, @PutExchange or @DeleteExchange on each method.
  3. Mark parameters as you would on a controller: @PathVariable, @RequestParam, @RequestHeader, @RequestBody.
@HttpExchange("/ledger")
public interface LedgerClient {

    @PostExchange("/reservations")
    LedgerReservation reserve(@RequestHeader("Idempotency-Key") String key,
                              @RequestBody ReserveRequest request);

    @DeleteExchange("/reservations/{id}")
    void release(@PathVariable("id") String reservationId,
                 @RequestHeader("Idempotency-Key") String key);
}
  1. On Boot 3.5, create the proxy yourself from a RestClient. The timeouts, token interceptor and status handlers on that client apply to every method.
@Bean
LedgerClient ledgerClient(RestClient.Builder builder, LedgerProperties props) {
    RestClient rest = builder.baseUrl(props.baseUrl()).build();
    return HttpServiceProxyFactory
            .builderFor(RestClientAdapter.create(rest))
            .build()
            .createClient(LedgerClient.class);
}
  1. In Boot 4 the proxies are auto-configured. You annotate a configuration class with @ImportHttpServices(group = "ledger", basePackages = "com.sorrel.payouts.ledger") and set spring.http.serviceclient.ledger.base-url.

Error responses behave as they do with retrieve(): a 4xx or 5xx becomes an exception (7.10). Put resilience annotations on the service method that calls the interface, not on the interface itself (7.05).

Also seen. OpenFeign in existing services. It still works, but it carries Spring Cloud for one job Spring now does itself. A plain RestClient class (7.01) when calls need different handling one by one.

When to break it. When the other team generates a client from its OpenAPI document and versions it with care (5.16), depending on that client can be reasonable. The cost is that their release schedule touches yours, so pin the version and read its dependency tree (1.03).

.NET anchor. This is Refit: [Post("/ledger/reservations")] on an interface, registered with AddRefitClient<ILedgerClient>(). The difference is small. Spring's proxy goes through the same RestClient and its interceptors that a hand-written client uses.

See also. 7.01, 7.05, 7.10, 1.03, 5.16, HTTP clients and resilience

7.03 Set connect and read timeouts on every client

Then.

  • Spring era: timeouts set in milliseconds on a request factory, and the factory handed to a RestTemplate.
HttpComponentsClientHttpRequestFactory factory = new HttpComponentsClientHttpRequestFactory();
factory.setConnectTimeout(1000);
factory.setReadTimeout(2000);
RestTemplate rest = new RestTemplate(factory);
  • Boot era: new RestTemplateBuilder().setConnectTimeout(Duration.ofSeconds(1)), or a JVM-wide default for HttpURLConnection on the command line. Hystrix and Ribbon each carried their own timeout keys as well, so one call could have three.

Recognise it by. -Dsun.net.client.defaultConnectTimeout and -Dsun.net.client.defaultReadTimeout in a start script, setReadTimeout(int) with a bare millisecond number, ribbon.ReadTimeout, and execution.isolation.thread.timeoutInMilliseconds.

The rookie version.

payouts:
  ledger:
    base-url: http://ledger.ledger.svc.cluster.local:8080
    connect-timeout: 30s
    read-timeout: 60s   # the ledger is sometimes slow, so be generous

What goes wrong. A generous timeout behaves like no timeout during an incident. Say a month-end spike sends each pod 20 payout requests a second, and the ledger stalls. Each request now waits the full 60 seconds, so after one minute 20 × 60 = 1,200 requests are stuck in the pod. Virtual threads make the waiting itself cheap, but each stuck request still holds its memory and a ledger connection. The pool of 20 ledger connections is taken in the first second, and every later request queues behind it. Memory climbs until the pod is killed. The claims portal that called Payouts gave up after 10 seconds anyway, so Payouts spent the other 50 working for nobody.

Do this now. A connect timeout bounds the wait to open a connection. A read timeout bounds the wait for data once the request has gone.

  1. Choose each number from measurement. Take the dependency's slowest normal response over a week, its 99th percentile, and add a margin. The ledger answers in about 200 ms, so Payouts uses connect 1 second and read 2 seconds.
  2. Keep the connect timeout short. On a cluster network a connection opens quickly or not at all.
  3. Set the values per client, on the request factory that client uses. Build the factory with Boot's ClientHttpRequestFactoryBuilder, so you keep the HTTP library Boot detected. With Apache HttpClient on the classpath, that is a pooled client (7.12). Do not write new SimpleClientHttpRequestFactory(): it uses the JDK's HttpURLConnection and silently drops the pool.
@Bean
RestClient ledgerRestClient(RestClient.Builder builder, LedgerProperties props) {
    var settings = ClientHttpRequestFactorySettings.defaults()
            .withConnectTimeout(props.connectTimeout())   // Duration, 1s
            .withReadTimeout(props.readTimeout());        // Duration, 2s
    return builder.baseUrl(props.baseUrl())
            .requestFactory(ClientHttpRequestFactoryBuilder.detect().build(settings))
            .build();
}
  1. Know what a timeout looks like. A read timeout surfaces as ResourceAccessException, caused by SocketTimeoutException. Map it on purpose (7.10), and treat it as "unknown" on a write (7.07).
  2. Time the hidden calls too. A client-credentials token request is a call to the identity provider, and it needs its own timeout (7.08).
  3. Remember what a read timeout measures. With these factories it bounds each wait for the next bytes, not the whole response. A server that trickles a byte a second never trips it. To bound the whole operation you need a deadline (7.15).

Boot can also set timeouts for every client it builds. On Boot 3.5 the properties are spring.http.client.connect-timeout and spring.http.client.read-timeout. In Boot 4 they are spring.http.clients.connect-timeout and spring.http.clients.read-timeout. Set a sensible floor there, and set the dependencies that differ, such as the slower bank gateway, in code as above.

Also seen. A resilience4j TimeLimiter, which bounds a call that returns a CompletableFuture. The JDK HttpClient's per-request HttpRequest.Builder.timeout(Duration), when you use that client directly.

When to break it. A call that is slow by nature, such as downloading a month's statement from the bank gateway, may need a read timeout of minutes. Give it its own client and its own bulkhead (7.06), so its threads cannot crowd out the payment path. The cost is a second client to configure and watch.

.NET anchor. SocketsHttpHandler.ConnectTimeout is the connect timeout. HttpClient.Timeout is different from a Java read timeout: it bounds the whole request, which is closer to a deadline. Java's read timeout bounds silence on the socket.

See also. 7.07, 7.08, 7.10, 7.15, 17.04, The Yard, chapter 11, HTTP clients and resilience

7.04 Retry with backoff and jitter, and only what is safe

Then.

  • Boot era: Spring Retry. You enabled it with @EnableRetry and annotated the method. It was the standard Spring answer for years. It was archived on 27 July 2026, superseded by the retry support in Spring Framework 7.
@Retryable(value = ResourceAccessException.class, maxAttempts = 3,
           backoff = @Backoff(delay = 200, multiplier = 2))
public PolicySummary find(String policyId) { ... }

@Recover
public PolicySummary recover(ResourceAccessException e, String policyId) { ... }

Recognise it by. org.springframework.retry.annotation.Retryable, @Backoff, @Recover, @EnableRetry, and the spring-retry artifactId. Check the import. Framework 7 has its own @Retryable and RetryTemplate, with the same simple names, in org.springframework.resilience.annotation and org.springframework.core.retry.

The rookie version.

for (int attempt = 1; attempt <= 3; attempt++) {
    try {
        return policyClient.find(policyId);
    } catch (RestClientException e) {
        if (attempt == 3) throw e;
    }
}
throw new IllegalStateException("unreachable");

What goes wrong. The loop retries at once, with no pause. When the policy system has a 300 ms hiccup, the 40 requests in flight across 2 pods become 120 requests inside 50 ms. That lands on the service at the moment it is weakest. The loop also catches every RestClientException, and HttpClientErrorException is one of them. So a 404 for a policy that does not exist is asked for 3 times, and the 404 still comes back.

Do this now. A retry repeats a call that failed. Make it safe first, and gentle second.

  1. Retry only failures that a second attempt could fix: connection failures, timeouts, and 502, 503 and 504. Never retry a 400, 404, 409 or 422: the answer will not change. The exception is a 409 or 429 that carries Retry-After, such as an idempotency store's "still running" (5.05, 9.10).
  2. Retry only calls that are safe to repeat. A GET is. A POST is not, unless it carries an idempotency key the receiver honours (7.07).
  3. Back off exponentially: wait 200 ms, then 400 ms. Add jitter, a random part of each wait, so two pods that failed together do not retry together.
  4. Cap the attempts, and do the arithmetic against your caller's patience. Three attempts with a 2-second read timeout cost up to 3 × 2 s + 0.2 s + 0.4 s = 6.6 seconds.

On Boot 3.5 use resilience4j, and put @Retry(name = "policy") on the service method that calls the client:

resilience4j:
  retry:
    instances:
      policy:
        max-attempts: 3
        wait-duration: 200ms
        enable-exponential-backoff: true
        exponential-backoff-multiplier: 2
        enable-randomized-wait: true
        randomized-wait-factor: 0.5
        retry-exceptions:
          - org.springframework.web.client.ResourceAccessException
          - org.springframework.web.client.HttpServerErrorException

HttpServerErrorException covers every 5xx. If the client maps statuses to its own exceptions (7.10), list those types here instead, or the retry stops matching. To match step 1 exactly, list its subclasses HttpServerErrorException.BadGateway, .ServiceUnavailable and .GatewayTimeout instead. With both enable- flags on, resilience4j combines them into an exponential backoff with a random part. In resilience4j max-attempts counts the first call. In Boot 4 you can use Framework 7's own annotation instead, enabled with @EnableResilientMethods. Its maxRetries does not count the first call, so maxRetries = 2 is three attempts.

@Retryable(includes = ResourceAccessException.class,
           maxRetries = 2, delay = 200, multiplier = 2, jitter = 100)
public PolicySummary find(String policyId) { ... }

Neither library has a retry budget, a cap on retries across all calls. The circuit breaker in 7.05 plays that part: when the dependency is failing, it stops the retries for you.

Also seen. Programmatic retry, with Framework 7's RetryTemplate or resilience4j's Retry.decorateSupplier, where an annotation cannot reach. Libraries that retry for you, such as the AWS SDK. Know they do it, so you do not stack your retries on theirs.

When to break it. Do not retry at all when a person is waiting and can press the button again, or when a lower layer, such as a service mesh, already retries. Two layers of 3 attempts are 9 calls.

.NET anchor. This is Polly's retry strategy: AddRetry(new RetryStrategyOptions { MaxRetryAttempts = 2, BackoffType = DelayBackoffType.Exponential, UseJitter = true }). Polly's MaxRetryAttempts counts retries, like Framework 7's maxRetries. Resilience4j counts attempts.

See also. 7.05, 7.06, 7.07, 6.11, 16.10, The Yard, chapter 11, HTTP clients and resilience

7.05 Put a circuit breaker around a downstream service

Then.

  • Boot era: Netflix Hystrix, through Spring Cloud Netflix. Each annotated method became a command with a timeout, a thread pool and a breaker. It carried a generation of Java services, and it is now in maintenance mode. Its last release, 1.5.18, was in 2018.
@HystrixCommand(fallbackMethod = "ledgerDown", commandProperties = {
    @HystrixProperty(name = "circuitBreaker.requestVolumeThreshold", value = "10"),
    @HystrixProperty(name = "circuitBreaker.errorThresholdPercentage", value = "50")})
public LedgerReservation reserve(Payout payout) { ... }

Recognise it by. @EnableCircuitBreaker, @EnableHystrix, com.netflix.hystrix, the spring-cloud-starter-netflix-hystrix artifactId, hystrix.command.default.* keys, and a /hystrix.stream endpoint feeding a dashboard.

The rookie version.

@CircuitBreaker(name = "downstream")
public LedgerReservation reserve(Payout payout) { ... }

@CircuitBreaker(name = "downstream")
public BankInstruction instruct(Payout payout) { ... }

What goes wrong. Two dependencies share one breaker, and it counts every exception. The bank gateway answers 422 for 6 payouts in a row, because the claimants' accounts are closed. That is the bank working correctly. But the shared instance is set to a window of 10 calls, and 6 failures in 10 is 60%, over the 50% threshold, so the breaker opens. Now ledger calls fail too, though the ledger is healthy. Every payout stops for the 20 seconds the breaker stays open, then again each time the next few closed accounts come through.

Do this now. A circuit breaker counts recent outcomes for one dependency. When too many fail, it opens and fails calls at once for a while, without touching the dependency. The Yard, chapter 11, explains the three states. For code:

  1. Give each dependency its own named instance: ledger, bankGateway, policy.
  2. Count only failures that mean the dependency is unwell: timeouts, connection errors and 5xx responses. Ignore 4xx responses. They are the dependency answering correctly.
  3. Count slow calls as well. Set the slow-call threshold below the read timeout, so the breaker opens on a ledger that is slow but not yet failing.
  4. Set a minimum number of calls, so 2 failures at 3 a.m. on a quiet night do not open it.
  5. Handle the open state. Resilience4j throws CallNotPermittedException. Map it to a 503 with a Retry-After header (6.09), or to a truthful fallback (7.11).
resilience4j:
  circuitbreaker:
    instances:
      ledger:
        sliding-window-type: COUNT_BASED
        sliding-window-size: 20
        minimum-number-of-calls: 10
        failure-rate-threshold: 50
        slow-call-duration-threshold: 1500ms
        slow-call-rate-threshold: 80
        wait-duration-in-open-state: 20s
        ignore-exceptions:
          - org.springframework.web.client.HttpClientErrorException

ignore-exceptions names the exception types the client throws. If the client maps a 404 to PolicyNotFound (7.10), a 404 is no longer an HttpClientErrorException, so list the mapped type too.

Annotate the service method with @CircuitBreaker(name = "ledger"). A starter is a dependency that brings everything one feature needs (1.01). The resilience4j starter is resilience4j-spring-boot3 on Boot 3.5 and resilience4j-spring-boot4 on Boot 4. It needs the Actuator and AOP starters beside it. AOP, aspect-oriented programming, is how the annotation works: Spring wraps the bean in a proxy that runs the breaker's logic around each call. In Boot 4 the AOP starter is renamed spring-boot-starter-aspectj.

Each pod keeps its own breaker. With 2 pods, one may open a few seconds before the other. That is expected.

Publish the state as a metric and put it on the dashboard (14.07). Do not put it in the readiness probe. An open ledger breaker would then take both healthy Payouts pods out of service for another team's outage (14.05).

Also seen. Spring Cloud Circuit Breaker, an abstraction over resilience4j with a CircuitBreakerFactory, in services that wanted to swap implementations. A service mesh's outlier detection, which ejects a bad pod rather than a whole dependency. Spring Framework 7 has retry and a concurrency limit in its core, but no circuit breaker. Resilience4j remains the answer for that.

When to break it. A dependency called a few times an hour never fills the window, so the breaker never decides anything. Use a timeout and a careful retry instead. The cost is that a dead dependency is discovered one slow call at a time.

.NET anchor. Polly's AddCircuitBreaker(new CircuitBreakerStrategyOptions { FailureRatio = 0.5, MinimumThroughput = 10, BreakDuration = ... }). Polly samples over a time window. Resilience4j can count the last N calls or the last N seconds, and you choose which.

See also. 7.06, 7.11, 6.09, 14.05, 16.10, The Yard, chapter 11, HTTP clients and resilience

7.06 Order the retry, breaker, bulkhead and time limiter

Then.

  • Boot era: a Hystrix command bundled everything into one class in a fixed order: a timeout, a thread pool per group as the bulkhead, the breaker, and a fallback. You could tune each part but not reorder them.
public class ReserveCommand extends HystrixCommand<LedgerReservation> {
    ReserveCommand(LedgerClient ledger, Payout payout) {
        super(HystrixCommandGroupKey.Factory.asKey("ledger"));
        this.ledger = ledger; this.payout = payout;
    }
    @Override protected LedgerReservation run() { return ledger.reserve(payout); }
    @Override protected LedgerReservation getFallback() { return LedgerReservation.none(); }
}

Recognise it by. Classes that extend HystrixCommand or HystrixObservableCommand, HystrixCommandGroupKey, and HystrixThreadPoolProperties.

The rookie version.

Supplier<LedgerReservation> call = () -> ledgerClient.reserve(key, request);
Supplier<LedgerReservation> guarded =
        CircuitBreaker.decorateSupplier(breaker,
            Retry.decorateSupplier(retry, call));

What goes wrong. Here the retry is inside the breaker. The breaker sees one outcome for every 3 attempts. With a minimum of 10 calls, it needs 30 failed ledger calls before it can open, not 10. During those calls the ledger gets 3 times the load. The breaker opens late and protects the ledger least when it most needs protecting.

Do this now. A bulkhead caps how many calls to one dependency run at once. A time limiter bounds how long one call may take. Wrap them from the outside in:

  1. Retry, outermost. Each attempt passes through the breaker and is counted. An open breaker ends the retries at once.
  2. Circuit breaker. It sees every real call and its timeouts. A full bulkhead counts against it too, which is fair: it means the ledger is slow.
  3. Bulkhead. It caps concurrent ledger calls at 20, so a slow ledger can hold at most 20 threads.
  4. Timeout, innermost. For a blocking RestClient, the read timeout is the time limiter. Resilience4j's TimeLimiter works on asynchronous return types such as CompletableFuture. Its annotation rejects a method with a plain return type, so a blocking method relies on the read timeout instead.
  5. Tell the retry not to retry CallNotPermittedException or BulkheadFullException. Retrying a call that was refused on purpose undoes the refusal. Add both to the retry's ignore-exceptions.

With annotations, resilience4j applies its aspects in a fixed default order, not the order you write them: Retry outermost, then CircuitBreaker, RateLimiter, TimeLimiter and Bulkhead. That matches the diagram. The *-aspect-order properties, such as resilience4j.retry.retry-aspect-order, change it. Prove the order you rely on with a test (16.10). Or compose by hand, so the order is in the code:

Supplier<LedgerReservation> call = () -> ledgerClient.reserve(key, request);
Supplier<LedgerReservation> guarded =
        Retry.decorateSupplier(retry,
            CircuitBreaker.decorateSupplier(breaker,
                Bulkhead.decorateSupplier(bulkhead, call)));
return guarded.get();

The retry, breaker and bulkhead objects come from the registries the starter auto-configures: RetryRegistry, CircuitBreakerRegistry and BulkheadRegistry, each looked up by the name ledger.

Use one library for the whole stack on a given call. If Framework 7's @Retryable wraps a resilience4j breaker, two separate aspect systems decide the order between them.

Also seen. Framework 7's @ConcurrencyLimit as the bulkhead, on Boot 4, where nothing else from resilience4j is needed. It makes extra callers wait for a slot rather than fail, so it does not fail fast. A thread-pool bulkhead, Bulkhead.Type.THREADPOOL, where the call must run on a separate pool.

When to break it. Put the retry inside the breaker when you want the breaker to count logical operations, as a user sees them, rather than attempts. The cost is a breaker that opens about 3 times later.

.NET anchor. AddStandardResilienceHandler() in Microsoft.Extensions.Http.Resilience builds the same shape, outermost first: rate limiter, total timeout, retry, circuit breaker, then a timeout per attempt. In Polly the order is the order of your Add* calls. In resilience4j annotations it is not the order you write them.

See also. 7.03, 7.04, 7.05, 3.09, 16.10, The Yard, chapter 11, HTTP clients and resilience

7.07 Never retry a non-idempotent call blindly

Then.

  • Boot era: Ribbon, Netflix's client-side load balancer, retried failed calls on the same server and then on others. With one setting it retried every method, including POST. It was right for reads against a pool of VMs where one could vanish. Kubernetes Services and Spring Cloud LoadBalancer have since replaced it.
ledger.ribbon.MaxAutoRetries=1
ledger.ribbon.MaxAutoRetriesNextServer=2
ledger.ribbon.OkToRetryOnAllOperations=true

Recognise it by. OkToRetryOnAllOperations, MaxAutoRetriesNextServer, com.netflix.ribbon, and @Retryable or @Retry on a method whose name starts with create, pay, send or instruct.

The rookie version.

@Retry(name = "bankGateway")
public BankInstruction instruct(Payout payout) {
    return bankGatewayClient.instruct(new InstructionRequest(
            payout.accountNumber(), payout.amount()));
}

What goes wrong. The bank gateway receives the instruction for £1,240.50 and processes it in 2.3 seconds. Payouts' read timeout fired at 2 seconds, so Payouts never saw the reply. The retry sends the instruction again, and the bank pays it again. The claimant receives £2,481.00. Instructing the bank is the saga's pivot step: once it has happened, it cannot be undone by Payouts. Getting the money back takes a phone call to the bank and a letter to the claimant.

Do this now. A call is idempotent when doing it twice has the same effect as doing it once.

  1. Classify every outbound call. A GET is safe. A PUT to a known ID and a DELETE are idempotent by design. A POST is unsafe, unless the receiver honours an idempotency key: an ID sent with the request, which the receiver uses to recognise a repeat and answer it without acting twice.
  2. Create the key once per business operation, before the first attempt, and store it with the saga's state. Every retry, and every recovery after a crash, reuses the stored key.
  3. Agree with the other team what a repeat returns: the original response, or a 409 that points at it. Put that in the contract test (16.16).
  4. Treat a timeout on an unsafe call as "unknown". Ask before you act again.
  5. Return the three outcomes as a sealed interface, so every caller must handle each one (2.12). The records are nested, and the code that uses them imports them.
public sealed interface InstructionOutcome {
    record Instructed(BankInstruction instruction) implements InstructionOutcome {}
    record Rejected(String reason) implements InstructionOutcome {}   // the bank said no
    record Unknown(Exception cause) implements InstructionOutcome {}  // we cannot tell
}

public InstructionOutcome instruct(Payout payout, SagaState saga) {
    String key = saga.instructionKey();          // saved before the first attempt
    try {
        return new Instructed(bankGatewayClient.instruct(key, InstructionRequest.from(payout)));
    } catch (HttpClientErrorException refused) {
        if (isKeyReused(refused)) return new Unknown(refused); // not a refusal
        return new Rejected(refused.getStatusText()); // any other 4xx: the bank did not act
    } catch (ResourceAccessException timeout) {
        return bankGatewayClient.findByKey(key)  // did the bank act?
                .<InstructionOutcome>map(Instructed::new)
                .orElseGet(() -> new Unknown(timeout));
    }
}

isKeyReused checks for the error the bank's contract defines for a key sent again with a different request. That is not a refusal: the first request may have been acted on, so it is Unknown (11.06). Test for it before mapping the 4xx to Rejected.

  1. Turn off retries you did not ask for. Apache HttpClient 5 has its own retry strategy, and HttpClients.custom().disableAutomaticRetries() turns it off for a client used for unsafe calls.

Also seen. A queue between Payouts and the bank gateway, with a consumer that deduplicates (10.07). The retry then belongs to the queue, and the duplicate check to the consumer.

When to break it. You may retry a POST without a key when the receiver treats the request body itself as the identity, for example a unique constraint on the payout ID. The cost is that you rely on a rule in someone else's database, so write it into the contract.

.NET anchor. The same rule applies to Polly. Microsoft.Extensions.Http.Resilience can be told to skip retries for unsafe HTTP methods, and the idempotency-key pattern is the same as in ASP.NET Core APIs.

See also. 5.05, 9.09, 9.10, 10.07, 11.06, 7.16, The Yard, chapter 11

7.08 Authenticate to internal services with client credentials

Then.

  • Boot era: the separate Spring Security OAuth project, with an OAuth2RestTemplate that fetched and cached the token. It was the standard way to call a protected service before Spring Security grew its own OAuth2 client support, which is what Boot configures today.
ClientCredentialsResourceDetails details = new ClientCredentialsResourceDetails();
details.setAccessTokenUri(tokenUri);
details.setClientId("payouts-api");
details.setClientSecret(secret);
OAuth2RestTemplate rest = new OAuth2RestTemplate(details);
  • Spring era: a shared service-account password sent as Basic authentication, set on the HTTP client's credentials and later through Spring's BasicAuthenticationInterceptor, or no authentication at all behind a network allow list.

Recognise it by. OAuth2RestTemplate, @EnableOAuth2Client, ClientCredentialsResourceDetails, the spring-security-oauth2 and spring-security-oauth2-autoconfigure artifactIds, and security.oauth2.client.* keys without the spring. prefix.

The rookie version.

public LedgerReservation reserve(String key, ReserveRequest request) {
    TokenResponse token = RestClient.create().post().uri(props.tokenUri())
            .contentType(MediaType.APPLICATION_FORM_URLENCODED)
            .body("grant_type=client_credentials&client_id=payouts-api&client_secret=" + secret)
            .retrieve().body(TokenResponse.class);
    return client.post().uri("/ledger/reservations")
            .header("Authorization", "Bearer " + token.accessToken())
            .header("Idempotency-Key", key)
            .body(request).retrieve().body(LedgerReservation.class);
}

What goes wrong. Every ledger call is now two calls. At the month-end peak of 20 payouts a second on each of 2 pods, the identity provider receives 40 token requests a second for tokens that would have lasted an hour. It rate-limits Payouts, and payouts fail with 429s from a service nobody thought was involved. The token call has no timeout, so a slow identity provider holds Payouts' threads too. The secret is concatenated into the body unencoded, so a secret containing & breaks the request.

Do this now. Client credentials is the OAuth2 flow for a service acting as itself. Payouts proves who it is with its own ID and secret, and receives a token to send to the ledger.

  1. Add spring-boot-starter-oauth2-client. In Boot 4 it is renamed spring-boot-starter-security-oauth2-client.
  2. Register the client in configuration, with the secret from a secret store (4.04).
spring:
  security:
    oauth2:
      client:
        registration:
          ledger:
            provider: sorrel-idp
            client-id: payouts-api
            client-secret: ${LEDGER_CLIENT_SECRET}
            authorization-grant-type: client_credentials
            scope: ledger.reserve
        provider:
          sorrel-idp:
            token-uri: https://idp.sorrel.internal/oauth2/token
  1. Use the manager built for background work. AuthorizedClientServiceOAuth2AuthorizedClientManager does not need an incoming HTTP request, so it also works from a scheduled job or an SQS listener.
  2. Add Spring Security's OAuth2ClientHttpRequestInterceptor to the ledger's RestClient. It asks the manager for a token and adds the Authorization header. The manager keeps the token and fetches a new one only near expiry (15.04).
@Bean
OAuth2AuthorizedClientManager clientManager(ClientRegistrationRepository registrations,
                                            OAuth2AuthorizedClientService clients) {
    return new AuthorizedClientServiceOAuth2AuthorizedClientManager(registrations, clients);
}

@Bean
RestClient ledgerRestClient(RestClient.Builder builder, OAuth2AuthorizedClientManager manager,
                            LedgerProperties props) {
    var oauth = new OAuth2ClientHttpRequestInterceptor(manager);
    oauth.setClientRegistrationIdResolver(request -> "ledger");
    oauth.setPrincipalResolver(request -> PAYOUTS); // one token for the service (15.04)
    return builder.baseUrl(props.baseUrl()).requestInterceptor(oauth).build();
}
  1. Give the token request a timeout of its own. Spring Security sends it through a separate token-response client, not through the ledger's RestClient. Wire it in four steps: - Build a RestClient with timeouts (7.03). It also needs the two OAuth2 message converters and the OAuth2 error handler that Spring Security's documentation lists, because it replaces the default one. - Hand it to a RestClientClientCredentialsTokenResponseClient with setRestClient. - Build a provider for the client-credentials grant that uses that token client. - Set the provider on the manager from step 3.
RestClient tokenRest = RestClient.builder()
        .requestFactory(ClientHttpRequestFactoryBuilder.detect().build(tokenTimeouts))
        .messageConverters(c -> {
            c.clear();
            c.add(new FormHttpMessageConverter());
            c.add(new OAuth2AccessTokenResponseHttpMessageConverter());
        })
        .defaultStatusHandler(new OAuth2ErrorResponseErrorHandler())
        .build();
var tokens = new RestClientClientCredentialsTokenResponseClient();
tokens.setRestClient(tokenRest);
manager.setAuthorizedClientProvider(OAuth2AuthorizedClientProviderBuilder.builder()
        .clientCredentials(cc -> cc.accessTokenResponseClient(tokens))
        .build());

tokenTimeouts is a ClientHttpRequestFactorySettings, as in 7.03.

Also seen. Mutual TLS from a service mesh, where the mesh proves identity and the code sends no token. Kubernetes service-account tokens, where the identity provider trusts the cluster.

When to break it. Inside a mesh that enforces mTLS and per-service authorisation policies, service tokens may add little. The cost is that permission becomes "which service" only, with no scopes such as ledger.reserve.

.NET anchor. Duende.AccessTokenManagement: AddClientCredentialsTokenManagement() and then AddClientCredentialsTokenHandler("ledger") on the HttpClient. Spring's interceptor plays the role of that DelegatingHandler.

See also. 15.04, 15.06, 4.04, 7.03, 7.01, The Yard, chapter 11, Security

7.09 Pass trace and correlation headers downstream

Then.

  • Boot era: Spring Cloud Sleuth added X-B3-TraceId and X-B3-SpanId headers to outbound calls. Its last minor version is 3.1, and it does not work with Boot 3. Its core moved into Micrometer Tracing.
  • Spring era: a ClientHttpRequestInterceptor on each RestTemplate that copied a hand-made request ID from the logging context into a header. It was the only option before tracing libraries existed.

Recognise it by. X-B3-TraceId, spring-cloud-starter-sleuth, and MDC.get("requestId") inside an interceptor.

What goes wrong. A client built with RestClient.create() or new RestTemplate() sends no trace header. The ledger starts a fresh trace for every Payouts call. When a payout of £1,240.50 fails, its trace ends at Payouts.

Do this now. Build every client from the auto-configured RestClient.Builder. Boot then sends the W3C traceparent header by default, and accepts W3C and B3 headers on the way in. You add no code. For a business ID, such as the claim reference, an interceptor on the builder may still copy it into an agreed header. Test once that the header arrives (7.14).

See also. 13.04, 13.10, 12.04, 3.04, 7.01, Actuator and observability

7.10 Turn a client's error responses into exceptions deliberately

Then.

  • Spring era: a ResponseErrorHandler, often a subclass of DefaultResponseErrorHandler, set with restTemplate.setErrorHandler(...). It was one handler per client for every status.

Recognise it by. setErrorHandler, DefaultResponseErrorHandler, and hasError(ClientHttpResponse).

What goes wrong. By default retrieve() throws HttpClientErrorException for a 4xx and HttpServerErrorException for a 5xx. Unmapped, a policy 404 becomes a 500 from Payouts, and the retry cannot tell "not there" from "down".

Do this now. Decide each status deliberately, in the client, and turn it into a type Payouts owns:

return client.get().uri("/policies/{id}", policyId)
        .retrieve()
        .onStatus(status -> status.value() == 404, (request, response) -> {
            throw new PolicyNotFound(policyId);
        })
        .onStatus(HttpStatusCode::is5xxServerError, (request, response) -> {
            throw new PolicySystemUnavailable(response.getStatusCode().value());
        })
        .body(PolicySummary.class);

Rules shared by every call go on the builder with defaultStatusHandler. Mapping changes the exception types, so update the resilience configuration (7.04, 7.05) to match. Otherwise the breaker counts 404s again:

resilience4j:
  retry:
    instances:
      policy:
        retry-exceptions:
          - org.springframework.web.client.ResourceAccessException
          - com.sorrel.payouts.policy.PolicySystemUnavailable
  circuitbreaker:
    instances:
      policy:
        ignore-exceptions:
          - org.springframework.web.client.HttpClientErrorException  # unmapped 4xx
          - com.sorrel.payouts.policy.PolicyNotFound

See also. 6.09, 6.04, 7.04, 7.05, Validation and error responses

7.11 Add a fallback that tells the truth

Then.

  • Boot era: Hystrix fallback methods that returned a default value. Netflix designed them for things like a recommendations row, where a generic list beats an error page. On a money path the same pattern invents an answer.
@HystrixCommand(fallbackMethod = "defaultLimit")
public Money dailyLimit(String claimantId) { return policyClient.limit(claimantId); }

public Money defaultLimit(String claimantId) { return Money.gbp("5000.00"); }

Recognise it by. fallbackMethod on @HystrixCommand, getFallback() overrides, @FeignClient(fallback = ...), and feign.hystrix.enabled.

The rookie version.

@CircuitBreaker(name = "ledger", fallbackMethod = "reserveLater")
public LedgerReservation reserve(Payout payout) { ... }

private LedgerReservation reserveLater(Payout payout, Throwable t) {
    return new LedgerReservation("PENDING", payout.amount());
}

What goes wrong. The fallback returns something that looks like a reservation. The saga reads it as success and moves on to instruct the bank. For 20 minutes the ledger is down, and 37 payouts are paid with no ledger reservation behind them. The ledger team's reconciliation finds the gap 2 days later. The fallback also catches Throwable, so a 400 for a malformed request becomes "pending" too.

Do this now. A fallback is the method the library calls instead of failing. It must return the truth in a shape the caller cannot mistake for success.

  1. For writes, usually have no fallback. Fail clearly, or accept the work as pending with a 202 and a status resource (5.06), and let the saga retry it later.
  2. For reads, a fallback may return an older answer, labelled as older, with its age.
  3. Make the return type say which answer it is. A sealed interface does this, and the compiler makes every caller handle each case (2.12).
public sealed interface PolicyLookup {
    record Fresh(PolicySummary policy) implements PolicyLookup {}
    record Stale(PolicySummary policy, Instant fetchedAt) implements PolicyLookup {}
    record Unavailable(String reason) implements PolicyLookup {}
}
  1. Catch a narrow exception. The fallback method takes the same parameters plus the exception. Resilience4j chooses the fallback whose exception type matches best, so you can write one for an open breaker and none for a 400.
@CircuitBreaker(name = "policy", fallbackMethod = "fromCache")
public PolicyLookup lookup(String policyId) {
    return new PolicyLookup.Fresh(policyClient.find(policyId));
}

private PolicyLookup fromCache(String policyId, CallNotPermittedException e) {
    return cache.find(policyId)
            .<PolicyLookup>map(c -> new PolicyLookup.Stale(c.policy(), c.fetchedAt()))
            .orElse(new PolicyLookup.Unavailable("policy system circuit open"));
}
  1. Count every fallback as a metric. A fallback that runs all day is an outage nobody has noticed.
  2. At the edge of Payouts, Unavailable becomes a 503 ProblemDetail with a Retry-After header (6.02).

Also seen. A static default where the business has signed it off, such as showing "limit unknown" on a screen. A queue to hold the work until the dependency returns (21.05).

When to break it. A display-only read, such as the claimant's name on a status page, may fall back to a placeholder. The cost is small, as long as no decision is ever made on it.

.NET anchor. Polly's AddFallback(new FallbackStrategyOptions<T> { ... }). The same rule applies: the FallbackAction should return a result type that says it is a fallback.

See also. 7.05, 7.13, 2.12, 5.06, 6.02, 21.05, HTTP clients and resilience

7.12 Configure the HTTP connection pool

What goes wrong. Apache HttpClient keeps a pool of open connections and, by default, allows only a few per destination host. With virtual threads on, 60 payouts can call the ledger at once, and most of them queue for a connection inside Payouts. The ledger answers in 200 ms, yet Payouts' 99th percentile rises to 3 seconds. Nobody looks at the pool, because the ledger's graphs are green.

Do this now. When Apache HttpClient 5 is on the classpath, Boot picks it first. Size its pool to match the bulkhead (7.06), and bound the wait for a free connection. Use Boot's builder, so the timeouts from 7.03 still apply:

var factory = ClientHttpRequestFactoryBuilder.httpComponents()
        .withConnectionManagerCustomizer(pool -> pool
                .setMaxConnPerRoute(20)
                .setMaxConnTotal(40))
        .withDefaultRequestConfigCustomizer(request -> request
                .setConnectionRequestTimeout(Timeout.ofMilliseconds(500)))
        .withHttpClientCustomizer(http -> http
                .evictIdleConnections(TimeValue.ofSeconds(30)))
        .build(settings);   // the timeouts from 7.03
builder.requestFactory(factory);

Watch the pool's metrics next to the call latency.

.NET anchor. SocketsHttpHandler.MaxConnectionsPerServer has no limit by default, so a .NET developer rarely meets this queue. Java pools cap connections per host, and the cap is low. Set it on purpose.

See also. 18.03, 3.09, 7.06, 7.17, HTTP clients and resilience

7.13 Cache a slow lookup that rarely changes

What goes wrong. Every payout asks the policy system for the product rules of the claim's policy type. There are 14 product types, and their rules change once a month. Yet at the month-end peak Payouts makes 40 identical calls a second, and every policy-system outage becomes a Payouts outage.

Do this now. Cache the lookup with Spring's cache abstraction and Caffeine, an in-memory cache library. Add spring-boot-starter-cache and com.github.ben-manes.caffeine:caffeine, and set spring.cache.type=caffeine:

@Cacheable(cacheNames = "productRules", unless = "#result == null")
public ProductRules rulesFor(String productCode) {
    return policyClient.productRules(productCode);
}

Enable caching with @EnableCaching. Set the size and expiry with spring.cache.caffeine.spec=maximumSize=500,expireAfterWrite=10m. Spring caches through a proxy around the bean, so call the method from another bean. A call from inside the same class goes straight to the method, not through the proxy, and skips the cache (4.08). Each pod has its own cache, so 2 pods can disagree for up to 10 minutes. Never cache an error.

.NET anchor. Like IMemoryCache, but you never call the cache yourself. The proxy does it, so a self-call is never cached.

See also. 18.08, 4.08, 7.11, Caching, scheduling and events

7.14 Test a client against a fake server

Then.

  • Spring era: MockRestServiceServer.createServer(restTemplate), the same idea as today, bound to a RestTemplate.
  • Boot era: WireMock 2 under JUnit 4, as a rule on a fixed port, which clashed when two builds ran on one CI agent.
@Rule
public WireMockRule wireMock = new WireMockRule(8089);

Recognise it by. WireMockRule, the com.github.tomakehurst:wiremock-jre8 artifact, MockRestServiceServer.createServer, and @RunWith(SpringRunner.class).

The rookie version.

@MockitoBean LedgerClient ledgerClient;

@Test
void reservesTheAmount() {
    when(ledgerClient.reserve(any(), any())).thenReturn(new LedgerReservation("R-1", AMOUNT));
    payoutService.pay(claim);
    verify(ledgerClient).reserve(any(), any());
}

What goes wrong. This tests PayoutService, not the client. The URL, the JSON field names, the Idempotency-Key header, the 409 mapping and the timeouts are never exercised. When the ledger renamed amountMinor to amount, this test stayed green. In production every reservation failed with a 400 for 40 minutes.

Do this now. Test the client at two levels.

  1. Shape, fast and in memory. MockRestServiceServer replaces the client's request factory. You state the request you expect and the response to give. This checks the URL, method, headers, body and how each status is mapped.
class PolicyClientTest {
    RestClient.Builder builder = RestClient.builder();
    MockRestServiceServer server = MockRestServiceServer.bindTo(builder).build();
    PolicyClient client = new PolicyClient(builder, new PolicyClientProperties("http://policy"));

    @Test
    void readsAPolicySummary() {
        server.expect(requestTo("http://policy/policies/P-100"))
              .andExpect(method(HttpMethod.GET))
              .andRespond(withSuccess("""
                  {"policyId":"P-100","status":"ACTIVE"}""", MediaType.APPLICATION_JSON));
        assertThat(client.find("P-100").status()).isEqualTo("ACTIVE");
        server.verify();
    }
}

Write one test per status the client maps: a 200, a 404, a 409 and a 503. For the ledger, also assert the request itself. header("Idempotency-Key", "K-1") checks the key is sent, and content().json(...) checks the body field by field. Those two assertions pin down exactly what Payouts sends, so a rename such as amountMinor becomes a visible change to a test.

  1. Wire, over a real socket. Because MockRestServiceServer replaces the request factory, it cannot test timeouts, pools or connection resets. WireMock is a real HTTP server for tests. Its stable line is 3.13.x, and 4.x is still in beta. Under JUnit 5 it runs as an extension on a free port. Point the real client, with the real timeouts, at wireMock.baseUrl().
@RegisterExtension
static WireMockExtension wireMock = WireMockExtension.newInstance()
        .options(wireMockConfig().dynamicPort())
        .build();

wireMock.stubFor(post("/ledger/reservations")
        .willReturn(aResponse().withStatus(200).withFixedDelay(3_000)));

assertThatThrownBy(() -> ledgerClient.reserve("K-1", request))
        .isInstanceOf(ResourceAccessException.class)
        .hasCauseInstanceOf(SocketTimeoutException.class);

Stub a dropped connection too, with aResponse().withFault(Fault.CONNECTION_RESET_BY_PEER), and check that the client reports it as a failure the retry recognises.

  1. Agree the shape itself with the other team in a contract test (16.16). Your fake only proves what you believe the ledger does.

Also seen. @RestClientTest, a Boot test slice that wires MockRestServiceServer to the auto-configured builder. A Testcontainers container running the other team's real image, for a few end-to-end checks.

When to break it. A mock of the client is the right tool when testing the code that uses it, such as the saga. The cost is that it proves nothing about HTTP, so the client still needs its own tests.

.NET anchor. MockRestServiceServer is like RichardSzalay.MockHttp's MockHttpMessageHandler. WireMock is WireMock.Net, used the same way.

See also. 16.09, 16.10, 16.16, 16.06, 7.03, Testing Spring Boot

7.15 Keep a deadline across several hops

What goes wrong. The claims portal gives up on Payouts after 2 seconds (9.10). Payouts calls the policy system, the ledger and the bank gateway in turn, each with its own timeouts and retries. In the worst case those add up to over 20 seconds, ten times the caller's patience. Payouts goes on working, and holding threads, long after the caller has left.

Do this now. Set a deadline at the edge: the moment by which the whole request must finish. Carry it with the request, and check it before each call.

public record Deadline(Instant at) {
    public Duration remaining(Clock clock) {
        return Duration.between(clock.instant(), at);
    }
    public void check(Clock clock, Duration floor) {
        if (remaining(clock).compareTo(floor) < 0) throw new DeadlineExceeded(at);
    }
}

Create it in the controller as 1.8 seconds from now, a little inside the portal's 2, using an injected Clock (2.16). Pass it as a parameter. The read timeout sits on the factory and cannot shrink per call, so bound the wait with a future:

deadline.check(clock, Duration.ofMillis(200));
return CompletableFuture
        .supplyAsync(() -> ledgerClient.reserve(key, request), calls)
        .orTimeout(deadline.remaining(clock).toMillis(), TimeUnit.MILLISECONDS)
        .join();   // CompletionException wrapping TimeoutException when late

calls is a SimpleAsyncTaskExecutor with virtual threads and a ContextPropagatingTaskDecorator, so the trace still travels. The ledger call itself runs on until its read timeout. Skip a retry that would pass the deadline. Send the remaining time downstream in an agreed header.

See also. 7.03, 7.04, 3.04, 2.16, 13.04

7.16 Handle a failure halfway through two calls

Then.

  • J2EE era: a distributed XA transaction through JTA, which asked every resource to prepare and then commit together. It worked across databases and message brokers that spoke XA. HTTP services never did.
UserTransaction tx = (UserTransaction) ctx.lookup("java:comp/UserTransaction");
tx.begin();
payoutsDb.insert(payout);
ledgerQueue.send(reserveMessage);
tx.commit();
  • Spring era: the same through JtaTransactionManager and a standalone transaction manager such as Atomikos or Bitronix.

Recognise it by. javax.transaction.UserTransaction, JtaTransactionManager, XADataSource, and com.atomikos or bitronix.tm imports.

The rookie version.

public void pay(Payout payout) {
    LedgerReservation r = ledgerClient.reserve(payout.idempotencyKey(), ReserveRequest.from(payout));
    try {
        bankGatewayClient.instruct(payout.idempotencyKey(), InstructionRequest.from(payout));
    } catch (RestClientException e) {
        ledgerClient.release(r.id(), "release-" + payout.id());
        throw e;
    }
}

What goes wrong. There are three gaps. If the bank call times out after the bank acted, the code releases the reservation, so the claimant is paid and the ledger shows nothing. If the pod is stopped between the two calls, during a deploy, nothing records that a reservation exists. If the release itself fails, the exception from the bank call is lost. In one deploy of 2 pods, 3 reservations totalling £3,912.75 were left open for 2 days, until the ledger team's reconciliation found them.

Do this now. This is a small saga: a sequence of steps across services, each with an undo step called a compensation. Part 11 covers sagas in full.

  1. Write down the intent before each call. The SagaState document in payout_sagas records the current step, and is saved before the call and again after it.
  2. Classify each failure. A 4xx or a refused connection means the step did not happen. A timeout or a reset after sending means you do not know.
  3. Compensate only definite failures, and only before the pivot step. If the bank refused, release the reservation.
  4. Never compensate an unknown pivot. Ask the bank by idempotency key. If it still cannot say, park the saga for a recovery job or a person.
switch (outcome) {
    case Instructed ok -> saga.advance(SagaStep.COMPLETED, ok.instruction().reference());
    case Rejected no   -> saga.compensate(SagaStep.RELEASE, no.reason());
    case Unknown u     -> saga.park(SagaStep.PARKED, u.cause().getMessage());
}
sagas.save(saga);
  1. Make every step idempotent, so recovery can safely run a step again (11.07).
  2. Run a recovery job that finds sagas stuck in one step for longer than expected (11.09).

InstructionOutcome is the sealed interface defined in 7.07, so the switch must handle all three cases: Instructed, Rejected and Unknown.

Also seen. Choreography, where each service reacts to the others' events instead of one orchestrator calling them (11.03). A workflow engine, such as Temporal or Step Functions, when there are many long sagas (11.11).

When to break it. If the first call is a read and only the second changes anything, there is nothing to undo, and a plain try and retry is enough.

.NET anchor. TransactionScope does not span HTTP calls either. The .NET answers are the same patterns: MassTransit sagas, or Durable Functions as the workflow engine.

See also. 7.07, 9.06, 9.14, 11.02, 11.05, 11.06, 11.09, Transactions, propagation and isolation

7.17 Find other services on Kubernetes without a registry

Then.

  • Boot era: Netflix Eureka as the registry and Ribbon as the client-side balancer. A @LoadBalanced RestTemplate resolved http://ledger/ through the registry. It was right on virtual machines with no platform DNS to lean on.

Recognise it by. @EnableEurekaClient, @EnableDiscoveryClient, eureka.client.serviceUrl.defaultZone, and @LoadBalanced.

What goes wrong. A team carries Eureka onto Kubernetes. Now two systems decide where ledger is, and they disagree for the seconds after a pod moves.

Do this now. Use the Kubernetes Service name. The ledger is http://ledger.ledger.svc.cluster.local:8080, read from payouts.ledger.base-url. Kubernetes spreads connections across the ledger's pods. It balances connections, not requests, so a pooled keep-alive connection stays on one pod. When the ledger scales from 2 pods to 4, the new pods get little Payouts traffic until old connections close. Give pooled connections a limited lifetime and evict idle ones (7.12).

See also. 7.12, 17.08, 17.06

7.18 Log outbound calls usefully

Then.

  • Boot era: logging.level.org.apache.http.wire=DEBUG, which logged every byte, including Authorization headers and bank details.

What goes wrong. Without outbound logs, a slow payout shows only "took 4.1 s". With wire logs, the log store holds claimants' account numbers and live tokens.

Do this now. Log one line per call from a ClientHttpRequestInterceptor: method, path, status and duration. The trace ID is already on the line from the logging context (13.06). Never log headers or bodies.

@Override
public ClientHttpResponse intercept(HttpRequest request, byte[] body,
                                    ClientHttpRequestExecution execution) throws IOException {
    long start = System.nanoTime();
    ClientHttpResponse response = execution.execute(request, body);
    log.info("outbound {} {} -> {} in {} ms", request.getMethod(), request.getURI().getPath(),
            response.getStatusCode().value(), (System.nanoTime() - start) / 1_000_000);
    return response;
}

The auto-configured builder also records a timer for each call. Read latency from that metric, not from logs (14.06).

See also. 12.01, 12.06, 13.06, 14.03, 14.06

⚠Review checklist
  • If you see RestClient.create() or new RestTemplate() in production code: the client misses the service's Jackson settings, tracing and timeouts. See 7.01.
  • If you see a dependency on another team's client or API jar: their dependencies and release schedule become yours. See 7.02.
  • If you see an HTTP client with no timeout, or a read timeout of tens of seconds: one slow dependency can take every thread. See 7.03.
  • If you see a retry loop that catches RestClientException with no pause: it retries 4xx answers and hits a struggling service in a burst. See 7.04.
  • If you see one circuit breaker name shared by two dependencies, or no ignore-exceptions for 4xx: a healthy dependency gets cut off. See 7.05.
  • If you see a retry composed inside a circuit breaker, or a retry that retries CallNotPermittedException: the breaker opens late and protects nothing. See 7.06.
  • If you see @Retry or @Retryable on a POST with no idempotency key: a timeout can become a double payment. See 7.07.
  • If you see a token fetched by hand inside a business call: the identity provider gets a request per call, with no timeout. See 7.08.
  • If you see a fallback on a write that returns something shaped like success: the saga carries on with money nobody recorded. See 7.11.
  • If you see a client tested only through @MockitoBean: the URL, JSON and timeouts are untested. See 7.14.
  • If you see a compensation call inside a catch block, with no saved saga state: a crash or an unknown outcome leaves money in limbo. See 7.16.
  • If you see wire-level HTTP logging switched on: tokens and bank details go into the log store. See 7.18.

Part IV · The how-to8. MongoDB API and DocumentDB#

Payouts keeps its payouts, sagas, outbox and idempotency keys in Amazon DocumentDB, AWS's managed document database. DocumentDB speaks the MongoDB API, so the service reaches it through MongoDB's Java driver and Spring Data MongoDB, but its engine is AWS's own. This part shows how to map, query, update, index and test those documents so they stay correct with 2 pods writing at once. It also shows which MongoDB features DocumentDB lacks on the engine Payouts runs, and how to check before you rely on one.

★What a veteran knows
  • The driver cannot tell DocumentDB from MongoDB, so it will happily send an operator DocumentDB refuses. Amazon's supported list, for your engine version, is the real contract of your data layer.
  • The database is better at saying no than your code is. A unique index, a version number or a condition in the update filter each turns a race into a refused write.
  • An annotation on a field is a request to some code you cannot see. Ask the database what it actually has: getIndexes() for indexes, explain() for plans.
  • Design the document around the write that must be atomic. Read shapes can always be built later with a second query or an aggregation.
  • A query that is fast against 200 test documents proves nothing. A plan read against production-sized data proves a lot.
  • Everything unbounded reaches its bound in production: arrays inside documents, lists returned by queries, page numbers, connection pools.
  • Read from the primary, the one instance in a cluster that takes writes, unless the use case was designed to tolerate a stale answer. Replica reads are a reporting tool, not a default.
◷How we got hereOn 15 May 2020 Kyle Kingsbury published "Jepsen: MongoDB 4.2.6", a test he ran "independently, without…

On 15 May 2020 Kyle Kingsbury published "Jepsen: MongoDB 4.2.6", a test he ran "independently, without compensation". MongoDB claimed "among the strongest data consistency, correctness, and safety guarantees of any database available today". Kingsbury found that "even at the strongest levels of read and write concern, it failed to preserve snapshot isolation". Transactions ignored the safer settings users had chosen at the database or collection level and fell back to the weakest ones. One transaction read a value that a later transaction had not yet written: "unless MongoDB has built a time machine, it cannot return values which it doesn't yet know will be written." Eleven days later he added a note. MongoDB had found a bug in its transaction retry mechanism and scheduled a patch for 4.2.8. The report was about MongoDB, not DocumentDB, which is a different engine. The lesson carries anyway. Set what you need on each operation, and test the database you actually run.

8.01 Map a document with a record

Then. - Spring era: the 2.x Java driver, with each document built by hand as a map. Every field name was a string and every read was a cast. It was the API there was, and it was honest about what a document is.

DBCollection payouts = mongo.getDB("payouts").getCollection("payouts");
BasicDBObject doc = new BasicDBObject("claimId", "C-4471")
        .append("amountMinor", 124050L)
        .append("status", "PENDING");
payouts.insert(doc);
DBObject found = payouts.findOne(new BasicDBObject("claimId", "C-4471"));
long amount = (Long) found.get("amountMinor");
  • Boot era: a mutable class with a no-argument constructor, getters and setters, mapped by Spring Data. Spring Data needed a way to create an empty object and fill it, and setters were that way. Records became a standard Java feature in Java 16, and Spring Data now calls a record's canonical constructor instead.

Recognise it by. com.mongodb.DBObject, BasicDBObject, DBCollection, mongo.getDB(...). A @Document class with public Payout() {} and a setter per field. @PersistenceConstructor, the older name of @PersistenceCreator.

The rookie version.

Payout payout = Payout.pending("C-4471", Money.gbp("1240.50"), key, clock.instant());
repository.save(payout);
return payout.id();          // null

What goes wrong. A document is one record in a document database, a JSON-like object stored in a collection, the equivalent of a table. Spring Data MongoDB is the Spring library that maps a Java type to it, much as EF Core maps a class to a table. Its repository is an interface, here PayoutRepository, whose implementation Spring Data writes for you, with save, findById and the rest. Spring Boot, the framework the service runs on, configures it from application.yml, the service's settings file. A record cannot change, so save cannot write the generated id into it. Instead save returns a new record holding the id and the version. The code above returns null. The controller builds Location: /payouts/null and the client stores it. Worse, the original record still has a null version, so a later save of it is treated as new and inserts a second document. Only the unique index on idempotencyKey (8.16) stops a second payout of £1,240.50 for claim C-4471.

Do this now.

  1. Declare the document as a record annotated with @Document("payouts"). Each component becomes a field of the stored document.
  2. Mark the id with @Id from org.springframework.data.annotation, not the one from JPA, Java's standard for relational mapping. An annotation such as @Id is Java's form of a C# attribute. A String id is generated as an ObjectId, MongoDB's 12-byte id type, and read back as its hex string.
  3. Add @Version Long version to every document that is updated after it is created (8.05).
  4. Keep working with the instance save or insert returns. Treat the one you passed in as spent.
  5. Add @TypeAlias("payout"). Spring Data writes a _class field into each document so it knows what to create on read. Without an alias it holds the full class name, and moving the class to another package breaks reads of old documents.
  6. Remember that an enum is stored by its constant's name. Renaming PAID to SETTLED makes every stored payout unreadable.
  7. Give the record small methods that return changed copies, such as paid(). They are the only way to change a payout.
@Document("payouts")
@TypeAlias("payout")
public record Payout(
        @Id String id,
        @Version Long version,
        String idempotencyKey,
        String claimId,
        Money amount,
        PayoutStatus status,
        Instant requestedAt) {

    public Payout paid() {
        return new Payout(id, version, idempotencyKey, claimId, amount, PayoutStatus.PAID, requestedAt);
    }
}

The stored form is BSON, MongoDB's binary relative of JSON. It has types JSON lacks, such as ObjectId, date and Decimal128. Money is stored as a nested document inside the payout, in the shape 8.10 chooses.

Also seen. MongoTemplate, Spring Data's general-purpose client for queries and updates (8.04), with the same record, in code that needs no repository interface. Morphia, a separate object mapper, in older services that never used Spring. The driver's own PojoCodecProvider, in services that use the bare driver.

When to break it. A plain org.bson.Document, which is a map, is right for a migration or an admin tool that must read every shape a collection has ever held (8.19). The cost is the old cost: string keys and casts, with no compiler to help.

.NET anchor. A C# class with [BsonId] and [BsonElement], or a C# record with init properties. The .NET driver sets Id on the object you passed to InsertOne. Spring Data cannot do that to a record, so the habit of reading the id from your own object fails here.

See also. 2.03, 8.04, 8.05, 8.18, 8.19, The Yard, chapter 8, Records, Document data: Amazon DocumentDB and the MongoDB API

8.02 Choose between embedding and referencing

Then. - Spring era: a collection per relational table, with the joins done in Java. Teams moving from SQL kept the shape they knew. It was right when the data had been designed for a relational database first and moved later. - Boot era: @DBRef, Spring Data's way to link documents. It stores a MongoDB DBRef, an object of the form {"$ref": "claims", "$id": ...}, and loads the target with a second query. It was the documented way to point at another document for years.

@Document("payouts")
public class Payout {
    @Id private String id;
    @DBRef private Claim claim;
    @DBRef(lazy = true) private List<PayoutLine> lines;
}

Recognise it by. @DBRef, com.mongodb.DBRef, "$ref" and "$id" in stored documents, and collections named like child tables, such as payout_lines or payout_status_changes.

The rookie version.

@Document("payouts")
public record Payout(@Id String id, @Version Long version,
                     @DBRef Claim claim,
                     @DBRef List<BankInstruction> instructions,
                     PayoutStatus status) { }

What goes wrong. The tests pass against a MongoDB container. On DocumentDB they cannot work, because AWS lists DBRefs as unsupported on every engine version. Even on MongoDB the shape hurts. Listing 50 payouts makes 1 query for the payouts and 100 more for claims and instructions. And the bank instruction now lives in a different document from the payout, so the write that marks the payout instructed and the write that records the instruction can disagree after a crash.

Do this now.

  1. Embed what is read and written with its owner and has no life without it. The amount, the bank instruction and a bounded status history (8.09) go inside the payout.
  2. Reference what another team or another aggregate owns, a cluster of objects that is loaded and changed as one unit. Store its id as a plain String: claimId for the policy system's claim, ledgerReservationId for the ledger's reservation.
  3. Copy the few fields you need from the referenced thing, at the moment you need them. The claimant's bank details at the time of instruction are a fact about the payout, and must not change when the claim changes later.
  4. Give anything that grows without limit its own collection, keyed by the payout's id. Events go to outbox, saga progress to payout_sagas.
  5. Put the fields that must change together in one document. AWS states that every single CRUD statement on DocumentDB is atomic, so one document is one consistent write (9.05).
  6. Stay well inside the limits: 16 MiB per document and 200 levels of nesting.
  7. When you must combine collections, prefer two queries, the second with $in. $lookup on DocumentDB supports equality matches, and correlated subqueries only from engine 8.0.2. Payouts runs 5.0.
@Document("payouts")
public record Payout(
        @Id String id,
        @Version Long version,
        String idempotencyKey,           // unique (8.16)
        String claimId,                  // reference: the policy system owns claims
        String ledgerReservationId,      // reference: the ledger owns reservations
        Money amount,                    // embedded value
        BankInstruction instruction,     // embedded: no life without the payout
        List<StatusChange> history,      // embedded, kept short (8.09)
        PayoutStatus status,
        Instant requestedAt) { }

Also seen. @DocumentReference, a newer Spring Data annotation that stores only the id and loads the target with one more query per document. It works on DocumentDB but brings back the N+1 problem, one query for the list plus one per item (18.02), and nothing cascades. $lookup inside a reporting aggregation (8.14).

When to break it. Reference something you always read together when it is large or written by another process at a high rate. Two writers on one document means @Version conflicts and retries (8.05).
