Embed a copy of data owned elsewhere when you need the value as it was, accepting that it will go stale.

.NET anchor. EF Core's owned types (OwnsOne, OwnsMany) are embedding. A navigation property to another aggregate root is referencing. The .NET driver's MongoDBRef is the same DBRef, with the same DocumentDB problem.

See also. 8.09, 8.14, 9.05, 18.02, 21.04, The Yard, chapter 8, Document data: Amazon DocumentDB and the MongoDB API

8.03 Write derived queries and know their limits

Then. - Spring era: queries written as JSON strings and run through MongoTemplate. It was the most direct route from the shell to Java, and many teams wrote the shell query first.

List<Payout> paid = mongoTemplate.find(
        new BasicQuery("{ status: 'PAID', 'amount.currency': 'GBP' }"),
        Payout.class);
  • Boot era: an @Query JSON string on every repository method, including ones a method name could have expressed.

Recognise it by. BasicQuery, @Query("{ ... }") on methods with one or two simple conditions, and filters built from BasicDBObject.

The rookie version.

List<Payout> findByStatusAndRequestedAtBetweenAndClaimIdStartingWithAndLedgerReservationIdIsNullOrderByRequestedAtDesc(
        PayoutStatus status, Instant from, Instant to, String claimPrefix);

List<Payout> findByClaimantNameContainingIgnoreCase(String name);

List<Payout> findByStatus(PayoutStatus status);

What goes wrong. A repository is an interface that Spring Data implements for you. A derived query is one Spring Data builds from the method's name. The first name above is too long for a reviewer to check against the index. The second becomes a case-insensitive $regex with no anchor, which reads every document (8.13). The third returns an unbounded List. After a ledger outage that lasted a day, 20,000 payouts sat in PENDING. The recovery job loaded them all into a pod with a 512 MiB limit, which was killed.

Do this now.

  1. Use derived queries for one to three conditions on indexed fields. They are short, typed and checked when the application starts. A misspelt property name fails the start-up, not the first request.
Optional<Payout> findByIdempotencyKey(String key);
List<Payout> findTop100ByStatusOrderByRequestedAtAsc(PayoutStatus status);
boolean existsByClaimIdAndStatus(String claimId, PayoutStatus status);
long countByStatus(PayoutStatus status);
  1. Bound every query that returns many documents: Top100, First, a Pageable (a page number and size, 8.08), or a range key (8.08).
  2. Always name the sort. AWS states that DocumentDB guarantees no implicit order of results, so a list with no OrderBy may come back in a different order each time.
  3. Past three conditions, build the query with Criteria, Spring Data's builder for filters, and run it through MongoTemplate (8.04). The field names are strings, so keep them next to the document type. query and where below are static imports from Query and Criteria.
Query stuck = query(where("status").is(PayoutStatus.PENDING)
                .and("requestedAt").lt(clock.instant().minus(Duration.ofMinutes(15))))
        .with(Sort.by("requestedAt"))
        .limit(100);
List<Payout> page = mongoTemplate.find(stuck, Payout.class);
  1. Use @Query with placeholders when the shape is fixed but a name cannot express it, for example @Query("{ 'status': ?0, 'history.status': { $ne: 'FAILED' } }"). Spring binds ?0 safely. Never build the string by concatenation (15.08).
  2. Know the keywords that turn into $regex: IgnoreCase, Like, StartingWith and Containing. Treat each as a scan until an explain plan says otherwise (8.07).

Also seen. Querydsl, through QuerydslPredicateExecutor and generated Q classes, for type-checked dynamic filters. Query by Example, with Example.of(probe), for search screens where any field may be blank.

When to break it. A four-condition derived name is acceptable in a test helper or a rarely used admin tool where nobody tunes it. The cost is a name that reviewers stop reading.

.NET anchor. The nearest .NET habit is a LINQ Where lambda against IMongoCollection<T>.AsQueryable(). The compiler checks a lambda. Spring Data checks a method name at start-up instead, which is later than the compiler but earlier than production.

See also. 8.04, 8.07, 8.08, 8.13, 15.08, Document data: Amazon DocumentDB and the MongoDB API

8.04 Update one field atomically with MongoTemplate

Then. - Spring era: the 2.x driver's update with a hand-built $set. It did the right thing on the server, and it is still what Spring sends today. What replaced it is the typed Update builder, which maps field names and types for you.

WriteResult r = collection.update(
        new BasicDBObject("_id", id).append("status", "RESERVED"),
        new BasicDBObject("$set", new BasicDBObject("status", "INSTRUCTED")));
if (r.getN() == 0) { /* someone else moved it */ }

Recognise it by. DBCollection.update, WriteResult.getN(), new BasicDBObject("$set", ...).

The rookie version.

Payout p = repository.findById(id).orElseThrow();
repository.save(new Payout(p.id(), p.version(), p.idempotencyKey(), p.claimId(), p.ledgerReservationId(),
        p.amount(), p.instruction(), p.history(), PayoutStatus.PAID, p.requestedAt()));

What goes wrong. save replaces the whole document, not the one field that changed. Pod A's saga step writes ledgerReservationId. Thirty milliseconds earlier, pod B's LedgerConfirmListener read the payout without it. Pod B saves its copy and the reservation id is gone. @Version (8.05) would at least turn this into an error. Without it nothing complains. When the bank instruction later fails, the compensation step cannot find the reservation to release, and £1,240.50 stays held in the ledger.

Do this now.

  1. Change only the fields that change, on the server, with MongoTemplate, Spring Data's general-purpose client for queries and updates. Boot creates one, and you inject it like any other bean. updateFirst sends one update command with $set, $inc or $push. The $push with $slice below keeps the history bounded (8.09).
  2. Put the expected state in the filter. "Move to INSTRUCTED only if it is still RESERVED" makes the update a compare-and-set. Two pods cannot both make the move.
  3. Check the result. A modified count of 0 means the document was not in the expected state. Read it and decide, do not assume.
  4. Use findAndModify with returnNew(true) when you need the document after the change in the same round trip.
  5. Use $inc for counters, never read-add-save.
  6. Make sure the update moves the version too, or a stale save elsewhere can overwrite it (8.05). Spring Data adds the increment when you pass the entity class and the update does not set the version itself. A test that reads the version before and after proves it in your version.
UpdateResult r = mongoTemplate.updateFirst(
        query(where("_id").is(id).and("status").is(PayoutStatus.RESERVED)),
        new Update()
                .set("status", PayoutStatus.INSTRUCTED)
                .set("updatedAt", clock.instant())
                .push("history").slice(-20).each(new StatusChange(PayoutStatus.INSTRUCTED, clock.instant())),
        Payout.class);
if (r.getModifiedCount() == 0) {
    throw new IllegalStateException("payout " + id + " is no longer RESERVED");
}

Payout after = mongoTemplate.findAndModify(
        query(where("_id").is(id)), new Update().inc("bankAttempts", 1),
        FindAndModifyOptions.options().returnNew(true), Payout.class);

AWS states that on DocumentDB every single CRUD statement, findAndModify included, is atomic. The filter and the change cannot be split by another writer.

Every field an update sets, such as updatedAt and bankAttempts, must also be a component of the record. A field the record lacks is silently dropped the next time anyone saves the record, which is the loss of 8.15.

Also seen. Spring Data's @Update annotation on a repository method, which declares the same $set next to a derived filter. A read, a change and a save guarded by @Version, when the new state depends on logic over the whole document (8.05).

When to break it. Replace the whole document when the change really is a rewrite, such as a migration to a new shape (8.19), and you hold the version. The cost is that every field must be correct in your copy, including fields you did not know about.

.NET anchor. UpdateOneAsync with Builders<Payout>.Update.Set(...) in the .NET driver. In EF Core the closest is ExecuteUpdate, which updates on the server without tracking.

See also. 8.05, 8.09, 8.15, 9.05, 9.11, 11.02, Document data: Amazon DocumentDB and the MongoDB API

8.05 Prevent lost updates with @Version

Then. - Spring era: a version number kept by hand. The update filter named the version read, the update incremented it, and the code checked that one document matched. It was correct, and it is exactly what @Version now does for you on every save.

WriteResult r = collection.update(
        new BasicDBObject("_id", id).append("version", 3),
        new BasicDBObject("$set", new BasicDBObject("status", "CANCELLED"))
                .append("$inc", new BasicDBObject("version", 1)));
if (r.getN() == 0) throw new ConcurrentModificationException(id);
  • Boot era: a lastModified timestamp compared before saving, borrowed from relational habits. It worked with one instance. With several pods, two writes in the same millisecond or a skewed clock let a stale write through.

Recognise it by. A version field incremented in code, getN() == 0 checks, and @LastModifiedDate used as a guard rather than as information.

The rookie version.

@Document("payouts")
public record Payout(@Id String id, String claimId, Money amount, PayoutStatus status) { }

// PayoutSaga, pod A, just before it sends the instruction to the bank
repository.save(repository.findById(id).orElseThrow().instructed());

// PayoutService.cancel, pod B, 40 ms later
repository.save(repository.findById(id).orElseThrow().cancelled());

What goes wrong. Both pods read the payout while it was RESERVED. Pod A saves INSTRUCTED and sends the instruction, then pod B saves CANCELLED over it. The last save wins and nothing reports an error. This is a lost update. The bank pays £1,240.50, Payouts says the payout was cancelled, and reconciliation finds the gap 3 days later.

Do this now.

  1. Add @Version Long version to every document that is updated after it is created. Use the wrapper Long: a null version is how Spring Data knows a document is new and must be inserted.
  2. Understand the mechanism. This is optimistic locking: nothing is locked while you work, and the database checks at the last moment. On each save Spring Data sends the filter {_id: id, version: n} and writes version as n + 1. If no document matches, it throws OptimisticLockingFailureException.
  3. On that exception, read again and apply the business rule again. Do not blindly resend your copy, which would only lose the other write a different way.
  4. Bound the retries. Three attempts is plenty for 2 pods. Persistent conflicts mean two processes are fighting over one document, which is a design problem (8.02).
  5. Make every other write path move the version as well, including template updates (8.04) and scripts.
  6. Test it with two copies of the same version. The second save must fail.
public Payout cancel(String id) {
    for (int attempt = 1; ; attempt++) {
        Payout current = repository.findById(id).orElseThrow(() -> new PayoutNotFound(id));
        if (current.status() != PayoutStatus.PENDING && current.status() != PayoutStatus.RESERVED) {
            throw new IllegalStateException("payout " + id + " is " + current.status());
        }
        try {
            return repository.save(current.cancelled());
        } catch (OptimisticLockingFailureException e) {
            if (attempt == 3) throw e;
        }
    }
}

Run against the race above, pod B's first save fails. Its second attempt reads INSTRUCTED, past the pivot, and refuses to cancel. That is the point: the retry repeats the decision, not the write. If pod B had saved first, pod A's save would fail instead, and its retry would read CANCELLED and send nothing. That is why the saga saves before it calls the bank.

Also seen. A conditional update with the expected state in the filter (8.04), which needs no version at all for a single transition. A lease, a lockedBy and lockedUntil pair, for long work one pod must own. Leases need an expiry and a plan for the pod that dies holding one.

When to break it. Append-only documents, such as outbox events and audit records, are never updated and need no version. The cost appears the day someone adds an update to one.

.NET anchor. EF Core's [ConcurrencyCheck] or a rowversion column, failing with DbUpdateConcurrencyException. The difference is that SQL Server moves a rowversion itself. Here Spring Data increments the version in the write it sends, so a write that bypasses Spring Data, such as a fix in mongosh, the MongoDB shell, leaves it where it was.

See also. 5.11, 8.04, 9.11, The Yard, chapter 8, Document data: Amazon DocumentDB and the MongoDB API

8.06 Create indexes deliberately

Then. - Boot era: indexes created from annotations at start-up. Spring Data used to build every @Indexed and @CompoundIndex it found when the application started. Spring Data's reference says automatic index creation "is turned OFF by default as of version 3.0". Code from before then still carries the annotations, and often nothing else creates the indexes. - Spring era: an index script on a wiki page, run by hand in the shell with ensureIndex, the shell's old name for createIndex.

db.payouts.ensureIndex({ idempotencyKey: 1 }, { unique: true, background: true })

Recognise it by. @Indexed and @CompoundIndexes with no spring.data.mongodb.auto-index-creation setting and no index code. ensureIndex in scripts and in Java code. auto-index-creation: true in the production profile of a large collection.

The rookie version.

@Document("payouts")
@CompoundIndexes({
        @CompoundIndex(def = "{'status': 1}"),
        @CompoundIndex(def = "{'status': 1, 'requestedAt': 1}"),
        @CompoundIndex(def = "{'claimId': 1, 'status': 1}") })
public record Payout(@Id String id, @Indexed String claimId, PayoutStatus status,
                     @Indexed Instant requestedAt, @Indexed(unique = true) String idempotencyKey) { }
// application.yml: spring.data.mongodb.auto-index-creation: true

What goes wrong. Six indexes plus _id, two of them redundant, and every write maintains all seven. AWS suggests five or fewer per collection as a good guideline. Worse, the build happens when a pod starts. AWS states that by default an index build blocks all other operations on its collection, and that only one build runs on a collection at a time. Someone adds one more annotation to a collection of 3.1 million payouts. The new pod starts at 11:00 and writes to payouts stall for the length of the build.

Do this now.

  1. Start from the queries, not the fields. For each query shape, write down its filter and its sort.
  2. Build one compound index per shape, ordered as equality fields first, then the sort field, then range fields. findTop100ByStatusOrderByRequestedAtAsc wants {status: 1, requestedAt: 1}.
  3. Drop indexes that are a prefix of another. {status: 1, requestedAt: 1} already serves a filter on status alone.
  4. Create indexes explicitly, by name, with IndexOperations. On a new or small collection a start-up runner is fine. An ApplicationRunner is a bean whose run method Boot calls once, after the application has started, much like an IHostedService. @Component asks Spring to create one instance and pass its constructor arguments in. createIndex does nothing if the same index already exists. Spring Data's older ensureIndex is deprecated in favour of it.
  5. On a populated collection, build the index as a migration in a quiet window, not at start-up (8.20).
  6. Ask the database what exists. Run db.payouts.getIndexes() in the nightly run against DocumentDB, and read a plan (8.07).
  7. Know the quotas: 64 indexes per collection, 32 keys in a compound index, and 2,048 bytes per index key. DocumentDB does not compress indexes, so each one costs memory.
@Component
class PayoutIndexes implements ApplicationRunner {
    private final MongoTemplate mongo;
    PayoutIndexes(MongoTemplate mongo) { this.mongo = mongo; }

    @Override public void run(ApplicationArguments args) { ensure(); }

    void ensure() {
        IndexOperations ops = mongo.indexOps(Payout.class);
        ops.createIndex(new Index().on("idempotencyKey", Sort.Direction.ASC)
                .unique().named("payouts_idempotency_key_unique"));
        ops.createIndex(new Index().on("status", Sort.Direction.ASC)
                .on("requestedAt", Sort.Direction.ASC).named("payouts_status_requested"));
    }
}

Some index types do not exist on DocumentDB. Hashed, wildcard and 2d indexes are unsupported on every engine version, though 2dsphere is supported. Partial indexes need engine 5.0 or later. A sparse index is used only when the query has an $exists clause on its field.

Also seen. auto-index-creation: true in tests and on laptops, where collections are tiny. A migration tool such as Mongock running index change units (8.20).

When to break it. A brand-new service with small collections can let Spring Data build indexes from annotations. The cost arrives the day a collection grows and a new annotation blocks it during a deploy.

.NET anchor. In the .NET driver you call Indexes.CreateOneAsync(new CreateIndexModel<T>(...)) yourself, usually at start-up. EF Core's HasIndex creates indexes through migrations. MongoDB has no built-in migrations, so the decision of when to build is yours.

See also. 8.07, 8.16, 8.17, 8.20, The Yard, chapter 8, Document data: Amazon DocumentDB and the MongoDB API

8.07 Read an explain plan

Then. - Spring era: the database profiler. On a self-run MongoDB, db.setProfilingLevel(1, 100) recorded slow operations in the system.profile collection, and teams read it to find scans. It was right for a server you ran yourself. AWS states that DocumentDB does not support MongoDB's system.* collections, so that habit has nothing to read.

Recognise it by. setProfilingLevel, queries against system.profile, and the 2.x driver's DBCursor.explain().

The rookie version.

@Test
void findsStuckPayoutsQuickly() {
    long start = System.nanoTime();
    repository.findTop100ByStatusOrderByRequestedAtAsc(PayoutStatus.PENDING);
    assertThat(Duration.ofNanos(System.nanoTime() - start))
            .isLessThan(Duration.ofMillis(50));
}

What goes wrong. The container holds 200 documents, and any plan is fast on 200 documents. Production holds 3.1 million. The stuck-payout job runs every minute, reads every document each time and takes 4 seconds. The primary instance sits at 80% CPU, and every other write waits behind it.

Do this now.

  1. Get the exact query Spring sends. Set logging.level.org.springframework.data.mongodb.core.MongoTemplate=DEBUG in a test run and copy the filter and sort it prints.
  2. Load a realistic volume into a MongoDB container, ideally a copy of production's shape and counts with the personal data removed.
  3. Run the query with explain("executionStats") in mongosh, the MongoDB shell.
db.payouts.find({ status: "PENDING" })
  .sort({ requestedAt: 1 })
  .limit(100)
  .explain("executionStats")
  1. Read the winning plan, the plan the query planner chose. COLLSCAN means a collection scan, reading every document. IXSCAN means an index scan, and names the index in indexName. A separate SORT stage means the index did not provide the order, so the server sorted in memory.
  2. Compare three numbers in executionStats: nReturned, totalKeysExamined and totalDocsExamined. A good plan for this query shows about 100 of each. A plan that returns 100 and examines 3,100,000 documents is a scan, however fast it felt.
  3. Run the same explain against DocumentDB, in the nightly environment. AWS states that query plans and the output of explain() may differ between DocumentDB and MongoDB. Engine 5.0 uses the planner AWS calls Planner v1 by default, and 8.0 uses Planner v3. Find the winning plan's stage and the index it names, whatever the shape around them.
  4. Test a candidate index with hint, which forces the planner to use a named index. On DocumentDB a $regex needs a hint to use an index at all (8.13).

Also seen. MongoDB Compass, which draws the same plan as a tree. An explain run from Java through the driver, for a test that fails the build when a known query stops using its index.

When to break it. A small reference collection, such as a few hundred currency rules, can be scanned on every read. The cost is nil until it grows, so note the assumption beside the query.

.NET anchor. SQL Server's actual execution plan in SSMS. COLLSCAN is a table scan, IXSCAN an index seek or range scan, and totalDocsExamined plays the part of the logical reads from SET STATISTICS IO ON.

See also. 8.06, 8.13, 8.14, 18.01, Document data: Amazon DocumentDB and the MongoDB API

8.08 Paginate with a range key instead of skip

Then. - Boot era: page numbers through Spring Data's Pageable, which becomes a skip, a limit and a separate count. It was right for admin screens that show "page 3 of 12" over a few thousand documents, and it is still right there.

Page<Payout> findByStatus(PayoutStatus status, Pageable pageable);

Page<Payout> page = repository.findByStatus(PayoutStatus.PAID, PageRequest.of(3, 50));

Recognise it by. PageRequest.of(, a Page<...> return type, .skip( on a Query, and ?page= parameters on an endpoint.

The rookie version.

int page = 0;
Page<Payout> batch;
do {
    batch = repository.findByStatus(PayoutStatus.PAID, PageRequest.of(page++, 500));
    batch.forEach(exporter::write);
} while (batch.hasNext());

What goes wrong. The nightly export covers 2.4 million paid payouts. skip does not jump. The server walks past every skipped document, so page 4,000 reads 2,000,000 documents to return 500. Each page is slower than the last, and every Page also runs a count. The job grew to 5 hours 40 minutes. There is no sort, and DocumentDB gives no implicit order, so pages overlapped and some payouts were exported twice and others never. New payouts arriving during the run shifted every later page.

Do this now.

  1. Sort by a key that is unique and indexed. _id is both. For time order, sort by requestedAt and then _id, so that ties have a fixed order.
  2. Ask for "the next 500 after the last key I saw", not "page 4,000".
  3. Make sure an index serves the filter and the sort together: {status: 1, _id: 1} here.
  4. Stop when a batch comes back short.
List<Payout> findTop500ByStatusAndIdGreaterThanOrderByIdAsc(PayoutStatus status, String afterId);

String after = "000000000000000000000000";
List<Payout> batch;
do {
    batch = repository.findTop500ByStatusAndIdGreaterThanOrderByIdAsc(PayoutStatus.PAID, after);
    batch.forEach(exporter::write);
    if (!batch.isEmpty()) after = batch.getLast().id();
} while (batch.size() == 500);

Each batch is now one index range read, whatever its position. The export takes the same time per batch at the end as at the start. Documents inserted during the run land after the cursor or before it, never in the middle of a page.

  1. For a time-ordered range key, the filter is requestedAt > last or requestedAt == last and _id > lastId, built with Criteria.orOperator, over an index on {status: 1, requestedAt: 1, _id: 1}.
  2. Spring Data can do the bookkeeping. A method returning Window<Payout> and taking a ScrollPosition from ScrollPosition.keyset() scrolls by key, and the window tells you where to continue.
  3. Over HTTP, hand the client an opaque cursor that encodes the last key, not a page number (5.07).

Also seen. A repository method returning Stream<Payout>, which keeps one server cursor open for the whole export. It avoids skip, but an open cursor counts against the instance's cursor quota, 450 on an r5.large, the DocumentDB instance size Payouts runs on, and a long export holds one for hours.

When to break it. An admin screen that must jump to page 7 of 20 over a filtered set of about 1,000 payouts can use Pageable. The cost is small at that size and grows with every page.

.NET anchor. EF Core's Skip(n).Take(m) has the same cost on SQL Server. The keyset version is Where(p => p.Id > lastId).OrderBy(p => p.Id).Take(500), the same idea in LINQ.

See also. 5.07, 8.06, 8.07, 20.07, Document data: Amazon DocumentDB and the MongoDB API

8.09 Keep arrays in a document bounded

What goes wrong. Every poll of the bank gateway, once every 30 seconds, pushed a StatusChange into the payout's history array. One payout stuck in retries for 9 days collected 26,000 entries, 2,880 a day. Every read of it loaded them all, and every update rewrote a document that kept growing. A document on DocumentDB may not exceed 16 MiB, and the write that crosses the line fails.

Do this now. Decide the maximum before the first $push. Keep the newest entries only, with $push and a $slice modifier, written in Spring as new Update().push("history").slice(-20).each(change). Check $slice inside $push against the feature contract for your engine before relying on it (8.12). Put anything that grows without a natural limit, such as every bank poll or every event, in its own collection keyed by payoutId and indexed on it.

See also. 8.02, 8.04, 8.12, 9.05, Document data: Amazon DocumentDB and the MongoDB API

8.10 Store money and dates correctly

Then. - J2EE era: java.util.Date fields, stored as BSON dates. They were the only date type Java had, and they still store correctly. They are mutable and have no idea of time zones, so java.time replaced them (2.02). - Spring era: Joda-Time's DateTime in documents, with converters to and from BSON dates. Joda-Time was the sound choice before Java 8. Its own site now asks users to migrate to java.time.

Recognise it by. java.util.Date and org.joda.time.DateTime fields on @Document classes, and converter classes with Joda in their names.

The rookie version.

@Document("payouts")
public record Payout(@Id String id,
                     double amount, String currency,
                     LocalDateTime requestedAt,
                     LocalDate paymentDate) { }

What goes wrong. A double cannot hold most decimal fractions exactly. One payout of £1,240.50 looks fine. The daily $sum over 18,000 of them drifts by fractions of a penny, and the ledger reconciliation fails by £0.01. LocalDateTime has no zone, so "09:12" means nothing until someone guesses where. Spring Data converts a LocalDate or LocalDateTime to a BSON date through a time zone, by default the JVM's own. A pod on UTC and a laptop on British Summer Time store the same payment date an hour apart, and one of them reads back the previous day.

Do this now.

  1. Keep the domain type from 2.01: Money(BigDecimal amount, Currency currency). The service computes with it everywhere, and the database never sees it directly.
  2. Choose the stored form on purpose. Payouts stores minor units: a StoredMoney(long minor, String currency) sub-document, an integer number of pence plus an ISO currency code. Integers sum exactly in $sum and compare exactly in a filter on any engine, so the report in 8.14 needs no type check. Decimal128 would also be exact, but it must be checked against AWS's supported data types for your engine (8.12).
  3. Do not let Spring Data pick the form. It has no mapping for Money itself, so it maps the BigDecimal inside it. In Spring Data MongoDB 4.5, which Boot 3.5 uses, a BigDecimal is stored as a string by default. In 5.x it is passed to the driver as Decimal128, and Boot 4 adds spring.data.mongodb.representation.big-decimal. The same class would store a different type after the upgrade.
  4. Write a pair of converters. A converter is a class Spring Data calls to turn one type into another on the way in and out. Register both in the service's one MongoCustomConversions bean, beside the ClaimId converters, as 8.18 shows. Boot applies them to every repository and to MongoTemplate.
  5. Convert with the currency's own number of decimal places, so yen and pounds both work.
  6. Store a point in time as an Instant. It becomes a BSON date, which counts milliseconds from 1970 in UTC. Truncate to milliseconds in memory, with clock.instant().truncatedTo(ChronoUnit.MILLIS), so the value you hold equals the value you read back.
  7. Store a business date, such as the day the bank pays, as an ISO string like "2026-10-24". It sorts correctly as text and no time zone touches it. Spring Data would turn a LocalDate into a BSON date, so add a LocalDate-to-String converter pair to the same bean, or keep the component a String.
  8. Never use LocalDateTime for something that happened.
public record StoredMoney(long minor, String currency) {
    static StoredMoney from(Money m) {
        int digits = m.currency().getDefaultFractionDigits();
        return new StoredMoney(m.amount().movePointRight(digits).longValueExact(),
                m.currency().getCurrencyCode());
    }
    Money toMoney() {
        Currency c = Currency.getInstance(currency);
        return new Money(BigDecimal.valueOf(minor, c.getDefaultFractionDigits()), c);
    }
}

@WritingConverter
class MoneyWriter implements Converter<Money, Document> {
    public Document convert(Money m) {
        StoredMoney s = StoredMoney.from(m);
        return new Document("minor", s.minor()).append("currency", s.currency());
    }
}
@ReadingConverter
class MoneyReader implements Converter<Document, Money> {
    public Money convert(Document d) {
        return new StoredMoney(d.getLong("minor"), d.getString("currency")).toMoney();
    }
}

{ "amount": { "minor": 124050, "currency": "GBP" },
  "requestedAt": { "$date": "2026-10-24T09:12:07.412Z" },
  "paymentDate": "2026-10-24" }

longValueExact throws if the amount has more decimal places than the currency allows. The Money constructor already refuses such a value (2.01), so this is a second guard, not the first.

Also seen. Decimal128 through @Field(targetType = FieldType.DECIMAL128), where the ledger or a rate needs more precision than minor units give. Amounts stored as strings such as "1240.50", which cannot be summed by the database and sort wrongly as text.

When to break it. Exchange rates and interest calculations need more decimal places than any currency has. Store those as Decimal128. The cost is a second representation of numbers that every reader must handle.

.NET anchor. C#'s decimal is the natural type for money and maps to Decimal128 with [BsonRepresentation(BsonType.Decimal128)]. DateTime with an unspecified Kind is the .NET form of the LocalDateTime trap. DateTimeOffset is the safe choice, as Instant is here.

See also. 2.01, 2.02, 5.13, 8.14, 8.18, Numbers, money and time, Document data: Amazon DocumentDB and the MongoDB API

8.11 Connect to DocumentDB with TLS, retryable writes and read preference set right

Then. - Boot era: the client built by hand in a configuration class, with the whole connection string in Java. It gave one place to see every option, which mattered before Boot's properties covered TLS. Boot's spring.data.mongodb.uri and SSL bundles replaced it.

@Configuration
public class MongoConfig extends AbstractMongoConfiguration {
    @Override public MongoClient mongoClient() {
        return new MongoClient(new MongoClientURI(
            "mongodb://payouts:…@docdb.sorrel.internal:27017/payouts?tls=true&retryWrites=false"));
    }
    @Override protected String getDatabaseName() { return "payouts"; }
}
  • Boot era: a JKS trust store, the file of certificates the JVM trusts, built with keytool from AWS's certificate bundle and passed with -Djavax.net.ssl.trustStore. These are still AWS's own Java instructions, and they work. The cost is that the setting replaces the trust store for the whole JVM, not only for the database.

Recognise it by. AbstractMongoConfiguration, MongoClientURI, MongoClientOptions, -Djavax.net.ssl.trustStore=rds-truststore.jks, and a comment saying "do not remove" next to retryWrites=false.

The rookie version.

spring:
  data:
    mongodb:
      uri: mongodb://payouts:${MONGODB_PASSWORD}@docdb.sorrel.internal:27017/payouts?tls=true&replicaSet=rs0&readPreference=secondaryPreferred&retryWrites=false

Payout saved = repository.insert(payout);
return repository.findById(saved.id()).orElseThrow(() -> new PayoutNotFound(saved.id()));

What goes wrong. readPreference=secondaryPreferred sends reads to a replica, a read-only copy of the cluster that trails the primary. AWS states that reads from replicas are eventually consistent, and that a read after a write can be served only by the primary. So the insert goes to the primary and the read may go to a replica that has not seen it. About 1 in 300 POST /payouts calls answered 404 for a payout that existed. Worse, the saga read its own state from payout_sagas on a replica, saw step 1 not yet done, and asked the ledger to reserve £1,240.50 a second time.

Do this now.

  1. Know your engine version. AWS's SDK, CLI and CloudFormation create a 5.0 cluster unless told otherwise, which is how Payouts came to run 5.0. aws docdb describe-db-clusters shows EngineVersion.
  2. Use a driver compatible with MongoDB 5.0 or later. AWS requires it for 5.0 and 8.0 clusters.
  3. Set retryWrites=false on every engine before 8.0.2 and on every elastic cluster. Drivers turn retryable writes on by default, and those engines refuse every write that carries them. Keep a test that fails the build if the option disappears.
  4. Turn TLS on with an SSL bundle. AWS enables TLS on clusters by default and publishes the CA bundle at https://truststore.pki.rds.amazonaws.com/global/global-bundle.pem. Engine 8.0 requires TLS 1.2 or later. A Spring Boot SSL bundle is a named set of certificates that a client can use without touching the JVM's own trust store.
  5. Leave the read preference at its default, the primary, for the service. Add replicaSet=rs0 so the driver discovers the cluster's members.
  6. Give replica reads to the code that was designed for them, such as reports, through a separate template (see the second listing).
  7. Through an SSH tunnel from a laptop, remove replicaSet=rs0. AWS states that replica-set mode through a tunnel results in an error.
spring:
  data:
    mongodb:
      uri: mongodb://payouts:${MONGODB_PASSWORD}@docdb.sorrel.internal:27017/payouts?replicaSet=rs0&retryWrites=false
      ssl:
        bundle: docdb
  ssl:
    bundle:
      pem:
        docdb:
          truststore:
            certificate: file:/etc/payouts/global-bundle.pem

In Boot 4 the first keys become spring.mongodb.uri and spring.mongodb.ssl.bundle. The bundle section is unchanged.

@Component
class PayoutReportQueries {
    private final MongoTemplate replicas;

    PayoutReportQueries(MongoDatabaseFactory factory, MongoConverter converter) {
        this.replicas = new MongoTemplate(factory, converter);
        this.replicas.setReadPreference(ReadPreference.secondaryPreferred());
    }
}

Creating the template inside the class leaves Boot's own MongoTemplate, which reads from the primary, as the only bean of that type.

Also seen. A JKS bundle under spring.ssl.bundle.jks.*, for teams that already keep a trust store file. The JVM-wide trust store, in older services.

When to break it. A read-only reporting service can set secondaryPreferred for everything, because no request reads its own writes. The cost is that every answer may be a little behind.

.NET anchor. The .NET driver reads the same connection-string options. In .NET on Windows you would import AWS's .p7b bundle into the certificate store, and in a Linux container you would add the PEM to the system's CA store. Both trust it for every connection the process makes, the same trade-off as the JVM-wide trust store. Read preference is like SQL Server's ApplicationIntent=ReadOnly, which routes a connection to a readable secondary with the same staleness.

See also. 8.12, 8.24, 9.13, 15.06, 17.07, The Yard, chapter 7, Document data: Amazon DocumentDB and the MongoDB API

8.12 Check that an operator works on DocumentDB before you use it

Then. - Modern: a warning comment beside the code that needs it, or a wiki page kept by the one person who had read AWS's lists. It worked while that person was on the team. A feature contract replaced it: a short text file in the repository with one line per MongoDB feature the service relies on, checked by a test and a nightly run.

Recognise it by. Comments such as // DocumentDB or // do not remove, and links to a wiki page instead of a file in the repository.

The rookie version.

Aggregation monthly = newAggregation(
        match(where("status").is(PayoutStatus.PAID)),
        facet(group("amount.currency").sum("amount.minor").as("totalMinor")).as("byCurrency")
                .and(group("status").count().as("payouts")).as("byStatus"));
List<Document> rows = mongoTemplate.aggregate(monthly, "payouts", Document.class).getMappedResults();

What goes wrong. The pipeline was green against the mongo:5.0 container and merged on a Tuesday. AWS lists $facet as supported only from engine 8.0.2. Payouts runs 5.0. The monthly finance report failed at 06:00 on the 1st, and finance waited 2 days for the rewrite.

Do this now.

  1. Know exactly what you run: the engine version, and whether the cluster is instance-based or elastic. Elastic clusters lack transactions, change streams, retryable writes, collation, views, partial indexes and text indexes.
  2. Look every new operator, stage, index type and driver option up in AWS's two lists: "Supported MongoDB APIs, operations, and data types in Amazon DocumentDB" and "Functional differences: Amazon DocumentDB and MongoDB". AWS states that a command missing from the supported list is not supported.
  3. Find what Spring sends on your behalf. Derived query keywords such as IgnoreCase become $regex. @DBRef becomes a DBRef. @HashIndexed and @WildcardIndexed build index types DocumentDB lacks. Aggregation.facet becomes $facet.
  4. Record the commands the test suite sends, with a driver command listener, a hook the MongoDB driver calls for every command. Collect every $ key and compare the set with the contract at the end of the run. Bring the listing below into each MongoDB test with @Import(RecordOperators.class). collectDollarKeys is your own few lines of recursion over the command's keys and values. A final test, or an @AfterAll method, fails when SEEN holds an operator the contract file does not list.
  5. Add one line to the contract per feature, with the engine version and the date it was checked.
  6. Let the nightly run against the shared DocumentDB instance prove the contract. It is the only place the real engine answers.
@TestConfiguration
class RecordOperators {
    static final Set<String> SEEN = ConcurrentHashMap.newKeySet();

    @Bean
    MongoClientSettingsBuilderCustomizer recordOperators() {
        return builder -> builder.addCommandListener(new CommandListener() {
            @Override
            public void commandStarted(CommandStartedEvent event) {
                collectDollarKeys(event.getCommand(), SEEN);   // walks the BsonDocument
            }
        });
    }
}

The gaps a Spring service on engine 5.0 meets most often, as AWS lists them:

  • Only from 8.0: collation, views, $merge, $bucket, $graphLookup, and the $set, $unset and $replaceWith stages. $facet and $setWindowFields need 8.0.2.
  • On no engine version: $where, $unionWith, $densify, $fill, DBRefs, capped collections, tailable cursors and noCursorTimeout().
  • Different: $elemMatch is not supported inside $all, allowDiskUse works only in aggregations, and no result order is guaranteed without a sort.

Also seen. A per-feature integration test that runs only in the nightly suite against DocumentDB. It is slower to write than a contract line, and worth it for a feature a release depends on.

When to break it. A one-off query run by hand in the shell does not need a contract line. The cost appears when someone pastes it into the code.

.NET anchor. EF Core tests on SQLite standing in for SQL Server is the same trap: the same code, a different engine, some queries that behave differently. Cosmos DB's API for MongoDB is a close cousin of DocumentDB, with its own list.

See also. 8.13, 8.14, 8.22, 8.23, The Yard, chapter 7, Document data: Amazon DocumentDB and the MongoDB API

8.13 Avoid queries that scan with $regex

What goes wrong. The support screen searched claimants with findByClaimantNameContainingIgnoreCase(name). Spring Data derives a $regex from Containing, StartingWith, Like and IgnoreCase. AWS states that DocumentDB uses an index for $regex only with hint(), and works best with a prefix and without the i, m or o options. This query had neither, so every search read all 3.1 million payouts.

Do this now. Store a normalised copy of the searched field, such as claimantNameKey in lower case with accents removed, and index it. Search it with an exact match, or with an anchored prefix such as ^smi and no options, and name the index with Query.withHint("payouts_claimant_key"). On engine 5.0, AWS lists a find with both $regex and $options as an error, so test any IgnoreCase method on a real cluster. Collation, which gives case-insensitive indexes, needs engine 8.0. A text index exists from 5.0, one per collection.

See also. 8.03, 8.07, 8.12, 15.08, Document data: Amazon DocumentDB and the MongoDB API

8.14 Build a report with an aggregation pipeline

Then. - Spring era: map-reduce, with JavaScript map and reduce functions run inside the database, through MongoTemplate.mapReduce. Before the aggregation framework it was the only way to group on the server. AWS lists mapReduce as supported only from engine 8.0.

MapReduceResults<CurrencyTotal> totals = mongoTemplate.mapReduce(
        "payouts",
        "function() { emit(this.amount.currency, this.amount.minor); }",
        "function(key, values) { return Array.sum(values); }",
        CurrencyTotal.class);

Recognise it by. mapReduce(, MapReduceResults, .js files containing emit(, and the 2.x driver's DBCollection.aggregate(List<DBObject>).

The rookie version.

Map<Currency, BigDecimal> totals = new HashMap<>();
for (Payout p : repository.findAll()) {
    if (p.status() == PayoutStatus.PAID
            && !p.requestedAt().isBefore(from) && p.requestedAt().isBefore(to)) {
        totals.merge(p.amount().currency(), p.amount().amount(), BigDecimal::add);
    }
}

What goes wrong. findAll brings 3.1 million documents over the network to compute 4 numbers. The report pod has a 512 MiB memory limit and was killed on most nights. On the nights it finished, it took 11 minutes and kept the primary busy the whole time.

Do this now.

  1. Push the work to the database with an aggregation pipeline: a list of stages, each transforming the stream of documents from the one before, like a chain of LINQ operators.
  2. Put $match first, on indexed fields, so the pipeline reads only the documents it needs. Read its plan with explain as for a find (8.07).
  3. Shrink the documents early. $group keeps only what it accumulates, and $project drops fields you do not need.
  4. Put $sort last. AWS states that on DocumentDB a $sort keeps its order only when it is the last stage of the pipeline.
  5. Map the output to a small record. The group's key arrives as _id, so mark that component with @Id.
  6. Run reports against replicas through the reporting template (8.11), so they never compete with payouts.
  7. Check each stage against your engine (8.12). A pipeline may have at most 500 stages, and allowDiskUse is accepted for aggregations: pass AggregationOptions.builder().allowDiskUse(true).build() to the aggregation's withOptions.
Aggregation daily = newAggregation(
        match(where("status").is(PayoutStatus.PAID)
                .and("requestedAt").gte(from).lt(to)),
        group("amount.currency")
                .sum("amount.minor").as("totalMinor")
                .count().as("payouts"),
        sort(Sort.Direction.DESC, "totalMinor"));

List<CurrencyTotal> rows = replicas         // the reporting template from 8.11
        .aggregate(daily, Payout.class, CurrencyTotal.class)
        .getMappedResults();

record CurrencyTotal(@Id String currency, long totalMinor, long payouts) { }

The same report now reads one index range and returns 4 small documents. Because amounts are integers (8.10), the totals match the ledger to the penny.

On engine 5.0, avoid the stages AWS lists for later engines: $bucket, $merge and the $set stage from 8.0, and $facet and $setWindowFields from 8.0.2. $lookup supports equality joins, and correlated subqueries only from 8.0.2.

Also seen. The @Aggregation annotation, which declares a pipeline as JSON strings on a repository method. It suits a fixed report with one or two parameters.

When to break it. Load and compute in Java when the rule is too intricate for a pipeline and the set is small, such as 200 payouts for one claim. The cost is network and memory, which stay small only while the set does.

.NET anchor. The .NET driver's fluent Aggregate().Match(...).Group(...), or LINQ GroupBy translated to $group. In SQL terms, $match is WHERE and $group is GROUP BY.

See also. 8.07, 8.10, 8.11, 8.12, 18.04, Document data: Amazon DocumentDB and the MongoDB API

8.15 Read only the fields you need

What goes wrong. The payout list endpoint loaded 50 whole payouts to show 4 columns. Each held its bank instruction, with the bank's full response, and 20 history entries: about 40 KB. One screen moved 2 MB from the database. Then someone made it worse. They returned the document type with only some fields loaded, a later handler saved one, and save replaced the stored payout with the half-empty copy.

Do this now. Declare a small record with only the fields the screen needs, and return it from the repository: List<PayoutSummary> findTop50ByStatusOrderByRequestedAtDesc(PayoutStatus status). Spring Data reads only that record's fields. With MongoTemplate, restrict the fields on the query with query.fields().include("claimId").include("status"). With @Query, add fields = "{ 'claimId': 1, 'status': 1 }". Never load a document type partially, and never save a projection back.

See also. 5.03, 8.04, 18.02, Document data: Amazon DocumentDB and the MongoDB API

8.16 Enforce uniqueness with a unique index, not check-then-insert

Then. - Boot era: a check followed by an insert, inside a synchronized method or behind a lock document. It was right when the service ran as one instance, because synchronized stops two threads in one JVM. It cannot stop two pods. The unique index replaced it because only the database sees every writer.

public synchronized Payout create(String claimId, Money amount, String key) {
    return repository.findByIdempotencyKey(key)
            .orElseGet(() -> repository.save(Payout.pending(claimId, amount, key, Instant.now())));
}

Recognise it by. synchronized on a create method, a findBy... followed by save or insert, and a locks collection with lockedBy fields.

The rookie version.

public Payout create(CreatePayoutRequest request, String key) {
    Optional<Payout> existing = repository.findByIdempotencyKey(key);
    if (existing.isPresent()) return existing.get();
    Payout saved = repository.save(
            Payout.pending(request.claimId(), request.amount(), key, clock.instant()));
    saga.start(saved);
    return saved;
}

What goes wrong. The client's 2-second timeout fires while the first POST /payouts is still working, and it retries with the same Idempotency-Key. The retry lands on the other pod. Both pods check, both find nothing, both insert and both start a PayoutSaga. Claim 4471 is paid twice, 4 seconds apart, as it was in chapter 8.

Do this now.

  1. Put a unique index on the key, created explicitly (8.06). The database then refuses a second document with the same value, whoever sends it.
  2. When uniqueness is per something, make the index compound, for example unique on {claimId: 1, attempt: 1}.
  3. Use insert, not save. insert always creates a document. save overwrites one with the same id, which hides a duplicate instead of refusing it.
  4. Catch DuplicateKeyException, from org.springframework.dao, and read the winner. Compare what the winner was created from with this request. The same key with a different body is a client error.
  5. Read the winner from the primary. A replica may not have it yet (8.11).
  6. Keep a pre-check if you like, as a cheap answer for the common case. The index decides.
  7. Before building a unique index on a collection that already holds data, find existing duplicates with an aggregation that groups by the key and keeps counts above 1. The build fails while any remain.
public Payout create(CreatePayoutRequest request, String key) {
    try {
        Payout saved = repository.insert(
                Payout.pending(request.claimId(), request.amount(), key, clock.instant()));
        saga.start(saved);
        return saved;
    } catch (DuplicateKeyException e) {
        Payout winner = repository.findByIdempotencyKey(key).orElseThrow();
        if (!winner.matches(request.claimId(), request.amount())) {
            throw new IdempotencyKeyConflict(key);
        }
        return winner;
    }
}

If the pod dies between the insert and saga.start, the winner exists with no saga. The stuck-payout query of 8.03 finds PENDING payouts older than 15 minutes, so the recovery job starts it.

AWS limits an index key to 2,048 bytes. Reject idempotency keys longer than 255 characters at the API (6.01), long before the index has to.

Also seen. An upsert with $setOnInsert, through mongoTemplate.upsert, which creates the document only if none matches. Two concurrent upserts can still both insert, so it needs the unique index too, and its operator needs a line in the feature contract (8.12). A separate idempotency_keys collection whose _id is the key, because the _id index is always unique (9.10).

When to break it. Uniqueness across two collections, or across services, cannot be one index. Use a claim document in one place, such as idempotency_keys, or design the operation to be idempotent (9.09). The cost is a second write that must be cleaned up when the first fails.

.NET anchor. EF Core's HasIndex(p => p.IdempotencyKey).IsUnique(), with the second insert throwing a DbUpdateException that wraps SQL Server error 2601 or 2627. The pattern of catching it and reading the winner is the same.

See also. 5.05, 8.03, 8.06, 9.09, 9.10, The Yard, chapter 8, Document data: Amazon DocumentDB and the MongoDB API

8.17 Expire documents with a TTL index

What goes wrong. Payouts keeps each HTTP idempotency key for 24 hours. Nobody wrote the clean-up, so idempotency_keys grew to 40 million documents and its index stopped fitting in memory. After a TTL index was added, a time-to-live index that deletes documents once a date field is old enough, a second bug appeared. The code assumed a key vanished at exactly 24 hours, and refused a legitimate new request 24 hours and 6 minutes after the first, because the old key was still there.

Do this now. Put the TTL index on an Instant field, with @Indexed(expireAfterSeconds = 86_400) or explicitly with new Index().on("createdAt", Sort.Direction.ASC).expire(Duration.ofHours(24)). AWS states that TTL deletes are best effort and not guaranteed within a specific time, and that expiry starts only after the index build completes. So treat expiry as storage clean-up, not as logic. The code checks createdAt itself and treats an older key as absent. An insert would still hit the unique _id, so take the old key over with a conditional update whose filter includes createdAt older than 24 hours.

See also. 8.06, 9.10, Document data: Amazon DocumentDB and the MongoDB API

8.18 Store a value type with a custom converter

What goes wrong. Payouts wrapped claim ids in a record, ClaimId(String value), to stop them being mixed up with payout ids. Spring Data stored it as a nested document, "claimId": {"value": "C-4471"}. The policy team's reconciliation job matched on a plain string and found no payouts at all, and the index on claimId no longer served it.

Do this now. Write a pair of converters, a @WritingConverter from ClaimId to String and a @ReadingConverter back, and register them in one MongoCustomConversions bean, which Boot picks up. The @Bean method goes in a @Configuration class, Spring's equivalent of registering a service in Program.cs. The stored field is then the plain string, and queries that pass a ClaimId are converted too.

@WritingConverter
enum ClaimIdToString implements Converter<ClaimId, String> {
    INSTANCE;
    public String convert(ClaimId id) { return id.value(); }
}
@ReadingConverter
enum StringToClaimId implements Converter<String, ClaimId> {
    INSTANCE;
    public ClaimId convert(String value) { return new ClaimId(value); }
}
@Bean
MongoCustomConversions mongoCustomConversions() {
    return new MongoCustomConversions(List.of(ClaimIdToString.INSTANCE, StringToClaimId.INSTANCE));
}

See also. 2.03, 8.01, 8.10, Document data: Amazon DocumentDB and the MongoDB API

8.19 Evolve a document's shape with a schema version field

What goes wrong. A release replaced amountMinor and currency with a nested amount. The new code could not read the 3.1 million old payouts, and the rollback could not read the 2,000 new ones written in the first hour. There was no way to tell the two shapes apart except by guessing from which fields were present.

Do this now. Give each document a schemaVersion integer, written by every insert and update. Readers accept every version still stored, and turn old shapes into the current record in one place, a @ReadingConverter from org.bson.Document or a small factory method. Register the converter in the service's one MongoCustomConversions bean, beside the ClaimId pair of 8.18: new MongoCustomConversions(List.of(ClaimIdToString.INSTANCE, StringToClaimId.INSTANCE, new PayoutReader())). Writers write only the newest version, and only once every running pod can read it. Old documents change shape when they are next written, or through a backfill (20.07). Remove support for a version only when a count shows none remain.

See also. 8.01, 8.20, 20.03, 20.07, 20.11, Document data: Amazon DocumentDB and the MongoDB API

8.20 Run index and data migrations

Then. - Boot era: mongobee, a small library of @ChangeLog classes with @ChangeSet methods run at start-up and recorded in a collection. It was the first common answer to "Flyway for Mongo".

What goes wrong. A migration that built a new index on payouts ran in a start-up runner. Both pods started together during a deploy at 14:00, and both tried to build it. AWS states that only one index build runs on a collection at a time, and that by default a build blocks every other operation on the collection. Writes stalled for the length of the build in the middle of the afternoon.

Do this now. Run migrations once, not once per pod. A Kubernetes Job before the deploy is the simplest form. Mongock (io.mongock) keeps a change log and a lock so that only one runner applies each change. Its maintainers now point new projects at its successor, Flamingock. Check either tool's use of sessions and transactions against your engine (8.12). Build large indexes in a quiet window. Make data changes small and resumable, in batches keyed by _id (8.08, 8.21).

See also. 8.06, 8.19, 17.08, 20.03, 20.07, Document data: Amazon DocumentDB and the MongoDB API

8.21 Write in bulk

What goes wrong. A backfill set a new schemaVersion on 1.2 million payouts by reading each one and calling save. At about 3 ms a round trip, two per payout, it took 2 hours, and each save rewrote the whole document. saveAll did not help, because for documents that already exist it saves them one at a time.

Do this now. Send many writes in one command with mongoTemplate.bulkOps(BulkOperations.BulkMode.UNORDERED, Payout.class), add updateOne or insert calls, and execute(). Batches of about 1,000 stay well inside DocumentDB's limit of 100,000 writes in one batch command. UNORDERED carries on past a failed write, while ORDERED stops at the first. Either way execute() throws a BulkOperationException naming the failed writes, and the rest stay applied, so log those. Add .inc("version", 1) to each update, so @Version sees the change (8.05). AWS states that each write inside a bulk operation is atomic but the bulk as a whole is not, so a crash leaves part of a batch applied. Make each write safe to repeat, with a filter such as schemaVersion: 1, so the job can be run again.

See also. 8.04, 8.05, 8.08, 18.04, 20.07, Document data: Amazon DocumentDB and the MongoDB API

8.22 Use change streams on DocumentDB

What goes wrong. A change stream is a feed of the inserts, updates and deletes on a collection, which a client can follow and resume. The outbox relay was rewritten to follow outbox this way instead of polling it. On DocumentDB it received nothing, because AWS disables change streams by default and they must be enabled for each collection. After an outage over a weekend, the relay could not resume either. It had kept its resume token, the position to continue from, in memory, and the stream's history had expired.

Do this now. Enable the stream per collection, as AWS documents, with db.adminCommand({modifyChangeStreams: 1, database: "payouts", collection: "outbox", enable: true}). Store the resume token in a document after each event is handled, and open the stream with watch().resumeAfter(token). AWS keeps 3 hours of history by default, extendable to 7 days, so plan for an outage longer than that with a full re-scan. DocumentDB has no oplog, the MongoDB log some tools tail instead. Events from aborted transactions never appear. Elastic clusters have no change streams at all. Polling the outbox (9.08) remains the simpler choice.

See also. 8.12, 9.07, 9.08, Document data: Amazon DocumentDB and the MongoDB API

8.23 Test repositories against a real Mongo container

Then. - Boot era: Flapdoodle's embedded MongoDB, a library that downloaded and started a real mongod process for the tests, auto-configured by Boot 2. It gave a real server before Docker was everywhere. Testcontainers replaced it, and Boot 3 no longer configures it. - Spring era: Fongo, an in-memory imitation of MongoDB written in Java. It was fast and needed nothing installed. It also accepted queries no real server would and rejected some it would accept. - Modern: @DynamicPropertySource, copying the container's address into spring.data.mongodb.uri by hand. @ServiceConnection now does that for you.

Recognise it by. de.flapdoodle.embed.mongo, com.github.fakemongo:fongo, @DynamicPropertySource methods that set a MongoDB URI, and @RunWith(SpringRunner.class) on a @DataMongoTest.

The rookie version.

@DataMongoTest
@Testcontainers
class PayoutRepositoryTest {
    @Container @ServiceConnection
    static MongoDBContainer mongo = new MongoDBContainer("mongo:latest");

    @Autowired PayoutRepository repository;
    // tests rely on auto-index-creation: true in application-test.yml
}

What goes wrong. mongo:latest is a moving tag. One morning the suite ran on a newer MongoDB, with features DocumentDB 5.0 lacks, and nothing said so. The test profile also switched on automatic index creation, which production did not. So the duplicate-key test passed in the build while production had no unique index at all, which is how claim 4471 came to be paid twice in chapter 8.

Do this now.

  1. Start a real MongoDB with Testcontainers, a library that runs a Docker container for the length of the tests. A slice test, @DataMongoTest, starts only Spring's MongoDB parts. Declare the container once, as a @Bean in a @TestConfiguration class named MongoTestContainer, as 16.05 shows. Mark it @ServiceConnection, which tells Boot to connect to that container.
  2. Pin the image to the MongoDB API your engine emulates: mongo:5.0 for Payouts. That is this book's choice. AWS offers no way to run DocumentDB outside AWS and gives no guidance on local testing.
  3. Know your Testcontainers line. Boot 3.5 manages 1.21.4, with the artifact org.testcontainers:mongodb and the class org.testcontainers.containers.MongoDBContainer, which starts a single-node replica set itself. In Boot 4 it is 2.0.5, org.testcontainers:testcontainers-mongodb and org.testcontainers.mongodb.MongoDBContainer, and a transaction test needs .withReplicaSet() (9.04).
  4. Create indexes the way production does, by calling the same PayoutIndexes code, and keep automatic index creation off in tests.
  5. Clean up yourself. @DataMongoTest rolls nothing back. Delete documents before each test, and do not drop the collection, which drops its indexes too.
  6. Remember what the green proves: the query works on MongoDB 5.0. Whether it works on DocumentDB is the feature contract's question and the nightly run's job (8.12).
@DataMongoTest
@Import({MongoTestContainer.class, PayoutIndexes.class})
class PayoutRepositoryTest {
    @Autowired PayoutRepository repository;
    @Autowired PayoutIndexes indexes;

    @BeforeEach void clean() { repository.deleteAll(); indexes.ensure(); }

    @Test void refusesASecondPayoutForTheSameKey() {
        Payout first = Payout.pending("C-4471", Money.gbp("1240.50"), "k-1", NOW);
        repository.insert(first);
        assertThatThrownBy(() -> repository.insert(first)).isInstanceOf(DuplicateKeyException.class);
    }
}

In Boot 4, @DataMongoTest moves from org.springframework.boot.test.autoconfigure.data.mongo to org.springframework.boot.data.mongodb.test.autoconfigure.

Also seen. MongoDBAtlasLocalContainer, for services on MongoDB Atlas, which has nothing to do with DocumentDB. A static @Container field with @Testcontainers in each class, as in the rookie version. It works, but each class starts its own container (16.08).

When to break it. Domain logic with no query in it needs no container. A plain unit test is faster and says more (16.01). Every container a suite starts adds to the time of every build.

.NET anchor. Testcontainers for .NET's MongoDbBuilder in an xUnit fixture. The trap is the familiar one of running EF Core tests against SQLite when production runs SQL Server.

See also. 8.06, 8.12, 9.04, 16.05, 16.08, The Yard, chapter 7, Testing Spring Boot, Document data: Amazon DocumentDB and the MongoDB API

8.24 Tune the connection pool and timeouts

What goes wrong. Each pod's driver keeps a connection pool, a set of open connections reused across requests. Three services shared one r5.large instance, whose quota is 1,100 active connections and 3,400 in all. During a rolling deploy the three ran 9 pods, each with a pool of 200, and the instance refused new connections. The driver's default wait for a server then held each request far past the caller's 2-second timeout.

Do this now. Set the pool and the timeouts in the connection string: maxPoolSize=10&minPoolSize=2&maxIdleTimeMS=60000&serverSelectionTimeoutMS=250&connectTimeoutMS=250&socketTimeoutMS=500. Peak pods times maxPoolSize, summed over every service on the instance, must stay under its quota. Payouts gives 3 × 10 = 30 (18.03). With pools of 20 for the other two, the total is 30 + 2 × 3 × 20 = 150, under 1,100. Graph DatabaseConnections against DatabaseConnectionsLimit. The timeouts add up to 250 + 250 + 500 = 1,000 ms at worst, half the caller's 2 seconds, leaving the rest to the ledger and bank (7.15). socketTimeoutMS covers every operation, so a longer report needs its own MongoClient.

See also. 7.03, 7.15, 8.11, 18.03, Document data: Amazon DocumentDB and the MongoDB API

⚠Review checklist
  • If you see code that uses the object it passed to save instead of the one save returned: the id and version are missing, and a second save inserts a duplicate. See 8.01.
  • If you see @DBRef on a field: DocumentDB does not support DBRefs, and each reference costs a query. See 8.02.
  • If you see a derived query with four or more conditions, or one that returns an unbounded List: nobody can check it against an index, and one day it loads everything. See 8.03.
  • If you see findById followed by save to change one field: the save replaces the whole document and loses concurrent changes. See 8.04.
  • If you see a document that is updated after creation with no @Version: two writers lose one update silently. See 8.05.
  • If you see @Indexed with nothing that creates it, or auto-index-creation: true on a large collection: either there is no index or a deploy blocks the collection. See 8.06.
  • If you see a query's speed in a test offered as proof it uses an index: a container holds too few documents for any plan to be slow. See 8.07.
  • If you see PageRequest.of(page++, ...) in a batch job: skip reads every skipped document, and with no sort the pages overlap. See 8.08.
  • If you see a $push with no limit on the array: the document grows towards 16 MiB on every write. See 8.09.
  • If you see double for an amount or LocalDateTime for an event: sums drift by pennies and times shift by zone. See 8.10.
  • If you see readPreference=secondaryPreferred in a service that reads its own writes: reads miss writes and the saga repeats steps. See 8.11.
  • If you see a new operator, stage or index type with no line in the feature contract: it may not exist on Payouts' engine. See 8.12.
  • If you see Containing, Like or IgnoreCase on a large collection: it becomes a $regex that scans. See 8.13.
  • If you see findAll() followed by a loop that sums: the whole collection crosses the network to compute a few numbers. See 8.14.
  • If you see a document type loaded with only some fields, or a projection saved back: the save wipes the missing fields. See 8.15.
  • If you see a findBy... check followed by an insert: two pods both pass the check. See 8.16.
  • If you see code that assumes a TTL index deletes at an exact time: AWS makes TTL deletes best effort. See 8.17.
  • If you see a migration or index build in a start-up runner on a populated collection: every pod runs it and the build blocks writes. See 8.20.
  • If you see a backfill that calls save or saveAll per document: it takes hours where a bulk write takes minutes. See 8.21.
  • If you see a change stream consumer that keeps its resume token in memory: after a restart it cannot continue. See 8.22.
  • If you see mongo:latest in a test, or test settings that create indexes production does not: the green build tests a different database. See 8.23.
  • If you see maxPoolSize chosen without counting pods: a rolling deploy exceeds the instance's connection quota. See 8.24.

Part IV · The how-to9. Transactions and consistency#

A payout touches three things that fail independently: the payouts collection, the outbox that feeds SNS, and the services at the other end. This part shows what @Transactional really does in a Spring Boot service on DocumentDB, when a multi-document transaction is worth its limits, and when one document is the better unit. It then builds the two mechanisms that parts 10 and 11 rely on. The transactional outbox publishes events without a dual write. Idempotency makes every retry and every redelivery safe. It ends with consistency choices per use case, and the XA transactions you will find in older code.

★What a veteran knows
  • A transaction you have not seen begin, in a log or a failing test, is a transaction you do not have. On a Mongo service, @Transactional does nothing until a transaction manager exists.
  • Draw the boundary around one document first. A transaction is for the rare rule that two documents must agree, and on DocumentDB it has limits that a batch job will find.
  • Code that writes to the database and then to something else has a gap between the two. The outbox does not close the gap. It moves the gap to a place where repeating the second write is safe.
  • Nobody offers exactly-once delivery: not SQS, not SNS, not the network. Exactly-once effect is on offer, if every handler is idempotent.
  • An idempotency key is created once, before the first attempt, and stored. A key generated inside the retry makes every attempt a new request.
  • Decide on strong reads and display from eventual ones. The primary answers questions that move money. A replica or a projection answers questions a person reads.
  • XA was the right answer when every resource spoke it. DocumentDB, SNS and SQS do not, so the answer now is a local write plus a message that is safe to repeat.
◷How we got hereIn January 2007, at the CIDR conference in Asilomar, California, Pat Helland presented a paper called "Life…

In January 2007, at the CIDR conference in Asilomar, California, Pat Helland presented a paper called "Life beyond Distributed Transactions: an Apostate's Opinion". It opened with a confession. He had spent "a nontrivial portion" of his career advocating platforms that guaranteed global serializability. A decade of experience had led him "to liken these platforms to the Maginot Line", and a footnote reminded readers that the fortress "was quickly bypassed by the Germans in 1940". Large applications, he wrote, were not built on distributed transactions, and projects that tried them would "founder because the performance costs and fragility make them impractical". In their place he described entities, at-least-once messages, idempotent processing, and tentative work such as "reserved inventory" that the application itself must manage. The paper said its views were his own, not his employer's. Nineteen years later a ledger reservation in Payouts is exactly his tentative work, and this part turns his list into Spring code.

9.01 Know what @Transactional does and where it applies

Then.

  • J2EE era: container-managed transactions on Enterprise JavaBeans (EJBs). The application server opened a transaction around each business method of a session bean, the EJB kind that holds business logic, declared in ejb-jar.xml or later with @TransactionAttribute. It was right while the server owned every connection the code used.
@Stateless
public class PayoutServiceBean {
    @TransactionAttribute(TransactionAttributeType.REQUIRED)
    public void markPaid(String payoutId) { /* JDBC through the server's DataSource */ }
}
  • Spring era: transactions declared in XML. A <tx:advice> named the methods. An <aop:config> pointcut, an expression that matches methods by package and name, applied it to every service class. AOP, aspect-oriented programming, is Spring's machinery for wrapping extra behaviour around methods you did not change. It let teams leave the application server and keep declarative transactions. Annotations replaced it because the rule then sits on the method it governs.
<tx:advice id="txAdvice" transaction-manager="txManager">
    <tx:attributes><tx:method name="*" rollback-for="Exception"/></tx:attributes>
</tx:advice>
<aop:config>
    <aop:advisor advice-ref="txAdvice" pointcut="execution(* com.sorrel.payouts..*Service.*(..))"/>
</aop:config>

Recognise it by. javax.ejb.TransactionAttribute, <tx:advice>, <tx:annotation-driven/>, TransactionProxyFactoryBean with PROPAGATION_REQUIRED,-Exception. Also jakarta.transaction.Transactional where Spring's org.springframework.transaction.annotation.Transactional was meant. Spring honours the Jakarta one, with rollback attributes named rollbackOn and dontRollbackOn. Since Framework 6 (Boot 3) it ignores the old javax.transaction.Transactional without a word, so code moved from Boot 2 with that import has no transaction.

The rookie version.

@Transactional
public Payout request(PayoutCommand cmd) throws PolicyLookup {
    Payout payout = payouts.insert(Payout.pending(cmd, clock.instant()));
    outbox.append(OutboxEvent.payoutRequested(payout, clock.instant()));
    policyClient.confirmCover(cmd.claimId());     // HTTP call, throws a checked exception
    return payout;
}

What goes wrong. Three things, each enough on its own. First, the annotation does nothing yet. Spring Data MongoDB states that transaction support is disabled unless a MongoTransactionManager is declared, and Boot declares none. Each insert commits as it happens. Second, with a manager declared, PolicyLookup still commits. Java has two kinds of exception. A checked exception must be declared with throws, as here. An unchecked one extends RuntimeException and need not be. Spring's rule rolls back on unchecked exceptions and commits on checked ones. So claim C-4471 had no cover, yet its PayoutRequested event reached the saga, and the ledger reserved £1,240.50. Third, the HTTP call runs inside the transaction. On DocumentDB a transaction has a one-minute execution limit, and each instance has an upper bound on open transactions: 200 on an r5.large instance. A policy system answering in 40 seconds fills those slots with transactions that are only waiting.

Do this now.

  1. Know the mechanism. Spring reads @Transactional through a proxy, a wrapper object it puts in front of your bean, an object that Spring creates and injects. On a call from another bean, the proxy asks the transaction manager, a PlatformTransactionManager for one kind of resource, to begin. It then calls your method, and commits on a normal return or rolls back on an unchecked exception.
  2. Declare the manager. For DocumentDB it is a MongoTransactionManager bean, with the session setting in 9.04. Without it there is no error, only no transaction.
  3. Annotate public methods that other beans call (9.02). One business operation is one transactional method.
  4. Choose the rollback rule. Use unchecked exceptions for failures that must undo the work. Where a checked exception must roll back, say so with rollbackFor.
  5. Keep remote calls out. Look up the policy before the transaction, and publish after it through the outbox (9.07).
  6. Prove it began. Write a test that fails after the first write and asserts nothing was stored. In a log, set logging.level.org.springframework.data.mongodb.MongoTransactionManager=DEBUG and look for "Creating new transaction".
public Payout request(PayoutCommand cmd) {
    Cover cover = policyClient.confirmCover(cmd.claimId());   // outside: it may be slow
    return requests.record(cmd, cover);                       // another bean, one transaction
}

// in PayoutRequests, a separate @Service
@Transactional
public Payout record(PayoutCommand cmd, Cover cover) {
    Payout payout = payouts.insert(Payout.pending(cmd, cover, clock.instant()));
    outbox.append(OutboxEvent.payoutRequested(payout, clock.instant()));
    return payout;
}

Also seen. TransactionTemplate, the programmatic form, tx.execute(status -> ...). Choose it when the boundary is a block inside a method, or when you want no proxy at all (9.02).

When to break it. A write to one document needs no transaction. AWS states that every single CRUD statement on DocumentDB is atomic (9.05). Leaving @Transactional off saves round trips and a slot in the instance's quota. The cost is that whoever adds a second write must remember to add the transaction.

.NET anchor. TransactionScope or DbContext.Database.BeginTransactionAsync(). A TransactionScope is ambient: any code inside it takes part. Spring's annotation works only through the proxy, and only with a manager for that resource. And a scope that is not completed rolls back whatever the exception, where Spring commits on a checked one. C# has no checked exceptions, so this rule has no .NET counterpart to warn you.

See also. 9.02, 9.03, 9.04, 9.07, The Yard, chapter 15, Transactions, propagation and isolation, How Spring actually works

9.02 Avoid the self-invocation trap

Then.

  • Spring era: AopContext.currentProxy(), with the proxy exposed in XML, so a bean could call itself through its own proxy. It worked, and it tied business code to Spring's AOP classes.
// applicationContext.xml: <aop:aspectj-autoproxy expose-proxy="true"/>
public void confirmFromLedger(LedgerConfirmation c) {
    ((PayoutService) AopContext.currentProxy()).markPaid(c.payoutId(), c.reference());
}
  • Spring era: AspectJ weaving, with <tx:annotation-driven mode="aspectj"/> and spring-aspects. It rewrites the class's bytecode so even a call on this is transactional. It was right for teams that needed it everywhere and could run a weaving step at build time, or a Java agent, a library the JVM loads at start-up to rewrite classes as they load. Most dropped it because the setup was fragile and proxies covered most cases.

Recognise it by. AopContext.currentProxy(), exposeProxy = true, mode = AdviceMode.ASPECTJ, the spring-aspects and spring-instrument artifacts, and a bean that injects itself, such as @Autowired private PayoutService self;.

The rookie version.

public void confirmFromLedger(LedgerConfirmation c) {
    markPaid(c.payoutId(), c.reference());          // this.markPaid: the proxy never sees it
}

@Transactional
public void markPaid(String payoutId, String ledgerRef) {
    payouts.markPaid(payoutId, ledgerRef);
    outbox.append(OutboxEvent.payoutCompleted(payoutId, clock.instant()));
}

What goes wrong. The Yard's chapter 15 tells how the team found this. Here is what it costs. The two writes are not in a transaction, so a pod stopped between them leaves a payout marked paid with no PayoutCompleted event. Over a month of rolling deploys, 14 claimants were paid and never told. The test suite was green throughout. Every test called markPaid directly, from outside the bean, so every test went through the proxy.

Do this now.

  1. Find the cases. For each annotated method, list its callers. The same trap applies to every annotation that works through a proxy: @Transactional, @Async, @Cacheable, Framework 7's @Retryable, and the @CircuitBreaker and @Retry of Resilience4j, the Java counterpart of Polly.
  2. Move the annotated method into its own bean. The boundary becomes a type you can name, such as PayoutTransitions. This is the default fix.
  3. Or put the annotation on the outer method, when all of it belongs in one transaction and it makes no remote call.
  4. Or use a TransactionTemplate, which needs no proxy (listing below).
  5. Know the other silent cases. Spring proxies a class with no interface by generating a subclass. A subclass cannot override a private or final method, so those are never intercepted. Spring's documentation also warns that the proxy is not ready in initialisation code, for example a @PostConstruct method.
  6. Test through the real caller. Call confirmFromLedger, make the second write fail, and assert that the first was rolled back.
@Service
public class PayoutService {
    private final TransactionTemplate tx;

    PayoutService(PlatformTransactionManager manager /* , repositories */) {
        this.tx = new TransactionTemplate(manager);
    }

    public void confirmFromLedger(LedgerConfirmation c) {
        tx.executeWithoutResult(status -> {
            payouts.markPaid(c.payoutId(), c.reference());
            outbox.append(OutboxEvent.payoutCompleted(c.payoutId(), clock.instant()));
        });
    }
}

Also seen. Self-injection with @Lazy, a constructor parameter of the bean's own type that Spring fills with its proxy. It works, and it hides the boundary from the next reader. AspectJ mode, in services that already weave for another reason.

When to break it. Self-injection is a fair stopgap in a large class you cannot split this sprint. The cost is a class that depends on itself, and a reviewer who must know why.

.NET anchor. Castle DynamicProxy, which Autofac's interceptors use, has the same rule. Only calls through the proxy are intercepted, and only virtual methods. TransactionScope has no such trap because it is code you run, not an interceptor.
