See also. 9.01, 3.05, 7.06, The Yard, chapter 15, How Spring actually works, Transactions, propagation and isolation

9.03 Choose a propagation setting deliberately

What goes wrong. Propagation is what a @Transactional method does when a transaction is already open. The outbox writer was given REQUIRES_NEW "so the event is saved even if the payout fails". The event committed on its own. The payout's transaction then rolled back on a write conflict, and the relay published PayoutRequested for a payout that did not exist. The ledger reserved £1,240.50 for nothing.

Do this now. Leave the default, REQUIRED, which joins the caller's transaction or starts one. Mark helpers that must never run alone MANDATORY, which throws when no transaction is open. The outbox writer is the example. Keep REQUIRES_NEW, which suspends the caller's transaction and starts a separate one, for records that must survive the caller's rollback, such as a failure log. On DocumentDB it holds a second open transaction against the instance's quota. Avoid NESTED. It needs savepoints, which MongoDB transactions do not have, so MongoTransactionManager does not allow it. Inside an open transaction it throws NestedTransactionNotSupportedException, and with none open it behaves like REQUIRED.

@Transactional(propagation = Propagation.MANDATORY)
public void append(OutboxEvent event) {
    mongo.insert(event);
}

See also. 9.01, 9.07, Transactions, propagation and isolation

9.04 Use a multi-document transaction on DocumentDB, within its limits

Then.

  • Boot era: two-phase commit by hand. MongoDB before 4.0 had no multi-document transactions, and its documentation described a pattern instead. A transactions document moved through initial, pending, applied and done. Each changed document carried a pendingTransactions array, so a recovery job could finish or undo the work. It was right when one document was all the database could change atomically. DocumentDB 3.6 clusters are in the same position: AWS supports transactions from 4.0.
db.transactions.insertOne({_id: t, state: "initial", payout: "p-81", claim: "C-4471"})
db.transactions.updateOne({_id: t, state: "initial"}, {$set: {state: "pending"}})
db.payouts.updateOne({_id: "p-81", pendingTransactions: {$ne: t}}, {$push: {pendingTransactions: t}})
db.transactions.updateOne({_id: t, state: "pending"}, {$set: {state: "applied"}})

Recognise it by. A transactions or pending_operations collection with a state field, pendingTransactions arrays on business documents, and a recovery job that walks them.

The rookie version.

@Transactional
public void markReconciled(LocalDate day) {
    try (Stream<Payout> due = payouts.streamByStatusAndPaidOn(PayoutStatus.PAID, day)) {
        due.forEach(p -> payouts.save(p.reconciled()));
    }
    runs.insert(ReconciliationRun.completed(day, clock.instant()));   // new collection
}

What goes wrong. Against the mongo:5.0 container, with 300 payouts, the job passed. On DocumentDB it failed three ways in turn. The Stream reads through a cursor, and AWS states that DocumentDB does not support cursors within a transaction. After a rewrite to a list, the first run in a fresh environment failed again, because reconciliation_runs did not exist yet and DocumentDB cannot create a collection inside a transaction. Then came month end. Saving 36,000 payouts took longer than one minute, the transaction was aborted with error code 251, and nothing was marked.

Do this now.

  1. Check the cluster can. AWS requires engine 4.0 or later and a driver compatible with MongoDB 4.0 or later. Elastic clusters have no transactions.
  2. Declare a MongoTransactionManager (9.01).
  3. Turn causal consistency off for its sessions. AWS states that DocumentDB supports sessions for transactions but not causal consistency, the guarantee that a session reads its own earlier writes. It rejects it with error 303. Spring Data's manager opens its session with causal consistency on, and asks the database factory for it. TransactionOptions on the manager cannot change that: they set read concern (how current a read must be), write concern (how many copies must acknowledge a write) and read preference, not session options. So give Spring a database factory whose sessions have it off (listing).
  4. Create every collection and index at start-up, before any transaction touches it (8.06).
  5. Stay small. Finish well inside one minute. Keep the transaction log under AWS's 32 MB. Use no cursors: load a bounded batch by id instead.
  6. Expect the isolation you get. AWS states that DocumentDB uses snapshot isolation and upgrades a lower read concern to it. Writes use majority write concern and are always journaled. The linearizable read concern, MongoDB's strongest, is refused with an error.
  7. Retry the whole transaction from outside when it aborts on a conflict or a timeout (9.11).
  8. Watch the quota. Each open transaction holds a slot: 50 on a t3.medium, 200 on an r5.large. CloudWatch shows the limit as TransactionsOpenLimit.
  9. Test against a replica set, a primary with copies, because MongoDB runs transactions only on one. Testcontainers, the library that runs Docker containers for tests, provides one (8.23). Boot 3.5 manages Testcontainers 1.21.4, whose container starts a replica set itself. In Boot 4 it is 2.0.5, and the container needs .withReplicaSet().
@Configuration
class MongoTransactionConfig {
    @Bean
    MongoDatabaseFactory mongoDatabaseFactory(MongoClient client) {
        return new SimpleMongoClientDatabaseFactory(client, "payouts") {
            @Override public ClientSession getSession(ClientSessionOptions options) {
                return client.startSession(ClientSessionOptions.builder(options)
                        .causallyConsistent(false).build());
            }
        };
    }
    @Bean
    MongoTransactionManager transactionManager(MongoDatabaseFactory f) { return new MongoTransactionManager(f); }
}

Declaring the factory replaces Boot's own, so MongoTemplate and the manager share it. A template on a different factory would not join the manager's transaction. AWS's own Java example sets the same option, causallyConsistent(false). On MongoDB, commit and rollback behave as before. Run it against a DocumentDB cluster before relying on it (8.12).

Also seen. The driver's ClientSession.withTransaction(...), as in AWS's sample, which retries transient failures itself. MongoTemplate.withSession(session) for code that manages the session by hand.

When to break it. A batch over thousands of documents does not belong in one transaction. Update each payout on its own, with a filter that skips those already done, so a rerun continues where the last stopped. The cost is that a reader can see half a run, so the run's record says "in progress" until the end.

.NET anchor. session.StartTransaction() and session.WithTransaction(...) in the .NET driver are the same calls. The difference from SQL Server is size and time. SQL Server itself puts no time limit on a transaction. DocumentDB aborts one after one minute, whatever the client asks.

See also. 8.06, 8.11, 8.12, 8.23, 9.01, 9.05, 9.11, Document data: Amazon DocumentDB and the MongoDB API, Transactions, propagation and isolation

9.05 Make one document the unit of consistency

Then.

  • Spring era: a running total kept in step with the rows it summarised, inside one SQL transaction. On a relational database the transaction kept them equal and cost little. Ported to documents, it became two independent writes.
BEGIN;
INSERT INTO payout (id, claim_id, amount_minor, status) VALUES (?, ?, ?, 'PENDING');
UPDATE claim_exposure SET committed_minor = committed_minor + ? WHERE claim_id = ?;
COMMIT;

Recognise it by. Collections named *_summary, *_totals or *_exposure, a $inc on a second collection right after an insert, and comments such as "keep in sync with payouts".

The rookie version.

ClaimExposure e = exposures.findById(cmd.claimId()).orElseThrow();
if (e.committed().plus(cmd.amount()).amount().compareTo(e.approved().amount()) > 0) {
    throw new ExposureExceeded(cmd.claimId());
}
Payout payout = payouts.insert(Payout.pending(cmd, clock.instant()));
exposures.save(e.commit(cmd.amount()));

What goes wrong. Claim C-4471 is approved for £5,000.00 and has £3,800.00 committed. Two instalments of £1,240.50 arrive 30 ms apart on 2 pods. Both read £3,800.00, both pass the check, and both insert. The claim now has £6,281.00 committed against £5,000.00 approved. Separately, a pod stopped between the insert and the save leaves a payout that the exposure document does not count, so the next check lets through more than it should.

Do this now.

  1. Name the invariant: the payouts committed on a claim never exceed the amount approved.
  2. Find the smallest document that can hold everything the invariant mentions. Here the claim's exposure document owns the approved amount, the remaining amount and the list of commitments. A claim has a handful of instalments, so the list stays bounded (8.09).
  3. Make the check the filter of one conditional update. AWS states that each single CRUD statement on DocumentDB is atomic, so no writer can come between the filter and the change.
  4. Put the idempotency in the same filter: refuse a commitment whose payout id is already in the list (9.09).
  5. Read the result. A modified count of 0 means the rule refused, or the commitment was already there. Read the document from the primary to tell which. If it was already there, this is a retry after a crash, so carry on and create the payout. That only works if the payout id is the same on every attempt: derive it from the request's idempotency key (9.10), never generate it here.
  6. Order the remaining writes so a crash leaves a safe state. Commit the exposure first, then insert the payout. A crash between leaves money held, not overspent, and a recovery job releases commitments with no payout after 10 minutes.
  7. Do not trust updateMany for an invariant. AWS states that each document's change is atomic, but the operation as a whole is not.
String payoutId = cmd.payoutId();                      // the same on every retry (9.10)
long minor = StoredMoney.from(cmd.amount()).minor();
Query room = query(where("_id").is(cmd.claimId())
        .and("remainingMinor").gte(minor)
        .and("commitments.payoutId").ne(payoutId));
Update commit = new Update()
        .inc("remainingMinor", -minor)
        .push("commitments", new Commitment(payoutId, cmd.amount(), clock.instant()));
if (mongo.updateFirst(room, commit, ClaimExposure.class).getModifiedCount() == 0
        && !alreadyCommitted(cmd.claimId(), payoutId)) {
    throw new ExposureExceeded(cmd.claimId());
}
return payouts.insertOrFindExisting(Payout.pending(payoutId, cmd, clock.instant()));

alreadyCommitted reads the exposure document from the primary and looks for the payout id in its list. insertOrFindExisting is the insert of 8.16: on a duplicate _id it returns the payout already stored.

Also seen. A @Version on the exposure document, with the check in Java and a retry on conflict (8.05). Choose it when the rule is too complex for a filter. A multi-document transaction over both writes (9.04), at the price of its limits.

When to break it. Some invariants span two documents written by different processes and must hold at every instant. Use a transaction for those (9.04), and accept its limits. When the documents belong to different services, no transaction can help. Use a reservation and a saga (11.02).

.NET anchor. The aggregate rule from domain-driven design, one aggregate per transaction, is the same rule in EF Core. SQL Server lets you cheat with a wider transaction, and DocumentDB makes cheating expensive. The conditional update is UPDATE ... WHERE remaining >= @amount with a check on the row count, or ExecuteUpdate and its return value.

See also. 8.02, 8.04, 8.05, 8.09, 8.10, 9.04, 9.09, 11.02, The Yard, chapter 8, Document data: Amazon DocumentDB and the MongoDB API

9.06 Recognise the dual-write problem

Then.

  • J2EE era: an XA transaction, one transaction that a coordinator commits across several resources, here the database and a broker reached through JMS, Java's standard messaging API. The row and the message committed together (9.14). It was right while both resources spoke XA.
  • Spring era: "best efforts one-phase commit". Commit the database, then the message, in a fixed order, and accept a rare duplicate or loss. Spring Data's ChainedTransactionManager packaged it, and JmsTemplate with sessionTransacted did something similar.
@Transactional   // DataSourceTransactionManager
public void request(Payout payout) {
    payoutDao.insert(payout);
    jmsTemplate.convertAndSend("payout.requested", payout);   // sent after the commit, usually
}

Recognise it by. JmsTemplate.convertAndSend inside a @Transactional method, setSessionTransacted(true), ChainedTransactionManager, and a @TransactionalEventListener(phase = TransactionPhase.AFTER_COMMIT) that sends to a broker.

The rookie version.

@Transactional
public Payout request(PayoutCommand cmd) {
    Payout payout = payouts.insert(Payout.pending(cmd, clock.instant()));
    snsTemplate.convertAndSend("payout-events", PayoutRequested.from(payout));
    return payout;
}

What goes wrong. A dual write is one operation that writes to two systems sharing no transaction. snsTemplate is Spring Cloud AWS's helper for publishing to SNS (10.02). Here the publish happens at once and cannot be rolled back. If the commit then fails, on a conflict or because the pod was stopped during a deploy, the ledger receives PayoutRequested for a payout that does not exist. It reserves £1,240.50 against nothing. Move the publish after the commit, or into an AFTER_COMMIT listener, and the failure flips. A pod stopped between the commit and the publish leaves a payout PENDING that no saga will ever start. In one month of about 440,000 payouts there were 3 of one and 1 of the other. That is rare enough to pass every test and frequent enough for finance to find.

Do this now.

  1. List every operation that changes Payouts' data and also tells another system: an SNS publish, an SQS send, an HTTP call to the ledger or the bank, an email, a cache write.
  2. For each, ask two questions. If the process dies between the two writes, what state is left? Who notices, and when?
  3. Choose a fix by case. When the other side needs an event, use the transactional outbox (9.07). When the other side is a step in a workflow, record the intent first and run a saga (7.16, 11.02). When the second write is a cache or a search index, derive it from the first and make it rebuildable.
  4. Do not fix it with a retry around the second write. A retry shortens the window and does not remove it, because the pod can die during the retries.
  5. Add detection anyway. A scheduled check for payouts PENDING for more than 10 minutes with no saga finds whatever the design missed.
# Transactional methods that also publish or call out: each is a dual write to review
grep -rn -A12 '@Transactional' payouts-api/src/main/java \
  | grep -E 'snsTemplate|sqsTemplate|snsClient|sqsClient|ledgerClient|bankGatewayClient'

Also seen. Change data capture, where a separate process reads the database's own change feed and publishes from it. On DocumentDB that feed is change streams (8.22). "Listen to yourself", where the service publishes first and updates its own database from its own event. It suits event-sourced designs and makes every read eventual.

When to break it. Accept a dual write when losing the second write is harmless: a metrics counter, a cache eviction that also expires on its own, or a courtesy email the claimant can check in the portal. The cost is an occasional loss. Write down that it was a choice.

.NET anchor. SaveChangesAsync() followed by IPublishEndpoint.Publish is the same bug. MassTransit and NServiceBus both ship a transactional outbox for this reason. TransactionScope promoted to MSDTC across SQL Server and MSMQ was the .NET counterpart of XA.

See also. 7.16, 8.22, 9.07, 9.08, 9.14, 10.02, 11.02, The Yard, chapter 8

9.07 Publish events reliably with a transactional outbox

Then.

  • Spring era: a transaction synchronisation registered by hand, which sent the message in its afterCommit callback. It removed the ghost event of 9.06, and kept the lost event: a crash after the commit lost the message. It was right for teams that accepted that. @TransactionalEventListener is its modern form, with the same gap.
TransactionSynchronizationManager.registerSynchronization(new TransactionSynchronizationAdapter() {
    @Override public void afterCommit() {
        jmsTemplate.convertAndSend("payout.requested", payout);
    }
});

Recognise it by. TransactionSynchronizationManager.registerSynchronization, TransactionSynchronizationAdapter, afterCommit(), and @TransactionalEventListener methods that call a broker.

The rookie version.

public Payout request(PayoutCommand cmd) {
    Payout payout = payouts.insert(Payout.pending(cmd, clock.instant()));
    outbox.insert(new OutboxEvent(null, "PayoutRequested", payout.id()));   // id only
    return payout;
}

What goes wrong. There is no transaction around the two inserts, so the gap of 9.06 is still there, one line lower. A pod stopped between them leaves a payout with no event. The event also carries only the payout's id. The relay, or each consumer, must load the payout later to learn what happened. By then it is RESERVED, so payout-audit records a PayoutRequested with the wrong status. And every consumer now calls payouts-api to fetch the data, which at 09:00 on the first of the month adds 3 calls for every payout.

Do this now. A transactional outbox is a collection your service writes events into, in the same transaction as the state change they describe. A separate relay publishes them later (9.08). Either both writes happen or neither does.

  1. Create the outbox collection and its index at start-up. DocumentDB cannot create a collection inside a transaction.
  2. Model the outbox document as a record (first listing). Its payload is the whole message a consumer will read: the envelope of 10.12, with everything the consumer needs frozen at the moment of the change.
  3. Create the event id when the event is created, as a UUID. It is the outbox document's _id and the envelope's eventId, so it travels with the message, and consumers deduplicate on it (10.07).
  4. Write the event in the same transaction as the change, with a MANDATORY writer (9.03) and the manager from 9.04.
  5. Write one event per state change, from the code that makes the change. A change made in two places gets two event writers, and one will be forgotten.
  6. Keep the payload small. SNS topics accept 256 KiB by default, and the relay sends the payload as the message. For more, store the data and send a reference (10.14).
  7. Never call SNS from the request thread. The relay publishes.
@Document("outbox")
public record OutboxEvent(
        @Id String id,               // event id: consumers deduplicate on it
        String type,                 // "PayoutRequested"
        int schemaVersion,           // the event's version, for consumers (10.12)
        String aggregateId,          // the payout's id
        String payload,              // the envelope's JSON, as published (10.12)
        Instant occurredAt,
        Map<String, String> traceContext, // traceparent and friends, for the relay (13.05)
        OutboxStatus status,         // PENDING, PUBLISHED, FAILED
        Instant leaseUntil,          // which relay holds it, and until when (9.08)
        int attempts,
        Instant publishedAt) { }

@Transactional
public Payout record(PayoutCommand cmd, Cover cover) {
    Instant now = clock.instant();
    Payout payout = payouts.insert(Payout.pending(cmd, cover, now));
    UUID eventId = UUID.randomUUID();
    String json = eventJson.write(new EventEnvelope<>(eventId, "PayoutRequested",
            1, now, payout.id(), PayoutRequestedData.from(payout)));
    outbox.append(OutboxEvent.pending(eventId, "PayoutRequested", 1, payout.id(), json, now,
            traceContexts.current()));
    return payout;
}

eventJson is a small bean around Jackson's ObjectMapper that rethrows its checked JsonProcessingException as unchecked, so a serialisation failure rolls the transaction back (9.01). OutboxEvent.pending stores the id as a string and sets status PENDING, leaseUntil equal to occurredAt and no attempts. traceContexts is a small Payouts bean that returns the current trace context as a map, built as 13.05 shows, and empty when there is no trace.

Also seen. An outbox embedded in the payout: a short pendingEvents array written by the same single-document update, with no transaction at all (9.05). The relay finds payouts with pending events and removes each one with $pull after publishing it. It avoids DocumentDB's transaction limits, at the cost of a relay that searches the payouts collection. Spring Modulith, Spring's library for modular monoliths, keeps a similar record for in-process listeners in its event publication registry.

When to break it. Events whose loss is harmless, such as an analytics feed, can go straight to SNS. The outbox's costs are real: a second write in every transaction, a relay to run and watch, a delay of one poll interval, and duplicates that consumers must handle.

.NET anchor. MassTransit's transactional outbox, AddEntityFrameworkOutbox<TDbContext>() or its MongoDB version, and NServiceBus's Outbox do this for you. In Payouts it is the team's own code, about 200 lines, which means the team can read it.

See also. 9.03, 9.04, 9.06, 9.08, 10.07, 10.12, 10.14, The Yard, chapter 8, Caching, scheduling and events

9.08 Relay the outbox to SNS

Then.

  • Boot era: the relay as a job in Quartz, a scheduling library, with a clustered JDBC job store, so that only one node ran it at a time. It was right when there was no lighter way to stop two nodes running the same job. Leases on the outbox itself now do that without a scheduler of their own.
spring.quartz.job-store-type=jdbc
spring.quartz.properties.org.quartz.jobStore.isClustered=true
spring.quartz.properties.org.quartz.jobStore.clusterCheckinInterval=20000

Recognise it by. org.quartz.* imports, QRTZ_ tables in an old schema, spring.quartz.* properties, and @DisallowConcurrentExecution on a job class.

The rookie version.

@Scheduled(fixedDelay = 1000)
void relay() {
    for (OutboxEvent e : outbox.findByStatus(OutboxStatus.PENDING)) {
        outbox.save(e.published());
        publisher.publish(e);
    }
}

What goes wrong. It marks each event published before publishing it. During a 6-minute network fault, 212 events were marked PUBLISHED and never sent, and 212 claimants were never told. The loop reads every pending event at once, so after the fault it loaded 9,000 into memory. Both pods ran it, so most events reached each queue twice. And the first publish that threw ended the run, so one failure held up everything behind it until the next second.

Do this now.

  1. Publish, then mark. A crash between the two leaves the event PENDING, and the next run publishes it again. This is at-least-once delivery: never lost, sometimes repeated. Consumers deduplicate on the event id (10.07).
  2. Claim each event with a lease. findAndModify changes one document and returns it in one atomic step, so 2 pods never hold the same event at once. A pod that dies holding one loses it when the lease ends.
  3. Bound the work. Take at most 100 events per run, and give the SNS client timeouts (7.03).
  4. Count attempts. After 10, mark the event FAILED and alert. One bad event must not hold up the rest. The listing counts but does not stop: add .and("attempts").lt(10) to its query, and let the job of step 7 mark those that reach 10 FAILED.
  5. Sort by occurredAt and index status with it. Know that a standard topic does not keep order. Consumers guard each transition (9.09), or the topic is FIFO with the payout id as the message group, the key within which FIFO keeps order (10.10).
  6. Put the event id, type and version in message attributes, so consumers and filter policies, the rules on an SNS subscription that choose what it receives, can read them without parsing the body (10.13). A numeric filter on the version needs a Number attribute.
  7. In a separate job, delete published events after 7 days and mark events with 10 attempts FAILED.
  8. Measure the age of the oldest PENDING event. It is the relay's health in one number, like the oldest message on a queue (14.08).
@Scheduled(fixedDelayString = "${payouts.outbox.poll-delay:PT1S}")
void relayBatch() {
    for (int i = 0; i < 100; i++) {
        Instant now = clock.instant();
        OutboxEvent event = mongo.findAndModify(
                query(where("status").is(PENDING).and("leaseUntil").lte(now)).with(Sort.by("occurredAt")),
                new Update().set("leaseUntil", now.plusSeconds(30)).inc("attempts", 1),
                OutboxEvent.class);
        if (event == null) return;                  // nothing due
        publisher.publish(event);                   // throws on failure: the lease runs out, retried
        mongo.updateFirst(query(where("_id").is(event.id())),
                new Update().set("status", PUBLISHED).set("publishedAt", clock.instant()),
                OutboxEvent.class);
    }
}

@Scheduled needs @EnableScheduling on a configuration class. Every pod runs the relay, and the leases keep them apart. The publisher is PayoutEventPublisher, here with the plain AWS SDK v2. Its sns field is the one SnsClient bean of 10.03, built with the timeouts of step 3, and properties is the @ConfigurationProperties record that holds payouts.*:

public void publish(OutboxEvent event) {
    sns.publish(PublishRequest.builder()
            .topicArn(properties.payoutEventsTopicArn())
            .message(event.payload())
            .messageAttributes(Map.of(
                    "eventId", attribute("String", event.id()),
                    "eventType", attribute("String", event.type()),
                    "eventVersion", attribute("Number", String.valueOf(event.schemaVersion()))))
            .build());
}

private static MessageAttributeValue attribute(String type, String value) {
    return MessageAttributeValue.builder().dataType(type).stringValue(value).build();
}

Also seen. A relay that follows the outbox with a change stream instead of polling it (8.22). It is faster, needs streams enabled on the collection, and must keep its resume token. SnsTemplate from Spring Cloud AWS as the publisher (10.02).

When to break it. An internal tool that will only ever run as 1 pod can drop the lease and update by id. The cost arrives the day someone scales it to 2. A poll delay longer than 1 second is fine where nobody waits on the event.

.NET anchor. MassTransit's outbox delivery service is a hosted BackgroundService that polls with a lock in the same way. @Scheduled plays the part of a BackgroundService with a PeriodicTimer.

See also. 3.10, 7.03, 8.22, 9.07, 9.09, 10.02, 10.03, 10.07, 10.10, 10.13, 14.08, Caching, scheduling and events

9.09 Design operations to be idempotent

Then.

  • J2EE era: exactly-once processing by XA. A message-driven bean took a JMS message and wrote the database in one XA transaction. After a crash the message was back on the queue and the database unchanged, so handlers did not need to be idempotent. It was right while the broker and the database both took part in XA. Neither SQS nor DocumentDB does.
@MessageDriven(activationConfig = @ActivationConfigProperty(
        propertyName = "destination", propertyValue = "jms/LedgerConfirm"))
@TransactionAttribute(TransactionAttributeType.REQUIRED)
public class LedgerConfirmBean implements MessageListener {
    public void onMessage(Message m) { payoutDao.addReserved(payoutIdOf(m), amountOf(m)); }
}

Recognise it by. javax.jms.MessageListener, @MessageDriven, Session.SESSION_TRANSACTED, XAConnectionFactory, and handlers that add to a total.

The rookie version.

@SqsListener("payouts-ledger-events")
void on(LedgerReserved event) {
    mongo.updateFirst(query(where("_id").is(event.payoutId())),
            new Update().set("status", PayoutStatus.RESERVED).inc("reservedMinor", event.amountMinor()),
            Payout.class);
    notifications.send(event.payoutId(), "Your payout is being processed");
}

What goes wrong. @SqsListener is Spring Cloud AWS's annotation for a method that consumes an SQS queue. This one reads the ledger's LedgerReserved from payouts-ledger-events, as the choreographed saga does (11.03). AWS states that standard queues deliver at least once, and more than one copy of a message may arrive. The visibility timeout is how long SQS hides a received message before offering it again. A slow database made one handler outlast it, and SQS delivered the message again. The payout's reserved amount became £2,481.00 for a reservation of £1,240.50, and the claimant got 2 emails. Messages may also arrive out of order. A late duplicate of LedgerReserved arrived after BankInstructed and moved the status backwards.

Do this now. An operation is idempotent when doing it twice has the same effect as doing it once. Design for it in this order:

  1. Set, do not add. Write the reserved amount from the event with $set. A repeat writes the same value.
  2. Guard each transition. Put the expected current status in the filter. A repeat, or a late message, matches nothing.
  3. Identify every operation with a stable id created once: an idempotency key for a request, an event id for a message. Never create it inside a retry.
  4. Record what you applied, when steps 1 and 2 are not enough. Write the id in the same atomic write as the effect: a bounded list on the document, or a key store in the same transaction (9.10).
  5. Carry idempotency to the next system. Send the bank your key (7.07). Route side effects such as emails through the outbox, so they carry the event id.
  6. Treat "already done" as success. Return normally, so the message is deleted and not retried.
@SqsListener("payouts-ledger-events")
void on(LedgerReserved event) {
    UpdateResult r = mongo.updateFirst(
            query(where("_id").is(event.payoutId()).and("status").is(PayoutStatus.PENDING)),
            new Update().set("status", PayoutStatus.RESERVED)
                    .set("ledgerReservationId", event.reservationId())
                    .set("reservedMinor", event.amountMinor())
                    .inc("version", 1),
            Payout.class);
    if (r.getModifiedCount() == 0) {
        log.info("LedgerReserved {} already applied or out of order", event.eventId());
    }
}

The version moves because this write bypasses save (8.05). The notification is an outbox event written by the saga, keyed by this event id.

Also seen. An inbox: a processed_messages collection keyed by message id, checked and written with the effect (10.07). A PUT to a client-chosen id, which HTTP already defines as idempotent (5.05).

When to break it. Duplicates are harmless for reads, cache refreshes and metrics, and there idempotency costs more than it saves. Never accept duplicates for anything that moves money or contacts a person.

.NET anchor. Azure Service Bus and SQS are both at-least-once. Service Bus duplicate detection, like SQS FIFO deduplication (10.11), stops a repeated send within a window. Neither makes the handler idempotent. The visibility timeout plays the part of Service Bus's lock duration, and in both a redelivery after a slow handler is still yours to absorb.

See also. 5.05, 7.07, 8.05, 9.05, 9.10, 10.06, 10.07, 10.11, 11.07, The Yard, chapter 11

9.10 Store and check idempotency keys

Then.

  • Boot era: a cache of seen keys. In memory it was a ConcurrentHashMap, which forgot everything on restart and knew nothing of the other pod. In Redis it was setIfAbsent with an expiry, which was shared and fast, but not atomic with the business write. It was right for one instance, or for work where a lost key was harmless.
public PayoutResponse create(String key, CreatePayoutRequest body) {
    if (!redis.opsForValue().setIfAbsent("idem:" + key, "1", Duration.ofHours(24))) {
        throw new DuplicateRequestException(key);
    }
    return PayoutResponse.from(payoutService.request(body.toCommand()));
}

Recognise it by. A ConcurrentHashMap named seen or processed, setIfAbsent, SETNX, @Cacheable used to remember requests, and a 409 for every repeat.

The rookie version.

public ResponseEntity<PayoutResponse> execute(String key, Supplier<ResponseEntity<PayoutResponse>> work) {
    if (keys.existsById(key)) {
        return ResponseEntity.status(HttpStatus.CONFLICT).build();
    }
    ResponseEntity<PayoutResponse> response = work.get();
    keys.save(new IdempotencyKey(key, clock.instant()));
    return response;
}

What goes wrong. The claims portal timed out at 2 seconds and retried at 2.1, while the first request was still running. Both passed existsById. The payout's unique index (8.16) refused the second payout, and the portal got a 500 and retried again. A retry after success got a 409, which the portal showed as "payment failed". The claimant was in fact paid £1,240.50, and phoned to ask why it had failed. And a test harness that sent the key "1" collided with a real caller that used the same key.

Do this now. The HTTP contract is in 5.05. This is the store behind it.

  1. Scope the key. The document id is the caller's identity from the token, then the header value: portal:7f3a.... The _id index is always unique, so no extra index is needed.
  2. Fingerprint the request. Store a SHA-256 hash of the canonical body: serialise the request record with the service's ObjectMapper, so field order is fixed, and hash the bytes with MessageDigest.getInstance("SHA-256"). The same key with a different body is a client bug, and gets a 422.
  3. Claim before working. Insert an IN_PROGRESS record first, outside any transaction, so a concurrent request sees it at once. Exactly one insert wins.
  4. Let the loser read the record. COMPLETED with the same hash replays the stored status and body. IN_PROGRESS gets a 409 with Retry-After: 1. A different hash gets a 422.
  5. Do the work, then complete the record with the response. If the pod dies in between, the record stays IN_PROGRESS until its lease ends. A later retry then takes it over with a conditional update on lockedUntil and runs the work again. That is safe because the payout carries the key under a unique index, and creating it returns the existing payout on a duplicate (8.16). The layers do different jobs. The key store replays the response, and the unique index protects the money.
  6. If the work throws, delete the IN_PROGRESS record, so the client's retry can run. Put the lockedUntil you set in the delete's filter, so a slow request never deletes a record that another one has taken over.
  7. Expire keys after 24 hours with a TTL index, which deletes documents once a date field is old enough, and check the age in code, because TTL deletion is best effort (8.17).
  8. Store only what a replay needs: status, Location and body. Never a token.
@Document("idempotency_keys")
public record IdempotencyKey(
        @Id String id,              // caller + ":" + Idempotency-Key header
        String requestHash,         // SHA-256 of the canonical request body
        State state,
        Instant lockedUntil,        // lease while IN_PROGRESS
        Integer responseStatus,
        String responseBody,        // JSON to replay
        Instant createdAt) {
    public enum State { IN_PROGRESS, COMPLETED }
}

public ResponseEntity<PayoutResponse> execute(String caller, String key, Object request,
        Supplier<ResponseEntity<PayoutResponse>> work) {
    String id = caller + ":" + key, hash = fingerprint(request);
    Instant now = clock.instant(), lease = now.plus(LEASE);
    try {
        mongo.insert(IdempotencyKey.started(id, hash, now, lease));        // the claim
    } catch (DuplicateKeyException taken) {
        IdempotencyKey found = mongo.findById(id, IdempotencyKey.class);
        if (!takeOverExpired(found, hash, now, lease)) return replayOrRefuse(found, hash, now);
    }
    ResponseEntity<PayoutResponse> response = work.get();   // safe to repeat (8.16)
    mongo.updateFirst(query(where("_id").is(id).and("lockedUntil").is(lease)),   // still ours
            completedWith(response), IdempotencyKey.class);
    return response;
}

LEASE is a constant longer than the slowest request. takeOverExpired is the conditional update of step 5: it sets the new lease only where the state is IN_PROGRESS, the hash matches and lockedUntil has passed, and says whether it matched. Both helpers handle a null, when the key expired between the insert and the read. The delete of step 6 is left out for space.

Also seen. The key on the payout alone, with its unique index (8.16), where no response needs replaying. A consumer's inbox, the same pattern keyed by message id (10.07).

When to break it. An operation with a natural key, such as one payout per claim instalment, needs no separate store. The store costs a write per request and a collection to watch.

.NET anchor. ASP.NET Core has no built-in support, and many samples check IDistributedCache.GetAsync and then SetAsync. That is the same check-then-act race as the rookie version. The fix is the same too: an insert that only one request can win.

See also. 5.05, 8.16, 8.17, 9.09, 10.07, 15.01, The Yard, chapter 8, Document data: Amazon DocumentDB and the MongoDB API

9.11 Retry after an optimistic-locking failure

What goes wrong. The retry loop from 8.05 was moved inside a @Transactional method. On a conflict it read the payout again. But a transaction on DocumentDB reads from a snapshot, so the second read returned the same stale version. All 3 attempts failed identically, and the ledger's confirmation of £1,240.50 went to the dead-letter queue.

Do this now. Retry the whole unit from outside the transaction. Each attempt then gets a fresh transaction, reads fresh data and makes the decision again. Put the retry on the calling bean, never inside the transactional method. Two retries with a short, jittered delay is plenty for 2 pods. In Boot 4, use Framework 7's @Retryable, enabled by @EnableResilientMethods on a configuration class. Its maxRetries does not count the first call, so 2 means the 3 attempts of 8.05. Its delay defaults to 1 second, so set a shorter delay and add a jitter, both in milliseconds. On Boot 3.5, write the loop of 8.05 or use Resilience4j's retry. Spring Retry is archived. In a listener, rethrowing is also a retry: SQS delivers the message again after its visibility timeout.

// CancelPayout calls PayoutTransitions, whose cancel method is @Transactional
@Retryable(includes = OptimisticLockingFailureException.class, maxRetries = 2, delay = 50, jitter = 25)
public Payout cancel(String payoutId) {
    return transitions.cancel(payoutId);
}

See also. 7.04, 8.05, 9.02, 9.04, 10.06

9.12 Choose strong or eventual consistency for each use case

Then.

  • J2EE era: one relational database for everything, so every read was strong without anyone choosing it. It was right while one database held all the data.
  • Boot era: eventual consistency by default, from the NoSQL years, with reads from replicas and caches everywhere. It was right for catalogues and feeds, and wrong for money.
spring.data.mongodb.uri=mongodb://payouts@docdb:27017/payouts?readPreference=secondaryPreferred
spring.cache.type=redis
spring.cache.redis.time-to-live=600000

Recognise it by. readPreference=secondaryPreferred on the main connection, ReadPreference.nearest(), @Cacheable on a method whose answer decides a payment, and local copies of another team's data used in an if.

The rookie version.

public Payout requestInstalment(PayoutCommand cmd) {
    ClaimView claim = claimViews.findById(cmd.claimId()).orElseThrow();   // fed by SQS events
    if (claim.status() == ClaimStatus.CLOSED) {
        throw new ClaimClosed(cmd.claimId());
    }
    return requests.record(cmd);
}

What goes wrong. ClaimView is a projection, a local copy of the policy system's claims, updated from its events. The fraud team closed claim C-4471 at 10:02:11. The ClaimClosed event sat behind a backlog in the queue for 4 minutes. At 10:04 Payouts read the copy, saw the claim open, and paid £1,240.50. The copy was not wrong. It was used for a decision it could not support.

Do this now. Strong consistency means a read sees every write that finished before it. Eventual means it will, given time.

  1. List the reads of each use case. For each, ask whether a decision about money, or a refusal, depends on it.
  2. Decide on strong reads. In Payouts that means the primary, which is the default read preference (8.11), or the filter of a conditional write (9.05). Inside a transaction, DocumentDB reads from a snapshot.
  3. Know the ceiling. AWS states that DocumentDB refuses the linearizable read concern, MongoDB's strongest. Writes are always majority and journaled.
  4. For data another service owns, a strong read means asking the owner at decision time, with a timeout (7.03). Better still, let the owner decide: the ledger refuses a reservation on a closed claim.
  5. Display from eventual reads: replicas for reports (8.11), projections for screens, caches for lookups. Show their age with an asOf field.
  6. Write the choice down next to the read, so the next developer keeps it.
Use case Consistency Read from
Idempotency check, saga state, status before a transition strong primary, conditional write
Claim still open before paying strong PolicyClient at decision time
Claimant's payout status page eventual, seconds primary or replica
Monthly finance report eventual, minutes replica template (8.11)

Also seen. A cache invalidated by events. It narrows the lag and never removes it. CQRS, with a separate read model for every screen, which makes every read eventual on purpose.

When to break it. If the owner is down and the projection is fresh, for example a measured lag under 5 seconds, the business may accept a decision on it for small amounts. The cost is a few payments made on stale data. Record that the decision used the copy (7.11).

.NET anchor. SQL Server's readable secondaries with ApplicationIntent=ReadOnly are the same trade, and a CQRS read model in .NET is a projection like ClaimView. The rule is the same: decide on the source of truth, display from the copy.

See also. 7.03, 7.11, 8.11, 9.05, 9.13, 10.01, The Yard, chapter 11, Document data: Amazon DocumentDB and the MongoDB API

9.13 Read your own writes after an asynchronous step

What goes wrong. The portal sent POST /payouts, got 202, and polled GET /payouts/p-81. The payout was on the primary, but the status page read a replica that had not caught up, and answered 404 for up to 9 seconds. Claimants pressed "pay" again, and support took 30 calls in a morning.

Do this now. Return what you wrote. The 202 carries the status and a Location (5.06). Serve a resource that the caller has just changed from the primary. Give each response the payout's version, as the ETag of 5.11, and let the client send back the version it last saw. The server reads the replica first, and reads the primary instead when the replica has no copy or an older version. Do not plan on the driver's causally consistent sessions. On MongoDB they order reads after writes made in the same session, not after a listener's write in another process. And AWS states that DocumentDB does not support causal consistency and rejects it with error 303. Show "processing" honestly while the saga runs.

See also. 5.06, 5.11, 8.11, 9.04, 9.12

9.14 Recognise distributed XA transactions in old code and replace them

Then.

  • J2EE era: JTA, Java's standard transaction API, in the application server. WebLogic, WebSphere or JBoss coordinated one transaction across an XADataSource and a JMS XAConnectionFactory, by two-phase commit: every resource first promises it can commit, then all commit. It was right when every resource spoke XA and the server lived on a fixed machine with a durable disk.
  • Spring era: a standalone JTA manager such as Atomikos or Bitronix, embedded in the application and wired into Spring's JtaTransactionManager. It gave XA without the application server.
<bean id="atomikosTm" class="com.atomikos.icatch.jta.UserTransactionManager"
      init-method="init" destroy-method="close"/>
<bean id="transactionManager" class="org.springframework.transaction.jta.JtaTransactionManager">
    <property name="transactionManager" ref="atomikosTm"/>
</bean>
  • Boot era: spring-boot-starter-jta-atomikos and spring.jta.* properties, and Spring Data's ChainedTransactionManager. Boot 3.0 removed its Atomikos support, and Spring Data Commons deprecated the chained manager in 2.5.

Recognise it by. javax.transaction.UserTransaction, JtaTransactionManager, XADataSource, XAConnectionFactory, com.atomikos or bitronix.tm imports, spring.jta.* keys, ChainedTransactionManager, and a tmlog or transaction-logs directory on a volume.

The rookie version.

@Bean
PlatformTransactionManager transactionManager(MongoTransactionManager mongo,
                                              JmsTransactionManager jms) {
    return new ChainedTransactionManager(jms, mongo);   // "atomic" across both
}

What goes wrong. The old payouts-batch ran Oracle and ActiveMQ under Atomikos. In the move to DocumentDB, a developer found that neither DocumentDB nor SQS takes part in XA, and reached for the chained manager. It looks atomic and is not. It commits one resource and then the other, and nothing undoes the first if the second fails. In a rehearsal, stopping the pod during commit 50 times gave 2 confirmations applied twice. The old system had its own scar. After a crash, Atomikos kept the state of in-doubt transactions in its log on local disk. On Kubernetes that disk vanishes with the pod.

Do this now.

  1. List every XA or chained transaction, the resources it spans, and the rule that needs them to agree.
  2. Replace each pair by its pattern (table).
  3. Migrate one flow at a time. Run the new path beside the old and compare counts in a reconciliation report.
  4. Test the crash paths. Stop the pod between every pair of steps and check that nothing is lost and nothing applied twice.
  5. Remove the JTA manager last, with its log directory and its spring.jta.* properties.
XA pair in old code Replace with
database write and outgoing message transactional outbox and relay (9.07, 9.08)
incoming message and database write idempotent consumer (9.09, 10.07)
two databases in one service one document (9.05), or one DocumentDB transaction (9.04)
two services saga with compensation (11.02, 11.05)

Also seen. XA kept where everything still speaks it, such as IBM MQ and Db2 on an application server, often with Narayana as the transaction manager.

When to break it. Keep XA for a legacy pair that both support it, on hosts with durable disks, at low volume, with a team able to resolve an in-doubt transaction by hand. The cost is locks held across the prepare phase, a coordinator log to protect, and outcomes that sometimes need a person.

.NET anchor. TransactionScope promoted to a distributed transaction under MSDTC, across SQL Server and MSMQ, is the same design. The replacement path is the same as well: MassTransit's or NServiceBus's outbox and idempotent handlers.

See also. 7.16, 9.04, 9.05, 9.06, 9.07, 9.09, 10.07, 11.02, Transactions, propagation and isolation, Appendix C: The Java you'll inherit

⚠Review checklist
  • If you see @Transactional in a Mongo service with no MongoTransactionManager bean: nothing is transactional and no error says so. See 9.01.
  • If you see a transactional method that throws a checked exception or makes an HTTP call: the checked exception commits, and the call holds a transaction open against a one-minute limit. See 9.01.
  • If you see an annotated method called from another method of the same class, or a private or final annotated method: the proxy never sees the call. See 9.02.
  • If you see REQUIRES_NEW on an outbox or state write: it commits even when the caller rolls back. See 9.03.
  • If you see a transaction that streams results, creates a collection, or loops over a whole day's payouts: DocumentDB refuses cursors and new collections inside one, and aborts it after one minute. See 9.04.
  • If you see a MongoTransactionManager with no session customisation for DocumentDB: its sessions ask for causal consistency, which DocumentDB rejects. See 9.04.
  • If you see a check in Java followed by writes to two documents to enforce one rule: two pods both pass the check. See 9.05.
  • If you see an SNS, SQS or HTTP call next to a database write in one method: one of them can happen without the other. See 9.06.
  • If you see an outbox event that holds only an id, or is written outside the state change's transaction: consumers read later state, and a crash loses the event. See 9.07.
  • If you see a relay that marks events published before publishing, or reads every pending event at once: events are lost in a fault, and memory fills after one. See 9.08.
  • If you see $inc, += or an email send in a message handler with no guard: a redelivery applies it twice. See 9.09.
  • If you see existsById on a key followed by the work: two concurrent requests both pass, and a repeat gets a 409 instead of the original answer. See 9.10.
  • If you see a retry loop inside a @Transactional method: every attempt rereads the same snapshot. See 9.11.
  • If you see a decision about money made from a projection, a cache or a replica: it can act on a state that is minutes old. See 9.12.
  • If you see a status page served from a replica straight after the caller's own write: the caller sees its change undone. See 9.13.
  • If you see ChainedTransactionManager, JtaTransactionManager or com.atomikos: the atomicity is best effort or depends on a coordinator log a pod will lose. See 9.14.

Part IV · The how-to10. Messaging with SNS and SQS#

Payouts tells other services what happened through messages, not calls. It publishes events such as PayoutCompleted to an SNS topic, and SNS copies each one into the SQS queues of the services that care. This part shows how to publish and consume those messages, with Spring Cloud AWS and with the plain AWS SDK. It covers duplicates, slow work, poison messages, dead-letter queues, FIFO ordering, filter policies and LocalStack tests. It also shows the JMS listeners and SDK v1 loops you will find in older code.

★What a veteran knows
  • A queue does not remove a failure. It moves it to later and somewhere quieter, so every queue needs an owner, a dead-letter queue and an alarm on the age of its oldest message.
  • Every message arrives at least twice in the end, and some arrive out of order. Write the consumer that is correct on the second delivery, because that is the only correct consumer.
  • The visibility timeout is a promise about your slowest processing, not a tuning knob. Work it out from the timeouts and retries inside the handler.
  • A dead-letter queue nobody watches is where money goes to be forgotten. On Payouts, one message in ledger-confirm-dlq pages the person on call.
  • Check the limits of the whole path, not of one service. SQS takes 1 MiB, but an event that goes through SNS is held to 256 KiB unless the topic is changed.
  • An event is a public API with consumers you have never met. Give it an ID, a type and a version, and never remove a field someone reads.
◷How we got hereOn 3 November 2004 Amazon announced that "The Amazon Simple Queue Service is now available for beta testing".

On 3 November 2004 Amazon announced that "The Amazon Simple Queue Service is now available for beta testing". It offered a "reliable, highly scalable hosted queue for buffering messages" between the parts of a distributed system. Jeff Barr, who wrote the AWS blog, later remembered how people took it: "Huh? Why would Amazon do that?" SQS stayed in beta for 20 months. In July 2006 Barr announced that "SQS is now in production", at 10 cents for every thousand messages sent. Werner Vogels wrote about the idea at its centre the same day. A message that a consumer does not delete before its lease runs out comes back, and that "Makes failure handling very simple." That lease is the visibility timeout in this part. Twenty years later it still decides whether a payout event is handled once, twice or not at all. SNS followed in April 2010. In 2021 Barr wrote that customers "think of SQS as an infinite buffer in the cloud."

10.01 Choose SNS fan-out to SQS over point-to-point queues

Then.

  • J2EE era: a JMS broker such as ActiveMQ or IBM MQ, with queues for one consumer and topics for many. Consumers were message-driven beans that the application server called. It was right when the company ran a broker in its own data centre and every service spoke JMS.
@MessageDriven(activationConfig = {
    @ActivationConfigProperty(propertyName = "destinationType", propertyValue = "javax.jms.Topic"),
    @ActivationConfigProperty(propertyName = "destination", propertyValue = "jms/PayoutEvents")})
public class LedgerConfirmBean implements MessageListener {
    public void onMessage(Message message) { /* ... */ }
}
  • Spring era: the same broker through Spring's JmsTemplate and DefaultMessageListenerContainer, configured in XML. The cloud services replaced the broker that somebody had to patch, size and fail over.

Recognise it by. javax.jms.* imports, @MessageDriven, MessageListener, JmsTemplate, @JmsListener, activemq or com.ibm.mq artifactIds, and JNDI names such as jms/PayoutEvents.

The rookie version.

public void completed(Payout payout) {
    String body = json.write(PayoutCompleted.from(payout));
    sqs.sendMessage(r -> r.queueUrl(ledgerConfirmUrl).messageBody(body));
    sqs.sendMessage(r -> r.queueUrl(notifyClaimantUrl).messageBody(body));
    sqs.sendMessage(r -> r.queueUrl(payoutAuditUrl).messageBody(body));
}

What goes wrong. The three sends are three separate operations, and nothing makes them happen together. The second send times out during a network blip. The ledger is confirmed, the claimant hears nothing, and a retry of the whole method sends the ledger a second copy. Payouts now also knows every consumer by name. When the fraud team wants payout events, Payouts must change code, redeploy, and get permission to write to a queue in another team's account. The publisher has become the place where every consumer's needs meet.

Do this now. SQS (Simple Queue Service) is a managed queue: a producer sends a message, and a consumer receives it, works on it and deletes it. SNS (Simple Notification Service) is a managed topic: a publisher sends one message, and SNS delivers a copy to every subscription. Put them together and you get fan-out.

  1. Publish once, to the payout-events topic. Payouts knows the topic, not the consumers.
  2. Each consumer owns its queue and subscribes it to the topic. Adding the fraud team is their change, not yours.
  3. Give each queue a policy that lets SNS send to it. Without one, SNS cannot deliver.
  4. Turn on raw message delivery on each subscription, so the SQS body is your event. Without it the body is an SNS JSON envelope with your event inside its Message field.
  5. Give each queue a dead-letter queue (10.08). Give each subscription one as well, for messages SNS could not deliver.
  6. Publish from the outbox relay, not from business code, so the event and the database write cannot disagree (9.07, 9.08).
{
  "Effect": "Allow",
  "Principal": { "Service": "sns.amazonaws.com" },
  "Action": "sqs:SendMessage",
  "Resource": "arn:aws:sqs:eu-west-2:111122223333:ledger-confirm",
  "Condition": {
    "ArnEquals": { "aws:SourceArn": "arn:aws:sns:eu-west-2:111122223333:payout-events" }
  }
}

The condition stops any other topic using your queue. SNS retries delivery to SQS for a long time: 100,015 attempts over 23 days. A missing queue policy is different. It is a client-side error, SNS does not retry it, and the message is discarded unless the subscription has a dead-letter queue. Remember also that a standard queue delivers at least once and may deliver out of order (10.07, 10.10).

Also seen. Amazon EventBridge, an event bus with routing rules, when events cross many teams and accounts. Kafka or Kinesis, when consumers must replay history. A plain SQS queue, when there is one consumer by design, such as a work queue that only Payouts reads.

When to break it. A command to one service is not an event. "Generate the remittance file" has exactly one handler, and a direct queue is honest about that. The cost is that a second consumer later means changing the sender.

.NET anchor. Azure Service Bus topics and subscriptions are the closest shape. The difference is ownership. A Service Bus subscription lives inside the topic, while here the queue is a separate resource the consumer owns and configures. MassTransit's Amazon SQS transport builds this same SNS-to-SQS shape for you.

See also. 9.07, 9.08, 10.08, 10.13, 11.03, 21.03, Messaging and WebSockets

10.02 Publish an event to SNS with SnsTemplate

Then.

  • Boot era: Spring Cloud AWS 2.x and its NotificationMessagingTemplate, built on AWS SDK v1. The packages were org.springframework.cloud.aws.messaging, then io.awspring.cloud.messaging from 2.3, when the project left the Spring Cloud release train. It was the Spring way to reach SNS for years. The 2.x line is in maintenance mode and has had no release since February 2023.
@Bean
NotificationMessagingTemplate notifications(AmazonSNS amazonSns) {
    return new NotificationMessagingTemplate(amazonSns);
}

// in the publisher
notifications.sendNotification("payout-events", json, "PayoutCompleted");

Recognise it by. NotificationMessagingTemplate, spring-cloud-aws-messaging or spring-cloud-starter-aws-messaging artifactIds, com.amazonaws.services.sns.AmazonSNS, and properties under cloud.aws.* such as cloud.aws.region.static.

The rookie version.

@Transactional
public void complete(Payout payout) {
    Payout done = repository.save(payout.markCompleted());
    snsTemplate.convertAndSend("payout-events", done);
}

What goes wrong. Three things. First, the payload is the Payout document, serialised whole. The claimant's sort code and account number go to three queues and into the audit store. When the team renames a field in the document, the notification service breaks. Second, nothing says what kind of event this is, so consumers cannot filter (10.13) and have to guess from a status field. Third, the publish happens inside the transaction, before it commits. When the commit fails, three services hear about a payout of £1,240.50 that never completed (9.06).

Do this now. Spring Cloud AWS is the community project that wires AWS services into Spring Boot. Its SnsTemplate is a ready-made bean for publishing to SNS.

  1. Pick the line that matches your Boot version. Spring Cloud AWS 3.4.x is the last line for Boot 3.5 (3.4.2 is its last release). Boot 4 needs 4.x (4.2.0, released on 29 September 2026).
  2. Import its BOM, a bill of materials that fixes the versions of all its modules, and add the SNS starter. A starter is one dependency that pulls in a module, the libraries it needs and its auto-configuration: the code that creates beans such as SnsTemplate for you at startup. The artifactIds above with starter in the name are the same idea in an older line.
<dependencyManagement>
  <dependencies>
    <dependency>
      <groupId>io.awspring.cloud</groupId>
      <artifactId>spring-cloud-aws-dependencies</artifactId>
      <version>3.4.2</version>
      <type>pom</type>
      <scope>import</scope>
    </dependency>
  </dependencies>
</dependencyManagement>
<dependency>                         <!-- in <dependencies> -->
  <groupId>io.awspring.cloud</groupId>
  <artifactId>spring-cloud-aws-starter-sns</artifactId>
</dependency>
  1. Set the region with spring.cloud.aws.region.static. Put the topic ARN, the Amazon Resource Name that identifies the topic, in payouts.events.topic-arn (4.02). Credentials come from the pod's role, never from the file (15.07).
  2. Publish an event record, not the document (10.12). Put the event ID, type and version in headers, as 9.08 does. The template sends headers as SNS message attributes: name-value pairs outside the body that filter policies can read.
@Component
public class PayoutEventPublisher {
    private final SnsTemplate sns;
    private final String topicArn;

    public PayoutEventPublisher(SnsTemplate sns, EventProperties props) {
        this.sns = sns;
        this.topicArn = props.topicArn();
    }

    public void publish(EventEnvelope<?> event) {
        sns.convertAndSend(topicArn, event, Map.of("eventId", event.eventId().toString(),
                "eventType", event.eventType(), "eventVersion", event.eventVersion()));
    }
}
  1. Call it only from OutboxRelay, after the outbox row is committed (9.08).
  2. Look at one real message in a test queue. Count its attributes. The template also sends Spring's own id, timestamp and contentType headers as attributes, so this event carries 6, not 3. Raw delivery to SQS allows at most 10, and SNS discards messages with more.

In Boot 4, with Spring Cloud AWS 4.x, objects are serialised with Jackson 3. Version 4.1 added batch and asynchronous SNS templates.

Also seen. snsTemplate.sendNotification(topic, message, subject) for a plain string with an SNS subject. The plain SnsClient (10.03), which some teams prefer. Spring Cloud AWS is run by its community, not by AWS or the Spring team, and its line is tied to your Boot version, so each Boot upgrade includes it.

When to break it. A library shared by several services should not pull in Spring Cloud AWS. Use the SDK there. The cost is writing the serialisation and attribute mapping yourself.

.NET anchor. The SDK's IAmazonSimpleNotificationService.PublishAsync is the low level. SnsTemplate sits where MassTransit's IPublishEndpoint.Publish<T> does: a framework layer that serialises an object and picks the destination. Unlike MassTransit, it does not create topics or queues for you.

See also. 10.03, 10.12, 9.06, 9.08, 4.02, 15.07, The Yard, chapter 3, Messaging and WebSockets

10.03 Publish an event with the plain AWS SDK v2

Then.

  • Boot era: AWS SDK for Java v1, with clients built by AmazonSNSClientBuilder and requests filled in with withXxx methods. It went into maintenance in July 2024 and reached end of support on 31 December 2025. It gets no more updates, including security fixes.
AmazonSNS sns = AmazonSNSClientBuilder.standard()
        .withRegion(Regions.EU_WEST_2).build();
MessageAttributeValue type = new MessageAttributeValue()
        .withDataType("String").withStringValue("PayoutCompleted");
PublishResult result = sns.publish(new PublishRequest(topicArn, json)
        .withMessageAttributes(Map.of("eventType", type)));

Recognise it by. com.amazonaws.services.sns.* imports, the aws-java-sdk-sns and aws-java-sdk-bom artifactIds, AmazonSNSClientBuilder, PublishResult, and setter chains named withXxx.

The rookie version.

public void publish(OutboxEvent event) {
    try (SnsClient sns = SnsClient.create()) {
        sns.publish(PublishRequest.builder()
                .topicArn(topicArn)
                .message(event.payload())
                .build());
    }
}

What goes wrong. Each call builds a new client. It resolves the region and credentials again, creates a new HTTP connection pool, and opens a new TLS connection to SNS. At the month-end peak the relay publishes about 20 events a second on each of 2 pods, so that is 40 new clients and 40 TLS handshakes a second. Publishing latency triples, and the credentials lookup adds its own calls. The message also has no attributes, so no consumer can filter it, and the returned message ID is thrown away.

Do this now. AWS SDK for Java v2 is AWS's own Java library, in packages software.amazon.awssdk.*. Each service has a client, and each call takes an immutable request built with a builder.

  1. Import software.amazon.awssdk:bom and add the sns artifact. Version 2.57.3 was current on 22 October 2026, and new versions appear most weeks.
  2. Build one SnsClient as a bean. Clients are safe to share between threads. Spring calls close() on the bean at shutdown.
  3. Set the region and the HTTP client's timeouts on the builder. Credentials come from the default chain, which finds the pod's role (15.07).
  4. Send the event type and version as message attributes, for filter policies (10.13).
  5. Keep the messageId() from the response with the outbox row. It ties a log line to an SNS delivery.
  6. Let exceptions propagate to the relay. The SDK already retries some failures with backoff. The relay leaves the row unpublished and tries again on its next pass (9.08).
@Bean
SnsClient snsClient() {
    return SnsClient.builder()
            .region(Region.EU_WEST_2)
            .httpClientBuilder(ApacheHttpClient.builder()
                    .connectionTimeout(Duration.ofSeconds(1))
                    .socketTimeout(Duration.ofSeconds(5)))
            .build();
}

public String publish(OutboxEvent event) {
    PublishResponse response = sns.publish(r -> r
            .topicArn(topicArn)
            .message(event.payload())
            .messageAttributes(Map.of(
                    "eventType", stringAttribute(event.eventType()),
                    "eventVersion", numberAttribute(event.eventVersion()))));
    return response.messageId();
}

private static MessageAttributeValue stringAttribute(String value) {
    return MessageAttributeValue.builder().dataType("String").stringValue(value).build();
}

numberAttribute is the same with dataType("Number"). To send several events in one call, use publishBatch, with at most 10 entries. Read the response's failed() list, because a batch can partly succeed.

Also seen. SnsTemplate (10.02), which is less code in a Boot service. SnsAsyncClient, which returns a CompletableFuture. With virtual threads the blocking client is usually enough (3.01).

When to break it. A one-off script may call SnsClient.create() and close it at the end. In a service, a client per call is never right.

.NET anchor. AmazonSimpleNotificationServiceClient, registered once with AddAWSService<IAmazonSimpleNotificationService>(). The .NET SDK is asynchronous first, with PublishAsync. The Java SDK v2 has separate blocking and asynchronous clients, and the blocking one is the usual choice.

See also. 10.02, 10.13, 9.08, 3.01, 7.03, 15.07, Messaging and WebSockets

10.04 Consume from SQS with @SqsListener

Then.

  • Boot era: Spring Cloud AWS 2.x, with its own @SqsListener in org.springframework.cloud.aws.messaging.listener.annotation, later io.awspring.cloud.messaging. A deletionPolicy said when to delete. @NotificationMessage unwrapped the SNS envelope. It ran on SDK v1.
@SqsListener(value = "ledger-confirm", deletionPolicy = SqsMessageDeletionPolicy.ON_SUCCESS)
public void onEvent(@NotificationMessage PayoutCompleted event) {
    ledger.confirm(event.payoutId());
}
  • Boot era: JMS on SQS, through amazon-sqs-java-messaging-lib and Spring's @JmsListener. It let JMS code move to SQS unchanged. The library now runs on SDK v2 and Jakarta JMS, with its last release, 2.1.4, in December 2024.

Recognise it by. SqsMessageDeletionPolicy, @NotificationMessage, @EnableSqs, SimpleMessageListenerContainerFactory, SQSConnectionFactory, and the spring-cloud-aws-messaging artifactId. The current annotation is io.awspring.cloud.sqs.annotation.SqsListener.

The rookie version.

@SqsListener("ledger-confirm")
public void onEvent(PayoutCompleted event) {
    try {
        ledger.confirm(event.payoutId(), event.amount());
    } catch (Exception e) {
        log.error("ledger confirm failed for {}", event.payoutId(), e);
    }
}

What goes wrong. The method always returns normally, so the listener reports success and the message is deleted. The ledger was down for 6 minutes, and 312 confirmations were logged and gone. The dead-letter queue stayed empty, so there was nothing to redrive. The Spring Cloud AWS documentation is plain about it: with the default mode, "it is important to propagate the error."

Do this now. @SqsListener marks a method that Spring Cloud AWS calls for each message on a queue. A listener container behind it polls the queue, converts each body from JSON into your parameter type, and deletes the message when the method returns.

  1. Add spring-cloud-aws-starter-sqs, from the same BOM as 10.02.
  2. Write one listener class per queue, with the queue name on the annotation.
  3. Let exceptions out. The default acknowledgement mode, ON_SUCCESS, deletes the message only when the method returns normally. A failed message stays and is received again after its visibility timeout (10.06).
  4. Make the handler safe to run twice (10.07). Acknowledgements are sent in batches: by default every second, or every 10 messages, on a standard queue. A message stays in flight until its batch is acknowledged, so a crash in that second means a redelivery.
  5. Turn on raw message delivery on the subscription (10.01). Otherwise the body is the SNS envelope, and conversion into your record fails.
  6. Set the concurrency deliberately. By default the container handles up to 10 messages at once from each queue, fetches up to 10 per poll, and waits up to 10 seconds per poll (10.16). maxMessagesPerPoll may not be larger than maxConcurrentMessages, so lower both together, or the container fails at startup.
@Component
public class LedgerConfirmListener {
    private final LedgerClient ledger;

    public LedgerConfirmListener(LedgerClient ledger) {
        this.ledger = ledger;
    }

    @SqsListener(value = "ledger-confirm", maxConcurrentMessages = "5", maxMessagesPerPoll = "5")
    public void onEvent(EventEnvelope<PayoutCompletedData> event) {
        ledger.confirm(event.eventId(), event.payoutId(), event.data().amount());
    }
}

The numbers are written as strings, "5", because the annotation's attributes accept property placeholders. maxConcurrentMessages = "${payouts.ledger.max-concurrent}" reads the value from configuration, so each environment can set its own. A Java annotation attribute has one fixed type, and only a String can hold both a number and a placeholder.

The listener stays thin: it converts the message and makes one call, with the event ID as the ledger's idempotency key. Entry 10.07 adds the key store that makes a second delivery harmless. In Boot 4, with Spring Cloud AWS 4.x, conversion uses Jackson 3, and from 4.1 the container can run listeners on virtual threads.

Also seen. A loop over the plain SDK (10.05), when you need control the container does not give. SqsTemplate.receive for an occasional pull. AWS Lambda with an SQS trigger, for consumers that are not services. Spring Integration AWS, which is now part of Spring Cloud AWS 4.

When to break it. Some failures will never succeed: a body that fails validation, or an unknown payout. Do not throw those 5 times. Park them with the reason and return normally (6.11, 10.17). The cost is a parking queue someone must watch.

.NET anchor. Azure Service Bus's ServiceBusProcessor with AutoCompleteMessages = true behaves the same way. An exception from ProcessMessageAsync abandons the message, and a normal return completes it. Swallowing the exception there loses messages in exactly the same way.

See also. 10.05, 10.07, 10.15, 10.16, 6.11, 16.11, 17.05, The Yard, chapter 14, Messaging and WebSockets

10.05 Consume with the plain AWS SDK v2: long polling and batches

Then.

  • Boot era: the same loop on SDK v1, with AmazonSQS and getMessages(). It was how every non-Spring consumer worked, and many Spring ones too. SDK v1 has been out of support since 31 December 2025.
AmazonSQS sqs = AmazonSQSClientBuilder.defaultClient();
ReceiveMessageRequest request = new ReceiveMessageRequest(queueUrl)
        .withMaxNumberOfMessages(10).withWaitTimeSeconds(20);
for (Message m : sqs.receiveMessage(request).getMessages()) {
    handle(m);
    sqs.deleteMessage(queueUrl, m.getReceiptHandle());
}

Recognise it by. com.amazonaws.services.sqs.AmazonSQS, AmazonSQSClientBuilder, the aws-java-sdk-sqs artifactId, getReceiptHandle(), and AmazonSQSBufferedAsyncClient.

The rookie version.

while (true) {
    List<Message> messages = sqs.receiveMessage(r -> r.queueUrl(queueUrl)).messages();
    for (Message m : messages) {
        sqs.deleteMessage(r -> r.queueUrl(queueUrl).receiptHandle(m.receiptHandle()));
        handle(m);
    }
}

What goes wrong. This asks for one message at a time, the default, and uses short polling, also the default. A short poll asks only a sample of SQS's servers and returns at once, often empty. With fewer than 1,000 messages waiting you usually get fewer than you asked for. On a quiet night the loop spins, and each pod sends about a hundred empty requests a second, each on the bill. It also deletes before handling. When a pod is killed mid-batch during a deploy, those messages are gone.

Do this now. A receive gives you messages and a receipt handle for each. The handle, not the message ID, is what you need to delete it or change its visibility.

  1. Build one SqsClient bean, as in 10.03. Look up the queue URL once at startup with getQueueUrl.
  2. Use long polling: waitTimeSeconds(20), the maximum. SQS holds the request until a message arrives or the time is up. Set the HTTP client's socket timeout longer than the wait, or every empty poll ends in a timeout.
  3. Ask for maxNumberOfMessages(10), the most one receive returns.
  4. Ask for the ApproximateReceiveCount attribute, so you can log how often a message has failed.
  5. Handle each message on its own. Catch its failure, so one bad message cannot stop the loop, and record each success as you go.
  6. Delete the recorded successes together with deleteMessageBatch, in a finally block. Then the successes are deleted even if something escapes the catch. Check the response's failed() list.
  7. Leave failures alone. They come back after the visibility timeout (10.06).
void pollOnce() {
    List<Message> messages = sqs.receiveMessage(r -> r
            .queueUrl(queueUrl).maxNumberOfMessages(10).waitTimeSeconds(20)
            .messageSystemAttributeNames(MessageSystemAttributeName.APPROXIMATE_RECEIVE_COUNT))
            .messages();
    List<DeleteMessageBatchRequestEntry> done = new ArrayList<>();
    try {
        for (Message m : messages) {
            if (handledSafely(m)) done.add(DeleteMessageBatchRequestEntry.builder()
                    .id(m.messageId()).receiptHandle(m.receiptHandle()).build());
        }
    } finally {
        if (!done.isEmpty()) sqs.deleteMessageBatch(r -> r.queueUrl(queueUrl).entries(done));
    }
}

private boolean handledSafely(Message m) {
    try {
        handler.handle(m);
        return true;
    } catch (RuntimeException e) {
        log.warn("message {} failed on receive {}; it will come back", m.messageId(),
                m.attributes().get(MessageSystemAttributeName.APPROXIMATE_RECEIVE_COUNT), e);
        return false;
    }
}

If the fourth of 10 messages fails, the other 9 are deleted, and only the fourth returns.

  1. Run the loop on a thread you own and stop it cleanly. Implement SmartLifecycle, so Spring starts the loop after the context is ready and stops it before shutdown (17.05).
  2. To handle the 10 messages in parallel, submit them to a virtual-thread executor and bound it with a semaphore (3.01, 3.09). Delete only after each one finishes.

Also seen. @SqsListener (10.04), which writes this loop, the acknowledgement batching and the shutdown for you. The two are the split in this part. The container is less code and less to get wrong. The loop is AWS's own library, with nothing between you and the API, and it suits a library or a batch job. SqsAsyncClient, in reactive code.

When to break it. A nightly job that drains a queue and exits may use a short poll to see that the queue is empty. The cost is that a short poll can come back empty while messages remain, so poll a few times before you stop.

.NET anchor. IAmazonSQS.ReceiveMessageAsync with WaitTimeSeconds = 20, inside a BackgroundService.ExecuteAsync loop. SmartLifecycle plays the part of IHostedService: it starts after the application and stops before it.

See also. 10.03, 10.04, 10.06, 3.01, 3.09, 17.05, Messaging and WebSockets

10.06 Set the visibility timeout to fit the work

The rookie version.

ledger-confirm queue, created from the shared template:
  VisibilityTimeout       30          (seconds, the SQS default)

LedgerConfirmListener, per message:
  ledger call             connect 1 s, read 2 s
  retries                 4 attempts, backoff 1 s, 2 s, 4 s
  worst case              4 x 3 s + 7 s = 19 s, plus the bank status check

What goes wrong. When a consumer receives a message, SQS hides it from other consumers for the visibility timeout. If the message is not deleted in that time, it becomes visible and is delivered again. That is the lease from the history at the top of this part. Here the handler's worst case is close to the timeout. On a slow day the bank status check, which has no timeout, takes 15 seconds. The total passes 30, so pod 2 receives the same message while pod 1 is still working on it. The ledger is asked to confirm £1,240.50 twice. The opposite mistake hurts too. A team sets 12 hours, the maximum, "so it never comes back twice". When a pod is killed holding 10 messages, those 10 claimants wait 12 hours for their notification.

Do this now.

  1. Choose one retry layer (7.04). The rookie handler retries 4 times, and SQS delivers the message up to maxReceiveCount times, 5 on ledger-confirm (10.08). That is 4 × 5 = 20 ledger calls for one message. On Payouts the layer is SQS: remove the handler's retries, make one attempt, and throw on failure.
  2. Work out the worst case for one message from its timeouts (7.03). Do not measure the average. Give the bank check a 10-second timeout. The ledger call is then 1 + 2 = 3 seconds and the bank check 10, so 13 seconds.
  3. Add what happens around the handler. Spring Cloud AWS acknowledges in batches, by default once a second on a standard queue, and the message stays in flight until then (10.04). That makes 14 seconds.
  4. Set the timeout to at least twice that total, 28 seconds. Payouts uses 60. With SQS as the only retry layer, the visibility timeout is also the wait between attempts, so 5 receives 60 seconds apart give a ledger blip about 5 minutes to clear.
  5. Set it on the queue, as the VisibilityTimeout attribute, in the queue's infrastructure code. It accepts 0 to 43,200 seconds, which is 12 hours. Spring Cloud AWS can also set it per receive, and by default it leaves the queue's value alone.
  6. Put a deadline on the work itself, so it cannot outlive the lease (7.15).
  7. For a message that is occasionally slow, extend its lease while you work. ChangeMessageVisibility sets a new timeout counted from the moment of the call.
sqs.changeMessageVisibility(r -> r
        .queueUrl(queueUrl)
        .receiptHandle(message.receiptHandle())
        .visibilityTimeout(120));     // 120 s from now, not from the receive

The new value applies to this receive only. If the message comes back, it gets the queue's timeout again. SQS refuses a value beyond the maximum time the message has left. In a Spring Cloud AWS listener, a Visibility parameter gives the method the same control.

  1. On a FIFO queue, one poll can bring several messages from one group, and the container handles them in order. The later ones wait, with their visibility clocks running.
