If you set a message visibility for the listener, the container's messageVisibility option, the container extends the visibility of all the group's waiting messages before it starts each one. So a message does not reappear while it waits its turn (10.10).
  2. Watch the handler's p99 duration (14.06). When it creeps towards the timeout, change one or the other before production does it for you.

Also seen. A heartbeat for long jobs: a scheduled task that extends the lease every 60 seconds until the work is done. Taking the long work off the queue altogether: record it in DocumentDB, acknowledge the message, and process the record separately with its own status (5.06).

When to break it. Setting the visibility to 0 makes a message visible again at once. That is right at shutdown, to hand back messages you have not started. It is wrong as a fast retry: each immediate receive counts towards maxReceiveCount, so a short blip can dead-letter the message in seconds.

.NET anchor. Azure Service Bus peek-lock, with LockDuration on the queue and RenewMessageLockAsync to extend it. ServiceBusProcessor renews locks for you up to MaxAutoLockRenewalDuration. The SQS SDK does not renew anything, so extending is your code.

See also. 7.03, 7.04, 7.15, 10.04, 10.07, 10.08, 14.06, The Yard, chapter 11, Messaging and WebSockets

10.07 Consume an SQS message safely when it may arrive twice

Then.

  • J2EE era: an XA transaction, coordinated by the application server, that covered both the JMS broker and the database. Receiving the message and writing the result committed together or not at all. It was right when the broker and the database both spoke XA and sat in one data centre. SQS, SNS and DocumentDB offer no XA, so the guarantee is gone (9.14).
@MessageDriven
@TransactionAttribute(TransactionAttributeType.REQUIRED)
public class LedgerConfirmBean implements MessageListener {
    @PersistenceContext EntityManager em;
    public void onMessage(Message m) { em.persist(confirmationFrom(m)); }
}

Recognise it by. @TransactionAttribute, XAConnectionFactory, JtaTransactionManager, javax.transaction.UserTransaction, and Atomikos or Bitronix artifactIds.

The rookie version.

@SqsListener("ledger-confirm")
public void onEvent(EventEnvelope<PayoutCompletedData> event) {
    if (processedEvents.existsById(event.eventId())) {
        return;                                        // seen it before
    }
    ledger.confirm(event.payoutId(), event.data().amount());
    processedEvents.save(new ProcessedEvent(event.eventId()));
}

What goes wrong. The idea is right. The order is not. A standard queue delivers at least once, and sometimes it delivers two copies at nearly the same time. Pod 1 and pod 2 each receive one copy, 40 ms apart. Both check, both find nothing, and both confirm £1,240.50 in the ledger. There is a second gap as well. A pod that crashes after the ledger call and before the save leaves no record. The message comes back, and the ledger is asked again.

Do this now. An operation is idempotent when doing it twice has the same effect as doing it once. Part 9 defines the pattern and the key store (9.09, 9.10). For a listener it has three layers.

  1. Use the event's own ID, from the envelope (10.12). Do not use the SQS message ID. The outbox relay may publish one event twice after a timeout (9.08), and each publish becomes a different SQS message. A redrive from a dead-letter queue also gives every message a new ID (10.09).
  2. Claim the ID before the side effect. Insert it into idempotency_keys, which has a unique index on the key (8.16). The insert either succeeds or fails with a duplicate-key error. The database decides, not a read followed by a write.
  3. Make the downstream call idempotent too. Send the event ID to the ledger as its Idempotency-Key (5.05, 7.07). That closes the crash gap: a repeat after a crash is a repeat the ledger recognises.
@SqsListener("ledger-confirm")
public void onEvent(EventEnvelope<PayoutCompletedData> event) {
    String key = "ledger-confirm:" + event.eventId();
    KeyClaim claim = idempotency.claim(key);
    if (claim == KeyClaim.DONE) return;                       // a duplicate: acknowledge it
    if (claim == KeyClaim.IN_PROGRESS) throw new RetryLater(key); // another pod has it
    try {
        ledger.confirm(event.eventId(), event.payoutId(), event.data().amount());
        idempotency.markDone(key);
    } catch (RuntimeException e) {
        idempotency.release(key);
        throw e;
    }
}
  1. Treat an IN_PROGRESS claim older than the visibility timeout as abandoned, and take it over. Its owner has crashed (10.06).
  2. Where you can, make the effect itself idempotent. A conditional update that marks a ledger entry confirmed only while it is still unconfirmed matches nothing the second time (8.04).
  3. Keep the keys longer than a duplicate can arrive. That is the dead-letter queue's retention, counted from the message's first arrival on a standard queue (10.08), plus a full retention again for any message you redrive (10.09). A TTL index expires them (8.17). DocumentDB deletes expired documents on a best-effort schedule, so expect them to linger.

Also seen. FIFO deduplication (10.11). It stops a producer's retry within 5 minutes, and nothing else, so it does not replace this. Natural keys: the audit consumer writes its record with the event ID as _id, so a duplicate insert fails harmlessly.

When to break it. notify-claimant could accept the occasional duplicate email and skip the key store. That is a business decision, not a technical one. Ask the people who answer the complaints, and write the answer down (21.08).

.NET anchor. NServiceBus's Outbox and MassTransit's inbox deduplicate incoming messages by ID inside the framework. Here you write it, and the ID must be the event's, not the transport's.

See also. 9.08, 9.09, 9.10, 8.04, 8.16, 8.17, 5.05, 7.07, 10.06, The Yard, chapter 8, Document data: Amazon DocumentDB and the MongoDB API

10.08 Configure a dead-letter queue and maxReceiveCount

Then.

  • Boot era: an error queue handled in code. The listener caught the exception, sent the body to a queue named -errors with the reason as an attribute, and deleted the original. It recorded why a message failed, which SQS's own dead-lettering still does not do. It also ran on every failure, transient or not, and lost the message when the second send failed.
} catch (Exception e) {
    sqs.sendMessage(new SendMessageRequest(errorQueueUrl, m.getBody())
            .addMessageAttributesEntry("error", text(e.getMessage())));
    sqs.deleteMessage(queueUrl, m.getReceiptHandle());
}

Recognise it by. sendMessage inside a catch block, queues named -errors or -failed, an errorQueueUrl property, and a retryCount attribute that the code increments and re-sends.

The rookie version.

{
  "ledger-confirm": {
    "RedrivePolicy": { "deadLetterTargetArn": "...:ledger-confirm-dlq", "maxReceiveCount": "1" },
    "MessageRetentionPeriod": "345600"
  },
  "ledger-confirm-dlq": { "MessageRetentionPeriod": "345600" }
}

What goes wrong. A dead-letter queue (DLQ) is a queue that receives messages the source queue gave up on. A redrive policy on the source says where, and after how many receives. Here one failed receive is enough. On a Friday at 18:00 the ledger has a 2-second blip, and 40 confirmations go straight to the DLQ. Nobody is alerted. Both queues keep messages for 4 days, 345,600 seconds, the default. On a standard queue a message keeps its original enqueue time when it moves, so the DLQ does not restart the clock. On Tuesday at 18:00 the 40 confirmations expire, unread.

Do this now.

  1. Give each queue its own DLQ, named after it: ledger-confirm-dlq. It must be in the same account and Region, and a FIFO queue's DLQ must be FIFO too.
  2. Choose maxReceiveCount, the number of receives before SQS moves the message. It counts receives, not your retries. With a 60-second visibility timeout, 5 receives give about 5 minutes for a transient fault to clear. The API's default is 10.
{
  "deadLetterTargetArn": "arn:aws:sqs:eu-west-2:111122223333:ledger-confirm-dlq",
  "maxReceiveCount": "5"
}
  1. Keep messages in the DLQ longer than in the source. Set it to 14 days, 1,209,600 seconds, the maximum. On a standard queue the DLQ clock started when the message first arrived. On a FIFO queue it restarts when the message moves.
  2. Restrict which queues may use the DLQ with a redrive allow policy.
{
  "redrivePermission": "byQueue",
  "sourceQueueArns": ["arn:aws:sqs:eu-west-2:111122223333:ledger-confirm"]
}
  1. Alarm when the DLQ's ApproximateNumberOfMessagesVisible is above 0 (14.08). Each message there is a decision a person must make.
  2. Give each SNS subscription a DLQ too, for messages SNS could not deliver to the queue (10.01).

SQS's dead-letter queue guide adds one detail. On a standard queue with maxReceiveCount above 3, a message received 3 or more times without being deleted is moved to the back of the queue. Its later retries are therefore not back to back, and order shuffles further.

Also seen. A parking queue for failures that will never succeed, written by the listener with the reason attached (6.11, 10.17). An error handler in the listener container that does the same.

When to break it. AWS warns against a DLQ on a FIFO queue when the exact order must hold, because moving one message out breaks it. Then a failing message should stop its group and page someone (10.10). The cost is that the group waits for a person.

.NET anchor. Azure Service Bus has a dead-letter subqueue on every queue, with MaxDeliveryCount and a DeadLetterReason on each message. In SQS the DLQ is a separate queue you create and attach, and it records no reason.

See also. 10.01, 10.09, 10.17, 6.11, 14.08, 20.08, Messaging and WebSockets

10.09 Redrive messages from a dead-letter queue after a fix

Then.

  • Boot era: a replay job that received from the DLQ, sent each body back to the source queue and deleted it. Before SQS could move messages itself, every team wrote one. It can still skip or change messages, which SQS's own redrive cannot.
for (Message m : sqs.receiveMessage(dlqUrl).getMessages()) {
    sqs.sendMessage(sourceQueueUrl, m.getBody());     // attributes are lost here
    sqs.deleteMessage(dlqUrl, m.getReceiptHandle());
}

Recognise it by. SDK v1's AmazonSQS in a class named DlqReplayJob or RedriveJob, an admin endpoint such as /admin/dlq/replay, and a receive, send, delete loop between two queue URLs.

The rookie version.

// Put them back where they came from: the topic.
for (Message m : sqs.receiveMessage(r -> r.queueUrl(dlqUrl).maxNumberOfMessages(10)).messages()) {
    sns.publish(r -> r.topicArn(payoutEventsArn).message(m.body()));
    sqs.deleteMessage(r -> r.queueUrl(dlqUrl).receiptHandle(m.receiptHandle()));
}

What goes wrong. The messages in ledger-confirm-dlq failed in one consumer. Publishing them to payout-events sends them to every subscriber. notify-claimant handled those events days ago. Its key store had expired the IDs, so 230 claimants receive a second "your claim has been paid" message. payout-audit records 230 completions twice. The republished messages also lose their attributes, so filter policies no longer route them (10.13).

Do this now. Move the messages back to the queue they failed from, and let SQS do it. A message move task is SQS's built-in redrive, started with the StartMessageMoveTask API, the CLI or the console.

  1. Fix the cause and deploy it first. The procedure around a production redrive is in 20.08.
  2. Start the task on the DLQ's ARN. With no destination, SQS returns each message to the queue it came from. A destination ARN sends them to another queue of the same type instead.
  3. Set a rate. The maximum allowed is 500 messages a second. Size it for the slowest downstream, not for SQS.
StartMessageMoveTaskResponse task = sqs.startMessageMoveTask(r -> r
        .sourceArn("arn:aws:sqs:eu-west-2:111122223333:ledger-confirm-dlq")
        .maxNumberOfMessagesPerSecond(20));
log.info("redrive started, task handle {}", task.taskHandle());
  1. Watch it with ListMessageMoveTasks, which shows up to the 10 most recent tasks. CancelMessageMoveTask stops a task while it is running.
  2. Know the limits. A task runs for at most 36 hours, and an account may have 100 active at once. SQS cannot filter or change messages during a redrive.
  3. Expect new identities. Each redriven message is a new message with a new message ID and a new enqueue time, so its retention restarts. A consumer that deduplicates on the event ID handles that (10.07).
  4. An SNS subscription's DLQ is different. A message move task accepts only a DLQ whose source is another SQS queue, not one fed by an SNS subscription. To deliver those messages again, you need code.

Also seen. A replay consumer you write yourself, when some messages must be skipped or corrected first. The console's "Start DLQ redrive" button, which starts the same task.

When to break it. Some messages should not go back at all. A confirmation for a payout that has since been cancelled by hand is stale. Record what it held in the audit trail, then delete it. The cost is a person reading each one.

.NET anchor. Azure Service Bus has no server-side move from the dead-letter subqueue. You receive from $DeadLetterQueue and resend in code, or use Service Bus Explorer. SQS does the move for you, at the rate you set.

See also. 10.07, 10.08, 10.13, 14.08, 20.08, Messaging and WebSockets

10.10 Keep order where it matters with FIFO queues and message groups

Then.

  • Boot era: a sequence number in every event, and a consumer that remembered the last number seen for each payout and ignored anything older. It works on any queue and it is still a good guard. FIFO queues took over where events must be handled in strict order, not only filtered.
long last = lastSeen.getOrDefault(event.payoutId(), 0L);
if (event.sequence() <= last) {
    return;                                    // stale or duplicate, ignore
}

Recognise it by. A sequence or version field on events, a lastSeen map or collection, and listeners pinned to one thread with maxConcurrentMessages = "1" to keep order.

The rookie version.

sns.publish(r -> r
        .topicArn(payoutEventsFifoArn)
        .messageGroupId("payouts")                 // one group for everything
        .messageDeduplicationId(event.eventId().toString())
        .message(json));

What goes wrong. A FIFO queue (first in, first out) keeps strict order within a message group, and only there. With one group for every payout, every event in the system is in one line. SQS will not hand out more messages from a group while earlier ones are in flight. So one consumer works at a time, however many pods there are. One failing event for one payout blocks the 900 behind it for 5 receives × 60 seconds = 5 minutes. All 900 had nothing to do with that payout.

Do this now.

  1. Decide whether you need order. Most consumers do not, if they check the payout's current state (8.05). ledger-confirm does: a reservation must be confirmed before it is released, for the same payout.
  2. Use the entity's key as the group ID: the payout ID. Events for one payout stay in order. Events for different payouts run in parallel.
sns.publish(r -> r
        .topicArn(props.topicArn())                    // ...:payout-events.fifo
        .messageGroupId(event.payoutId())              // order per payout
        .messageDeduplicationId(event.eventId().toString())
        .message(json)
        .messageAttributes(attributes));
  1. Use a FIFO topic and FIFO queues end to end. Their names end in .fifo. A FIFO topic can deliver to standard queues, but only a FIFO queue keeps the order. FIFO topics cannot deliver to email, SMS or HTTP endpoints.
  2. Set a deduplication ID on every send (10.11).
  3. Know the throughput. Without high-throughput mode, a FIFO queue manages 300 transactions per second per partition and per API action, or 3,000 messages with batching. High-throughput mode needs DeduplicationScope set to messageGroup and FifoThroughputLimit to perMessageGroupId. Its limits differ by Region, so read the quota page for yours. Many distinct group IDs spread the load across partitions.
  4. Do not ask for a group. A consumer cannot request messages from a particular group.
  5. Spring Cloud AWS handles each group in order, different groups in parallel, and acknowledges each message at once on FIFO queues. When one message fails, it skips the rest of that group in the batch, and they come back after their visibility timeout.

AWS's guide to FIFO deduplication promises exactly-once delivery only when the subscription has no filter policy. With one, it calls delivery "at-most-once", "as messages can be filtered out based on your subscription filter policies". That is the filter doing its job: a message that does not match is delivered zero times. The real risk is a wrong policy, which drops events the consumer needed without any error, so test it (10.13, 10.19).

Also seen. Kafka or Kinesis, which order by partition key in the same way. A standard queue with a version check in the consumer, which tolerates reordering instead of preventing it (8.05).

When to break it. FIFO everywhere costs throughput, and one bad message holds back its group. When a consumer can check state and ignore a stale event, a standard queue is simpler. The cost is writing that check.

.NET anchor. Azure Service Bus sessions, with SessionId and a ServiceBusSessionProcessor. SQS message groups are the same idea without session state, and a consumer cannot lock a group it chooses.

See also. 10.06, 10.08, 10.11, 10.13, 8.05, Messaging and WebSockets

10.11 Deduplicate messages on FIFO queues

What goes wrong. The relay publishes PayoutCompleted to the FIFO topic, and the call times out, though SNS accepted it. The relay sends again. With no deduplication ID and content-based deduplication off, a FIFO send fails with an error. With content-based deduplication on, SNS hashes the body, and the relay's body includes a publishedAt time that changed. The hash differs, and the consumer gets two copies.

Do this now. Set MessageDeduplicationId to the event's ID on every send. SQS and SNS FIFO accept a repeat with the same ID within 5 minutes and do not deliver it. Content-based deduplication uses a SHA-256 hash of the body, not the attributes, so use it only for bodies that never vary. An explicit ID overrides it. In high-throughput mode deduplication applies within each message group. After 5 minutes a repeat goes through, so a relay that was down for an hour still sends duplicates. The consumer's check stays necessary (10.07).

See also. 9.08, 10.07, 10.10

10.12 Design an event: envelope, ID, type and version

Then.

  • J2EE era: a JMS ObjectMessage carrying a serialised Java object. Producer and consumer shared the class, usually in a common jar, and Java's own serialisation did the rest. It was right for one team, one language and one release schedule. JSON replaced it because any language can read JSON and a person can read it in a queue. Java deserialisation of untrusted bytes also became a well-known route to running an attacker's code.
ObjectMessage message = session.createObjectMessage(payout);   // Payout implements Serializable
producer.send(message);

Recognise it by. ObjectMessage, createObjectMessage, events that implements Serializable with a serialVersionUID, and a shared payouts-events jar that every consumer must upgrade together.

The rookie version.

{
  "payoutId": "p-7781",
  "status": "COMPLETED",
  "amount": 1240.5,
  "date": "24/10/2026 14:02"
}

What goes wrong. There is no event ID, so no consumer can tell a duplicate from a second event (10.07). There is no type, so consumers guess from status, which is the name of an internal enum. The amount is a binary floating-point number: it has lost its second decimal place, and an amount such as 0.10 cannot be held exactly, so sums drift by fractions of a penny. The date is local time without a zone. On the night the clocks go back, the audit consumer puts two events in the wrong order. Nothing says which version of this shape it is, so the first change breaks someone.

Do this now. An envelope is the outer part of an event: the same fields on every Payouts event. The payload inside it, data, varies by type. payoutId belongs in the envelope only because every Payouts event is about exactly one payout. Readers can then log it, and the publisher can use it as the FIFO group key, without knowing the event type. A service whose events have different subjects would keep the subject in data.

public record EventEnvelope<T>(
        UUID eventId,          // set once, when the outbox row is written
        String eventType,      // "PayoutCompleted", a fact in the past tense
        int eventVersion,      // 1, raised only for a breaking change
        Instant occurredAt,    // UTC, from the injected Clock
        String payoutId,       // the subject, also the FIFO group key
        T data) {}

public record PayoutCompletedData(String claimId, Money amount, String bankReference) {}
  1. eventId is generated once, when the event is written to the outbox (9.07). It stays the same through every retry and redrive. Consumers deduplicate on it.
  2. eventType names what happened. Use one type per business fact: PayoutRequested, LedgerReserved, BankInstructed, PayoutCompleted, PayoutFailed.
  3. eventVersion changes only when a change would break a reader. Adding an optional field is not one. How to change it is in 20.02.
  4. occurredAt is an Instant, written in ISO 8601 with a Z (2.02).
  5. data holds what consumers need, not the document. Money is a decimal string and a currency (2.01, 5.13).
  6. Copy eventType and eventVersion into message attributes too, so filter policies can route without reading the body (10.13). SNS has a publish option, MessageStructure=json, that sends a different body to each kind of subscriber, such as one for email and one for SQS. With that option SNS sends no message attributes, so publish a plain string body, the default.
  7. Carry trace context as an attribute as well (13.05).
{
  "eventId": "6f1c2a52-6a8e-4c0b-9a63-2b7a1d0c9e41",
  "eventType": "PayoutCompleted",
  "eventVersion": 1,
  "occurredAt": "2026-10-24T13:02:11.204Z",
  "payoutId": "p-7781",
  "data": { "claimId": "cl-55120", "amount": { "value": "1240.50", "currency": "GBP" },
            "bankReference": "SRL-0091-4471" }
}
  1. Make consumers ignore fields they do not know, and prove it with a test that adds one (16.17). That is what lets the producer add fields.

Also seen. CloudEvents, a CNCF specification with id, source, type and specversion attributes. Choose it when events leave the company or a tool expects it. Avro or Protobuf with a schema registry, common with Kafka. A thin event that carries only the payout ID, so consumers call back for the rest.

When to break it. A thin event keeps personal data out of three queues. It costs a call back to payouts-api for every event, and the consumer may read the payout before the change is visible (9.13). A fat event costs size: through SNS the limit is 256 KiB (10.14).

.NET anchor. MassTransit's envelope, with messageId, messageType URNs and the message inside, is the same idea, chosen for you. The CloudEvents SDK for .NET gives you the standard one.

See also. 9.07, 10.07, 10.13, 10.14, 20.02, 13.05, 2.01, 2.02, 5.10, 5.13

10.13 Route messages with SNS subscription filter policies

Then.

  • Boot era: one SNS topic per event type, payout-completed and payout-failed, and each consumer subscribed to the topics it wanted. It needed no filtering at all. It also meant a new topic, new permissions and new subscriptions for every new event type. Filter policies made one topic per producer workable, and since November 2022 they can match the body as well as the attributes.

Recognise it by. Topic ARNs per event type in configuration, such as payouts.topics.completed-arn, and consumers with three or four nearly identical subscriptions.

The rookie version.

@SqsListener("notify-claimant")
public void onEvent(EventEnvelope<JsonNode> event) {
    if (!event.eventType().equals("PayoutCompleted")) {
        return;                                   // not ours
    }
    notifier.tellClaimant(event);
}

What goes wrong. Each payout produces 5 events, and notify-claimant wants 1 of them. The listener's parameter type has to accept every shape of every event, which is why it ended up as JsonNode, with no type checking. The consumer is now coupled to every event Payouts publishes. When Payouts adds a sixth type, or changes the shape of one this consumer never wanted, the conversion or the early return is where it breaks. The other 4 events are also delivered, received, parsed and deleted for nothing. At 20,000 payouts a day that is 80,000 messages a day of work for the consumer's pods, and 80,000 more chances to fail before the check. The request charges are small. The coupling is the real cost.

Do this now. A filter policy is a JSON document on a subscription. SNS delivers a message to that subscription only if the message matches.

  1. Put the fields you route on into message attributes when you publish: eventType and eventVersion (10.12).
  2. Attach a policy to the consumer's subscription. Attribute matching is the default scope. Set FilterPolicyScope to MessageBody to match fields in the body instead.
{
  "eventType": ["PayoutCompleted", "PayoutFailed"],
  "eventVersion": [{ "numeric": [">=", 1] }]
}
  1. Use the operators you need: a list of exact values, anything-but, prefix, numeric and exists. Matching is case-sensitive. A numeric match needs a Number attribute. SnsTemplate sends an int header with the custom type Number.java.lang.Integer, so prove in a LocalStack test (10.19) that your filter matches it, or publish that attribute with the SDK as plain Number (10.03).
  2. Stay inside the limits. A policy may have at most 5 keys and at most 150 combinations of values, and must be under 256 KB. A topic may have 200 policies by default, and an account 10,000. Attribute matching ignores Binary attributes.
  3. Keep the policy with the consumer's infrastructure code. The consumer owns its subscription, so it owns what it receives.
  4. Test it end to end, with a real topic and queue (10.19). A policy with a typo matches nothing and reports no error.

Also seen. EventBridge rules, which match on richer patterns, for events shared across many teams. A topic per event type, still reasonable for a producer with two event types.

When to break it. payout-audit wants everything, so it has no policy. A rule the policy cannot express, such as "only claims from one broker", may stay in code. Keep the policy coarse and the code fine. The cost is paying for the messages the code discards.

.NET anchor. Azure Service Bus subscription rules: a SqlRuleFilter such as eventType = 'PayoutCompleted', or a CorrelationRuleFilter. SNS policies are JSON patterns, with no SQL and smaller limits.

See also. 10.01, 10.10, 10.12, 10.19, Messaging and WebSockets

10.14 Send a payload larger than the message limit

What goes wrong. A PayoutCompleted event for a bulk claim carries the bank's settlement lines and reaches 310 KiB. The test sends it straight to SQS, which accepts up to 1 MiB, and passes. In production it goes through SNS, whose topics accept 256 KiB by default, and every publish fails.

Do this now. Prefer a claim check: store the large part in S3 or DocumentDB and send its key in the event. If the body must travel whole, there are two tools.

  1. Raise the topic's MaximumMessageSize, up to 1 MiB, possible since 18 September 2026. That topic can then deliver only to SQS, Lambda and Firehose, with at most 100 subscriptions.
  2. Use the SQS Extended Client Library, com.amazonaws:amazon-sqs-java-extended-client-lib. Version 2.x is on SDK v2 and moves bodies to S3, up to 2 GB. It still offloads anything over 256 KiB by default. Raise that with withPayloadSizeThreshold. Consumers need the library and S3 read access too. In Spring Cloud AWS 4.1 and later, setting spring.cloud.aws.sqs.extended.bucket wraps the auto-configured client. This library sends to SQS. For the SNS path, the publisher needs the SNS Extended Client Library, which does the same on publish.

See also. 10.12, 10.18, 8.02

10.15 Acknowledge messages manually or automatically

Then.

  • Boot era: Spring Cloud AWS 2.x's deletionPolicy, with the values ALWAYS, NEVER, NO_REDRIVE and ON_SUCCESS.

What goes wrong. A team switches payout-audit to manual acknowledgement to control it. One branch of the listener, for events it skips, returns without acknowledging. Those messages come back every visibility period until they reach the DLQ, and its alarm wakes someone for messages that were handled correctly.

Do this now. To acknowledge a message is to tell SQS you are done, which deletes it. Spring Cloud AWS has three modes: ON_SUCCESS, the default, ALWAYS, which also acknowledges after an error, and MANUAL.

@SqsListener(value = "payout-audit", acknowledgementMode = "MANUAL")
public void onEvent(EventEnvelope<JsonNode> event, Acknowledgement ack) {
    auditStore.append(event);
    ack.acknowledge();
}

Keep ON_SUCCESS unless you need to acknowledge at another point, such as after an asynchronous step. In MANUAL, every path must acknowledge or throw. With the plain SDK, acknowledging means DeleteMessage (10.05).

See also. 10.04, 10.05, 10.07

10.16 Control consumer concurrency and back-pressure

What goes wrong. A backlog builds on ledger-confirm. Say a hypothetical autoscaler takes Payouts from 2 pods to 4. Each listener handles 10 messages at once, the default, so 40 ledger calls are now in flight. The ledger team agreed to 20. The ledger slows, the backlog grows, and the autoscaler adds pods.

Do this now. Back-pressure means the consumer takes work only as fast as it can finish it. A queue gives you that for free: waiting messages cost almost nothing.

  1. Set maxConcurrentMessages on each listener from the downstream's limit divided by the most pods you run: 20 ÷ 4 = 5 (10.04).
  2. Set maxMessagesPerPoll at or below it. The container refuses to start otherwise, and its default is 10. A smaller poll also means fetched messages do not wait locally with their visibility clock running (10.06).
  3. Scale pods on queue age, not CPU, and cap the replica count (14.08, 17.08).
  4. For a hard limit inside one pod across several listeners, use a shared limiter (3.09).

From Spring Cloud AWS 4.1 the container can use virtual threads, which changes the cost of a thread, not the downstream's limit.

See also. 3.09, 10.04, 10.06, 14.08, 17.08

10.17 Handle a poison message

What goes wrong. A poison message fails every time, whoever receives it. A producer's bug writes "amount": 1240.5 where the consumer expects an object. Conversion fails before the listener method runs, on every receive. With no DLQ, the message cycles for the queue's 4-day retention, and each receive logs a stack trace.

Do this now.

  1. Give every queue a DLQ, so a poison message leaves after maxReceiveCount receives (10.08).
  2. Separate the permanent failures you can detect, such as a validation error or an unknown eventVersion. Park them at once with the reason, then return normally (6.11).
  3. Log the event ID and the reason once, at the place that decides (12.05).
  4. Never switch to ALWAYS to make one bad message go away. It deletes the good messages that fail for transient reasons too.
  5. Validate messages as you would request bodies (6.12).

See also. 6.11, 6.12, 10.08, 10.12, 12.05

10.18 Grant least-privilege IAM to publishers and consumers

Then.

  • Boot era: an IAM user's access keys in cloud.aws.credentials.access-key and secret-key, often with sqs:* and sns:* on every resource.

What goes wrong. Payouts' role has sqs:* on *. A bug in a test script run against production purges notify-claimant, which belongs to another team. 1,100 notifications are lost.

Do this now. Give each service exactly the actions its code calls, on the ARNs it uses, through the pod's role (15.07).

{
  "Statement": [
    { "Effect": "Allow", "Action": "sns:Publish",
      "Resource": "arn:aws:sns:eu-west-2:111122223333:payout-events" },
    { "Effect": "Allow",
      "Action": ["sqs:ReceiveMessage", "sqs:DeleteMessage", "sqs:ChangeMessageVisibility",
                 "sqs:GetQueueUrl", "sqs:GetQueueAttributes"],
      "Resource": "arn:aws:sqs:eu-west-2:111122223333:ledger-confirm" }
  ]
}

The SNS-to-SQS permission is the queue policy, not this role (10.01). New queues are encrypted with SQS-owned keys by default since 2022. That encrypts the body, not the attributes, so keep personal data out of attributes. A queue with a customer-managed KMS key also needs kms:Decrypt for consumers, and a key policy that lets SNS use the key.

See also. 10.01, 15.06, 15.07

10.19 Test SNS and SQS with LocalStack

Then.

  • Boot era: ElasticMQ, an in-memory server that speaks the SQS API, started inside the test. It was fast and needed no Docker, but it has no SNS.
  • Boot era: LocalStack through Testcontainers 1.x, with a :latest tag and an enum per service. It worked without an account until 2026.
@Container
static LocalStackContainer aws = new LocalStackContainer(
        DockerImageName.parse("localstack/localstack:latest"))
        .withServices(LocalStackContainer.Service.SQS, LocalStackContainer.Service.SNS);

Recognise it by. org.elasticmq artifacts, LocalStackContainer.Service, localstack/localstack:latest, and a mocked AmazonSQS in tests named *IT.

The rookie version.

@MockitoBean
SnsTemplate snsTemplate;

@Test
void publishesCompletedEvent() {
    relay.publishPending();
    verify(snsTemplate).convertAndSend(eq(topicArn), any(EventEnvelope.class), anyMap());
}

What goes wrong. The test proves that a method was called. It says nothing about what reached a queue. In production the eventVersion attribute was sent as a string, the notify-claimant filter policy compared it as a number, and nothing matched. Claimants received no notifications for 2 days, while this test stayed green. Mocking a library you do not own tests your assumptions about it, not the library (16.02).

Do this now. LocalStack is an emulator of AWS services that runs in a container. Testcontainers starts it for the test and removes it afterwards.

  1. Add the module. Boot 3.5 manages Testcontainers 1.21.x: the artifact is org.testcontainers:localstack, and the class is org.testcontainers.containers.localstack.LocalStackContainer. Boot 4 manages Testcontainers 2.0, which renames modules to testcontainers-<name> and moves classes into org.testcontainers.<name>.
  2. Deal with the token. Since 23 March 2026 the localstack/localstack image needs an auth token for current releases. In CI, pass a CI token in LOCALSTACK_AUTH_TOKEN from the pipeline's secrets. The other choice is to pin an older tag, such as 4.12, and accept that it gets no updates. Spring Cloud AWS 4.2's Docker Compose support also covers Floci, floci/floci, as an alternative image.
  3. Create the topic, queues, subscriptions, raw delivery settings and filter policies in the container, from the same definitions as production where you can.
  4. Point Spring Cloud AWS at the container.
@Container
static LocalStackContainer aws = new LocalStackContainer(
        DockerImageName.parse("localstack/localstack:4.12"));   // pinned: see step 2

@DynamicPropertySource
static void awsProperties(DynamicPropertyRegistry registry) {
    registry.add("spring.cloud.aws.endpoint", () -> aws.getEndpoint().toString());
    registry.add("spring.cloud.aws.region.static", aws::getRegion);
    registry.add("spring.cloud.aws.credentials.access-key", aws::getAccessKey);
    registry.add("spring.cloud.aws.credentials.secret-key", aws::getSecretKey);
}
  1. Assert at the far end. Run the relay, then receive from notify-claimant and ledger-confirm with an SDK client, waiting with Awaitility. Check the body, the attributes, and that a filtered-out event did not arrive.
  2. Start the container once per test run, not per class (16.08). Listener tests are 16.11.

An emulator tests your wiring, not AWS. Limits, IAM and throughput need a real account. This is the same gap DocumentDB has against a Mongo container.

Also seen. Floci, the other image Spring Cloud AWS's Docker Compose support covers. ElasticMQ, for tests that need only SQS. A sandbox AWS account for the checks an emulator cannot make. A mock of PayoutEventPublisher, which is yours, in unit tests of the relay's logic.

When to break it. A test of how an outbox row maps to an envelope needs no container. Test the mapping alone. The cost of LocalStack is seconds of start-up and a token to manage.

.NET anchor. Testcontainers for .NET has the same module, Testcontainers.LocalStack, with a LocalStackBuilder. The token rule applies there too, because it belongs to the image.

See also. 16.02, 16.08, 16.11, 16.12, 10.13, The Yard, chapter 7, Testing Spring Boot

10.20 Delay a message

What goes wrong. The saga wants to check payout p-7781 again in 10 minutes. A developer puts Thread.sleep(Duration.ofMinutes(10)) in the listener. The message's visibility timeout is 60 seconds, so another pod receives it after one minute and sleeps as well. After 5 receives SQS moves the message to the DLQ (10.08), and 10 minutes later 5 sleeping copies wake up and act at once.

Do this now. Ask SQS to hold the message instead.

  1. A message timer delays one message: set DelaySeconds on the send, from 0 to 900 seconds, which is 15 minutes.
  2. A delay queue delays every message, through the queue's DelaySeconds attribute, with the same 15-minute maximum.
  3. A delay is part of the SQS send, so send to the queue directly, not through SNS.
sqs.sendMessage(r -> r
        .queueUrl(sagaChecksUrl)
        .messageBody(json)
        .delaySeconds(600));      // visible in 10 minutes

For a later retry of a message you already hold, change its visibility instead (10.06). For anything longer than 15 minutes, store the due time in DocumentDB and poll for it with a scheduled job that runs on one pod (3.10).

See also. 3.10, 10.06, 11.08

⚠Review checklist
  • If you see a service sending the same event to several queues in turn: the sends are not atomic, and every new consumer needs a change in the producer. See 10.01.
  • If you see an SQS queue subscribed to SNS with no queue policy, or a subscription without raw delivery: SNS discards the messages, or the listener cannot parse the envelope. See 10.01.
  • If you see a document passed to convertAndSend, or a publish inside @Transactional: personal data leaks into queues, and events describe writes that never committed. See 10.02.
  • If you see an SnsClient or SqsClient created inside a method: a new connection pool and TLS handshake per call. See 10.03.
  • If you see a listener that catches every exception and returns: failures are acknowledged and deleted, and the DLQ stays empty. See 10.04.
  • If you see a receive loop without waitTimeSeconds, or a delete before the handling: empty polls on the bill, and messages lost in a deploy. See 10.05.
  • If you see a queue left at the default visibility timeout, or set to 12 hours: duplicates while work is still running, or messages stuck after a crash. See 10.06.
  • If you see a duplicate check that reads, then acts, then writes, or that uses the SQS message ID: two pods pass it at once, and redrives slip through. See 10.07.
  • If you see a maxReceiveCount of 1, a DLQ with the source's retention, or a DLQ with no alarm: a blip dead-letters messages that then expire unread. See 10.08.
  • If you see messages from one consumer's DLQ republished to the topic: every other consumer handles them a second time. See 10.09.
  • If you see one constant messageGroupId for a whole FIFO queue: everything is serial, and one failure blocks the lot. See 10.10.
  • If you see a FIFO send without a deduplication ID that is stable across retries: the retry is delivered twice. See 10.11.
  • If you see an event with no ID, type or version, or money as a JSON number: duplicates cannot be detected and the first change breaks a consumer. See 10.12.
  • If you see a listener that returns early for event types it does not want: a missing filter policy. See 10.13.
  • If you see a large event tested by sending straight to SQS: SNS rejects it above 256 KiB by default. See 10.14.
  • If you see acknowledgementMode = "MANUAL" with a branch that neither acknowledges nor throws: handled messages come back until they reach the DLQ. See 10.15.
  • If you see sqs:* or sns:* in a role, or access keys in configuration: one bug can empty another team's queue. See 10.18.
  • If you see @MockitoBean SnsTemplate as the only test of publishing: attributes, filter policies and raw delivery are untested. See 10.19.
  • If you see Thread.sleep in a listener to wait for later: the message is redelivered while it sleeps. See 10.20.

Part IV · The how-to11. Sagas and long-running workflows#

A payout touches three systems that share no transaction: the ledger, the bank gateway and Payouts' own database. This part shows how to make that one business operation reliable anyway. It covers the saga, a sequence of local steps where each completed step has an undo, in both of its forms: an orchestrator that drives the steps from a state document, and a chain of services reacting to each other's events. It then covers compensations, the pivot step that cannot be undone, idempotent steps, timeouts, stuck sagas, and how to test the paths that only fail in production.

★What a veteran knows
  • Draw the steps on paper before you write a line of code. Mark which steps can be undone, which cannot, and which can only be retried. The order of those three groups is the design.
  • A saga's state lives in the database, never in a variable. If a pod restart in the middle of a step loses track of where the payout was, the code was never a saga.
  • "Unknown" is the outcome that matters. Code that turns a timeout into "failed" will, sooner or later, undo a step that actually happened.
  • A compensation is a new business action, not a rollback. It runs later, with other writes in between, and it must be as idempotent and as retryable as the step it undoes.
  • Every saga will get stuck one day. The question is whether a dashboard tells you within 15 minutes, or a claimant phones you after 3 days.
  • On Payouts the money path is orchestrated and the after-effects are choreographed. Most mature systems end up mixed, and it is fine to decide that on purpose.
◷How we got hereIn January 1987 Hector Garcia-Molina and Kenneth Salem, two computer scientists at Princeton University,…

In January 1987 Hector Garcia-Molina and Kenneth Salem, two computer scientists at Princeton University, published a technical report called "Sagas". They presented it in May that year at ACM SIGMOD in San Francisco. Their problem was the long-lived transaction, which "hold[s] on to database resources for relatively long periods of time, significantly delaying the termination of shorter and more common transactions". Their answer was to cut it into a sequence of shorter transactions. The database would guarantee that either all of them completed, or "compensating transactions are run to amend a partial execution". They called the idea "relatively simple". Their examples were monthly bank statements, statistics over a whole database, and insurance claims. The paper was about one database, not about services. Distributed systems adopted the pattern decades later, when the shared database had gone and the transaction around it had gone with it.

11.01 Recognise when you need a saga

Then.

  • J2EE era: a distributed transaction. An application server such as WebLogic or WebSphere ran a transaction manager that enlisted two databases, and often a broker for JMS, Java's standard messaging API, in one transaction. It committed them all with two-phase commit, through a protocol called XA: every resource votes "prepared", then the coordinator tells them all to commit.
@Stateless
public class PayoutBean {
    @Resource(mappedName = "jdbc/PayoutsXA") private DataSource payouts;
    @Resource(mappedName = "jdbc/LedgerXA")  private DataSource ledger;

    @TransactionAttribute(TransactionAttributeType.REQUIRED)
    public void pay(PayoutRequest request) { /* write both, commit together */ }
}
  • Spring era: the same two-phase commit without the application server, through Spring's JtaTransactionManager and an embedded transaction manager such as Atomikos or Bitronix.

XA was right when every resource was a database or a broker in one data centre, and every one spoke the XA protocol. HTTP services, SQS and DocumentDB offer no XA interface, and a coordinator that fails between the two phases leaves every resource locked until it returns. Sagas replaced XA because they need nothing from the other side except an API that is safe to call twice. Entry 9.14 covers removing it.

Recognise it by. javax.transaction.UserTransaction, javax.sql.XADataSource, org.springframework.transaction.jta.JtaTransactionManager, com.atomikos.*, bitronix.tm.*, spring-boot-starter-jta-atomikos (a starter is a Boot dependency that brings in a library and its setup), and data sources whose JNDI names end in XA.

The rookie version.

@Transactional
public void pay(Payout payout) {
    payouts.save(payout.withStatus(PayoutStatus.RESERVED));
    ledgerClient.reserve(payout.idempotencyKey(), ReserveRequest.from(payout));
    bankGatewayClient.instruct(payout.idempotencyKey(), InstructionRequest.from(payout));
    payouts.save(payout.withStatus(PayoutStatus.PAID));
}

What goes wrong. @Transactional is Spring's annotation for "run this method in a database transaction". Once a MongoTransactionManager is declared (9.01), it covers DocumentDB and nothing else. Without one, it does nothing at all. The bank refuses a payout of £1,240.50. The exception rolls back both payout writes, so the payout document looks as if nothing happened. The ledger still holds the £1,240.50 reservation, because the HTTP call to it was never part of the transaction, and nothing will ever release it. The transaction is also held open across 2 network calls. DocumentDB aborts a transaction after 1 minute, and each instance has an upper bound on open transactions. A slow bank turns into failed writes for everyone else.

Do this now. You need a saga when one business operation changes state in two or more systems that cannot share a transaction. A saga is a sequence of local transactions, one per system, where each step that completed has a compensation: a later action that undoes its business effect. Work through these questions in order:

  1. List every system the operation changes. For Payouts: the ledger, the bank gateway, and Payouts' own payouts and outbox collections.
  2. Ask whether the changes can live in one document. If they can, one atomic write is enough and you do not need a saga (9.05).
  3. Ask whether only the first change can fail for business reasons. If every later change is a local write plus a message that can be retried until it succeeds, the transactional outbox is enough (9.07). Sending the claimant an email after a payout is that case.
  4. If two or more remote steps can each fail, you need a saga. Payouts can be refused by the ledger, then refused by the bank, after the ledger has said yes.
  5. For each step, write down whether it can be undone, whether it can be retried safely, and who owns it.
  6. Decide where the saga's state lives. On Payouts it is a document in payout_sagas (11.02).

A saga gives up one property of a database transaction: isolation. Other code can see a payout halfway through. Entry 11.10 deals with that. It also makes the outcome eventually consistent: for a few seconds the ledger knows something the bank does not.

Also seen. A nightly reconciliation job that compares the two systems and reports differences to a person. Keep one alongside a saga, as the net under the net.

When to break it. If the second system is idempotent and will accept a retry for as long as it takes, a plain retry from a durable queue is cheaper than a saga. The cost is that you can never stop halfway and undo, so this only works when no later step can refuse.

.NET anchor. TransactionScope promoted to MSDTC is the .NET form of XA, with the same limits. NServiceBus sagas, MassTransit state machines and Durable Functions orchestrations are the .NET forms of a saga.

See also. 7.16, 9.05, 9.06, 9.07, 9.14, 11.02, 11.10, Transactions, propagation and isolation

11.02 Orchestrate a saga with a state-machine document

Then.

  • Spring era: the process lived in a status column on the main table. A Quartz job ran every few minutes, selected rows in each status, did the next thing and updated the column. It was right for an overnight, single-database world, where a few minutes' delay was normal.
public class PayoutStatusJob implements Job {
    public void execute(JobExecutionContext context) throws JobExecutionException {
        for (Payout p : payoutDao.findByStatus("RESERVED")) {
            bankService.send(p);
            p.setStatus("SENT"); payoutDao.update(p);
        }
    }
}

Its weaknesses were the unrecorded intent and the missing compensation path. A crash between send and update sent the payment again on the next run. The saga document below keeps the same idea, a stored status that drives the work, and adds intent, keys and undo.

Recognise it by. org.quartz.Job, JobExecutionContext, SchedulerFactoryBean, status columns compared as strings, and @Scheduled methods, Spring's timer annotation, looping over findByStatus.

The rookie version.

public void pay(Payout payout) {
    CompletableFuture
        .supplyAsync(() -> ledgerClient.reserve(payout.idempotencyKey(), ReserveRequest.from(payout)))
        .thenApply(r -> bankGatewayClient.instruct(payout.idempotencyKey(), InstructionRequest.from(payout)))
        .thenAccept(outcome -> payouts.save(payout.withStatus(PayoutStatus.PAID)))
        .exceptionally(e -> { log.error("payout {} failed", payout.id(), e); return null; });
}

What goes wrong. CompletableFuture is Java's nearest thing to a Task, and the saga exists only as a chain of them in one pod's memory. The controller has already returned 202. A deploy stops the pod between the reservation and the bank call, and nothing anywhere records that £1,240.50 is reserved. A bank refusal reaches exceptionally, which logs it and stops, so the reservation is never released. The chain also ignores the bank's outcome and marks every payout PAID. The fix is to make the state durable and give it one owner.

Do this now. In orchestration, one component, the orchestrator, decides every step and calls each participant. On Payouts that is PayoutSaga, and its memory is one SagaState document per payout in payout_sagas:

@Document("payout_sagas")
public record SagaState(
        @Id String payoutId,
        @Version Long version,          // optimistic lock: two writers cannot both win
        SagaStep step,                  // what to do next
        String reserveKey,              // idempotency keys, created with the saga
        String instructionKey,
        String reservationId,           // needed by the compensation
        BankDetails bankDetails,        // copied at the start, never reread (11.10)
        int attempts,
        Instant nextAttemptAt,
        Instant leaseUntil,             // which worker owns it, and until when
        Instant stepDeadline,
        String lastError,
        Instant updatedAt) { }          // set when step changes (11.09)

@Document, @Id and @Version are Spring Data MongoDB's mapping annotations, the counterpart of an EF Core entity configuration. SagaStep is an enum: RESERVE, INSTRUCT, RELEASE, COMPLETED, FAILED and PARKED. These are the saga's own states. The payout keeps its PayoutStatus: PENDING, RESERVED, INSTRUCTED, PAID, FAILED or CANCELLED. The saga moves it in the same transaction as each step, along the transitions of 2.13. It never sets CANCELLED, which only PayoutService.cancel does (8.05). The saga moves like this:

The mechanism, in steps:

  1. POST /payouts saves the payout as PENDING and a new SagaState at RESERVE, in one transaction, and returns 202 Accepted (5.06). Both idempotency keys are generated here, once, and nextAttemptAt and leaseUntil are set so the worker can find it (11.07).
  2. A worker in each pod polls for due sagas. It claims one with findAndModify, MongoDB's find-and-update in one atomic command, which sets leaseUntil as it reads (11.07). Only one pod runs a given saga at a time.
  3. The worker runs exactly one step, then saves the next step, with the payout's matching status, in a conditional write that also gives up the lease. After a reservation the payout becomes RESERVED. The @Version field turns a stale save into an OptimisticLockingFailureException instead of a lost update.
  4. The last forward step is a local write. When the bank accepts, it moves the saga to COMPLETED, the payout through INSTRUCTED to PAID with the bank reference, and adds PayoutCompleted to the outbox collection, in one transaction (9.07). OutboxRelay publishes it to SNS later (9.08).
void advance(SagaState saga) {
    switch (saga.step()) {
        case RESERVE  -> reserve(saga);
        case INSTRUCT -> instruct(saga);       // the pivot: 11.06
        case RELEASE  -> release(saga);        // the compensation: 11.05
        case COMPLETED, FAILED, PARKED -> { }  // finished, or waiting for a person
    }
}

Listing every value, the finished ones included, makes adding a step a visible decision. The compiler will not insist: only a switch that returns a value or matches patterns must cover every case (2.12). The whole process is readable in one class, and "where is payout p-1042?" is one query on payout_sagas.

Also seen. Eventuate Tram Sagas, which builds a saga definition in Java with a step, its participant and its compensation. Axon Framework's @Saga classes, in event-sourced systems. A workflow engine such as Temporal, Camunda or AWS Step Functions holding the state for you (11.11).

When to break it. A saga with 2 steps and no pivot needs only a durable job with a retry. The full version costs one more collection, worker and dashboard.

.NET anchor. A MassTransit MassTransitStateMachine<T> with its saga repository is the closest match: states, events, and a persisted instance per process. An NServiceBus Saga<TData> stores its data the same way. The difference is that here you write the worker loop yourself, unless you adopt an engine.

See also. 2.12, 2.13, 5.06, 8.04, 8.05, 9.04, 9.07, 9.08, 11.05, 11.06, 11.07, The Yard, chapter 8, Document data: Amazon DocumentDB and the MongoDB API

11.03 Choreograph the same saga with events

Then.

  • J2EE era: message-driven beans, EJBs the server calls once per message, chained through JMS queues. Each bean consumed a message, did its work, and sent the next message, inside an XA transaction that spanned the queue and the database. The XA transaction made consume, write and send one atomic unit, which is what the outbox and an idempotent consumer do today.
@MessageDriven(mappedName = "jms/LedgerReserved")
public class InstructBankBean implements MessageListener {
    public void onMessage(Message message) {
        // read the payout ID, call the bank, send to jms/BankInstructed
    }
}
  • Boot era: the same chain with @JmsListener methods and JmsTemplate against ActiveMQ or IBM MQ, usually without XA, and so usually with duplicate handling bolted on after an incident.

Recognise it by. javax.ejb.MessageDriven, javax.jms.MessageListener, onMessage(Message), @JmsListener, JmsTemplate, and queue names that read like steps, such as jms/LedgerReserved.

The rookie version.

@SqsListener("payouts-ledger-events")
void onLedgerReserved(LedgerReserved event) {
    Payout payout = payouts.findById(event.payoutId()).orElseThrow();
    String ref = bankGatewayClient.instruct(UUID.randomUUID().toString(),
            InstructionRequest.from(payout));
    payouts.save(payout.withStatus(PayoutStatus.PAID));
    snsTemplate.sendNotification("payout-events", new PayoutCompleted(payout.id(), ref), null);
}

What goes wrong. @SqsListener is the annotation from Spring Cloud AWS, the library that wires AWS services into Spring, for a method that consumes an SQS queue (10.04). snsTemplate is its SNS publisher (10.02). SQS delivers a message at least once, so LedgerReserved for one payout sometimes arrives twice. Each delivery generates a new idempotency key, so the bank pays £1,240.50 twice. The listener also writes the payout and then publishes to SNS, two systems with no shared transaction (9.06). A crash between them completes the payout and tells nobody.

Do this now. In choreography there is no orchestrator. Each service listens for events and reacts by doing its own step and publishing its own event. Nobody calls anybody to say "now do yours". On Payouts the same saga runs like this:

  1. PayoutController saves the payout as PENDING with PayoutRequested in the outbox, in one transaction. OutboxRelay publishes it to payout-events.
  2. The ledger service receives PayoutRequested on its own queue, reserves the money, and publishes LedgerReserved. If it refuses, it publishes a refusal, and Payouts marks the payout FAILED.
  3. LedgerEventsListener in Payouts receives LedgerReserved on payouts-ledger-events, the queue Payouts subscribes to the ledger's own topic, ledger-events. It moves the payout to RESERVED with a conditional update and instructs the bank with the payout's stored key.
  4. On success it moves the payout through INSTRUCTED to PAID, with PayoutCompleted in the outbox. On refusal it writes FAILED with PayoutFailed.
  5. The ledger hears PayoutFailed and releases its own reservation. That is the compensation, and the ledger owns it. ClaimantNotificationListener and PayoutAuditListener react to both outcomes.
@SqsListener("payouts-ledger-events")
void onLedgerReserved(LedgerReserved event) {
    Optional<Payout> reserved = payouts.markReserved(event.payoutId(), event.reservationId());
    if (reserved.isEmpty()) return;               // already PAID or FAILED: a late duplicate
    Payout payout = reserved.get();
    var outcome = bankGatewayClient.instruct(payout.idempotencyKey(), InstructionRequest.from(payout));
    switch (outcome) {
        case Instructed ok -> recorder.completed(payout, ok.instruction().reference());
        case Rejected no   -> recorder.failed(payout, no.reason());
        case Unknown u     -> throw new BankOutcomeUnknown(payout.id(), u.cause());
    }
}

markReserved uses findAndModify to move the status from PENDING or RESERVED to RESERVED, and returns empty when the payout has already moved on. A duplicate delivery therefore finds RESERVED and repeats the bank call with the same key, which the bank treats as the same instruction. A late duplicate finds PAID or FAILED and stops. recorder writes the status and the outbox event in one transaction, on condition that the payout is still RESERVED, so two deliveries running at once cannot write 2 PayoutCompleted events. InstructionOutcome and its three records are the sealed interface of 7.07. An unknown outcome throws, so the message is not acknowledged. SQS delivers it again after the visibility timeout, the period a received message stays hidden from other consumers (10.06). After 5 receives, the maxReceiveCount set on the queue's redrive policy, it moves to the queue's dead-letter queue, which is this design's version of PARKED (10.08).

The state of the saga is the payout's status, plus whatever each other service holds. No single document says where the whole saga is.

Also seen. Axon Framework sagas, which react to events with @SagaEventHandler and send commands: choreography on the outside, orchestration on the inside. Kafka with a consumer per step, in organisations that run Kafka rather than SNS and SQS.

When to break it. Choreography with no correlation ID and no audit trail is unworkable past 3 steps. If you cannot trace one payout across every service, add tracing (13.05) and payout-audit before you add a fourth step.

.NET anchor. MassTransit or NServiceBus consumers subscribed to each other's events, with no saga class, are the same shape. So is a chain of Azure Functions with Service Bus triggers.

See also. 9.06, 9.07, 10.04, 10.06, 10.07, 10.08, 10.12, 13.05, 11.04, Messaging and WebSockets

11.04 Choose orchestration or choreography

The rookie version.

@SqsListener("notify-claimant")
void onPayoutFailed(PayoutFailed event) {
    notifier.tell(event.claimId(), "Your payout is delayed");
    if (event.reason().equals("BANK_TIMEOUT")) {
        publisher.publish(new PayoutRequested(event.payoutId(), event.claimId(), event.amount()));
    }
}

What goes wrong. The team chose choreography so that services would be decoupled. Then a business rule arrived, "retry a payout the bank timed out", and the nearest listener took it. The saga's logic now lives partly in the notification listener. During a 40-minute bank outage each failure requests the payout again, which fails again. One claimant receives 6 "delayed" messages for one payout of £1,240.50. Nobody reviewing the payment code sees the loop, because it is in another listener's file. The reason itself is a warning: a bank timeout is an unknown outcome, not a failure, so each new request risks paying twice (11.06).

Do this now. Both styles are sound, and experienced engineers disagree about the default. Decide per saga, with these questions:

  1. Does the order of steps matter, with decisions between them? Reserve, then instruct only if reserved, then release only if refused. That is orchestration's strength: the rules sit in one class.
  2. Is there a pivot step? An irreversible step needs someone to decide, with full knowledge, whether to go ahead. An orchestrator can check everything first (11.06).
  3. Who must answer "where is this payout?" With an orchestrator it is one query. With choreography it is a trace across services.
  4. Are the reactions independent? Notifying the claimant, writing the audit trail and confirming the ledger posting each depend only on PayoutCompleted. No reaction affects another. That is choreography's strength: add a fourth subscriber without touching Payouts.
  5. Who owns each step? If another team owns a step and its undo, letting it react to your events keeps their logic in their service.
  6. Can an undo overtake the step it undoes? In the choreographed version a release can reach the ledger before a slow reservation has landed. The money then stays held, and only a reconciliation job will find it. An orchestrator releases only after it has seen the reservation's result.

The case for orchestration as the default: one place to read the process, explicit compensation, and a clear owner for timeouts and stuck sagas. Its cost is a central component that knows every participant. The case for choreography as the default: no central component, independent deployment, and natural fan-out. Its cost is a process that exists only as an emergent property, which is hard to see, change and test as a whole.

Payouts' answer is mixed. PayoutSaga orchestrates the money path: reserve and instruct. Everything after PayoutCompleted is choreographed through payout-events. A rule of thumb that covers most cases: orchestrate decisions, choreograph notifications.

Also seen. Orchestration through events: the orchestrator sends command messages and waits for reply events, instead of calling over HTTP. It keeps one owner of the logic and gains a queue's buffering. Axon and Eventuate Tram both work this way.

When to break it. A team that owns every service in the saga may choreograph decisions too, if they trace every event and test the chain end to end. The cost is that the rules are spread across listeners, so changing the process means changing several deployables at once.

.NET anchor. The same split exists in MassTransit: a state machine saga is orchestration, and plain consumers of published events are choreography. The trade-offs are the same in either language.

See also. 10.01, 10.13, 11.02, 11.03, 11.06, 21.03, 21.04, Messaging and WebSockets

11.05 Write compensating actions

Then.

  • Spring era: the reconciliation batch. A Spring Batch job ran overnight, compared the payouts table with the ledger's extract, and wrote a report of differences. The operations team then corrected each one by hand. It was right when volumes were low and a day's delay was acceptable.
@Bean
public Step reconcileStep() {
    return stepBuilderFactory.get("reconcile")
            .<LedgerLine, Difference>chunk(500)
            .reader(ledgerExtractReader()).processor(matcher()).writer(reportWriter())
            .build();
}

Recognise it by. org.springframework.batch.*, @EnableBatchProcessing, ItemReader, ItemProcessor and ItemWriter, StepBuilderFactory and JobBuilderFactory, and jobs named reconcile or fixup.

The rookie version.

private void compensate(SagaState saga, Payout payout) {
    ledgerClient.post(UUID.randomUUID().toString(),
            new Posting(payout.accountId(), payout.amount().negate(), "reversal"));
    sagas.save(saga.withStep(SagaStep.FAILED));
}

What goes wrong. The bank refused the payout, so the saga must undo the reservation. The rookie code posts a negative amount with a fresh key. The ledger is slow and the first call times out after the ledger has applied it. The worker tries 4 times in all, each with a new key, and every attempt lands. The account now shows 4 reversals of £1,240.50, a credit of £4,962.00 that nobody paid. Undoing by posting the opposite amount was also the wrong action. A reservation is a hold, and the right undo is to release the hold, which leaves a clean history.

Do this now. A compensating action undoes the business effect of a completed step. It is not a database rollback. Time has passed, and other writes may have happened in between. Write each one by these rules:

  1. Use the domain's own undo. Release the reservation. Do not delete it or post its opposite. Ask the owning team for an explicit release operation if they have none. On Payouts that was a negotiation with the ledger team (The Yard, chapter 11).
  2. Make it idempotent. Use a key derived from the saga, such as "release-" + payoutId. Every attempt sends the same key. Releasing an already released reservation must succeed.
  3. Make it retryable until it succeeds. A compensation that gives up leaves money held forever. Retry with backoff, and after a cap, park the saga and alert a person (11.09).
  4. Record the intent first. Move the saga to RELEASE and save before calling. A crash then resumes the compensation, not the forward step.
  5. Undo only what happened, once it is certain. If reservationId is empty, the reservation's outcome is unknown. Send the reservation again with the same reserveKey. The ledger answers with the hold it already made, or makes it now, and either way you have an ID to release. If it refuses, there is nothing to release. Asking whether a reservation exists is not enough: a slow first request can land after the answer, and that hold is never released.
  6. Undo in reverse order. With more steps, compensate the most recent completed step first.
private void release(SagaState saga) {
    String reservation = saga.reservationId() != null
            ? saga.reservationId()
            : settleReservation(saga);   // reserve again with reserveKey: the hold's ID, or null if refused
    if (reservation != null) {
        ledgerClient.release(reservation, "release-" + saga.payoutId());  // same key every attempt
    }
    finisher.failed(saga);      // saga FAILED, payout FAILED, PayoutFailed in the outbox: one transaction
}

If release throws, the saga stays at RELEASE and the worker tries again later.

Also seen. Compensation by the participant itself, as in 11.03, where the ledger releases its own reservation when it hears PayoutFailed. It moves the undo to the team that understands it. Keep the reconciliation job too. It finds the cases the compensations missed.

When to break it. Some effects have no undo. An email to the claimant cannot be unsent. The compensation is then a second, corrective message. Design for it by sending such messages only after the pivot (11.06).

.NET anchor. MassTransit's routing slips call this "compensate" on each activity, in reverse order. Durable Functions leaves it to your orchestrator code. The rules above apply to both.

See also. 7.07, 7.16, 9.09, 9.10, 11.06, 11.07, 11.09, The Yard, chapter 11, HTTP clients and resilience

11.06 Handle the pivot step that cannot be undone

The rookie version.

try {
    String ref = bankGatewayClient.instruct(saga.instructionKey(), InstructionRequest.from(payout));
    payouts.markCompleted(payout.id(), ref);
    outbox.save(OutboxEvent.of(new PayoutCompleted(payout.id(), ref)));
} catch (Exception e) {
    ledgerClient.release(saga.reservationId(), "release-" + saga.payoutId());
    payouts.markFailed(payout.id(), e.getMessage());
}

What goes wrong. The bank accepts the instruction for £1,240.50. Then DocumentDB fails over to a new primary, and markCompleted throws. The catch treats every exception as "the payout failed". It releases the reservation and marks the payout FAILED. The claimant is paid, but the ledger shows nothing and Payouts shows a failure. The claims handler sees FAILED and resubmits. The claimant is paid twice, and the second payment is now reserved and recorded properly, so it looks correct.

Do this now. The pivot step is the step after which the saga can no longer go back. On Payouts it is the bank instruction: once the bank has it, money leaves Sorrel. Every step falls into one of 3 kinds, and they must come in this order:

  1. Compensatable steps come before the pivot. Reserving in the ledger can be released.
  2. The pivot comes once. Instructing the bank.
  3. Retriable steps come after the pivot. They cannot be undone, so they must be certain to succeed eventually. Recording COMPLETED and the outbox event is a local write, retried until DocumentDB accepts it. Confirming the ledger posting is retried by LedgerConfirmListener until the ledger accepts it.

The rules that follow:

  1. Check everything before the pivot. Is the claim still approved? Is the policy still in force? Are the bank details verified? Each check that can fail belongs in a compensatable step or before the saga starts.
  2. After the pivot, only go forward. No exception after a successful instruction may lead to compensation. Catch failures of the local write, leave the saga at INSTRUCT with the bank reference unrecorded, and retry.
  3. Never compensate an unknown pivot. A timeout means you do not know. Ask the bank by instructionKey. Sending the same instruction again with the same key is one way to ask, if the bank's contract says so and the bank still remembers the key (7.07). Only a refusal of the instruction itself is definite. An error such as "key reused with a different request" is unknown, not a refusal (11.10). The 7.07 wrapper tests for that error first and returns Unknown, before it maps any other 4xx to Rejected.
  4. Park what you still cannot resolve. After the step's deadline, move the saga to PARKED with the reason, and alert a person (11.08, 11.09).
private void instruct(SagaState saga) {
    var outcome = bankGatewayClient.instruct(saga.instructionKey(), InstructionRequest.from(saga));
    switch (outcome) {
        case Instructed ok -> finisher.completed(saga, ok.instruction().reference()); // retried till it commits
        case Rejected no   -> sagas.save(saga.next(SagaStep.RELEASE, no.reason()));   // definite: undo
        case Unknown u     -> sagas.save(saga.retryLater(u.cause().getMessage(), clock));
    }
}

The call returns the InstructionOutcome of 7.07: Payouts' wrapper turns the bank's reply, a 4xx or a timeout into one of its three records. If finisher.completed throws, the saga is still at INSTRUCT. The next attempt sends the same key, the bank answers with the same reference, and the write is tried again.

A bank that later returns the money, because the account was closed, does not reopen this saga. That is a new business event with its own process, recorded against the payout rather than undoing this saga.

Also seen. Moving the pivot later. Some teams make the bank instruction a two-stage "prepare, then release funds" call, if the bank offers one. The pivot is then the release, and preparing becomes compensatable.

When to break it. Occasionally a step after the pivot can legitimately fail for good, such as a notification to a claimant whose address is invalid. Record it and alert a person. Do not unwind the payment. The cost is a manual task in a queue.

.NET anchor. No .NET library marks a pivot for you either. A Durable Functions orchestrator or a MassTransit state machine needs the same ordering, written by hand: compensatable activities first, the irreversible one once, and retried activities after it.

See also. 7.07, 7.16, 9.12, 11.05, 11.08, 11.09, Sealed types and pattern matching

11.07 Make every saga step idempotent and retryable

Then.

  • Boot era: Spring Retry. A @Retryable method was retried in process, with @Recover as the method called after the last attempt. It was the standard Spring answer for years. Its repository was archived on 27 July 2026, superseded by retry support in Spring Framework 7 itself.
@Retryable(value = LedgerUnavailable.class, maxAttempts = 4, backoff = @Backoff(delay = 500))
public LedgerReservation reserve(Payout payout) { ... }

@Recover
public LedgerReservation giveUp(LedgerUnavailable e, Payout payout) { ... }

In-process retry is still useful for a brief glitch. It is not enough for a saga, because the retry state dies with the pod.

Recognise it by. org.springframework.retry.annotation.Retryable, @Recover, @EnableRetry, @Backoff, and the spring-retry artifactId.

The rookie version.

@Scheduled(fixedDelay = 5_000)
void runPendingSagas() {
    for (SagaState saga : sagas.findByStep(SagaStep.RESERVE)) {
        var r = ledgerClient.reserve(UUID.randomUUID().toString(), ReserveRequest.from(saga));
        sagas.save(saga.reserved(r.id()));
    }
}

What goes wrong. @Scheduled runs a method on a timer, in every pod. payouts-api has 2 pods, so both pick up the same saga. Each uses a new idempotency key, so the ledger sees 2 different requests. Then a deploy restarts one pod after its call reached the ledger but before it saved, and the new pod reserves a third time. One payout of £1,240.50 ends up with 3 reservations, £3,721.50 held on the claimant's account. Only one reservationId is saved, so the other 2 are never released.

Do this now. Idempotent means doing it twice has the same effect as doing it once. Every step will run more than once, after a timeout, a crash or a duplicate message, so every step must be idempotent. Build it in at 4 layers:

  1. One key per step, created once. Generate reserveKey and instructionKey when the saga is created, and store them in SagaState. Every attempt, on any pod, sends the stored key (7.07, 9.10).
  2. One worker per saga at a time. Claim a saga with a lease: a time until which one worker owns it. findAndModify sets the lease and returns the document in one atomic write, so 2 pods cannot both claim it. A pod that dies loses the lease when the time passes.
  3. Conditional state changes. Save the next step with @Version, so a stale worker gets an OptimisticLockingFailureException and discards its result (9.11).
  4. Idempotent consumers. In a choreographed step, guard with the status check of 11.03, and deduplicate by event ID where the step has no natural guard (10.07).
SagaState claimNext(Instant now) {      // query, where: static imports from Query, Criteria
    return mongoTemplate.findAndModify(
            query(where("step").in(SagaStep.RESERVE, SagaStep.INSTRUCT, SagaStep.RELEASE)
                    .and("nextAttemptAt").lte(now)
                    .and("leaseUntil").lt(now)),
            new Update().set("leaseUntil", now.plusSeconds(60)).inc("attempts", 1),
            FindAndModifyOptions.options().returnNew(true),
            SagaState.class);
}

MongoTemplate is Spring Data MongoDB's lower-level API, for the queries and updates a repository cannot express (8.04). Create every saga with leaseUntil set to Instant.EPOCH and nextAttemptAt set to the creation time, because a lt or lte condition does not match a missing or null field. For the same reason, reset leaseUntil to Instant.EPOCH, not null, when a step's result is saved, or the next step waits for the lease to expire. Set the lease longer than the slowest step, including its HTTP timeouts and retries (7.03). Three attempts at the bank, each up to 1 second to connect and 2 to read, with the waits of 7.04, take about 10 seconds. The status check of 7.07 adds up to 3 more, so 60 is ample.

Retry at two speeds. Within one attempt, retry a transient failure 2 or 3 times with a short backoff, using Resilience4j, the library closest to Polly, on Boot 3.5 (7.04). In Boot 4, Spring Framework 7's own @Retryable can do this. Across attempts, set nextAttemptAt with exponential backoff and jitter, a random part of each wait. Park the saga after a cap on attempts, and reset attempts to 0 when the step changes, so the cap applies per step.

Also seen. ShedLock, which runs a @Scheduled method on one pod at a time (3.10). It stops 2 pods running the loop together but serialises every saga behind one lock. A per-saga lease scales better.

When to break it. A read-only step, such as fetching the policy, needs no key. It still needs to tolerate running twice, which a read does.

.NET anchor. Hangfire's distributed locks and MassTransit's saga concurrency, which uses optimistic versions in most repositories, solve the same problem. Polly is the in-process layer, like Resilience4j.

See also. 3.10, 7.03, 7.04, 7.07, 8.04, 8.05, 9.09, 9.10, 9.11, 10.07, The Yard, chapter 8, HTTP clients and resilience

11.08 Time out a step and decide what happens next

What goes wrong. The bank gateway answers "pending", then goes quiet. Each call has a 2-second read timeout, but the step has no limit. The saga retries every few minutes for 9 days, until the claimant phones.

Do this now. An HTTP timeout bounds one call (7.03). A step deadline bounds the whole step across every retry. Store it in SagaState.stepDeadline when the step starts. The worker checks it on every claim, before running the step. Once it has passed, what happens depends on where the step sits:

  1. Before the pivot, compensate. A reservation with no recorded outcome is settled by reserveKey, then released (11.05).
  2. At the pivot, never compensate. Move the saga to PARKED and alert a person who can phone the bank (11.06).
  3. After the pivot, keep retrying and alert.

Choose deadlines from the business, such as the bank's agreed processing time, not a round number.

In a choreographed saga nobody owns the clock, so schedule a check: an SQS message delayed by up to 15 minutes, saying "check payout p-1042" (10.20). For a longer wait, store the due time in DocumentDB and poll for it.

See also. 7.03, 7.15, 10.20, 11.05, 11.06, 11.09

11.09 Find and repair stuck sagas

What goes wrong. A change to the creation code stops setting leaseUntil on new sagas, and the worker never claims them. For 3 days 212 payouts sit at RESERVE, unnoticed.

Do this now.
