  1. Define stuck. A saga is stuck when it is unfinished and on one step longer than Payouts' slowest normal step, 15 minutes. A PARKED saga always counts.
  2. Make the query cheap. Keep updatedAt on SagaState, set only when step changes, so retries still count. Index { step: 1, updatedAt: 1 } (8.06).
  3. Measure it. Register a Micrometer gauge, payouts.sagas.stuck, tagged by step, over a count that a scheduled query refreshes, not a query run at every scrape (14.02). Alert as soon as it is above 0, since the definition already waits 15 minutes (14.07).
  4. Repair through an audited, internal endpoint, never by editing documents (5.22). The actions: retry now, resolve with a bank reference, and release, allowed only before the pivot. Run any re-drive sweep on one pod (3.10).

In a choreographed saga the dead-letter queue is the stuck list. Watch its depth, and redrive after a fix (10.09).

See also. 3.10, 5.22, 8.06, 10.09, 14.02, 14.07, 14.08, 20.08, Actuator and observability

11.10 Protect a saga in flight with a semantic lock

What goes wrong. A saga gives up isolation, so other code sees a payout halfway through. While the saga for claim C-4471 is at INSTRUCT, a claims handler changes the bank details on the claim. The first bank call timed out. The retry rereads the claim and instructs £1,240.50 to the new account with the same idempotency key. The bank rejects the mismatch, the saga takes that as a refusal, and it releases the reservation for a payment that had in fact succeeded.

Do this now. A semantic lock is an application-level flag that says "a saga is using this". It is not a database lock.

  1. Set payoutInFlight on the claim when the saga starts, in the same transaction as the saga document.
  2. Make every other change to the claim conditional on the flag being empty. A refused change returns 409 Conflict (5.04).
  3. Clear the flag when the saga reaches COMPLETED or FAILED. A PARKED saga keeps it until a person resolves it.
  4. Copy what the pivot needs, such as the bank details, into SagaState at the start, so the saga never rereads it.
UpdateResult result = mongoTemplate.updateFirst(
        query(where("_id").is(claimId).and("payoutInFlight").isNull()),
        new Update().set("bankDetails", newDetails),
        Claim.class);
if (result.getModifiedCount() == 0) throw new ClaimLocked(claimId);   // 409: a payout is in flight

See also. 5.04, 5.11, 8.04, 9.12, 11.01

11.11 Know when to use Step Functions, Temporal or Camunda instead

What goes wrong. A team with one 3-step saga adopts a workflow engine for it. They now run a new cluster, learn a new programming model, and debug a new failure mode, to replace about 200 lines of code.

Do this now. A workflow engine stores a saga's state and runs its retries, timers and compensations for you. Consider one when you have many saga types, waits of days or weeks, steps done by people, or a business that wants to see the process drawn.

  • AWS Step Functions: a managed state machine written in Amazon States Language, JSON with Retry and Catch on each state. Java starts it with the SDK's SfnClient. Nothing to run, but the logic lives outside your code.
  • Temporal: durable execution. You write the workflow as ordinary Java behind @WorkflowInterface, and the engine replays it after a crash. The code must be deterministic, and you run a Temporal cluster or pay for Temporal Cloud.
  • Camunda: workflows drawn in BPMN, a diagram the business can read, with Java code for each task.
  • Axon Framework: sagas inside an event-sourced system. Choose it for event sourcing, not sagas alone.

See also. 11.02, 11.04, 21.09

11.12 Test a saga's failure paths

What goes wrong. The saga's tests cover the happy path and one refusal. The first time the bank times out after acting, production finds the bug that 7.16 describes, with real money.

Do this now. List every failure at every step, and test each one. For each step that means: a refusal, a timeout before the other side acted, a timeout after it acted, and a crash between the call and the save. Use fakes of LedgerClient and BankGatewayClient that can be told to fail in each of those ways, and that remember what they did. Assert on money, not on calls: how much is held, and how many payments were made.

@ParameterizedTest
@EnumSource(BankFailure.class)
void noBankFailureLosesOrDuplicatesMoney(BankFailure failure) {
    bank.failNextWith(failure);                    // a fake, not a mock
    sagaRunner.runUntilQuiet(payoutId);            // claim and advance until nothing is due
    assertThat(bank.paymentsFor(payoutId)).isLessThanOrEqualTo(1);
    assertThat(ledger.heldFor(payoutId)).isEqualTo(expectedHold(failure));
}

@ParameterizedTest with @EnumSource runs the test once per value of BankFailure, an enum of the four failures above, like xUnit's [Theory]. expectedHold returns what the ledger should still hold for that failure once the saga is quiet.

Run the end-to-end path separately, against real MongoDB and LocalStack, an AWS emulator in a container (16.12). On Boot 4, Testcontainers 2.x needs withReplicaSet() for the saga's transactions. The 1.x that Boot 3.5 manages starts a replica set itself (9.04).

See also. 16.02, 16.10, 16.12, 16.13, 16.14, Testing Spring Boot

⚠Review checklist
  • If you see @Transactional around calls to the ledger or the bank: the database rolls back and the other systems do not. See 11.01.
  • If you see a saga whose progress is held in local variables or a catch block: a pod restart loses money in flight. See 11.02.
  • If you see a listener that acts on an event with no conditional status update, or with a new key per delivery: a duplicate message repeats the step. See 11.03.
  • If you see a business decision, such as a retry, inside a notification or audit listener: the saga's logic is now hidden in a file nobody reviews with it. See 11.04.
  • If you see a compensation that deletes a record, posts an opposite amount, or uses a fresh key per attempt: retries multiply the undo. See 11.05.
  • If you see a catch-all after the bank call that releases the reservation: a local failure undoes a payment the bank made. See 11.06.
  • If you see a timeout on the bank call treated as a refusal: the saga compensates a pivot that happened. See 11.06.
  • If you see a @Scheduled step runner with no lease, or idempotency keys generated per attempt: 2 pods run the same step with different keys. See 11.07.
  • If you see a step with an HTTP timeout but no step deadline: the saga retries for days and nobody notices. See 11.08.
  • If you see a new saga with no stuck-saga metric or alert: the first sign of trouble is a claimant's phone call. See 11.09.
  • If you see an update to a claim that ignores whether a payout is in flight: the saga acts on data changed under it. See 11.10.
  • If you see a workflow engine proposed for one short saga: a cluster and a programming model to replace a few hundred lines. See 11.11.
  • If you see saga tests that cover only success and one refusal: the timeout-after-success path is untested. See 11.12.

Part IV · The how-to12. Logging#

A log line is the only witness to what Payouts did at 02:14 when nobody was watching. This part covers writing that line well: through the SLF4J facade, at a level the team agrees on, as structured JSON, with the payout's identifiers attached and its personal data left out. It shows how to log an exception once, how to run Logback or Log4j2 behind the same code, how to change a level without a deploy, and how to read the logging setup you inherit. Trace IDs in log lines belong to part 13.

★What a veteran knows
  • A log line is written once and read under pressure by someone who did not write it. Write it for that person: what was being done, to which payout, and what happened.
  • Logs are for diagnosis, metrics for counting, traces for following a request, and audit records for proof. A team that uses one for another's job ends up paging on log counts.
  • Every logging API on the classpath must end up in one backend, or its lines go nowhere. When a line is missing, check the dependency tree before the configuration.
  • The log store is a copy of production data with weaker access control than the database. On Payouts, anything you would not paste into the team chat stays out of it.
  • An exception appears once, with its stack trace, at the place that decides what happens next. Three copies of one failure look like three incidents.
  • DEBUG in production is a tool you switch on for minutes, on one logger, on purpose. Then you switch it off.
◷How we got hereOn 24 November 2021 an email reached the Apache Software Foundation's security address.

On 24 November 2021 an email reached the Apache Software Foundation's security address. Chen Zhaojun of the Alibaba Cloud Security team had found a flaw in Log4j 2, with a proof of concept. A logged string could make the library look a name up through JNDI, Java's directory interface, and run code loaded from an LDAP directory server. The cause was a 2013 community contribution that added JNDI lookup support. Apache committed a fix on 5 December. On 9 December the Alibaba engineer warned that the bug was being discussed on WeChat. Apache published version 2.15.0 on 10 December, the day the CVE went public with a CVSS score of 10.0. On 13 December Jen Easterly, the director of CISA, told industry it was "one of the most serious I've seen in my entire career, if not the most serious". The US Cyber Safety Review Board reported in July 2022 that one federal cabinet department had spent 33,000 hours on its response. It called Log4j an "endemic vulnerability".

12.01 Log with SLF4J and placeholders

Then.

  • J2EE era: System.out.println and e.printStackTrace(). Right for a program with one user and a console. On a server they give no level, no logger name and no way to turn anything off.
  • J2EE era: java.util.logging (JUL), the logger built into the JDK since 1.4. It needed no dependency, which is why old libraries chose it.
private static final Logger LOG = Logger.getLogger(PayoutService.class.getName());

LOG.log(Level.INFO, "Payout {0} reserved", payoutId);
if (LOG.isLoggable(Level.FINE)) {
    LOG.fine("Ledger answered " + response);
}
  • Spring era: Jakarta Commons Logging (LogFactory.getLog(...)), a facade that Spring itself used, and log4j 1.x called directly. Both took one Object message, so every debug call was concatenated inside an isDebugEnabled() guard. SLF4J's placeholders made the guard unnecessary for most calls.

Recognise it by. java.util.logging.Logger, Level.FINE, org.apache.commons.logging.LogFactory, org.apache.log4j.Logger, System.out.println in service code, printStackTrace(), and if (log.isDebugEnabled()) around every call.

The rookie version.

private final Logger log = LoggerFactory.getLogger(PayoutService.class);

public Payout pay(Claim claim, PolicySummary policy) {
    log.debug("Paying claim " + claim.id() + " for " + claim.amount()
            + " under policy " + policy);
    Payout payout = payouts.save(Payout.requested(claim));
    log.info("Payout " + payout.id() + " requested for claim " + claim.id());
    return payout;
}

What goes wrong. Production runs at INFO, so nobody reads the debug line. Java still builds it. Every call converts policy to a string, joins six pieces, and throws the result away. In a nightly batch of 5,000 claims, that is 5,000 strings built for nothing, each carrying the whole policy summary. The INFO line has a second cost. Its text is different for every payout, so the log store cannot group "the same message" across payouts. Searching for all requested payouts means a regular expression instead of a field.

Do this now. SLF4J (the Simple Logging Facade for Java) is an API with no logging of its own. Your code calls it, and a backend behind it writes the lines. A Boot starter is one dependency that brings a feature's libraries and their auto-configuration, such as spring-boot-starter-web. Every starter brings SLF4J with Logback as the backend, through spring-boot-starter-logging.

  1. Import org.slf4j.Logger and org.slf4j.LoggerFactory. Never import the backend's classes in service code.
  2. Declare one logger per class, as a private static final field. Its name is the class's full name, com.sorrel.payouts.PayoutService. Names form a tree by package, so logging.level.com.sorrel.payouts=DEBUG sets every logger beneath that package.
  3. Keep the message text fixed and pass values as arguments to {} placeholders. SLF4J formats the message only if the level is enabled.
  4. Remember that the arguments themselves are still evaluated. A placeholder saves the formatting, not a method call you put in the argument list (12.10).
  5. For values you will search on, use the SLF4J 2 fluent API and add them as key-value pairs, or put them in the MDC, a per-thread map that the backend adds to every line (12.04).
  6. Know where those values show up. In structured JSON they are fields (12.03). Boot's default text pattern prints neither, so the line below reads only "payout requested" on a laptop unless the pattern adds %kvp (12.07).
private static final Logger log = LoggerFactory.getLogger(PayoutService.class);

public Payout pay(Claim claim) {
    log.debug("paying claim {} for {}", claim.id(), claim.amount());
    Payout payout = payouts.save(Payout.requested(claim));
    log.atInfo()
       .setMessage("payout requested")
       .addKeyValue("payoutId", payout.id())
       .addKeyValue("claimId", claim.id())
       .log();
    return payout;
}

The facade is also what lets old libraries share one output. Bridges route their APIs into SLF4J, and one backend writes everything.

Also seen. The Log4j2 API (LogManager.getLogger()) in teams that standardised on Log4j2. It adds lambda arguments, at the price of tying code to one backend (12.08). System.Logger, in the JDK since Java 9, for a library that must have no dependencies at all. Lombok's @Slf4j in older code. Lombok is a compiler plug-in that generates code from annotations, and @Slf4j generates the same field. Payouts does not use it.

When to break it. A one-off command-line tool may print to the console. A test may too. The cost is that nothing about the output can be configured, so it must never reach payouts-api.

.NET anchor. SLF4J is ILogger<PayoutService> from Microsoft.Extensions.Logging, and Logback is the provider behind it, like Serilog or NLog. Two differences matter. The Java logger is a static field, not an injected service. And .NET message templates have named holes, {PayoutId}, that become structured fields. SLF4J's {} is positional and names nothing, so fields come from key-value pairs or the MDC.

See also. 12.03, 12.04, 12.10, 12.12, Appendix I: Your library, translated

12.02 Choose log levels the team agrees on

Then.

  • J2EE era: JUL's seven levels, SEVERE, WARNING, INFO, CONFIG, FINE, FINER and FINEST, and log4j 1.x's FATAL. SLF4J settled on five, and the old names map onto them: SEVERE to ERROR, FINE to DEBUG, FINEST to TRACE.

Recognise it by. Level.SEVERE, Level.FINEST, log.fatal(, org.apache.log4j.Priority, and logging.properties files with .level= lines.

The rookie version.

public LedgerReservation reserve(Payout payout) {
    log.info("Entering reserve() for {}", payout.id());
    try { return ledger.reserve(payout.idempotencyKey(), toRequest(payout));
    } catch (ResourceAccessException e) {
        log.error("Ledger timed out, retrying", e);
        throw e;                       // the retry around this call then succeeds
    } finally {
        log.info("Leaving reserve()");
    }
}

What goes wrong. Payouts had an alert on any ERROR line in a 5-minute window. One night the ledger was slow for 40 seconds, in the middle of the nightly batch. The ledger retry allows 3 attempts (7.04). 120 payouts failed once or twice each, and every failed attempt wrote an ERROR line: about 200 of them. Every payout then succeeded on a later attempt. The on-call engineer was paged at 02:14 for nothing. After the third such night the team muted the alert, and the next real failure went unseen for an hour. The entering and leaving lines added to the noise. A payout that needed 3 attempts wrote 8 lines from this one method, 6 INFO and 2 ERROR, and none of them said that the payout had succeeded.

Do this now. A level is a promise to the reader about what to do with the line. Write the team's meanings down in the repository, then hold reviews to them.

  1. ERROR: an operation failed and nothing else will handle it. Someone should look. One line per failure, with the stack trace (12.05).
  2. WARN: something unexpected that the service handled, which matters if it repeats. A fallback taken, a retry budget exhausted on a non-critical call, a configuration value that looks wrong.
  3. INFO: a business event a support engineer would want, once each. Payout requested, ledger reserved, bank instructed, payout completed. Also startup facts such as the active profiles.
  4. DEBUG: detail for developers. Off in production, and switched on per logger when needed (12.09).
  5. TRACE: step-by-step detail, almost never on.

Then apply three rules that follow from those meanings:

  • A retry attempt is DEBUG. Only the final failure is ERROR, logged once by the code that handles it (12.05). Resilience4j, the library behind Payouts' retries, does not log each attempt for you. To see them, register a consumer on retryRegistry.retry("ledger").getEventPublisher().onRetry(...) and log at DEBUG there.
  • A client's mistake, such as a 400 or a 404, is not an error in Payouts. Log it at INFO without a stack trace, or not at all.
  • Alert on metrics, not on log counts (14.07). Logs explain the alert. They should not raise it.
logging:
  level:
    root: INFO
    com.sorrel.payouts: INFO
    com.sorrel.payouts.ledger: INFO

Setting root explicitly costs one line and removes the question of what the default is.

Also seen. Log4j2's own API keeps FATAL, which SLF4J does not have. SLF4J markers (MarkerFactory.getMarker("PAGER")) tag a line for special routing, which some teams use instead of a level. Prefer a metric for anything that should page.

When to break it. During an incident, turn DEBUG on for one logger for a few minutes. The cost is volume, so turn it off again and say so in the incident channel.

.NET anchor. LogLevel has Trace, Debug, Information, Warning, Error and Critical. SLF4J has no Critical. "Logging": { "LogLevel": { "Default": "Information" } } in appsettings.json is logging.level.root=INFO, and a namespace key there is a package key here.

See also. 12.05, 12.09, 14.07, 7.04

12.03 Turn on structured JSON logging in Boot

Then.

  • Boot era: logstash-logback-encoder, a third-party Logback encoder that writes each event as one JSON object. Boot had no JSON output of its own before 3.4, so this was the standard answer.
<appender name="JSON" class="ch.qos.logback.core.ConsoleAppender">
  <encoder class="net.logstash.logback.encoder.LogstashEncoder"/>
</appender>
<root level="INFO">
  <appender-ref ref="JSON"/>
</root>
  • Boot era: Log4j2's JsonLayout, and later its JsonTemplateLayout, in services on Log4j2.

Recognise it by. net.logstash.logback.encoder.LogstashEncoder, the logstash-logback-encoder artifactId, StructuredArguments.kv(...) in log calls, <JsonLayout> or <JsonTemplateLayout> in log4j2.xml.

The rookie version.

logging.pattern.console={"time":"%d","level":"%p","logger":"%c","msg":"%m"}%n

What goes wrong. It looks like JSON until a message contains a quote. The bank gateway returns account "closed", the line is no longer valid JSON, and the log store keeps it as unparsed text. A stack trace is worse. It spans 87 lines, and the collector reads each line as a separate event, so one failure becomes 87 fragments, none with the payout ID. Nothing escapes newlines or quotes, because a pattern layout was never meant to produce JSON.

Do this now. Structured logging means each event is one machine-readable object with named fields, instead of a line of text. Boot 3.4 added it built in, for both Logback and Log4j2, and Payouts on Boot 3.5 has it.

  1. Pick the format your log platform reads. Boot offers three: ecs (Elastic Common Schema, a standard set of field names), logstash and gelf (the Graylog format). Ask the platform team which one their pipeline parses.
  2. Set logging.structured.format.console. In Kubernetes, write to the console: the node's log agent collects each pod's standard output.
  3. Set it in the Deployment's environment, not in application.yml. Boot reads LOGGING_STRUCTURED_FORMAT_CONSOLE as that property, so the cluster gets JSON and a laptop keeps plain text (4.03, 12.07).
  4. Set spring.application.name. The ECS service name defaults to it, through logging.structured.ecs.service.name.
  5. Use the MDC and SLF4J key-value pairs for fields (12.01, 12.04). They appear as fields of the JSON object, and the stack trace becomes one escaped field.
# application.yml, shared by every environment
spring:
  application:
    name: payouts-api

# the payouts-api Deployment, in the container's env list
- name: LOGGING_STRUCTURED_FORMAT_CONSOLE
  value: ecs
- name: LOGGING_STRUCTURED_ECS_SERVICE_ENVIRONMENT
  value: production

If you also need a file, set logging.structured.format.file and logging.file.name. Boot's file appender rotates the file when it reaches 10 MB. On Kubernetes, prefer the console.

When no built-in format fits, implement Boot's StructuredLogFormatter interface and name your class in the format property. For smaller changes, Boot has logging.structured.json.include, .exclude, .rename and .add, which drop, rename or add fields of a built-in format.

Also seen. logstash-logback-encoder, still maintained and still a good choice when you need its extras, such as its StructuredArguments. Log4j2's JsonTemplateLayout, with an event template, on services that configure Log4j2 directly. A sidecar that parses text lines with regular expressions, which is fragile and should go.

When to break it. On a laptop, JSON is hard to read, so run plain text locally. Also keep text where the only consumer is a person reading a terminal. The cost is that a local log cannot be pasted into the log store's query tools.

.NET anchor. This is builder.Logging.AddJsonConsole(), or Serilog with CompactJsonFormatter. In .NET, the named holes of a message template become fields automatically. Here they do not: fields come only from the MDC and key-value pairs, so a value written into the message text is just text.

See also. 12.04, 12.07, 12.08, 13.06, Actuator and observability

12.04 Add context to every line with MDC

Then.

  • Boot era: a hand-written servlet filter that put a correlation ID from a header into the MDC, and Spring Cloud Sleuth, which added traceId and spanId for you. Both were right before Boot had tracing built in. Micrometer Tracing now does the trace part (13.06).
public void doFilter(ServletRequest req, ServletResponse res, FilterChain chain)
        throws IOException, ServletException {
    MDC.put("correlationId", ((HttpServletRequest) req).getHeader("X-Correlation-Id"));
    try { chain.doFilter(req, res); } finally { MDC.remove("correlationId"); }
}
  • J2EE era: log4j 1.x's NDC, a nested stack of context strings pushed and popped by hand.

Recognise it by. javax.servlet.Filter classes that call MDC.put, org.apache.log4j.NDC, X-Correlation-Id or X-B3-TraceId headers, and spring.sleuth.* keys.

The rookie version.

@SqsListener("ledger-confirm")
void onMessage(EventEnvelope<PayoutCompletedData> event) {
    MDC.put("payoutId", event.payoutId());
    service.confirm(event.payoutId());
}

What goes wrong. @SqsListener is Spring Cloud AWS's annotation for a method that receives messages from an SQS queue. The MDC (Mapped Diagnostic Context) is a map held per thread, and the backend adds its entries to every line that thread writes. The listener's threads come from a pool and are reused. Nothing removes payoutId, so it stays on the thread after the message is done. The next message on that thread was malformed and failed to deserialise before the listener ran. The container's error line carried payoutId=p-1043 from the previous message. Someone spent 40 minutes investigating a payout that was fine.

Do this now.

  1. Put context in the MDC where a unit of work starts: a request filter, a listener method, a scheduled job. One unit of work, one payout ID.
  2. Remove it when that work ends, always. MDC.putCloseable returns an MDC.MDCCloseable, so try-with-resources removes the key even when an exception is thrown.
  3. Agree the keys as a team and keep them few: payoutId, claimId, sagaId. Never a name, an email or an account number (12.06).
  4. In a text pattern, print an entry with %X{payoutId}. With structured logging (12.03) the entries appear as fields with no extra configuration.
  5. The MDC belongs to one thread. Work handed to an executor, or to a method marked @Async (which Spring runs on another thread), does not see the caller's entries unless a TaskDecorator, Spring's wrapper around each submitted task, copies them (3.04).
  6. Do not add your own trace or correlation ID. Micrometer Tracing puts the trace ID in the MDC for you (13.06).
@SqsListener("ledger-confirm")
void onMessage(EventEnvelope<PayoutCompletedData> event) {
    try (MDC.MDCCloseable p = MDC.putCloseable("payoutId", event.payoutId());
         MDC.MDCCloseable c = MDC.putCloseable("claimId", event.data().claimId())) {
        service.confirm(event.payoutId());
        log.info("ledger posting confirmed");
    }
}

For HTTP, use the same try-with-resources in the method where the payout ID is first known: the controller for /payouts/{id}, the service for a new payout. A servlet filter suits values in headers or the path, such as the idempotency key. On virtual threads (3.01) each request gets a new thread, which hides the leak in HTTP code. The listener pool above still shows it, so remove the keys anyway.

Also seen. SLF4J 2's addKeyValue for a value that belongs to one line only, not to the whole unit of work. In reactive code (Reactor, the library behind Spring WebFlux), the MDC does not follow the work between threads, and teams use Micrometer's context-propagation library instead.

When to break it. A value relevant to a single line goes on that line as a key-value pair, not in the MDC. Putting it in the MDC costs a removal you must not forget.

.NET anchor. using (logger.BeginScope(new Dictionary<string, object> { ["PayoutId"] = id })), or Serilog's LogContext.PushProperty. The using block is the try-with-resources. The difference: .NET scopes flow across await through AsyncLocal<T>. The MDC is a ThreadLocal and never crosses to another thread by itself.

See also. 3.04, 3.01, 12.03, 12.06, 13.06, 13.07

12.05 Log an exception once, with its stack trace

Then.

  • J2EE era: e.printStackTrace() in every catch block. With checked exceptions on every call, catch-print-continue was the shortest code that compiled, and stderr was where the operator looked.
  • Spring era: log and rethrow at each layer. Before a central handler such as @ControllerAdvice was common, a layer could not trust its caller to log, so each one did.

Recognise it by. e.printStackTrace(), log.error(e.getMessage()), catch blocks that log and then throw e, and ExceptionUtils.getStackTrace(e) concatenated into a message.

The rookie version.

public LedgerReservation reserve(Payout payout) {
    try {
        return ledger.reserve(payout.idempotencyKey(), toRequest(payout));
    } catch (RestClientException e) {
        log.error("Reserve failed: " + e.getMessage());
        throw new LedgerUnavailable(e);
    }
}

What goes wrong. Two things. The line keeps only the message, so the stack trace and the cause chain are gone, and some messages are null. Then the same failure is logged again in PayoutService, and a third time in the @RestControllerAdvice. A 6-minute ledger outage failed 360 payouts and wrote 1,080 ERROR lines with three different messages. The on-call engineer counted three problems. The only line with a stack trace was the last one, and it showed the advice, not the ledger call.

Do this now.

  1. Decide who handles the exception. That is the code that turns it into a response or a decision: the @RestControllerAdvice (6.03), the SQS listener, or the saga step that records the failure. That code logs.
  2. Everywhere else, either handle the exception completely and do not rethrow, or wrap it with its cause and throw without logging (2.09).
  3. Pass the exception as the last argument. SLF4J treats a trailing Throwable as the exception, not a placeholder value, and prints the full stack trace with every Caused by.
  4. Write the message about what was being done, with identifiers. The exception already says what went wrong.
  5. Match the level to the meaning (12.02). A domain refusal, such as a claim already paid, is INFO with no stack trace (6.04). A technical failure is ERROR with one.
  6. With structured logging the stack trace is one field of one event (12.03).
@ExceptionHandler(LedgerUnavailable.class)
ProblemDetail ledgerUnavailable(LedgerUnavailable e, HttpServletRequest request) {
    log.error("ledger unavailable while handling {} {}",
            request.getMethod(), request.getRequestURI(), e);
    return ProblemDetail.forStatusAndDetail(HttpStatus.SERVICE_UNAVAILABLE,
            "The ledger is unavailable. Try again later.");
}

The handler is a method of the advice class from 6.03. ProblemDetail is Spring's type for a standard JSON error body, like ASP.NET Core's ProblemDetails. The line needs no payout ID in its text, because the MDC already carries it (12.04).

The lower layer becomes a plain wrap, as in the ledger client of 6.09:

} catch (RestClientException e) {
    throw new LedgerUnavailable(e);
}

Also seen. Logback's %rEx conversion word, which prints the root cause first, set through Boot's logging.exception-conversion-word. logstash-logback-encoder's ShortenedThrowableConverter, which trims long traces. In structured output, Boot 3.5's logging.structured.json.stacktrace.* properties do the same jobs: root cause first, and a maximum length or depth.

When to break it. When you swallow an exception on purpose, for a fallback, log it once at WARN with the exception, because no one else will. When a framework callback discards whatever you throw, log before you throw. The cost is a duplicate line when the framework changes its mind.

.NET anchor. logger.LogError(ex, "Payout {PayoutId} failed", id) takes the exception first. SLF4J takes it last. ASP.NET Core's exception-handling middleware plays the role of the advice, and throw; versus wrapping in a new exception is the same choice as here.

See also. 2.09, 6.03, 6.04, 6.11, 12.02, Exceptions and resources

12.06 Keep personal data and secrets out of logs

Then.

  • Boot era: request and response logging filters, switched on to debug an integration before tracing existed. They wrote headers and bodies, which means tokens and bank details.
@Bean
CommonsRequestLoggingFilter requestLogging() {
    CommonsRequestLoggingFilter filter = new CommonsRequestLoggingFilter();
    filter.setIncludePayload(true);
    filter.setIncludeHeaders(true);
    return filter;
}
  • Boot era: logging.level.org.apache.http.wire=DEBUG, which logged every byte of every outbound call (7.18).

Recognise it by. CommonsRequestLoggingFilter, setIncludePayload(true), setIncludeHeaders(true), logging.level.org.apache.http.wire, and filters that wrap requests in ContentCachingRequestWrapper to log bodies.

The rookie version.

public record BankAccount(String holderName, String sortCode, String accountNumber) {}

public void instruct(Payout payout, BankAccount account) {
    log.info("instructing bank for {} to {}", payout.id(), account);
    bankGateway.instruct(payout, account);
}

What goes wrong. A record generates toString from every component. The line reads BankAccount[holderName=..., sortCode=..., accountNumber=...] in full. Payouts makes about 20,000 payouts a day, so the log store gains 20,000 names and account numbers a day. That store keeps 90 days, is searchable by every engineer at Sorrel, and is shipped to a third-party service. A claimant's request to see or erase their data now includes the logs, and nobody can say exactly which lines hold it. A bearer token in a log is worse: anyone with log access can replay it until it expires.

Do this now.

  1. Log identifiers, not objects. payoutId and claimId let a support engineer look the rest up in a system with access control.
  2. Make sensitive types safe by default. Override toString on the record, so the mistake above prints nothing harmful.
  3. Never log request or response bodies, headers, tokens, connection strings or the whole environment at startup.
  4. Write the team's list of fields that are never logged: names, addresses, email addresses, phone numbers, dates of birth, bank details, tokens and secrets.
  5. Test it. Capture the log output of one payout in a test and assert that the account number is not in it (16.20).
  6. If personal data does reach the log store, treat it as an incident: fix the code, and ask the platform team to purge the lines.
public record BankAccount(String holderName, String sortCode, String accountNumber) {
    @Override
    public String toString() {
        String last4 = accountNumber.substring(Math.max(0, accountNumber.length() - 4));
        return "BankAccount[****" + last4 + "]";
    }
}

Also seen. A masking layout or converter in Logback that replaces patterns such as card numbers with regular expressions. It is a safety net for what slips through, never the primary control, because a regex cannot know what a name looks like. Zalando's Logbook library logs HTTP traffic with built-in obfuscation, for teams that must keep request logs.

When to break it. Never for secrets. For personal data that must be recorded, such as who approved a payout, write it to an audit store with its own access rules and retention (12.11), not to the diagnostic log.

.NET anchor. C# records have the same trap: their generated ToString prints every property. .NET 8 added Microsoft.Extensions.Compliance.Redaction, which classifies properties and redacts them in the logger. SLF4J has no equivalent, so Java teams make the type's toString safe instead.

See also. 12.04, 12.11, 7.18, 15.13, 15.14, 16.20, Security

12.07 Configure Logback per environment

Then.

  • Boot era: one logback.xml per environment, chosen by a system property, or Logback's <if condition=...> blocks, which need the Janino library.

What goes wrong. Three copies of the file drift. Someone added the JSON encoder to the production copy, then later fixed a logger name only in the development copy. For 2 weeks production logged the old package at DEBUG.

Do this now. Use properties first, and XML only when properties cannot say it.

  1. Put the levels in application.yml. Set the structured format in the Deployment's environment (12.03), so a laptop never gets JSON.
  2. Override for local runs in application-local.yml (4.03): DEBUG for com.sorrel.payouts, and, to see key-value pairs and MDC entries, logging.pattern.console: "%d{HH:mm:ss} %-5p %logger{36} %m %kvp %X%n".
  3. When you need XML, for an extra appender for example, name the file logback-spring.xml, not logback.xml. Boot then loads it after the Spring environment is ready, so <springProfile> and <springProperty> work in it.
  4. Once the file exists, it decides the appenders. logging.structured.format.console then works only through Boot's structured appender, included as below.
<configuration>
  <include resource="org/springframework/boot/logging/logback/defaults.xml"/>
  <springProperty name="app" source="spring.application.name"/>
  <springProfile name="local">
    <include resource="org/springframework/boot/logging/logback/console-appender.xml"/>
  </springProfile>
  <springProfile name="!local">
    <include resource="org/springframework/boot/logging/logback/structured-console-appender.xml"/>
  </springProfile>
  <root level="INFO"><appender-ref ref="CONSOLE"/></root>
</configuration>

See also. 4.03, 12.03, 12.12

12.08 Use Log4j2 instead of Logback

Then.

  • Spring era: log4j 1.x, configured in log4j.properties. Log4j2 is a rewrite, not an upgrade of it. Apache announced log4j 1.x's end of life on 5 August 2015, and its last version is 1.2.17.
log4j.rootLogger=INFO, stdout
log4j.appender.stdout=org.apache.log4j.ConsoleAppender
log4j.appender.stdout.layout=org.apache.log4j.PatternLayout
log4j.appender.stdout.layout.ConversionPattern=%d %-5p [%t] %c - %m%n
  • Boot era: Log4j2 services patched in December 2021. Many first added -Dlog4j2.formatMsgNoLookups=true to the start command as an emergency measure. It works only from 2.10, and Apache soon declared it insufficient, because some code paths still performed lookups. Upgrading was the fix.

Recognise it by. org.apache.log4j.* imports, log4j.properties, log4j-1.2-api, log4j2.xml, -Dlog4j2.formatMsgNoLookups=true in Dockerfiles or Helm charts, and spring-boot-starter-log4j2.

The rookie version.

<dependency>
  <groupId>org.springframework.boot</groupId>
  <artifactId>spring-boot-starter-log4j2</artifactId>
</dependency>
<dependency>
  <groupId>org.apache.logging.log4j</groupId>
  <artifactId>log4j-core</artifactId>
  <version>2.14.1</version>
</dependency>

What goes wrong. Two mistakes. Logback was never excluded, so two SLF4J backends are on the classpath. SLF4J warns at startup that it found several providers and uses the first it finds. On Payouts that was Logback. The new log4j2-spring.xml was silently ignored for a week. The pinned version is the second mistake, copied from an old answer online. It overrides the version Boot manages, and 2.14.1 sits inside one of the ranges Log4Shell affects, [2.13.0, 2.15.0) (CVE-2021-44228, CVSS 10.0). The dependency scan failed the build, which was the good outcome.

Do this now. The field is split, and both choices are sound.

The case for Log4j2: its async loggers hand each event to a background thread through a lock-free queue (the LMAX Disruptor), so a request thread spends less time logging. It has a garbage-free mode for low-latency services. Its plugin system is rich. Some organisations standardise on it across all their Java, and one configuration style is worth having.

The case for Logback: it is Boot's default and needs no exclusions. Most Boot examples and answers assume it. Its AsyncAppender gives a similar background queue for the services that need one.

Pick Logback unless one of those Log4j2 reasons applies to you. To switch:

  1. Exclude spring-boot-starter-logging. It reaches you through spring-boot-starter, which every starter depends on. Declare spring-boot-starter yourself with the exclusion: Maven then uses your declaration wherever the starter appears, because the declaration nearest your project wins (1.02).
  2. Add spring-boot-starter-log4j2 with no version. It brings Log4j2, the SLF4J binding (log4j-slf4j2-impl) and the bridge for java.util.logging.
  3. Keep service code on the SLF4J API. Nothing in PayoutService changes.
  4. Keep using logging.level.* and logging.structured.format.console. Boot applies them to Log4j2 too. For anything more, add log4j2-spring.xml, so <SpringProfile> works in it, and use Boot's StructuredLogLayout there to keep JSON output.
  5. Confirm with the Maven wrapper script, ./mvnw dependency:tree -Dincludes=ch.qos.logback. It should print no Logback.
  6. Never pin log4j-core. If a security fix is out before Boot manages it, override the log4j2.version property (this works when spring-boot-starter-parent is the parent; with an imported BOM, import Log4j's own log4j-bom before Boot's), and remove the override at the next Boot upgrade.
<dependency>
  <groupId>org.springframework.boot</groupId>
  <artifactId>spring-boot-starter</artifactId>
  <exclusions>
    <exclusion>
      <groupId>org.springframework.boot</groupId>
      <artifactId>spring-boot-starter-logging</artifactId>
    </exclusion>
  </exclusions>
</dependency>
<dependency>
  <groupId>org.springframework.boot</groupId>
  <artifactId>spring-boot-starter-log4j2</artifactId>
</dependency>

To make every logger asynchronous, add com.lmax:disruptor and set the system property log4j2.contextSelector to org.apache.logging.log4j.core.async.AsyncLoggerContextSelector. Decide what happens when the queue fills: block the caller or drop events. Know also that events still in the queue are lost if the pod is killed without a graceful shutdown.

Log4Shell is the lesson about version management, not about Log4j2 as a choice. Apache fixed it in 2.15.0, then follow-up flaws in later releases, among them 2.16.0 (CVE-2021-45046) and 2.17.0 (CVE-2021-45105). A service on a version Boot manages got those fixes with a Boot upgrade. A service with a pin did not.

Also seen. The Log4j2 API (org.apache.logging.log4j.LogManager) used directly, for its lambda arguments. log4j-1.2-api, a bridge that lets code written for log4j 1.x run on Log4j2 during a migration.

When to break it. Stay on Logback when nothing above applies. The switch costs an exclusion in every module and a check in every dependency update that something has not brought Logback back (1.03, 1.09).

.NET anchor. This is swapping the default logging providers for NLog: builder.Logging.ClearProviders() and builder.Host.UseNLog(). In .NET the swap is code. In Java it is the classpath, and leaving both backends on it fails quietly instead of at compile time.

See also. 1.02, 1.03, 1.09, 12.01, 12.12, 15.12, 19.06, Appendix I: Your library, translated

12.09 Change a log level at runtime

Then.

  • Boot era: Logback's JMXConfigurator, driven from JConsole, or scan="true" in logback.xml with the file edited in place. Neither fits an immutable container.

What goes wrong. To see the ledger calls, someone changed logging.level in the configuration and redeployed. Both pods restarted, and the state that caused the bug was gone. The DEBUG setting stayed for 3 weeks.

Do this now. Use Actuator's loggers endpoint. Only health is exposed by default, so make the list health,prometheus,loggers in management.endpoints.web.exposure.include. Payouts serves Actuator on port 8081, and its Actuator security chain lets only the OPERATOR role reach loggers (14.09). Send an operator's token.

kubectl port-forward pod/payouts-api-7d9f8-abcde 8081:8081 &
L=localhost:8081/actuator/loggers/com.sorrel.payouts.ledger
# read the current level of one logger
curl -s -H "Authorization: Bearer $TOKEN" $L
# set it to DEBUG on this pod only
curl -s -X POST $L -H "Authorization: Bearer $TOKEN" \
  -H 'Content-Type: application/json' -d '{"configuredLevel":"DEBUG"}'
# reset it to the configured level
curl -s -X POST $L -H "Authorization: Bearer $TOKEN" \
  -H 'Content-Type: application/json' -d '{"configuredLevel":null}'

The change applies to one pod and lasts until it restarts. With 2 pods, repeat it through a port-forward to each. logging.group.<name> lets you name several loggers and change them together.

See also. 12.02, 14.01, 14.09, Actuator and observability

12.10 Keep logging out of hot paths and loops

What goes wrong. The nightly reconciliation checked the day's 20,000 payouts. It wrote an INFO line per payout, and a DEBUG line whose argument was saga.describe(), which serialised the whole saga history. DEBUG was off, but the argument was still built every time. The job went from 4 minutes to 11.

Do this now.

  1. In a loop, log a summary at the end, with counts, and one line per failure.
  2. When a debug argument is expensive, pass a supplier through the fluent API, so it runs only if the level is enabled. An isDebugEnabled() guard does the same job.
  3. Count things with a metric, not with log lines (14.02).
  4. A plain console appender writes on the calling thread. If logging shows up in a profile, measure before reaching for an async appender (18.01).
log.atDebug()
   .setMessage("saga state {}")
   .addArgument(() -> saga.describe())
   .log();

See also. 12.01, 12.08, 14.02, 18.01

12.11 Keep audit records separate from diagnostic logs

Then.

  • Spring era: a logger named AUDIT with its own file appender, so that audit lines went to a separate file. Better than mixing them, and still a log.

What goes wrong. A complaint arrived 14 months after a payout, asking who had approved it. The answer had been an INFO line, and the log store keeps 90 days. Logs are also the wrong kind of store for proof. Anyone can switch a logger off, an async appender may drop lines under load, and lines can be lost when a pod dies.

Do this now. An audit record is data the business keeps on purpose: who did what, to which payout, when, and with what result.

  1. Model it as a record and store it in DocumentDB, append-only, with a retention the business sets.
  2. Write it as an OutboxEvent in the same write as the change (9.07). PayoutAuditListener stores each event from payout-audit under its event ID, so a redelivery is stored once (15.14).
  3. Keep logging for diagnosis. The two may share a payout ID and a trace ID, nothing more.
public record AuditRecord(String eventId, String payoutId, String actor, String action,
                          PayoutStatus from, PayoutStatus to, Instant at) {}

See also. 9.07, 12.06, 15.14

12.12 Read an old logging setup

What goes wrong. An inherited service logged nothing at all after a dependency upgrade. The upgrade brought SLF4J 2, and the only backend was an old 1.7 binding, slf4j-log4j12. SLF4J 2 ignores 1.7 bindings, printed warnings at startup, and fell back to a logger that discards everything.

Do this now. Read the classpath first, then the files.

  1. Run ./mvnw dependency:tree -Dincludes=org.slf4j,ch.qos.logback,org.apache.logging.log4j,log4j,commons-logging.
  2. Find exactly one backend: logback-classic or log4j-core with log4j-slf4j2-impl. Old 1.7 bindings such as slf4j-log4j12 or log4j-slf4j-impl must go.
  3. Check that no bridge sits beside a binding that writes back to the API it bridges: jul-to-slf4j with slf4j-jdk14, log4j-over-slf4j with slf4j-log4j12 or slf4j-reload4j, or Boot's log4j-to-slf4j with log4j-slf4j2-impl. Each pair makes a loop. Some stop with an error at startup, others overflow the stack.
  4. Then the files. logback.xml loads before Spring, so <springProfile> in it does nothing. log4j.properties with no log4j 1.x on the classpath is dead.

See also. 1.03, 12.01, 12.07, 12.08, Appendix C: The Java you'll inherit

⚠Review checklist
  • If you see string concatenation inside a log call: the string is built even when the level is off, and the message cannot be grouped. See 12.01.
  • If you see log.error on a retry attempt or a client's 4xx: alerts fire for failures that recovered, and the team learns to ignore them. See 12.02.
  • If you see a hand-built JSON logging.pattern.console: a quote or a stack trace breaks the line. See 12.03.
  • If you see MDC.put with no matching removal: the value leaks onto the next unit of work on that pooled thread. See 12.04.
  • If you see log.error(e.getMessage()), or a catch that logs and rethrows: the stack trace is lost and one failure is logged several times. See 12.05.
  • If you see a record, a request body, a header or a token passed to a log call: personal data and credentials go into a store that everyone can read. See 12.06.
  • If you see a logback.xml with <springProfile>, or one logging file per environment: the profile blocks do nothing, or the copies drift. See 12.07.
  • If you see spring-boot-starter-log4j2 without excluding spring-boot-starter-logging, or a pinned log4j-core: two backends compete, and the pin can hold a known vulnerability. See 12.08.
  • If you see a redeploy to change a log level: the restart can erase the state you wanted to see. See 12.09.
  • If you see a log line per item inside a large loop, or an expensive method call as a debug argument: the job slows down for lines nobody reads. See 12.10.
  • If you see audit facts written only with log.info: they disappear when the log store's retention ends. See 12.11.

Part IV · The how-to13. Correlation and tracing#

A payout touches payouts-api, the ledger, the bank gateway, an SNS topic and three SQS queues. When one fails, a log search by timestamp is guesswork. This part shows how one trace ID follows a payout through all of them. It covers the two ways a Boot service gets traces, Micrometer Tracing and the OpenTelemetry Java agent, and how the context crosses HTTP calls, message queues and threads. It ends with sampling, custom spans, and handing the ID back to the caller.

★What a veteran knows
  • Tracing is only as good as its weakest hop. One client built by hand, or one queue that drops the header, cuts every trace in two at that point.
  • Pick one tracing mechanism per service and say which in the README. Micrometer Tracing and the Java agent together give you duplicate spans and an argument about which one is right.
  • The trace ID is for engineers, and a business ID is for people. Log both, and never make a support analyst search by a 32-character hex string when a claim reference would do.
  • Boot keeps 1 trace in 10 by default. Check the sampling rate before you tell anyone "the trace is missing, so the request never arrived".
  • An outbox breaks the trace unless you store the context with the event. The relay runs later, on another thread, with no idea which request wrote the row.
  • On Payouts the first question in any incident is "what is the trace ID?". The answer is in the error response, the log line and the dead-letter message, because each of those was set up on purpose.
◷How we got hereIn April 2010 Google published a technical report by Benjamin H.

In April 2010 Google published a technical report by Benjamin H. Sigelman and seven colleagues: "Dapper, a Large-Scale Distributed Systems Tracing Infrastructure". It described a system they had run in production for over two years. Its motivating engineer could see that a search was slow, but "may not be able to guess which service is at fault, nor why it is behaving poorly." Dapper's answer was to carry a trace context across every hop, to put the instrumentation in "a rather small number of common libraries", and to sample. On 7 June 2012 Twitter open-sourced Zipkin. Johan Oskarsson and Franklin Hu had started it in Twitter's first Hack Week as "a basic version of the Google Dapper paper for Thrift". The post was frank about the trade: "By only sampling a portion of all the requests we reduce the overhead of tracing, allowing us to always have it enabled in production." Every tool in this part descends from those two decisions.

13.01 Understand traces, spans and trace IDs

Then.

  • Boot era: a hand-rolled correlation ID. A servlet filter, Java's form of ASP.NET Core middleware, read X-Correlation-Id, made a UUID if it was missing, and put it in the MDC (the Mapped Diagnostic Context, a per-thread map that the logger adds to every line, 13.06). Every client then had to copy it onto outbound calls by hand. It was right for its time: it needed no backend and worked in any log tool.
String id = Optional.ofNullable(request.getHeader("X-Correlation-Id"))
        .orElse(UUID.randomUUID().toString());
MDC.put("correlationId", id);
try { chain.doFilter(request, response); }
finally { MDC.remove("correlationId"); }
  • Boot era: Spring Cloud Sleuth, which did the same job with real trace and span IDs in X-B3-* headers. Its last minor version is 3.1, it does not work with Boot 3, and its core moved into Micrometer Tracing.

Recognise it by. X-Correlation-Id or X-Request-Id read in a Filter, MDC.put("correlationId", ...), UUID.randomUUID() in a filter, and spring-cloud-starter-sleuth in the POM, the Maven build file pom.xml.

The rookie version.

public Payout pay(Claim claim) {
    String requestId = UUID.randomUUID().toString();
    log.info("paying claim {} request {}", claim.id(), requestId);
    ledgerClient.reserve(toReserve(claim));
    return bankGatewayClient.instruct(claim);
}

What goes wrong. The ID is made inside one method of one service. The ledger never sees it, the bank gateway never sees it, and the next method in Payouts makes its own. It also gives no timings. When a payout of £1,240.50 takes 9 seconds, the log shows a start line and an end line. It cannot say whether the 9 seconds went on the ledger, the bank gateway or DocumentDB.

Do this now. Learn the four words first, because every tool uses them.

  1. A trace is the whole journey of one request through every service it touches. It has a trace ID: 16 bytes, written as 32 hex characters.
  2. A span is one timed piece of work inside a trace: the incoming POST /payouts, the call to the ledger, one DocumentDB query. Each span has its own 8-byte span ID, a start time, a duration, a name and some attributes.
  3. Spans form a tree. Each span except the first records its parent span ID. The ledger's span for "reserve" is a child of Payouts' span for the outbound call.
  4. The trace context is the trace ID, the current span ID and a "sampled" flag. It travels between services in a header such as traceparent (13.04). Inside a service it sits in a ThreadLocal, a variable that holds a separate value for each thread.

A tracing library does three jobs:

  • Instrumentation creates spans around work it knows about: HTTP in and out, database calls, messages.
  • Propagation writes the context into outgoing requests and reads it from incoming ones.
  • Export sends finished spans to a backend, where you see the tree as a timeline. They usually go through an OpenTelemetry Collector, a separate process that receives spans and forwards them.

OpenTelemetry (OTel) is the vendor-neutral standard for all three. It defines the API, the SDK, the wire protocol (OTLP) and the agent. Spring's own layer is Micrometer Tracing, which hides the tracer behind one API and can sit on top of OpenTelemetry. Both are full entries below: 13.02 and 13.03.

The trace ID also goes into every log line (13.06). That is what joins logs to traces. You find the error in the log, copy its trace ID, and open the timeline.

Also seen. A business correlation ID alongside the trace, such as the claim reference or the Idempotency-Key. Carry it as baggage, key-value pairs that travel with the trace context, or in the MDC (13.10). It survives sampling and means something to a person.

When to break it. A batch job that runs alone on one pod gains little from distributed tracing. A job ID in the MDC is enough. The cost appears the day the job starts calling other services.

.NET anchor. This is System.Diagnostics.Activity. An Activity is a span, Activity.TraceId is the trace ID, and ActivitySource creates them. ASP.NET Core propagates traceparent by default, and OpenTelemetry .NET exports. Java splits the same ideas between Micrometer Tracing and OpenTelemetry. One difference bites later: Activity.Current lives in an AsyncLocal and follows await, while Java's context stays on its thread (13.07).

See also. 13.02, 13.03, 13.04, 13.06, 12.04, Actuator and observability

13.02 Trace with Micrometer Tracing and the OpenTelemetry bridge

Then.

  • Boot era: Spring Cloud Sleuth with Brave, Zipkin's Java tracer. Adding its starter, one dependency that brings a library and the code that configures it, traced Spring MVC, RestTemplate and messaging with no code. It was the obvious choice for a Boot 2 service, and it is gone on Boot 3.
<dependency>
  <groupId>org.springframework.cloud</groupId>
  <artifactId>spring-cloud-starter-sleuth</artifactId>
</dependency>
<!-- spring.sleuth.sampler.probability=1.0 -->
<!-- spring.zipkin.base-url=http://zipkin:9411 -->
  • Boot era: OpenTracing, an API standard with Jaeger as a common tracer: io.opentracing.Tracer, GlobalTracer.get(), and starters such as opentracing-spring-jaeger-cloud-starter. OpenTracing and OpenCensus merged into OpenTelemetry, which replaced both.

Recognise it by. spring-cloud-starter-sleuth, spring-cloud-sleuth-zipkin, org.springframework.cloud.sleuth.* imports, spring.sleuth.* and spring.zipkin.* keys, brave.Tracer, io.opentracing.* and io.jaegertracing.

The rookie version.

<dependency>
  <groupId>io.micrometer</groupId>
  <artifactId>micrometer-tracing-bridge-otel</artifactId>
</dependency>
<dependency>
  <groupId>io.micrometer</groupId>
  <artifactId>micrometer-tracing-bridge-brave</artifactId>
</dependency>

What goes wrong. Two bridges is two tracers, and Boot has to choose one. Nothing is exported either, because there is no exporter and no Actuator, Boot's module for health, metrics and tracing. Fix that, deploy, and the next surprise arrives: a tester posts one payout of £1,240.50 and finds no trace. By default Boot samples only 10% of requests, so 9 tests in 10 leave nothing behind. The team concludes that tracing is broken and turns it off.

Do this now. Micrometer Tracing is a facade over a tracer, as SLF4J, the logging API most Java code writes to, is a facade over a logger. Boot 3.0 and later auto-configure it: at startup Boot sees the jars on the classpath, the set of jars the application runs with, and creates the objects for you. The OpenTelemetry bridge makes OpenTelemetry the tracer underneath. Spring MVC and the auto-configured HTTP clients create spans through the Observation API, Micrometer's single hook that produces both a metric and a span.

  1. Add the three dependencies. Boot manages their versions.
<dependency>
  <groupId>org.springframework.boot</groupId>
  <artifactId>spring-boot-starter-actuator</artifactId>
</dependency>
<dependency>
  <groupId>io.micrometer</groupId>
  <artifactId>micrometer-tracing-bridge-otel</artifactId>
</dependency>
<dependency>
  <groupId>io.opentelemetry</groupId>
  <artifactId>opentelemetry-exporter-otlp</artifactId>
</dependency>
  1. Point the exporter at the collector and set the sampling rate per environment, through environment variables on Kubernetes (4.15).
spring:
  application:
    name: payouts-api
management:
  otlp:
    tracing:
      endpoint: http://otel-collector.observability:4318/v1/traces
  tracing:
    sampling:
      probability: ${PAYOUTS_TRACE_SAMPLING:0.1}
  1. Build every HTTP client from the injected RestClient.Builder (7.01). Boot's documentation warns that otherwise "automatic trace propagation won't work!"
  2. Read the current trace in code through io.micrometer.tracing.Tracer, which Boot provides as a bean, an object Spring creates and injects into your constructor: tracer.currentSpan().
  3. In tests, @SpringBootTest does not auto-configure the reporting components, so a test does not try to reach a collector.

In Boot 4, add org.springframework.boot:spring-boot-starter-opentelemetry in place of the bridge and exporter. The endpoint key becomes management.opentelemetry.tracing.export.otlp.endpoint. Boot's OpenTelemetry-with-Zipkin auto-configuration is due to be removed in Boot 4.2, so export OTLP now.

Also seen. The Brave bridge, micrometer-tracing-bridge-brave, with zipkin-reporter-brave. Choose it when the backend is Zipkin and nothing else. The OpenTelemetry Java agent (13.03) is the other serious option. Here is the honest comparison:

  • Micrometer Tracing is in the POM, versioned by Boot, visible in code review and testable.
  • It traces only what Spring and Micrometer instrument. A library outside that set produces no spans until someone wires it in.
  • Payouts uses it because its spans and metrics come from one Observation and its versions move with Boot.

When to break it. When the platform team injects the OpenTelemetry agent into every pod in the namespace, follow the platform. Remove the bridge rather than run both. The cost is one more thing outside the build that can change under you.

.NET anchor. This is AddOpenTelemetry().WithTracing(b => b.AddAspNetCoreInstrumentation().AddHttpClientInstrumentation().AddOtlpExporter()). Micrometer's Observation is close to an ActivitySource that also records a Meter histogram. The difference is that Boot does the wiring from the classpath, with no builder code.

See also. 13.01, 13.03, 13.09, 7.01, 14.01, 19.04, Actuator and observability

13.03 Trace with the OpenTelemetry Java agent

Then.

  • Boot era: a vendor's agent, such as New Relic, Dynatrace, AppDynamics or Elastic APM. Each was a -javaagent jar with its own wire format, its own backend and its own licence. They did real work long before an open standard existed. Moving vendors meant changing every pod.
java -javaagent:/opt/newrelic/newrelic.jar -jar payouts-api.jar

Recognise it by. -javaagent: in a Dockerfile ENTRYPOINT or in JAVA_TOOL_OPTIONS, newrelic.yml, elastic-apm-agent, appdynamics directories in the image, and vendor annotations such as @Trace.

The rookie version.

ENV JAVA_TOOL_OPTIONS="-javaagent:/otel/opentelemetry-javaagent.jar"
# pom.xml still has micrometer-tracing-bridge-otel and the OTLP exporter

What goes wrong. Now there are two tracers in one JVM. The agent instruments the HTTP server and the outbound calls, and so does Micrometer Tracing. A payout of £1,240.50 shows 2 server spans for one request, sometimes in 2 separate traces. The log line carries Micrometer's traceId in one MDC field and the agent's trace_id in another, and they can differ. Nobody sets a service name either, so the backend shows a generic placeholder name instead of payouts-api.

Do this now. A Java agent is a jar the JVM loads before your application, through -javaagent. It can rewrite classes as they load. The OpenTelemetry Java agent uses that to add spans to the libraries it recognises, with no code and no dependency in your POM. It attaches to any Java 8 or later application.

  1. Remove micrometer-tracing-bridge-* and the OTLP exporter from the POM. Keep Actuator for metrics and health.
  2. Put the agent jar in the image, at a version you chose, from the project's GitHub releases. Bump it deliberately, as you bump Boot.
ADD https://github.com/open-telemetry/opentelemetry-java-instrumentation/releases/download/v2.33.0/opentelemetry-javaagent.jar /otel/opentelemetry-javaagent.jar
  1. Attach it through JAVA_TOOL_OPTIONS, so the ENTRYPOINT stays unchanged.
  2. Configure it with OTEL_* environment variables. They are the standard SDK settings, not Boot properties. The agent ignores management.tracing.*.
env:
  - name: JAVA_TOOL_OPTIONS
    value: "-javaagent:/otel/opentelemetry-javaagent.jar"
  - name: OTEL_SERVICE_NAME
    value: payouts-api
  - name: OTEL_EXPORTER_OTLP_ENDPOINT
    value: http://otel-collector.observability:4318
  - name: OTEL_EXPORTER_OTLP_PROTOCOL
    value: http/protobuf
  - name: OTEL_TRACES_SAMPLER
    value: parentbased_traceidratio
  - name: OTEL_TRACES_SAMPLER_ARG
    value: "0.1"
  1. Set the protocol and the sampler explicitly. The agent's defaults are not Boot's, and port 4318 is the OTLP HTTP port, while 4317 is gRPC. The endpoint is a base URL: the agent adds /v1/traces itself. Boot's property in 13.02 takes the full path, so copying one into the other doubles or drops it.
  2. For the trace ID in code, use the OpenTelemetry API: Span.current().getSpanContext().getTraceId(), from io.opentelemetry.api.trace. For custom spans, use @WithSpan (13.08).
  3. The agent adds trace_id, span_id and trace_flags to the MDC map of each event in Logback, Boot's default logging library. Put those names in the log pattern (13.06). They are not in SLF4J's MDC thread local, so MDC.get("trace_id") in code returns null.

The agent covers more than Spring does: the JDK HTTP client, the MongoDB driver, the AWS SDK v2 and the executors in java.util.concurrent. That is its strength. Here is the honest comparison:

  • The agent instruments libraries the team never thought about, and it works the same way across services that are not all Spring.
  • Its behaviour is not in the POM or the code. A new agent version can change span names or attributes without a line of your code changing.
  • It adds work at startup, because classes are rewritten as they load. Measure that on your own service.

Also seen. The OpenTelemetry Operator on Kubernetes, which injects the agent into pods carrying an annotation. Choose it when the platform team owns tracing for the whole cluster. The OpenTelemetry Spring Boot starter, which is library instrumentation configured from application.yml, sits between the two approaches.

When to break it. A service that must start very fast, or one where every dependency change goes through review, may refuse the agent. The cost is writing and maintaining the instrumentation the agent would have given you.

.NET anchor. This is OpenTelemetry .NET automatic instrumentation, set up with CORECLR_ENABLE_PROFILING and CORECLR_PROFILER, or the same Kubernetes operator. The OTEL_* variables are the same names in both worlds.

See also. 13.02, 13.06, 13.08, 13.09, 17.01, 17.07, Actuator and observability

13.04 Propagate traceparent across HTTP calls

Then.

  • Boot era: B3 headers from Zipkin and Sleuth: X-B3-TraceId, X-B3-SpanId, X-B3-ParentSpanId and X-B3-Sampled, or the single b3 header. Jaeger clients sent uber-trace-id. Each tracer had its own format, which was workable while one company used one tracer.
X-B3-TraceId: 4bf92f3577b34da6a3ce929d0e0e4736
X-B3-SpanId: 00f067aa0ba902b7
X-B3-Sampled: 1

Recognise it by. X-B3-* and b3 header names in code or proxy config, uber-trace-id, spring.sleuth.propagation.type, and management.tracing.propagation.type=B3 in newer services that still talk to old ones.

The rookie version.

public LedgerReservation reserve(HttpServletRequest incoming, ReserveRequest body) {
    return RestClient.create().post()
            .uri(ledgerUrl + "/ledger/reservations")
            .header("traceparent", incoming.getHeader("traceparent"))
            .body(body)
            .retrieve()
            .body(LedgerReservation.class);
}

What goes wrong. The header is copied unchanged, so it names the caller's span as the parent. The ledger's span hangs off the caller, not off Payouts. In the timeline the ledger call is a sibling of Payouts' own span, not its child, and the 6 seconds Payouts spent waiting on the ledger appear to belong to whoever called Payouts. When the incoming request had no header, this passes a null header value, which the HTTP library either rejects or sends empty. The bare client also loses its timeouts and the settings of Jackson, Boot's JSON library (7.01).

Do this now. The W3C Trace Context standard defines one header, traceparent, in four dash-separated fields:

traceparent: 00-4bf92f3577b34da6a3ce929d0e0e4736-00f067aa0ba902b7-01
  • 00 is the version.
  • The next 32 hex characters are the trace ID.
  • The next 16 are the parent span ID: the span of whoever sent this request.
  • 01 is the flags, and its last bit says "sampled".

A companion header, tracestate, carries vendor data. baggage carries your own key-value pairs (13.10).

  1. Do nothing on the server side. With Micrometer Tracing on the classpath, Spring MVC reads the incoming header and starts a child span. With no header, it starts a new trace.
  2. Build every client from the auto-configured RestClient.Builder, RestTemplateBuilder or WebClient.Builder. The client starts a span for the call and writes a new traceparent naming that span as the parent.
  3. Know the defaults. Boot sends W3C headers only, and accepts W3C, single b3 and multi-header B3 on the way in. A Boot 3 service therefore understands an old Sleuth caller without configuration.
  4. If an old service downstream reads only B3, set management.tracing.propagation.produce=W3C,B3 to send both until it is upgraded.
  5. At the public edge, decide whether to trust an incoming traceparent. Internal callers, yes. The internet, usually not.
  6. Prove propagation once, with a test that asserts the ledger stub received a traceparent with the same trace ID as the request (7.14).

Also seen. An X-Amzn-Trace-Id header from AWS load balancers and X-Ray. It is a separate format, and a load balancer adds it whether or not you trace. Leave it alone unless you use X-Ray.

When to break it. A call to an outside supplier, such as the bank gateway, may not want your trace IDs. Some suppliers log every header they receive. Strip traceparent and baggage on that client with a ClientHttpRequestInterceptor that removes the headers. The cost is that the trace stops at your outbound span.

.NET anchor. HttpClient from IHttpClientFactory sends traceparent by default through its diagnostics handler, and ASP.NET Core reads it. Spring is the same, with one catch: a client you build yourself does not get it. In .NET even a bare new HttpClient() propagates.

See also. 7.01, 7.09, 7.14, 13.02, 13.10, HTTP clients and resilience

13.05 Propagate trace context through SNS and SQS

Then.

  • Boot era: the correlation ID inside the event body, as a correlationId field in the JSON. It worked across any broker and any language, and it still makes sense as a business field.
{ "type": "PayoutCompleted", "payoutId": "p-7781",
  "correlationId": "3f1c9e0a-6b2d-4e8f-9a31-5c7d0e2b4a18" }
  • Boot era: the X-Ray SDK, which carried its trace in the AWSTraceHeader message system attribute. That attribute is AWS's own and does not use up one of your attributes.

Recognise it by. A correlationId field in every event record, AWSTraceHeader in consumer code, com.amazonaws.xray imports, and listeners that call MDC.put with a value read from the body.

The rookie version.

ReceiveMessageResponse response = sqs.receiveMessage(ReceiveMessageRequest.builder()
        .queueUrl(notifyClaimantUrl)
        .waitTimeSeconds(20)
        .maxNumberOfMessages(10)
        .build());
for (Message m : response.messages()) {
    String traceparent = m.messageAttributes().get("traceparent").stringValue();
    handle(m, traceparent);
}

What goes wrong. SQS returns message attributes only when the receive asks for them by name. This request asks for none, so messageAttributes() is empty and get("traceparent") returns null. The consumer throws a NullPointerException on every message. After 5 receives, the limit set in 10.08, each message goes to notify-claimant-dlq, and the claimant for a payout of £1,240.50 is never told. A null check would only start a fresh trace per message: quieter, and just as useless.

Do this now. A queue has no headers. It has message attributes: named, typed values sent next to the body. Trace context goes there, as traceparent. Count your attributes. SQS allows at most 10 per message, and names must not start with AWS. or Amazon.. traceparent, tracestate and baggage can take 3 of them.

Payouts' path has two extra breaks, drawn here:

  1. Store the context with the outbox row. The relay runs on a scheduled thread with no request around it (9.08). The 9.07 OutboxEvent record has a Map<String, String> traceContext field for it, empty when there is no trace. As PayoutService writes the event, fill it on the request thread with Boot's Propagator bean (io.micrometer.tracing.propagation). It writes traceparent, and tracestate and baggage when present. The relay sends that map, not its own context.
Map<String, String> traceContext = new HashMap<>();
TraceContext current = tracer.currentTraceContext().context();
if (current != null) propagator.inject(current, traceContext, Map::put);
// pass traceContext to OutboxEvent.pending(...)
  1. Turn on raw message delivery on each SQS subscription, with RawMessageDelivery=true. Without it, the SQS body is the SNS JSON envelope, with the attributes inside it rather than on the message. Raw delivery allows at most 10 attributes, and SNS discards a message with more.
  2. Publish attributes with a String message structure. SNS sends message attributes only when the message structure is String, not JSON.

With Spring Cloud AWS. Spring Cloud AWS, the community project that wires SQS and SNS into Boot (10.02), maps each SQS message attribute to a header of the same name. Set spring.cloud.aws.sqs.observation-enabled=true, and the @SqsListener container (10.04) opens an observation per message and continues the trace from traceparent. It asks for all attributes by default, and SqsTemplate writes the propagator's headers as attributes. SnsTemplate has no observation support, so put the stored context in the headers it sends as SNS attributes:

public void publish(OutboxEvent event) {
    Map<String, Object> headers = new HashMap<>(event.traceContext());
    headers.put("eventId", event.id());
    headers.put("eventType", event.type());
    headers.put("eventVersion", event.schemaVersion());
    snsTemplate.convertAndSend(props.topicArn(), event.payload(), headers);
}

SnsTemplate also sends Spring's id, timestamp and contentType headers as attributes, so this message carries up to 9 of the 10.

With the plain AWS SDK v2. On the publish, add each entry of traceContext as a MessageAttributeValue with dataType("String"), next to eventId, eventType and eventVersion (9.08). On the consumer, ask for the attributes by name and continue the trace:

ReceiveMessageRequest request = ReceiveMessageRequest.builder()
        .queueUrl(notifyClaimantUrl).maxNumberOfMessages(10).waitTimeSeconds(20)
        .messageAttributeNames("traceparent", "tracestate", "baggage")
        .build();
// for each message m:
Span span = propagator.extract(m.messageAttributes(),
                (attrs, key) -> attrs.containsKey(key) ? attrs.get(key).stringValue() : null)
        .name("notify-claimant receive").kind(Span.Kind.CONSUMER).start();
try (Tracer.SpanInScope scope = tracer.withSpan(span)) {
    handle(m);
} finally {
    span.end();
}

With the OpenTelemetry agent. The agent instruments SDK v2 SQS and SNS calls. By default it writes context only on an SQS send, as X-Ray's AWSTraceHeader system attribute, and nothing on an SNS publish. The experimental otel.instrumentation.aws-sdk.experimental-use-propagator-for-messaging option adds W3C attributes for both, while the total stays within 10. The relay still has no context of its own, so step 1 applies.

Also seen. A correlationId in the event envelope (10.12) as well as the attribute. Keep it: it survives a redrive, a replay and a consumer in another language.

When to break it. A message replayed from the DLQ days later should start a new trace linked to the old one, not extend one that closed long ago. The cost is one more ID to follow by hand.

.NET anchor. The Azure Service Bus SDK carries the context in a Diagnostic-Id application property for you. SQS and SNS do not. In .NET you would read traceparent off MessageAttributes and start an Activity, with Propagators.DefaultTextMapPropagator as Micrometer's Propagator.

See also. 9.07, 9.08, 10.02, 10.03, 10.04, 10.05, 10.12, 16.11, Messaging and websockets

13.06 Put the trace ID in every log line

Then.

  • Boot era: Sleuth's log format, [payouts-api,traceId,spanId], added to Boot's default pattern. Early Sleuth versions used MDC keys named after the B3 headers.
<pattern>%d %5p [${appName},%X{traceId:-},%X{spanId:-}] %logger : %m%n</pattern>
<!-- Sleuth 1.x: %X{X-B3-TraceId:-} -->

Recognise it by. %X{X-B3-TraceId}, %X{traceId} in a hand-written logback-spring.xml, [appname,traceId,spanId,exportable] in old log lines, and %X{correlationId} from a hand-rolled filter.

The rookie version.

logging:
  pattern:
    console: "%d{HH:mm:ss.SSS} %-5level %logger{36} - %msg%n"

What goes wrong. Boot's default console pattern includes the correlation ID. This custom pattern replaces it and leaves it out. The logs look tidier and no line carries a trace ID. When a payout of £1,240.50 fails at 02:14, the error line says what failed but not which request. With 2 pods and 40 payouts a minute, nobody can join it to the trace, or to the ledger's logs for the same call.

Do this now. Micrometer Tracing puts the current trace and span IDs in the MDC as traceId and spanId. The MDC, the Mapped Diagnostic Context, is a per-thread map that SLF4J adds to each log line (12.04).

  1. Keep Boot's default pattern if you can. With Micrometer Tracing present, Boot adds a correlation ID built from those two values, such as [803B448A0489F84084905D3093480352-3425F23BB2432450].
  2. To change only that part, set logging.pattern.correlation, not the whole console pattern.
  3. Prefer structured JSON logs (12.03). The MDC entries become JSON fields, so the log store can search by trace ID without parsing text. Check the field names in one real line before you build dashboards on them.
  4. With the Java agent instead (13.03), the MDC keys are trace_id, span_id and trace_flags. Boot's correlation pattern looks for traceId and spanId, so it prints nothing. Use the agent's names: logging.pattern.correlation=[%X{trace_id:-},%X{span_id:-}].
  5. Make sure the MDC is set where the work runs. HTTP requests are covered. SQS listeners need the observation turned on (13.05), and executors need a decorator (13.07).
  6. Add the business IDs, such as payoutId and claimId, to the MDC yourself (12.04). They are what a person searches for.
logging.pattern.correlation=[${spring.application.name:},%X{traceId:-},%X{spanId:-}] 
logging.include-application-name=false

That listing restores the old Sleuth layout. Set logging.include-application-name=false so the name is not printed twice.

Also seen. Exporting logs through OpenTelemetry itself, with an appender that sends each log record to the collector with its trace context attached. Choose it when the platform has moved logs into the same backend as traces.

When to break it. A log line written at startup or by a scheduled job has no trace, and the field is empty. That is correct. Do not invent a trace for it. The cost of a fake one is a "trace" with no spans that wastes the next reader's time.

.NET anchor. In .NET, ActivityTrackingOptions on the logger factory, or Serilog's trace enrichers, add TraceId and SpanId to each log scope. Boot's correlation pattern plays the same part.

See also. 12.03, 12.04, 12.08, 13.03, 13.07, Actuator and observability

13.07 Keep context across @Async, executors and virtual threads

What goes wrong. The trace lives in a ThreadLocal, and a task handed to an executor runs on another thread. The audit write after a payout of £1,240.50 logs with no trace ID, so its line joins nothing. CompletableFuture.supplyAsync with no executor runs on the shared common pool, which nothing decorates.

Do this now. Boot's documentation is direct: for @Async methods (3.05) or an AsyncTaskExecutor, register a ContextPropagatingTaskDecorator, "otherwise the observability context is lost when switching threads". A TaskDecorator wraps each task as it is submitted. This one captures every registered ThreadLocal on the submitting thread and restores it on the worker.

@Bean
TaskDecorator taskDecorator() {
    TaskDecorator context = new ContextPropagatingTaskDecorator();
    TaskDecorator mdc = mdcDecorator();   // 3.04's, no longer a bean of its own
    return task -> context.decorate(mdc.decorate(task));
}

Boot applies a TaskDecorator bean to its own executor, virtual-thread or not. On Boot 3.5 it does so only when the bean is unique, so 3.04's MDC decorator beside this one means neither is applied. Declare one bean that applies both, as above. Boot 4 combines several itself. An executor you build yourself needs setTaskDecorator. Always pass an executor to CompletableFuture. The Java agent instruments java.util.concurrent and needs no decorator.

.NET anchor. In .NET, Activity.Current follows await and Task.Run by itself. Java needs the decorator.

See also. 3.04, 3.05, 3.06, 13.06, Threads are cheap now

13.08 Add custom spans and attributes

Then.
