  • Boot era: Sleuth's @NewSpan, @SpanTag and @ContinueSpan, or OpenTracing's tracer.buildSpan("instruct").start(). Micrometer Tracing kept the three annotations.

What goes wrong. A payout spends 6 seconds in PayoutSaga between the ledger call and the bank call, and the trace shows a gap. Someone adds a span with lowCardinalityKeyValue("payoutId", id). Low-cardinality values also become metric tags, so the service now creates a new time series per payout (14.03).

Do this now. Wrap the work in an Observation, which gives a span and a timer at once:

Observation.createNotStarted("payout.instruct", registry)
        .lowCardinalityKeyValue("bank", "gateway-a")
        .highCardinalityKeyValue("payout.id", payout.id())
        .observe(() -> bankGatewayClient.instruct(payout));

registry is the ObservationRegistry bean Boot provides. Put a value with few possible values, such as a status, in lowCardinalityKeyValue. Put an ID in highCardinalityKeyValue, which goes on the span only. For annotations such as @Observed and @NewSpan, set management.observations.annotations.enabled=true and add spring-boot-starter-aop (spring-boot-starter-aspectj in Boot 4). They work through AOP: Spring wraps the bean in a proxy that opens the span around each call. A call from one method to another in the same class skips the proxy and gets no span (3.05). With the Java agent, use @WithSpan from opentelemetry-instrumentation-annotations, and Span.current().setAttribute(...).

See also. 13.02, 13.03, 14.02, 14.03, Actuator and observability

13.09 Sample traces sensibly

What goes wrong. Boot samples 10% of requests by default, through management.tracing.sampling.probability=0.1. In a test environment that sees 30 payouts a day, the one failure somebody wants to see is probably not kept. In production the opposite happens: someone sets the probability to 1.0 to debug an incident, forgets it, and the trace backend's bill grows tenfold.

Do this now.

  1. Set the rate per environment: 1.0 in development and test, a measured fraction in production.
  2. Let the first service decide. The sampled flag travels in traceparent, and downstream services follow it, so a trace is kept whole or not at all. Boot's sampler applies the probability only to a request with no incoming context.
  3. To keep every failed or slow trace, sample in the OpenTelemetry Collector instead, with tail-based sampling. It decides once the trace is complete, so errors survive. The services must then send everything, at 1.0. The cost is a collector holding every span in memory until it decides.
  4. With the Java agent, set OTEL_TRACES_SAMPLER and OTEL_TRACES_SAMPLER_ARG instead (13.03).

Logs are not sampled, so a logged trace ID may point at a trace that was never kept.

See also. 13.02, 13.03, 13.06, 14.06

13.10 Return a correlation ID to callers

Then.

  • Boot era: a filter that echoed X-Correlation-Id or X-Request-Id back on the response, usually the filter from 13.01.

What goes wrong. A claims handler reports "payout £1,240.50 failed at 10:42". Support searches by amount and time and finds 3 candidates. The 500 response carried no ID the caller could quote.

Do this now.

  1. Add the trace ID to every error body. In the @RestControllerAdvice that builds the ProblemDetail error body (6.02, 6.03), call problem.setProperty("traceId", span.context().traceId()), where span is tracer.currentSpan(), checked for null.
  2. For every response, set a header such as X-Trace-Id in a filter, Spring's form of middleware. Agree the name across services. A @Component filter runs after Boot's tracing filter, so the span exists.
@Component
class TraceIdHeaderFilter extends OncePerRequestFilter {
    private final Tracer tracer;
    TraceIdHeaderFilter(Tracer tracer) { this.tracer = tracer; }

    @Override
    protected void doFilterInternal(HttpServletRequest request, HttpServletResponse response,
            FilterChain chain) throws ServletException, IOException {
        Span span = tracer.currentSpan();
        if (span != null) response.setHeader("X-Trace-Id", span.context().traceId());
        chain.doFilter(request, response);
    }
}
  1. Carry a business ID as baggage. Set management.tracing.baggage.remote-fields=claim-ref to send it as its own header, and management.tracing.baggage.correlation.fields=claim-ref to put it in the MDC. Set it where the claim is known: try (BaggageInScope b = tracer.createBaggageInScope("claim-ref", claimRef)) { ... }. Baggage not named in remote-fields travels only in the W3C baggage header, so a B3 hop drops it.

Baggage reaches every downstream service, so never put personal data in it (12.06).

See also. 6.02, 6.03, 12.06, 13.04, 7.09

⚠Review checklist
  • If you see a UUID.randomUUID() used as a request ID inside a service method: it never leaves the method and gives no timings. See 13.01.
  • If you see two micrometer-tracing-bridge-* dependencies, or a bridge with no exporter: Boot picks one tracer, and nothing reaches the backend. See 13.02.
  • If you see a team saying "tracing is broken" in a test environment: Boot keeps 1 request in 10 by default. See 13.02 and 13.09.
  • If you see -javaagent:opentelemetry-javaagent.jar in a service that still has the Micrometer bridge: two tracers make duplicate spans and two trace IDs. See 13.03.
  • If you see traceparent copied from the incoming request onto an outbound call: the downstream span hangs off the wrong parent. See 13.04.
  • If you see a ReceiveMessageRequest with no messageAttributeNames: SQS returns no attributes, so the trace context is lost. See 13.05.
  • If you see an SNS-to-SQS subscription without raw message delivery, or an outbox row with no trace context: the trace stops at the topic or at the relay. See 13.05.
  • If you see a custom logging.pattern.console with no %X{traceId}: no log line can be joined to its trace. See 13.06.
  • If you see CompletableFuture.supplyAsync with no executor, or an executor with no task decorator: the task runs with no trace and no MDC. See 13.07.
  • If you see an ID passed to lowCardinalityKeyValue: it becomes a metric tag with a time series per payout. See 13.08.
  • If you see management.tracing.sampling.probability: 1.0 in production configuration with no tail sampling in the collector: every request is exported and the backend's cost follows. See 13.09.
  • If you see a 500 response body with no trace ID: support cannot find the failing request. See 13.10.

Part IV · The how-to14. Metrics, health and alerting#

Logs tell you what happened to one payout. Metrics tell you what is happening to all of them, right now, in numbers you can graph and alert on. This part shows how Payouts exposes metrics with Micrometer and Actuator, how to add a business metric without wrecking the metrics system, and how to measure latency so the numbers survive being added up across pods. It also covers health checks that do not restart healthy pods, alerts that wake someone only when a customer is affected, queue monitoring, and the JVM numbers worth reading.

★What a veteran knows
  • Count what the business cares about first. "Payouts completed per minute" has caught more incidents on Payouts than any CPU graph.
  • A tag is a dimension, not a label for a single event. If a tag's values grow with traffic, it belongs in a log line or a trace, not a metric.
  • An average latency is a comfortable lie. Measure with a histogram, and read the 99th percentile across every pod at once.
  • Liveness asks about this process and nothing else. Every dependency you add to it is a way for another team's outage to restart your pods.
  • Page a person for a symptom a customer can feel. Put the causes on the dashboard, where the person who was paged will look next.
  • A queue's depth says how much work is waiting. The age of the oldest message says whether anyone is doing it.
  • An alert nobody acts on is noise, and noise trains people to ignore the alert that matters. Delete it or fix it the week it first fires for no reason.
◷How we got hereIn 2012 Matt T.

In 2012 Matt T. Proud, an engineer at SoundCloud, started what his colleagues later called "an ambitious pet project". SoundCloud had moved to microservices, with "hundreds of services, with many thousand instances". Its monitoring was "mostly based on StatsD and Graphite", and that setup had "a number of serious limitations". The team wanted a multi-dimensional data model, operational simplicity, decentralised collection and a powerful query language, and "could not identify a system that combined them all". Proud's project aimed to. "Shortly thereafter, we decided to develop it into SoundCloud's monitoring system: Prometheus was born." Julius Volz and Björn Rabenstein told the story on the SoundCloud blog on 26 January 2015, thanking Proud "who initially started the Prometheus project". A year later Google's Site Reliability Engineering book gave the same idea its checklist: "The four golden signals of monitoring are latency, traffic, errors, and saturation." Labelled metrics, pulled by a server and queried in one language, are what Micrometer and this part assume.

14.01 Expose metrics with Micrometer and Actuator

Then.

  • Spring era: Dropwizard Metrics, first released as Coda Hale's Metrics. You built a MetricRegistry by hand, created timers and meters in it, and attached a reporter that pushed to Graphite or published to JMX, Java Management Extensions, the JVM's built-in management interface. It worked well with one host per service.
MetricRegistry metrics = new MetricRegistry();
Timer payTimer = metrics.timer(MetricRegistry.name(PayoutService.class, "pay"));
JmxReporter.forRegistry(metrics).build().start();
  • Spring era: JMX only. A bean is an object that Spring creates and wires, as .NET's container does for a registered service. A bean marked @ManagedResource exposed counters as @ManagedAttribute getters, and an operator read them in JConsole, the JDK's desktop JMX viewer. This needed no extra server, which suited a few long-lived application servers.
  • Boot era: Boot 1.x Actuator's own metrics, through CounterService and GaugeService, read as flat JSON from /metrics. Boot 2.0 replaced them with Micrometer, whose dimensional metrics carry tags that flat names could not.
@Autowired private CounterService counterService;
counterService.increment("payouts.completed");

Recognise it by. com.codahale.metrics.*, the io.dropwizard.metrics:metrics-core and metrics-spring artifactIds, org.springframework.boot.actuate.metrics.CounterService, GaugeService, endpoints at /metrics and /health without /actuator, @ManagedResource, and -Dcom.sun.management.jmxremote.port in a start script.

The rookie version.

@Service
public class PayoutService {
    private final MeterRegistry registry = new SimpleMeterRegistry();
    private final Counter paid = registry.counter("payouts.completed");

    public void markPaid(Payout payout) {
        // ... save the payout as PAID
        paid.increment();
    }
}

What goes wrong. The code compiles, the counter counts, and nobody ever sees the number. SimpleMeterRegistry keeps meters in the pod's memory, and nothing reads it. Boot built its own registry for the service and wired it to the Prometheus endpoint, and this class never touched it. On the day the bank gateway rejected 312 payouts in an hour, the "payouts completed" panel showed no data at all. Everyone assumed the panel was broken rather than the payouts.

Do this now. Micrometer is a metrics facade: one API in your code, many monitoring systems behind it, much as ILogger sits in front of a logging library. A meter is one measurement, such as a counter or a timer. A meter registry holds the meters and exports them. Actuator is Spring Boot's module of management endpoints under /actuator.

  1. Add spring-boot-starter-actuator. A starter is one dependency that brings everything a feature needs. This one brings Micrometer and auto-configures a registry: Boot creates the bean because the library is present, with meters for HTTP requests, the JVM, the process and the MongoDB driver's connection pool.
  2. Add the registry for your monitoring system. Sorrel's cluster runs Prometheus, a server that scrapes, meaning it fetches each pod's metrics over HTTP on a schedule. The artifact is io.micrometer:micrometer-registry-prometheus, and Boot then serves /actuator/prometheus.
  3. Expose that endpoint. Only health is exposed over HTTP by default.
  4. Inject Boot's MeterRegistry wherever you record a meter (14.02).
  5. Check it. Payouts serves Actuator on port 8081 (14.09), so run kubectl port-forward <pod> 8081, then curl -s localhost:8081/actuator/prometheus | grep http_server_requests.
  6. Tell Prometheus where to scrape: port 8081, path /actuator/prometheus. With the Prometheus Operator that is a PodMonitor or ServiceMonitor resource, usually the platform team's.

The keys go in src/main/resources/application.yml.

management:
  endpoints:
    web:
      exposure:
        include: health,prometheus
  metrics:
    tags:
      application: payouts-api

Micrometer names use dots, such as http.server.requests. The Prometheus registry rewrites them with underscores and a unit, so the timer appears as http_server_requests_seconds_count and _sum. Search for the Prometheus form on the dashboard and the dotted form in code. The common application tag lets one dashboard query cover every service that shares a Prometheus.

Also seen. micrometer-registry-otlp, which pushes metrics to an OpenTelemetry collector instead of being scraped. Choose it when the platform runs a collector for traces already. micrometer-registry-cloudwatch2 for services that report straight to CloudWatch. The OpenTelemetry Java agent records its own metrics with no Micrometer at all (13.03).

When to break it. A batch job that lives for 40 seconds may finish between two scrapes. Push its metrics instead, through OTLP or a push gateway. The cost is a second path for metrics that the platform team must run.

.NET anchor. Micrometer's MeterRegistry does two jobs that .NET splits. It creates meters, as System.Diagnostics.Metrics.Meter does, and it holds and exports them, as the OpenTelemetry MeterProvider with the Prometheus exporter does. The other difference is that Boot registers the HTTP, runtime and pool meters for you as soon as the starter is on the classpath, the set of jars the application runs with. The rookie mistake is the same in both: a meter that no exporter reads.

See also. 14.02, 14.09, 14.10, 13.03, 4.02, The Yard, chapter 11, Actuator and observability

14.02 Add a business metric

Then.

  • Spring era: a Dropwizard Meter, which counted events and computed one-, five- and fifteen-minute rates inside the process. It suited a dashboard that read a single host. Prometheus computes rates at query time instead, across every pod, so the counter only needs to count.
Meter completed = metrics.meter("payouts.completed");
completed.mark();
double perSecond = completed.getOneMinuteRate();

Recognise it by. getOneMinuteRate(), Meter.mark(), counterService.increment(...), and gauge names that start with gauge. in old JSON output.

The rookie version.

public void recordBacklog(int pending) {
    registry.gauge("payouts.outbox.pending", new AtomicInteger(pending));
}

What goes wrong. A gauge is a meter that reports a current value each time it is read, such as a queue length. Micrometer registers the gauge once, on the first call, against that first AtomicInteger. Every later call creates a new object that the gauge never sees. The gauge also holds its object through a weak reference, so after the next garbage collection it has nothing to read and reports NaN. When SNS was unavailable for 25 minutes, the outbox grew to 4,000 unsent events. The panel showed 17, then a gap.

Do this now. Choose the meter type by the question you will ask of it.

  1. A counter only goes up. Use it for events: payouts completed, payouts failed. Prometheus's rate() turns it into events per second.
  2. A timer records how long something took, and counts it at the same time (14.06).
  3. A distribution summary records sizes that are not durations, such as payout amounts.
  4. A gauge reads a current value from a long-lived object, through a function, at scrape time.

Then follow these rules.

  • Build meters once, in a constructor, and keep them in fields. When a tag's value is known only at record time, keep a MeterProvider from withRegistry(...) and add the tag with withTags(...).
  • Count at the point of truth: after the payout is saved as PAID, not when the request arrives.
  • Use one meter name with a bounded tag, such as outcome, rather than one name per outcome.
  • Keep the gauge's function cheap. It runs on every scrape, on every pod.
@Component
public class PayoutMetrics {
    private final Meter.MeterProvider<Counter> completed;
    private final Meter.MeterProvider<DistributionSummary> amounts;
    public PayoutMetrics(MeterRegistry registry, OutboxBacklog backlog) {
        completed = Counter.builder("payouts.completed").withRegistry(registry);
        amounts = DistributionSummary.builder("payouts.amount").withRegistry(registry);
        Gauge.builder("payouts.outbox.pending", backlog, OutboxBacklog::pendingCount).register(registry);
    }
    public void paid(Money amount) {
        completed.withTags("outcome", "paid").increment();
        amounts.withTags("currency", amount.currency().toString()).record(amount.amount().doubleValue());
    }
    public void failed() { completed.withTags("outcome", "failed").increment(); }
}

The amount carries its currency as a tag, because pounds and euros do not add up. OutboxBacklog is a singleton bean, so the gauge's weak reference is never the only one. Its pendingCount() reads a cached count that the OutboxRelay refreshes, rather than querying DocumentDB on every scrape.

Also seen. @Counted and @Timed on a method. They work through AOP, aspect-oriented programming: Spring wraps the bean in a proxy that records the meter around each call from another bean. They need management.observations.annotations.enabled=true and the AOP starter, renamed spring-boot-starter-aspectj in Boot 4 (13.08). Without both, the annotations do nothing. The Observation API records a timer and a trace span from one call (13.08). Choose it when you want both for the same operation.

When to break it. A number the business reports on, such as the total paid this month, does not belong in a metric. Metrics are sampled and may lose a scrape. Read money totals from DocumentDB or the ledger, and keep the metric for trends.

.NET anchor. meter.CreateCounter<long>("payouts.completed") and CreateObservableGauge in System.Diagnostics.Metrics. The observable gauge takes a callback, which avoids the dangling-object mistake by design. Micrometer's object-and-function form does the same thing once you hand it a long-lived object.

See also. 14.01, 14.03, 14.06, 9.08, 13.08, Actuator and observability

14.03 Avoid high-cardinality tags

Then.

  • Spring era: hierarchical names for Graphite and StatsD, where each dimension was a segment of the name, such as payouts.pod-1.ledger.reserve.count. Dashboards used wildcards on the segments. It was the only model those tools had, and putting an ID in a segment caused the same damage as an ID in a tag.
metrics.timer(MetricRegistry.name("payouts", podName, "ledger", "reserve"));

Recognise it by. Dotted names with a host or ID in the middle, MetricRegistry.name(...) with runtime values, and GraphiteReporter or StatsDReporter in the configuration.

The rookie version.

Counter.builder("payouts.completed")
       .tag("outcome", "paid")
       .tag("payoutId", payoutId)
       .tag("claimant", claim.claimantEmail())
       .register(registry)
       .increment();

What goes wrong. A tag is a name and value attached to a meter, such as outcome=paid. Each distinct combination of tag values is a separate time series, a stream of numbers that Prometheus stores and indexes. Cardinality is how many such combinations a meter has. Payouts makes about 20,000 payouts on a normal day. This counter creates 20,000 new series a day, each of which never counts past 1. Every one also stays in the pod's registry, so the heap grows until the pod restarts. Prometheus memory climbs for the whole cluster, and the platform team drops the payouts-api scrape target to protect everyone else. The claimant's email address is now stored in a monitoring system with no data-protection controls (12.06).

Do this now.

  1. Tag only with values from a small, known set: outcome, currency, method, status, a client application's name.
  2. Before adding a tag, multiply. Four methods, 12 URI templates and 8 status codes give 4 × 12 × 8 = 384 series per pod. A histogram multiplies that by its bucket count (14.06).
  3. Put IDs in logs and traces, which are built to search for one event (12.04, 13.08).
  4. Keep URIs as templates. Boot's http.server.requests tags uri with the route template, /payouts/{id}. An outbound call whose URI is built by string concatenation passes that string as the template, so each concrete path becomes its own uri value (7.01).
  5. Cap anything that could still grow, with a MeterFilter bean. A MeterFilter is a rule Micrometer applies to each meter as it is registered, to rename, change or deny it. Boot applies every MeterFilter bean to its registries.
@Bean
MeterFilter capClientUris() {
    return MeterFilter.maximumAllowableTags(
            "http.client.requests", "uri", 50, MeterFilter.deny());
}

Past 50 distinct uri values, new ones are dropped rather than registered. A gap in the graph is cheaper than a broken Prometheus.

Also seen. A MeterFilter.ignoreTags(...) bean to remove a tag a library adds. Exemplars, which attach a sample trace ID to a histogram bucket, so you can jump from a slow bucket to one slow request without tagging every request.

When to break it. A tag with a few hundred stable values, such as a partner bank's code, is acceptable if someone has counted the series. The cost is real memory in Prometheus, so agree it with the platform team first.

.NET anchor. counter.Add(1, new("outcome", "paid")) in System.Diagnostics.Metrics creates series exactly as Micrometer tags do, and the OpenTelemetry SDK has its own cardinality limit per instrument. The rule is the same in both: bounded values only.

See also. 14.02, 14.06, 7.01, 12.04, 12.06, 13.08, Actuator and observability

14.04 Separate liveness from readiness

Then.

  • Boot era: one /health endpoint for every probe. It aggregated every health indicator, a bean that reports one component as UP or DOWN, including the database, into one status. Older Boot versions had no notion of an application's availability, so the aggregate was the only answer there was.
livenessProbe:  { httpGet: { path: /health, port: 8080 } }
readinessProbe: { httpGet: { path: /health, port: 8080 } }

Recognise it by. Probes pointing at /health or /actuator/health with no group path, and custom HealthIndicator classes for downstream services, with no management.endpoint.health.group.* keys.

The rookie version.

management:
  endpoint:
    health:
      group:
        liveness:
          include: livenessState,mongo,ledger

What goes wrong. The liveness probe tells Kubernetes when to restart a container, and the readiness probe tells it when to send traffic. With the defaults, three failed liveness probes 10 seconds apart restart the container. So a DocumentDB failover that lasts 30 seconds now restarts both Payouts pods. The restart does not fix the database. It cuts off payouts that were in flight, and adds a full startup to the outage. The ledger entry is worse. A slow ledger, which is another team's problem, restarts Payouts in a loop.

Do this now. Boot tracks an availability state for the application, through the ApplicationAvailability interface. Health groups expose it as /actuator/health/liveness and /actuator/health/readiness. Boot 3.5 turns these groups on when it detects Kubernetes, and Boot 4 turns them on everywhere. "By default, Spring Boot does not add other health indicators to these groups."

  1. Leave liveness alone. It reports livenessState, which is CORRECT unless your code says otherwise.
  2. Add to readiness only what stops this pod, and only this pod, from serving. A full local work queue qualifies. A shared database does not, because removing every pod from service helps nobody.
  3. Warm up in an ApplicationRunner, a bean whose run method Boot calls once the application has started (4.09). Boot reports ACCEPTING_TRAFFIC only after the runners have finished.
  4. Change the state from code when something local breaks. Publish ReadinessState.REFUSING_TRAFFIC to stop new work, or LivenessState.BROKEN when only a restart will help.
@Component
class OutboxRelayWatchdog {
    private final ApplicationEventPublisher events;

    OutboxRelayWatchdog(ApplicationEventPublisher events) { this.events = events; }

    void relayStuck() {
        // the relay's thread is blocked and cannot be freed in place: ask for a new container
        AvailabilityChangeEvent.publish(events, this, LivenessState.BROKEN);
    }
}

ApplicationEventPublisher is Spring's in-process event bus, injected like any other bean. Call relayStuck from a check on a thread of its own, such as a timer that sees no finished relay run for 5 minutes. A check on the relay's own thread would be stuck too. At shutdown Boot moves readiness to refusing traffic by itself, while liveness stays correct. The probe thresholds on the Kubernetes side are 17.04.

Also seen. management.endpoint.health.probes.add-additional-paths=true, which also serves the groups on the main server port as /livez and /readyz. Choose it when Actuator runs on a separate management port (14.09). Then a probe also proves that the port serving payouts is answering.

When to break it. A pod whose only job is one dependency, such as a relay that does nothing without its queue, may put that dependency in readiness. The cost is that a dependency outage takes the pod out of service, so make sure nothing else is routed to it.

.NET anchor. ASP.NET Core health checks with tags, mapped twice: MapHealthChecks("/healthz/live", new HealthCheckOptions { Predicate = _ => false }) and a /healthz/ready that selects checks tagged ready. Boot's groups are the same idea. The difference is that Boot already maps both groups, and connects readiness to graceful shutdown.

See also. 14.05, 14.09, 17.04, 17.05, 4.09, The Yard, chapter 14, Actuator and observability

14.05 Add a health indicator for a dependency, carefully

Then.

  • Boot era: an AbstractHealthIndicator that called the downstream service's own /health on every check, and was counted in the single /health every probe read.

What goes wrong. A LedgerHealthIndicator calls the ledger on each check. Both pods' probes, plus the monitoring scrape, now call the ledger every few seconds. When the ledger slows, the indicator times out, the aggregate goes DOWN, and Payouts is removed from service, even though 3 of its 5 endpoints never touch the ledger.

Do this now. Implement HealthIndicator. It is in org.springframework.boot.actuate.health on Boot 3.5, and moves to org.springframework.boot.health.contributor in Boot 4. Make it cheap: report state Payouts already holds, such as the breaker from 7.05, instead of making a call. Keep it out of the liveness and readiness groups. It then appears in /actuator/health for people who are allowed to see details (14.09), and the probes ignore it.

@Component
class LedgerHealthIndicator implements HealthIndicator {
    private final CircuitBreakerRegistry breakers;

    LedgerHealthIndicator(CircuitBreakerRegistry breakers) { this.breakers = breakers; }

    @Override
    public Health health() {
        var state = breakers.circuitBreaker("ledger").getState();
        return Health.up().withDetail("breaker", state.name()).build();
    }
}

It reports UP with the breaker's state as a detail, so the aggregate never goes DOWN for the ledger. Boot names an indicator after its bean, less the HealthIndicator suffix, so this one is ledger.

See also. 14.04, 14.07, 7.05, 4.06, Actuator and observability

14.06 Measure latency with histograms and percentiles

Then.

  • Spring era: a Dropwizard Timer, whose reservoir sampled recent durations and computed percentiles inside each process. One host's 99th percentile was accurate. Two hosts' percentiles cannot be combined into one, which did not matter until services ran as many pods.
Timer.Context ctx = payTimer.time();
try { pay(claim); } finally { ctx.stop(); }
double p99 = payTimer.getSnapshot().get99thPercentile();

Recognise it by. getSnapshot(), get99thPercentile(), ExponentiallyDecayingReservoir, and dashboards that show a mean or p99 series per host.

The rookie version.

Timer.builder("payouts.ledger.reserve")
     .publishPercentiles(0.99)          // computed inside each pod
     .register(registry);

avg(payouts_ledger_reserve_seconds{quantile="0.99"})

What goes wrong. publishPercentiles computes the 99th percentile in each pod and exports the result. Pod A handled 900 reserves with a p99 of 400 ms. Pod B handled 100 with a p99 of 6 seconds, because its connections to the ledger had gone bad. The average of the two is 3.2 seconds, which describes no request at all. The true p99 across both pods cannot be computed from these two numbers. The mean is no better. If 98% of reserves take 180 ms and 2% take 8 seconds, the mean is 0.98 × 180 + 0.02 × 8,000 = 336 ms. That looks healthy while 1 payout in 50 waits 8 seconds.

Do this now. A percentile is the value below which a given share of measurements fall: p99 is the latency that 99 of 100 requests beat. A histogram counts measurements into fixed ranges called buckets. Bucket counts from many pods can be added together, and the percentile is then estimated from the sum.

  1. Publish a histogram, not client-side percentiles. For your own timers, call publishPercentileHistogram().
  2. Turn it on for Boot's meters through configuration, per meter name.
  3. Add SLO boundaries, the latency you have promised, so one bucket sits exactly on the line.
  4. Query the percentile across all pods in PromQL, Prometheus's query language, with histogram_quantile, after summing the buckets.
reserve = Timer.builder("payouts.ledger.reserve")    // in the constructor
        .publishPercentileHistogram()
        .register(registry);

LedgerReservation r = reserve.record(() -> ledgerClient.reserve(payout));

management:
  metrics:
    distribution:
      percentiles-histogram:
        http.server.requests: true
      slo:
        http.server.requests: 200ms,1s

histogram_quantile(0.99,
  sum by (le, uri) (rate(http_server_requests_seconds_bucket[5m])))

le is the bucket's upper bound, the label that Prometheus needs to rebuild the distribution. The SLO bucket lets you read "share of requests under 1 second" directly, which makes a better alert than a percentile (14.07).

Also seen. Client-side publishPercentiles for a single-instance job, where nothing needs combining. The Observation API, which gives the same timer plus a trace span (13.08).

When to break it. Every histogram multiplies a meter's series by its bucket count. On a timer with many tags, enable it only on the meters you alert on. The cost of leaving the rest off is no percentile for them, only a rate and a mean.

.NET anchor. Histogram<double> from meter.CreateHistogram<double>(...), exported with explicit bucket boundaries set through an OpenTelemetry view. Micrometer chooses default buckets for you, and slo adds the boundaries you care about.

See also. 14.03, 14.07, 7.01, 13.08, 18.01, 18.10, Actuator and observability

14.07 Alert on symptoms, not causes

Then.

  • Spring era: Nagios checks per host on CPU, disk, heap use and process count, each with a warning and a critical threshold. With few hosts and no load balancer, a busy host often was the outage.

What goes wrong. Payouts pages someone when CPU passes 80% on either pod. It fires most nights in the reconciliation batch, while payouts succeed. After a month, the person on call mutes it. Then the bank gateway rejects payouts from 02:14 with CPU at 12%, and nothing pages.

Do this now. A symptom is something a customer or another team can feel. A cause is one reason for it. Page on symptoms.

  • The share of POST /payouts answering 5xx.
  • The share of requests slower than the 1-second SLO bucket (14.06).
  • Payouts not completing: payouts_completed_total{outcome="paid"} falling to zero in working hours (14.02).
  • Messages ageing on a queue, or reaching a dead-letter queue (14.08).

CPU, heap, pod restarts and the breaker's state go on the dashboard, to explain a page.

sum(rate(http_server_requests_seconds_count{method="POST",uri="/payouts",status=~"5.."}[5m]))
  / sum(rate(http_server_requests_seconds_count{method="POST",uri="/payouts"}[5m])) > 0.02

Put the expression in a Prometheus alerting rule with for: 5m, so one bad scrape cannot page.

See also. 14.02, 14.06, 14.08, 14.10, The Yard, chapter 13, Actuator and observability

14.08 Monitor queues by the age of the oldest message and DLQ depth

Then.

  • Spring era: queue depth read from a JMS broker's JMX beans, with an alert above a fixed number.

What goes wrong. ledger-confirm holds 600 messages, which is normal after a batch. This time the LedgerConfirmListener had stopped, and the 600 messages were 3 hours old.

Do this now. SQS publishes queue metrics to CloudWatch, under the QueueName dimension.

  1. Alarm on ApproximateAgeOfOldestMessage for each source queue, above the longest a message should wait. Age rises when consumers fall behind, whatever the depth.
  2. Alarm on ApproximateNumberOfMessagesVisible above 0 on each dead-letter queue: ledger-confirm-dlq, notify-claimant-dlq and payout-audit-dlq. A dead-letter queue (DLQ) holds messages that failed too often, and each needs a person's decision (10.08).
  3. Do not alarm on NumberOfMessagesSent for a DLQ. It ignores messages the redrive policy moves.
  4. Know two quirks. On a standard queue, a message received 3 or more times without being deleted drops out of the age metric, so a poison message hides. On a DLQ, age counts from when the message was moved, not when it was first sent.

A Micrometer counter of listener failures shows the problem before the DLQ does.

See also. 10.08, 10.09, 10.17, 14.07, 20.08, Messaging and WebSockets

14.09 Secure the Actuator endpoints

Then.

  • Boot era: Boot 1.x served every endpoint at the root path, and services turned its checks off with management.security.enabled=false and endpoints.sensitive=false to make the dashboards work. Endpoints were few, and the network was trusted.

Recognise it by. management.security.enabled, endpoints.sensitive, endpoints.<id>.sensitive keys, and paths such as /env and /heapdump with no /actuator in front.

The rookie version.

management:
  endpoints:
    web:
      exposure:
        include: "*"     # to reach /actuator/prometheus

What goes wrong. The developer wanted one endpoint and exposed all of them, on the main port. With a chain that permits /actuator/**, as in 15.05's rookie version, that includes /actuator/env, which lists configuration sources, and /actuator/heapdump, which downloads the heap. The heap holds every claimant's bank details that are in memory, and the DocumentDB password. One request from anywhere on the ingress takes it.

Do this now.

  1. Serve Actuator on its own port with management.server.port: 8081. The ingress routes only 8080, so nothing outside the cluster reaches 8081.
  2. List exactly what you expose: health,prometheus, plus loggers for changing a level at runtime (12.09). The default is health only.
  3. Keep health details hidden. show-details defaults to never. Use when-authorized, with roles in management.endpoint.health.roles, if people need them.
  4. Give Actuator a security chain of its own. Spring Security's filters run on the management port too, so the API chain in 15.05, which ends in denyAll(), would refuse Prometheus's scrape. EndpointRequest is Boot's request matcher for Actuator endpoints, whatever their port and base path.
@Bean
@Order(1)
SecurityFilterChain actuator(HttpSecurity http) throws Exception {
    return http
            .securityMatcher(EndpointRequest.toAnyEndpoint())
            .authorizeHttpRequests(auth -> auth
                    .requestMatchers(EndpointRequest.to("health", "prometheus")).permitAll()
                    .requestMatchers(EndpointRequest.to("loggers")).hasRole("OPERATOR")
                    .dispatcherTypeMatchers(DispatcherType.ERROR).permitAll()
                    .anyRequest().denyAll())
            .oauth2ResourceServer(o -> o.jwt(Customizer.withDefaults()))
            .build();
}

@Order(1) puts this chain ahead of the API chain, and its securityMatcher makes it handle Actuator requests only. Prometheus scrapes without a token, so the scrape is open, on a port only the cluster can reach. loggers needs a token with the OPERATOR role, mapped as in 15.02. The ERROR dispatch is permitted for the reason given in 15.05. An endpoint exposed later is refused until someone writes a rule for it.

  1. Point the probes at the port that serves payouts, through /livez and /readyz (14.04, 17.04). Those paths are on 8080, so the API chain must permit them, or every probe is refused and Kubernetes restarts the pod.

Also seen. Actuator on the main port, behind the API chain, with a role for everything except health. It suits a platform with no second port in its manifests, and every scrape then needs a credential.

When to break it. On a laptop, include: "*" is a quick way to explore the endpoints. Set it as an environment variable for that run, not in a file in the repository, so it cannot reach an image.

.NET anchor. ASP.NET Core has no Actuator. The nearest is MapHealthChecks and the OpenTelemetry exporter's MapPrometheusScrapingEndpoint(), bound to a management port with .RequireHost("*:8081"). The difference is the default. In .NET you add each endpoint yourself. Actuator ships many, some of them dangerous, and exposure is the switch.

See also. 5.22, 14.01, 14.04, 15.05, 15.06, 17.04, Actuator and observability

14.10 Read the JVM metrics that matter

Then.

  • Spring era: jstat -gcutil and JConsole, attached over remote JMX to one host at a time, to read heap generations and GC counts by eye.

What goes wrong. The team watches jvm.memory.used for the heap, which stays flat at 60% of its maximum. The pod is still OOMKilled, because the kernel counts the whole container: heap, metaspace, thread stacks and direct buffers.

Do this now. Read these, in this order.

  1. The container's total memory against its limit, from the cluster's own metrics, such as container_memory_working_set_bytes (17.02).
  2. jvm.gc.live.data.size, the old generation's size after the last collection. A floor that rises over days is a leak (18.06).
  3. jvm.memory.used with area="nonheap" and jvm.buffer.memory.used, the memory outside the heap.
  4. jvm.gc.pause: how often, and the longest pause. Long pauses show up as p99 latency (14.06).
  5. process.cpu.usage, against the CPU limit, not the node.
  6. jvm.threads.live, which counts platform threads only. With virtual threads on, watch the connection pools instead, such as mongodb.driver.pool.waitqueuesize (18.03).

See also. 14.01, 14.07, 17.02, 17.09, 18.03, 18.06, The Yard, chapter 13, The JVM at runtime: memory, GC and containers

⚠Review checklist
  • If you see new SimpleMeterRegistry() or any registry built by hand in production code: the meters never reach Prometheus. See 14.01.
  • If you see registry.gauge(...) called with a new object on every call: the gauge keeps the first object, then reports NaN after garbage collection. See 14.02.
  • If you see a tag whose value is an ID, an email, a full URL or a free-text message: series grow with traffic until Prometheus or the pod runs out of memory. See 14.03.
  • If you see a database or another service in the liveness group: another team's outage restarts your pods in a loop. See 14.04.
  • If you see a health indicator that calls a downstream service: the probes multiply its load and its slowness takes your pods out of service. See 14.05.
  • If you see publishPercentiles on a multi-pod service, or an average of percentiles on a dashboard: the number describes no real request. See 14.06.
  • If you see a page on CPU, heap or pod restarts: it fires when customers are fine and stays quiet when they are not. See 14.07.
  • If you see a queue alarm on depth alone, or a DLQ with no alarm: a stopped consumer or a failed message goes unnoticed for hours. See 14.08.
  • If you see exposure.include: "*" or Actuator on the public port: the heap dump and the environment are one request away. See 14.09.
  • If you see a memory alert on the heap alone: the container is killed on total memory while the heap graph is green. See 14.10.

Part IV · The how-to15. Security#

Payouts moves real money to real bank accounts, so every request has to say who sent it, and the service has to decide what that caller may do. This part shows how payouts-api checks the tokens it receives, how it decides by scope, by role and by the data itself, and how it holds the tokens it sends. It also covers secrets, AWS permissions without keys, injection into Mongo queries, CORS, CSRF, tests, vulnerable dependencies, field encryption and the audit trail.

★What a veteran knows
  • Authentication is the easy half. Most breaches in an API come from a caller who was correctly identified and then shown someone else's data.
  • A signature check without an audience check accepts every token your identity provider has ever issued, for every service in the company.
  • A rule that silently does nothing looks exactly like a rule that works. Test the refusal, not only the success.
  • The token you send needs as much care as the one you receive. On Payouts, the token request was the call nobody had timed or counted.
  • A secret is only as safe as its widest reader. Count who can read the repository, the pod's environment, the logs and the heap dump.
  • The closed default is the safe default. A new endpoint should be refused until someone writes its rule.
◷How we got hereOn Thursday 26 July 2012 Eran Hammer published a post on his blog, hueniverse.com, called "OAuth 2.0 and the…

On Thursday 26 July 2012 Eran Hammer published a post on his blog, hueniverse.com, called "OAuth 2.0 and the Road to Hell". He had spent three years and "over two dozen drafts" as lead author and editor of the new standard. "Last month I reached the painful conclusion that I can no longer be associated with the OAuth 2.0 standard," he wrote. He had resigned, withdrawn his name and left the working group. "OAuth 2.0 is a bad protocol. WS-* bad," he wrote. One compromise had been "to rename it from a protocol to a framework". Bearer tokens had dropped signatures at the protocol level, so 2.0 "relies solely on TLS". In the hands of most developers, he warned, it was "likely to produce insecure implementations." RFC 6749 was published that October, edited by D. Hardt of Microsoft, and it credits Hammer with editing many of the drafts. The checks in this part, on issuer, audience, expiry and scope, are the care his warning asked for.

15.01 Protect an API as an OAuth2 resource server with JWTs

Then.

  • Boot era: The separate Spring Security OAuth project, with @EnableResourceServer and a ResourceServerConfigurerAdapter. Before Spring Security had resource-server support of its own, this was how a Boot service accepted OAuth2 tokens. Its keys lived under security.oauth2.resource.*, without the spring. prefix. The project is no longer maintained, and its README points to the OAuth2 client and resource-server support in Spring Security itself, and to Spring Authorization Server.
@Configuration
@EnableResourceServer
public class ResourceServerConfig extends ResourceServerConfigurerAdapter {
    @Override
    public void configure(HttpSecurity http) throws Exception {
        http.authorizeRequests().antMatchers("/payouts/**").authenticated();
    }
}
  • Boot era: Keycloak's own adapters, with a class annotated @KeycloakConfiguration that extended KeycloakWebSecurityConfigurerAdapter. They were convenient when Keycloak was the only identity provider. They build on WebSecurityConfigurerAdapter, which Spring Security 6.0 removed, so they cannot run on Boot 3. Keycloak deprecated them in 2022, pointing Spring users to Spring Security, and removed them in Keycloak 25.
  • Boot era: Opaque tokens, random strings that only the provider can read, checked on every request by RemoteTokenServices, which called the provider's check_token endpoint.

Recognise it by. org.springframework.security.oauth2.config.annotation.web.configuration.EnableResourceServer, ResourceServerConfigurerAdapter, RemoteTokenServices, the spring-security-oauth2 and spring-security-oauth2-autoconfigure artifactIds, security.oauth2.resource.jwk.key-set-uri, keycloak-spring-boot-starter, and keycloak.auth-server-url.

The rookie version.

@PostMapping("/payouts")
ResponseEntity<PayoutResponse> create(@RequestHeader("Authorization") String auth,
                                      @RequestBody CreatePayoutRequest request) throws IOException {
    String payload = auth.substring("Bearer ".length()).split("\\.")[1];
    Map<?, ?> claims = mapper.readValue(Base64.getUrlDecoder().decode(payload), Map.class);
    if (!"payouts-api".equals(claims.get("aud"))) {
        return ResponseEntity.status(403).build();
    }
    return ResponseEntity.status(201).body(payoutService.create(request));
}

What goes wrong. The code reads the middle part of the token and never checks the signature. Anyone can write that part. A tester base64-encodes {"aud":"payouts-api"}, adds 2 dots and any text, and creates a payout of £1,240.50. Expiry is not checked either, so a token copied from a log 3 months ago still works. The check is repeated in each controller method, and the 1 method that forgets it is open to anyone.

Do this now. A resource server is OAuth2's name for an API that accepts access tokens. A JWT (JSON Web Token) is a signed token in 3 base64url parts, joined by dots: a header, the claims, and a signature. Spring Security checks the token in a servlet filter, code that runs on every request before any controller, like ASP.NET Core middleware.

  1. Add spring-boot-starter-oauth2-resource-server. A starter is a Maven dependency that pulls in a set of libraries and switches on Boot's automatic configuration for them, so adding it is most of the setup. In Boot 4 it is renamed spring-boot-starter-security-oauth2-resource-server.
  2. Name the issuer and the audience.
spring:
  security:
    oauth2:
      resourceserver:
        jwt:
          issuer-uri: https://idp.sorrel.internal
          audiences: payouts-api
  1. Boot builds a JwtDecoder from these settings. It reads the provider's discovery document, the JSON published under the issuer at /.well-known/openid-configuration, and finds the JWK set, the provider's public signing keys, and caches them. Each token's signature is checked against those keys. Then iss must equal the issuer and exp must lie in the future. With audiences set, aud must contain payouts-api.
  2. Set audiences. Without it, Spring checks no audience, and a token issued to any of Sorrel's 40 services is accepted by Payouts.
  3. Turn the filter on in the chain with oauth2ResourceServer(o -> o.jwt(Customizer.withDefaults())) (15.05).
  4. Read the caller in a controller with a parameter @AuthenticationPrincipal Jwt jwt. jwt.getSubject() is the caller's ID.

A request with no token, a bad signature or an expired token gets 401, with a WWW-Authenticate: Bearer header. For a bad or expired token the header also says why. The request never reaches your controller.

To add a rule of your own, declare the decoder yourself. Boot then creates none, and the audiences property no longer applies, so the audience check goes in your validators.

@Bean
JwtDecoder jwtDecoder(OAuth2ResourceServerProperties props) {
    String issuer = props.getJwt().getIssuerUri();
    NimbusJwtDecoder decoder = JwtDecoders.fromIssuerLocation(issuer);
    decoder.setJwtValidator(new DelegatingOAuth2TokenValidator<>(
            JwtValidators.createDefaultWithIssuer(issuer),
            new JwtClaimValidator<List<String>>("aud",
                    aud -> aud != null && aud.contains("payouts-api"))));
    return decoder;
}

Also seen. Opaque tokens checked by introspection, a call to the provider for every request, with oauth2ResourceServer(o -> o.opaqueToken(...)). Choose it when a token must stop working the moment it is revoked, and accept a network call per request. An API gateway that validates tokens and forwards headers is also common. Then the service must accept requests only from the gateway.

When to break it. The Kubernetes probes call /actuator/health with no token, so that path is open (15.05). Behind a service mesh that enforces mutual TLS and per-service policies, some teams accept requests with no token. The cost is that a decision can then depend only on which service called, never on which person.

.NET anchor. AddAuthentication().AddJwtBearer(o => { o.Authority = "https://idp.sorrel.internal"; o.Audience = "payouts-api"; }). Authority is issuer-uri and Audience is audiences. The difference is the default: ASP.NET Core validates the audience unless you turn it off, and Spring validates it only when you name one.

See also. 15.02, 15.05, 15.11, 7.08, Security

15.02 Authorise endpoints by scope and role

Then.

  • Spring era: XML rules such as <intercept-url pattern="/payouts/**" access="hasRole('ROLE_PAYOUTS')"/>, and @Secured("ROLE_ADMIN") on methods.
  • Boot era: antMatchers inside authorizeRequests(), joined with .and(), and @EnableGlobalMethodSecurity(prePostEnabled = true) to switch on @PreAuthorize. Spring Security 6.0 removed antMatchers in favour of requestMatchers. @EnableMethodSecurity replaced @EnableGlobalMethodSecurity, and authorizeHttpRequests replaced authorizeRequests.
http.authorizeRequests()
    .antMatchers(HttpMethod.POST, "/payouts/**").hasAuthority("SCOPE_payouts.write")
    .antMatchers("/payouts/**").hasAuthority("SCOPE_payouts.read")
    .anyRequest().authenticated()
    .and().csrf().disable();

Recognise it by. antMatchers, mvcMatchers, authorizeRequests(), .and(), @EnableGlobalMethodSecurity, @Secured, and <intercept-url in XML.

The rookie version.

// hasRole("payouts.write") gave every caller 403, so it was loosened to this:
.authorizeHttpRequests(auth -> auth
        .requestMatchers("/actuator/health/**").permitAll()
        .anyRequest().authenticated())

What goes wrong. hasRole("payouts.write") checks for the authority ROLE_payouts.write. The token carries the scope payouts.write, which Spring turns into SCOPE_payouts.write. The 2 never match, so every caller got 403. The fix that made the test pass was authenticated(). Now any valid token from Sorrel's identity provider can create a payout. That includes the token the notification service uses to read claim statuses.

Do this now. An authority is a string the caller holds, checked by hasAuthority. Each scope in the JWT's scope claim becomes an authority with the prefix SCOPE_. A role is an authority whose name starts with ROLE_. hasRole('X') adds that prefix and checks ROLE_X.

  1. Use URL rules for the coarse decision: which scope may call which method on which path. The most specific rule goes first, and anyRequest() goes last.
.authorizeHttpRequests(auth -> auth
        .requestMatchers("/actuator/health/**").permitAll()
        .requestMatchers(HttpMethod.POST, "/payouts/**").hasAuthority("SCOPE_payouts.write")
        .requestMatchers(HttpMethod.GET, "/payouts/**").hasAuthority("SCOPE_payouts.read")
        .dispatcherTypeMatchers(DispatcherType.ERROR).permitAll()
        .anyRequest().denyAll())

denyAll() at the end closes any endpoint nobody wrote a rule for. The ERROR line lets Spring's error handling through: without it, an unhandled exception is forwarded to /error, denyAll() refuses that, and the caller gets 403 instead of 500 (15.05).

  1. Map roles for people. A claim handler's token carries "roles": ["payouts-approver"], which Spring ignores by default. A JwtAuthenticationConverter bean maps it. A converter reads one claim, so combine 2 of them to keep the scopes as well.
@Bean
JwtAuthenticationConverter jwtAuthenticationConverter() {
    var scopes = new JwtGrantedAuthoritiesConverter();
    var roles = new JwtGrantedAuthoritiesConverter();
    roles.setAuthoritiesClaimName("roles");
    roles.setAuthorityPrefix("ROLE_");
    var converter = new JwtAuthenticationConverter();
    converter.setJwtGrantedAuthoritiesConverter(jwt -> Stream.concat(
            scopes.convert(jwt).stream(), roles.convert(jwt).stream()).toList());
    return converter;
}
  1. Put rules about one operation on the method. Add @EnableMethodSecurity to one configuration class, then annotate PayoutService.approve with @PreAuthorize("hasRole('payouts-approver')"). Without @EnableMethodSecurity every @PreAuthorize is ignored, and nothing warns you.
  2. Remember that @PreAuthorize works through a proxy, a wrapper object Spring puts in front of the bean to run the check. A call from another method of the same class skips the check (4.08).

Also seen. @Secured("ROLE_ADMIN"), which takes full authority names, and @RolesAllowed("ADMIN"), which adds the ROLE_ prefix. Neither takes expressions, and both are ignored unless switched on with @EnableMethodSecurity(securedEnabled = true, jsr250Enabled = true). A custom AuthorizationManager bean, for a rule too long to read as an expression.

When to break it. A service with 1 caller and 1 scope can use anyRequest().hasAuthority(...) alone. The cost arrives with the second caller, which then gets everything the first one had.

.NET anchor. A policy, options.AddPolicy("PayoutsWrite", p => p.RequireClaim("scope", "payouts.write")), used as [Authorize(Policy = "PayoutsWrite")]. [Authorize(Roles = "payouts-approver")] is hasRole. ASP.NET Core reads roles from the claim type in RoleClaimType. Spring needs the converter, and ASP.NET Core has no equivalent of the SCOPE_ prefix.

See also. 15.01, 15.03, 15.05, 15.11, 4.08, 9.02, Security

15.03 Authorise by data: may this caller see this payout

Then.

  • Spring era: Spring Security ACL. Permissions are rows in relational tables, one per object and user, and hasPermission checks them through a PermissionEvaluator. It suits systems where people grant access to single objects, such as shared documents. For a rule the data already holds, such as "the claimant owns this payout", the rows only copy it.
@PreAuthorize("hasPermission(#payoutId, 'com.sorrel.payouts.Payout', 'read')")
public Payout find(String payoutId) { ... }
  • Boot era: @PostFilter("filterObject.claimantId == authentication.name") on a method that returns a list. It loads every row and drops the others in memory.

Recognise it by. The spring-security-acl artifactId, AclPermissionEvaluator, JdbcMutableAclService, the tables acl_object_identity and acl_entry, hasPermission(, @PostFilter and @PreFilter.

The rookie version.

@GetMapping("/payouts/{id}")
@PreAuthorize("hasAuthority('SCOPE_payouts.read')")
PayoutResponse get(@PathVariable String id) {
    return payoutRepository.findById(id)
            .map(PayoutResponse::from)
            .orElseThrow(() -> new PayoutNotFound(id));
}

What goes wrong. The claims portal lets claimants see their own payouts, so their tokens carry payouts.read. A claimant changes p-10431 in the address bar to p-10432 and sees another claimant's payout of £1,240.50, with the last 4 digits of their bank account. The IDs are sequential, so a short script reads 5,000 payouts in a minute. Every check passed: the token was genuine, and the scope was right. OWASP's API Security Top 10 calls this broken object level authorization.

Do this now. Write the rule in domain terms first. On Payouts a claimant sees payouts for their own claims, and a service holding payouts.read sees all of them.

  1. Turn the token into a caller type in the controller, once. A sealed interface (2.12) lists the kinds of caller. Claimants and services both hold payouts.read, so the scope cannot tell them apart. The azp (authorised party) claim can: it names the client the token was issued to, which is the claims portal for a claimant and the service itself for a client-credentials token. Some providers call it client_id.
Caller callerOf(Jwt jwt) {
    String client = jwt.getClaimAsString("azp");
    return serviceClients.contains(client)
            ? new Caller.Service(client)
            : new Caller.Claimant(jwt.getSubject());
}

serviceClients is a set bound from payouts.security.service-clients (4.02). A client nobody listed gets the narrowest view, a claimant's, and a service's subject owns no payouts.

  1. Put the owner into the query, so a payout that is not yours does not exist for you.
public sealed interface Caller {
    record Service(String clientId) implements Caller {}
    record Claimant(String claimantId) implements Caller {}
}

public Payout find(String payoutId, Caller caller) {
    Optional<Payout> payout = switch (caller) {
        case Caller.Service s -> payouts.findById(payoutId);
        case Caller.Claimant c -> payouts.findByIdAndClaimantId(payoutId, c.claimantId());
    };
    return payout.orElseThrow(() -> new PayoutNotFound(payoutId));
}
  1. Answer 404 for another claimant's payout, not 403. A 403 confirms that the payout exists.
  2. Filter lists in the query, with findByClaimantId(claimantId, pageable), never in memory.
  3. Put the check in PayoutService, not only in the controller. Then the admin endpoint and any later route go through it too.
  4. Test the refusal: claimant CL-2093 asks for another claimant's payout and gets 404. The check lives in the query, so this test needs the real PayoutService and a database, not a mocked service (15.11).

The switch has no default. When someone adds a third kind of caller, the code stops compiling until they decide what it may see.

Also seen. @PreAuthorize("@payoutAccess.canRead(#id, authentication)"), which calls a bean before the method runs and costs a second read. @PostAuthorize("returnObject.claimantId() == authentication.name"), which checks the loaded object and answers 403. A policy engine such as Open Policy Agent, when many services share the same rules.

When to break it. Support staff sometimes need to read any payout. Give them a scope of their own rather than an exception in the query. The cost is that every such read must be recorded, with who and why (15.14).

.NET anchor. Resource-based authorisation: IAuthorizationService.AuthorizeAsync(User, payout, "OwnsPayout") with an AuthorizationHandler<OwnsPayoutRequirement, Payout>. The @PreAuthorize bean is Spring's version of it. Putting the owner in the query is closer to an EF Core global query filter.

See also. 15.02, 15.11, 15.14, 2.12, 8.03, Security

15.04 Call other services with client credentials and cache the token

Then.

  • Boot era: OAuth2RestTemplate from the Spring Security OAuth project kept the token in an OAuth2ClientContext and fetched a new one after it expired. Entry 7.08 shows how it was wired.
  • Boot era: ServletOAuth2AuthorizedClientExchangeFilterFunction on a WebClient, in services that were not reactive. Before RestClient had an OAuth2 interceptor, this was how Spring Security's own client attached tokens.
var oauth = new ServletOAuth2AuthorizedClientExchangeFilterFunction(manager);
oauth.setDefaultClientRegistrationId("ledger");
WebClient ledger = WebClient.builder().apply(oauth.oauth2Configuration()).build();

Recognise it by. OAuth2ClientContext, OAuth2RestTemplate, ClientCredentialsAccessTokenProvider, ServletOAuth2AuthorizedClientExchangeFilterFunction, and a ledger call that ends in .block().

The rookie version.

private volatile String token;
private volatile Instant expiresAt = Instant.EPOCH;

String token() {
    if (Instant.now().isBefore(expiresAt)) return token;
    TokenResponse response = fetchToken();
    token = response.accessToken();
    expiresAt = Instant.now().plusSeconds(response.expiresIn());
    return token;
}

What goes wrong. 3 things, all at the hour.

  • There is no margin. A token is valid when Payouts checks it at 10:59:59.900 and expired when the ledger reads it 150 ms later. Those ledger calls get 401, and their payouts fail.
  • Nothing stops a stampede. At expiry, every thread that asks sees an expired token, and each fetches its own. Under load that is 200 token requests in 1 second, and the identity provider starts to refuse them.
  • Nothing clears a bad token. When the identity provider withdraws a signing key early, the ledger rejects every token signed with it, and Payouts keeps sending its token for up to an hour.

Do this now. A client-credentials token is the token a service gets for itself, with its own ID and secret (7.08). It has a life: it is requested, cached, used until shortly before it expires, and replaced. This flow has no refresh token. The client asks again with its credentials.

  1. Let Spring Security hold the token. OAuth2AuthorizedClientService stores tokens, and the AuthorizedClientServiceOAuth2AuthorizedClientManager asks for a new one when the cached one is close to expiry. Entry 7.08 wires the manager into the ledger's RestClient.
  2. Set the margin, called the clock skew, to cover a slow call and clocks that disagree.
@Bean
OAuth2AuthorizedClientManager clientManager(ClientRegistrationRepository registrations,
                                            OAuth2AuthorizedClientService clients) {
    var provider = OAuth2AuthorizedClientProviderBuilder.builder()
            .clientCredentials(cc -> cc.clockSkew(Duration.ofSeconds(90)))
            .build();
    var manager = new AuthorizedClientServiceOAuth2AuthorizedClientManager(registrations, clients);
    manager.setAuthorizedClientProvider(provider);
    return manager;
}

The manager takes no lock. Threads that ask in the same instant may each fetch a token, but with the margin that happens before expiry, and only for the length of one token request.

  1. Store the token under the service, not the user. The service keeps 1 token per registration and principal name. If a ledger call runs inside a claimant's request, the default principal is that claimant. Then every claimant gets a separate Payouts token, and the cache does nothing. Give the OAuth2ClientHttpRequestInterceptor from 7.08 a principal resolver that always returns the same Authentication, named payouts-api: oauth.setPrincipalResolver(request -> PAYOUTS), where PAYOUTS is a constant holding UsernamePasswordAuthenticationToken.authenticated("payouts-api", null, List.of()).
  2. Drop the token when the other side rejects it. On a 401, call removeAuthorizedClient("ledger", "payouts-api") on the service, or call setAuthorizationFailureHandler(OAuth2ClientHttpRequestInterceptor.authorizationFailureHandler(clients)) on the interceptor, which does it for you. The interceptor's default failure handler does nothing. The next call then fetches a fresh token. Retry the failed call once only if it is safe to repeat (7.07).
  3. Count the token requests. Each of the 2 pods keeps its own cache, so with 1-hour tokens Payouts should ask about 2 times an hour. A graph that shows 40 a second at month-end, one per ledger call, finds the bug in step 3.
  4. Give the token request a timeout of its own (7.03), and never log the token.

Also seen. A mesh sidecar that adds the token, so the code holds none. A token cache shared by all pods, in Redis, when the identity provider limits how many tokens a client may hold.

When to break it. A very sensitive call may use a fresh, short-lived token every time. The cost is a token request per call, so it suits a few calls an hour, not 40 a second.

.NET anchor. Duende.AccessTokenManagement caches client-credentials tokens and renews them before expiry, and MSAL's AcquireTokenForClient keeps them in the application's token cache. Spring's OAuth2AuthorizedClientService plays the role of that cache. The per-principal key has no counterpart in either, which is why it surprises .NET developers.

See also. 7.08, 7.03, 7.07, 15.06, Security

15.05 Configure a SecurityFilterChain

Then.

  • Boot era: A class extending WebSecurityConfigurerAdapter that overrode configure(HttpSecurity). Spring Security deprecated it in 5.7, released in May 2022, and recommended a SecurityFilterChain bean instead. Spring Security 6.0 removed it in November 2022. The bean is plain Spring configuration, and a service can declare several.
@EnableWebSecurity
public class SecurityConfig extends WebSecurityConfigurerAdapter {
    @Override
    protected void configure(HttpSecurity http) throws Exception {
        http.csrf().disable().authorizeRequests().antMatchers("/actuator/health").permitAll()
            .anyRequest().authenticated().and().oauth2ResourceServer().jwt();
    }
}
  • Spring era: An <http> element in security-context.xml, and a DelegatingFilterProxy named springSecurityFilterChain in web.xml.

Recognise it by. extends WebSecurityConfigurerAdapter, configure(HttpSecurity http), configure(AuthenticationManagerBuilder auth), .and() between sections, and springSecurityFilterChain in web.xml.

The rookie version.

.authorizeHttpRequests(auth -> auth
        .requestMatchers("/actuator/**").permitAll()
        .requestMatchers("/payouts/**").authenticated()
        .anyRequest().permitAll())

management.endpoints.web.exposure.include: "*"

What goes wrong. Every Actuator endpoint is now exposed and open. /actuator/heapdump returns a heap dump to anyone on the cluster network. That file holds the bank API key and every cached token in memory. anyRequest().permitAll() adds a second hole later. 6 months on, someone adds /claims/{id}/payouts, and it is open to the internet on its first day.

Do this now. Spring Security is a list of servlet filters in front of Spring MVC. A SecurityFilterChain bean says which filters and which rules apply to which requests. Boot supplies a default chain until you declare one.

The bean goes in a SecurityConfig class annotated @Configuration, @EnableWebSecurity and @EnableMethodSecurity.

@Bean
SecurityFilterChain api(HttpSecurity http) throws Exception {
    return http
            .authorizeHttpRequests(auth -> auth
                    .requestMatchers("/livez", "/readyz").permitAll()
                    .requestMatchers(POST, "/payouts/**").hasAuthority("SCOPE_payouts.write")
                    .requestMatchers(GET, "/payouts/**").hasAuthority("SCOPE_payouts.read")
                    .dispatcherTypeMatchers(DispatcherType.ERROR).permitAll()
                    .anyRequest().denyAll())
            .oauth2ResourceServer(o -> o.jwt(Customizer.withDefaults()))
            .sessionManagement(s -> s.sessionCreationPolicy(SessionCreationPolicy.STATELESS))
            .csrf(csrf -> csrf.disable())
            .build();
}
  1. Rules match in order, and the first match decides. Put anyRequest() last. Spring Security refuses to start if a rule follows it.
  2. End with denyAll(), so a new endpoint is closed until its rule exists. Open only the probe paths, /livez and /readyz, which Payouts serves on port 8080 for Kubernetes (14.04, 17.04). Actuator itself runs on port 8081, behind its own chain (14.09).
  3. Permit the ERROR dispatch. When a controller throws an exception nobody handles, the servlet container forwards the request to /error, and the chain checks that too. Without the line, denyAll() turns every 500 into a 403. POST and GET are static imports of HttpMethod's constants; the scope rules are 15.02's.
  4. STATELESS means Spring creates no HTTP session. Every request carries its own token.
  5. CSRF protection is off only because this chain uses no cookies (15.10).
  6. Use the lambda style shown here. Spring Security 7, used by Boot 4, removed the chained style with .and().
  7. For a second kind of client, add a second chain. The claim handlers' admin pages log in with a session cookie, so they get a chain of their own with securityMatcher("/admin/**") and @Order(1). The first chain whose matcher fits handles the request, and the others are never consulted. A chain with no securityMatcher matches everything, so it goes last.
  8. To see why a request was refused, set logging.level.org.springframework.security=DEBUG locally. The log shows which chain matched and which rule refused it.

A missing or bad token gets 401. A valid token without the authority gets 403.

Also seen. web.ignoring() in a WebSecurityCustomizer bean, which skips Spring Security entirely for some paths. Spring logs a warning when you use it and suggests permitAll() instead, because ignored paths also lose the security headers.

When to break it. Static files served at very high volume can be ignored rather than permitted. The cost is that they get no security headers, so ignore only files that hold nothing private.

.NET anchor. AddAuthentication, AddAuthorization, and app.UseAuthentication() and app.UseAuthorization() in Program.cs, with MapGroup("/payouts").RequireAuthorization(). In ASP.NET Core an endpoint is open until you protect it. In Spring every endpoint needs a login as soon as spring-boot-starter-security is on the classpath, which the resource-server starter brings in. Your chain then decides the exceptions. Setting options.FallbackPolicy in ASP.NET Core is the nearest thing to anyRequest().denyAll().

See also. 15.01, 15.02, 15.10, 14.09, 4.08, Security

15.06 Load secrets from AWS Secrets Manager or Kubernetes

Then.

  • Boot era: A properties file on each server, outside the jar, picked up with spring.config.additional-location. On a fleet of virtual machines that an operations team owned, the file was as safe as the box. Pods have no box that lasts, and the file had to be copied by hand.
# /opt/payouts/config/application.properties, copied to each server by hand
payouts.bank.api-key=sk_live_4f9a1c7e2b
spring.data.mongodb.password=Winter2016
  • Boot era: Spring Cloud AWS 2.x, which read Secrets Manager in a separate bootstrap phase configured in bootstrap.yml, before the rest of the configuration. spring.config.import, below, replaced that phase (4.04).
  • Boot era: Encrypted values in the YAML with jasypt, covered in 4.04.

Recognise it by. spring.config.location or spring.config.additional-location pointing at /opt or /etc, bootstrap.yml with aws.secretsmanager.* keys, the spring-cloud-starter-aws-secrets-manager-config artifactId, and AWSSecretsManagerClientBuilder from AWS SDK v1, which reached end of support on 31 December 2025.

The rookie version.

public BankInstruction instruct(Payout payout) {
    String apiKey = secretsManager.getSecretValue(GetSecretValueRequest.builder()
            .secretId("payouts/bank").build()).secretString();
    log.debug("calling bank with key {}", apiKey);
    return bankRestClient.post().uri("/instructions")
            .header("X-Api-Key", apiKey)
            .body(BankInstructionRequest.from(payout))
            .retrieve().body(BankInstruction.class);
}

What goes wrong. Every payout makes a Secrets Manager call first. At the month-end peak of 20 payouts a second on each of 2 pods, that is 40 calls a second. Each is a network round trip and a billed request. On a busy month-end morning Secrets Manager is slow for a few minutes, and payouts time out with an error from a service nobody thought was in the path. The day someone turns on DEBUG to find out why, the log line prints the bank key.

Do this now. AWS Secrets Manager stores a named secret, usually a JSON object, with versions. Read it once at startup, bind it to a typed record (4.02), and treat rotation as a restart. Spring Cloud AWS and the plain AWS SDK v2 both do this well.

With Spring Cloud AWS:

  1. Add io.awspring.cloud:spring-cloud-aws-starter-secrets-manager, managed by the Spring Cloud AWS BOM. A POM is Maven's project file, the counterpart of a .csproj. A BOM (bill of materials) is a POM that fixes the versions of a family of libraries. You import it once in <dependencyManagement>, and then name its libraries without versions. Use its 3.4.x line on Boot 3.5 and 4.x on Boot 4.
  2. Import the secret.
spring:
  config:
    import: "aws-secretsmanager:payouts/bank?prefix=payouts.bank."
  1. Each key of the JSON becomes a property, and the prefix goes in front of it. A secret holding {"api-key": "..."} binds to payouts.bank.api-key in BankProperties, as in 4.04.
  2. Leave off the optional: prefix. If the secret cannot be read, the service then refuses to start, which is what you want (4.10).

With the plain AWS SDK v2:

  1. Add software.amazon.awssdk:secretsmanager, managed by the SDK's BOM.
  2. Read the secret once, in a @Bean method, and parse it into a record.
@Bean
SecretsManagerClient secretsManagerClient() {
    return SecretsManagerClient.create();
}

@Bean
BankCredentials bankCredentials(SecretsManagerClient secrets, ObjectMapper json) throws IOException {
    String value = secrets.getSecretValue(r -> r.secretId("payouts/bank")).secretString();
    return json.readValue(value, BankCredentials.class);
}

BankCredentials is a record whose apiKey component carries @JsonProperty("api-key"), so it reads the same secret as the Spring Cloud AWS version.

Choose Spring Cloud AWS when you want secrets to arrive as ordinary properties, and you already use its SQS or SNS support. Choose the plain SDK when you want no extra framework, and no wait for a Spring Cloud AWS release when Boot moves.

Either way the pod needs no access key. It gets its AWS permissions from its role (15.07).

Rotation. Secrets Manager keeps the previous version under the staging label AWSPREVIOUS when AWSCURRENT moves to the new one. Ask the bank to accept both keys for a while, rotate, then roll the pods (17.06).

Also seen. The platform team syncs secrets into Kubernetes Secrets, with the External Secrets Operator or the Secrets Store CSI driver. The service then reads mounted files as a config tree (4.04), and needs no AWS permission for secrets. Parameter Store SecureString values, imported with aws-parameterstore:. Spring Cloud Vault, where Vault is the company's store.

When to break it. Short-lived database credentials change while the service runs, so they must be read again. Use AWS's caching client for Secrets Manager, so that the read stays out of the hot path. The cost is a refresh interval to choose and test.

.NET anchor. The Azure Key Vault configuration provider, builder.Configuration.AddAzureKeyVault(...), or a Secrets Manager configuration provider for AWS. spring.config.import is how Spring adds a configuration provider. Binding the result to a record is IOptions<T>.

See also. 4.04, 4.02, 4.10, 15.07, 17.07, 12.06, Dependency injection and configuration

15.07 Give a pod AWS permissions without access keys

Then.

  • Boot era: AWS_ACCESS_KEY_ID and AWS_SECRET_ACCESS_KEY in a Kubernetes Secret. Later, kube2iam's iam.amazonaws.com/role pod annotation, read by a node agent that handed the pod a role's credentials.

What goes wrong. An access key never expires on its own. Payouts' key was 3 years old. It appears in any dump of the pod's environment, and works from any laptop until someone rotates it.

Do this now. Link the pod's Kubernetes service account, the identity a pod runs as, to an IAM role, a set of AWS permissions code can assume briefly. On EKS, with IRSA (IAM roles for service accounts) you annotate the service account. With EKS Pod Identity the platform team associates the account with the role, and the YAML carries no annotation.

apiVersion: v1
kind: ServiceAccount
metadata:
  name: payouts-api
  namespace: payouts
  annotations:
    eks.amazonaws.com/role-arn: arn:aws:iam::123456789012:role/payouts-api

The Deployment's pod spec names it with serviceAccountName: payouts-api. Without it the pod runs as default and gets no role.

Both give the pod short-lived credentials. The SDK's default credentials chain finds and renews them, so SecretsManagerClient.create() needs no credentials code. For IRSA, SDK v2 also needs the software.amazon.awssdk:sts module on the classpath. Grant the role only what Payouts uses (10.18). It is the counterpart of Azure workload identity.

See also. 15.06, 10.18, 17.07, Security

15.08 Stop operator injection in Mongo queries

Then.

  • Spring era: 2.x driver code that parsed a request parameter straight into a query with com.mongodb.util.JSON.parse(request.getParameter("q")) and a BasicDBObject.

What goes wrong. A search endpoint takes its body as Map<String, Object> and passes body.get("claimantId") to Criteria.where("claimantId").is(...). A caller sends {"claimantId": {"$ne": null}}. The map is written as a sub-document, and the database reads $ne as an operator. The query becomes "claimant is not null", and the response holds every claimant's payouts.

Do this now. Operator injection is SQL injection's cousin for MongoDB: input that arrives as an operator instead of a value.

  1. Bind the request to a record with typed fields, such as PayoutSearch(@Pattern(regexp = "CL-\\d+") String claimantId, PayoutStatus status), and take it as @Valid @RequestBody PayoutSearch search (6.01). Jackson then answers 400 to an object where a String belongs. Without @Valid, @Pattern is ignored.
  2. Pass only typed values to derived queries (8.03) or Criteria.
  3. Never build query JSON by concatenation, as in new BasicQuery("{ claimantId: '" + id + "' }"), and never call Document.parse on client input.
  4. Take field names for sorting and filtering from an allow-list (5.08).

See also. 5.08, 6.01, 8.03, Document data: Amazon DocumentDB and the MongoDB API

15.09 Configure CORS only where a browser calls

Then.

  • Boot era: @CrossOrigin on every controller, or addCorsMappings in a WebMvcConfigurer with allowedOrigins("*"). Outside the security chain, a browser's preflight request reached Spring Security first and failed with 401.

What goes wrong. CORS (cross-origin resource sharing) is a browser rule. It decides whether a page from one origin, the scheme, host and port of a URL, may read responses from another. A developer copies allowedOriginPatterns("*") with allowCredentials(true) into every service. On the admin chain, which uses a session cookie, any website a claim handler visits can now call Payouts as that handler and read the answer, in every browser that sends the cookie cross-site. The cookie's SameSite attribute may stop the browser sending it cross-site. Do not rely on that.

Do this now. Configure CORS only on a service a browser calls from another origin. For Payouts that is the claims portal. Service-to-service calls ignore CORS entirely. Name the exact origins, methods and headers, and let the chain apply them with http.cors(Customizer.withDefaults()).

@Bean
CorsConfigurationSource corsConfigurationSource() {
    var config = new CorsConfiguration();
    config.setAllowedOrigins(List.of("https://portal.sorrel.co.uk"));
    config.setAllowedMethods(List.of("GET"));
    config.setAllowedHeaders(List.of("Authorization", "traceparent"));
    var source = new UrlBasedCorsConfigurationSource();
    source.registerCorsConfiguration("/payouts/**", config);
    return source;
}

The portal only reads payouts (15.03), so only GET is allowed. CORS is not access control. curl ignores it.

See also. 15.05, 15.10, Security

15.10 Handle CSRF in a stateless API

Then.
