  • Boot era: http.csrf().disable() as the first line of every security class.

What goes wrong. CSRF protection is on by default. The resource server skips it for requests with a bearer token, but MockMvc's jwt() test helper (15.11) sends no Authorization header, so the first test POST /payouts gets 403. So CSRF goes off everywhere, including the admin chain, which uses a session cookie. Another site can now make a handler's browser post an approval.

Do this now. CSRF (cross-site request forgery) is another site making the user's browser send a request. The browser adds cookies by itself, never an Authorization header.

  1. In a bearer-token chain with no session, disable CSRF: csrf(csrf -> csrf.disable()) with STATELESS (15.05).
  2. Keep CSRF on in any chain that uses cookies, such as a login session or a backend-for-frontend, a server that keeps the tokens and gives the browser a cookie.
  3. For a browser app that echoes the token from a cookie, use CookieCsrfTokenRepository.withHttpOnlyFalse(). Spring Security 6's default, XorCsrfTokenRequestAttributeHandler, expects a masked token, not the raw cookie value, so a Spring Security 5 setup can fail with 403. The reference's single-page-app setup accepts both.

See also. 15.05, 15.09, Security

15.11 Test secured endpoints

What goes wrong. The controller tests use @AutoConfigureMockMvc(addFilters = false), so no security filter runs. They stay green while the rule from 15.02 is loosened to authenticated(). Nothing tested that a payouts.read token cannot create a payout.

Do this now. Run the real chain in a @WebMvcTest, and send fake tokens with spring-security-test. Its jwt() post-processor builds an authenticated JWT without a signature or an identity provider.

@WebMvcTest(PayoutController.class)
@Import(SecurityConfig.class)
class PayoutControllerSecurityTest {
    @Autowired MockMvc mvc;
    @MockitoBean PayoutService payoutService;
    @MockitoBean JwtDecoder jwtDecoder;

    @Test
    void readScopeCannotCreate() throws Exception {
        mvc.perform(post("/payouts").contentType(APPLICATION_JSON).content(BODY)
                        .with(jwt().authorities(new SimpleGrantedAuthority("SCOPE_payouts.read"))))
           .andExpect(status().isForbidden());
    }
}

jwt() is a static import from SecurityMockMvcRequestPostProcessors. BODY is a request body as in 16.04. The refusal comes before the body is read, but the success case also needs its Idempotency-Key header. The mocked JwtDecoder stops the slice looking for the identity provider.

Write 3 cases per endpoint here: no token gets 401, the wrong scope gets 403, and the right scope succeeds. The fourth, another claimant's payout gets 404 (15.03), cannot run in this slice, because the mocked PayoutService holds no query. Run it in a @SpringBootTest with @AutoConfigureMockMvc and a real database, with jwt().jwt(j -> j.subject("CL-2093").claim("azp", "claims-portal")). In Boot 4 the test slice lives in the spring-boot-webmvc-test module.

See also. 15.02, 15.03, 16.04, 16.06, Testing Spring Boot

15.12 Keep dependencies free of known vulnerabilities

What goes wrong. A CVE is a published vulnerability with an ID and a CVSS score from 0 to 10. Payouts' build passed for 5 months over a library with a critical one. The fix was in a Boot patch 6 releases ahead. Log4Shell, CVE-2021-44228, was published on 10 December 2021 with a score of 10.0. A team that knew where log4j-core sat in its trees could patch that day.

Do this now.

  1. Run OWASP's dependency-check-maven plugin from the parent POM (1.02), which every module inherits, like Directory.Build.props. Fail the build above a score with failBuildOnCVSS. An API key for the NVD, the US National Vulnerability Database it downloads, is strongly recommended, not required.
  2. Find who pulls the library in with ./mvnw dependency:tree -Dincludes=<groupId>:<artifactId> (1.03).
  3. Fix it in this order: the latest Boot patch, then a managed version in the parent's <dependencyManagement> (1.02), then an exclusion if nothing uses it.
  4. Suppress a finding only with a reason in <notes> and an until date on <suppress>, so it counts again later.
  5. Merge the weekly Renovate or Dependabot pull requests while they are small (19.06).

See also. 1.02, 1.03, 19.06, The Yard, chapter 9, Maven vs csproj

15.13 Encrypt sensitive fields

Then.

  • Boot era: jasypt's StandardPBEStringEncryptor inside a converter, with its password beside the database password.

What goes wrong. Account numbers sit in plain text in payouts. A backup restored to a test cluster, or a query result in a ticket, exposes all 18,400. Cluster storage encryption protects the disks, not the data from anyone who can query it.

Do this now. Encrypt the few fields that hurt if read with a key the database never sees.

  1. Use envelope encryption through the AWS Encryption SDK for Java (com.amazonaws:aws-encryption-sdk-java) and AWS KMS. KMS holds the key, and each value gets a fresh data key, stored encrypted in the ciphertext.
  2. Use the payout ID as the encryption context, so ciphertext copied to another document fails to decrypt.
  3. Map it with a value type and a custom converter (8.18).
  4. Store the last 4 digits for display, and a keyed hash for "has this account been paid before?". Every encrypt and decrypt calls KMS, so decrypt only for the bank instruction.
  5. Grant kms:GenerateDataKey and kms:Decrypt on that 1 key to the Payouts role only (15.07).

See also. 8.18, 15.07, 12.06, Document data: Amazon DocumentDB and the MongoDB API

15.14 Record who did what

Then.

  • Boot era: Actuator's AuditEventRepository and the /auditevents endpoint, holding login events in memory until restart.

What goes wrong. A payout of £1,240.50 went to the wrong account. Investigators ask who changed the bank details on 3 March. The document says lastModifiedBy: "payouts-api", and the logs from March were deleted after 90 days. Nobody can say.

Do this now. Write an audit event for every business action, as data, not as a log line (12.11).

  1. Record the person (the JWT's sub), the service that acted for them (the azp or client_id claim), the action, the payout ID, the changed fields with sensitive values masked, the time and the trace ID.
  2. Write it as an OutboxEvent in the same write as the change (9.07). The event then exists exactly when the change does.
  3. Give the subscriptions filter policies (10.13), so only payout-audit receives audit events.
  4. Let PayoutAuditListener copy events from the payout-audit queue into an append-only store: its credentials may insert, not update or delete.

Spring Data's @CreatedBy and @LastModifiedBy, with AuditorAware and @EnableMongoAuditing, stamp the last writer on the document. Useful, but not a trail.

See also. 9.07, 12.11, 10.04, 10.13, 15.03, Security

⚠Review checklist
  • If you see a controller that splits the Authorization header and decodes the JWT itself: the signature and expiry go unchecked, and anyone can write a token. See 15.01.
  • If you see issuer-uri without audiences, or a custom JwtDecoder with no audience validator: tokens meant for other services are accepted. See 15.01.
  • If you see hasRole(...) with a scope name, or a rule loosened to authenticated(): any valid token can do anything. See 15.02.
  • If you see @PreAuthorize with no @EnableMethodSecurity in the service: every method rule is silently ignored. See 15.02.
  • If you see findById(id) on a path ID in a claimant-facing endpoint: any caller can read any payout by changing the ID. See 15.03.
  • If you see @PostFilter on a list method: every row is loaded, and the filter hides an authorisation rule in memory. See 15.03.
  • If you see a token kept in a field with an expiry check and no margin: calls fail at the boundary, and threads stampede the identity provider. See 15.04.
  • If you see a client-credentials call made inside a user's request with the default principal: Payouts holds 1 token per user. See 15.04.
  • If you see /actuator/** permitted, or anyRequest().permitAll(): the heap dump and every new endpoint are open. See 15.05.
  • If you see web.ignoring() for anything but static files: the paths skip Spring Security entirely. See 15.05.
  • If you see getSecretValue in a request path: every request becomes a Secrets Manager call, and a slow Secrets Manager becomes a Payouts outage. See 15.06.
  • If you see a real key in a properties file, in the repository or on a server: everyone who can read the file holds the key. See 15.06.
  • If you see AWS_ACCESS_KEY_ID in a Kubernetes Secret: a long-lived key that works from anywhere. See 15.07.
  • If you see a Map<String, Object> request body passed into a query: a caller can send operators. See 15.08.
  • If you see allowedOriginPatterns("*") with allowCredentials(true): any website can act as a signed-in user. See 15.09.
  • If you see csrf.disable() in a chain with a login session: cross-site requests ride on the user's cookie. See 15.10.
  • If you see addFilters = false in a controller test: the security rules are never tested. See 15.11.
  • If you see a dependency-check suppression with no reason or date: a real risk stays hidden after the code changes. See 15.12.
  • If you see a bank account number stored as a plain string: every database reader holds it. See 15.13.
  • If you see lastModifiedBy offered as the audit trail: it records the last writer, not who did what. See 15.14.

Part IV · The how-to16. Testing#

This part is about the tests a Payouts developer writes every week. It starts with a plain unit test and what to mock, then works outward through the Spring test slices, containers, fake HTTP servers and queues, to a few end-to-end tests of the saga. It covers what makes a suite fast or slow, what makes a test flaky, and what a coverage number does not tell you. It ends with the JUnit 4 tests you will find in older services, and how to move them on.

★What a veteran knows
  • A test earns its place by failing for the right reason. Before you trust a new test, break the code it guards and watch it go red.
  • Choose the test by the question. A unit test answers a decision, a slice, which starts one layer of Spring, answers that layer, a container answers a query, and a full context answers the wiring. Suites get slow when one kind of test does every job.
  • Mock the edge of your system, through a type you own. A mock of a library's API only tests your memory of that API.
  • The Spring context cache, which lets test classes with the same configuration share one started application, is the biggest lever on a slow suite. On Payouts, cutting 31 distinct test configurations to 4 took the build from 11 minutes to 3.
  • Thread.sleep in a test is either too long, which makes the suite slow, or too short, which makes it flaky. Often it is both, on different machines.
  • A flaky test is a bug report with no title. The cause is usually time, order or shared state, and rarely the machine.
  • Always ask "green against what?". A test against MongoDB in a container proves the query on MongoDB, and nothing yet about DocumentDB.
◷How we got hereOn 12 April 2015 Richard North pushed a commit called "Initial commit" to a new repository on GitHub.

On 12 April 2015 Richard North pushed a commit called "Initial commit" to a new repository on GitHub. He was chief engineer at Deloitte Digital, and his team's tests had hit a wall. "We were struggling with a few MySQL features that didn't have equivalents in H2," he said in a 2017 interview. H2 is an in-memory Java database that many teams used in place of the real one. The team faced "the unpleasant prospect" of limiting their product to what H2 could imitate. North saw a gap for "an H2-like tool that was actually a facade to a Docker-based database container". The first commit held JUnit rules that started MySQL and Nginx in containers. Version 1.0.0 reached Maven Central on 9 February 2016. North and Sergei Egorov later built a company, AtomicJar, around the library, and on 11 December 2023 Docker announced it had bought it. Every container in this part's listings descends from that commit.

16.01 Write a fast unit test with JUnit 5

Then.

  • Boot era: JUnit 4. Test classes and methods were public, set-up went in @Before, and a runner chosen with @RunWith changed how the class ran. It served Java well for over a decade and still runs in many older services (16.22).
@RunWith(MockitoJUnitRunner.class)
public class PayoutTest {
    @Before
    public void setUp() { now = Instant.parse("2026-10-24T09:00:00Z"); }

    @Test(expected = IllegalStateException.class)
    public void paidPayoutCannotBeReservedAgain() { paid.reserve("R-2", now); }
}
  • Spring era: TestNG, chosen for the groups, ordering and data providers that JUnit 4 lacked. You will still meet it in a few older suites.

Recognise it by. import org.junit.Test, org.junit.Assert.*, @RunWith, @Before, @BeforeClass, public void test methods, and org.testng.annotations.Test.

The rookie version.

@SpringBootTest
class PayoutTest {
    @Autowired PayoutService payoutService;

    @Test
    void paidPayoutCannotBeReservedAgain() {
        Payout paid = payoutService.payNow("C-4471", Money.gbp("1240.50"), "k-1");
        assertThrows(IllegalStateException.class, () -> payoutService.reserve(paid.id()));
    }
}

What goes wrong. The rule under test lives in Payout, a record with no dependencies. This test starts the whole application to check it: every bean (each object Spring creates and wires), the MongoDB connection and the SQS listeners. At Sorrel that takes about 20 seconds. The test now fails on a laptop with Docker stopped, for a reason that has nothing to do with the rule. When it does fail, the cause could be the rule, the service, the repository or the database. A test that cannot say which of four things broke is a slow way to start debugging.

Do this now. JUnit is Java's standard test framework. JUnit 5 has three parts. The Platform finds and runs tests, and Maven's Surefire plugin talks to it. Jupiter is the API you write against, in org.junit.jupiter.api. Vintage runs JUnit 4 tests on the Platform. Boot 3.5 manages Jupiter 5.12.2. In Boot 4 it is JUnit 6, which keeps the Jupiter API, gives all three parts one version number and needs Java 17.

  1. Test the object that makes the decision, created with new. No Spring, and no annotation on the class.
  2. Leave the class and methods package-private. JUnit 5 does not need public.
  3. Test one behaviour per method, and name the method as a sentence about it.
  4. Know the lifecycle. JUnit creates a new instance of the test class for every test method, so fields start fresh each time. A @BeforeAll method must be static for the same reason.
  5. Group tests by the state they start from with @Nested inner classes.
  6. assertThrows returns the exception, so you can check what it says.
class PayoutTest {
    private final Instant now = Instant.parse("2026-10-24T09:00:00Z");
    private final Payout pending = Payout.pending("C-4471", Money.gbp("1240.50"), "k-1", now);

    @Test void reservingAPendingPayoutMovesItToReserved() {
        assertThat(pending.reserve("R-1", now).status()).isEqualTo(PayoutStatus.RESERVED);
    }

    @Test void aPaidPayoutCannotBeReservedAgain() {
        Payout paid = pending.reserve("R-1", now).instruct("B-9", now).paid(now);
        var e = assertThrows(IllegalStateException.class, () -> paid.reserve("R-2", now));
        assertThat(e).hasMessageContaining("PAID");
    }
}

Tests like these run in milliseconds. Payouts has 412 of them, and together they take under 2 seconds, which is what lets a developer run them on every save.

Also seen. @TestInstance(Lifecycle.PER_CLASS), when set-up is expensive and the tests only read it. The cost is that one test can now change what the next one sees. Spock, a Groovy test framework, in teams that use Gradle.

When to break it. When the rule depends on Spring itself, such as validation annotations or a transaction, a plain object cannot see it. Spring adds those by wrapping the object in a proxy, a generated class that intercepts each call. Use a slice, a Spring test that starts only one layer of the application (16.04, 16.05), and pay a second or two instead of milliseconds.

.NET anchor. @Test is xUnit's [Fact], and a new instance per test is xUnit's default too. NUnit shares one instance per fixture, which is what PER_CLASS gives you. @BeforeEach plays the part of the xUnit constructor, and @AfterEach of Dispose.

See also. 16.02, 16.03, 16.14, 16.22, 2.16, The Yard, chapter 6, Testing

16.02 Mock only what you do not own

Then.

  • Boot era: PowerMock, with @RunWith(PowerMockRunner.class) and @PrepareForTest, to mock static methods, constructors and final classes. It was the only way to test code built around static gateways and singletons. Mockito's inline mock maker, the part of Mockito that builds mocks and the default since Mockito 5, does most of that now, and well-shaped code needs none of it.
@RunWith(PowerMockRunner.class)
@PrepareForTest(LedgerGateway.class)
public class PayoutServiceTest {
    @Test public void pays() {
        PowerMockito.mockStatic(LedgerGateway.class);
        when(LedgerGateway.reserve("C-4471")).thenReturn("R-1");
    }
}
  • Spring era: EasyMock and jMock, with record-and-replay expectations: expect(...), then replay(mock), then verify(mock).

Recognise it by. org.powermock, @PrepareForTest, PowerMockito.mockStatic, org.easymock.EasyMock.replay, RETURNS_DEEP_STUBS, and an explicit mockito-inline dependency in the POM, Maven's pom.xml build file.

The rookie version.

RestClient rest = mock(RestClient.class, RETURNS_DEEP_STUBS);
when(rest.post().uri("/ledger/reservations").body(request)
        .retrieve().body(LedgerReservation.class))
    .thenReturn(new LedgerReservation("R-1", Money.gbp("1240.50")));

LedgerClient client = new RestLedgerClient(rest);
assertThat(client.reserve(request).id()).isEqualTo("R-1");

What goes wrong. A deep stub is a mock whose every method returns another mock, so the chain compiles and answers whatever you wrote down. The test describes how the client calls Spring, line by line, and not what Payouts does. When a developer changed .body(...) to .toEntity(...) to read a response header, 14 tests failed and no behaviour had changed. Meanwhile, nothing that fails in production ever runs: the URL, the JSON field names, the 409 handling. A real RestClient throws on a 409, and this mock never will.

Do this now. Mockito is the Java mocking library in Boot's test starter. A starter is one dependency that brings everything a feature needs, and spring-boot-starter-test brings JUnit, Mockito, AssertJ, Awaitility and Spring's test support. mock() or @Mock makes a fake, when(...).thenReturn(...) gives it answers, and verify(...) checks it was called. The rule has two halves. Mock the systems you do not own, and do it through a type you do own.

  1. Find the edges of Payouts: the ledger, the bank gateway, the policy system and AWS. Payouts cannot run them truthfully in a test, and must never call the bank for real.
  2. Put an interface Payouts owns at each edge: LedgerClient, BankGatewayClient, PolicyClient, PayoutEventPublisher. Its methods take and return Payouts' own records, such as ReserveRequest and LedgerReservation, not HTTP types.
  3. In tests of the code that uses an edge, mock that interface or write a small fake.
  4. Test the adapter behind each interface against a fake server or a container (16.09, 16.11). Never mock RestClient, SqsTemplate or MongoTemplate, Spring's own clients for HTTP, SQS and MongoDB.
  5. Keep everything inside the edge real: records, Money, PayoutService itself.
  6. Leave MockitoExtension strict. It has always failed a test that sets up an answer nobody uses.
@ExtendWith(MockitoExtension.class)
class PayoutServiceTest {
    @Mock LedgerClient ledger;
    @Mock BankGatewayClient bank;
    @Mock PayoutRepository repository;   // its queries have their own tests (16.05)

    @Test void releasesTheReservationWhenTheBankRefuses() {
        when(repository.save(any())).thenAnswer(call -> call.getArgument(0));
        when(ledger.reserve(any(), any())).thenReturn(new LedgerReservation("R-1", AMOUNT));
        when(bank.instruct(any(), any())).thenReturn(new Rejected("account closed"));
        new PayoutService(repository, ledger, bank, CLOCK).pay(CLAIM);

        verify(ledger).release(eq("R-1"), any());
    }
}

Also seen. A hand-written fake, such as a FakeBankGateway that records instructions and can be told to refuse. It is better than a mock once many tests share the behaviour. Mockito.mockStatic inside try-with-resources, as a temporary step for legacy static calls.

When to break it. For a stable JDK type, use the real thing set up for the test, such as Clock.fixed, rather than wrapping or mocking it (16.13). The cost of every wrapper is one more class to read.

.NET anchor. It is the .NET rule "do not mock HttpClient, mock your typed client's interface". In .NET you cannot easily mock HttpClient, so you write a fake HttpMessageHandler. Mockito can mock RestClient, which is exactly why the trap is so easy to fall into here.

See also. 16.06, 16.09, 16.11, 7.14, The Yard, chapter 6, Testing

16.03 Write assertions that explain their failures

Then.

  • Boot era: JUnit 4's assertEquals(expected, actual), often with the arguments the wrong way round, and Hamcrest matchers such as assertThat(payout.getStatus(), is(equalTo(PAID))). Hamcrest gave readable, composable checks years before the fluent libraries. It is still in Boot's test starter, and MockMvc's jsonPath matchers use it.
  • Spring era: FEST-Assert, the fluent library that AssertJ was forked from.

Recognise it by. org.hamcrest.Matchers.*, org.hamcrest.MatcherAssert.assertThat, org.junit.Assert.assertEquals, and org.fest.assertions.

The rookie version.

List<Payout> stuck = repository.findStuck(cutoff);
assertTrue(stuck.size() == 2 && stuck.get(0).status() == PayoutStatus.RESERVED);

What goes wrong. When this fails in CI, the log says expected: <true> but was: <false> and nothing else. The list might be empty, or 3 long, or in another order, or hold the wrong status. The developer pulls the branch, starts a debugger and spends 20 minutes learning what the message could have said. The test also depends on order. findStuck does not sort, so get(0) passes on one database and fails on the next.

Do this now. AssertJ is the fluent assertion library in Boot's test starter. You write assertThat(actual) and then a chain of checks, and a failure prints the actual value.

  1. Assert on the value itself, never on a boolean you computed.
  2. For collections, extract the fields that matter and use containsExactly or containsExactlyInAnyOrder. A failure lists what was there and what was missing.
  3. Compare records with isEqualTo, which uses their equals. For documents with generated IDs or timestamps, use usingRecursiveComparison().ignoringFields("id", "updatedAt").
  4. Compare a BigDecimal, such as an exchange rate, with isEqualByComparingTo. Its equals counts the scale, so 1.165 and 1.1650 are not equal.
  5. Check exceptions with assertThatThrownBy(...), then isInstanceOf and hasMessageContaining.
  6. Add context with as(...) when the values alone would not say which case failed.
  7. When several independent facts belong to one test, use SoftAssertions.assertSoftly, which reports every failure, not only the first.
assertThat(repository.findStuck(cutoff))
        .as("payouts reserved before %s", cutoff)
        .extracting(Payout::claimId, Payout::status)
        .containsExactlyInAnyOrder(
                tuple("C-4471", PayoutStatus.RESERVED),
                tuple("C-4502", PayoutStatus.RESERVED));

assertThat(quote.rate()).isEqualByComparingTo("1.1650");

When this fails, the message shows the actual tuples, for example [("C-4471", RESERVED), ("C-4502", INSTRUCTED)], and which one did not match. Nobody needs a debugger.

Also seen. Hamcrest in older tests and in MockMvc expectations, where it is the natural fit. JUnit's own assertEquals for a single value, which is fine when the message is enough.

When to break it. A custom assertion method, such as assertThatPayout(p).isPaidWith("B-9"), pays off once many tests check the same shape. The cost is one more class to keep in step with the record.

.NET anchor. AssertJ is the Java FluentAssertions or Shouldly: assertThat(x).isEqualTo(y) is x.Should().Be(y). assertTrue(a && b) gives the same useless message as Assert.True(a && b) in xUnit.

See also. 16.01, 16.05, 16.15, 2.01, Testing

16.04 Test a controller with @WebMvcTest

Then.

  • Spring era: MockMvcBuilders.standaloneSetup, which built MockMvc around one controller by hand, with no Spring context. It was fast, but it ran without the service's settings for Jackson, the JSON library Spring uses, validation and error handling unless you added each one.
MockMvc mvc = MockMvcBuilders.standaloneSetup(new PayoutController(service))
        .setControllerAdvice(new PayoutErrors())
        .build();
  • Boot era: the same @WebMvcTest slice under JUnit 4, with @RunWith(SpringRunner.class) and Boot's @MockBean.

Recognise it by. standaloneSetup, @RunWith(SpringRunner.class), org.springframework.boot.test.mock.mockito.MockBean, and controller tests that start a server and call it with TestRestTemplate.

The rookie version.

@Test
void rejectsANegativeAmount() {
    var controller = new PayoutController(service);
    var body = new CreatePayoutRequest("C-4471", new BigDecimal("-5.00"), "GBP", PAYEE);
    ResponseEntity<?> response = controller.create("k-1", body);
    assertThat(response.getStatusCode()).isEqualTo(HttpStatus.BAD_REQUEST);
}

What goes wrong. Calling the method skips everything between the HTTP request and the method. JSON parsing, header binding, @Valid and the @RestControllerAdvice that builds the ProblemDetail body, the standard error format of RFC 9457 (6.02), never run. The test failed at first, because nothing validated the amount. So the developer added an if to the controller that returned a bare 400, and the test went green. In production the real constraint fired first, but the advice had a bug and answered with Spring's default error body. The claims portal, which reads application/problem+json, showed "unknown error" for 3 weeks.

Do this now. The application context is Spring's container of the objects an application is built from, each one a bean. A slice test starts only one layer of that context. @WebMvcTest starts the Spring MVC layer, and MockMvc sends requests through it in-process, with no network port.

  1. Name the controller: @WebMvcTest(PayoutController.class). Without it the slice loads every controller, and you must mock the dependencies of all of them.
  2. Know what the slice holds: controllers, @RestControllerAdvice classes, Jackson configuration, converters, filters and validation. It leaves out @Service, @Repository and other @Component classes.
  3. Replace the service with @MockitoBean (16.06).
  4. Write the request JSON by hand, in a text block. Serialising your own request record with the same Jackson settings would only prove the code agrees with itself.
  5. Assert the status, the headers and the body, with jsonPath. The order of errors is not fixed, so match an entry with hasItem, not by its index.
  6. Write one test per mapping a client relies on: 202 with a Location (5.06), 400 with field errors, 409 for a reused key, 404.
  7. If Spring Security is on the classpath, the slice includes its filter chain. 15.11 shows how to test with it.
@WebMvcTest(PayoutController.class)
class PayoutControllerTest {
    @Autowired MockMvc mvc;
    @MockitoBean PayoutService service;

    @Test void rejectsANegativeAmountWithAProblemDetail() throws Exception {
        mvc.perform(post("/payouts").header("Idempotency-Key", "k-1")
                .contentType(MediaType.APPLICATION_JSON)
                .content("""
                    {"claimId":"C-4471","amount":{"value":"-5.00","currency":"GBP"},"payee":{"name":"R. Okafor","sortCode":"40-11-62","accountNumber":"31926819"}}"""))
           .andExpect(status().isBadRequest())
           .andExpect(jsonPath("$.errors[*].pointer", hasItem("#/amount/value"))); // in any order
        verifyNoInteractions(service);
    }
}

In Boot 4, @WebMvcTest moves from org.springframework.boot.test.autoconfigure.web.servlet to org.springframework.boot.webmvc.test.autoconfigure, in the spring-boot-webmvc-test module.

Also seen. MockMvcTester, an AssertJ-style wrapper around MockMvc in newer Spring versions. REST Assured's MockMvc module, in teams that like its given().when().then() style.

When to break it. A controller with real logic in it is the problem, not the test. Move the logic into the service (5.02) and test it there. A @SpringBootTest over HTTP is right for the few tests that need the whole path, such as security with real tokens (16.07).

.NET anchor. The nearest thing is WebApplicationFactory<T> with every service replaced, though @WebMvcTest starts far less. MockMvc is like TestServer: requests go through the real pipeline without a socket.

See also. 16.06, 16.07, 6.02, 6.13, 15.11, The Yard, chapter 6, Testing Spring Boot

16.05 Test a repository with @DataMongoTest and Testcontainers

Then.

  • Boot era: Flapdoodle's embedded MongoDB. Adding de.flapdoodle.embed.mongo to the test scope was enough for Boot 2 to download and start a real mongod for the tests, with the version in a property. It gave a real server before Docker was on every laptop. Boot 3 no longer configures it, and Testcontainers replaced it.
# src/test/resources/application.properties, Boot 2
spring.mongodb.embedded.version=4.0.2
  • Spring era: Fongo, an in-memory imitation of MongoDB written in Java, wired in as a Mongo bean in a test configuration.

Recognise it by. de.flapdoodle.embed.mongo in the POM, spring.mongodb.embedded.* keys, com.github.fakemongo.Fongo, and @RunWith(SpringRunner.class) above @DataMongoTest.

The rookie version.

@DataMongoTest
class PayoutRepositoryTest {
    @Autowired PayoutRepository repository;

    @Test
    void savesAndLoadsAPayout() {
        Payout saved = repository.save(Payout.pending("C-4471", Money.gbp("1240.50"), "k-1", NOW));
        assertThat(repository.findById(saved.id())).contains(saved);
    }
}

What goes wrong. This tests Spring Data, which has its own tests. The code Payouts wrote is a hand-written @Query behind findStuck, and it never runs. That query filtered on updated_at, while the record stored the field as updatedAt. MongoDB does not complain about a field that does not exist. It returns nothing. For 6 weeks the sweeper that repairs stuck sagas found 0 payouts, while 37 sat in RESERVED with money held in the ledger.

Do this now. Testcontainers is a library that starts Docker containers for tests and removes them afterwards. @DataMongoTest is the MongoDB slice: it starts the repositories and MongoTemplate, and none of your services. Entry 8.23 covers the image tag, indexes and DocumentDB. This entry covers what to test and how to wire it.

  1. Test what you wrote. That means every @Query, every derived query (one Spring Data builds from the method name) with more than one condition, every MongoTemplate update, the @Version check and every unique index. A plain save and load needs no test.
  2. Declare the container once, as a bean in a @TestConfiguration, a configuration class used only by tests, and mark it @ServiceConnection. That annotation, from spring-boot-testcontainers, builds the connection settings from the running container, so no URI is copied by hand.
  3. Add spring-boot-testcontainers and the Testcontainers MongoDB module in test scope, taking the artifact and package names for Boot 3.5 and Boot 4 from 8.23 and the handbook chapter Document data: Amazon DocumentDB and the MongoDB API.
  4. Bring in your own beans with @Import, because the slice leaves them out.
  5. Clean up before each test, as 8.23 explains, so two tests in one class never see each other's documents. Delete the documents and create the indexes again with production's PayoutIndexes code, but never drop the collection, which drops its indexes too.
  6. Seed the documents each test needs in the test itself, so a reader sees the data next to the assertion.
@TestConfiguration(proxyBeanMethods = false)
class MongoTestContainer {
    @Bean @ServiceConnection
    MongoDBContainer mongo() { return new MongoDBContainer("mongo:5.0"); }
}

@DataMongoTest
@Import({MongoTestContainer.class, PayoutIndexes.class})
class PayoutRepositoryTest {
    @Autowired PayoutRepository repository;
    @Autowired MongoTemplate mongo;
    @Autowired PayoutIndexes indexes;

    @BeforeEach void clean() { repository.deleteAll(); indexes.ensure(); }
}
  1. Pin the stored shape with one test per document type. Read the raw Document, in BSON, MongoDB's binary form of JSON, and check field names and types. Every old document in production depends on that shape, and a renamed record component changes it silently.
@Test void findsOnlyPayoutsReservedBeforeTheCutoff() {
    repository.saveAll(List.of(reserved("C-4471", NOW.minus(2, HOURS)), reserved("C-4502", NOW)));
    assertThat(repository.findStuck(NOW.minus(1, HOURS)))
            .extracting(Payout::claimId).containsExactly("C-4471");
}

@Test void storesTheAmountInMinorUnitsWithItsCurrency() {
    repository.save(reserved("C-4471", NOW));
    Document raw = mongo.getCollection("payouts").find().first();
    assertThat(raw).containsKey("updatedAt");
    assertThat(raw.get("amount", Document.class))
            .containsEntry("minor", 124050L).containsEntry("currency", "GBP");
}
  1. Test a lost update directly. Load the same payout twice, save one copy, then expect OptimisticLockingFailureException when saving the other (8.05).

Also seen. @Testcontainers with a @Container static field in each test class. It works, but every class then has its own container and, often, its own context (16.08). @DynamicPropertySource setting the MongoDB URI by hand, from before @ServiceConnection.

When to break it. A query so simple that a typo would break a dozen other tests may go without its own test. The cost is that when it breaks, the failure shows up somewhere less obvious.

.NET anchor. This is Testcontainers for .NET's MongoDbBuilder in a class fixture, testing a repository against a real server instead of EF Core's in-memory provider. Fongo was Java's in-memory provider, with the same kind of false greens.

See also. 8.05, 8.06, 8.23, 16.08, 16.03, The Yard, chapter 7, Testing Spring Boot, Document data: Amazon DocumentDB and the MongoDB API

16.06 Replace a bean in a Spring test with @MockitoBean

Then.

  • Modern: Spring Boot's own @MockBean and @SpyBean, from org.springframework.boot.test.mock.mockito. They made replacing a bean a one-line job, and most Boot tests of the last decade use them. Boot 3.4 deprecated them in favour of Spring Framework's @MockitoBean and @MockitoSpyBean, and Boot 4 removes them.
import org.springframework.boot.test.mock.mockito.MockBean;

@SpringBootTest
class PayoutFlowTest {
    @MockBean LedgerClient ledger;
}
  • Spring era: a test configuration with a @Primary bean, the one Spring prefers when two match, such as @Bean @Primary LedgerClient ledger() { return Mockito.mock(LedgerClient.class); }, or a bean of the same name that overrode the real one.

Recognise it by. org.springframework.boot.test.mock.mockito.MockBean, @SpyBean, @MockBean on a @Configuration class, @Primary beans that return Mockito.mock(...), and spring.main.allow-bean-definition-overriding=true in test properties.

The rookie version.

@TestConfiguration
class FakeLedgerConfig {
    static final LedgerClient LEDGER = Mockito.mock(LedgerClient.class);

    @Bean @Primary
    LedgerClient ledgerClient() { return LEDGER; }
}
// in a test: verify(FakeLedgerConfig.LEDGER).reserve(any());

What goes wrong. The mock is static, so every test class and every cached context share one mock, and nothing resets it. Its recorded calls pile up. verify(LEDGER).reserve(any()) passed when run alone and failed in the full build with "Wanted 1 time but was 3", because two earlier classes had also paid claims. The stubs leaked too. One test told the ledger to refuse, and a later test in another class failed with a refusal it never asked for. Surefire does not promise an order, so the failures came and went.

Do this now. @MockitoBean replaces a bean in the test's application context with a Mockito mock, or adds one if no such bean exists. It arrived in Spring Framework 6.2, in org.springframework.test.context.bean.override.mockito.

  1. Put it on a field of the test class. Spring finds the bean by type and swaps in the mock.
  2. Stub and verify the field like any other mock. Spring resets it after each test, so neither stubs nor recorded calls leak.
  3. Use @MockitoSpyBean to wrap the real bean, so you can verify calls to it or stub one method. You will rarely need it.
  4. Use @TestBean to replace a bean with a real object you build, such as a FakeBankGateway. Spring calls a static factory method in the test class to make it.
  5. Know where they may go. Unlike @MockBean, they are not supported on @Configuration classes. Keep them on the test class or on a base class it extends.
  6. Every different set of replaced beans gives a different context, and so another start-up (16.07). Agree one set for the suite.
  7. To migrate, change the import and the annotation name, and move any @MockBean out of configuration classes.
@SpringBootTest
class PayoutFlowTest {
    @Autowired PayoutService payouts;
    @MockitoBean LedgerClient ledger;
    @MockitoBean BankGatewayClient bank;

    @Test void marksThePayoutFailedWhenTheLedgerRefuses() {
        when(ledger.reserve(any())).thenThrow(new LedgerRefused("insufficient funds"));
        Payout payout = payouts.pay(CLAIM);
        assertThat(payout.status()).isEqualTo(PayoutStatus.FAILED);
        verifyNoInteractions(bank);
    }
}

Also seen. A @Primary fake in a @TestConfiguration, which is fine when the fake is a real class that holds no state between tests. @MockBean in every Boot 3.x service you inherit, still working with a deprecation warning until the Boot 4 upgrade.

When to break it. When a fake server exists for the dependency, a full-context test should use the real client against it (16.09). A mocked LedgerClient hides the whole HTTP layer, so use it to test the code above the client, not the client.

.NET anchor. It is WebApplicationFactory.WithWebHostBuilder with ConfigureTestServices replacing a registration with a Moq object. In .NET you create and reset that mock yourself. Spring creates it per context and resets it per test.

See also. 16.02, 16.04, 16.07, 4.14, 19.04, The Yard, chapter 6, Testing Spring Boot, Migrating Spring Boot 3 to 4

16.07 Keep @SpringBootTest for what needs it, and reuse contexts

Then.

  • Spring era: SpringJUnit4ClassRunner with an XML test context, and @DirtiesContext on any class that changed a bean. The context cache dates from this era. So does the habit of defeating it.
@RunWith(SpringJUnit4ClassRunner.class)
@ContextConfiguration(locations = "classpath:payouts-test-context.xml")
@DirtiesContext(classMode = ClassMode.AFTER_EACH_TEST_METHOD)
public class PayoutFlowIT { }
  • Boot era: @RunWith(SpringRunner.class) with @SpringBootTest(webEnvironment = RANDOM_PORT) and an injected TestRestTemplate, used for every controller test because slices were not yet a habit.

Recognise it by. SpringJUnit4ClassRunner, @ContextConfiguration(locations = ...), @DirtiesContext, AFTER_EACH_TEST_METHOD, and *IT classes that each carry their own properties = ....

The rookie version.

@SpringBootTest(properties = "payouts.ledger.read-timeout=1s")
class LedgerTimeoutTest { @MockitoBean BankGatewayClient bank; }

@SpringBootTest(properties = "payouts.saga.step-timeout=5s")
@ActiveProfiles("saga")
class SagaTimeoutTest { @MockitoBean LedgerClient ledger; }

@SpringBootTest @DirtiesContext
class OutboxRelayTest { }

What goes wrong. Spring caches each test context and reuses it for any later class with exactly the same configuration. Here every class differs: in properties, in profile (a named set of configuration switched on together), in replaced beans. @DirtiesContext throws a context away on purpose. Each new combination is a new start, about 20 seconds at Sorrel. Payouts had 31 such combinations, so about 10 of its 11 build minutes were start-ups. Worse, on Boot 3.5 a cached context stays running until the JVM exits. Its SQS listeners keep polling. With 12 live contexts polling one queue in LocalStack, a container that imitates AWS (16.11), a test's message was often taken by another context's listener, and the test timed out.

Do this now. @SpringBootTest starts the whole application context, as production would. With webEnvironment = RANDOM_PORT it also starts a real server on a free port. Keep it for three jobs:

  1. Wiring. One test that the context starts with the real configuration catches a missing bean or a bad property before a deploy does.
  2. A few paths across layers. HTTP in, the database, the fake ledger and the queues, as in 16.12.
  3. Spring behaviour that spans layers. Security with the real filter chain, transactions, @Async.

Everything else is a unit test or a slice. Then make the full tests share one context:

  1. Define one meta-annotation for all of them. A meta-annotation is an annotation you write that carries others, so every class that uses it has the same configuration.
  2. Put the replaced beans in one abstract base class, so every subclass has the same set. Put the fake servers there too, with their @DynamicPropertySource method (16.09). A different method in each class is a different configuration, and so a different context.
  3. Undo state in @AfterEach instead of using @DirtiesContext: delete documents, reset circuit breakers, purge queues.
  4. Set logging.level.org.springframework.test.context.cache=DEBUG to see how many contexts a run builds.
@Target(ElementType.TYPE)
@Retention(RetentionPolicy.RUNTIME)
@SpringBootTest(webEnvironment = SpringBootTest.WebEnvironment.RANDOM_PORT)
@AutoConfigureMockMvc
@ActiveProfiles("test")
@Import(PayoutsTestContainers.class)
public @interface PayoutsIntegrationTest { }

@PayoutsIntegrationTest
abstract class IntegrationTestBase {
    @MockitoBean PolicyClient policy;   // the same replaced beans in every subclass
    @Autowired MongoTemplate mongo;

    @AfterEach void clean() { mongo.getCollectionNames().forEach(c -> mongo.remove(new Query(), c)); }
}

Two version notes. On both Boot 3.5 and Boot 4, @SpringBootTest needs @AutoConfigureMockMvc before you can inject MockMvc, which is why the annotation above carries it. In Boot 4 it no longer provides TestRestTemplate: add @AutoConfigureTestRestTemplate, or use the new RestTestClient.

Also seen. Surefire forks, which run tests in several JVMs, and JUnit's parallel execution, used to make a slow suite finish sooner. They help after the context count is down, not instead of it.

When to break it. A test that must change a bean's configuration, such as a breaker with tiny thresholds (16.10), may need its own context. Give such tests one shared variant, not one each, and accept one more start-up for it.

.NET anchor. @SpringBootTest is WebApplicationFactory<Program>. The context cache is what an xUnit IClassFixture or collection fixture gives you by hand. Spring builds and shares the fixture for you, keyed on configuration.

See also. 16.04, 16.06, 16.08, 16.12, 4.14, 1.04, The Yard, chapter 6, Testing Spring Boot

16.08 Reuse containers across tests

What goes wrong. A @Container annotation on an instance field, not a static one, tells Testcontainers' JUnit extension to start a new container for every test method. Payouts had 120 repository tests and MongoDB takes about 2 seconds to start, so 4 minutes of every build went on starting databases.

Do this now. Start each container once per test run, and isolate tests by their data, not by a fresh container.

  • Declare containers as @ServiceConnection beans in one @TestConfiguration that every test imports (16.05). They live as long as the cached context does.
  • Or hold the container in a static final field of a base class and start it in a static block. Testcontainers' Ryuk helper container removes it when the JVM exits.
  • Keep the same image and settings everywhere, so one configuration serves all.
  • On a laptop only, withReuse(true) plus testcontainers.reuse.enable=true in ~/.testcontainers.properties keeps a container across runs. Never on CI, where data would survive from one build to the next.
abstract class MongoContainerBase {
    static final MongoDBContainer MONGO = new MongoDBContainer("mongo:5.0");
    static { MONGO.start(); }   // once per JVM; Ryuk removes it at exit
}

.NET anchor. An xUnit collection fixture holding a Testcontainers for .NET container.

See also. 16.05, 16.07, 8.23

16.09 Test an HTTP client with WireMock

Then.

  • Boot era: WireMockRule under JUnit 4, from the com.github.tomakehurst:wiremock-jre8 artifact, usually on a fixed port.
  • Boot era: Spring Cloud Contract's @AutoConfigureWireMock, which started WireMock inside the Spring context and published its port as a property. It suited teams already on Spring Cloud.
@SpringBootTest(properties = "payouts.ledger.base-url=http://localhost:${wiremock.server.port}")
@AutoConfigureWireMock(port = 0)
class LedgerClientIT {
    @Test void reserves() { stubFor(post("/ledger/reservations").willReturn(okJson(BODY))); }
}

Recognise it by. com.github.tomakehurst:wiremock-jre8, WireMockRule, WireMockClassRule, @AutoConfigureWireMock, and wiremock.server.port.

The rookie version.

@RegisterExtension
static WireMockExtension ledger = WireMockExtension.newInstance()
        .options(wireMockConfig().port(8089)).build();

@Test void reserves() {
    ledger.stubFor(any(anyUrl()).willReturn(okJson("""
        {"reservationId":"R-1"}""")));
    assertThat(ledgerClient.reserve(payout).id()).isEqualTo("R-1");
}

What goes wrong. There are two faults. The fixed port 8089 clashes when two builds share a CI agent, and about 1 build in 10 failed with "Address already in use". The catch-all stub is worse. It answers any method, any URL and any body. The client had a typo, /ledger/reservation, and sent the amount in pounds instead of minor units. The test stayed green, and for 25 minutes after the deploy every reservation got a 404.

Do this now. WireMock is a real HTTP server for tests. You tell it which requests to expect and what to answer, and afterwards you can ask what it received. The stable line is 3.13.x, which is now in maintenance mode, and 4.x is still in beta. Pin 3.13.x in the parent POM. Entry 7.14 shows timeouts and dropped connections. This entry shows the set-up and the matching.

  1. Add org.wiremock:wiremock in test scope. If its Jetty or Jackson clash with the service's own, use org.wiremock:wiremock-standalone, which bundles its dependencies under other package names.
  2. Register a WireMockExtension in a static field, on a dynamic port.
  3. Point the client at it. In a Spring test, @DynamicPropertySource adds a property whose value is known only at runtime.
@RegisterExtension
static WireMockExtension ledger = WireMockExtension.newInstance()
        .options(wireMockConfig().dynamicPort()).build();

@DynamicPropertySource
static void ledgerUrl(DynamicPropertyRegistry registry) {
    registry.add("payouts.ledger.base-url", ledger::baseUrl);
}

A static extension starts its server before the first test of each class and stops it after the last, on a new port each time. That suits a client test in a class of its own. It breaks the shared context of 16.07: the cached context keeps the first class's URL, so the next class calls a port nobody is listening on. There, hold one WireMockServer for the whole run in the base class, as 16.08 holds containers, and reset it after each test.

static final WireMockServer LEDGER = new WireMockServer(wireMockConfig().dynamicPort());
static { LEDGER.start(); }

@DynamicPropertySource
static void ledgerUrl(DynamicPropertyRegistry registry) {
    registry.add("payouts.ledger.base-url", LEDGER::baseUrl);
}

@AfterEach void resetLedger() { LEDGER.resetAll(); }   // stubs and recorded requests
  1. Stub narrowly: the method, the exact path, and the body fields that matter. A request that matches no stub gets a 404, and WireMock prints the nearest stub with the difference marked. Read that diff before changing a stub.
  2. Stub for the answer, verify for the effect. A reservation must be sent once, with its key, so verify it.
  3. Check the body with equalToJson. It compares JSON, not text, so spacing and field order do not matter.
@Test void sendsOneReservationWithItsIdempotencyKey() {
    ledger.stubFor(post(urlEqualTo("/ledger/reservations"))
            .withRequestBody(equalToJson("""
                {"payoutId":"p-1","amountMinor":124050,"currency":"GBP"}"""))
            .willReturn(okJson("""
                {"reservationId":"R-1"}""")));

    assertThat(ledgerClient.reserve(payout).id()).isEqualTo("R-1");

    ledger.verify(1, postRequestedFor(urlEqualTo("/ledger/reservations"))
            .withHeader("Idempotency-Key", equalTo("k-1")));
}
  1. For a sequence of answers, such as a 503 and then a 200, use a scenario: stubs tied to named states, each moving WireMock to the next (16.10).
  2. The extension clears stubs and recorded requests between tests, so set up each test's stubs inside it. A WireMockServer you hold yourself clears nothing until you call resetAll().

Also seen. MockRestServiceServer, for fast tests of the request's shape with no socket (7.14). MockServer, an alternative fake server. WireMock run as a container, when several services share one set of stubs.

When to break it. A shared stub for a happy path that many tests need may live in a @BeforeEach. Keep a test's own stubs in the test, though, or a reader cannot tell which stub made it pass.

.NET anchor. WireMock.Net works the same way: WireMockServer.Start() on a random port, then Given(Request.Create().WithPath(...).UsingPost()) and RespondWith(...). equalToJson is its JsonMatcher.

See also. 7.14, 7.10, 16.10, 16.16, 16.02, HTTP clients and resilience, Testing Spring Boot

16.10 Test retries, timeouts and circuit breakers

Then.

  • Boot era: Hystrix through Spring Cloud Netflix, with @HystrixCommand and its timeout in a nested annotation. Tests waited out real timeouts and called Hystrix.reset() between classes. Hystrix is in maintenance mode, its last release was 1.5.18 in 2018, and Resilience4j replaced it.
@HystrixCommand(fallbackMethod = "reserveLater", commandProperties = @HystrixProperty(
        name = "execution.isolation.thread.timeoutInMilliseconds", value = "2000"))
public LedgerReservation reserve(Payout payout) { return ledger.reserve(payout); }
  • Spring era: Spring Retry's @Retryable with @EnableRetry. The project was archived in July 2026, and Spring Framework 7's own @Retryable takes its place.

Recognise it by. @HystrixCommand, com.netflix.hystrix, Hystrix.reset(), org.springframework.retry.annotation.Retryable, and @EnableRetry.

The rookie version.

@SpringBootTest
class LedgerRetryTest {
    @MockitoBean LedgerClient ledger;
    @Autowired LedgerGateway gateway;   // carries @Retry and @CircuitBreaker
    @Test void retriesThenSucceeds() {
        when(ledger.reserve(any(), any())).thenThrow(new LedgerUnavailable(503))
                .thenThrow(new LedgerUnavailable(503)).thenReturn(RESERVATION);
        assertThat(gateway.reserve(PAYOUT)).isEqualTo(RESERVATION);
    }
}

What goes wrong. The test runs on production timings, 2 waits of 500 ms. The breaker tests on the same settings needed 10 failed calls before the breaker could open (7.05), then waited out the 20 seconds it stays open. Nine such tests added about 50 seconds, most of it two breaker tests waiting. The bigger fault is the exception. The mock throws a Payouts exception, but the real client throws ResourceAccessException on a timeout. The retry's list of exceptions to retry did not include it. So in production a ledger timeout was never retried, and every test said it was. The breaker's state also outlived the test. One class left it open, and the next class failed with CallNotPermittedException, the exception an open breaker throws.

Do this now. Resilience4j is the library that gives Payouts its retry, circuit breaker, bulkhead and time limiter. Its annotations, such as @Retry(name = "ledger"), work through a Spring proxy, so they apply only to calls that arrive through the bean.

  1. Test the policy through the real stack: the real LedgerClient, a WireMock ledger (16.09), and the real Spring bean with its annotations.
  2. Shrink time, not rules. In the test profile, cut waits and windows. Keep the attempt count and the lists of retried and ignored exceptions as in production, because those are what you are testing.
resilience4j:
  retry:
    instances:
      ledger:
        wait-duration: 10ms              # production: 500ms
  circuitbreaker:
    instances:
      ledger:
        sliding-window-size: 4           # production: 20
        minimum-number-of-calls: 4       # production: 10
        wait-duration-in-open-state: 200ms   # production: 20s
payouts:
  ledger:
    read-timeout: 300ms                  # production: 2s
  1. Test a retry with a WireMock scenario: a 503, then a 503, then a 200. Assert success, and verify exactly 3 requests.
  2. Test a timeout with withFixedDelay longer than the read timeout. Check that the exception is the one the retry recognises, and that a call that is unsafe to repeat is not retried (7.07).
  3. Test the breaker: fail until it opens, then check that the next call fails fast and that the ledger received nothing.
@Autowired LedgerGateway gateway;
@Autowired CircuitBreakerRegistry breakers;   // the starter's registry of breakers

@Test void opensTheBreakerAndStopsCallingTheLedger() {
    ledger.stubFor(post("/ledger/reservations").willReturn(serviceUnavailable()));
    for (int i = 0; i < 4; i++) catchThrowable(() -> gateway.reserve(payout));
    assertThat(breakers.circuitBreaker("ledger").getState()).isEqualTo(CircuitBreaker.State.OPEN);

    ledger.resetRequests();
    assertThatThrownBy(() -> gateway.reserve(payout)).isInstanceOf(CallNotPermittedException.class);
    ledger.verify(0, postRequestedFor(urlEqualTo("/ledger/reservations")));
}

@AfterEach void closeBreakers() { breakers.getAllCircuitBreakers().forEach(CircuitBreaker::reset); }
  1. Reset every breaker after each test, as above. The registry is a bean in a cached context and keeps its state otherwise.
  2. For the open-to-half-open move, wait with Awaitility, a library that polls a condition until it holds (16.11), until a call is let through again, never with Thread.sleep. Unless automatic transition is switched on, the breaker changes state only when a call arrives, so do not wait on getState() alone.

Also seen. A plain unit test of the policy, with Retry.of("ledger", RetryConfig.custom()...build()) and Retry.decorateSupplier. It is fast, but it tests the configuration object, not the one Spring builds. Spring Framework 7's @Retryable in Boot 4, tested the same way.

When to break it. One slow test that runs on the exact production settings is worth having, so a typo in the production values cannot hide. Tag it and run it nightly (16.19).

.NET anchor. It is testing a Polly policy inside the HttpClient pipeline, against WireMock.Net, rather than a policy object on its own. Shrinking the timings plays the part that a FakeTimeProvider plays in a Polly test.

See also. 7.04, 7.05, 7.06, 7.07, 16.09, HTTP clients and resilience

16.11 Test an SQS listener

Then.

  • Boot era: Spring Cloud AWS 2.x, with @SqsListener, the annotation that makes a method receive from a queue, from org.springframework.cloud.aws.messaging.listener.annotation and QueueMessagingTemplate to send. Tests ran against ElasticMQ, an SQS-compatible server, embedded or in Docker. It was the light local SQS before LocalStack was common.
  • Boot era: a fixed Thread.sleep after sending, then the assertion.
queueMessagingTemplate.convertAndSend("ledger-confirm", event);
Thread.sleep(5000);
verify(ledgerClient).confirm(any(), eq("p-1"), any());

Recognise it by. org.springframework.cloud.aws.messaging, QueueMessagingTemplate, org.elasticmq, com.amazonaws.services.sqs.AmazonSQS in test code, and Thread.sleep after a send.

The rookie version.

@Test void confirmsThePayoutInTheLedger() throws Exception {
    sqsTemplate.send("ledger-confirm", completed("p-1"));   // a PayoutCompleted envelope
    Thread.sleep(3000);
    verify(ledger).confirm(any(), eq("p-1"), any());
}

What goes wrong. On a laptop the listener handled the message in 200 ms, so the test slept 2.8 seconds for nothing. On a busy CI agent it sometimes took 3.4 seconds, and the test failed 1 run in 15. Someone raised the sleep to 10 seconds. With 14 listener tests, the build then spent over 2 minutes asleep. Only one path is tested, too. A standard SQS queue may deliver a message twice, and nobody tested what the second delivery did.

Do this now. Test a listener at two levels.

  1. The logic, as a method call. An @SqsListener method is an ordinary method. LedgerConfirmListener from 10.07 takes a PayoutCompleted envelope and confirms the payout in the ledger. Call its onEvent(event) directly in a unit test, with a mocked LedgerClient and an in-memory fake of the idempotency store. Put most cases here: the duplicate, the unknown payout, the event from an older version.
@Test void confirmsOnceWhenTheSameEventArrivesTwice() {
    EventEnvelope<PayoutCompletedData> event = completed("p-1");   // a test helper
    listener.onEvent(event);
    listener.onEvent(event);
    verify(ledger, times(1)).confirm(eq(event.eventId()), eq("p-1"), any());
}
  1. The wiring, against LocalStack. LocalStack is a container that imitates AWS services, SQS and SNS among them. Since 23 March 2026 its image needs an auth token. Pass it from a CI secret in LOCALSTACK_AUTH_TOKEN, or pin an older tag and accept that it gets no updates. Entry 10.19 shows the container set-up.
  2. Send with SqsTemplate, Spring Cloud AWS's client for sending and receiving. Boot 3.5 uses Spring Cloud AWS 3.4.x, and Boot 4 needs 4.x. Sending straight to the queue skips SNS and its raw-delivery setting (10.04). 10.19 tests that hop.
  3. Wait for the effect with Awaitility, a library in Boot's test starter that polls a condition until it holds or a time runs out. The test finishes as soon as the work is done.
  4. Test what only the real container shows: the JSON converts to the record, a success deletes the message, an exception leaves it to come back, and a poison message reaches the dead-letter queue.
  5. Create the test queues with a short visibility timeout, how long a received message stays hidden before it comes back, such as 1 second. Set maxReceiveCount, the number of receives before a message moves to the dead-letter queue, to 2. They play the parts of Service Bus's lock duration and max delivery count. Otherwise the dead-letter test waits as long as production would.
@Test void confirmsTheEventAndSendsAPoisonMessageToTheDlq() {
    sqsTemplate.send("ledger-confirm", completed("p-1"));
    sqsTemplate.send("ledger-confirm", "{\"not\":\"an event\"}");

    await().atMost(Duration.ofSeconds(10)).untilAsserted(() ->
            verify(ledger).confirm(any(), eq("p-1"), any()));   // a @MockitoBean LedgerClient
    await().atMost(Duration.ofSeconds(30)).untilAsserted(() ->
            assertThat(sqsTemplate.receive("ledger-confirm-dlq", String.class)).isPresent());
}

Also seen. ElasticMQ, still a light choice when only SQS is needed. Floci, another AWS imitation that Spring Cloud AWS's Docker Compose support also knows. A test that disables the listener container and calls the method through the Spring bean, to include its proxies.

When to break it. Every LocalStack test costs a container and several seconds. Keep about 3 per listener, for the happy path, the redelivery and the dead letter, and test the rest as method calls.

.NET anchor. It is testing a BackgroundService SQS consumer: the handler as a plain method, plus a few runs against LocalStack through Testcontainers for .NET. Awaitility plays the part of a polling helper you would otherwise write around Task.Delay.

See also. 10.04, 10.07, 10.08, 10.17, 10.19, 16.12, Messaging and WebSockets

16.12 Test the outbox and the saga end to end

Then.

  • Boot era: a shared integration environment, where every team deployed and the tests ran against everyone else's services, often overnight. Before containers it was the only way to see the whole flow. Somebody else's deploy broke it most weeks.
  • Spring era: an embedded broker for JMS, Java's standard messaging API, and an in-memory database in one XA transaction, a two-phase commit across both, with the test rolling both back at the end.
BrokerService broker = new BrokerService();
broker.setPersistent(false);
broker.addConnector("vm://localhost");
broker.start();

Recognise it by. vm://localhost, org.apache.activemq.broker.BrokerService, com.atomikos, @Rollback on a test that sends messages, and test properties pointing at a shared int or sit host.

The rookie version.

@Test void paysAClaim() throws Exception {
    mvc.perform(post("/payouts").header("Idempotency-Key", "k-1")
            .contentType(MediaType.APPLICATION_JSON).content(CLAIM_4471_BODY))
       .andExpect(status().isAccepted());
    Thread.sleep(5000);
    assertThat(statusOf("k-1")).isEqualTo(PayoutStatus.PAID);
}

What goes wrong. It tests the one path that rarely breaks. A saga is worth its complexity on the failure paths, and none is tested here. One day the bank gateway answered 422 for a closed account after the ledger had reserved the money. The release call was never sent. £1,240.50 stayed reserved for 9 days, until the ledger team's reconciliation found it. The outbox was untested too. Nobody had checked that an event relayed twice was handled once.

Do this now. A saga is a sequence of local steps, each with a compensating step that undoes it if a later step fails. The outbox is a collection where an event is saved in the same write as the state change, for a relay to publish afterwards. Payouts tests both end to end, with a small number of tests.

  1. Build the harness once, in one shared context (16.07). It needs a MongoDB container, WireMock for the ledger and the bank gateway, and LocalStack with the payout-events topic and its queues. Hold WireMock as 16.09 shows for a shared context. If the saga uses multi-document transactions, the MongoDB container must be a replica set, MongoDB's primary-and-secondaries mode. Testcontainers 1.x makes one for you, and 2.x needs withReplicaSet().
  2. Drive the flow through the front door, POST /payouts, and wait with Awaitility.
  3. Assert every outcome: the payout's status, the saga state document, the requests the ledger received, and the event on payout-audit.
  4. Write one test per failure path that moves money. If the bank refuses, the reservation is released. If the ledger is down, the payout fails and the bank is never called. If the bank times out, the saga waits and does not compensate, because the bank step is the pivot that cannot be undone (11.06).
@Test void releasesTheReservationWhenTheBankRefuses() throws Exception {
    ledger.stubFor(post("/ledger/reservations").willReturn(okJson(RESERVED_R1)));
    ledger.stubFor(delete("/ledger/reservations/R-1").willReturn(noContent()));
    bank.stubFor(post("/instructions").willReturn(aResponse().withStatus(422)));

    mvc.perform(post("/payouts").header("Idempotency-Key", "k-1")
            .contentType(MediaType.APPLICATION_JSON).content(CLAIM_4471_BODY))
       .andExpect(status().isAccepted());

    await().atMost(Duration.ofSeconds(20)).untilAsserted(() ->
            assertThat(statusOf("k-1")).isEqualTo(PayoutStatus.FAILED));
    ledger.verify(1, deleteRequestedFor(urlEqualTo("/ledger/reservations/R-1")));
    assertThat(auditEventTypes()).contains("PayoutFailed");
}
  1. Test at-least-once delivery on purpose. Run the relay's publish method twice over the same outbox entries, as a crash between publishing and marking them sent would. Then check that each consumer acted once.
  2. Keep this suite small. Payouts has 7 such tests, and they run in about 70 seconds. The many variations of each step belong in unit tests of the saga (11.12).

Also seen. Docker Compose, started by Boot's Compose support, instead of Testcontainers, when developers also run the whole stack by hand. A staging environment with real AWS, for a short smoke test after each deploy.

When to break it. A failure path whose only logic is inside one step can be tested in that step's unit test. The cost of leaving it out here is that the wiring between steps for that path goes unchecked.

.NET anchor. It is a WebApplicationFactory test with Testcontainers for .NET, WireMock.Net and LocalStack, or MassTransit's saga test harness for the in-memory version.

See also. 9.07, 9.08, 11.02, 11.05, 11.06, 11.12, 16.07, 16.11

16.13 Control time in tests

Then.

  • Boot era: Joda-Time, the date library before java.time, and its DateTimeUtils.setCurrentMillisFixed(...), a global switch that froze the JVM's time until a test reset it.

What goes wrong. A test checked that a payout requested now went into today's bank file. The bank's cut-off is 17:00 London time (2.02), and the code read Instant.now(). The test passed all day. The nightly build ran at 18:00, so it was red every night, and the team learned to ignore it.

Do this now. Inject a Clock into anything that reads the time (2.16), and control it from the test.

  • For a fixed moment, pass Clock.fixed(Instant.parse("2026-11-24T16:59:59Z"), ZoneOffset.UTC). Test both sides of the cut-off, 16:59:59 and 17:00:00, in November, when London is on UTC. Add a summer pair too, when 17:00 in London is 16:00 UTC.
  • For time that moves, such as a step's timeout, write a mutable test clock.
  • In a Spring test, replace the Clock bean with @TestBean or a @Primary test bean.
  • Truncate to milliseconds, because MongoDB stores no finer (8.10).
  • To wait for asynchronous work, use Awaitility (16.11).
final class MutableClock extends Clock {
    private volatile Instant now;   // the code under test may read it on another thread
    MutableClock(Instant start) { this.now = start; }
    void advance(Duration d) { now = now.plus(d); }
    @Override public Instant instant() { return now; }
    @Override public ZoneId getZone() { return ZoneOffset.UTC; }
    @Override public Clock withZone(ZoneId zone) { throw new UnsupportedOperationException(); }
}

.NET anchor. TimeProvider with FakeTimeProvider, and its Advance method.

See also. 2.16, 2.02, 11.08, 16.19

16.14 Write parameterised tests

Then.

  • Boot era: JUnit 4's @RunWith(Parameterized.class), with a static @Parameters method returning Collection<Object[]> and the values passed through the constructor. One table needed one whole class. JUnitParams made it lighter.

What goes wrong. The fee rule had 9 copied tests, one per amount. When yen arrived, with no decimal places, the new case went into one copy and not the others. A loop inside one test is no better. It stops at the first failing case and hides which others fail.

Do this now. A parameterised test is one test method run once per row of data, each run reported on its own.

  • Use @ParameterizedTest with a source. @CsvSource suits small tables, and its textBlock form reads like a table. @ValueSource takes one value per run, @EnumSource one per enum constant, and @MethodSource takes objects from a static method.
  • Name each run with name = "...", so the report shows the case, not "[3]".
  • The annotations live in junit-jupiter-params, which Boot's test starter already brings.
@ParameterizedTest(name = "{0} {1} gives a fee of {2}")
@CsvSource(textBlock = """
    1240.50, GBP, 12.41
    100.00,  GBP,  1.00
    5000,    JPY,    50
    """)
void chargesOnePercentRoundedHalfUp(String amount, String currency, String fee) {
    Currency c = Currency.getInstance(currency);
    assertThat(FeePolicy.standard().feeFor(new Money(new BigDecimal(amount), c)))
            .isEqualTo(new Money(new BigDecimal(fee), c));
}

.NET anchor. xUnit's [Theory] with [InlineData] and [MemberData].

See also. 16.01, 2.01, 2.13

16.15 Build test data without noise

Then.

  • Boot era: Lombok, a compiler plugin that generates code from annotations, and its @Builder(toBuilder = true) on the entity, used mostly by tests. Sorrel no longer uses Lombok (The Yard, chapter 5).
  • Spring era: DbUnit XML datasets loaded with @DatabaseSetup("payouts.xml"), with the data far from the test that relied on it.

What goes wrong. Every test built a Payout with all 7 fields spelled out. A reader could not see which value mattered to the test. When an 8th field was added, 140 tests stopped compiling, and none of them cared about it.

Do this now. Give each test only the values it is about, and let the rest default to something valid.

  • Write a test data builder per aggregate, such as Payout, saved and loaded as one, in test sources, with defaults that make a valid object.
  • For common states, add named factories such as reserved(claimId, at), as in 16.05.
  • Avoid random generators such as Instancio for values that matter. A failure cannot be repeated unless the seed is logged.
final class PayoutBuilder {
    private String claimId = "C-4471";
    private Money amount = Money.gbp("1240.50");
    private PayoutStatus status = PayoutStatus.PENDING;
    private Instant updatedAt = Instant.parse("2026-10-24T09:00:00Z");

    static PayoutBuilder aPayout() { return new PayoutBuilder(); }
    PayoutBuilder status(PayoutStatus s) { this.status = s; return this; }
    PayoutBuilder updatedAt(Instant t) { this.updatedAt = t; return this; }
    Payout build() { return new Payout(null, null, "k-" + claimId, claimId, amount, status, updatedAt); }
}

.NET anchor. The same builder pattern, or AutoFixture, which has the same drawback as random generators.

See also. 16.03, 16.05, 2.03

16.16 Write a consumer-driven contract test

Then.

  • Boot era: the provider's client jar. The ledger team published ledger-client with its request and response classes, and compatibility was checked by whoever upgraded it (7.02).
  • Boot era: a shared integration environment, where a breaking change showed up when another team's tests went red, often days later.
<dependency>
    <groupId>com.sorrel.ledger</groupId>
    <artifactId>ledger-client</artifactId>
    <version>3.4.1</version>
</dependency>

Recognise it by. A *-client or *-api dependency from another team, their DTO packages such as com.sorrel.ledger.api in your imports, and test classes named *CompatibilityIT pointing at a shared host.

The rookie version.

// Copied from the ledger team's wiki, March 2025
ledger.stubFor(post("/ledger/reservations")
        .willReturn(okJson("""
            {"reservationId":"R-1","amountMinor":124050}""")));

What goes wrong. The stub is what Payouts believed on the day it was written. The ledger team later renamed the request field amountMinor to amount. Their own tests passed. Payouts' stub accepted any request body, so Payouts' tests passed too. In production every reservation failed with a 400 for 40 minutes. Neither team had a test that saw both sides.

Do this now. In a consumer-driven contract test, the consumer writes down the requests it makes and the parts of each response it relies on. The provider runs that contract against its real service, in its own build. A change that would break a consumer then fails the provider's build, before release. Pact is the common tool. Its contract file is called a pact, and a Pact Broker stores the pacts and records which versions have been verified.

  1. In Payouts, the consumer, write a Pact test for LedgerClient. Declare the interaction, and Pact starts a mock server that answers it.
  2. In the request, declare every field the client sends: Pact fails a request that carries a field the pact does not name. In the response, ask only for the fields Payouts reads, with type matchers instead of exact values. The ledger can then add response fields freely.
@ExtendWith(PactConsumerTestExt.class)
@PactTestFor(providerName = "ledger")
class LedgerClientPactTest {
    @Pact(consumer = "payouts-api")
    V4Pact reserve(PactDslWithProvider builder) {
        return builder.given("account A-1 has funds")
                .uponReceiving("a reservation for a payout")
                .path("/ledger/reservations").method("POST")
                .body(new PactDslJsonBody().stringType("payoutId", "p-1")
                        .integerType("amountMinor", 124050).stringType("currency", "GBP"))
                .willRespondWith().status(200)
                .body(new PactDslJsonBody().stringType("reservationId", "R-1"))
                .toPact(V4Pact.class);
    }
  1. Run the real client against Pact's server. The pact file is written only if the client made exactly the requests declared.
    @Test void reserves(MockServer server) {
        assertThat(clientFor(server.getUrl()).reserve(payout).id()).isEqualTo("R-1");
    }
}
  1. Publish the pact to the broker from CI, with Payouts' version and branch.
  2. The ledger team verifies every consumer's pacts in its own build, against its running service. Its code sets up each provider state, such as "account A-1 has funds".
  3. Before a deploy, each side asks the broker whether the versions are compatible, with the Pact CLI's can-i-deploy command.
  4. Agree it with the other team first. A contract test needs both teams' builds, so it is an agreement as much as a test. Start with the provider whose breaks cost most, which for Payouts is the ledger.

Also seen. Spring Cloud Contract. The provider writes contracts in Groovy or YAML, generates its own tests from them, and publishes a stubs jar that consumers run with Stub Runner. It suits a provider that wants to lead and an estate that is all Spring. A check of requests against the provider's OpenAPI document, which proves the shape but not what the consumer actually uses.

When to break it. A supplier such as the bank gateway will not run your pacts. Test against its sandbox on a schedule instead, and compare the answers with your stubs. The cost is that a change is found days late, not before release.

.NET anchor. PactNet uses the same pact format and the same broker, so a .NET consumer and a Java provider can share contracts.

See also. 7.02, 7.14, 16.09, 5.09, 5.10, 20.01, HTTP clients and resilience

16.17 Test JSON serialisation

What goes wrong. A developer changed the service's Jackson settings to fix one endpoint. Amounts went out as 1240.5 instead of "1240.50". The controller tests passed, because they built the expected JSON with the same settings. The claims portal parsed strings, and showed blank amounts for 2 days.

Do this now. Test the wire format directly, against JSON written by hand.

  • @JsonTest is a slice that starts only the service's Jackson configuration. It provides JacksonTester<T> fields that write and read one type.
  • Check the fields clients depend on: money as a string with its currency, times in ISO 8601 with a zone, enum names (5.13).
  • Check the read side too: a request with an unknown field is accepted (5.10).
  • In Boot 4, Jackson 3 moves to new package names. That upgrade is when these tests earn their keep.
@JsonTest
class PayoutResponseJsonTest {
    @Autowired JacksonTester<PayoutResponse> json;

    @Test void writesTheAmountAsAStringAndTheTimeInUtc() throws Exception {
        var content = json.write(PayoutResponse.from(PAID_PAYOUT));
        assertThat(content).extractingJsonPathStringValue("$.amount.value").isEqualTo("1240.50");
        assertThat(content).extractingJsonPathStringValue("$.requestedAt")
                .isEqualTo("2026-10-24T09:00:00Z");
    }
}

.NET anchor. A System.Text.Json test with the app's own JsonSerializerOptions, compared with a JSON literal.

See also. 5.10, 5.12, 5.13, 19.04

16.18 Test configuration binding

What goes wrong. Someone wrote payouts.ledger.read-timeout: 2 in the YAML, meaning seconds. A Duration with no unit binds as milliseconds. After the deploy every ledger call timed out at 2 ms, and nothing failed at start-up to say so.

Do this now. Test the @ConfigurationProperties record that holds payouts.ledger.* (4.02), and the rules on it, without starting the application.

  • ApplicationContextRunner builds a tiny context in milliseconds, with only the configuration you name.
  • Give it values with withPropertyValues, then check the bound record, or check that start-up fails.
  • Test the validation that should stop a bad deploy (4.10): a missing base URL must fail.
  • Write units in every Duration property, such as 2s, and test that one is read as you meant.
class LedgerPropertiesTest {
    private final ApplicationContextRunner runner = new ApplicationContextRunner()
            .withUserConfiguration(LedgerConfig.class);   // enables LedgerProperties

    @Test void readsATimeoutWithItsUnit() {
        runner.withPropertyValues("payouts.ledger.base-url=http://ledger", "payouts.ledger.read-timeout=2s")
              .run(context -> assertThat(context.getBean(LedgerProperties.class).readTimeout())
                      .isEqualTo(Duration.ofSeconds(2)));
    }

    @Test void refusesToStartWithoutABaseUrl() {
        runner.withPropertyValues("payouts.ledger.read-timeout=2s")
              .run(context -> assertThat(context).hasFailed());
    }
}

.NET anchor. Binding an IConfiguration built from an in-memory collection, with ValidateOnStart checked in a test.

See also. 4.02, 4.10, 4.14, 6.12

16.19 Find and fix a flaky test

What goes wrong. The outbox test failed about 1 run in 20. The team set Surefire to rerun failing tests twice, and the build went green. The flake was a real race in the relay. Three months later, 2 pods relayed the same events, and claimants got their emails twice.

Do this now. Treat a flaky test as a bug until you know which side of the test it is in.

  • Reproduce it first. Run it with @RepeatedTest(200), or in random order with @TestMethodOrder(MethodOrderer.Random.class).
  • Check the usual causes, in this order. Shared state: a cached context, a static field, documents not cleaned, a breaker left open. Time: now(), time zones, the bank cut-off. Waiting: Thread.sleep. Order: an unsorted query. Environment: fixed ports, unpinned images.
  • Fix the cause, in the code or the test.
  • If it cannot be fixed today, quarantine it. Tag it @Tag("quarantine"), exclude the tag from the pull-request build with Surefire's excludedGroups, and give it a ticket and an owner.

.NET anchor. The same causes as in xUnit, where parallel test collections play the part of the shared Spring context.

See also. 16.07, 16.08, 16.11, 16.13, 9.08

16.20 Test logging and metrics when they matter

What goes wrong. An alert in the log store searched for the marker PAYOUT_STUCK. A tidy-up changed the message to "Payout stuck". The alert never fired again, and 12 stuck payouts were found by a claimant's phone call.

Do this now. Test only the log lines and metrics that something else depends on: an alert, a dashboard, an audit.

  • For a metric, build the class with a SimpleMeterRegistry, an in-memory registry from Micrometer, the metrics library Boot uses, and read the meter back by name and tag.
