  • For a log line, use Boot's OutputCaptureExtension and a CapturedOutput parameter, or attach a ListAppender from Logback, Boot's default logging library, to the logger.
  • With JSON logging on (12.03), check the field the alert reads, not the wording around it.
@Test void countsACompletedPayoutByCurrency() {
    var registry = new SimpleMeterRegistry();
    new PayoutMetrics(registry).completed(Money.gbp("1240.50"));
    assertThat(registry.get("payouts.completed").tag("currency", "GBP").counter().count()).isEqualTo(1.0);
}

@Test @ExtendWith(OutputCaptureExtension.class)
void logsTheMarkerTheStuckPayoutAlertSearchesFor(CapturedOutput output) {
    sweeper.sweep();
    assertThat(output.getOut()).contains("PAYOUT_STUCK");
}

.NET anchor. FakeLogger from Microsoft.Extensions.Logging.Testing, and a MeterListener reading a Meter.

See also. 12.03, 12.11, 14.02, 14.07

16.21 Measure coverage without gaming it

Then.

  • Boot era: Cobertura, through cobertura-maven-plugin, which rewrote the compiled classes. JaCoCo, an agent at runtime, replaced it.

What goes wrong. A team raised its coverage gate from 75% to 90%. The new tests called the configuration classes and asserted nothing. The number reached 91%. The defect rate did not move, and the suite took 4 minutes longer.

Do this now. Use coverage to find untested code, and mutation testing to find unchecked code.

  • JaCoCo measures which lines and branches the tests ran. jacoco-maven-plugin has a prepare-agent goal that attaches it to Surefire and a report goal that writes the HTML report. Its check goal can set a floor.
  • Read the report for missed branches in code that decides about money.
  • PIT is a mutation-testing tool. It changes the code, for example < to <=, and reruns the tests. A change that no test notices is a line that runs but is never checked. Use pitest-maven with the pitest-junit5-plugin, on payouts-domain, nightly, because it is slow.
  • Treat coverage as a floor, never a target.

.NET anchor. Coverlet for coverage, and Stryker.NET for mutation testing.

See also. 16.01, 16.03, 1.04, The Yard, chapter 6

16.22 Read JUnit 4 tests and migrate them

Then.

  • Boot era: JUnit 4, with runners, rules (fields that wrap each test) and public methods. It is the test code in most Sorrel services older than 2020.

What goes wrong. Boot's test starter brings JUnit 5's Jupiter engine, not the Vintage engine that runs JUnit 4. A test annotated with org.junit.Test is then not found at all, with no warning. Payouts found 46 JUnit 4 tests that had not run since an upgrade. 3 of them failed when run. Testcontainers 2.0 removed JUnit 4 support, so container rules break on the Boot 4 upgrade as well.

Do this now. Make the old tests run, then move them.

JUnit 4 JUnit 5 (Jupiter)
org.junit.Test org.junit.jupiter.api.Test
@Before, @After @BeforeEach, @AfterEach
@BeforeClass, @AfterClass @BeforeAll, @AfterAll
@Ignore, @Category @Disabled, @Tag
@Test(expected = X.class), ExpectedException assertThrows(X.class, ...)
@RunWith(SpringRunner.class) nothing: Boot's test annotations include the Spring extension
@RunWith(MockitoJUnitRunner.class) @ExtendWith(MockitoExtension.class)
@Rule TemporaryFolder @TempDir
  • Count them with a search for import org.junit.Test, then add junit-vintage-engine in test scope until the migration ends.
  • Migrate class by class. OpenRewrite, a source-rewriting tool, has recipes for JUnit 4 to 5 (19.03).
  • Watch the message argument. JUnit 4's assertEquals(message, expected, actual) puts it first, and Jupiter's puts it last.
  • Remove the Vintage engine when the count reaches 0.

.NET anchor. Like moving from MSTest v1 to xUnit: the ideas map across, and the attributes change name.

See also. 16.01, 16.06, 19.03, 19.04, Testing

⚠Review checklist
  • If you see @SpringBootTest on a test of one domain rule: it waits for the whole application and fails for reasons unrelated to the rule. See 16.01.
  • If you see mock(RestClient.class, RETURNS_DEEP_STUBS), or a mock of SqsTemplate or MongoTemplate: the test pins the library calls and never runs the URL, JSON or error handling. See 16.02.
  • If you see assertTrue(a && b) or assertTrue(list.size() == 2): the failure will say only "expected true". See 16.03.
  • If you see a controller method called directly in a test: validation, JSON and error handling never run. See 16.04.
  • If you see a repository test that only saves and loads: the queries Payouts wrote are untested. See 16.05.
  • If you see a static Mockito mock exposed as a bean: its stubs and calls leak across test classes. See 16.06.
  • If you see a new combination of properties, profiles or replaced beans on a @SpringBootTest, or @DirtiesContext: another context start, and more listeners alive at once. See 16.07.
  • If you see @Container on an instance field: a new container for every test method. See 16.08.
  • If you see a WireMock stub on anyUrl(), or a fixed port: a wrong URL passes, and parallel builds clash. See 16.09.
  • If you see resilience tests on production timings, a mock that throws a home-made exception, or no breaker reset: slow tests that never test what is really retried. See 16.10.
  • If you see Thread.sleep after a send: slow when it passes, flaky when it fails. See 16.11.
  • If you see an end-to-end test of the happy path only: the compensation that releases money is untested. See 16.12.
  • If you see a WireMock stub copied from another team's documentation, with no contract: it stays green when they change. See 16.16.
  • If you see a rerun setting added to make a build green: a real race may be hiding behind it. See 16.19.
  • If you see import org.junit.Test in a module with no Vintage engine: the test never runs. See 16.22.

Part IV · The how-to17. Containers and Kubernetes#

Payouts runs as 2 pods in the payouts namespace on a shared cluster. This part is about the space between the Java process and the cluster that runs it. It shows how to build a small image that runs as a normal user, size the heap and the pod so the kernel never has to step in, write probes that restart only what is broken, and stop a pod without dropping a request or a message. It ends with the tools for when a pod dies anyway, and a cluster on a laptop to rehearse on.

★What a veteran knows
  • The kernel counts the whole process, not the heap. A heap graph that looks healthy says nothing about how close a pod is to being killed.
  • A liveness probe that checks a dependency turns that dependency's bad minute into a restart of every pod at once.
  • Java must be process 1 in its container, or it never hears the signal that asks it to stop. Check this before you tune anything about shutdown.
  • The heap flag and the memory limit belong in the same manifest and change in the same commit. Split them across a Dockerfile and a Helm chart and one of them will drift.
  • During every rolling update two versions of the service run side by side. Every change to an API, an event or a document must survive that minute.
  • A base image is a dependency like any library. Pin it, scan it, and upgrade it on a schedule.
  • Run as a numeric user ID that is not 0. Kubernetes can only check "not root" when the user is a number.
◷How we got hereOn Friday 15 March 2013, at PyCon US in Santa Clara, Solomon Hykes, a co-founder of the hosting company…

On Friday 15 March 2013, at PyCon US in Santa Clara, Solomon Hykes, a co-founder of the hosting company dotCloud, gave a lightning talk called "The future of Linux Containers". dotCloud used Linux containers itself, and people were curious about how. The talk's listing says it had been too complicated to explain "until now: Docker." Docker's own account, nine years later, has him telling the room that for developers, shipping to the server is hard. The code was public eight days after the talk, as version 0.1.0. In October dotCloud renamed itself Docker, Inc., and in 2014 it sold the hosting business that had produced the idea. The JVM took longer to notice. Until JDK 10 in 2018, and the 8u191 update that October, a JVM in a container read the host's memory and sized its heap for a machine it did not have.

17.01 Build a small, safe image

Then.

  • Spring era: a WAR file copied into the webapps directory of a shared Tomcat that the operations team owned, along with the JVM and its flags. It was right when servers were long-lived machines and one Tomcat hosted many applications. A self-contained jar in an image replaced it, so each service owns its own runtime and versions.
  • Boot era: the Dockerfile from the getting-started guides of the time. The egd flag sped up random-number seeding on virtual machines short of entropy.
FROM openjdk:8-jdk-alpine
VOLUME /tmp
ADD target/payouts-api-1.0.jar app.jar
ENTRYPOINT ["java","-Djava.security.egd=file:/dev/./urandom","-jar","/app.jar"]
  • Modern: layered images built with java -Djarmode=layertools -jar app.jar extract. It was right until Boot added the tools jar mode, whose extract --layers does the same job. layertools is now deprecated.

Recognise it by. FROM openjdk:, ADD target/*.jar, VOLUME /tmp, -Djava.security.egd, -Djarmode=layertools, a Dockerfile with no USER line, and in the POM <packaging>war</packaging> with a class extending SpringBootServletInitializer.

The rookie version.

FROM eclipse-temurin:25-jdk
COPY . /src
WORKDIR /src
RUN ./mvnw package -DskipTests
ENTRYPOINT ["java", "-jar", "payouts-api/target/payouts-api.jar"]

What goes wrong. It works, which is why it survives review. The image holds a full JDK, the source, .git, Maven's local repository and every test dependency. On Payouts that came to 1.1 GB, and every build pushed most of it, because COPY . /src changes whenever any file changes. So every layer after it is rebuilt, and Maven downloads the internet again. The vulnerability scanner reported findings in a compiler and build tools that production never runs. A developer's application-local.yml, with a test bank-gateway key in it, went into the image too. And the process runs as root. Anyone who gets a shell in the pod has root and a compiler.

Do this now. An image is a stack of read-only layers, one per instruction, and a layer is reused only if it and everything below it are unchanged. Build the jar in CI with ./mvnw package, then build an image that holds only what runs.

  1. Use a multi-stage build: an early stage does the work, and the final stage copies out only the result.
  2. Start the final stage from a JRE image, the Java runtime without the compiler and tools. eclipse-temurin:25-jre is one. Pin the tag, and in production pin the digest too.
  3. Split the jar into layers with Boot's tools jar mode. Dependencies change rarely and go first. Your own classes change on every commit and go last. A code change then pushes a layer of a few hundred kilobytes.
  4. Run as a numeric user that is not root.
  5. Add a .dockerignore that excludes .git, target from other modules, and any local configuration.
FROM eclipse-temurin:25-jre AS extract
WORKDIR /builder
COPY payouts-api/target/payouts-api.jar application.jar
RUN java -Djarmode=tools -jar application.jar extract --layers --destination extracted

FROM eclipse-temurin:25-jre
WORKDIR /application
COPY --from=extract /builder/extracted/dependencies/ ./
COPY --from=extract /builder/extracted/spring-boot-loader/ ./
COPY --from=extract /builder/extracted/snapshot-dependencies/ ./
COPY --from=extract /builder/extracted/application/ ./
USER 10001
ENTRYPOINT ["java", "-jar", "application.jar"]

The ENTRYPOINT is in exec form, a JSON list, so Java is process 1 (17.05). There are no JVM flags in the image. They go in the manifest, next to the limit (17.02). Then tell Kubernetes to enforce what the image promises. The settings go in the Deployment's pod template:

spec:
  template:
    spec:
      containers:
        - name: payouts-api
          securityContext:
            runAsNonRoot: true
            runAsUser: 10001
            allowPrivilegeEscalation: false
            readOnlyRootFilesystem: true
          volumeMounts:
            - { name: tmp, mountPath: /tmp }
      volumes:
        - { name: tmp, emptyDir: {} }

With runAsNonRoot: true, the kubelet refuses to start a container whose user is root. It can only check a numeric user, which is why the Dockerfile says 10001 and not app. A read-only root filesystem needs a writable /tmp, from an emptyDir volume, because embedded Tomcat writes its work files there.

Also seen. Distroless or Alpine bases for a smaller image. Distroless has no shell, which makes debugging harder (17.10). Alpine uses the musl C library, so pick a JDK built for it. The platform team's base image from Sorrel's registry: prefer it where one exists. Images built without a Dockerfile at all (17.11).

When to break it. A JDK base in the final stage is fair when the team needs jcmd inside the pod and the cluster forbids debug containers. The cost is a larger image and more scanner findings, so write the reason in the Dockerfile.

.NET anchor. A .NET multi-stage build usually compiles inside Docker on mcr.microsoft.com/dotnet/sdk and runs on mcr.microsoft.com/dotnet/aspnet. A first stage on eclipse-temurin:25-jdk running ./mvnw package would do the same here. Payouts builds the jar in CI, so this first stage only unpacks it. Recent .NET images ship a non-root app user and USER $APP_UID. Java base images mostly do not, so you add the user yourself.

See also. 17.05, 17.10, 17.11, 1.11, 15.12, The Yard, chapter 13, Packaging and native images

17.02 Size the heap inside a container limit

Then.

  • Boot era: ENV JAVA_OPTS="-Xms2g -Xmx2g" baked into the Dockerfile, sized for the virtual machine the service used to run on. It was right when the JVM owned the whole machine. In a pod the limit is set somewhere else, and the two numbers drift.
  • Boot era: JDK 8 before update 191. The JVM read the host's memory, not the container's. Teams used an experimental flag that read the cgroup limit, or fixed the heap as a fraction of it.
-XX:+UnlockExperimentalVMOptions -XX:+UseCGroupMemoryLimitForHeap -XX:MaxRAMFraction=2

Container awareness, on by default since JDK 10 and 8u191, replaced both. MaxRAMPercentage replaced the Fraction flags.

Recognise it by. -Xmx in a Dockerfile ENV or ENTRYPOINT, JAVA_OPTS that the image's start script expands, UseCGroupMemoryLimitForHeap, MaxRAMFraction, and a base image tagged 8u with a number below 191.

The rookie version.

env:
  - name: JAVA_TOOL_OPTIONS
    value: "-Xmx768m"
resources:
  limits:
    memory: 768Mi

What goes wrong. The heap is allowed to grow to the whole limit. Everything outside the heap still needs room: metaspace for class metadata, the code cache for compiled code, thread stacks, direct buffers and the garbage collector's own bookkeeping. On Payouts that is about 200 MiB under load. So 768 + 200 = 968 MiB is the most the process can use, against a limit of 768. The heap grows towards its maximum under steady load, which is normal for a JVM. At some point past 568 MiB of heap the total crosses the limit, and the kernel kills the process. There is no OutOfMemoryError, no stack trace and no heap dump. Kubernetes records OOMKilled and exit code 137, and the pod restarts. The opposite mistake is quieter. With no flag at all, the JVM takes 25% of the limit, so a 768 MiB pod gets a 192 MiB heap and spends its time collecting garbage.

Do this now. The heap is where Java keeps its objects. The limit is the ceiling the kernel enforces on the whole process. Size one inside the other.

  1. Measure the non-heap footprint once, under real load, with native memory tracking and jcmd (The Yard, chapter 13). Use the number, not a guess.
  2. Do the arithmetic and write it down: heap + measured non-heap + margin = limit. Payouts: 384 + 200 = 584 MiB, with the limit at 768 MiB.
  3. Set the heap in the manifest with JAVA_TOOL_OPTIONS, an environment variable every JVM reads at startup. It prints Picked up JAVA_TOOL_OPTIONS in the log, which tells you it took effect.
  4. Add -XX:+ExitOnOutOfMemoryError, so a full heap ends in a clear exit and a log line, not a slow death.
  5. Name the collector with -XX:+UseG1GC. Under about 1792 MB the JVM treats the container as a small machine and picks the Serial collector, even with 2 CPUs (17.03).
  6. Check what the running JVM chose. Actuator's jvm.memory.max metric with the tag area=heap shows it.
env:
  - name: JAVA_TOOL_OPTIONS
    # heap 384 + measured non-heap 200 = 584 MiB; limit 768 leaves 184 MiB margin
    value: "-Xmx384m -XX:+UseG1GC -XX:+ExitOnOutOfMemoryError"
resources:
  requests: { memory: 768Mi }
  limits:   { memory: 768Mi }

Cap the parts that can grow without bound if your measurement shows they move. Metaspace has no limit by default. -XX:MaxMetaspaceSize sets one, and -XX:MaxDirectMemorySize bounds direct buffers. A cap turns a silent kill into a Java error with a name. Virtual threads keep their stacks on the heap, so moving to them shifts memory from the non-heap side to the heap side (3.01).

Also seen. -XX:MaxRAMPercentage=75 and no -Xmx. The heap then follows the limit when someone raises it, which is convenient. The 75% is still a claim that the non-heap part fits in the other 25%, so check it once with a measurement. It fits large pods better than small ones.

When to break it. A batch job that runs for minutes and exits may give the heap a larger share, because its non-heap footprint is small and stable. Measure it first. The cost of guessing wrong is a kill with no evidence.

.NET anchor. DOTNET_GCHeapHardLimit and DOTNET_GCHeapHardLimitPercent are the nearest settings. Under a container limit, .NET's default heap hard limit is 75% of the limit, or 20 MB if that is larger, against Java's 25%. Both runtimes leave native memory outside the managed heap, and the kernel counts both.

See also. 17.03, 17.09, 17.10, 14.10, 3.01, The Yard, chapter 13, The JVM at runtime: memory, GC and containers

17.03 Set requests and limits

Then.

  • Spring era: one service per virtual machine, sized by a ticket to operations. The JVM saw the machine's real memory and CPUs, and the machine was the limit. Requests and limits replaced the ticket, and the scheduler now packs many pods onto one node.
  • Boot era: -XX:ParallelGCThreads=2 and -XX:CICompilerCount=2 hand-set in the Dockerfile, because a JVM in a container counted the host's CPUs. Container awareness made the JVM count the container's CPUs instead.

Recognise it by. A Deployment with no resources: block, -XX:ParallelGCThreads or -XX:CICompilerCount in a Dockerfile, and a memory requests value well below limits.

The rookie version.

resources:
  requests:
    memory: 256Mi
  limits:
    memory: 1Gi

What goes wrong. A request is what the scheduler reserves for the pod when it chooses a node. A limit is the ceiling enforced once the pod runs. This pod tells the scheduler it needs 256 MiB, so the scheduler places it on a node with 256 MiB free. Under load it uses 700 MiB. When the other pods on that node do the same, the node runs short, and the kernel kills something. The pod was within its own limit, and it died anyway. There is no CPU request, so under contention the pod gets whatever is left over. Spring starts slowly on a busy node, the startup probe runs out of time, and the pod restarts in a loop. There is no CPU limit either, so on current JDKs the JVM counts every CPU on the node, 16 on Sorrel's nodes. It sizes its garbage-collection threads and the common fork-join pool for 16 CPUs it will never get.

Do this now.

  1. Memory: request equals limit. Take the number from the measurement in 17.02. The scheduler then reserves what the pod really uses.
  2. CPU request: the steady-state use. CPU is counted in millicores: 500m is half a CPU. Read the pod's actual use from the cluster's metrics under normal load, and request that.
  3. CPU limit: give the JVM a number it can plan for. "cpu limits are enforced by CPU throttling", in the Kubernetes documentation's words: the kernel pauses the process for the rest of each period. A JVM starting up wants several CPUs for a short burst. A limit of 2 leaves room for that burst and tells the JVM to plan for 2.
  4. Never give a JVM service a CPU limit of 1 or less. With 1 CPU the JVM chooses the Serial garbage collector, which does all its work on one thread with the application stopped. A memory limit under about 1792 MB also makes JDK 25 choose Serial, even with 2 CPUs, and Payouts' 768 MiB is under it. Name the collector, -XX:+UseG1GC, in JAVA_TOOL_OPTIONS, and check it with jcmd 1 VM.flags or the startup log.
resources:
  requests: { cpu: 500m, memory: 768Mi }
  limits:   { cpu: "2",  memory: 768Mi }
  1. Check the result. kubectl get pod <name> -o jsonpath='{.status.qosClass}' prints the quality-of-service class. This pod is Burstable, because its CPU request and limit differ. A pod whose requests equal its limits for both CPU and memory is Guaranteed, and is the last to be evicted when a node runs short.

Also seen. No CPU limit at all, with only a request. Many platform teams prefer this, because throttling hurts bursty JVM startups and garbage collections. Pair it with -XX:ActiveProcessorCount=2, so the JVM still plans for a fixed number of CPUs. Which way Payouts goes is Sorrel's platform team's policy, not the service's choice.

When to break it. A memory request below the limit is fair for a non-critical batch workload on a cluster with spare room. The cost is that it may be the pod the kernel kills when the node runs short.

.NET anchor. The same manifest fields apply to a .NET service. .NET reads the CPU limit into Environment.ProcessorCount and sizes Server GC from it, much as the JVM sizes its collector threads.

See also. 17.02, 17.04, 17.08, 21.10, The Yard, chapter 13, The JVM at runtime: memory, GC and containers

17.04 Configure probes that do not kill healthy pods

Then.

  • Boot era: Boot 1's /health endpoint at the root, opened up with endpoints.health.sensitive=false or management.security.enabled=false. One endpoint answered every question. Separate liveness and readiness groups replaced it.
  • Boot era: a hand-written @GetMapping("/ping") that returned "pong". It proved the web server answered, and nothing else.
  • Boot era: initialDelaySeconds: 120 on the liveness probe, to stop it killing a slow start. Startup probes, generally available since Kubernetes 1.20, replaced the guess.

Recognise it by. endpoints.health.sensitive, management.security.enabled, a probe path: /health or /ping, a large initialDelaySeconds, and liveness and readiness probes with the same path.

The rookie version.

livenessProbe:
  httpGet: { path: /actuator/health, port: 8080 }
readinessProbe:
  httpGet: { path: /actuator/health, port: 8080 }

What goes wrong. A probe is a check the kubelet, the node's agent, runs against a container on a schedule. /actuator/health is the whole health tree. Boot adds a mongo health indicator by itself when Spring Data MongoDB is on the classpath. So when DocumentDB fails over to a new primary, both Payouts pods report DOWN. The liveness probe runs every 10 seconds and allows 3 failures, the Kubernetes defaults. Thirty seconds into the failover, the kubelet restarts both pods together. The database comes back to a service that is starting up and cannot take traffic for another 40 seconds. A 30-second database blip has become a 70-second Payouts outage. The default timeoutSeconds is 1, so a long garbage-collection pause can fail a probe on its own.

Do this now. Each probe has one consequence. Liveness restarts the container. Readiness removes the pod from the Service, and restarts nothing. Startup holds the other two back until the application has started. Give each the question that fits its consequence.

  1. Point liveness at the liveness health group and readiness at the readiness group. Boot turns both groups on by default.
  2. Keep liveness to livenessState only, which is its default. A restart fixes a wedged process. It never fixes a database, a ledger or a bank.
  3. Think hard before adding a dependency to readiness. If DocumentDB is down and every pod goes unready, the Service has no endpoints. Callers then get connection errors instead of a clear 503 with a ProblemDetail body. Payouts adds nothing to readiness (14.05).
  4. Give startup a budget by arithmetic: failureThreshold × periodSeconds.
  5. Raise timeoutSeconds above 1 for liveness, so one slow answer is not a failure.
startupProbe:
  httpGet: { path: /livez, port: 8080 }
  periodSeconds: 10
  failureThreshold: 30     # 30 x 10 s = 5 minutes to start
livenessProbe:
  httpGet: { path: /livez, port: 8080 }
  periodSeconds: 10
  timeoutSeconds: 3
  failureThreshold: 3      # 30 s of failures before a restart
readinessProbe:
  httpGet: { path: /readyz, port: 8080 }
  periodSeconds: 5
  timeoutSeconds: 3

Payouts runs Actuator on a separate management port, so its endpoints are not reachable through the public Service (14.09). A probe on that port has a catch. It runs on a separate web server, so it can pass while the main server has stopped accepting connections. One property puts the two groups on the main port as well, at /livez and /readyz:

management.server.port=8081
management.endpoint.health.probes.add-additional-paths=true

Also seen. A tcpSocket probe, which proves only that the port is open. An exec probe running curl, which needs curl in the image and costs a process start every period.

When to break it. A service that holds a resource only it can repair, such as a connection that never recovers after a network change, may add that check to liveness. The cost is that a wider outage then restarts every pod, so put a long failure window on it.

.NET anchor. In ASP.NET Core this is MapHealthChecks("/health/live", new HealthCheckOptions { Predicate = _ => false }) for liveness, and a tag predicate for readiness. Boot's groups do the same with properties, and Boot flips readiness to "not ready" on shutdown by itself.

See also. 17.03, 17.05, 14.04, 14.05, 14.09, The Yard, chapter 14, Actuator and observability

17.05 Shut down gracefully

Then.

  • Boot era: a hand-written Tomcat drain, from before Boot had a property for graceful shutdown. It paused the connector, shut its thread pool, then waited for the pool to finish. It did the right thing, and server.shutdown=graceful replaced it.
public class GracefulShutdown implements TomcatConnectorCustomizer,
        ApplicationListener<ContextClosedEvent> {
    private volatile Connector connector;
    public void customize(Connector c) { this.connector = c; }
    public void onApplicationEvent(ContextClosedEvent e) {
        connector.pause();
        ExecutorService pool = (ExecutorService) connector.getProtocolHandler().getExecutor();
        pool.shutdown(); pool.awaitTermination(30, TimeUnit.SECONDS);
  • Modern: server.shutdown=immediate, the default before Boot 3.4. Graceful is the default from 3.4, so a 3.5 service has it unless someone turned it off.

Recognise it by. TomcatConnectorCustomizer, ContextClosedEvent, connector.pause(), server.shutdown=immediate, and Runtime.getRuntime().addShutdownHook in application code.

The rookie version.

#!/bin/sh
# start.sh, the image's ENTRYPOINT
export JAVA_OPTS="$JAVA_OPTS -Dpayouts.region=$REGION"
java $JAVA_OPTS -jar /application/application.jar
echo "payouts-api exited with $?"

What goes wrong. The shell is now process 1 in the container, and Java is its child. To stop a pod, the runtime sends SIGTERM, the polite "please stop" signal, to process 1 only. The shell does not pass it on, and process 1 ignores signals it has no handler for. So Java never hears it. Spring's graceful shutdown, written for exactly this moment, never starts. Kubernetes waits out the whole 50-second grace period, then sends SIGKILL, which cannot be caught. Every request in flight is cut off. A payout of £1,240.50 that had reserved money in the ledger stops before it records the bank instruction. Two SQS messages being processed are never acknowledged. They come back after their visibility timeout and run a second time. And every deploy now takes 50 seconds per pod.

Do this now.

  1. Make Java process 1. Use the exec form, ENTRYPOINT ["java", "-jar", "application.jar"], and put flags in JAVA_TOOL_OPTIONS (17.02). If you need a script, end it with exec java ..., which replaces the shell with Java. Check with kubectl exec <pod> -- cat /proc/1/cmdline.
  2. Know what SIGTERM sets off. The JVM runs its shutdown hooks. Spring's hook closes the application context. Readiness goes to "not ready". Then the SmartLifecycle beans stop, a phase at a time, highest phase first. These are Spring beans with a start and a stop, such as message listener containers and schedulers. Listener containers sit in the default, highest phase, so they stop first. The web server's graceful drain is a later phase: it stops accepting connections and waits for requests in flight. Last, @PreDestroy methods run and beans are destroyed.
  3. Bound each phase. spring.lifecycle.timeout-per-shutdown-phase defaults to 30 seconds, and it applies to each phase, not to the whole shutdown. Payouts uses 20, because no request should take longer.
  4. Wait for the cluster first. The preStop sleep is a preStop hook, a command the kubelet runs inside the container before it sends SIGTERM, that does nothing but sleep. Kubernetes removes the pod from the Service while it starts stopping it, so some nodes still send it requests for a moment. A 5-second sleep lets them catch up (The Yard, chapter 14).
  5. Fit the worst case inside the grace period. terminationGracePeriodSeconds covers the hook and the whole shutdown. Payouts has two timed phases, the SQS listener containers and then the web server's drain. Then its task executor (3.05) waits up to 20 seconds. The worst case is 5 + 20 + 20 + 20 = 65 seconds, so Payouts sets 70, not the 40 of The Yard, chapter 14.
  6. Drain your own executors. A ThreadPoolTaskExecutor needs setWaitForTasksToCompleteOnShutdown(true) and setAwaitTerminationSeconds, or its queued tasks are dropped (3.11).
  7. Make a kill survivable anyway. A node can fail without any signal. The saga records each step before the next one, so a stuck saga can be found and finished (11.09). An SQS consumer must tolerate the redelivery (10.07).
spec:
  terminationGracePeriodSeconds: 70   # 5 preStop + 20 listeners + 20 web + 20 executor + 5
  containers:
    - name: payouts-api
      lifecycle:
        preStop:
          exec: { command: ["sleep", "5"] }

spring.lifecycle.timeout-per-shutdown-phase=20s

Keep @PreDestroy methods short. They run inside the same grace period, after the web server stops.

Also seen. tini, or Docker's --init, as process 1. It forwards signals to Java and reaps child processes. It is worth having when the container starts other processes, which a Spring service rarely does.

When to break it. A batch job may choose server.shutdown=immediate when its work is idempotent and restartable. The cost is redone work on every deploy.

.NET anchor. IHostApplicationLifetime.ApplicationStopping and HostOptions.ShutdownTimeout play the same part as Spring's context close and phase timeout. The process-1 rule is the same: a .NET image with a shell-script entrypoint has the same deaf shell.

See also. 17.04, 17.06, 3.11, 10.07, 11.09, The Yard, chapter 14, Actuator and observability

17.06 Roll out with zero downtime

What goes wrong. A rolling update replaces old pods with new ones a few at a time. Even with perfect probes and shutdown, both versions serve for about a minute. A new version of payouts-api renamed a JSON field in PayoutRequested. For 70 seconds the old pod's consumers received events they could not read, and 14 went to ledger-confirm-dlq.

Do this now.

  1. Write the surge settings down: maxSurge: 1 and maxUnavailable: 0. The defaults are 25% each, rounded, and change meaning with the replica count (The Yard, chapter 14).
  2. A new pod gets traffic only once ready (17.04).
  3. Set minReadySeconds: 10. A new pod must stay ready for 10 seconds before the rollout counts it and stops an old one. With readiness every 5 seconds, that is two more passing checks.
  4. Make every change work with the previous version, in both directions: expand first, contract in a later release (20.01, 20.02).
  5. Watch it with kubectl rollout status deployment/payouts-api, and go back with kubectl rollout undo deployment/payouts-api. An undo is safe only if the new version wrote nothing the old one cannot read (20.10).

See also. 17.04, 17.05, 20.01, 20.02, 20.09, 20.10, The Yard, chapter 14

17.07 Pass configuration and secrets to a pod

What goes wrong. A bank-gateway key put in a ConfigMap, Kubernetes' object for plain configuration, is readable by anyone who can read the namespace. Put in an environment variable, it appears in kubectl describe output, in /proc/1/environ, and in Actuator's env endpoint if someone exposes it.

Do this now.

  1. Plain settings go in a ConfigMap, passed as environment variables with envFrom. Boot's relaxed binding reads payouts.ledger.base-url from PAYOUTS_LEDGER_BASEURL: dots become underscores, dashes are removed, and the name is upper-cased (4.15).
  2. Secrets go in a Secret, mounted as files, one file per value. A Secret is only base64-encoded, so who can read it is decided by the cluster's access rules.
  3. Read the mounted files with a config tree. Each file name becomes a property name, and the file's contents its value:
containers:
  - name: payouts-api
    envFrom:
      - configMapRef: { name: payouts-api-config }   # PAYOUTS_LEDGER_BASEURL
    volumeMounts:
      - { name: secrets, mountPath: /etc/payouts/secrets, readOnly: true }
volumes:
  - name: secrets
    secret: { secretName: payouts-api-secrets }      # key: payouts.bank.api-key

spring.config.import=optional:configtree:/etc/payouts/secrets/
  1. Both are read once, at startup. Changing a ConfigMap restarts nothing. Roll the Deployment to pick the change up.

Also seen. AWS Secrets Manager read directly by the service, with the pod's IAM role (15.06, 15.07).

.NET anchor. .NET maps PAYOUTS__LEDGER__BASEURL, with a double underscore for each level. Boot uses a single underscore.

See also. 4.04, 4.15, 15.06, 15.07, Dependency injection and configuration

17.08 Run several replicas safely

What goes wrong. Payouts ran 1 replica to save memory. When the platform team drained a node for patching, the only pod stopped before its replacement was ready, and POST /payouts failed for 50 seconds. A second team scaled their service to 10 replicas with a pool of 50 connections each. That is 500 connections against one DocumentDB instance, before a rollout's surge pod adds 50 more.

Do this now.

  1. Run at least 2 replicas of anything that takes traffic.
  2. Add a PodDisruptionBudget, which limits how many pods voluntary disruptions such as node drains may take at once. minAvailable: 1 keeps one serving.
  3. Spread the pods over zones with topologySpreadConstraints on topology.kubernetes.io/zone, so one zone's failure does not take both.
  4. Keep no state in the pod: no in-memory sessions, and no cache that must agree across pods.
  5. Remember that every replica runs every @Scheduled method (3.10).
  6. Multiply: pool size × maximum replicas, plus the surge, must stay under the database's connection quota (8.24).
apiVersion: policy/v1
kind: PodDisruptionBudget
metadata: { name: payouts-api }
spec:
  minAvailable: 1
  selector: { matchLabels: { app: payouts-api } }
---
# in the Deployment's pod template spec
topologySpreadConstraints:
  - maxSkew: 1                     # zones differ by at most 1 pod
    topologyKey: topology.kubernetes.io/zone
    whenUnsatisfiable: ScheduleAnyway
    labelSelector: { matchLabels: { app: payouts-api } }

ScheduleAnyway still places a pod when only one zone has room.

See also. 3.10, 8.24, 17.06, 18.03, 21.10

17.09 Diagnose OOMKilled and CrashLoopBackOff

What goes wrong. kubectl get pods shows CrashLoopBackOff. That is not a cause. It means the container keeps exiting and the kubelet keeps restarting it, waiting longer between tries. The current container's logs may hold only the start of a new attempt, not the failure.

Do this now.

  1. Run kubectl describe pod <name>. Read Last State: Terminated, its Reason and Exit Code, then the Events at the bottom.
  2. Run kubectl logs <name> --previous for the log of the container that died.
  3. Match the evidence:
You see It means Go to
Reason: OOMKilled, exit code 137 the kernel killed the process at the memory limit 17.02
APPLICATION FAILED TO START in the previous log Spring could not start, usually configuration 4.10
Terminating due to java.lang.OutOfMemoryError the heap ran out 18.06
Liveness probe failed in Events the kubelet restarted a process it judged dead 17.04

See also. 4.10, 17.02, 17.04, 18.06, The Yard, chapter 13

17.10 Take a heap dump or thread dump from a pod

What goes wrong. A JRE image has no jcmd, so the runbook's command fails at 02:00. A heap dump written to a /tmp mounted as a memory-backed emptyDir counts against the pod's limit. On Payouts a 384 MiB dump got the 768 MiB pod OOMKilled halfway.

Do this now.

  1. Thread dump, a list of every thread and what it is doing: send the JVM signal 3. The dump goes to standard output, so read it with kubectl logs.
kubectl exec payouts-api-7d9f8 -- sh -c 'kill -3 1'
kubectl logs payouts-api-7d9f8 | tail -n 400
  1. Heap dump, a file of every object on the heap: use Actuator's heapdump endpoint on the management port, or jcmd 1 GC.heap_dump /dumps/payouts.hprof. Write to a disk-backed volume with room for the heap. Copy it out with kubectl cp.
  2. With no tools in the image, add a debug container: kubectl debug -it payouts-api-7d9f8 --image=eclipse-temurin:25-jdk --target=payouts-api. --target shares the container's processes. jcmd attaches only when it runs as the JVM's user, 10001, set by the Dockerfile's USER 10001 and the pod's runAsUser: 10001 (17.01). Run the debug container as 10001.
  3. A heap dump holds claimants' names and bank details. Treat it as personal data; delete it after use.

See also. 14.09, 18.05, 18.06, 17.01, The Yard, chapter 13

17.11 Build an image without a Dockerfile

What goes wrong. A team hand-maintains 40 Dockerfiles, one per service. Each drifts a little. Three still start from a base image last updated a year ago.

Do this now.

  1. Cloud Native Buildpacks turn source or a jar into an image with no Dockerfile. Boot's Maven plugin runs them, using a Docker daemon:
./mvnw spring-boot:build-image \
  -Dspring-boot.build-image.imageName=registry.sorrel.internal/payouts-api:1.4.0
  1. The result is layered and runs as a non-root user. The default Paketo builder's Java buildpack also adds a memory calculator. Each time the container starts, it sets -Xmx and the other memory flags in JAVA_TOOL_OPTIONS from the container's memory limit. Flags you set yourself win. Read what it chose in the log before adding your own (17.02).
  2. Jib, Google's jib-maven-plugin, builds and pushes an image from Maven with no daemon at all. That suits CI runners that cannot run Docker.
  3. Keep a Dockerfile when the platform team supplies a base image and you need full control of it.

See also. 17.01, 17.02, 1.11, Packaging and native images

17.12 Run a local cluster for testing

What goes wrong. The image was tagged payouts-api:latest. A latest tag makes Kubernetes pull on every start, so the local cluster went to the registry, found nothing, and reported ErrImagePull.

Do this now.

  1. kind, "Kubernetes in Docker", runs a whole cluster as containers on a laptop or a CI runner.
kind create cluster --name payouts
kind load docker-image payouts-api:dev --name payouts
kubectl apply -f k8s/
  1. Use a fixed tag such as :dev, which kind load copies into the cluster's nodes.
  2. Rehearse what manifests decide: probes, shutdown, rolling updates. Payouts' deploy test sends requests through a rollout and fails if any fail (The Yard, chapter 14).
  3. Do not expect it to stand in for AWS. IAM roles, DocumentDB and the load balancer are not there.

Also seen. k3d and minikube, which do the same job. The Kubernetes built into Docker Desktop. Testcontainers' K3s module, for a cluster started from a JUnit test.

See also. 16.08, 17.05, 17.06, The Yard, chapter 14

⚠Review checklist
  • If you see FROM openjdk, a JDK in the final stage, COPY . . before the build, or no USER line: the image is large, slow to push, full of tools, and runs as root. See 17.01.
  • If you see -Xmx equal to the memory limit, or set in the Dockerfile while the limit is in the manifest: the process outgrows its limit and dies with no evidence. See 17.02.
  • If you see a memory request below the limit, or no resources: block: the scheduler overpacks the node, and the JVM sizes itself for CPUs it will not get. See 17.03.
  • If you see a CPU limit of 1 or less, or a memory limit under about 1792 MB, with no collector named: the JVM picks the Serial collector, which stops the application for the whole of every collection. See 17.03.
  • If you see a liveness probe on /actuator/health, or liveness and readiness on the same path: a database failover restarts every pod at once. See 17.04.
  • If you see a shell-script entrypoint that runs java without exec: Java never receives SIGTERM, and every stop is a kill. See 17.05.
  • If you see a renamed field or a removed endpoint shipped in one release: the old and new pods disagree during the rollout. See 17.06.
  • If you see a secret in a ConfigMap or a plain environment variable: anyone who can read the namespace can read it. See 17.07.
  • If you see replicas: 1, or no PodDisruptionBudget: a node drain is an outage. See 17.08.
  • If you see a heap dump path on a memory-backed volume: taking the dump gets the pod killed. See 17.10.
  • If you see a latest tag in a local or production manifest: what runs depends on when the node pulled. See 17.12.

Part IV · The how-to18. Performance#

Payouts is rarely slow because Java is slow. It is slow because it waits: for the ledger, for the bank gateway, for a free connection to DocumentDB, or for a lock. This part shows how to find out where the time goes before you change anything. It covers removing repeated calls, sizing pools from arithmetic, reading thread dumps and heap dumps, and profiling with the JDK's own recorder. It ends with caching, startup time and load tests that tell the truth about latency.

★What a veteran knows
  • A performance goal is a percentile at a stated load: "99% of POST /payouts under 300 ms at 40 requests a second". Without the load and the percentile there is nothing to test against.
  • The slow part is nearly always waiting, not computing. Look at remote calls, pools and locks before you look at a loop.
  • A pool is a queue with a name. Making it bigger moves the queue to the database, where you cannot see it.
  • Take three thread dumps before you restart anything. A restart cures the symptom and destroys the evidence.
  • A cache without a maximum size is a memory leak with a hit rate.
  • A load test that waits for each slow reply before it sends the next request cannot see the slowness you are looking for. On Payouts the tool once reported a 99th percentile of 180 ms while the service's own histogram said 2.1 seconds.
◷How we got hereIn March 2013 Gil Tene, the chief technology officer of Azul Systems, a company that builds JVMs, gave a talk…

In March 2013 Gil Tene, the chief technology officer of Azul Systems, a company that builds JVMs, gave a talk at QCon London called "How NOT to Measure Latency". Its abstract warned that "coordinated data omission issues can literally skew measurement results by orders of magnitude." On 3 August 2013 he opened a thread called "Coordinated Omission" on the mechanical-sympathy mailing list. He had been "harping for a while now", he wrote, about a measurement problem that "can often render percentile data useless". His example was a benchmark of log4j2. A test thread stalled, and while it stalled it skipped the calls it would otherwise have timed. The slowest moments were the ones never recorded. He concluded the real figure was "at least 35,000x higher than reported". In a reply he added: "I rarely see load testers that don't suffer from it, including common testers used in the industry (JMeter, Grinder, HP LoadRunner)." His HdrHistogram library could correct for the samples a stalled tester never took. Most teams still had to learn it from their own outage.

18.01 Measure before you optimise

Then.

  • Spring era: timing by hand with System.currentTimeMillis() and a log line. It was the tool in every JDK, and before metrics libraries it was often the only number a team had.
long start = System.currentTimeMillis();
LedgerEntry entry = ledgerClient.reserve(payout);
log.info("ledger reserve took " + (System.currentTimeMillis() - start) + " ms");
  • Spring era: micro-optimisation by habit: StringBuilder for every concatenation, object pools for small objects, loops instead of iterators. On early JVMs, before modern garbage collectors (the part of the JVM that frees unused objects) and JIT compilers, some of these paid. On a current JVM they rarely do, and they make code harder to read.
  • Boot era: Dropwizard Metrics, also known as Codahale Metrics, with a MetricRegistry and registry.timer("ledger.reserve"). Micrometer later became Spring Boot's own metrics layer, with one API for many monitoring systems, and replaced it in Boot services.

Recognise it by. System.currentTimeMillis() pairs around a call, org.apache.commons.lang3.time.StopWatch or Spring's org.springframework.util.StopWatch in production code, com.codahale.metrics imports, and comments such as // faster than a stream.

The rookie version.

public static void main(String[] args) {
    FeeCalculator fees = new FeeCalculator();
    long start = System.currentTimeMillis();
    for (int i = 0; i < 1_000; i++) {
        fees.feeFor(SAMPLE_CLAIM);
    }
    System.out.println("1000 fees in " + (System.currentTimeMillis() - start) + " ms");
    // printed 41 ms, so the streams in FeeCalculator were rewritten as loops
}

What goes wrong. The loop measures a cold JVM. The JIT compiler, the part of the JVM that turns frequently run methods into machine code, has not yet compiled feeFor, so the first thousand calls run slowly in the interpreter. The JIT may also remove work whose result is never used, so a warm loop can measure nothing. currentTimeMillis is the wall clock, which can jump when the machine corrects its time. Even a correct number would not matter. A developer spent 2 days rewriting the fee code. Payouts' 99th percentile stayed at 2.4 seconds, because a payout request spent 1.8 seconds waiting for the bank gateway and less than 1 ms computing fees.

Do this now.

  1. Write the goal down as a percentile at a load. The 99th percentile, or p99, is the latency that 99% of requests beat. Averages hide the slow requests your callers complain about.
  2. Start from production. With Actuator, Boot's monitoring module (the spring-boot-starter-actuator dependency), Boot records a timer for every request, http.server.requests. Publish it as a histogram, so that p99 can be computed across pods (14.06), and read p99 per endpoint.
  3. Open a trace of one slow request, the timed record of its path through every service (13.01). It splits the time between the ledger, the bank gateway and DocumentDB, and shows what is left over in Payouts itself.
  4. If the time is waiting, look at pools (18.03), repeated calls (18.02) and locks (18.05). If it is CPU in your own code, profile it (18.07).
  5. Time a section that nothing else covers with a Micrometer Timer. It measures elapsed time with a monotonic clock. registry is the MeterRegistry bean, an object Spring creates and hands to your class's constructor.
public SagaState runStep(SagaStep step, SagaState state) {
    Timer.Sample sample = Timer.start(registry);
    try {
        return step.execute(state);
    } finally {
        sample.stop(registry.timer("payouts.saga.step", "step", step.name()));
    }
}
  1. Change one thing. Measure again at the same load, and keep the change only if the percentile moved.
  2. For a genuinely hot piece of pure Java, write a JMH benchmark. JMH, the Java Microbenchmark Harness from the OpenJDK project, warms the JVM up, runs separate forks and stops the JIT from discarding your work. Add org.openjdk.jmh:jmh-core and its annotation processor, jmh-generator-annprocess, in a module of their own. Mark the method @Benchmark and return its result, or pass it to a Blackhole.

Also seen. System.nanoTime() for a one-off measurement in a test, where you need elapsed time and nothing else. Commercial APM agents that time everything without code changes. They answer the same questions as traces and metrics, at a licence cost.

When to break it. Some choices are cheap to get right first time and costly later: an index on the field every query filters on, or one query instead of fifty. Make those without a benchmark. The cost of skipping measurement elsewhere is code that is harder to read and no faster.

.NET anchor. JMH is Java's BenchmarkDotNet, and it exists for the same reason: JIT warm-up and dead-code elimination fool hand-written loops. Timer.Sample plays the part of Stopwatch feeding a Histogram<T> from System.Diagnostics.Metrics. System.nanoTime() is Stopwatch.GetTimestamp().

See also. 13.01, 14.06, 18.07, 18.10, The Yard, chapter 4, Actuator and observability, How Java runs your code

18.02 Remove an N+1 call pattern

Then.

  • Spring era: Hibernate lazy loading. Hibernate is the JPA library that maps Java objects to SQL tables, much as EF Core does. An entity's collection, marked FetchType.LAZY, was loaded with its own SELECT the first time code touched it. Loop over 50 orders, touch each order's lines, and the database ran 51 queries. Lazy loading was right for screens that showed one entity at a time. It went wrong in lists. JOIN FETCH, @EntityGraph and Hibernate's @BatchSize were the fixes.
@OneToMany(mappedBy = "claim", fetch = FetchType.LAZY)
private List<PayoutLine> lines;   // one SELECT per claim, the first time it is read
  • Boot era: Spring Data MongoDB's @DBRef(lazy = true), the same pattern in a document database. DocumentDB does not support DBRefs at all (8.02).

Recognise it by. FetchType.LAZY on @OneToMany or @ManyToOne, @DBRef, hibernate.show_sql=true in a config file, and logs or traces that repeat the same query with a different ID.

The rookie version.

public List<PayoutView> recent() {
    return payoutRepository.findTop50ByOrderByRequestedAtDesc().stream()
            .map(p -> PayoutView.of(p, policyClient.findClaim(p.claimId())))
            .toList();
}

What goes wrong. Spring Data, the library that writes repository implementations from interfaces, builds the first query from the method name. The name N+1 describes the shape: one call to fetch a list of N things, then one more call for each of them. Here that is 1 query and 50 HTTP calls to the policy system, which owns claims. Each call takes about 40 ms, so the page takes 2 seconds, done one after another on a single thread. It looked fine in the test, which had 3 payouts. The finance team's dashboard refreshes every 30 seconds for 12 people, so the policy system receives 1,200 calls a minute from one screen. Some claims are paid in instalments, and the 50 payouts referred to only 31 distinct claims, so 19 of those calls fetched something already fetched.

Do this now.

  1. Find the pattern. A trace shows it as a ladder of identical spans (13.01). In a test, count the calls: a request count from WireMock, a fake HTTP server for tests (16.09), or a MongoDB driver command listener (8.12).
  2. Fetch the list, then collect the distinct keys.
  3. Fetch all of them in one call. For DocumentDB that is one $in query, such as findAllById(ids). For another service it is a batch endpoint, if its owners offer one. Ask them.
  4. Join in memory with a Map.
public List<PayoutView> recent() {
    List<Payout> payouts = payoutRepository.findTop50ByOrderByRequestedAtDesc();
    Set<String> claimIds = payouts.stream()
            .map(Payout::claimId)
            .collect(Collectors.toSet());
    Map<String, ClaimSummary> claims = policyClient.findClaims(claimIds).stream()
            .collect(Collectors.toMap(ClaimSummary::id, Function.identity()));
    return payouts.stream()
            .map(p -> PayoutView.of(p, claims.get(p.claimId())))   // null if not returned
            .toList();
}
  1. Bound the batch. Limit the page size (5.07), and split a large ID set into chunks the other side accepts.
  2. Add a test that fails when the call count grows with the list size. Stub the batch endpoint, load 50 payouts across 31 claims, and verify exactly 1 request to it (16.09).

Also seen. When there is no batch endpoint, make the calls in parallel with a bounded limit (3.03, 3.09). The page is faster, but the other service still receives N calls. A cache (18.08) helps when the same keys repeat across requests. Embedding the data you need in the payout document (8.02) removes the call entirely, at the cost of keeping a copy up to date.

When to break it. A loop over a list that is always small and bounded, such as the 3 steps of a saga, can make one call per item. The cost is that someone must keep it small. Write the bound down in a comment or an assertion.

.NET anchor. This is Entity Framework's N+1 with lazy-loading proxies, and JOIN FETCH is EF's .Include(). The HTTP version is the same bug as calling HttpClient inside a LINQ Select.

See also. 3.03, 3.09, 5.07, 8.02, 8.15, 18.04, Data access, JPA and migrations, Document data: Amazon DocumentDB and the MongoDB API

18.03 Size connection pools to the work

Then.

  • Boot era: very large request thread pools in Tomcat, the web server Boot embeds, such as server.tomcat.max-threads=1000, so that a slow dependency would not run out of threads. When each waiting request held an operating-system thread, a bigger pool did buy time. It also hid the real limit, and Boot later renamed the key to server.tomcat.threads.max.
  • Spring era: database pools sized "to be safe", in c3p0 or Commons DBCP, and in the 2.x and 3.x MongoDB Java drivers.
MongoClientOptions options = MongoClientOptions.builder()
        .connectionsPerHost(200)
        .threadsAllowedToBlockForConnectionMultiplier(10)
        .build();

Recognise it by. server.tomcat.max-threads, server.tomcat.threads.max with no comment, MongoClientOptions, connectionsPerHost, threadsAllowedToBlockForConnectionMultiplier, com.mchange.v2.c3p0 and org.apache.commons.dbcp imports.

The rookie version.

server:
  tomcat:
    threads:
      max: 800           # "the ledger was slow, so more threads"
spring:
  data:
    mongodb:
      uri: mongodb://docdb.sorrel.internal:27017/payouts?tls=true&maxPoolSize=400

What goes wrong. A connection pool is a set of open connections that requests borrow and return. Payouts runs 2 pods, so this asks for up to 800 connections to DocumentDB. During a rolling deploy a third pod starts before an old one stops (17.06): 1,200. Three services share one r5.large, a DocumentDB instance size whose quota is 3,400 connections in all and 1,100 active ones. Payouts alone could pass the active quota, before the other two services take any. More connections do not make DocumentDB faster: past a point, extra concurrent queries compete for the same CPU and memory, and every query slows down. The 800 platform threads, each backed by an operating-system thread with its own stack, cost Payouts memory outside the heap too.

Do this now. Size each pool from arithmetic, not from fear.

  1. Measure two numbers per pod at peak: operations per second, and how long each holds a connection. Payouts' peak is 20 payouts a second per pod, each making about 10 DocumentDB writes (21.10): at least 200 operations a second, each holding a connection for about 3 ms.
  2. Apply Little's law: the number in use on average equals the arrival rate times the time each one is held. Here 200 × 0.003 = 0.6 connections.
  3. Add headroom for bursts and slow moments. Use the p99 hold time, not the average, and the burst rate, not the mean. At 4 times the rate and a p99 hold of 12 ms, 800 × 0.012 = 9.6, so Payouts settles on 10.
  4. Check the other side's budget. Pods at peak, including the extra pods of a deploy, times the pool size, summed over every service on the instance, must stay under the quota (8.24). For Payouts that is 3 pods × 10 = 30.
  5. Bound the wait for a free connection, well inside the caller's deadline (7.15), and map the driver's timeout to a 503 in one place (6.03). Fail fast, do not queue.
@Bean
MongoClientSettingsBuilderCustomizer payoutsPool(PayoutsDbProperties props) {
    return settings -> settings.applyToConnectionPoolSettings(pool -> pool
            .maxSize(props.maxPoolSize())       // 10, from the arithmetic above
            .minSize(2)
            .maxWaitTime(500, TimeUnit.MILLISECONDS));
}

PayoutsDbProperties is a @ConfigurationProperties record bound from payouts.db.*. Set the pool in one place only, here or in the connection string (8.24).

  1. Graph the pool: mongodb.driver.pool.checkedout, the connections in use, and mongodb.driver.pool.waitqueuesize, the requests waiting for one. Actuator publishes both. A growing wait queue means the pool is the limit.
  2. With virtual threads on (3.01), threads the JVM schedules itself and parks cheaply while they wait, the request thread pool is no longer a limit at all. The connection pools and bulkheads are now the limits, so they must be set on purpose.

The same arithmetic sizes the HTTP client's pool for the ledger (7.12) and the bulkhead, the limit on concurrent ledger calls, in front of it (3.09). In Boot 4 the connection string property is spring.mongodb.uri instead of spring.data.mongodb.uri.

Also seen. HikariCP, Boot's default pool for JDBC databases, set with spring.datasource.hikari.maximum-pool-size and connection-timeout, with the same arithmetic. Sizing from the database's core count gives an upper bound, not the number you need.

When to break it. A nightly reconciliation job running alone may use a larger pool. The cost is a schedule that must keep it away from daytime traffic, and an alert if it overruns.

.NET anchor. Max Pool Size in an ADO.NET connection string, or maxPoolSize in a MongoDB .NET one, is the same setting, and the same arithmetic applies. The large Tomcat pool is Java's version of raising ThreadPool.SetMinThreads to cure thread starvation: it buys time and moves the queue.

See also. 3.01, 3.09, 7.12, 7.15, 8.24, 17.03, 21.10, The Yard, chapter 12, Document data: Amazon DocumentDB and the MongoDB API

18.04 Batch calls and writes

What goes wrong. The outbox relay (9.08) claims each event, publishes it to SNS, AWS's topic service, and marks it sent, each with its own call. After a 20-minute ledger outage there are 9,000 events waiting. Each costs two DocumentDB calls of about 3 ms and one SNS call of about 15 ms, so the backlog spends 9,000 × 21 ms = 189 seconds in round trips.

Do this now.

  • Publish to SNS with PublishBatch, and send to SQS, AWS's queue service, with SendMessageBatch. Each takes at most 10 entries.
  • Read the response entry by entry. A batch call can succeed as a whole while some entries fail, and its failed() list names them by entry id, so use the event id there. Mark only the others published, in one updateMulti on _id $in their ids. Failed ones stay PENDING.
  • For writes that differ per document, use a bulk operation: mongoTemplate.bulkOps(BulkMode.UNORDERED, OutboxEvent.class), run with execute() (8.21).
  • A call that times out may have landed some entries, and the retry repeats them. Make every entry idempotent (9.09), so consumers drop repeats by event id (10.07).

See also. 8.21, 9.08, 9.09, 10.02, 10.03, 10.07, 18.02

18.05 Read a thread dump

Then.

  • Spring era: kill -3 <pid>, which makes the JVM print a thread dump to its standard output, and jstack <pid>. Both still work, and kill -3 is the fallback in an image without jcmd (17.10). jstack was the usual name in runbooks before jcmd gathered the JDK's diagnostic commands into one tool.
  • Spring era: VisualVM's Threads tab, attached over JMX, a remote management protocol. It needed a port open into the process, which is awkward on a Kubernetes pod.
jstack -l 4211 > /tmp/dump.txt

Recognise it by. Runbooks that say jstack -l, -Dcom.sun.management.jmxremote.port in start scripts, and an exposed /actuator/threaddump as the only diagnostic.

The rookie version.

# p99 is 9 seconds and both pods look stuck
kubectl rollout restart deployment/payouts-api

What goes wrong. The restart works. Latency drops, and everyone goes back to work. At 14:05 the next day it happens again, and nobody knows why, because the only evidence was in the memory of the pods that were restarted. The cause was a synchronized method in ProductRulesCache. One thread held its lock while it called the policy system with no timeout. The other request threads queued behind it.

Do this now. A thread dump is a snapshot of every thread in the JVM: its name, its state and its stack.

  1. Before any restart, take three dumps from the stuck pod, 10 seconds apart. One dump is a moment. Three show which threads are not moving.
# jcmd is the JDK's diagnostic tool. The JVM is usually process 1 in the container.
for i in 1 2 3; do
  kubectl exec payouts-api-7d9f8c-x2kqp -- jcmd 1 Thread.print > dump-$i.txt
  sleep 10
done

A JRE-only image has no jcmd. Then send kill -3 1 and read the dump with kubectl logs, or use a debug container (17.10).

  1. Read each thread's state. RUNNABLE is running or in a system call. BLOCKED is waiting to enter a synchronized block. WAITING and TIMED_WAITING are parked, often on a pool or a queue.
  2. Group threads by their top frames. Here 180 threads are BLOCKED on the same object:
"http-nio-8080-exec-41" #96 daemon prio=5 os_prio=0 waiting for monitor entry
   java.lang.Thread.State: BLOCKED (on object monitor)
	at com.sorrel.payouts.policy.ProductRulesCache.rulesFor(ProductRulesCache.java:38)
	- waiting to lock <0x00000000e3b1c2d8> (a com.sorrel.payouts.policy.ProductRulesCache)

"http-nio-8080-exec-7" #62 daemon prio=5 os_prio=0 runnable
   java.lang.Thread.State: RUNNABLE
	at sun.nio.ch.Net.poll(java.base@25.0.1/Native Method)
	at sun.nio.ch.NioSocketImpl.park(java.base@25.0.1/NioSocketImpl.java:190)
	at sun.nio.ch.NioSocketImpl.implRead(java.base@25.0.1/NioSocketImpl.java:307)
	...
	at com.sorrel.payouts.policy.ProductRulesCache.rulesFor(ProductRulesCache.java:44)
	- locked <0x00000000e3b1c2d8> (a com.sorrel.payouts.policy.ProductRulesCache)
  1. Find the holder. Search for the address after - locked. That thread is the cause. Here it is waiting in Net.poll for a socket read inside the lock, with the HTTP client's frames (elided as ...) in between, so the fixes are a timeout (7.03) and no network call while holding a lock (3.07).
  2. Look for the line Found one Java-level deadlock, which the JVM prints when threads wait on each other in a cycle (3.12).
  3. With virtual threads on, Thread.print lists platform threads only. Use jcmd 1 Thread.dump_to_file -format=json /tmp/threads.json, which includes virtual threads. Copy it off with kubectl cp and query it with jq.
  4. Then restart if you must, and attach the dumps to the incident.

Also seen. /actuator/threaddump returns a dump over HTTP. It is convenient, but it must be secured (14.09), and it is no use when the service cannot answer HTTP. fastthread.io and similar tools group a dump's threads for you. Treat a dump as internal data before you upload it anywhere.

When to break it. If the service is losing money every second, restart one pod and take the dumps from the other. The cost is that you see only the pod you kept.

.NET anchor. jcmd Thread.print is dotnet-stack report, or dotnet-dump collect followed by clrstack -all in dotnet-dump analyze. Java's dumps are plain text and cheap, so take them often.

See also. 3.07, 3.12, 7.03, 17.10, 18.06, The Yard, chapter 12, Threads are cheap now, The JVM at runtime: memory, GC and containers

18.06 Find a memory leak in a heap dump

Then.

  • Spring era: jmap -dump:live,format=b,file=heap.hprof <pid> to write the dump, and jhat, a small web server in old JDKs, to browse it. jhat has long since left the JDK. jmap still works, and jcmd now covers the same ground.
  • Spring era: VisualVM's heap dump view on a developer's laptop, attached to a local copy of the service. It suited a leak you could reproduce.
jmap -histo:live 4211 | head -20

Recognise it by. Runbooks with jmap -dump, jmap -histo or jhat, and start scripts with -XX:+HeapDumpOnOutOfMemoryError but no -XX:HeapDumpPath, which writes the dump into the working directory of a container that is about to disappear.

The rookie version.

@Component
public class IdempotentResponses {
    private static final Map<String, PayoutResponse> SEEN = new ConcurrentHashMap<>();

    public PayoutResponse remember(String idempotencyKey, PayoutResponse response) {
        SEEN.put(idempotencyKey, response);
        return response;
    }
}

What goes wrong. Every Idempotency-Key Payouts sees stays in the map until the pod restarts. Each pod receives about 10,000 payouts a day, at about 2 KB an entry, in a 384 MiB heap. After 15 days without a deploy it held 150,000 entries, 300 MB. Heap used after each collection had climbed daily, and collections ran almost back to back. Then the pod threw java.lang.OutOfMemoryError: Java heap space. In the last hour before that, p99 rose from 250 ms to 4 seconds, as the garbage collector spent more and more time finding nothing to free.

Do this now.

  1. Confirm it is the heap. Graph heap used after each collection (14.10). A leak is a sawtooth whose floor rises. If the pod is OOMKilled, killed by the kernel at its memory limit, with exit code 137 and no Java error, the memory is outside the heap, and 17.09 and The Yard, chapter 13, apply instead.
  2. Arrange for a dump to be written on failure: -XX:+HeapDumpOnOutOfMemoryError -XX:HeapDumpPath=/dumps in JAVA_TOOL_OPTIONS. Mount /dumps as a disk-backed emptyDir volume with room for the heap, which survives a container restart within the pod. A memory-backed one counts against the pod's limit (17.10).
  3. Or take one from a live pod: jcmd 1 GC.heap_dump /dumps/payouts-1.hprof. The JVM pauses while it writes, so take the pod out of service first if you can (17.10). The file is about the size of the heap in use.
  4. Copy it off with kubectl cp, which needs tar in the image. A heap dump holds every object, including bank details and claimant names. Store it as personal data, and delete it when the incident closes.
  5. Open it in Eclipse Memory Analyzer, called MAT. Run the Leak Suspects report, then the dominator tree. The retained size of an object is the memory freed if it were collected. A small map can retain hundreds of megabytes.
  6. Ask MAT for the path to GC roots of the biggest object. GC roots are the references the JVM always keeps alive, such as static fields and running threads' stacks. Here it ends at the static field IdempotentResponses.SEEN.
  7. Fix the cause. Store idempotency keys in the idempotency_keys collection with an expiry (9.10, 8.17). A bounded cache (18.08) would stop the leak but keep the bug: a map in one pod forgets on restart and knows nothing of the other pod.

For a quick check without a full dump, run jcmd 1 GC.class_histogram twice, an hour apart, and compare the counts. The class whose count only grows is your suspect.

Common leaks in Spring services: static collections, caches with no maximum size, ThreadLocal values (one per thread) left on pooled threads, listeners registered and never removed, and metrics tagged with a payout ID (14.03).

Also seen. IntelliJ IDEA's heap dump viewer, for a small dump. The old-object sample event of JFR, the JDK's built-in recorder (18.07), which can point at a leak in a running service without a full dump.

When to break it. A service may hold a large data set on purpose, such as a reference table loaded at startup. The cost is that its size must be stated and alerted on, or nobody can tell growth from a leak.

.NET anchor. jcmd GC.heap_dump is dotnet-gcdump collect, and MAT plays the part of PerfView or Visual Studio's memory analysis. A static ConcurrentDictionary used as a cache leaks in .NET exactly as it does here.

See also. 8.17, 9.10, 14.03, 14.10, 17.09, 17.10, 18.08, The Yard, chapter 13, The JVM at runtime: memory, GC and containers

18.07 Profile with JFR and async-profiler

Then.

  • Spring era: VisualVM's sampler, or a commercial profiler such as YourKit or JProfiler attached as an agent. They were the best tools there were, but their overhead and licences kept them on developers' machines, and they were rarely allowed in production. JFR, built into every current JDK, replaced them for most production work.
  • Spring era: JFR as an Oracle commercial feature, unlocked with a flag in the start script.

Recognise it by. -agentpath: pointing at libyjpagent.so or libjprofilerti.so in a start script or Dockerfile, and -XX:+UnlockCommercialFeatures -XX:+FlightRecorder.

The rookie version.

public String toAuditJson(Payout payout) {
    try {
        return new ObjectMapper()                    // a new mapper on every call
                .registerModule(new JavaTimeModule())
                .writeValueAsString(payout);
    } catch (JsonProcessingException e) {
        throw new IllegalStateException(e);
    }
}

What goes wrong. Payouts uses 90% of its CPU limit at 20 requests a second, its month-end peak per pod, and nobody knows why. Someone guesses the DocumentDB driver and spends a week tuning it. A profile would have shown 60% of CPU inside toAuditJson. A new ObjectMapper starts with empty caches, so every call works out again how to serialise a Payout. A shared mapper does that once.

Do this now. JFR, the JDK Flight Recorder, is a low-overhead recorder built into the JVM. It samples stacks, allocations, locks, garbage collections and I/O.

  1. Start a 60-second recording in the pod at peak load. The profile settings sample more often than the default, for a little more overhead. If the image has no jcmd, use a debug container (17.10).
kubectl exec payouts-api-7d9f8c-x2kqp -- \
  jcmd 1 JFR.start duration=60s filename=/tmp/payouts.jfr settings=profile
  1. Copy the file off with kubectl cp. Open it in JDK Mission Control, the JDK's viewer for recordings, or summarise it with jfr summary and jfr print --events jdk.ExecutionSample.
  2. Find the methods with the most samples, then walk up to their callers. Here that leads to toAuditJson.
  3. For a flame graph, a picture in which each bar's width is the share of samples spent in that method, use async-profiler. It is not part of the JDK, so copy its release into the pod or a debug container. Run asprof -d 30 -e cpu -f /tmp/flame.html 1. Where the container blocks the kernel's performance events, use -e itimer instead of -e cpu. Use -e alloc to see allocations and -e wall to see where threads wait.
  4. Fix the cause. Here it is one line: inject the ObjectMapper bean Boot already configures, which is safe to share between threads.
  5. Measure again at the same load (18.01), and keep the change only if CPU and p99 moved.

Also seen. A continuous recording from startup with -XX:StartFlightRecording and a maxage, which keeps the recent past so that jcmd 1 JFR.dump can save it after an incident. IntelliJ IDEA's profiler, which runs JFR or async-profiler on a laptop.

When to break it. When the trace shows the time is spent waiting on another service (18.01), a CPU profile has little to show, and it will point you at whatever code happens to run. Use -e wall or the trace instead.

.NET anchor. JFR is close to EventPipe, recorded with dotnet-trace collect, and Mission Control plays the part of PerfView. The difference is that the recorder is already inside every JVM, so there is no agent to attach. jcmd or a start-up flag only switches it on.

See also. 17.10, 18.01, 18.06, How Java runs your code

18.08 Cache with Caffeine and expire correctly

Then.

  • Boot era: Guava's CacheBuilder, and Ehcache 2 configured in ehcache.xml. Both were sound. Caffeine succeeded Guava's cache, and Spring dropped its Guava cache manager for it. Ehcache 3 is a different API with a different package.
LoadingCache<String, ProductRules> rules = CacheBuilder.newBuilder()
        .maximumSize(500).expireAfterWrite(10, TimeUnit.MINUTES)
        .build(CacheLoader.from(policyClient::productRules));

Recognise it by. com.google.common.cache, net.sf.ehcache, an ehcache.xml with timeToLiveSeconds, GuavaCacheManager, and EhCacheCacheManager.

What goes wrong. A cache of policy summaries uses expireAfterAccess(10m) with no maximum size. The busiest policies are read every second, so they never expire, and a corrected policy is served stale for days. The rarely read ones pile up until the heap is full (18.06).

Do this now. Add com.github.ben-manes.caffeine:caffeine. Always set a maximum size. Prefer expireAfterWrite, which bounds how stale an entry can be. Add refreshAfterWrite to reload hot entries in the background while serving the old value.

LoadingCache<String, ProductRules> rules = Caffeine.newBuilder()
        .maximumSize(500)
        .expireAfterWrite(Duration.ofMinutes(10))
        .refreshAfterWrite(Duration.ofMinutes(1))
        .recordStats()
        .build(policyClient::productRules);

Publish the hit rate with Micrometer's CaffeineCacheMetrics.monitor(registry, rules, "productRules"). Never cache a failure: let the loader throw, and Caffeine stores nothing. Behind @Cacheable (7.13), the size and expiry go in spring.cache.caffeine.spec. Each pod has its own cache, so 2 pods can disagree until expiry.

See also. 7.13, 4.08, 18.06, Caching, scheduling and events

18.09 Make startup faster

Then.

  • Boot era: spring.main.lazy-initialization=true, which creates beans on first use, and spring-context-indexer, which precomputed the classpath scan. Lazy initialisation moves startup errors to the first request that needs the bean. The indexer is deprecated.

What goes wrong. payouts-api logs Started PayoutsApplication in 41.2 seconds. Each new pod must start and stay ready for 10 seconds (17.06) before the next begins, so a 2-pod rollout takes about 2 minutes. The CPU limit is 500m, half a core, and startup is mostly CPU: class loading and compiling.

Do this now. Measure first. In main, call app.setApplicationStartup(new BufferingApplicationStartup(2048)) before app.run(args), expose the startup Actuator endpoint, and read each step's time. Move remote cache warming and index builds out (8.20). Give startup enough CPU (17.03). Then use class data sharing (CDS), which saves parsed classes to an archive that later runs map in. A training run with -XX:ArchiveClassesAtExit and -Dspring.context.exit=onRefresh, which exits once the context has started, writes it. Each start then reads it with -XX:SharedArchiveFile, on the same JDK and the jar extracted with -Djarmode=tools. Recent JDKs extend this into an ahead-of-time cache: -XX:AOTCacheOutput writes it and -XX:AOTCache reads it.

See also. 4.09, 17.03, 17.04, 17.06, Packaging and native images

18.10 Load-test a service

Then.

  • Spring era: JMeter test plans, saved as .jmx XML and edited in its desktop GUI, with a thread group of a fixed number of users. JMeter was free and could drive almost any protocol. Its usual thread groups are closed, though: each user waits for its reply before sending again, which is the flaw in the history above.
  • Boot era: Gatling simulations written in Scala, under src/test/scala. Gatling's Java DSL now sits beside the Scala one, so a Java team need not learn Scala.

Recognise it by. .jmx files, jmeter-maven-plugin, src/test/scala classes that extends Simulation, import io.gatling.core.Predef._, and ab -n or wrk lines in a README.

The rookie version.

ScenarioBuilder pay = scenario("pay").exec(http("POST /payouts").post("/payouts")
        .header("Idempotency-Key", "load-test")          // the same key every time
        .body(ElFileBody("payout.json")).asJson());
{
    setUp(pay.injectClosed(constantConcurrentUsers(50).during(Duration.ofMinutes(2))))
            .protocols(http.baseUrl("https://payouts.staging.sorrel.internal"));
}

What goes wrong. The test keeps 50 virtual users busy, each sending a payout and waiting for the reply before sending the next. When Payouts stalls for 2 seconds, the users stall too and send nothing. The tool records 50 slow requests, one per user, while real clients arriving on their own schedule would have kept sending through the stall. It reports a p99 of 180 ms. Production's histogram says 2.1 seconds. This is coordinated omission: the tester slows down with the system and misses the worst moments. The fixed key makes it worse. After the first request, Payouts replays the stored response (9.10), so the test measures the idempotency store. And 2 minutes is too short for pools and garbage collection to show.

Do this now. Use an open model, in which requests arrive at a fixed rate whatever the service does, as real clients do.

  1. Write the test in Gatling, a load-testing tool whose tests are Java classes. Add io.gatling.highcharts:gatling-charts-highcharts in test scope and io.gatling:gatling-maven-plugin, and run it with mvn gatling:test.
  2. Inject at a rate, not a number of users, and send a fresh key per request.
public class PayoutsSimulation extends Simulation {
    ScenarioBuilder pay = scenario("pay").exec(http("POST /payouts").post("/payouts")
            .header("Idempotency-Key", session -> UUID.randomUUID().toString())
            .body(ElFileBody("payout.json")).asJson());
    {
        setUp(pay.injectOpen(constantUsersPerSec(40).during(Duration.ofMinutes(10))))
                .protocols(http.baseUrl("https://payouts.staging.sorrel.internal"));
    }
}
  1. Test a staging copy with production-sized data, and stub the bank gateway, never the real one.
  2. Run for at least 10 minutes, so garbage collection and pools show.
  3. Read p99 from the service's own http.server.requests histogram, and compare it with the tool's figure. If they disagree, believe the service.
  4. Against one pod, raise the rate in steps, with incrementUsersPerSec(10).times(5).eachLevelLasting(Duration.ofMinutes(5)), until p99 breaks the goal. The last rate that met it is one pod's capacity (21.10).

Also seen. k6, scripted in JavaScript, whose constant-arrival-rate executor is the same open model. wrk2, Gil Tene's fork of wrk, which holds a fixed rate with -R and corrects for coordinated omission.

When to break it. A short closed-model run is fine for finding a crash, a leak or a deadlock under concurrency, where nobody reads the percentiles. The cost is that someone will, so label its report.

.NET anchor. NBomber has both models: Simulation.Inject(rate, interval, during) is the open one, and Simulation.KeepConstant(copies, during) the closed one, with the same trap.

See also. 9.10, 14.06, 18.01, 18.03, 21.10, The Yard, chapter 12, Actuator and observability

⚠Review checklist
  • If you see a timing loop in a main method or a test, or System.currentTimeMillis() pairs around a call: the number measures a cold JVM or a wall clock, and code gets rewritten on a guess. See 18.01.
