  • If you see a repository or HTTP call inside a map, forEach or loop over results: one request becomes N+1 calls, and the other side pays for each. See 18.02.
  • If you see maxPoolSize or server.tomcat.threads.max raised with no arithmetic in the comment: the queue moves to the database, and the shared instance's connection quota fills. See 18.03.
  • If you see a publish or update per item in a relay or a backfill: round trips dominate, and backlogs drain slowly. See 18.04.
  • If you see a runbook that restarts pods before taking thread dumps: the evidence is lost, and the incident recurs. See 18.05.
  • If you see a static map or list that is only ever added to: it is a memory leak that ends in OutOfMemoryError. See 18.06.
  • If you see new ObjectMapper() inside a method that runs per request: every call rebuilds what a shared mapper caches, and CPU goes on it. See 18.07.
  • If you see a cache with no maximumSize, or expireAfterAccess on data that changes: hot entries go stale for ever and cold ones fill the heap. See 18.08.
  • If you see a load test with a fixed number of users that each wait for a reply: it hides stalls and reports a p99 far below production's. See 18.10.

Part IV · The how-to19. Upgrades and dependency hygiene#

A Java service is never finished, because everything under it keeps moving: the JDK, Spring Boot, and every library Boot does not manage. This part covers the upgrades a developer actually does: the javax to jakarta rename, Boot minors one at a time, mechanical changes with OpenRewrite, the move from Boot 3.5 to Boot 4, a new Java version, and the steady work of keeping dependencies current. It also shows the hand-picked version lists and upgrade checklists you will find in older services, and what replaced them.

★What a veteran knows
  • Changing the version number is the first half of an upgrade. The second half is finding out what that number changed, and most of it is not in the compiler's output.
  • Upgrade on a calendar, not in a crisis. Boot releases a minor every six months, in May and November, and a team that takes each one only ever does small upgrades.
  • The latest patch of the version you are on is the safest step you will ever take. Take it first, and on its own.
  • Keep the machine's changes and yours in separate commits. A reviewer can trust a recipe's diff and read yours, but not both at once.
  • Your configuration is not all in the repository. ConfigMaps, Helm values and environment variables need the same renames, and no tool you run on the code can see them.
  • Every library you add is a library you will one day upgrade or replace. Count that cost on the day you add it.
◷How we got hereOn 3 May 2019 Mike Milinkovich, executive director of the Eclipse Foundation, posted the result of a long…

On 3 May 2019 Mike Milinkovich, executive director of the Eclipse Foundation, posted the result of a long negotiation. Oracle had handed Java EE, the enterprise APIs behind servlets (Java's standard for code that answers HTTP requests), validation and persistence, to the Foundation, where it became Jakarta EE. The code had moved. The package names had not. "Following many months of good-faith negotiations," he wrote, the Foundation and Oracle "have been unable to agree" on terms for Oracle's Java trademarks. The javax namespace "may be used 'as is' only". Any change had to happen "under a new namespace, such as jakarta". He called it "the best outcome we could mutually achieve for the community." So Jakarta EE 9, released on 8 December 2020, changed nothing but the names. Spring Framework 6.0 went GA on 16 November 2022 on the new names, and Spring Boot 3.0 followed on 24 November. That is why a library built for Boot 2 can sit in a Boot 3 service and do nothing at all.

19.01 Move from javax to jakarta

Then.

  • J2EE era: Servlets and EJBs (Enterprise JavaBeans, components an application server ran) written against javax.servlet and javax.ejb, and wired together in web.xml. These were the Java EE APIs, and the javax prefix marked them as official Java extensions.
  • Spring era: Spring code used the same APIs: javax.inject.Inject, javax.annotation.PostConstruct, javax.validation.constraints.NotNull, and javax.persistence.Entity for JPA.
  • Boot era: Boot 1 and Boot 2 kept the javax names.
import javax.annotation.PostConstruct;
import javax.servlet.http.HttpServletRequest;
import javax.validation.constraints.NotBlank;

public class PayoutRequest {
    @NotBlank
    private String claimId;
}

The javax names were right for their time: they were the official names. The rename was a legal outcome, not a technical one, so the move is mechanical in your own code and hard only in your dependencies.

Recognise it by. import javax.servlet., javax.validation., javax.annotation.PostConstruct and javax.persistence. in the code. In the POM, Maven's csproj, javax.servlet:javax.servlet-api and javax.validation:validation-api. Also a META-INF/spring.factories file with an EnableAutoConfiguration key. Auto-configuration is the setup a library's jar applies by itself when it is on the classpath. The file is not part of the rename, but Boot 3.0 stopped reading auto-configuration from it, so you meet both in one upgrade.

The rookie version.

# Boot 3 needs jakarta, so rename everything
find src -name '*.java' \
  | xargs sed -i '' 's/import javax\./import jakarta./'
./mvnw verify   # 1 compile error, fixed by hand, then green

What goes wrong. The rename hits the JDK's own packages too. javax.crypto.Cipher in the field-encryption code becomes jakarta.crypto.Cipher, which does not exist. The compiler catches that one. It cannot catch the jars. payouts-api also depends on sorrel-audit-filter 2.3, an internal library that records who called each endpoint. Built for Boot 2, its filter implements javax.servlet.Filter, and it brings the old servlet API jar with it, so everything still compiles. Boot 3 runs Tomcat on jakarta.servlet, and to Tomcat a javax.servlet.Filter is just an object. Its auto-configuration is listed only in spring.factories, so Boot 3 never registers the filter at all. Nothing fails. For 9 days no audit record is written for 41,000 payout calls, until the audit team asks.

Do this now.

  1. List every javax EE artifact in the build, direct and transitive, with the Maven wrapper script in the repository: ./mvnw dependency:tree -Dincludes=javax.servlet,javax.validation,javax.annotation. A transitive dependency is one brought in by another library, not named in your POM.
  2. Upgrade the library that brings each one to a version built for Jakarta EE 9 or later. Some libraries publish a new artifact ID for it, and some a jakarta classifier, a suffix that picks a second build of the same artifact. An internal library needs a new release from its owners first, on jakarta imports and with its auto-configuration listed in META-INF/spring/org.springframework.boot.autoconfigure.AutoConfiguration.imports (4.11).
  3. Rename the imports in your own code with OpenRewrite, a tool that edits code by its types (19.03). Its recipe org.openrewrite.java.migrate.jakarta.JavaxMigrationToJakarta knows which packages moved.
  4. Leave the JDK's javax packages alone. javax.crypto, javax.net.ssl, javax.sql, javax.naming and javax.management belong to Java SE and never moved.
  5. Search strings as well as imports: web.xml, files under META-INF/services/, and configuration keys that start javax.persistence..
  6. Ban the old artifacts with the enforcer, the plugin that fails the build when a rule breaks (1.09). Put this execution beside 1.09's in the parent POM.
<execution>
  <id>ban-javax-ee</id>
  <goals><goal>enforce</goal></goals>
  <configuration>
    <rules>
      <bannedDependencies>
        <excludes>
          <exclude>javax.servlet:*</exclude>
          <exclude>javax.validation:*</exclude>
          <exclude>javax.annotation:javax.annotation-api</exclude>
        </excludes>
      </bannedDependencies>
    </rules>
  </configuration>
</execution>

javax.annotation.Nullable comes from a different jar, JSR 305's com.google.code.findbugs:jsr305. It was never part of Java EE, and it has no jakarta version. Replace it with JSpecify's org.jspecify.annotations.Nullable when you next touch the file (19.04).

Also seen. The Eclipse Transformer rewrites javax to jakarta inside compiled jars. It is a stopgap for a library whose source you cannot change, and you then own a modified jar. IntelliJ IDEA Ultimate's Refactor, Migrate Packages and Classes does the source rename in the IDE.

When to break it. You cannot move half a service: one deployable uses one servlet API. A library you cannot replace yet is a reason to stay on Boot 2.7 a little longer, not to mix the two. Staying costs you every fix since, so write down the date you will leave.

.NET anchor. The nearest thing is the move from System.Web to ASP.NET Core's Microsoft.AspNetCore namespaces. That was a rewrite of the framework, and this is only a rename. Your code changes little, but every compiled dependency must be rebuilt. A package built for System.Web fails loudly in ASP.NET Core. A jar built for javax may load and do nothing.

See also. 19.03, 19.07, 1.03, 1.09, 4.11, The Yard, chapter 3, Appendix C: The Java you'll inherit

19.02 Upgrade Spring Boot one minor version at a time

Then.

  • Spring era: Teams set a version for a dozen Spring jars by hand, then chose Hibernate (the ORM), Jackson (the JSON library) and the rest to match. A BOM (bill of materials) is a POM that lists tested versions for many libraries, and importing it sets all of them. The Spring IO Platform BOM, io.spring.platform:platform-bom, later offered one. Any upgrade meant re-testing the whole combination, so teams did it rarely.
  • Boot era: Boot's BOM made the upgrade one line, and teams treated it as one line. Many services sat on one Boot version for years and then jumped several at once.
<properties>
  <spring.version>4.3.25.RELEASE</spring.version>
  <jackson.version>2.9.10</jackson.version>
  <hibernate.version>5.2.18.Final</hibernate.version>
</properties>

Hand-picked versions were right when nobody published a tested set. Rare, large jumps were right when an upgrade cost weeks of manual testing. Boot's twice-yearly releases and a test suite that runs in minutes make small, frequent steps cheaper.

Recognise it by. A <spring.version> property, and Spring versions ending .RELEASE. Also io.spring.platform:platform-bom, and a POM history in which spring-boot.version changes once every few years.

The rookie version.

 <properties>
-  <spring-boot.version>3.1.5</spring-boot.version>
+  <spring-boot.version>3.5.16</spring-boot.version>
 </properties>

What goes wrong. A Boot version has three parts. In 3.5.16, 3 is the major, 5 the minor and 16 the patch. This pull request brings four minors at once: 3.2, 3.3, 3.4 and 3.5. The build shows 37 new compile warnings and 6 failing tests, and nobody can say which minor caused which. After the merge, a rolling deploy of 2 pods takes 70 seconds instead of 25. Boot 3.4 turned on graceful shutdown by default. On SIGTERM, the signal Kubernetes sends to stop a pod, the server stops taking new requests and waits for the ones in flight, up to spring.lifecycle.timeout-per-shutdown-phase, 30 seconds by default. Each old pod now waits about 22 seconds for its slowest bank call, and the pods are replaced one at a time. That is a good change. Finding it took 2 days, because it was one of 40 changes in one pull request.

Do this now.

  1. Move to the latest patch of the minor you are on. Patches carry bug and security fixes, so this step is cheap and keeps them apart from the rest.
  2. Clear the deprecation warnings. A deprecation is the library's notice that an API will be removed in a later release. Turn the warnings on with <showDeprecation>true</showDeprecation> in the <configuration> of maven-compiler-plugin, and fix every one in Spring's packages.
  3. Read the release notes for the next minor only (19.08). Note each changed default and each renamed property.
  4. Add spring-boot-properties-migrator to the application module's dependencies, for this step only. At startup it logs every property that was renamed or removed, and applies the new name for you while it is present.
  5. Change the version to the next minor's latest patch. Build, run every test, and deploy to a test environment.
  6. Read the migrator's log in that environment, where the real configuration lives. Rename the properties, then remove the migrator.
  7. Repeat for the next minor. One pull request per minor.
<dependency>
  <groupId>org.springframework.boot</groupId>
  <artifactId>spring-boot-properties-migrator</artifactId>
  <scope>runtime</scope>
</dependency>

The calendar matters as much as the method. Boot 3.5's open-source support ended on 30 June 2026. A team that takes each minor as it comes does 2 small upgrades a year and never meets that date unprepared.

Also seen. Skipping minors on a small service with strong tests and few integrations. It often works, and when it fails you are back to bisecting. Some teams let a bot, GitHub's Dependabot or the similar Renovate, propose each Boot patch (19.06).

When to break it. Security fixes do not wait. If a vulnerability is fixed only in a newer minor, make the jump in one pull request. Read every set of release notes in between before you merge. The cost is a bigger review and a bigger rollback.

.NET anchor. This is like moving from .NET 6 to 7 to 8 instead of straight to 8, with each step's "Breaking changes" page read in turn. .NET ships one major a year, and Boot ships a minor every six months. A Boot minor can change a default, as a .NET major does.

See also. 19.04, 19.06, 19.08, 1.07, 17.05, The Yard, chapter 3, Migrating Spring Boot 3 to 4

19.03 Use OpenRewrite for mechanical migrations

Then.

  • Boot era: An upgrade checklist on the wiki, applied by hand with the IDE's find and replace, one service at a time. Each team repeated the work and made its own mistakes.
  • Boot era: sed across the repository for renames, as in the rookie version of 19.01. It is fast, and it cannot tell a type from a comment or a string.
UPGRADE-BOOT-3.md
1. Replace WebSecurityConfigurerAdapter with a SecurityFilterChain bean
2. Rename spring.redis.* to spring.data.redis.*
3. Replace javax.* imports (but not javax.crypto)

Hand migration was right before there was a tool that understood Java types well enough to trust. It does not scale to forty services, and the checklist is only as good as whoever wrote it.

Recognise it by. UPGRADE-*.md files in old repositories. In newer ones, a rewrite.yml in the repository root, org.openrewrite.maven:rewrite-maven-plugin in a POM, and commits titled "Apply recipe".

The rookie version.

commit 9f1c2e0  "Boot upgrade"
    OpenRewrite upgrade recipe (latest), build fixes,
    and the ledger retry change from PAY-1182
    212 files changed, 1,604 insertions(+), 1,577 deletions(-)

What goes wrong. The reviewer cannot tell the machine's changes from the people's. 209 files are the recipe's work, and safe. 3 are hand edits, and one raises the retry count on the ledger call from 2 to 5. Nobody reads it, because it sits inside a 212-file diff. The recipe also ran with whatever recipe version was newest that day. When the branch was rebased and the recipe run again, the diff came out 19 files different. And the recipe changed application.yml, but not the Kubernetes ConfigMap that overrides it, which lives in another repository.

Do this now.

OpenRewrite is an open-source tool that edits source code by applying recipes, named sets of changes. It parses the code into a tree with full type information. So it changes javax.servlet.Filter where it is a type, and leaves a comment that mentions it alone. It also edits YAML, properties files and the POM. The engine is Apache-licensed. The Spring and Java recipe modules use the Moderne Source Available License, which lets you run them on your own code at no cost.

  1. Start from a clean branch with every test green.
  2. Add the plugin to the root POM's <build><plugins>, as below, with both versions pinned in <properties>, so the same recipe gives the same diff tomorrow. Spring recipes live in org.openrewrite.recipe:rewrite-spring. Java and Jakarta recipes live in org.openrewrite.recipe:rewrite-migrate-java.
  3. Run ./mvnw rewrite:discover to list the recipes the plugin can see.
  4. Run ./mvnw rewrite:dryRun. It writes a patch file under target/rewrite/ and changes nothing. Read the patch.
  5. Run ./mvnw rewrite:run, and commit the result on its own. Put the recipe name and version in the message.
  6. Build and test. Make your hand fixes in separate commits.
<plugin>
  <groupId>org.openrewrite.maven</groupId><artifactId>rewrite-maven-plugin</artifactId>
  <version>${rewrite-maven-plugin.version}</version>
  <configuration>
    <activeRecipes>
      <recipe>org.openrewrite.java.spring.boot3.UpgradeSpringBoot_3_5</recipe>
    </activeRecipes>
  </configuration>
  <dependencies>
    <dependency>
      <groupId>org.openrewrite.recipe</groupId><artifactId>rewrite-spring</artifactId>
      <version>${rewrite-spring.version}</version>
    </dependency>
  </dependencies>
</plugin>

The plugin has no <executions>, so it never runs in the normal build, only when you call one of its goals. Name the recipe for the next minor only. Each Boot recipe runs the one before it first, so on a 3.1 service UpgradeSpringBoot_3_5 makes the changes of four minors at once, which 19.02 warns against. It also moves the Boot version itself.

Know what a recipe cannot do. It does not see configuration outside the repository. It does not know your behaviour changed, as when graceful shutdown became the default (19.02). It cannot upgrade a library that has no recipe. Treat its output as a first draft that compiles, not a finished upgrade.

Also seen. IntelliJ's migration refactorings, for one service at a time. Moderne, the company that leads OpenRewrite, sells a platform that runs recipes across many repositories at once. Some organisations write their own recipe in rewrite.yml, composing built-in ones such as org.openrewrite.java.ChangeType and org.openrewrite.java.ChangePackage.

When to break it. A change across 3 files is quicker by hand than by learning a recipe. Writing your own recipe pays off only when the same change must land in many services, such as a renamed class in a shared Sorrel library. Then it pays off every time.

.NET anchor. The .NET Upgrade Assistant, now deprecated in favour of the GitHub Copilot modernization agent, and Roslyn code fixes do the same job, and dotnet format with analysers is the daily version. OpenRewrite reaches further across files. One recipe changes Java, YAML, properties and the POM together, which Roslyn's code fixes do not.

See also. 19.01, 19.02, 19.04, 2.19, 15.05, The Yard, chapter 3, Migrating Spring Boot 3 to 4

19.04 Upgrade from Boot 3.5 to Boot 4

Then.

  • Modern: Boot 3 idioms that Boot 4 removes, renames or moves. Each was right on Boot 3, and all still compile on 3.5.
import com.fasterxml.jackson.databind.ObjectMapper;
import org.springframework.boot.test.mock.mockito.MockBean;
import org.springframework.lang.Nullable;
import org.springframework.retry.annotation.Retryable;
import org.springframework.boot.actuate.health.HealthIndicator;

@MockBean swapped a bean, an object Spring creates and injects, for a Mockito mock in a test. It was Boot's way until Framework 6.2 added @MockitoBean. Spring Retry was the retry library until Framework 7 put @Retryable in core and the Spring Retry project was archived. Jackson 2's packages were the only Jackson until Jackson 3 moved them.

Recognise it by. spring-boot-starter-web, @MockBean, @SpyBean, com.fasterxml.jackson, spring.data.mongodb.uri, org.springframework.lang.Nullable, ListenableFuture, org.springframework.retry, resilience4j-spring-boot3, Spring Cloud AWS 3.x, and org.testcontainers:mongodb. A starter is a Boot dependency that brings the libraries for one job with their auto-configuration.

The rookie version.

 <properties>
-  <spring-boot.version>3.5.16</spring-boot.version>
+  <spring-boot.version>4.1.2</spring-boot.version>
 </properties>

What goes wrong. The compiler and the tests find the loud problems. @MockBean is gone, test slices such as @WebMvcTest, which start one layer of the application, have moved package, and Spring Cloud AWS 3.4 is built for Boot 3.5. The rookie fixes those. The quiet problem is outside the build. Boot 4 renamed the driver-level MongoDB properties from spring.data.mongodb.* to spring.mongodb.*. The test profile was updated. The payouts ConfigMap still sets SPRING_DATA_MONGODB_URI, and on Boot 4 nothing reads it. The 2 new pods start and pass readiness, because Boot does not add the Mongo health check to the readiness group by default. Every payout request then tries a MongoDB on the pod's own address, and 184 requests fail with a 500 before the rollback at 16:40. The upgrade was also two hops in one: 3.5 to 4.0 is the major, and 4.0 to 4.1 is a minor on top.

Do this now.

A major version removes what the minors before it deprecated, and moves the baseline under every library. Boot 4.0 went GA on 20 November 2025. It requires Java 17 or later, Spring Framework 7, Jakarta EE 11 and Servlet 6.1. It drops the Undertow web server, so use Tomcat or Jetty.

  1. On 3.5, take the latest patch, 3.5.16, and clear every deprecation. @MockitoBean and @MockitoSpyBean arrived with Framework 6.2, which Boot 3.4 brought.
  2. Read the Spring Boot 4.0 Migration Guide on the Boot wiki. Turn it into a checklist for this service.
  3. Check that every library that plugs into Boot has a Boot 4 line. For Payouts that means Spring Cloud AWS 4.x for SQS and SNS, resilience4j-spring-boot4 (Resilience4j is Java's Polly) and Testcontainers 2.x. If one has none, stop here.
  4. Run the mechanical changes with OpenRewrite in their own commit (19.03). Recent rewrite-spring releases carry org.openrewrite.java.spring.boot4.UpgradeSpringBoot_4_0, which also runs the 3.5 recipe first.
  5. Move to the latest 4.0 patch, 4.0.9 on 22 October 2026. Work through the table below.
  6. Run spring-boot-properties-migrator in a test environment with the real ConfigMaps and secrets. Rename what it reports, in every repository that sets it.
  7. Ship 4.0. Then take 4.1 as an ordinary minor (19.02), once your integrations name it. Spring Cloud AWS's compatibility table names Boot 4.0.x only.
On Boot 3.5 On Boot 4
spring-boot-starter-web spring-boot-starter-webmvc (the old name is deprecated)
@MockBean, @SpyBean @MockitoBean, @MockitoSpyBean (the old ones are removed)
Jackson 2, com.fasterxml.jackson Jackson 3, tools.jackson, and @JsonComponent becomes @JacksonComponent
Jackson2ObjectMapperBuilderCustomizer JsonMapperBuilderCustomizer
spring.data.mongodb.uri spring.mongodb.uri
@WebMvcTest in ...test.autoconfigure.web.servlet org.springframework.boot.webmvc.test.autoconfigure
@DataMongoTest in ...test.autoconfigure.data.mongo org.springframework.boot.data.mongodb.test.autoconfigure
TestRestTemplate from @SpringBootTest add @AutoConfigureTestRestTemplate, or use RestTestClient
org.springframework.boot.actuate.health org.springframework.boot.health.contributor
org.springframework.lang.Nullable org.jspecify.annotations.Nullable
Spring Retry @Retryable org.springframework.resilience.annotation.Retryable, with @EnableResilientMethods
ListenableFuture CompletableFuture
JUnit 5 JUnit 6 (Boot manages 6.0.x)
Testcontainers org.testcontainers:mongodb org.testcontainers:testcontainers-mongodb, and withReplicaSet() for transactions
management.otlp.tracing.endpoint management.opentelemetry.tracing.export.otlp.endpoint

Watch the count when you leave Spring Retry. Its maxAttempts counted the first call. Core's maxRetries does not: total attempts are 1 plus maxRetries. Copy the old PolicyClient's maxAttempts = 3 (7.04) across as maxRetries = 3, and every failing policy lookup is made 4 times, not 3. Use maxRetries = 2. An annotation with no count changes too, because core's default is 3 retries, 4 calls.

Also seen. Staying on 3.5 with commercial support, which runs to 30 June 2032. Every month the libraries' new releases target Boot 4, and the gap grows.

When to break it. A service with few Boot integrations can go from 3.5 to 4.1 in one step, if every integration names 4.1. Do not stay long on 4.0: its open-source support ends on 31 December 2026, and 4.1's on 31 July 2027.

.NET anchor. This is like moving from .NET 8 to 10 while your web, test and JSON packages all change at once. Jackson 3 is the sharpest part. Picture Newtonsoft.Json changing its namespace, so that every custom JsonConverter needs a new using.

See also. 19.02, 19.03, 19.08, 16.06, 7.04, 8.11, The Yard, chapter 3, Migrating Spring Boot 3 to 4

19.05 Upgrade the Java version

The rookie version.

<!-- pom.xml, the parent of payouts-api and payouts-domain -->
<properties>
  <maven.compiler.release>25</maven.compiler.release>  <!-- was 21 -->
</properties>

What goes wrong. maven.compiler.release tells the compiler which Java version's class files to write (1.08). The developer's laptop and CI both run JDK 25, so the build is green. The image still runs Java 21. Both pods fail at startup with UnsupportedClassVersionError, naming "class file version 69.0". A JVM refuses class files newer than itself. Nothing in the pull request touched the image, so nobody had looked at it.

Do this now. The runtime moves first, and the compiler last.

  1. Move from one LTS (long-term support) release to the next: 17, 21, 25. These are the versions vendors keep patching for years.
  2. Change the runtime: the JDK in CI, then the image's base (17.01). Run the existing jar on it. Older class files run on newer JVMs, so nothing you wrote changes yet.
  3. Upgrade the tools that read or write bytecode: Mockito; Byte Buddy, which Mockito uses to generate mock classes; JaCoCo, which measures coverage; and Lombok, a compiler plugin that writes getters and constructors, if it is still there. Old versions fail with errors such as "Unsupported class file major version 69". Boot manages most of them, so the latest Boot patch often brings versions that know the new JDK.
  4. Look for libraries that use JDK internals. ./mvnw dependency:copy-dependencies copies every jar into target/dependency. Then jdeps --jdk-internals --multi-release 25 target/dependency/*.jar lists direct uses of internal classes, which newer JDKs refuse. It cannot see access by reflection, which fails at runtime with InaccessibleObjectException, so run the whole test suite on the new JDK as well. Upgrade an offending library rather than adding --add-opens, the JVM flag that reopens a JDK package to reflection.
  5. When every image runs the new JDK, raise maven.compiler.release in the parent (1.08), in its own pull request.
  6. Adopt the new language features in later pull requests, a file at a time (2.19).

Also seen. The releases between LTS versions, such as 24. Each gets updates for a short time only, so a team that takes them upgrades far more often. It suits a service that needs a feature early. The Maven toolchains plugin, maven-toolchains-plugin, compiles and tests with a JDK other than the one running Maven. Choose it for a library that must be tested on two Java versions.

When to break it. A shared library that services on older JDKs depend on keeps the lower release, even after its own build moves to the new JDK. A release of 21 built on JDK 25 runs on both. Raise it when the last consumer's image has moved. The cost is that the library cannot use the new language features or APIs until then.

.NET anchor. <TargetFramework> is the nearest thing, and the rule is the same: an app built for net10.0 will not start on an image with only the .NET 8 runtime. Java is looser in the other direction. A Java 21 jar runs on a JDK 25 image with no setting, where a net8.0 app needs <RollForward>Major</RollForward> to run on .NET 10 alone.

See also. 1.08, 2.19, 17.01, 19.03, Getting a JDK, and the release train, Appendix A: Java 9 to 25

19.06 Keep dependencies current without breaking things

The rookie version.

dependabot[bot]  Bump com.fasterxml.jackson.core:jackson-databind in /payouts-api
                 14 checks passed, approved, merged 3 minutes after opening
dependabot[bot]  Bump org.mongodb:mongodb-driver-sync in /payouts-domain
                 14 checks passed, approved, merged 4 minutes after opening
... and 21 more this week

What goes wrong. Dependabot, GitHub's dependency bot, opens 23 pull requests a week across payouts-api and payouts-domain. The team merges anything green. Both libraries above are in Boot's BOM. The bot could bump them only because someone once wrote a <version> on each in a module. After the merge those modules sit outside the set Boot tested, and they stay there through the next Boot upgrade, which no longer moves them. Then the team stops reading the bot at all, and 61 pull requests are open when a real security fix arrives.

Do this now.

  1. Leave the version off every dependency Boot's BOM manages. The bot can only change versions written in a POM, so for those it proposes the Boot version alone, which you take a minor at a time (19.02).
  2. Where you must override a managed version (1.02), list it under ignore in .github/dependabot.yml, so a person decides when it moves.
  3. Group the rest. A groups entry with update-types of minor and patch turns a week of bumps into one pull request. One is reviewable. Twenty-three are not.
  4. Each month, run ./mvnw versions:display-dependency-updates and versions:display-plugin-updates. They list every newer version, including the ignored ones, so nothing is forgotten.
  5. Keep the enforcer's requireUpperBoundDeps rule on (1.09). An upgrade that leaves an older version winning then fails the build.
  6. Remove what you do not use. dependency:analyze lists declared but unused dependencies.
  7. Security findings jump the queue (15.12).
# .github/dependabot.yml
version: 2
updates:
  - package-ecosystem: maven
    directory: /
    schedule: { interval: weekly }
    ignore:
      - dependency-name: "com.fasterxml.jackson.core:jackson-databind"  # overridden, see 1.02
    groups:
      weekly:
        patterns: ["*"]
        update-types: ["minor", "patch"]

Major versions still arrive one pull request each, because they need reading.

Also seen. Renovate, a bot like Dependabot with more rules. Its packageRules group updates, and automerge merges patches once the build passes. Choose it when the team trusts its tests enough to stop reviewing patches. Some repositories have no bot, and a person reads the monthly versions report. It is slower, and it is rarely ignored.

When to break it. A security fix in a managed library that Boot has not shipped yet. Override that one version on purpose (1.02), with a comment naming the CVE and the Boot patch expected to make the override unnecessary. Remove it when that patch arrives. The cost is an override someone has to remember.

.NET anchor. dotnet list package --outdated is versions:display-dependency-updates, and Dependabot works the same way on NuGet. The difference is the BOM. Central Package Management's Directory.Packages.props puts versions in one place, but you choose them. With Boot, someone else has tested the set, and most versions move together when one property changes.

See also. 1.02, 1.09, 1.10, 15.12, 19.02, The Yard, chapter 9, The Yard, chapter 10, Maven vs csproj

19.07 Replace a library that has reached end of life

What goes wrong. payouts-api still uses the AWS SDK for Java v1, com.amazonaws, for one S3 call. v1 reached end of support on 31 December 2025 and gets no more releases. A scanner flags a vulnerability in a jar v1 depends on, and there is no v1 release to take. The fix becomes an unplanned migration in the week of a release.

Do this now.

  • Check a library's README and releases page before you rely on it. Download counts tell you nothing about whether anyone still fixes it.
  • Know the common ones you will inherit:
Finished Replace with
Hystrix (maintenance mode since 1.5.18, 2018) Resilience4j
Spring Cloud Sleuth (does not work with Boot 3) Micrometer Tracing
Spring Retry (archived 27 July 2026) Framework 7's @Retryable
AWS SDK v1 (end of support 31 December 2025) AWS SDK v2, software.amazon.awssdk
Log4j 1.x (end of life August 2015) Logback or Log4j2, through SLF4J
Joda-Time java.time
RestTemplate (the Framework 7 reference declares it deprecated) RestClient
Spring Cloud AWS 2.x (no release since February 2023) Spring Cloud AWS 3.4 or 4.x
  • Put the library behind your own class first, as LedgerClient hides the HTTP client, so the swap touches one place.
  • Replace it in its own pull request, before the upgrade that would force it.
  • When it is gone, ban it with the enforcer's bannedDependencies (19.01).

See also. 19.01, 1.09, 7.05, 12.12, 13.02, Appendix I: Your library, translated, Appendix C: The Java you'll inherit

19.08 Read the release notes that matter

What goes wrong. Boot 3.4's release notes deprecated @MockBean and @SpyBean in favour of @MockitoBean and @MockitoSpyBean. The team read the new features and skipped the deprecations. The tests kept passing with warnings. Boot 4 removed the old annotations, and 140 test classes failed to compile in one afternoon.

Do this now.

  • Each Boot minor has a release notes page on the Spring Boot wiki on GitHub, such as "Spring Boot 3.4 Release Notes". A major also has a migration guide. Patch releases are listed on the GitHub releases page.
  • Read the upgrade section first, then the deprecations, then the new features.
  • Search each page for "default", "removed", "renamed", "deprecated" and "requires". Every match becomes a line on the upgrade checklist.
  • At a major, read the notes of the projects you use directly: Framework, Security, Data MongoDB, Jackson, Testcontainers, Spring Cloud AWS.
  • For a patch, read the security fixes and the modules you use.

.NET anchor. Microsoft's "Breaking changes in .NET" pages are the migration guide. A Boot minor's notes are "What's new" and its breaking changes on one page.

See also. 19.02, 19.04, 17.05, The Yard, chapter 3, Migrating Spring Boot 3 to 4

⚠Review checklist
  • If you see sed or find and replace turning javax. into jakarta.: it renames JDK packages too, and misses the jars that still use javax. See 19.01.
  • If you see javax.servlet or javax.validation in the dependency tree of a Boot 3 service: a library built for Boot 2 is in the build, and it may load and do nothing. See 19.01.
  • If you see a Boot version change that skips minors: every minor's behaviour changes arrive together, and nobody can tell which caused what. See 19.02.
  • If you see spring-boot-properties-migrator merged to the main branch: it was for the upgrade, and while present it hides renamed properties instead of fixing them. See 19.02.
  • If you see recipe output and hand edits in one commit: the reviewer cannot find the human change. See 19.03.
  • If you see an OpenRewrite run with unpinned recipe versions: the same command gives a different diff tomorrow. See 19.03.
  • If you see an OpenRewrite Boot recipe several minors ahead of the service's version: it makes every minor's changes in one commit. See 19.03.
  • If you see a Boot 4 upgrade with no change to ConfigMaps or Helm values: renamed properties set outside the repository are silently ignored. See 19.04.
  • If you see resilience4j-spring-boot3 or Spring Cloud AWS 3.x in a Boot 4 build: they are built for Boot 3.5. See 19.04.
  • If you see a Spring Retry maxAttempts copied unchanged into maxRetries: every failing call is made once more. See 19.04.
  • If you see maven.compiler.release raised before the image's JDK: the pods fail at startup with UnsupportedClassVersionError. See 19.05.
  • If you see a bot's pull request that bumps a <version> written on a library Boot manages: that version overrides Boot's tested set and survives the next Boot upgrade. See 19.06.
  • If you see com.amazonaws, com.netflix.hystrix, Spring Cloud Sleuth or org.springframework.retry added in a pull request: it is a library nobody fixes any more. See 19.07.
  • If you see @SuppressWarnings("deprecation") on a Spring API: the removal will arrive later, all at once. See 19.08.

Part IV · The how-to20. Evolving a live system#

Payouts never stops. Claims are paid at 03:00 and on bank holidays, and during a deploy 2 pods keep serving while a third, running the next version, starts. This part is about changing that system while it runs: an API, an event, a stored document, a whole service. It shows the one pattern under almost all of it, expand and then contract, and the order of deploys that makes each step safe to roll back. It covers feature flags, backfills, reprocessing a dead-letter queue after a fix, and splitting and merging services. It also shows the older ways you will find written into runbooks: the cut-over weekend, the maintenance window and the shared database.

★What a veteran knows
  • During a rolling deploy the old version and the new one serve at the same time. Every change must be safe with both running, for minutes at least.
  • Readers change before writers. Deploy the code that can read the new shape, then the code that writes it, never both in one release.
  • The release you might roll back to is part of the design. If it cannot read what the new release writes, you have no rollback, only a roll forward.
  • Remove the old shape only on evidence. A count of old-shape documents, old-version events or old-field callers at zero is a reason. A date in a ticket is not.
  • Data outlives code. A message sits in a queue for days and a document for years, so the oldest shape still stored decides what a reader must accept.
  • A flag, a shim (a small adapter from the old shape to the new) or a dual write that is never removed becomes the system. Put the removal on the board when you add it.
◷How we got hereOn a holiday in the rainforests of the Queensland coast in 2001, Martin Fowler saw the huge strangler figs.

On a holiday in the rainforests of the Queensland coast in 2001, Martin Fowler saw the huge strangler figs. They "seed in the upper branches of a tree and gradually work their way down the tree until they root in the soil", killing the host. On 29 June 2004 Fowler wrote it up on his bliki as "StranglerApplication". The metaphor, he wrote, was "a way of doing a rewrite of an important system": "gradually create a new system around the edges of the old." His colleague Chris Stevenson had just done this on a real project, and with Andy Pols had presented a paper on it at XP 2004. Fowler's case was plain: "The most important reason to consider a strangler fig application over a cut-over rewrite is reduced risk." On 29 April 2019 he renamed the page "Strangler Fig Application", because readers had forgotten the botany and heard only the violence. He rewrote it in 2024 and ended: "Fortunately the new title strangled the old one."

20.01 Change an API without breaking clients by expanding, then contracting

Then.

  • J2EE era: a SOAP service described by a WSDL file. Each client generated stubs from it with wsimport, so any change meant regenerating every client. Teams batched changes into a new contract, PayoutServiceV2.wsdl, and ran both.
  • Spring era: the coordinated release. The provider and every client changed together and went live in one maintenance window on a Saturday night, with a runbook and a rollback plan for each system.
Release 2014-11: Sat 22:00 stop claims-portal, finance-export
                 22:15 deploy payouts 4.2, portal 7.1, export 3.9
                 23:30 smoke test, restart, sign-off

The window was right when there were 3 systems, one operations team and no 24-hour traffic. It stopped working when services deployed several times a day, owned by different teams, with traffic that never paused.

Recognise it by. jaxws-maven-plugin and wsimport in a client's POM (its Maven build file, Java's .csproj), versioned .wsdl files, a shared payouts-client jar (a packaged Java library, like a NuGet package's assembly) whose version is bumped in every consumer at once, and a release runbook listing several services.

The rookie version.

// One pull request: rename payeeName to claimantName in the response.
public record PayoutResponse(String id, String claimantName, MoneyJson amount,
                             PayoutStatus status) { }
// The same PR updates the claims portal's client, which lives in the same repo.
// PR description: "All clients updated."

What goes wrong. The pull request changes the provider and its one known client together. It deploys as a rolling update, in which Kubernetes replaces the pods one at a time. For 4 minutes 1 pod returns payeeName and the other returns claimantName. The portal, also mid-deploy, gets whichever pod answers, and 31 letters print with no name. The finance export, which nobody had listed, reads payeeName into its nightly file. At 02:00 it writes 1,906 empty names, one of them on a payout of £1,240.50.

Do this now. Expand and contract, also called parallel change, makes a breaking change as three releases that are each safe alone. 5.10 lists which JSON changes break clients. This entry is about the order.

  1. Expand. Release the provider with both shapes. Responses carry payeeName and claimantName with the same value. Requests accept either. @JsonAlias (5.10), Jackson's annotation for an extra accepted JSON name, is the shortest way, but it hides which name a client sent. To count old-name callers in step 3, take payeeName as its own deprecated component of the request record, copy it across when claimantName is absent, and increment a counter when it is set. Nothing else changes, and this release can be rolled back freely.
  2. Migrate. Each client moves to the new name on its own schedule. Mark the old field deprecated in the OpenAPI document (5.15) and tell the client teams the date you want.
  3. Measure. You cannot see which response fields a client reads. You can see who calls. Count calls with a counter tagged by the caller's identity from its OAuth2 token (15.01, 14.02), and watch the old-field counter from step 1. Run each consumer's contract test in your build (16.16): a test the consumer writes of the requests it sends and the fields it reads. A consumer whose contract still names payeeName fails the contract step, and the build tells you before production does.
  4. Contract. Remove the old field only when the request count is zero and no contract names it. This is the third release, and its rollback target is the expand release, which is still compatible.
public record PayoutResponse(String id,
        @Deprecated String payeeName,      // remove after every contract drops it
        String claimantName, MoneyJson amount, PayoutStatus status) {
    static PayoutResponse from(Payout p) {
        return new PayoutResponse(p.id(), p.claimantName(), p.claimantName(),
                MoneyJson.of(p.amount()), p.status());
    }
}

Keep each step in its own deploy. Two steps in one release bring back the 4-minute window above.

Also seen. A new API version (5.09), when a resource changes meaning and not only shape. A translation layer at a gateway that rewrites old requests into new ones. It works, but it is code that nobody owns and that outlives everyone who understood it.

When to break it. A field with one client, in the same team, that deploys after the provider can change in two releases, not three. The cost is that the order of those deploys is now a manual rule.

.NET anchor. The same sequence applies to an ASP.NET Core API. [Obsolete] on a DTO property is like @Deprecated here: it warns your compiler, never the client. Swashbuckle can mark the field deprecated in the OpenAPI document, which is what clients see.

See also. 5.09, 5.10, 5.15, 14.02, 16.16, 20.06, Controllers, routing and binding

20.02 Version events without breaking consumers

Then.

  • Spring era: JMS, Java's standard messaging API, with ObjectMessage, which carried a Java object in Java's own binary serialisation. The consumer needed the same class on its classpath, the set of jars it loads. Any incompatible change to the class threw InvalidClassException on the consumer.
public class PayoutCompletedEvent implements Serializable {
    private static final long serialVersionUID = 3L;
    private String payoutId;
    private BigDecimal amount;
}
// session.createObjectMessage(event)
  • Boot era: a shared payouts-events jar of event classes that every consumer depended on. A change to an event meant a new jar and a release of every consumer.

Both were right when producer and consumers were one team's code in one release. JSON events with an explicit type and version replaced them, because consumers can then deploy on their own schedule.

Recognise it by. javax.jms.ObjectMessage, createObjectMessage, implements Serializable with a serialVersionUID on a message class, and a payouts-events dependency in another team's POM.

The rookie version.

// bankReference was "SRL-0091-4471". It now says which payment scheme carried it.
public record PayoutCompletedData(String claimId, Money amount, BankReference bankReference) { }
public record BankReference(String scheme, String value) { }
// Same eventType, same eventVersion 1 in the envelope. Deployed on Tuesday.

What goes wrong. payout-events is an SNS topic, a channel that copies each message to every subscribed SQS queue. Three queues subscribe: ledger-confirm, notify-claimant and payout-audit. Each has its own consumer, owned and deployed separately. The new shape reaches all three at once. The audit consumer reads bankReference as a string, cannot parse an object there, and every completion goes to payout-audit-dlq, the queue's dead-letter queue, after 5 failed receives. Rolling Payouts back does not help. 2,400 new-shape messages are already in the queues, and they stay until they are consumed or expire.

Do this now. 10.12 designs the envelope, the fields every event carries: eventId, eventType, eventVersion and the payload, data. Here is how to change a version while every queue holds messages of both.

  1. Make additive changes inside a version. A new optional field needs no new version, provided every consumer is a tolerant reader, one that ignores fields it does not know (5.10).
  2. For a breaking change, define version 2 and change readers first. Each consumer deploys code that reads version 1 and version 2, turning version 1 into the current record in one place.
  3. Then let the producer publish version 2. The outbox (9.07), the collection each event is written to in the same transaction as its change, stores the version with each event, so events written before the deploy still go out as version 1.
  4. Keep reading version 1 for as long as one can still arrive. That is the outbox backlog, plus the dead-letter queue's retention, plus a full retention again for any message redriven from it (20.08). On a standard queue the dead-letter clock counts from the message's first arrival, not from its move (10.08). SQS keeps a message for 4 days by default and at most 14, and Payouts' dead-letter queues keep 14, so allow at least 14 days.
  5. Fail loudly on a version you do not know. The message then reaches the dead-letter queue, where it waits for a fix (20.08).
// json is the application's Jackson ObjectMapper; the listener takes EventEnvelope<JsonNode>
PayoutCompletedData read(EventEnvelope<JsonNode> event) throws JsonProcessingException {
    return switch (event.eventVersion()) {
        case 1 -> upgrade(json.treeToValue(event.data(), PayoutCompletedDataV1.class));
        case 2 -> json.treeToValue(event.data(), PayoutCompletedData.class);
        default -> throw new UnknownEventVersion(event.eventType(), event.eventVersion());
    };
}

private PayoutCompletedData upgrade(PayoutCompletedDataV1 v1) {
    return new PayoutCompletedData(v1.claimId(), v1.amount(),
            new BankReference("UNKNOWN", v1.bankReference()));   // v1 never named the scheme
}

When one consumer cannot move for months, publish both versions for a while. The version is already an SNS message attribute, eventVersion (10.12). Give each subscription a filter policy, a rule that lets through only messages whose attributes match (10.13). The audit subscription takes eventVersion 1 and the others take 2. Remove version 1 when its last subscription has moved.

Also seen. Avro or Protobuf with a schema registry, where the registry rejects an incompatible schema at publish time. It is the norm on Kafka, and rarer on SNS and SQS. A new event type, PayoutSettled, instead of a version 2, when the meaning has changed and not only the shape.

When to break it. Before the first consumer exists, change anything. With one consumer in your own team, deploying it first is enough, and step 4 is the only rule left.

.NET anchor. NServiceBus and MassTransit treat messages as contracts, and the same habits apply there: add, do not change, and introduce a new message type for a new meaning. Azure Service Bus subscription filters play the part of SNS filter policies.

See also. 5.10, 9.07, 10.12, 10.13, 16.16, 20.08, Messaging and WebSockets

20.03 Migrate a document shape with no downtime

Then.

  • Spring era: a maintenance window and a script in the legacy mongo shell, the predecessor of today's mongosh, run with the application stopped.
// Saturday 23:00, payouts-api scaled to 0
db.payouts.find({ amountMinor: { $exists: true } }).forEach(function (p) {
  p.amount = { value: p.amountMinor / 100, currency: p.currency };
  delete p.amountMinor; delete p.currency;
  db.payouts.save(p);
});

With the application stopped, nothing else wrote, so the script could not lose an update. The window went when payouts had to run every hour of the week, and the script grew too slow to fit it.

Recognise it by. .js files under a migrations or scripts folder, db.collection.save( and forEach(function in them, and mongo instead of mongosh in a runbook.

The rookie version.

// Release 31: the record changes, and a start-up runner converts every document.
@Bean ApplicationRunner migrate(MongoTemplate mongo) {
    return args -> mongo.findAll(LegacyPayout.class)
            .forEach(old -> mongo.save(Payout.from(old)));
}

What goes wrong. An ApplicationRunner is a bean Boot runs once at start-up, so every pod runs it. Both pods run the converter over 3.1 million documents, and race each other. Meanwhile the old pod, still serving during the rolling update, writes 600 payouts in the old shape that the converter has already passed. The new code throws on them. The team rolls back to release 30, which cannot read the 40,000 documents already converted. Every request that touches one of those payouts fails. findAll, from MongoTemplate, Spring Data's lower-level MongoDB API, also loads the whole collection into one pod's heap.

Do this now. 8.19 explains the schemaVersion field, an integer on every document saying which shape it has, and the reading converter, the one place that turns any stored shape into the current record. The live part is the release order.

  1. Release 1 learns to read version 2 and still writes version 1. Its rollback target is the current code, and nothing new has been written.
  2. Release 2 writes version 2. Its rollback target is release 1, which can read it. Nothing on disk is ever unreadable.
  3. Backfill the old documents in a separate job (20.07), not at start-up. It reads a batch, converts in Java, and writes each document back with a filter on its _id, its schemaVersion and its @Version value, the counter Spring Data uses to detect a concurrent write (8.05). The write increments that counter too, as every write path must. A live write in between makes the filter miss, and the job skips that document, because the application has already rewritten it.
  4. Count what is left with a query on schemaVersion: 1. Wait for zero.
  5. Release 3 removes the version 1 reader. Its rollback target, release 2, also reads version 2.

Payouts runs DocumentDB engine 5.0, and AWS lists the $set and $replaceWith aggregation stages as supported only from 8.0. They are the usual tools of a pipeline update, an update that computes new fields from a document's existing ones on the server. Do not plan on building the new fields from the old ones inside the database. The conversion happens in Java.

If queries will use a new field, build its index before release 2 needs it. AWS states that by default a DocumentDB index build blocks every other operation on the collection, so build it in a quiet hour (8.20).

Also seen. Lazy migration only: each document converts when it is next written, and the version 1 reader lives for ever. It suits a collection where old documents are rarely read. A new collection, filled by dual writes and a copy, then switched over. It suits a change of key or of collection-level design, at the price of two writes on every request.

When to break it. A collection that is small, and that no live path writes during the change, can be converted in one job between releases 2 and 3. Measure the job against a copy first.

.NET anchor. An EF Core migration changes a schema in one step and assumes the code changes with it. Here there is no schema, so the code carries the old shape instead. Cosmos DB users meet exactly this problem and solve it the same way.

See also. 8.06, 8.19, 8.20, 20.07, 20.10, 20.11, The Yard, chapter 8, Document data: Amazon DocumentDB and the MongoDB API

20.04 Replace an old service with a strangler fig

Then.

  • J2EE era: the big-bang rewrite. A new system was built beside the old one for 18 months, then switched on over a cut-over weekend, with the data migrated in one run.
  • Spring era: integration through the shared database. The new service opened a second DataSource, Java's connection factory, on the old system's database, and read and wrote its tables directly, so it could go live without the old system changing at all.
@Bean DataSource claimsCoreDataSource(@Value("${legacy.datasource.url}") String url) {
    BasicDataSource ds = new BasicDataSource();      // Commons DBCP
    ds.setUrl(url);
    return ds;
}
// In the new service:
jdbc.update("UPDATE CLAIMS_CORE.PAYMENT SET STATUS = 'PAID' WHERE ID = ?", id);

The rewrite was a reasonable bet when releases were rare and expensive anyway. The shared database was the quickest way to share data before services had APIs and events. Both were replaced because they put all the risk on one day, or tied the new system to the old system's tables for ever.

Recognise it by. A second DataSource bean, legacy.datasource.* or spring.datasource.legacy.* properties, SQL naming another system's schema, and a cutover-runbook with a weekend date.

The rookie version.

Plan: rebuild the whole payments module of claims-core as payouts-api.
Q1-Q3: build. Q4: migrate 3.1 million payments over one weekend.
Until then claims-core stays as it is, and new rules go into both.

What goes wrong. The old module keeps changing during the 9 months. 14 new rules land in claims-core and 11 of them reach the new code. The cut-over weekend finds 2,300 payments that the old rules would have held and the new ones would release. There is no partial rollback. Either everything moves back, or Payouts lives with the gap until Monday.

Do this now. A strangler fig replaces an old system one slice at a time, behind a single front door.

  1. Put a facade in front first. The facade is a router that every caller reaches. On Kubernetes an Ingress, the cluster's HTTP routing rule, can be that facade. On day one it sends everything to the old system. Nothing changes except where callers point.
  2. Choose a thin slice with a clear owner of its data. Reading a payout's status is a good first slice. Creating a payout is a poor one.
  3. Decide who owns the data for that slice. During the move, one side is the system of record and the other keeps a copy fed by events. Never let both write the same record.
  4. Prove it before it serves. Run the new code on real traffic in shadow and compare its answers (20.09).
  5. Route the slice. Add a path rule. Rolling back is removing the rule.
  6. Delete the old code for that slice. Otherwise both run, and new rules go into both.
apiVersion: networking.k8s.io/v1
kind: Ingress
metadata:
  name: payments
spec:
  rules:
    - host: payments.internal.sorrel
      http:
        paths:
          - path: /payouts                       # moved: the new service
            pathType: Prefix
            backend: { service: { name: payouts-api, port: { number: 8080 } } }
          - path: /                              # everything else: the old system
            pathType: Prefix
            backend: { service: { name: claims-core, port: { number: 8080 } } }

An Ingress routes by host and path, to Kubernetes Services. If claims-core runs outside the cluster, the facade is a proxy or gateway that can reach it there. To split by method or header, so that GETs move before POSTs, make the facade a gateway that can, such as one configured through the Kubernetes Gateway API.

Also seen. Branch by abstraction: put an interface in front of the old code inside the same codebase, then replace the implementation behind it. It is the strangler fig at the level of a class. Change data capture, which copies the old database's changes into the new system's store. It keeps a copy current without touching the old code, at the price of coupling to its tables.

When to break it. A small system with no active development and few callers can be replaced in one move. The cost is the one-day risk, so rehearse the cut-over on a copy until it is boring.

.NET anchor. Microsoft documents this exact pattern for moving from ASP.NET to ASP.NET Core. YARP, its reverse proxy, is the facade, and routes move from the old application to the new one a path at a time.

See also. 20.09, 20.12, 21.01, 21.04

20.05 Release behind a feature flag

Then.

  • Spring era: a long-lived release branch. The new bank integration lived on feature/new-bank for 4 months and was merged the week it went live.
  • Boot era: Togglz, a flag library in which each flag is an enum constant, often with a web console to switch it.
public enum PayoutFeatures implements Feature {
    @Label("New bank API") NEW_BANK_API;

    public boolean isActive() {
        return FeatureContext.getFeatureManager().isActive(this);
    }
}

Togglz was a good choice for one application with one database. Flag services with an open client API replaced it, because many services need the same flag, per caller, changed without a deploy.

Recognise it by. org.togglz imports, implements Feature, FeatureContext.getFeatureManager(), org.ff4j and ff4j.check( from FF4j, a similar library, and branch names that are months old.

The rookie version.

if (features.newBankApi()) {
    bankGateway.instructV2(payout);
} else {
    bankGateway.instruct(payout);
}
// The flag is a boolean in a ConfigMap, the Kubernetes object that holds a pod's settings.
// It went to true for both pods on Monday.

What goes wrong. The flag works as an on-off switch for the whole service, so the first real test of the new API is all traffic. On Monday at 09:00 it goes on, and 1 bank instruction in 50 is rejected for a field the old API did not need. By the time the flag is off again, 212 payouts are stuck at RESERVED: money held in the ledger, and no instruction at the bank. The flag is also never removed. A year later nobody knows whether false still works.

Do this now. A feature flag is a decision your code asks for at run time, so you can deploy code dark and release it later. 4.16 shows a flag read from configuration. A live release needs more: a change without a restart, a share of traffic, and a kill switch.

  1. Put the flag behind one Payouts interface, so the flag vendor appears in one class.
  2. Evaluate it with a stable key. Use the claim ID, so a claim sees the same path on every retry and on every pod.
  3. Roll out by percentage: 1 in 100 claims, then 10, then all. The percentage is a rollout rule on the flag in the flag service, which buckets claims by the key, so the code does not change between steps. Watch the business metric (14.02) at each step, not only error rates.
  4. Make both paths safe together. During the rollout both run, and so does whatever data each writes (20.03).
  5. Delete the flag when the rollout is complete. Put a removal date in the code and a ticket on the board.
public interface PayoutFlags {
    boolean useNewBankApi(ClaimId claim);
}

@Component
class OpenFeaturePayoutFlags implements PayoutFlags {
    private final Client client = OpenFeatureAPI.getInstance().getClient();

    public boolean useNewBankApi(ClaimId claim) {      // remove by 2027-01-31
        return client.getBooleanValue("payouts.new-bank-api", false,
                new ImmutableContext(claim.value(), Map.of()));
    }
}

@Component makes the class a Spring bean, which Spring creates once and injects wherever PayoutFlags is asked for. OpenFeature is a vendor-neutral flag API, a project of the CNCF, the Cloud Native Computing Foundation. Its Java SDK, dev.openfeature:sdk, talks to a provider: Unleash, LaunchDarkly, flagd or another, each with its own artifact. Register it once at start-up with OpenFeatureAPI.getInstance().setProviderAndWait(provider), which blocks until the provider is ready. The context's first argument is the targeting key, the value the provider buckets on. The default, false here, is what you get when the flag service cannot be reached. Choose it so that an outage leaves the safe path running.

Also seen. A configuration flag with a restart (4.16), when a whole-service switch is enough. A vendor's own SDK without OpenFeature, which is fine until you change vendors. Canary deploys, where 1 pod in 10 runs the new code. They test the code, but not per claim, and not without a deploy.

When to break it. A change you can roll back in minutes, with no effect outside the service, does not need a flag. Every flag doubles a code path to test, so add one only where a rollback would be slow or a mistake would cost money.

.NET anchor. Microsoft.FeatureManagement with its percentage and targeting filters is the closest match, often fed by Azure App Configuration. OpenFeature also has a .NET SDK, with providers for the same flag services.

See also. 4.02, 4.16, 14.02, 20.03, 20.09, 21.12

20.06 Deprecate and remove an endpoint

What goes wrong. GET /v1/payouts/search was replaced 18 months ago and still serves 3 requests a minute. Nobody knows from whom. It is deleted on a Friday, and on Monday the claims call centre's screen has been empty for 2 days.

Do this now.

  1. Find every caller. Count requests per OAuth2 client ID (15.01, 14.02), over a full month, so month-end jobs show up.
  2. Mark it deprecated in the OpenAPI document with @Operation(deprecated = true) (5.15). Tell each client team the date, in writing.
  3. Return Deprecation (RFC 9745) and Sunset (RFC 8594) headers on every response, set in the controller with ResponseEntity.ok().header(...) or in a servlet filter for the path, so a careful client can alert on them. Deprecation carries the date the endpoint was deprecated, and Sunset the date it stops answering.
  4. Run a brownout before the date: answer with an error for 10 minutes at a known time. Unknown callers find you then.
  5. On the date, return 410 Gone with a problem body that names the replacement (6.02). Delete the code a release later.

See also. 5.09, 5.15, 6.02, 14.02, 20.01

20.07 Backfill data safely

What goes wrong. A backfill sets channel: "LETTER" on 3.1 million payouts with one updateMany from a laptop. DocumentDB's CPU sits at 100% for 40 minutes and live writes time out. The VPN drops, and the shell reports an error with no count. AWS states that each document's update in a bulk operation such as updateMany is atomic and the whole is not. Nobody knows how far it got.

Do this now. A backfill writes new or corrected data into existing documents.

  1. Run it once, as a Kubernetes Job, a pod that runs to completion. Never in a start-up runner on every pod.
  2. Work in batches of about 1,000, ordered by _id, each written as one bulk command (8.21). Pause between them. Store the last _id done, so a restart resumes there (8.08).
  3. Filter each write on the condition you are fixing and its @Version, and increment the version (8.05): Update.update("channel", "LETTER").inc("version", 1). A document a live request changed is skipped.
  4. Make it idempotent: a second run changes nothing.
  5. Count first, with a dry run. Watch database CPU and latency. Rerun for what it skipped.

See also. 8.05, 8.08, 8.20, 8.21, 20.03

20.08 Reprocess a dead-letter queue after a fix

Then.

  • Boot era: a hand-written replay job with AWS SDK v1. It received from the dead-letter queue, sent each message back to the main queue and deleted it. Before AWS added a redrive API to SQS, every team wrote one.
AmazonSQS sqs = AmazonSQSClientBuilder.defaultClient();
for (Message m : sqs.receiveMessage(dlqUrl).getMessages()) {
    sqs.sendMessage(queueUrl, m.getBody());
    sqs.deleteMessage(dlqUrl, m.getReceiptHandle());
}

It worked, and it still has one use: it can skip or change messages, which the redrive API cannot. It was replaced because SQS now moves messages itself, at a rate you set, with a task you can watch and cancel. SDK v1 has been out of support since 31 December 2025.

Recognise it by. com.amazonaws.services.sqs.AmazonSQS, AmazonSQSClientBuilder (SDK v2 lives under software.amazon.awssdk), a class named DlqReplayJob or ReplayDeadLetters, and an admin endpoint that triggers it.

The rookie version.

# 10:02 the fix is merged. 10:03 put everything back.
aws sqs start-message-move-task \
  --source-arn arn:aws:sqs:eu-west-2:111122223333:ledger-confirm-dlq

What goes wrong. ledger-confirm-dlq holds 1,840 messages from a bug in LedgerConfirmListener. At 10:03 the rollout has replaced 1 pod of 2, so half the messages meet the old code, fail 5 more times and return to the dead-letter queue. The rest arrive with no rate limit and hit the ledger at once, which starts refusing calls. Worse, the listener's duplicate check used the SQS message ID. SQS gives every redriven message a new message ID. 212 messages whose ledger call had succeeded before the bug fired are confirmed twice.

Do this now. 10.09 covers the redrive mechanism. This is the procedure around it, after a production incident.

  1. Read a sample first. Receive 10 messages from the dead-letter queue and read them. Confirm that they failed for the bug you fixed, and not for something else.
  2. Ask whether each message still makes sense. A message from 3 days ago may describe a payout that has since been cancelled, or a claimant already called by hand. The handler must check current state and skip what is stale.
  3. Check the deadline. On a standard queue, a message keeps its original enqueue time when it moves to the dead-letter queue. It expires from there on the original clock, so messages near the end of their retention need attention first.
  4. Deploy the fix to every pod and confirm it. Check that the rollout is complete and that new messages succeed.
  5. Check the handler is idempotent on the event ID in the envelope, not the SQS message ID (10.07). A redriven message is a new message to SQS, with a new ID and a new retention period.
  6. Start a move task with a rate, on the dead-letter queue's ARN (its Amazon Resource Name), sized for the slowest downstream. AWS allows at most 500 messages a second.
  7. Watch it, and cancel it while it is running if the failures come back. Messages that fail again return to the dead-letter queue after maxReceiveCount receives, the redrive policy's limit, 5 on Payouts' queues (10.08).
# Move ledger-confirm-dlq back to its source queue at 20 messages a second.
DLQ=arn:aws:sqs:eu-west-2:111122223333:ledger-confirm-dlq
TASK_HANDLE=$(aws sqs start-message-move-task --source-arn "$DLQ" \
  --max-number-of-messages-per-second 20 --query TaskHandle --output text)

# Progress and status of recent tasks for this dead-letter queue.
aws sqs list-message-move-tasks --source-arn "$DLQ"

# Stop it if failures return. Only a running task can be cancelled.
aws sqs cancel-message-move-task --task-handle "$TASK_HANDLE"

AWS states that a redrive task runs for at most 36 hours, and that it cannot filter or modify messages. To skip or repair some messages, make the handler skip them, or move them with your own job as in Then.

Also seen. The SQS console's "Start DLQ redrive" button, which starts the same task. It suits a one-off, and leaves no record in the incident notes. The SDK v2 call startMessageMoveTask, for a runbook script or an admin tool.

When to break it. A dead-letter queue on a FIFO queue has already broken the order of its message groups. If order matters to the consumer, repair the affected records directly instead of replaying. An SNS subscription's own dead-letter queue is different again: AWS's SNS pages still describe moving those messages with your own code.

.NET anchor. An Azure Service Bus queue has a dead-letter subqueue, and resubmitting from it is code you write or a tool you run. The same rules apply: fix first, check idempotency, resubmit at a rate.

See also. 6.11, 10.07, 10.08, 10.09, 10.17, 14.08, Messaging and WebSockets

20.09 Run old and new code side by side

What goes wrong. A new fee calculation goes live for all payouts. It differs from the old one on 0.4% of them, all with an excess on a home policy. Over 2 days 96 payouts are short by an average of £18.20.

Do this now. Run the new code in shadow: call both implementations, serve the old result, and compare.

  1. Shadow only pure work: calculations, decisions, reads. Never call the bank, the ledger or SNS twice.
  2. Run the shadow call after the real one, with its own timeout, on a bounded executor (3.05). It must not slow or break the request, so give that executor ThreadPoolExecutor.DiscardPolicy, which drops work when the pool is full. The CallerRunsPolicy of 3.05 would run the shadow on the request thread.
  3. Record every difference with the claim ID and both results, as a metric and a log line (14.02). Record a failure or a timeout of the new code too, or a shadow that always throws looks like a perfect match.
  4. Investigate differences until they are zero or explained, then switch with a flag (20.05).
Money fee = feeCalculator.calculate(claim);
CompletableFuture.supplyAsync(() -> newFeeCalculator.calculate(claim), shadowExecutor)
        .orTimeout(500, TimeUnit.MILLISECONDS)
        .whenComplete((candidate, failure) -> {
            if (failure != null) mismatches.failed(claim.id(), failure);
            else if (!candidate.equals(fee)) mismatches.record(claim.id(), fee, candidate);
        });
return fee;

See also. 3.05, 14.02, 20.04, 20.05

20.10 Roll back a deploy that has written new data

What goes wrong. Release 44 adds a saga state, HELD, for payouts waiting on a fraud check, and publishes a new PayoutHeld event. After an hour of errors the team runs kubectl rollout undo, which puts the previous version's pods back (17.06). Release 43's SagaState enum has no HELD, so it cannot read the 380 payout_sagas documents now in that state. The PayoutHeld events are already in all three queues. Release 43's listeners do not know the type, and the dead-letter queues fill.

Do this now. Code rolls back. Data and published events do not.

  1. Before a release, ask what it writes that its predecessor cannot read: a new field, enum value, event type, document version or event version. If there is any, ship the reader first, in its own release (20.03).
  2. Prefer a flag off (20.05) to a rollback. The data stays readable, because the code that reads it stays.
  3. When the previous release cannot read the new data, roll forward with a fix. Rolling back then makes things worse.
  4. Treat published events as permanent. A rollback cannot recall a message already in three queues.

See also. 5.10, 17.06, 20.02, 20.03, 20.05

20.11 Rename a field in stored documents

What goes wrong. payeeName becomes claimantName in the Payout record, and in every document written after the deploy. Old documents now read as null. A finance report that queries payeeName loses every new payout, and its index serves nothing new.

Do this now. First ask whether the stored name must change. Spring Data's @Field("payeeName") on a field named claimantName renames it in Java only. That is often the whole job. To rename it on disk too:

  1. Read both names, preferring the new one, through the reading converter (8.19).
  2. Write both names, and build an index on the new one if queries need it (8.06).
  3. Move every query, report and aggregation to the new name. Search other teams' code too.
  4. Backfill the new name on old documents (20.07), keeping the old one. Convert in Java, as engine 5.0 has no pipeline update (20.03). Not $rename: it deletes payeeName while readers may still need it.
  5. Stop writing the old name, then remove it and its index. The $unset update operator, new Update().unset("payeeName"), works on engine 5.0. It is not the $unset stage that 8.12 lists as 8.0 only.

See also. 8.06, 8.12, 8.19, 20.03, 20.07

20.12 Split a service in two

Then.

  • J2EE era: an EAR, one archive holding several web modules and EJB jars (Enterprise JavaBeans, J2EE's server-managed components), deployed to one application server. Splitting meant moving one module to its own server. Every module still used the same database through one shared data source, looked up by name in JNDI, the server's directory of resources.
<application>
  <module><web><web-uri>payouts-web.war</web-uri></web></module>
  <module><ejb>notifications-ejb.jar</ejb></module>
</application>
<!-- both look up java:comp/env/jdbc/ClaimsDS -->
  • Spring era: the split by copy. The code was copied into a new repository and deployed, and both copies kept the shared schema.

The shared database was the natural integration point when one team owned everything. It was replaced because two services on one store cannot change that store independently, so they are still one system that deploys in two places.

Recognise it by. META-INF/application.xml, .ear packaging, java:comp/env/jdbc/ lookups, and two services whose configuration names the same database and collection.

The rookie version.

# claimant-notifications/application.yml: the new service, split out last sprint
spring:
  data:
    mongodb:
      uri: ${PAYOUTS_DOCDB_URI}      # the same cluster, database and user as payouts-api
      database: payouts              # reads payouts directly to build letters

What goes wrong. The new service reads payouts documents to address its letters. Three weeks later payouts-api renames payeeName to claimantName in its documents and deploys, as it always has, with its own tests green. It has no reason to look for a reader in another service. The notification service reads null for 3 hours, and 1,106 claimants get a letter that starts "Dear ,". Neither team broke a rule it knew about. The split moved the code and left the coupling.

Do this now. Split along a business capability (21.01), and move the data with the code.

  1. Split inside the codebase first. Make the part a Maven module (1.12), a separately built project inside the same repository, like a project in a .NET solution, with its own package. It may depend on the event records and nothing else of Payouts. Fix every compile error that reveals.
  2. Give it its own data. It owns its collections, and no other code reads them. What it needs from Payouts arrives in events (PayoutCompleted on notify-claimant) or through an API. It keeps its own copy of the claimant's name.
  3. Deploy it separately from the same repository. The new service gets its own Deployment, its own database user, granted only its own collections, and its own IAM role, the AWS identity that grants it its queue (10.18).
  4. Move the consumer without a gap. For a while both services consume notify-claimant. SQS gives each message to one of them, and may deliver a copy to the other. Both run the same module code against the same collections until step 5, so one check on the event ID (10.07) catches a copy wherever it lands. Then turn the listener off in payouts-api.
  5. Move the data last. Copy its collections to the new database. Switch reads and writes in one release, and keep the old copy until the new one has been checked.
  6. Give it everything a service needs: dashboards, alerts, an on-call owner, and its own release pipeline.
@Component
@ConditionalOnProperty(name = "payouts.notifications.listener-enabled",
                       havingValue = "true", matchIfMissing = true)
class ClaimantNotificationListener {
    @SqsListener("notify-claimant")
    void on(PayoutCompleted event) { notifications.send(event); }
}

@SqsListener, from Spring Cloud AWS, makes the method receive from the named queue. @ConditionalOnProperty creates the bean only when the property matches. Setting payouts.notifications.listener-enabled=false in payouts-api stops its listener, and the new service carries on alone.

Also seen. Moving the repository first and the data later, which often leaves the shared database for years. Splitting by technical layer, an "API service" and a "worker service" over one store. That is a deployment choice, not two services, and it is fine when one team owns both.

When to break it. Two processes may share one database while one team owns both and deploys them together. The cost is that they are one service for every change to the data, and the team should say so.

.NET anchor. The same split in .NET is a project in the solution becoming its own deployable, with its own DbContext and its own database. A shared DbContext across two services is the same trap as the shared collection above.

See also. 1.12, 10.07, 10.18, 21.01, 21.02, 21.04

20.13 Merge two services

What goes wrong. payout-fees and payouts-api were split 2 years ago. Every payout calls payout-fees over HTTP, they always deploy together, and a change to either needs both teams. When payout-fees is slow, Payouts is slow. Two services cost two pipelines, two dashboards and a network call for what is one capability.

Do this now. Merge when the services change together, share their data, or call each other on every request (21.02).

  1. Move the smaller service into the larger one's repository as a module, behind an interface.
  2. Replace the HTTP call with a call to that interface. Keep the old endpoint, served by the merged service, until its other callers have moved (20.06).
  3. Point the old name at the merged service: change the selector of the payout-fees Kubernetes Service to the merged pods, or its rule at the Ingress, so callers need no change on the day.
  4. Merge the data with clear ownership inside the one service.
  5. Remove the second Deployment, its queues, its IAM role and its alerts.

See also. 20.04, 20.06, 21.01, 21.02

20.14 Change a shared library many services use

What goes wrong. sorrel-observability-starter, a starter (a dependency that brings a library and the Spring Boot configuration that switches it on, 4.11) used by 26 services, changes its default log format in version 2.4. Nothing fails to compile. 26 teams upgrade over a month, and each one's log search breaks on a different day.

Do this now.
