  1. Use semantic versions honestly: major.minor.patch, where only a major bump may break a caller. A changed default is a breaking change even when every signature is the same, so it needs a new major version (4.11).
  2. Add before you remove. Mark the old method @Deprecated(since = "2.3", forRemoval = true), with the replacement in its Javadoc. The compiler then warns every caller.
  3. Support two major versions for a while, so no service is forced to upgrade on your schedule.
  4. Build two or three real consumers against the new version before the release.
  5. Let Renovate or Dependabot, bots that open dependency-upgrade pull requests, open them for every consumer, and watch who has not merged.

See also. 1.02, 4.11, 19.06, 21.07, Maven vs csproj

⚠Review checklist
  • If you see a pull request that adds a new field and removes the old one in the same release: during the rolling update and for every unknown client, the old field disappears with no warning. See 20.01.
  • If you see an event's payload change shape with the same type and version: every subscribed queue gets messages its consumer cannot read, and a rollback leaves them in the queues. See 20.02.
  • If you see an ApplicationRunner that converts stored documents, or a release that writes a new document shape its predecessor cannot read: every pod runs it, and the rollback cannot read the data. See 20.03.
  • If you see a new service writing to another system's tables or collections: the old system can no longer change its data without breaking it. See 20.04.
  • If you see a feature flag that is one boolean for the whole service, with no key and no removal date: the first real test is all traffic, and the flag never leaves. See 20.05.
  • If you see a redrive started before the rollout finished, with no rate, or a consumer that deduplicates on the SQS message ID: messages fail again, a downstream is flooded, and redriven messages are processed twice. See 20.08.
  • If you see a second service configured with another service's database and collection: the split moved the code and kept the coupling. See 20.12.

Part IV · The how-to21. Design judgement#

Most of this book is about how to do a thing. This part is about whether to do it, and where. It covers where one service should end and the next begin, when to leave a module where it is, when to call and when to send a message, who owns which data, and what Payouts does when the bank is down all day. It ends with the tools for deciding in the open: the decision record, the back-of-envelope estimate, the review question and the complexity budget.

★What a veteran knows
  • A service boundary is a team boundary first. If two services always change in the same pull request, they are one service with a network call in the middle.
  • The cheapest split is the one you have not made yet. A module boundary inside one deployable costs a test. A network boundary costs a team's attention for as long as both services live.
  • Ask every design "what happens when this is down for a day?", not "for a minute". The minute is handled by retries. The day is handled by a decision someone in the business has made.
  • A collection has one writer. The moment a second service writes to it, nobody owns its shape, and nobody can change it.
  • Numbers end design arguments sooner than taste does. Ten minutes of arithmetic on the back of an envelope settles most questions of scale before anyone builds for scale they will never see.
  • A decision that is not written down gets made again, every time someone new joins. On Payouts the decision log is in the repository, next to the code it explains.
◷How we got hereIn 1967 Melvin Conway submitted a paper called "How Do Committees Invent?" to the Harvard Business Review.

In 1967 Melvin Conway submitted a paper called "How Do Committees Invent?" to the Harvard Business Review. "HBR rejected it on the grounds that I had not proved my thesis," he later wrote. He sent it to Datamation, the major computing magazine of the day, which published it in April 1968. The paper opens on a definition: "That kind of intellectual activity which creates a whole from its diverse parts may be called the design of a system." Its claim was blunt. Organisations "are constrained to produce designs which are copies of the communication structures of these organizations." The idea had no name until Fred Brooks cited it in The Mythical Man-Month and called it "Conway's Law." The rejected paper outlived the objection. Every entry below that draws a boundary between services is, underneath, drawing one between people.

21.01 Draw service boundaries around business capabilities

Then.

  • J2EE era: tiers. The web tier, the EJB tier (Enterprise JavaBeans, J2EE's server-managed business components) and the data tier were often separate deployables, sometimes on separate machines. A boundary was a technical layer, and every feature crossed all three.
  • Spring era: SOA, service-oriented architecture, with one SOAP service per business entity: CustomerService, PolicyService, PaymentService. Each exposed create, read, update and delete operations over a WSDL contract, an XML file that describes a SOAP service's operations. It was right for exposing old systems of record to many callers in one standard way.
@WebService(serviceName = "PaymentService")
public class PaymentServiceImpl implements PaymentServicePort {
    public PaymentType getPayment(String paymentId) { ... }
    public void updatePayment(PaymentType payment) { ... }
}
  • Boot era: the first microservices wave cut the same entity services smaller, one per noun, each with its own Spring Boot app.

Recognise it by. javax.jws.WebService, *.wsdl files, wsimport or cxf-codegen-plugin, which generate Java classes from a WSDL, in the POM (pom.xml, Maven's build file, the counterpart of a .csproj), and service names that are nouns with get, update and delete operations and no verbs from the business.

The rookie version.

claim-service     GET/PUT /claims/{id}
payee-service     GET/PUT /payees/{id}
amount-service    POST    /amounts/validate
payout-service    POST    /payouts   calls the three above, then the ledger and the bank

What goes wrong. Each service owns a noun, and no service owns a decision. Paying one claim makes 5 synchronous calls in a row, and only the last one moves the money. A change such as "pay a claimant to an account other than the policy's" touches payee-service, claim-service and payout-service, in that order, in 3 deploys. The rule "a payout over £10,000 needs a second approval" has no home, so it ends up in two of them, and they disagree by a penny on rounding.

Do this now. A business capability is something the business does, described as a verb: pay an approved claim, record a payment, issue a policy. A bounded context is the area inside which a word means exactly one thing. The term comes from Eric Evans' book Domain-Driven Design. Draw the boundary around the capability.

  1. List the decisions the capability makes. For Payouts: is this claim payable, how much, to whom, and has it already been paid.
  2. List the data those decisions need to own. Data that is only read, such as the policy, stays with its owner and is fetched or copied (21.04).
  3. Check the words. "Account" in Payouts is the claimant's bank account. In the ledger it is a ledger account. Two meanings mean two contexts, and the boundary goes between them.
  4. Check the team. One team should be able to change, test and deploy the capability alone. Payouts owns payouts-api, and its 6 people can ship a change without asking the ledger team.
  5. Name the service after the capability, and its endpoints after what the business asks for: POST /payouts, not PUT /payees/{id}.

The test of a good boundary is the change log. Over a quarter, most changes to Payouts should touch only Payouts.

Also seen. Boundaries drawn around a volatile part, such as a pricing rule that changes weekly, so it can deploy on its own. Boundaries drawn around a supplier, such as one adapter service in front of the bank gateway, when several teams call it.

When to break it. A capability that a team of 2 cannot staff may sit in a neighbouring team's service for a while. The cost is that its changes queue behind someone else's priorities. Write that down, with the condition for moving it.

.NET anchor. The tiered split is the classic Web, BLL and DAL projects of a .NET solution, deployed as one or several applications. The SOAP entity services are the WCF services of the same years. Microsoft's eShopOnContainers reference application splits by capability instead: Catalog, Basket, Ordering. The Java advice is the same. Only the build tool differs.

See also. 21.02, 21.04, 20.12, 20.04, The Yard, chapter 11

21.02 Decide when not to split a service

Then.

  • Boot era: the microservices wave of roughly 2015 to 2018. Spring Cloud Netflix made a service cheap to start, with Eureka for discovery and Hystrix for resilience, so teams started many. Segment was one company that went back. In July 2018 its engineer Alexandra Noonan described merging "over 140 services" into one, after "3 full-time engineers spending most of their time just keeping the system alive". Splitting was right where teams were large and independent. It was wrong where one team owned all the pieces.
@SpringBootApplication
@EnableEurekaClient
@EnableHystrix
public class PayoutIdempotencyServiceApplication { ... }

Recognise it by. @EnableEurekaClient, @EnableHystrix, spring-cloud-starter-netflix-* artifactIds (an artifactId is the name part of a Maven dependency, and a starter is a dependency that brings in everything one feature needs), and a repository per service where most services have fewer than 10 classes and the same 2 committers.

The rookie version.

payouts-api           POST /payouts, starts the saga
payouts-saga          runs the steps, its own database
payouts-outbox-relay  reads the outbox, publishes to SNS, its own database
payouts-idempotency   POST /keys/check, its own database

What goes wrong. Nothing scales differently and nothing is owned by another team, so the split buys nothing and costs a lot. The idempotency check becomes an HTTP call, and when it times out nobody knows whether the key was stored. The outbox stops working. A transactional outbox works because the payout document and its outgoing event are written in the same database, in one step (9.07). The relay then publishes the events to SNS, AWS's publish-subscribe service. With the relay in its own database, the write and the event are separate again: the dual-write problem the outbox existed to solve. One payout of £1,240.50 now crosses 4 deployables, and a trace shows 11 hops.

Do this now. Keep one deployable with strong internal boundaries, and split only for a reason you can name.

  1. Put each part in its own package: com.sorrel.payouts.web, .saga, .outbox, .idempotency. Make classes package-private, Java's default access with no modifier, unless another package needs them. Package-private is visible only inside its own package.
  2. Use Maven modules where a boundary must be enforced by the compiler. A multi-module Maven build is like a .NET solution with several projects, and a module sees only the modules it declares as dependencies. Payouts already has payouts-domain, which cannot see the web layer because it does not depend on it.
  3. Write the rule down as a test. ArchUnit is a library that reads compiled classes and fails a test when a dependency breaks a rule.
class ModuleBoundaryTest {

    private final JavaClasses classes =
            new ClassFileImporter().importPackages("com.sorrel.payouts");

    @Test
    void theSagaDoesNotReachIntoTheWebLayer() {
        noClasses().that().resideInAPackage("..payouts.saga..")
                .should().dependOnClassesThat().resideInAPackage("..payouts.web..")
                .check(classes);
    }
}

ArchUnit comes from the com.tngtech.archunit:archunit test dependency. noClasses() is a static import from ArchRuleDefinition, and .. in a package pattern matches any number of package levels.

  1. Split when one of these is true and you can show it: a different team will own the part, it must scale or fail separately and you have measured why, it releases on a different cadence, or it is a security boundary.

Also seen. Spring Modulith, a Spring project that treats each top-level package under the application class as a module and verifies the dependencies between them in a test: ApplicationModules.of(PayoutsApplication.class).verify(). Choose it when you want the module structure documented as well as enforced.

When to break it. Split early when a part has a very different runtime profile, such as a batch job that needs 4 GiB for an hour a night. The cost is a second pipeline, a second dashboard and a contract between the two.

.NET anchor. The modular monolith in .NET is one host with a class library per module, internal types and InternalsVisibleTo for tests. NetArchTest plays ArchUnit's part. Java's package-private is narrower than internal: it stops at the package, not the assembly. Sub-packages get no special access either, so .saga.steps cannot see a package-private class in .saga.

See also. 21.01, 21.07, 9.07, 20.12, 20.13, The Yard, chapter 4, Access modifiers and packages

21.03 Choose synchronous or asynchronous communication

Then.

  • J2EE era: JMS, the Java Message Service, on a broker such as IBM MQ, with message-driven beans, EJBs that run when a message arrives, consuming it. It was right for reliable delivery between systems that were not always up at the same time.
  • Spring era: the ESB, or enterprise service bus. Every call between systems, synchronous or not, went through a central product such as Mule ESB, which routed, transformed and logged it. It was right when systems spoke many protocols and one integration team owned the translation.
<flow name="payment-request">
    <jms:inbound-endpoint queue="payments.in"/>
    <mulexml:xslt-transformer xsl-file="canonical-to-bank.xsl"/>
    <http:outbound-endpoint address="http://bank-gateway/pay"/>
</flow>

Recognise it by. @MessageDriven, javax.jms.MessageListener, JmsTemplate, Mule <flow> XML, and .xsl files that turn one team's XML into another's.

The rookie version.

public PayoutResponse pay(PayoutRequest request) {
    Payout payout = payoutService.create(request);
    ledgerClient.reserve(payout.idempotencyKey(), toReserve(payout));
    bankGatewayClient.instruct(payout.idempotencyKey(), toInstruction(payout));
    notificationClient.notifyClaimant(payout.claimId(), payout.amount());
    auditClient.record(payout);
    return PayoutResponse.from(payout);
}

What goes wrong. The claimant notification service is down for 20 minutes. Every payout in that window has already moved money at the bank, and then returns a 500 because the email could not be sent. The caller retries. The idempotency key saves the bank step, but the team spends a day proving it. The availability arithmetic is against this design. If each of 4 synchronous dependencies is up 99.9% of the time, and they fail independently, all 4 are up 0.999⁴ = 99.6% of the time. That is about 35 hours a year when a payout fails, against about 9 for one dependency.

Do this now. Synchronous means the caller waits for the answer. Asynchronous means the caller hands over a message and carries on. Ask four questions of each interaction.

  1. Does the caller need the answer to carry on? Payouts needs the policy to decide whether a claim is payable, and the ledger's reservation ID before it instructs the bank. Those are synchronous.
  2. Must it happen even if the other side is down right now? The claimant must be told, but not within the request. That is asynchronous.
  3. How many parties care? PayoutCompleted interests the ledger, the claimant notifier and the audit store. One event on SNS, fanned out to 3 SQS queues, serves all of them. SQS is AWS's message queue.
  4. Who sets the pace? With a queue, the consumer reads at its own speed. A slow audit store builds a backlog instead of slowing payouts down.

For Payouts the result is:

  • Policy lookup: synchronous, with a timeout (7.03).
  • Ledger reserve and bank instruction: synchronous calls inside saga steps, each with an idempotency key, so a step can be retried (11.07).
  • Facts about payouts: asynchronous, written to the outbox and relayed to SNS (9.08).

Asynchronous does not remove a dependency. It moves the waiting from a thread to a queue, and adds a dead-letter queue to watch, duplicates to handle and a delay before anyone sees the result.

Also seen. Request-reply over a queue, with a reply-to address, when the other side is reachable only by messaging. A callback or webhook, when the other side takes minutes, as a bank sometimes does. gRPC for synchronous internal calls where the payloads are large and the schema is shared.

When to break it. A synchronous call to a slow, non-essential service is acceptable inside an internal admin tool with one user. The cost is that the tool fails when that service does, and someone has to accept that in writing.

.NET anchor. The synchronous side is a typed HttpClient. The asynchronous side is MassTransit or NServiceBus publishing to Azure Service Bus topics and subscriptions, which map closely onto SNS topics and SQS queues. One difference bites: a Service Bus subscription lives inside its topic, while an SQS queue is a separate resource that SNS can write to only if the queue's policy allows it (10.01). The ESB era looked the same on both platforms, with BizTalk Server in the place of Mule.

See also. 10.01, 9.07, 9.08, 11.07, 7.03, 21.05, The Yard, chapter 11, Messaging and WebSockets

21.04 Decide who owns which data

Then.

  • J2EE era: the shared enterprise database. One large Oracle or DB2 database held every application's tables, and applications integrated by reading each other's. It was right for its time: one source of truth, joins and transactions across everything, one team of DBAs, and reports that were one query away. The habit outlived the era, and in Spring code, with JdbcTemplate, Spring's thin helper over JDBC, it looks like this:
BigDecimal balance = jdbcTemplate.queryForObject(
        "SELECT BALANCE FROM LEDGER.ACCOUNT WHERE ACCOUNT_ID = ?",
        BigDecimal.class, accountId);
  • Spring era: the canonical data model, from SOA. One XML schema for "Customer" or "Payment" that every system had to speak. It was right for making many old systems agree on a shape. It became the thing every change waited for, because changing it meant every team at once.

Recognise it by. SQL that names another team's schema (LEDGER.ACCOUNT), a second DataSource bean (a connection pool, registered as an object in Spring's container) for a database the team does not own, CREATE DATABASE LINK or synonyms in migration scripts, and a shared canonical-model.xsd.

The rookie version.

@Bean
MongoTemplate ledgerMongo(MongoClient client) {
    return new MongoTemplate(client, "ledger");   // the ledger team's database
}

boolean isReserved(String reservationId) {
    return ledgerMongo.exists(
            query(where("_id").is(reservationId).and("status").is("HELD")),
            "reservations");
}

What goes wrong. MongoTemplate is Spring Data MongoDB's helper for queries, and the @Bean method registers a second one pointed at the ledger's database. The ledger API takes 200 milliseconds, the collection read takes 3, and the shortcut looks harmless. Then the ledger team renames status to state as part of a migration that only their code knew about. Payouts reads every reservation as missing and holds 140 payouts as not reserved. The ledger team never knew Payouts read their collection, so their tests could not have caught it. Payouts' service account also needs read access to the ledger's database, which the next security review flags.

Do this now. Every piece of data has exactly one owner, and the owner is the only writer.

  1. Write down the owner of each collection. Payouts owns payouts, payout_sagas, outbox and idempotency_keys. The ledger owns reservations and balances. The policy team owns policies.
  2. Other services read the owner's data through its API or its events. Never through its database, even read-only.
  3. When you need someone else's data often, keep a local copy built from their events, called a projection. Store when it was last updated, and treat it as possibly stale.
  4. When you need a fact as it was at a moment, copy it into your own record and own the copy. A payout stores the claimant's bank account at the time of payment. If the policy changes next week, the payout must still show where the money went.
  5. Give reporting its own route. Every Payouts event reaches the payout-audit queue through the payout-events topic, and the reporting store is built from that, not from the payouts collection.

Also seen. A shared database with one schema per service, and database permissions that stop each service reading the others' schemas. It keeps one cluster to run while keeping ownership. Choose it when running several database clusters is the larger cost.

When to break it. A one-off data migration or an incident investigation may read another team's data directly, with that team's agreement and with a time limit. The cost is that the access must be removed afterwards, and someone has to check it was.

.NET anchor. The shared database is the SQL Server that every .NET application connected to, with linked servers and cross-database views. The modern equivalent is one EF Core DbContext per service, over a database only that service touches. The rule does not depend on the platform.

See also. 21.01, 21.07, 9.05, 9.12, 10.12, 20.03, The Yard, chapter 8, Document data: Amazon DocumentDB and the MongoDB API

21.05 Decide what happens when a dependency is down for a day

Then.

  • Spring era: the nightly batch. Systems exchanged files once a night, and Spring Batch jobs read them. Spring Batch is Spring's framework for record-by-record batch jobs. A partner down for a day meant the file came a night late. It was right for work that the business already measured in days.
@Bean
public Job paymentFileJob(JobBuilderFactory jobs, Step readPaymentFile) {
    return jobs.get("paymentFileJob").start(readPaymentFile).build();
}
  • J2EE era: store-and-forward on a JMS broker. Messages waited on IBM MQ until the other side came back, sometimes for days.

Recognise it by. @EnableBatchProcessing, JobBuilderFactory and StepBuilderFactory (current Spring Batch builds jobs with new JobBuilder(name, jobRepository) instead), <batch:job> XML, FlatFileItemReader, JobLauncher, and cron schedules such as 0 0 2 * * * next to file paths.

The rookie version.

payouts:
  bank:
    retry:
      max-attempts: 4
      backoff: 30s
    on-exhausted: mark-failed   # release the reservation, tell the claimant

What goes wrong. The bank gateway is down from 09:00 to 17:00 on a Monday. Every payout is tried 4 times over about 90 seconds and is marked failed. By evening 412 payouts have failed, their ledger reservations have been released, and each claimant has an email saying the payment failed. On Tuesday, operations resubmit them from a spreadsheet, as new payouts with new idempotency keys. 3 of them had reached the bank in the minutes before the outage was declared, with an unknown outcome, and are paid twice. Retries handle a blip. Nobody had decided what happens in a day.

Do this now. For each dependency, the team and the business decide the behaviour in advance, in writing.

  1. Choose a mode. Wait: accept the work and finish it when the dependency returns. Degrade: carry on with less, such as a cached policy summary for a read-only screen. Refuse: fail quickly and say so. For the bank, Payouts waits, because the payout is owed whether or not the bank is up today.
  2. Hold the work at a safe point. The saga stays at its INSTRUCT step, before the bank call, which is the pivot: the step that cannot be undone (11.06). While the bank's circuit breaker is open (7.05), the call is refused unsent with CallNotPermittedException, and the worker moves nextAttemptAt forward. The reservation stays in place. A call that timed out is unknown instead, and waits to ask the bank with the same key (11.06).
  3. Keep waiting work in your own database, not only on a queue. An SQS queue keeps a message for 4 days by default and 14 days at most. A saga document waits as long as the business needs, and can be listed and queried.
  4. Set a limit from the business. Claimants are promised payment within 5 working days, so a held saga's step deadline is 2 days. Then it moves to PARKED, for a person (11.08).
  5. Tell people. GET /payouts/{id} shows the payout as RESERVED, not yet sent to the bank, the claimant gets a "delayed" message, and an alert fires on the age of the oldest waiting saga (14.08).
  6. Recover slowly. When the bank returns, the saga worker picks up held sagas as they fall due. Each is claimed with a lease, so no saga runs on two pods (11.07), and each sends its original instruction key. A resilience4j @RateLimiter on the bank client holds the rate the bank has agreed, say 5 a second. It counts per pod, so with 2 pods give each half. 412 payouts then take under 2 minutes, and nothing is sent twice.
  7. Rehearse it. Turn the bank stub off for an hour in the test environment, once a quarter.

Also seen. A manual route for the worst case, such as a payment file uploaded to the bank's portal by a person, with its own controls. Choose it when the outage outlasts the business limit.

When to break it. For a dependency whose answer is only useful now, such as a fraud score at request time, waiting makes no sense. Refuse, and accept that the work is lost or re-requested.

.NET anchor. Polly handles the minute in .NET as resilience4j, Java's resilience library, does here. The day is handled by a durable workflow, such as Azure Durable Functions waiting on an external event. Payouts uses its saga document for the same job.

See also. 11.06, 11.07, 11.08, 11.09, 7.05, 14.08, 10.08, 21.06, The Yard, chapter 11

21.06 Design for the failure of every dependency

What goes wrong. A design lists the ledger and the bank and stops. Then the identity provider that issues tokens fails. Once the cached tokens expire, every outbound call fails with it, because nobody had counted it as a dependency.

Do this now. List every dependency, including the ones that feel like infrastructure, and fill in one row each. Review the table whenever a dependency is added.

Dependency When slow When down for a day How we notice
Policy system timeout at 2 s, fail the request refuse new payouts error rate on PolicyClient
Ledger breaker opens, saga step waits saga holds before reserve breaker state metric
Bank gateway saga step retries with its key saga holds before the pivot (21.05) age of oldest waiting saga
DocumentDB requests time out, readiness stays up (14.04) Payouts is down, and says so error rate, connection pool wait time
SNS outbox grows, relay retries outbox grows, nothing is lost outbox depth
Identity provider token fetch times out outbound calls fail once cached tokens expire token fetch error count

Some rows will say "we are down". That is an acceptable answer when it is a decision, and a bad one when it is a surprise.

See also. 21.05, 7.03, 7.05, 7.08, 14.05, 14.07

21.07 Keep a shared library from becoming a distributed monolith

Then.

  • Boot era: the company "common" jar, holding domain classes such as Policy and Payment alongside logging setup, so every service used the same types. It was right while a few services were written by one team. With 40 services, one change to Payment meant 40 releases.

What goes wrong. A distributed monolith is a set of services that must be deployed together. A field renamed in the shared Payment class arrives as null in 3 services that had not upgraded, because Jackson, the JSON library Boot configures, ignores the unknown new name by default, and the platform team has to coordinate a release across 6 teams.

Do this now.

  1. Share technical code only: logging setup, tracing, a Money type with no business rules. Never another service's request or response classes (7.02).
  2. Keep its own dependencies few and declared. Each one becomes every user's dependency.
  3. Version it with semantic versioning, release it on a schedule, and keep old versions working long enough for teams to move.
  4. Prefer copying a small helper to sharing it. Duplication between services is cheaper than coupling between them.

See also. 20.14, 7.02, 19.06, The Yard, chapter 10

21.08 Write an ADR for a technical decision

Then.

  • Spring era: the architecture document. A long Word file, written once before the project, approved by an architecture review board and stored on a shared drive. It was right when a system was designed up front and released once a year.
  • Boot era: the wiki page and the chat thread. Decisions were made in Slack or in a meeting, and a Confluence page was sometimes updated later, overwriting what it said before.

Recognise it by. Files such as docs/SAD-v3.2.docx or architecture-overview.pptx, a wiki page called "Architecture" last edited years ago, and code comments that say // see the design doc, with no link.

The rookie version.

# Use SQS for notifications

We decided to use SQS for notifications.

Status: done

What goes wrong. A year later someone proposes moving claimant notifications to synchronous HTTP, because the queue "adds latency". The record does not say what was considered, what the alternative cost, or what problem the queue solved. Nobody remembers the 20-minute notification outage that made 0 payouts fail because of it. The team spends 2 weeks rebuilding the argument, and half of it is wrong.

Do this now. An architecture decision record, or ADR, is a short document that records one decision, why it was needed, what was chosen and what follows from it. Michael Nygard proposed the common shape. The decision log in the epilogue of The Yard follows it, with two additions worth copying: who turned out to be right, and when to reopen the decision.

  1. Keep ADRs in the repository, under docs/adr/, numbered: 0016-hold-payouts-while-the-bank-is-down.md. They are reviewed in a pull request like code.
  2. One decision per record. A record that decides four things is four records.
  3. Write it when the decision is made, not afterwards. The context is clearest while people are still arguing.
  4. List the options you rejected, and why. That paragraph saves the most time later.
  5. State the consequences, including the bad ones. "We will run a scheduled job and watch its age" is a cost, so write it down.
  6. End with a reopen condition that can be checked: a number, a date or an event. "If it stops working" cannot be checked.
  7. Never change what an accepted record decided. When a decision changes, write a new record that supersedes the old one, and change only the old one's status line. The one other edit is the Who was right line, filled in once the outcome is known.
# 16. Hold payouts while the bank gateway is down

Status:        Accepted, 2026-10-12
Context:       What happened, with the numbers. Who wanted what, and why.
Options:       1. Fail after 4 retries and ask claimants to resubmit.
               2. Hold the saga before the bank step and resume.   (chosen)
               3. Park bank instructions on an SQS queue and replay them.
Decision:      One line per decision, each with its reason.
Consequences:  What gets better. What gets worse. What it costs to run.
Who was right: Filled in later, honestly.
Reopen when:   Held payouts exceed 2,000, or a hold lasts longer than 2 days.
Supersedes:    nothing

Write an ADR for a decision that is expensive to reverse, that another team depends on, or that someone will question in a year. A library version bump needs a commit message, not an ADR.

Also seen. adr-tools, Nat Pryce's command-line scripts that create and number records in the same format. MADR, a Markdown template with a longer section on the options. Choose either if the team wants a fixed template, and keep the same folder.

When to break it. In the first weeks of a prototype that may be thrown away, decisions change daily and a record per decision is noise. Write one record when the prototype becomes the product, summarising what was decided. The cost is that the reasons behind the early choices are mostly lost.

.NET anchor. ADRs are the same on any platform. The .NET team itself publishes its larger design decisions as Markdown documents in the public dotnet/designs repository on GitHub, reviewed by pull request.

See also. 21.11, 21.12, The Yard, epilogue

21.09 Decide whether to build or buy

What goes wrong. The team writes its own workflow engine for a 3-step saga, because the products looked large. A year later it has timers, retries, a user interface and a bug in its scheduling, and nobody else in the company can run it. Or the opposite: the team buys a platform to send 3 kinds of email and spends a quarter on its integration.

Do this now. There are three choices: build, adopt open source, or buy a managed service. Ask four questions.

  1. Is it the business? Paying claims correctly is Payouts' business, so the payout rules are built. Sending email is not, so it is bought.
  2. What does it cost to run, not to start? Count who is paged at night, upgrades, and security patches.
  3. What does leaving cost? Prefer something with a standard interface you can replace.
  4. How small is the built version? The PayoutSaga orchestrator and its SagaState document are about 200 lines, and the team understands all of them. A workflow engine is a product (11.11).

Put the answer in an ADR (21.08), with the size at which you would reconsider.

See also. 11.11, 21.08, 21.12

21.10 Estimate capacity on the back of an envelope

What goes wrong. A design review argues for an hour about whether DocumentDB can "handle the load", and nobody has said what the load is. The team adds a cache and a second read replica for traffic of 16 requests in flight on each pod.

Do this now. Write the arithmetic down, with each assumption on its own line, before the meeting. Start from a business number, not a technical one. Little's law says that, on average, the number of requests in flight equals the arrival rate times the time each one takes.

Payouts on a normal day           20,000
Over 8 working hours              20,000 / 28,800 s     = 0.7 per second
Month-end peak, 15 minutes        20 per second per pod, 40 across 2 pods
Time per payout request           about 0.8 s, assumed
In flight per pod (Little's law)  20/s x 0.8 s          = 16 requests
In flight, ledger hung 30 s       20/s x 30 s           = 600 requests per pod
Writes per payout                 about 10 (payout, saga, outbox, key, updates)
Peak writes per pod               20 x 10               = 200 per second
Stored per payout                 about 8 KB across 4 collections
A year of normal days             20,000 x 365 x 8 KB   = about 58 GB

The answer is that the load is small, and the risk is a slow dependency, not volume, which is why every client has a timeout (7.03). Then measure, and replace each assumption with a number from production (18.01).

See also. 18.01, 3.01, 7.03, 14.06, The Yard, chapter 13

21.11 Review a design with the right questions

What goes wrong. A design review spends its hour on naming and on the choice of library, and approves a design that pays a claim twice when the bank times out. The review never asked what happens on a failure.

Do this now. Send the design out a day before. Ask these questions in order, and write down each answer.

  • What happens when each dependency is slow for a minute, and down for a day? (21.05, 21.06)
  • Who owns each piece of data, and who writes it? (21.04)
  • What makes each write safe to repeat? Name the idempotency key. (9.09)
  • Which step cannot be undone, and what happens if it times out? (11.06)
  • How will we know it is broken, before a claimant tells us? Name the metric and the alert.
  • What is the load, as a number? (21.10)
  • How do we roll it back after it has written data? (20.10)
  • Which decisions are expensive to reverse? Those get ADRs. The rest can be changed next week. (21.08)

A review ends with a list of decisions and their owners, not with approval.

See also. 21.05, 21.06, 21.08, 21.10, 9.09, 11.06, 20.10

21.12 Choose which complexity to accept

What goes wrong. A team adds event sourcing (state rebuilt from logged changes), a second region and a FIFO queue (SQS's ordered kind) to a service that makes about 20,000 payouts a day. Each needs its own tests, dashboards and on-call skills. A year later two of the six people understand it all, both on holiday in August.

Do this now. Treat complexity as a budget, and spend it where a failure costs money or trust.

  1. Name the failure each piece prevents. The outbox prevents a lost event. The idempotency key prevents a double payment. The saga prevents money reserved and never released.
  2. Accept the piece if that failure is likely and expensive. Payouts accepts all three: each failure moves real money.
  3. Refuse the piece if it guards against scale or failures you have not measured. Payouts refuses a second region and event sourcing, with a reopen condition in an ADR.
  4. Give every accepted piece an owner, a test of its failure path, and a line in the runbook.

The question is never whether a design is simple. It is whether each part of it pays for itself.

See also. 21.08, 21.10, 9.07, 9.10, 11.01

⚠Review checklist
  • If you see a new service whose endpoints are a noun with get, update and delete: it owns data but no decision, and every business change crosses several services. See 21.01.
  • If you see a proposal to split a module out of payouts-api with no named reason beyond "cleaner": the split costs a network call, a pipeline and often the outbox's guarantee. See 21.02.
  • If you see a request handler that calls a notification or audit service synchronously after the money has moved: a non-essential outage turns into failed payouts. See 21.03.
  • If you see a MongoTemplate, DataSource or connection string for another team's database: their next migration breaks you without warning. See 21.04.
  • If you see a retry policy that ends in "mark failed" for a payout: a day-long outage becomes hundreds of failed payouts and manual resubmission. See 21.05.
  • If you see a design that lists only the business dependencies: the token issuer or the database fails, and nobody planned for it. See 21.06.
  • If you see request or response classes in a shared library: every service now upgrades in lockstep. See 21.07.
  • If you see an ADR with no options, no consequences or no reopen condition, or an accepted ADR whose decision is being edited: the next person cannot tell what was decided or why. See 21.08.
  • If you see a home-grown engine for something the company can buy or adopt: the team is now maintaining a product. See 21.09.
  • If you see a cache, replica or queue added "for scale" with no load estimate: the cost is real and the benefit is assumed. See 21.10.
  • If you see a new architectural pattern with no named failure it prevents: it is complexity without a reason. See 21.12.

Part IVPart IV indexes#

Four ways into Part IV. Look up a mistake you have seen in a pull request, an import you have found in old code, an old way you want to replace, or an entry by its number. The first, third and fourth indexes are generated from the parts, so they always match them.

Find it by mistake

1. Build and project

  • If you see spring-boot-starter-parent as the parent of a new Sorrel service: it has dropped the company parent and every rule in it. See 1.01.
  • If you see a <version> on a dependency in a module POM, with no comment: it silently overrides the parent, and nobody will know when it can go. See 1.02.
  • If you see a security finding closed because no POM names the jar: transitive jars ship too. See 1.03.
  • If you see -pl without -am in a script or README: the module builds against a stale copy in the local repository. See 1.04.
  • If you see mvn instead of ./mvnw in CI, or a plugin with no version: two machines build the same commit differently. See 1.05.
  • If you see <repositories> in a POM, or a CI job with no settings file: builds bypass the mirror, and nobody can count what they used. See 1.06.
  • If you see a module switching its parent to spring-boot-starter-parent: a POM has one parent, so the company's is lost. See 1.07.
  • If you see <source> and <target> in the compiler plugin: calls to newer APIs compile, then fail at runtime on the older Java. See 1.08.
  • If you see an import from a jar the module does not declare, or <fail>false</fail> on the enforcer: an upgrade elsewhere will break it, and the warning will not be read. See 1.09.
  • If you see -SNAPSHOT or a version range in a dependency on the main branch: the build can change with no commit. See 1.10.
  • If you see a test library without <scope>test</scope>: it ships to production. See 1.11.
  • If you see spring-boot-maven-plugin under <plugins> in the root POM: every module is repackaged, the domain module included. See 1.12.
  • If you see a Maven profile named after an environment: the jar you tested is not the jar you ship. See 1.13.
  • If you see a build-tool migration justified by test time: the tests will be as slow in the new tool. See 1.14.

2. Core Java

  • If you see double amounts, or new BigDecimal(someDouble): pennies are lost or invented in arithmetic. See 2.01.
  • If you see equals between two BigDecimal amounts: 1240.5 and 1240.50 are not equal. See 2.01.
  • If you see LocalDateTime.now() or a LocalDateTime field for something that happened: the value depends on the pod's zone. See 2.02.
  • If you see a record with a List or Map component and no copyOf in its constructor: the value can change under its owner. See 2.03.
  • If you see equals(Payout other) without @Override, or equals without hashCode: hash collections keep duplicates. See 2.04.
  • If you see Optional.get(), an Optional field, or a method returning Optional that also returns null: absence is unhandled again. See 2.05.
  • If you see null checks that return null deep in the domain: a missing value turns into a silent decision. See 2.06.
  • If you see a getter returning an internal ArrayList, or Arrays.asList followed by add: shared mutation or a run-time exception. See 2.07.
  • If you see forEach adding to an outside collection, or parallelStream with shared state: results are lost without an error. See 2.08.
  • If you see catch (Exception e) that rethrows with e.getMessage() only: the cause and its stack trace are gone. See 2.09.
  • If you see Files.lines, Files.list or an S3 stream outside try-with-resources: file handles leak until the pod fails. See 2.10.
  • If you see == between strings or boxed numbers: it passes tests and fails on real data. See 2.11.
  • If you see default in a switch over a sealed type: the compiler can no longer flag a new case. See 2.12.
  • If you see status transitions in if chains, or an enum stored by ordinal(): rules drift and stored data renumbers. See 2.13.
  • If you see += on a string in a loop, or String.format without a locale for machine output: slow builds and unparseable files. See 2.14.
  • If you see SimpleDateFormat in a field, or YYYY in a pattern: garbled dates under load and wrong years in December. See 2.15.
  • If you see Instant.now() or LocalDate.now() without a clock in a service: the rule cannot be tested. See 2.16.
  • If you see a timestamp or a random int used as an id: two pods produce the same id. See 2.17.
  • If you see an int summing pence or milliseconds: it wraps silently to a negative number. See 2.18.
  • If you see a fix and a modernisation in the same pull request: the fix cannot be reviewed or reverted alone. See 2.19.
  • If you see var with an empty diamond, or on a method call whose type matters: the reader cannot tell what the variable is. See 2.20.

3. Concurrency

  • If you see Executors.newFixedThreadPool(n, Thread.ofVirtual().factory()): pooling virtual threads brings back the ceiling and hides a limit inside an executor. See 3.01.
  • If you see a network call inside synchronized, or between lock() and unlock(): every caller queues behind the slowest call. See 3.02.
  • If you see parallelStream(), or supplyAsync with no executor, around an HTTP or database call: the waiting happens on the JVM's shared common pool. See 3.03.
  • If you see SecurityContextHolder or MDC read inside runAsync, submit or an @Async method: the context is empty, or belongs to another request. See 3.04.
  • If you see an @Async method called from its own class: it runs on the caller's thread. See 3.05.
  • If you see @Async with no named executor, or an executor with no queue capacity: overload grows the heap and a deploy loses the queue. See 3.05.
  • If you see a runAsync or supplyAsync whose future is never joined or handled: its exception disappears. See 3.06.
  • If you see a mutable HashMap, counter or non-final field in a @Service: every request thread shares it. See 3.07.
  • If you see lock() without unlock() in finally: the first exception leaves the lock held. See 3.08.
  • If you see Semaphore.acquire() with no timeout on a request path, or release() outside finally: permits leak until the pod pays nothing. See 3.09.
  • If you see a new @Scheduled method with no lock and no idempotency: it runs once per pod. See 3.10.
  • If you see an ExecutorService created in a constructor or a field, not as a bean: it is never shut down. See 3.11.

4. Spring configuration and dependency injection

  • If you see @Autowired on a private field in production code: dependencies are hidden, the field cannot be final, and a unit test gets nulls. See 4.01.
  • If you see @Value("${...:default}") reading the same key in two classes: defaults and units drift apart, and a misspelt key is hidden by the default. See 4.02.
  • If you see a new application-<environment>.yml copied from application.yml: the files fork and drift. See 4.03.
  • If you see a profile check such as acceptsProfiles in business code: the production path is the one no test runs. See 4.03.
  • If you see a password, token or API key in any YAML or properties file: it stays in git history, and rotating it needs a release. See 4.04.
  • If you see a record holding a secret with no toString() override: one log line prints the secret. See 4.04.
  • If you see @Primary added in the same change as a second bean of that type: it hides which bean each client receives. See 4.06.
  • If you see @Lazy on a constructor parameter, or spring.main.allow-circular-references: a cycle has been papered over. See 4.07.
  • If you see final, private or static on a method that carries @Transactional, @Cacheable, @Async or @CircuitBreaker: the proxy cannot intercept it. See 4.08.
  • If you see a test that asserts an annotation is present: it proves nothing about what happens at runtime. See 4.08.
  • If you see a network call in a @PostConstruct method: it runs before proxies are ready and can stop every pod starting. See 4.09.
  • If you see a @ConfigurationProperties record without @Validated: bad values fail the first request instead of startup. See 4.10.
  • If you see @Component in a shared library, or scanBasePackages naming another team's package: consumers cannot override it or switch it off. See 4.11.
  • If you see spring.autoconfigure.exclude with no comment: nobody will know what it removed or why. See 4.12.
  • If you see an @EventListener doing work that must not be lost or must reach another service: in-memory events vanish on a restart. See 4.13.
  • If you see src/test/resources/application.yml: it hides the main configuration from every test. See 4.14.
  • If you see an environment variable such as PAYOUTS_LEDGER_READ_TIMEOUT, with an underscore where the property has a dash: it binds to nothing. See 4.15.

5. REST API design

  • If you see a @GetMapping that changes state, or a verb in a URL path: crawlers, proxies and retries repeat GETs freely. See 5.01.
  • If you see a repository, two downstream clients or a catch (Exception e) in a controller: the next entry point will skip the rules, and errors leak internals. See 5.02.
  • If you see a @Document class as a @RequestBody or a controller return type: clients can set any field, and storage changes break them. See 5.03.
  • If you see "success": false inside a 200 response: clients, dashboards and retry policies read failures as success. See 5.04.
  • If you see a POST that creates a payout without an Idempotency-Key: one client retry pays the claimant twice. See 5.05.
  • If you see a controller that waits for the bank gateway or another slow step: client timeouts cause duplicate requests, and waiting requests hold threads. See 5.06.
  • If you see a list endpoint with no limit, or offset paging on a growing collection: memory and latency grow with the data. See 5.07.
  • If you see a sort or filter parameter passed straight into a query: unindexed scans and operator injection. See 5.08.
  • If you see a response field renamed, retyped or removed in place: every client breaks on deploy day. See 5.09.
  • If you see a new enum value in a response, or a consumer with a closed enum: the first new value sends messages to a dead-letter queue. See 5.10.
  • If you see PUT or PATCH without If-Match on a resource people edit: the second writer silently undoes the first. See 5.11.
  • If you see new ObjectMapper() in application code: it ignores the service's JSON settings and modules. See 5.12.
  • If you see a double amount or a LocalDateTime in a JSON record: lost pennies and times that may not exist. See 5.13.
  • If you see a hand-written API YAML in a code-first service, or a schema built from a storage class: the documentation lies or leaks. See 5.15.
  • If you see a PATCH body bound to a record: absent fields become nulls and wipe stored data. See 5.17.
  • If you see file.getBytes() or a byte[] download: memory per request equals the file size. See 5.19.
  • If you see a rate limit held in a pod's memory or keyed by getRemoteAddr(): the limit multiplies with pods and lumps clients together. See 5.21.
  • If you see an /admin path in a public controller: public tokens reach operational actions. See 5.22.

6. Validation and error handling

  • If you see constraint annotations on a request record but no @Valid on the @RequestBody: nothing is checked, and bad input reaches the domain. See 6.01.
  • If you see a 200 response with an ok: false or success: false flag: clients, gateways and dashboards all count it as a success. See 6.02.
  • If you see try { ... } catch (Exception e) in a controller method: errors are handled nine different ways and logged more than once. See 6.03.
  • If you see one exception type thrown for both a business refusal and a timeout: it cannot have the right status for both. See 6.04.
  • If you see a @RequestParam page size or ID with no constraint: a client can make the service do unbounded work. See 6.05.
  • If you see a ConstraintValidator with a repository or client injected: validation now does I/O, fails as a 400, and checks stale data. See 6.07.
  • If you see e.getMessage() of a technical failure in a response, or include-stacktrace set to anything but never: internals leak to callers. See 6.08.
  • If you see a downstream status code or body passed through to your caller: your API now depends on someone else's. See 6.09.
  • If you see a listener that catches every exception and returns normally: every failure is acknowledged and the message is lost. See 6.11.
  • If you see a @ConfigurationProperties record without @Validated: a bad value starts the service and fails later, under load. See 6.12.
  • If you see 404 for an empty collection, or 200 with no body for a missing item: clients cannot tell absence from emptiness. See 6.14.

7. Calling other services and resilience

  • If you see RestClient.create() or new RestTemplate() in production code: the client misses the service's Jackson settings, tracing and timeouts. See 7.01.
  • If you see a dependency on another team's client or API jar: their dependencies and release schedule become yours. See 7.02.
  • If you see an HTTP client with no timeout, or a read timeout of tens of seconds: one slow dependency can take every thread. See 7.03.
  • If you see a retry loop that catches RestClientException with no pause: it retries 4xx answers and hits a struggling service in a burst. See 7.04.
  • If you see one circuit breaker name shared by two dependencies, or no ignore-exceptions for 4xx: a healthy dependency gets cut off. See 7.05.
  • If you see a retry composed inside a circuit breaker, or a retry that retries CallNotPermittedException: the breaker opens late and protects nothing. See 7.06.
  • If you see @Retry or @Retryable on a POST with no idempotency key: a timeout can become a double payment. See 7.07.
  • If you see a token fetched by hand inside a business call: the identity provider gets a request per call, with no timeout. See 7.08.
  • If you see a fallback on a write that returns something shaped like success: the saga carries on with money nobody recorded. See 7.11.
  • If you see a client tested only through @MockitoBean: the URL, JSON and timeouts are untested. See 7.14.
  • If you see a compensation call inside a catch block, with no saved saga state: a crash or an unknown outcome leaves money in limbo. See 7.16.
  • If you see wire-level HTTP logging switched on: tokens and bank details go into the log store. See 7.18.

8. MongoDB API and DocumentDB

  • If you see code that uses the object it passed to save instead of the one save returned: the id and version are missing, and a second save inserts a duplicate. See 8.01.
  • If you see @DBRef on a field: DocumentDB does not support DBRefs, and each reference costs a query. See 8.02.
  • If you see a derived query with four or more conditions, or one that returns an unbounded List: nobody can check it against an index, and one day it loads everything. See 8.03.
  • If you see findById followed by save to change one field: the save replaces the whole document and loses concurrent changes. See 8.04.
  • If you see a document that is updated after creation with no @Version: two writers lose one update silently. See 8.05.
  • If you see @Indexed with nothing that creates it, or auto-index-creation: true on a large collection: either there is no index or a deploy blocks the collection. See 8.06.
  • If you see a query's speed in a test offered as proof it uses an index: a container holds too few documents for any plan to be slow. See 8.07.
  • If you see PageRequest.of(page++, ...) in a batch job: skip reads every skipped document, and with no sort the pages overlap. See 8.08.
  • If you see a $push with no limit on the array: the document grows towards 16 MiB on every write. See 8.09.
  • If you see double for an amount or LocalDateTime for an event: sums drift by pennies and times shift by zone. See 8.10.
  • If you see readPreference=secondaryPreferred in a service that reads its own writes: reads miss writes and the saga repeats steps. See 8.11.
  • If you see a new operator, stage or index type with no line in the feature contract: it may not exist on Payouts' engine. See 8.12.
  • If you see Containing, Like or IgnoreCase on a large collection: it becomes a $regex that scans. See 8.13.
  • If you see findAll() followed by a loop that sums: the whole collection crosses the network to compute a few numbers. See 8.14.
  • If you see a document type loaded with only some fields, or a projection saved back: the save wipes the missing fields. See 8.15.
  • If you see a findBy... check followed by an insert: two pods both pass the check. See 8.16.
  • If you see code that assumes a TTL index deletes at an exact time: AWS makes TTL deletes best effort. See 8.17.
  • If you see a migration or index build in a start-up runner on a populated collection: every pod runs it and the build blocks writes. See 8.20.
  • If you see a backfill that calls save or saveAll per document: it takes hours where a bulk write takes minutes. See 8.21.
  • If you see a change stream consumer that keeps its resume token in memory: after a restart it cannot continue. See 8.22.
  • If you see mongo:latest in a test, or test settings that create indexes production does not: the green build tests a different database. See 8.23.
  • If you see maxPoolSize chosen without counting pods: a rolling deploy exceeds the instance's connection quota. See 8.24.

9. Transactions and consistency

  • If you see @Transactional in a Mongo service with no MongoTransactionManager bean: nothing is transactional and no error says so. See 9.01.
  • If you see a transactional method that throws a checked exception or makes an HTTP call: the checked exception commits, and the call holds a transaction open against a one-minute limit. See 9.01.
  • If you see an annotated method called from another method of the same class, or a private or final annotated method: the proxy never sees the call. See 9.02.
  • If you see REQUIRES_NEW on an outbox or state write: it commits even when the caller rolls back. See 9.03.
  • If you see a transaction that streams results, creates a collection, or loops over a whole day's payouts: DocumentDB refuses cursors and new collections inside one, and aborts it after one minute. See 9.04.
  • If you see a MongoTransactionManager with no session customisation for DocumentDB: its sessions ask for causal consistency, which DocumentDB rejects. See 9.04.
  • If you see a check in Java followed by writes to two documents to enforce one rule: two pods both pass the check. See 9.05.
  • If you see an SNS, SQS or HTTP call next to a database write in one method: one of them can happen without the other. See 9.06.
  • If you see an outbox event that holds only an id, or is written outside the state change's transaction: consumers read later state, and a crash loses the event. See 9.07.
  • If you see a relay that marks events published before publishing, or reads every pending event at once: events are lost in a fault, and memory fills after one. See 9.08.
  • If you see $inc, += or an email send in a message handler with no guard: a redelivery applies it twice. See 9.09.
  • If you see existsById on a key followed by the work: two concurrent requests both pass, and a repeat gets a 409 instead of the original answer. See 9.10.
  • If you see a retry loop inside a @Transactional method: every attempt rereads the same snapshot. See 9.11.
  • If you see a decision about money made from a projection, a cache or a replica: it can act on a state that is minutes old. See 9.12.
  • If you see a status page served from a replica straight after the caller's own write: the caller sees its change undone. See 9.13.
  • If you see ChainedTransactionManager, JtaTransactionManager or com.atomikos: the atomicity is best effort or depends on a coordinator log a pod will lose. See 9.14.

10. Messaging with SNS and SQS

  • If you see a service sending the same event to several queues in turn: the sends are not atomic, and every new consumer needs a change in the producer. See 10.01.
  • If you see an SQS queue subscribed to SNS with no queue policy, or a subscription without raw delivery: SNS discards the messages, or the listener cannot parse the envelope. See 10.01.
  • If you see a document passed to convertAndSend, or a publish inside @Transactional: personal data leaks into queues, and events describe writes that never committed. See 10.02.
  • If you see an SnsClient or SqsClient created inside a method: a new connection pool and TLS handshake per call. See 10.03.
  • If you see a listener that catches every exception and returns: failures are acknowledged and deleted, and the DLQ stays empty. See 10.04.
  • If you see a receive loop without waitTimeSeconds, or a delete before the handling: empty polls on the bill, and messages lost in a deploy. See 10.05.
  • If you see a queue left at the default visibility timeout, or set to 12 hours: duplicates while work is still running, or messages stuck after a crash. See 10.06.
  • If you see a duplicate check that reads, then acts, then writes, or that uses the SQS message ID: two pods pass it at once, and redrives slip through. See 10.07.
  • If you see a maxReceiveCount of 1, a DLQ with the source's retention, or a DLQ with no alarm: a blip dead-letters messages that then expire unread. See 10.08.
  • If you see messages from one consumer's DLQ republished to the topic: every other consumer handles them a second time. See 10.09.
  • If you see one constant messageGroupId for a whole FIFO queue: everything is serial, and one failure blocks the lot. See 10.10.
  • If you see a FIFO send without a deduplication ID that is stable across retries: the retry is delivered twice. See 10.11.
  • If you see an event with no ID, type or version, or money as a JSON number: duplicates cannot be detected and the first change breaks a consumer. See 10.12.
  • If you see a listener that returns early for event types it does not want: a missing filter policy. See 10.13.
  • If you see a large event tested by sending straight to SQS: SNS rejects it above 256 KiB by default. See 10.14.
  • If you see acknowledgementMode = "MANUAL" with a branch that neither acknowledges nor throws: handled messages come back until they reach the DLQ. See 10.15.
  • If you see sqs:* or sns:* in a role, or access keys in configuration: one bug can empty another team's queue. See 10.18.
  • If you see @MockitoBean SnsTemplate as the only test of publishing: attributes, filter policies and raw delivery are untested. See 10.19.
  • If you see Thread.sleep in a listener to wait for later: the message is redelivered while it sleeps. See 10.20.

11. Sagas and long-running workflows

  • If you see @Transactional around calls to the ledger or the bank: the database rolls back and the other systems do not. See 11.01.
  • If you see a saga whose progress is held in local variables or a catch block: a pod restart loses money in flight. See 11.02.
  • If you see a listener that acts on an event with no conditional status update, or with a new key per delivery: a duplicate message repeats the step. See 11.03.
  • If you see a business decision, such as a retry, inside a notification or audit listener: the saga's logic is now hidden in a file nobody reviews with it. See 11.04.
  • If you see a compensation that deletes a record, posts an opposite amount, or uses a fresh key per attempt: retries multiply the undo. See 11.05.
  • If you see a catch-all after the bank call that releases the reservation: a local failure undoes a payment the bank made. See 11.06.
  • If you see a timeout on the bank call treated as a refusal: the saga compensates a pivot that happened. See 11.06.
  • If you see a @Scheduled step runner with no lease, or idempotency keys generated per attempt: 2 pods run the same step with different keys. See 11.07.
  • If you see a step with an HTTP timeout but no step deadline: the saga retries for days and nobody notices. See 11.08.
  • If you see a new saga with no stuck-saga metric or alert: the first sign of trouble is a claimant's phone call. See 11.09.
  • If you see an update to a claim that ignores whether a payout is in flight: the saga acts on data changed under it. See 11.10.
  • If you see a workflow engine proposed for one short saga: a cluster and a programming model to replace a few hundred lines. See 11.11.
  • If you see saga tests that cover only success and one refusal: the timeout-after-success path is untested. See 11.12.

12. Logging

  • If you see string concatenation inside a log call: the string is built even when the level is off, and the message cannot be grouped. See 12.01.
  • If you see log.error on a retry attempt or a client's 4xx: alerts fire for failures that recovered, and the team learns to ignore them. See 12.02.
  • If you see a hand-built JSON logging.pattern.console: a quote or a stack trace breaks the line. See 12.03.
  • If you see MDC.put with no matching removal: the value leaks onto the next unit of work on that pooled thread. See 12.04.
  • If you see log.error(e.getMessage()), or a catch that logs and rethrows: the stack trace is lost and one failure is logged several times. See 12.05.
  • If you see a record, a request body, a header or a token passed to a log call: personal data and credentials go into a store that everyone can read. See 12.06.
  • If you see a logback.xml with <springProfile>, or one logging file per environment: the profile blocks do nothing, or the copies drift. See 12.07.
  • If you see spring-boot-starter-log4j2 without excluding spring-boot-starter-logging, or a pinned log4j-core: two backends compete, and the pin can hold a known vulnerability. See 12.08.
  • If you see a redeploy to change a log level: the restart can erase the state you wanted to see. See 12.09.
  • If you see a log line per item inside a large loop, or an expensive method call as a debug argument: the job slows down for lines nobody reads. See 12.10.
  • If you see audit facts written only with log.info: they disappear when the log store's retention ends. See 12.11.

13. Correlation and tracing

  • If you see a UUID.randomUUID() used as a request ID inside a service method: it never leaves the method and gives no timings. See 13.01.
  • If you see two micrometer-tracing-bridge-* dependencies, or a bridge with no exporter: Boot picks one tracer, and nothing reaches the backend. See 13.02.
  • If you see a team saying "tracing is broken" in a test environment: Boot keeps 1 request in 10 by default. See 13.02 and 13.09.
  • If you see -javaagent:opentelemetry-javaagent.jar in a service that still has the Micrometer bridge: two tracers make duplicate spans and two trace IDs. See 13.03.
  • If you see traceparent copied from the incoming request onto an outbound call: the downstream span hangs off the wrong parent. See 13.04.
  • If you see a ReceiveMessageRequest with no messageAttributeNames: SQS returns no attributes, so the trace context is lost. See 13.05.
  • If you see an SNS-to-SQS subscription without raw message delivery, or an outbox row with no trace context: the trace stops at the topic or at the relay. See 13.05.
  • If you see a custom logging.pattern.console with no %X{traceId}: no log line can be joined to its trace. See 13.06.
  • If you see CompletableFuture.supplyAsync with no executor, or an executor with no task decorator: the task runs with no trace and no MDC. See 13.07.
  • If you see an ID passed to lowCardinalityKeyValue: it becomes a metric tag with a time series per payout. See 13.08.
  • If you see management.tracing.sampling.probability: 1.0 in production configuration with no tail sampling in the collector: every request is exported and the backend's cost follows. See 13.09.
  • If you see a 500 response body with no trace ID: support cannot find the failing request. See 13.10.

14. Metrics, health and alerting

  • If you see new SimpleMeterRegistry() or any registry built by hand in production code: the meters never reach Prometheus. See 14.01.
  • If you see registry.gauge(...) called with a new object on every call: the gauge keeps the first object, then reports NaN after garbage collection. See 14.02.
  • If you see a tag whose value is an ID, an email, a full URL or a free-text message: series grow with traffic until Prometheus or the pod runs out of memory. See 14.03.
  • If you see a database or another service in the liveness group: another team's outage restarts your pods in a loop. See 14.04.
  • If you see a health indicator that calls a downstream service: the probes multiply its load and its slowness takes your pods out of service. See 14.05.
  • If you see publishPercentiles on a multi-pod service, or an average of percentiles on a dashboard: the number describes no real request. See 14.06.
  • If you see a page on CPU, heap or pod restarts: it fires when customers are fine and stays quiet when they are not. See 14.07.
  • If you see a queue alarm on depth alone, or a DLQ with no alarm: a stopped consumer or a failed message goes unnoticed for hours. See 14.08.
  • If you see exposure.include: "*" or Actuator on the public port: the heap dump and the environment are one request away. See 14.09.
  • If you see a memory alert on the heap alone: the container is killed on total memory while the heap graph is green. See 14.10.

15. Security

  • If you see a controller that splits the Authorization header and decodes the JWT itself: the signature and expiry go unchecked, and anyone can write a token. See 15.01.
  • If you see issuer-uri without audiences, or a custom JwtDecoder with no audience validator: tokens meant for other services are accepted. See 15.01.
  • If you see hasRole(...) with a scope name, or a rule loosened to authenticated(): any valid token can do anything. See 15.02.
  • If you see @PreAuthorize with no @EnableMethodSecurity in the service: every method rule is silently ignored. See 15.02.
  • If you see findById(id) on a path ID in a claimant-facing endpoint: any caller can read any payout by changing the ID. See 15.03.
  • If you see @PostFilter on a list method: every row is loaded, and the filter hides an authorisation rule in memory. See 15.03.
  • If you see a token kept in a field with an expiry check and no margin: calls fail at the boundary, and threads stampede the identity provider. See 15.04.
  • If you see a client-credentials call made inside a user's request with the default principal: Payouts holds 1 token per user. See 15.04.
  • If you see /actuator/** permitted, or anyRequest().permitAll(): the heap dump and every new endpoint are open. See 15.05.
  • If you see web.ignoring() for anything but static files: the paths skip Spring Security entirely. See 15.05.
  • If you see getSecretValue in a request path: every request becomes a Secrets Manager call, and a slow Secrets Manager becomes a Payouts outage. See 15.06.
  • If you see a real key in a properties file, in the repository or on a server: everyone who can read the file holds the key. See 15.06.
  • If you see AWS_ACCESS_KEY_ID in a Kubernetes Secret: a long-lived key that works from anywhere. See 15.07.
  • If you see a Map<String, Object> request body passed into a query: a caller can send operators. See 15.08.
  • If you see allowedOriginPatterns("*") with allowCredentials(true): any website can act as a signed-in user. See 15.09.
  • If you see csrf.disable() in a chain with a login session: cross-site requests ride on the user's cookie. See 15.10.
  • If you see addFilters = false in a controller test: the security rules are never tested. See 15.11.
  • If you see a dependency-check suppression with no reason or date: a real risk stays hidden after the code changes. See 15.12.
  • If you see a bank account number stored as a plain string: every database reader holds it. See 15.13.
  • If you see lastModifiedBy offered as the audit trail: it records the last writer, not who did what. See 15.14.

16. Testing

  • If you see @SpringBootTest on a test of one domain rule: it waits for the whole application and fails for reasons unrelated to the rule. See 16.01.
  • If you see mock(RestClient.class, RETURNS_DEEP_STUBS), or a mock of SqsTemplate or MongoTemplate: the test pins the library calls and never runs the URL, JSON or error handling. See 16.02.
  • If you see assertTrue(a && b) or assertTrue(list.size() == 2): the failure will say only "expected true". See 16.03.
  • If you see a controller method called directly in a test: validation, JSON and error handling never run. See 16.04.
  • If you see a repository test that only saves and loads: the queries Payouts wrote are untested. See 16.05.
  • If you see a static Mockito mock exposed as a bean: its stubs and calls leak across test classes. See 16.06.
  • If you see a new combination of properties, profiles or replaced beans on a @SpringBootTest, or @DirtiesContext: another context start, and more listeners alive at once. See 16.07.
  • If you see @Container on an instance field: a new container for every test method. See 16.08.
  • If you see a WireMock stub on anyUrl(), or a fixed port: a wrong URL passes, and parallel builds clash. See 16.09.
  • If you see resilience tests on production timings, a mock that throws a home-made exception, or no breaker reset: slow tests that never test what is really retried. See 16.10.
  • If you see Thread.sleep after a send: slow when it passes, flaky when it fails. See 16.11.
  • If you see an end-to-end test of the happy path only: the compensation that releases money is untested. See 16.12.
  • If you see a WireMock stub copied from another team's documentation, with no contract: it stays green when they change. See 16.16.
  • If you see a rerun setting added to make a build green: a real race may be hiding behind it. See 16.19.
  • If you see import org.junit.Test in a module with no Vintage engine: the test never runs. See 16.22.

17. Containers and Kubernetes

  • If you see FROM openjdk, a JDK in the final stage, COPY . . before the build, or no USER line: the image is large, slow to push, full of tools, and runs as root. See 17.01.
  • If you see -Xmx equal to the memory limit, or set in the Dockerfile while the limit is in the manifest: the process outgrows its limit and dies with no evidence. See 17.02.
  • If you see a memory request below the limit, or no resources: block: the scheduler overpacks the node, and the JVM sizes itself for CPUs it will not get. See 17.03.
  • If you see a CPU limit of 1 or less, or a memory limit under about 1792 MB, with no collector named: the JVM picks the Serial collector, which stops the application for the whole of every collection. See 17.03.
  • If you see a liveness probe on /actuator/health, or liveness and readiness on the same path: a database failover restarts every pod at once. See 17.04.
  • If you see a shell-script entrypoint that runs java without exec: Java never receives SIGTERM, and every stop is a kill. See 17.05.
  • If you see a renamed field or a removed endpoint shipped in one release: the old and new pods disagree during the rollout. See 17.06.
  • If you see a secret in a ConfigMap or a plain environment variable: anyone who can read the namespace can read it. See 17.07.
  • If you see replicas: 1, or no PodDisruptionBudget: a node drain is an outage. See 17.08.
  • If you see a heap dump path on a memory-backed volume: taking the dump gets the pod killed. See 17.10.
  • If you see a latest tag in a local or production manifest: what runs depends on when the node pulled. See 17.12.

18. Performance

  • If you see a timing loop in a main method or a test, or System.currentTimeMillis() pairs around a call: the number measures a cold JVM or a wall clock, and code gets rewritten on a guess. See 18.01.
  • If you see a repository or HTTP call inside a map, forEach or loop over results: one request becomes N+1 calls, and the other side pays for each. See 18.02.
  • If you see maxPoolSize or server.tomcat.threads.max raised with no arithmetic in the comment: the queue moves to the database, and the shared instance's connection quota fills. See 18.03.
  • If you see a publish or update per item in a relay or a backfill: round trips dominate, and backlogs drain slowly. See 18.04.
  • If you see a runbook that restarts pods before taking thread dumps: the evidence is lost, and the incident recurs. See 18.05.
  • If you see a static map or list that is only ever added to: it is a memory leak that ends in OutOfMemoryError. See 18.06.
  • If you see new ObjectMapper() inside a method that runs per request: every call rebuilds what a shared mapper caches, and CPU goes on it. See 18.07.
  • If you see a cache with no maximumSize, or expireAfterAccess on data that changes: hot entries go stale for ever and cold ones fill the heap. See 18.08.
  • If you see a load test with a fixed number of users that each wait for a reply: it hides stalls and reports a p99 far below production's. See 18.10.

19. Upgrades and dependency hygiene

  • If you see sed or find and replace turning javax. into jakarta.: it renames JDK packages too, and misses the jars that still use javax. See 19.01.
  • If you see javax.servlet or javax.validation in the dependency tree of a Boot 3 service: a library built for Boot 2 is in the build, and it may load and do nothing. See 19.01.
  • If you see a Boot version change that skips minors: every minor's behaviour changes arrive together, and nobody can tell which caused what. See 19.02.
  • If you see spring-boot-properties-migrator merged to the main branch: it was for the upgrade, and while present it hides renamed properties instead of fixing them. See 19.02.
  • If you see recipe output and hand edits in one commit: the reviewer cannot find the human change. See 19.03.
  • If you see an OpenRewrite run with unpinned recipe versions: the same command gives a different diff tomorrow. See 19.03.
  • If you see an OpenRewrite Boot recipe several minors ahead of the service's version: it makes every minor's changes in one commit. See 19.03.
  • If you see a Boot 4 upgrade with no change to ConfigMaps or Helm values: renamed properties set outside the repository are silently ignored. See 19.04.
  • If you see resilience4j-spring-boot3 or Spring Cloud AWS 3.x in a Boot 4 build: they are built for Boot 3.5. See 19.04.
  • If you see a Spring Retry maxAttempts copied unchanged into maxRetries: every failing call is made once more. See 19.04.
  • If you see maven.compiler.release raised before the image's JDK: the pods fail at startup with UnsupportedClassVersionError. See 19.05.
  • If you see a bot's pull request that bumps a <version> written on a library Boot manages: that version overrides Boot's tested set and survives the next Boot upgrade. See 19.06.
  • If you see com.amazonaws, com.netflix.hystrix, Spring Cloud Sleuth or org.springframework.retry added in a pull request: it is a library nobody fixes any more. See 19.07.
  • If you see @SuppressWarnings("deprecation") on a Spring API: the removal will arrive later, all at once. See 19.08.

20. Evolving a live system

  • If you see a pull request that adds a new field and removes the old one in the same release: during the rolling update and for every unknown client, the old field disappears with no warning. See 20.01.
  • If you see an event's payload change shape with the same type and version: every subscribed queue gets messages its consumer cannot read, and a rollback leaves them in the queues. See 20.02.
  • If you see an ApplicationRunner that converts stored documents, or a release that writes a new document shape its predecessor cannot read: every pod runs it, and the rollback cannot read the data. See 20.03.
  • If you see a new service writing to another system's tables or collections: the old system can no longer change its data without breaking it. See 20.04.
  • If you see a feature flag that is one boolean for the whole service, with no key and no removal date: the first real test is all traffic, and the flag never leaves. See 20.05.
  • If you see a redrive started before the rollout finished, with no rate, or a consumer that deduplicates on the SQS message ID: messages fail again, a downstream is flooded, and redriven messages are processed twice. See 20.08.
  • If you see a second service configured with another service's database and collection: the split moved the code and kept the coupling. See 20.12.

21. Design judgement

  • If you see a new service whose endpoints are a noun with get, update and delete: it owns data but no decision, and every business change crosses several services. See 21.01.
  • If you see a proposal to split a module out of payouts-api with no named reason beyond "cleaner": the split costs a network call, a pipeline and often the outbox's guarantee. See 21.02.
  • If you see a request handler that calls a notification or audit service synchronously after the money has moved: a non-essential outage turns into failed payouts. See 21.03.
  • If you see a MongoTemplate, DataSource or connection string for another team's database: their next migration breaks you without warning. See 21.04.
  • If you see a retry policy that ends in "mark failed" for a payout: a day-long outage becomes hundreds of failed payouts and manual resubmission. See 21.05.
  • If you see a design that lists only the business dependencies: the token issuer or the database fails, and nobody planned for it. See 21.06.
  • If you see request or response classes in a shared library: every service now upgrades in lockstep. See 21.07.
  • If you see an ADR with no options, no consequences or no reopen condition, or an accepted ADR whose decision is being edited: the next person cannot tell what was decided or why. See 21.08.
  • If you see a home-grown engine for something the company can buy or adopt: the team is now maintaining a product. See 21.09.
  • If you see a cache, replica or queue added "for scale" with no load estimate: the cost is real and the benefit is assumed. See 21.10.
  • If you see a new architectural pattern with no named failure it prevents: it is complexity without a reason. See 21.12.
